en: Preface to the Commentary on the Meaning of the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tathāgatābhisaṃbodhi-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*.

The tradition of the Vidyādhara-piṭaka has long been transmitted through various lineages and translations. Among scholars of the world, many have maintained a focus on the aspect of form (*sākāra*), [while neglecting the aspect of emptiness].

While the Middle Way has been affirmed, the methods of its yogic practice remain hidden and unclarified; that the flow of the Dharma is obstructed is a source of concern for those who propagate the Path.

This *Vairocana Sūtra* is the secret treasury of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), which penetrates deeply into the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and serves as the fountainhead of all doctrines.
It was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India named Śubhakarasiṃha (in the Tang language, Shupojialu senghe).

Śubhakarasiṃha was a master whose virtuous and fearless deeds encompassed the Eight Piṭakas and whose fame crowned the Five Heavens; he was truly a patriarch in the transmission and reception of this sūtra.

Recently, an imperial decree invited him, and he served as a constant attendant. Master Yixing was a man born for the world, possessing clear discernment and profound penetration, with wisdom that encompassed all transformations and adaptabilities.
The present Emperor has honored him by inviting him to private banquets within the inner palace, as recorded in detail in the National History. I have heard this.
The Tripiṭaka Master, the treasury of the Dharma-jewel, was moved by my request; having received the imperial decree, he translated this sūtra with me acting as the scribe (*śodhaka*).
The monk-translator Ratnacandra was well-versed in the characteristics of various teachings and proficient in local dialects.

Were it not for the Meditation Master, one could not have probed its profound mysteries; were it not for the Tripiṭaka Master, one could not have elucidated its ultimate subtleties. Within this [work] is fully contained...

The training precepts of the three vehicles and the dhāraṇī-mantra practices of the Supreme Vehicle are intended to cause practitioners to know that the characteristics and nature of the world are inherently unborn.

Therefore, by resorting to the conditioned, they extensively demonstrate the signless; each point is examined and scrutinized to exhaustively reveal the dependent origination of the entire dharma-realm.
One should know that all the words and phrases within these immeasurable deeds converge upon and point toward this ultimate goal.
This is not a repository of secret teachings; it is divided into thirty-one chapters.

Fearing that those who uphold and recite it might cling to the literal text and lose the intended meaning, the Meditation Master further requested that the Tripiṭaka Master explain its significance, which was subsequently recorded. There is no word left unexhausted and no dharma left unfulfilled.

Both the superficial and the profound are explained, synthesizing the subtle words of various sūtras. Where there were doubts regarding specific passages, they were further clarified through the sūtras.

I have searched through and resolved the methods and principles, and have fully listed their positions and sequences below; subsequently, I revised and supplemented the text, titled it "Yi-shi" (Exegesis on the Meaning), and compiled it into fourteen fascicles.

Since there were one or two omissions and some minor, convoluted passages in the Sanskrit original, in the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, when the Chan Master passed away, the Dharma Master Zhiyan—whose dignified conduct was honored by the entire Buddhist community—had received his training together with the Chan Master under [the same master].

The Chan Master Wubei was also well-versed in Sanskrit. On the eve of his death, he entrusted the Dharma Master [Dao]zhang with the task of seeking various Sanskrit manuscripts and requested that the Tripitaka Master examine them in detail.
However, before the Dharma Master could record the texts and locate the original manuscripts, the Tripitaka Master passed away;
thus, there was no one left to consult. How tragic! As the Chan Master approached his end, he lamented that he had not yet been able to fathom the profound principles of this sutra.

It is truly said that there are lingering regrets in the propagation [of the teachings] and that it is difficult to encounter them at an auspicious time. Indeed, within the scriptures, there are hidden meanings;

preceding and succeeding passages clarify one another, and principles and facts are presented in mutual relation. These are the Buddha’s skillful means. Unless one receives instruction from a master or seeks out the explanations of their meaning, it has never been the case that anyone could enter its gates.
I, Wen Gu, have once associated with the circle of various worthies and have had the privilege of hearing [their teachings].
This sutra reaches the ultimate, peerless, and wondrous practice; I do not dare to fathom its depths.
Yet, disregarding my own ignorance, I have focused my mind in reverent devotion and have briefly set forth its beginning and end through my clumsy thoughts.
General Principles for the Re-engraving of the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-tathāgatābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*:
The current text contains numerous discrepancies and omissions that render it difficult to read; this edition has therefore been collated against ancient Tibetan manuscripts.
I have collated and corrected [the text], yet where the original contained errors or doubts, I have recorded those errors and doubts lest they be omitted;
however, where the textual corruption was certain and beyond doubt, I have corrected it immediately.
A notation of "one manuscript" (*biao shu yiben*) indicates a different version; when three manuscripts are cited, there are seven fascicles, or ten.
Regarding the fourteen fascicles, these were collated and prepared together; as for the "Yamamoto" (Mountain Version) text, it is the edition verified by Daisōjō Dengyō Daishi.
As for the ten fascicles brought by Daisōjō Chishō Daishi, they were recorded directly from the Chishō manuscript.
As for the commentary (*sho*), it is the twenty-fascicle version brought by Daisōjō Kōbō Daishi.
Regarding the Sanskrit characters used as subscripts for the mantras and their Sanskrit names, all extant editions write them separated from the main text;

fearing that these may have been added by later generations and do not reflect the intention of the commentator, I have here followed the original manuscripts entirely, either writing them as side-by-side annotations or as separate characters.
The fact that the sutra commentaries were corrupted and lost originally stems from the Sage’s own intention; it was intended as a safeguard against those who would treat the Dharma with arrogance.
I dare not alter a single character therein. However, since there are several versions transmitted through the oral instructions of former sages, I have appended them here;
these are now all removed, and readers should instead rely upon the guidance and exhortations of their teachers.

*Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra-vyākhyāna*, Fascicle One.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Ichigyō. Chapter One:
Abiding in Mind through the Gate of Mantra.
Regarding the *Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*: "Vairocana" is the Sanskrit term for this.
"Sun" (*sūrya*) is an alternative name for this [wisdom], signifying the dispelling of darkness and the universal illumination of all. However, the worldly sun has spatial dimensions;

when it shines upon the exterior, it cannot reach the interior. Its light illuminates one side but does not reach the other side, and its radiance exists only during the day, failing to shine through the night.
The sunlight of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is not like this; it acts universally, reaching every place.
This great illumination has no distinction of internal or external, nor of direction or location, nor of day and night.
Furthermore, as the sun travels over Jambudvīpa, all grasses, trees, and forests grow according to their respective natures, and the various affairs of the world are thereby accomplished.
Likewise, the Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom shines universally throughout the Dharma-realm, and is further able to impartially bring forth and develop immeasurable multitudes.
The production of various roots of goodness, and even the accomplishment of all mundane and supramundane sublime undertakings, does not occur without depending upon this.
Furthermore, just as when thick clouds obscure the sun and it seems to vanish, yet the sun is not destroyed;
and when a fierce wind blows away the clouds and the sunlight shines forth, yet the light was not newly produced—the sun of the Buddha-mind is also like this. Although obscured by ignorance...
It is obscured and veiled by the heavy clouds of afflictions and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet it does not diminish;
when the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is realized, it is perfectly luminous and boundless, yet it does not increase.
For various reasons such as these, the sun of the world cannot serve as a metaphor for it; however, because they share a slight degree of similarity, it is given the grand name [“Sun”].

Mahāvairocana, "the Great Vairocana," is one who has attained Buddhahood; in the pure Sanskrit language, this should be called *sambodhi*, which carries the meaning of perfect enlightenment and perfect knowledge.

This means that by means of wisdom as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), he clearly and fully awakens to and knows all phenomena—whether sentient or non-sentient, permanent or impermanent, and so forth—across the past, future, and present.

Therefore, it is called "Awakening" (*bodhi*), and since a Buddha is one who has awakened, for the sake of brevity the text simply says "attaining Buddhahood through the empowerment of spiritual transformations.

While older translations may render this as "empowerment by spiritual power" (*ṛddhibala-adhiṣṭhāna*) or "protected by the Buddha's mindfulness," this refers to the self-realization of *samyak-saṃbodhi* that transcends all stages of the mind-ground, manifesting the awakening that all phenomena are primordially unborn. This is the locus [of realization].

Language is ultimately exhausted and mental activity is likewise stilled; yet, apart from the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, even Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage do not possess this as their domain, let alone those still caught in the cycle of birth and death.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by virtue of the power of his past vows of great compassion, thought to himself: "If I were to remain only within such a state, then all sentient beings..."

Because they cannot derive benefit from this, he dwells in the samādhi of the empowerment of sovereign spiritual power, universally manifesting for all sentient beings various gateways to the realms of existence, bodies that are pleasing to behold, and various teachings suited to their dispositions and what they ought to hear;
according to their various mental activities, he opens the gateways of contemplative insight. However, these manifestations and transformations do not originate from Vairocana.
That body—whether arising from speech or from mind—is such that at all times and in all places, its limits of arising and ceasing cannot be apprehended.
It is like a magician who, through the power of incantations, empowers medicinal herbs to manifest various unprecedented phenomena that delight the hearts of the five senses;
yet once the empowerment is withdrawn, they vanish. So it is with the Tathāgata.
The illusion of the vajra is likewise: it ceases when conditions subside and arises when stimuli are activated. Being suchness within phenomena, it is without end;
therefore, it is called "the empowerment of spiritual power" (*adhiṣṭhāna*). According to the Sanskrit manuscript, the title should be fully stated as *Mahāvaipulyasūtra*.
*Indra* refers to Śakra Devendra; this scripture is said to be the source of all [dharmas].
The secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s essential teachings within the various doctrines of the Mahāyāna is uniquely majestic and honored, just as the thousand-eyed one is the lord of Śakra;
however, fearing that the title of this scripture would be too extensive, it has not been recorded here in full.
Regarding the chapter titled "The Chapter on Entering the Mantra Gate and Abiding in Mind": the Sanskrit original contains two titles;

the first is *Tattvayogācaraṇa-paṭala* (The Chapter on Practicing the Yoga of Reality), and the second is *Mantramukhāvatāra-cittasthāpana-paṭala* (The Chapter on Entering the Mantra Gate and Abiding in Mind).

I humbly suggest that since the meanings of "entering" (*avatāra*) and "abiding" (*sthāpana*) already encompass the sense of "practicing" (*yogācaraṇa*), one may omit the cumbersome wording and adopt only the latter title. Furthermore, "mantra" in Sanskrit is *mantra*, which means "true speech. As for...

Regarding the sounds that are neither false nor divergent, Nāgārjuna’s commentary refers to them as "esoteric designations" (*guhyapada*); the old translations call them "mantras," which is not a literal translation.
This chapter summarizes the general purport of the sutra: that the very mind of sentient beings is itself the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
To realize this as it truly is is what constitutes being an "omniscient one. Therefore, this teaching is for all bodhisattvas.

Taking true speech as the gateway, one awakens bodhicitta within one’s own mind; thus, the mind itself possesses the myriad practices, the mind is seen as perfect enlightenment, and the mind is realized as great nirvāṇa.
One gives rise to the mind of skillful means and adorns the buddha-field with the purity of the mind.
From cause to fruit, all are practiced by dwelling the mind in non-abiding; therefore, this is called the "Chapter on Entering the Gate of Mantra and Dwelling in the Mind. Entering...
The Mantra Gate briefly comprises three matters: first, the gate of body-secrecy; second, the gate of speech-secrecy; and third, the gate of mind-secrecy.

These matters shall be explained in detail below. By means of these three skillful means, the practitioner purifies their own three karmas and is thereby empowered by the three secrets of the Tathāgata, eventually becoming able to fulfill the *bhūmi* and *pāramitā* in this very life.
Because they no longer undergo kalpas of time to fully cultivate all remedial practices (*pratipakṣa*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"There may be bodhisattvas who, at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), immediately ascend to the bodhisattva stage and attain non-retrogression;

or there may be those who, at the moment of first generating the mind, immediately attain unsurpassed bodhi and then turn the wheel of Dharma. Nāgārjuna considered this to be like a person traveling a great distance who rides upon a sheep.

One who travels on foot takes a long time to arrive, whereas one riding a horse is somewhat faster; yet, for one who rides upon spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*), they reach their destination in the mere instant of forming a thought.
One must not say that it is impossible to arrive within the space of a single thought, for such is the nature of spiritual power.
This is the profound purport of this sutra.
The Sūtra says: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Bhagavān was dwelling in the Palace of the Dharmadhātu Sustained by the Tathāgata.

Regarding the five meanings at the beginning of the sūtra, they are explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. However, the Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra lacks the general introduction (*nidāna*).
The Ācārya states that the *Vairocana* Mahāyāna version consists of one hundred thousand verses; because it is so vast and difficult to maintain, [it has been abridged].
The Sage who transmitted the Dharma extracted its essential tenets, totaling more than three thousand verses.

Although the textual meaning of these mantra practices is largely complete, because they are not the original text of a major sūtra, a general introduction (sūtra-preface) was not originally inscribed;

I have now added one by analogy, which does no harm to the meaning. Regarding the term *Bhagavān*, according to the masters of the treatises, it possesses six meanings; in this present school, *Bha*...
"Ga" has the meaning of "able to destroy. It is like a person who, wielding a sharp weapon, subdues many;
though this name did not originally exist for him, worldly consensus observes his deeds and thus designates him as "the Destroyer. The World-Honored One is likewise:
with the light of great wisdom, he destroys all consciousness, ignorance, and afflictions. These things are fundamentally unborn from the beginning and possess no characteristics.
However, Huiyuan said: "When wisdom emerges, darkness and delusion are naturally eliminated; therefore, the meaning of the name is 'to destroy. The *Vyākhyā* also states:
*Bhaga* means 'to destroy' and *vān* means 'able'; because he is able to destroy lust, anger, and ignorance, he is called Bhagavān.

Although the followers of the Two Vehicles destroy the three poisons, they do not do so completely or clearly, like a fragrant vessel where residual odors remain, or like grass, wood, and firewood [that have been consumed]."

Because fire has limited power, its ashes and charcoal are not entirely consumed; however, the Tathāgata is like the fire at the end of an eon (*kalpoddāha*), which consumes everything until nothing remains—neither smoke nor charcoal—and is therefore named Bhagavān.
Furthermore, according to the *Śakravyākaraṇa-śabda-śāstra*, "Bhaga" refers to a woman, signifying the causal conditions for desire and the meaning of being able to extinguish afflictions (*kleśa*);
it also signifies that from which [all things] arise. This is the teaching of the *Vajraśekhara* school.
This meaning is then inverted as follows: "The woman" refers to Prajñāpāramitā, the Mother of Buddhas, whose unimpeded knowledge and vision give birth to all beings.
Those who aspire to seek her through the causal conditions will attain correspondence with her; their afflictions and conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) will all be forever stilled.
This is not like the heat of worldly desire, which, though it may slightly subside, actually increases further. [This is according to] the Secret Teaching (*Guhyamantra*).
Because it cannot be proclaimed directly, there are many such cryptic expressions; students should contemplate them by applying this principle to similar cases.

Furthermore, "Bhagavān" (the Blessed One) carries the sense of "possessor": just as one who possesses much wealth is called a "possessor of wealth," or one who possesses gold is called a "possessor of gold," so too the Tathāgata, being endowed with supreme virtues, is named the "Possessor of All Virtues. This is explained in the *Śāstra*.
It is also said that *bhaga* signifies "virtue" (*guṇa*) and *vān* signifies "possessing"; thus, it is called "Possessing Virtue.

Furthermore, *bhaga* signifies "fame" (*yaśas*), and *vān* signifies "possessing"; thus, it is called "Possessing Fame. The meaning is that among all the worlds, there is no one whose virtue and fame equal those of the Buddha.
In the sutras, this is frequently translated as "World-Honored One" (*Lokanātha*), which is a general title praising his virtues. This is the Western [usage].
In the conventions of speech, when addressing a Venerable One, one does not dare to directly state his name; rather, one must first extol his meritorious virtues. For example, it is said:
"The Greatly Wise Śāriputra, the One with Supernatural Powers Maudgalyāyana, the Ascetic Mahākāśyapa, the Upāli who Upholds the Vinaya," and so forth.
Therefore, in this sutra, the phrase "the Bhagavān Vairocana" is used, following the literary style of this region.
Alternatively, it may be because the World-Honored One occupies the lower position.
The Sūtra states: "The Bhagavān abides in the empowerment of the Tathāgata. Here, "Bhagavān" refers to the original *dharmakāya* of this Vairocana;
what follows as "Tathāgata" refers to the body of the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-kāya*). The place where he abides is called the "Buddha-reception" (*buddha-pratigraha*).
As for "using the body," it means that this very body abides as the dwelling place empowered by the Buddha—the heart-king of the Tathāgata—abiding therein just as all Buddhas abide.
Since it arises from the empowering power that pervades all places, it is non-dual and indistinguishable from the signless *dharmakāya*;
yet, through sovereign spiritual power, it causes all sentient beings to perceive the color of the secret body.
Hearing the sound of the secret of speech, one awakens to the dharma of the secret of mind;

according to their respective capacities and dispositions, these are variously different, and this very state of abiding is called the "place of empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Next, to further explain and praise this place of empowered abiding, it is said:
"The vast and great Vajra-Dharmadhātu Palace. "Great" means being without limit; "vast" means being immeasurable; and "Vajra" is used as a metaphor.
It transcends all linguistic expression and mental activity, being utterly without support; it does not indicate any phenomena as having beginning, middle, or end;
it is inexhaustible and indestructible; it is free from all faults and transgressions; it is unchangeable and cannot be shattered. For these reasons, it is called "Vajra.
Just as a worldly vajra jewel possesses three supreme qualities—first, its indestructibility; second, its status among jewels...
Because it is superior to these, it is the most victorious among the three types of battle equipment.
This is largely identical in its intended meaning to the three kinds of vajra-samādhis described in the *Śāstra*. The "Dharmadhātu" is the vast essence of vajra-wisdom;
this essence of wisdom is what is called the Tathāgata’s body of reality-wisdom (*dharmakāya*), which, through empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), is adorned with true merits.

Because it is the realm of the sublime abode where the sovereign mind dwells, it is called a "palace" (*kūṭāgāra*). This palace is the place where the ancient Buddhas attained *bodhi*, known as the Palace of Maheśvara.
The *Śāstra* states that the five kinds of *anāgāmins* who dwell there are called the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens;
beyond these lie the abodes of the *daśabhūmi* Bodhisattvas, which are also named "Pure."
The one who dwells in heaven is the Great Sovereign Heavenly King (Maheśvara-rāja).

According to the principles clarified in this school, because it is the abode of the divine mind through sovereign empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it is called the Palace of the Sovereign Heaven (*Īśvaradeva-maṇḍala*). Wherever the Tathāgata manifests his response, there is no place that is not this palace;
it is not located solely beyond the three realms (*tridhātu*).
All the Vajradharas have assembled; next, the wondrous retinue is clarified. One might ask:
while the Tathāgata resides in this palace, does he dwell in solitude, or does he have a retinue?

Therefore it is said that within this place there is a constant assembly of boundless retinues, namely the Vajradharas and others. In Sanskrit, they are called *Vajradhara*. This "Vajra" [is as follows:]...
*Vajra* means the *vajra-gada* (thunderbolt-club); since *dhara* has the meaning of "to hold," the old translation calls him the "Vajradhara Deva" (God who Holds the Vajra).

The current term "Vajradhara" (Holder of the Vajra) encompasses both shallow and profound interpretations, which is superior in terms of its doctrinal meaning. Therefore, for the sake of convenience in following the text, both terms are retained.
If expressed according to the common conventions of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is said that the *janma-kāya* Buddha (the Buddha of the birth-body) always possesses five hundred [attendants].
The Vajra-holding deity attends and guards [the practitioner], yet the profound intention of this school is that the *vajra* is the Tathāgata’s Vajra-Wisdom Seal (*jñāna-mudrā*).
This wisdom seal is immeasurable in number, and those who can uphold it are likewise boundless. Why is this so?
For wherever the King of the Mind dwells, there must necessarily be sands of *citta-anuvyañjana* (mental factors) as its retinue.

Now, when the Mind-King Vairocana attains spontaneous awakening, at that moment all mental factors (citta-saṃskāra) enter without exception into the Vajradhātu, becoming the various wisdom-seals (jñāna-mudrā) of the Tathāgata’s internally realized merit.
Such wisdom-seals can be maintained only by a Buddha together with another Buddha; in terms of the meaning of Bodhi, they comprise immeasurable and boundless gold.
Regarding the meaning of the *vajra-mudrā* as Buddha, there are immeasurable and boundless Vajradharas;
because all these qualities are of a single characteristic and a single flavor, reaching the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is called an "assembly.

If even a small portion were not equalized or if a single dharma were not fulfilled, it would not be called the "complete assembly. Nevertheless, it is sustained by the empowerment of sovereign spiritual power (*vibhūti-ṛddhi*).
Therefore, from the heart-king Vairocana, there immediately manifested the majestic and extraordinary body of the Honored One;
at that time, each and every member of the retinue of immeasurable Dharma-gates manifested as a Vajradhara, manifesting the fierce and great power of the Tathāgata.
Just as Śakra, holding a vajra in his hand, destroys the armies of the Asuras, so too did these various Vajradharas.

In this way, each [of these] is compared by means of a single attribute: they wield the weaponry of great emptiness through a single gateway, thereby being able to destroy and eliminate all afflictions and the stubborn attachments of ignorance held by sentient beings.

The Tathāgata’s playful manifestation of supernatural transformations through faith and resolve gives rise to a great jeweled king of palaces, high and without center or periphery, adorned with various kinds of supreme great jewel-kings;
the bodhisattvas, whose bodies serve as lion thrones, have already assembled because there must be a place for preaching the Dharma.
Therefore, next, the palace where he dwells and the lion throne are explained. As for "faith and resolve," it begins with—
From the initial generation of the true resolve until the attainment of Buddhahood, the stage in between is collectively termed the *adhimukti-bhūmi* (the Stage of Resolute Belief).
In Sanskrit, it is called *vicitrīṇī*, which carries the meanings of "leaping with joy," "sportive play," and "spiritual transformation.

This refers to the period from the first generation of the resolve onward, during which one deeply plants roots of goodness, gives rise to various vows and practices, adorns the Buddha-fields, and brings sentient beings to maturity, remaining constant throughout.
Because his sublime progress is uninterrupted, it carries the meaning of "leaping upward" or "bounding forth.
Just as a person who leaps and exults can universally delight the hearts of the multitude through skillful action of the three karmas, this bounding is termed "playful sport" (*vikrīḍita*).
Such playful sport is the sovereign supernormal power (*abhijñā*) of the Bodhisattva. Thus [it is said]: "Vairocana, in his original practice of the Bodhisattva path..."

At that time, by means of the samādhi of the swift power of a single essence, he made offerings to immeasurable spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and traversed all the gates of the immeasurable perfections (*pāramitā*).
Having fully perfected the dharmas of benefiting oneself and others, he was able to attain this palace of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-kūṭāgāra*),
adorned with secrets and integrated from the jewels of Tathāgata-wisdom, which is the most supreme among all that arises from true retribution.
The first is like the cintāmaṇi, the king of all jewels; therefore it is called the "Great Pavilion King Born of Playful Supernatural Transformations.
Its height is infinite, and one should know that its breadth is likewise boundless, for no limit can be found, nor is there a center.
This is the dwelling place of the body that pervades all places; one should know it to be thus.
These towers and pavilions also pervade all places. Next, to clarify the characteristics of the towers' adornments:
it is as if someone were to decorate a diamond with various colors of diamonds, yet their essential nature remains without distinction;
so too is it here, for the jewels of the towers are likewise interspersed with the various jewel-kings of the Tathāgata’s merits.
"O King, why is this? Because there is no dharma that transcends such a jewel-nature.

This foremost mark of quiescence, through the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s spiritual authority, causes those who are to be liberated to perceive it through various gateways of dharma—whether by seeing, hearing, touching, or knowing—and they enter the Dharma-realm by means of these very gateways, just as Sudhana entered the [Vajra-body Samādhi]."
Regarding the causes and conditions for the palace, this should be explained in detail herein. That the body of the Bodhisattva serves as the lion throne was previously stated:
the Vajradharmadhātu Palace is itself the body of the Tathāgata; next, it was said that the Great Pavilion King of Jewels is also the body of the Tathāgata;

now, it is said that the lion throne is likewise so. One should know that it is the same here. As for why it is called the "body of the Bodhisattva": [it is because... (The text continues with the specific reason).
This means that when one was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, one sequentially cultivated the stages (*bhūmi*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*) up to the eleventh stage;
it should be understood that each subsequent stage takes the preceding stage as its foundation. Therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva body serves as the lion throne.
The *Śāstra* explains: "For example, the lion strides alone among all beasts without fear; the Buddha is likewise."
Because he subdues all ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths without fear, he is called the Lion among Men;
whether it be a couch or the ground upon which he sits, all are termed the Lion Throne (*siṃhāsana*).

In the explicit meaning of this school, the "Lion" refers to the courageous and valiant bodhicitta, which has attained the great power of diligence from the very moment the thought of enlightenment was first conceived.
Being free from cowardice like a lion, whatever he seizes or strikes down, he inevitably captures without fail;
this is the meaning of his sovereign power in delivering sentient beings so that no effort is in vain. To explain it briefly:
because the Bodhisattvas, with their profound resolve, revere the Dharma and even bear the Buddha’s lion-throne upon their own bodies, it is said that the body of a Bodhisattva is the lion-throne.
...and the Vajra named Gaganāmala-vajradhara, up to the Lord of Secrets Vajrapāṇi—
accompanied by a host of vajra-samādhis equal in number to the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as their chief...
The Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, and other great bodhisattvas surround him before and behind as he expounds the Dharma;
this next section lists the assembly of those who heard it together. A question is asked:
"For what reason does the Sūtra spoken by the Buddha first clarify the dwelling place and the retinue? The answer is: "It is like a king who, when he has affairs of state..."
It is required that he first go out to reside in the outer court to deliberate and determine punishments and rewards; the chronicler records this, saying:

"At such a time, the King was at such a place, assembled with such-and-such great ministers to discuss and issue such an edict, desiring that those within his realm believe in and submit to it, practicing it without doubt.
Therefore, the Dharma King is likewise: when about to preach the Great Dharma, he must do so before a great assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Within the assembly of bodhisattvas, he causes them to act as witnesses; by this cause and condition, those who hear it give rise to faith.

Because of this faith, they are able to enter into such a Dharma to practice and attain realization, thereby generating even greater faith. For this reason, the location and the assembly are listed first.
The "Space-Untainted Vajra-Wielder" is the very essence of bodhicitta, free from all grasping, contention, and conceptual play.
The treatise states: Just as the pure void is without obstruction, without defilement, without stain, and without conceptual discrimination, so too is this mind the Vajra-Jñāna-Mudrā.
One who can maintain this mudrā is named Ākāśa-Vimala-Dharaṇīndhara-Vajrapāṇi.
Next, regarding Ākāśa-Caryā-Dharaṇīndhara-Vajrapāṇi: "caryā" (wandering) signifies non-abiding, progressive advancement, and miraculous transformation.

In meaning, because one takes the pure bodhicitta as the basis and dwells nowhere among all phenomena while constantly cultivating the myriad practices and giving rise to great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is called "Wandering in Space.
Furthermore, the Vajradhara who is stainless like space is the letter-gateway *A*, the seed of equality;
his cultivation of non-abiding practice is like planting seeds through skillful means, from which roots and sprouts emerge.
Because it arises gradually, the Vajra Seal of the Practice of Setting Forth is next explained. Third, regarding the Birth of Ākāśagarbha-vajradhara:

just as when a sprout has already emerged, the four great elements and the seasons act as conditions so that it grows and flourishes moment by moment without being obstructed by space, so too is the bodhicitta;
by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means and the myriad practices as conditions, one attains the reality.
That which is born as the truly born is called "born of great emptiness," and is therefore named "born of space. Fourth, regarding the one clad in variegated garments who holds a vajra:
just as sprouts grow and stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits gradually flourish until the king of trees of bodhicitta blossoms with ten thousand virtues, so it is likewise;
thus it is said that he is "endowed with various colors. Furthermore, by means of...
The various phenomena of the *dharmadhātu* color this stainless *bodhicitta*, which thus becomes the maṇḍala of great compassion;
for this reason, it is called "clad in variegated garments. Fifth is the Vajradhara named Subhūṣaṇapada (Excellent Gait).
This term "subha" (*śubha*) in Sanskrit is *viśuddhara*, meaning "exquisite adornment" and "seed-syllable. For example, it is like a fruit that, once ripened, returns once more to become a seed.

Furthermore, "skillfully walking" refers to the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) of all Buddhas; it means skillfully knowing the appropriate timing—whether beings are ready to be delivered or not—and various circumstances of penetration or obstruction.

By employing the expedient means of body, speech, and mind, one responds downwardly to the diverse capacities of sentient beings, precisely adhering to the rules and regulations so that everything becomes a Buddha-act;
for this reason, it is given this name. The sixth stage is called "Abiding in the Equality of All Dharmas, Grasping the Vajra."

This refers to abiding in the equality of all Buddhas; that is, all dharmas—cause and effect, self and other, conditioned and unconditioned—enter into this wisdom of suchness and are ultimately equal, identical to the single limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because one can maintain this wisdom, it is given this name. Furthermore, the five preceding phrases are also all the true merits of the Tathāgata.
Although there is no distinction between deep and shallow in virtue, it is taught in a sequential order merely for the sake of differentiation and ease of understanding.

Seventh, regarding the "Compassion for the Immeasurable Realm of Sentient Beings" of the Vajradhara: this compassion is also termed "rescue and deliverance," meaning that, abiding naturally within the equal nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one spontaneously gives rise to a mind of compassionate empathy that regards all sentient beings as being of one's own essence.
Because the realms of all sentient beings are immeasurable, this great compassion is likewise without limit;
as this is one of the Tathāgata’s virtues, the holder [of this mantra] takes it as his name. Eighth is the Nārāyaṇa-strength Vajradhara.
Having already given rise to a mind of pity, he is able to provide rescue and protection if he possesses great power; therefore, he is explained next. This is compared in the sutra.
The strength of sixty elephants is not equal to the strength of one fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*); even so, up until the final stage, the strength of Nārāyaṇa is supreme.
Because every single pore of the Buddha’s birth-body is equal to the strength of Nārāyaṇa, it is used as a metaphor for the Dharma-realm body.
The ninth [type of] great Nārāyaṇa strength belongs to the Vajradhara, who is the deity who holds the secret.
Supernatural power is like the incurable disease of an icchantika, and the realization of the limit of reality by those of the two vehicles is like a person who has already died.
Because the Buddhas, the Kings of Physicians, clearly perceive the Tathāgata-nature, they are able to give a definitive lion’s roar regarding the causes and conditions for healing;
their minds are not timid or weak. Since even the bodhisattvas cannot do so, this further clarifies that [this power] is unique and not shared.
The tenth, the Wondrous Vajra-holder of all the Great Nārāyaṇa powers, possesses a wondrous name that has no equal and no superior meaning.
It is like the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*), which, having reached the ultimate limit of refined excellence, can no longer be increased;
it is constant, unchanging, uninterrupted, and unmixed. The Tathāgata is likewise: all his merits are entirely incomparable and unsurpassed.
Whatever is performed is done solely for the sake of this one causal condition; therefore, it is called "Wondrous Vajra-holder.

The eleventh is the "Victorious Swift Vajra-holder. "Victorious" refers to the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*); because Great Emptiness pervades all places, it is able to give rise to swift supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Those who abide in this vehicle attain unshakable perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) at the very moment they first resolve their minds toward awakening.
Because one proceeds from birth and death to nirvāṇa, it is called "Supreme Swift" (dvādaśa-vimala-vajradhara).
This Stainless Vajra-holder is precisely the bodhicitta that is free from all obscurations.

For example, just as the nature of pure gold is inherently stainless, yet when refined through various smelting processes and polished with various jewels, its radiance increases manifold—so too should one know that even its original substance was still accompanied by subtle impurities.
Abiding in the ability to maintain this ultimate pure vajra-seal, he is named for that reason the Thirteenth, the Vajrapāṇi of Swift Blade-Grasping.
This character "blade" (khaḍga) in the Sanskrit signifies the most wrathful among the wrathful and the sharpest among the sharp; its translation is "like the edge of a blade.
Holding this vajra-like sharp wisdom, he completely severs all places that are difficult to cut and subdues all places that are difficult to subdue.
He is so named because he has completely subdued all [afflictions]; this is the fourteenth. As for the Vajra-wielder Tathāgatavarmadhara (Tathāgata-Armor Wearer):
"Tathāgata-armor" refers to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). Because his body is adorned by this, he protects and sustains sentient beings and performs the buddha-work;
he cannot be harmed by any afflictions, nor can anyone subdue or destroy him—hence he is so named. This is the fifteenth.
The phrase "the arising of the Vajradhara-holder" refers to the locus of names, which is the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
The merits of the self-realization of all Buddhas arise from the *tathāgata*-nature; this empowered body arises from the merits of the Tathāgata’s own realization.

Because it is not separate from the gate of the letter *A*, it is called the "Tathāgata-phrase. It gives rise to the sixteenth dwelling, the Vajradhara who is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

This refers to abiding in the wisdom of great emptiness; it means contemplating the true mark of dependent origination as being without arising or ceasing, neither interrupted nor permanent, and neither coming nor going, nor one nor different—wherein all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) cease, just like *nirvāṇa*.
Because one maintains such a seal of wisdom, one receives this name. Seventeenth, the Tathāgata’s Ten Powers: the one who gives rise to them is Vajradhara. This refers to...
From where does such wondrous skillful means of the Buddha’s wisdom arise? It arises from the ten powers of the Tathāgata;
because he maintains this seal, he receives this name. (18) The Vajradhara of the Stainless Eye is none other than the five eyes of the Tathāgata.
Because the bodhicitta is ultimately pure, he contemplates all phenomena through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because he clearly perceives all that is seen, heard, sensed, and known without any obstruction, and because he can maintain such a vajra-seal (*vajramudrā*), he is thus named.
The nineteenth [title] is Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets. In Sanskrit, *pāṇi* means "the palm of the hand";
since holding a vajra with the palm is synonymous with grasping it with the hand, these two names appear interchangeably in the sūtras. In the West, this is called *ya*.
He is called "Secret" (*Guhyaka*) because his body, speech, and mind are swift, hidden, and difficult to comprehend; thus, the old translations sometimes call him "Secret Trace" (*Guhyapada*).
If explained according to the superficial meaning, the Lord of Secrets (*Guhyakādhipati*) is the King of Yakṣas, who wields the vajra and constantly attends upon and protects the Buddha;
hence he is called Vajrapāṇi. However, according to the profound meaning therein, as for the term "Yakṣa":
This refers to the secrets of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind, which only Buddhas and Buddhas can know; even Bodhisattvas such as Maitreya cannot reach such secret supernormal powers.
It is the most secret among secrets, namely the Lord of the Mind Secret (*cittaguhyaka*), and is thus called the "Lord of Secrets" (*Guhyakādhipati*).
Because he is able to maintain this seal (*mudrā*), he is called the "Vajra-holder" (*Vajradhara*). As it says:
These leaders, equal in number to the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, are accompanied by hosts of Vajradharas;

if the Sanskrit original were preserved in its entirety, there would be multiple vocatives for each name in the list, such as "O Vimalākāśa," "O Gaganagañja," and so forth, up to "O Guhyapati. This is because these are the foremost among the Vajradharas.
Each one possesses immeasurable retinues and categories; the original texts should exist in their entirety.

However, if one grasps the essential framework, the secondary details will follow accordingly, and there will be no deficiency in the application of the "Principle of the Essential Penetration" (zongtong).

As for what is called "the number of atoms in ten Buddha-fields," this refers to the Tathāgata’s seal of differentiated wisdom; its number is immeasurable, beyond the reach of calculation or metaphor.

That which can be known is further illustrated by taking each of the ten powers of the Tathāgata and correlating them with a single atom of a Buddha-field to represent the number of those in the assembly.
The nature of the oceans of worlds, the world-systems, and the meaning of a single Buddha-field are explained in detail within the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanatory Commentary).
Nevertheless, through the empowerment of the inner-realized virtues of this Vairocana, from each and every seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*), [the manifestations arise].
Each manifests the form, color, and nature of a Vajradhara, with distinct characteristics that correspond to the original conditions and dispositions of sentient beings to attract and guide them.
If practitioners cultivate this diligently, they can cause their three karmas to become identical to those of the Honored One;
by entering through this single gate, one enters the Dharma-realm, which is the universal gateway for entering all dharma-realms.
Next, the assembly of Bodhisattvas is listed, with four noble beings as their leaders.

While it was previously explained that all the Vajradharas are exclusively the wisdom-seals (*jñāna-mudrā*) of the Tathāgatas, these Bodhisattvas have a meaning that encompasses both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as compassion (*karuṇā*);
therefore, they receive distinct names. Furthermore, they represent the internally realized merits of Vairocana, just as there are ten Buddhas corresponding to the Vajradharas.
Those as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field should know that these bodhisattvas’ relative dharmaparyāyas also number ten times the atoms of a buddha-field;
through the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), each appears from a single gate of the *dharmadhātu* in the form of a single spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Furthermore, according to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, when the Buddha attained enlightenment in his birth-body (*janma-kāya*), Ānanda, Guhyapada, the Malla, and others [were present].

These are called the inner retinue: Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and other such noble ones, as well as Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and the various non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before buddhahood; these are called the great retinue.
Now, it is said that the Buddha’s empowered body (*adhiṣṭhita-kāya*) is likewise: those Vajradharas who each hold the secret seals (*guhyamudrā*) of the Tathāgata are called the inner retinue.
All Bodhisattvas, through the skillful means of great compassion, universally embrace immeasurable sentient beings;
because they assist the Dharma King and perform the deeds of the Tathāgata, they are called the "Great Retinue. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"Those who wish to become the inner retinue of all Buddhas, and those who wish to obtain a great retinue, should study the Prajñāpāramitā. As for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, "Samanta" means "universal" or "all-pervading."
The meaning of "Sarvārthasiddha" (Accomplisher of All Aims) refers to the most excellent and virtuous aim;

that is, because the vows and practices arising from the bodhicitta, as well as his body, speech, and mind, are entirely equal and pervasive in all places, being purely and excellently virtuous and endowed with all qualities, he is named thus.
As for the Bodhisattva Maitreya, this means that among the Buddha’s four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), compassion (*maitrī*) is now taken as the foremost designation. This...
Maitreya arises from the lineage of the Tathāgata; because he can ensure that the seed of the Buddha is never severed throughout all worlds, he is called Maitreya.
As stated above, Samantabhadra represents the virtue of self-realization whose original vows have already been fulfilled;
wishing to transform sentient beings so that they may attain this path, he is explained next. Regarding the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī: "Mañju" refers to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha.
It is like *sarpis* (clarified butter), which is pure and supreme; *śrī* is translated as "Auspiciousness" (*śubha*), meaning that which is endowed with all virtues.

It is also called "Wondrous Virtue" (*Guṇasāgara*) or "Wondrous Sound" (*Ghoṣa*). This refers to how, by the power of great compassion, he proclaims the wondrous sound of the Dharma so that all may hear it;
therefore, Maitreya clarifies this next. As for the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, "obstruction" (*nīvaraṇa*) refers to—
This means that the various mental defilements of sentient beings can obscure the Tathāgata’s pure eye, preventing it from opening and becoming luminous.
If one employs the non-conceptual Dharma to extinguish all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), it is like the clearing away of clouds and mist so that the sun’s orb shines forth;

therefore, he is called the Tathāgata Avaraṇaviṣkambhin. Because everything the Tathāgata has taught is for the sake of this single purpose, the name "Ghoṣadatta" (Bestowed with Wondrous Sound) follows next.

Furthermore, although a practitioner may study the Prajñāpāramitā, if they lack meditative concentration (dhyāna), they are like a blind person who, despite encountering sunlight, is unable to do anything;
therefore, next follows Mañjuśrī’s Samādhi of Sublime Wisdom that Dispels Obstructions.
These four Bodhisattvas are the four virtues of the Buddha-body; if there is any deficiency in them, one cannot achieve Buddhahood.
Because supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*) is the foremost, it is listed as the primary [attribute] to encompass the sands-of-the-Ganges of all virtues.
Regarding the "Great Bodhisattvas" (*mahā-bodhisattva*), the original Sanskrit text should be rendered as such. The *Śāstra* explains: "Bodhi" refers to the path of all Buddhas;
"Sattva" refers to sentient beings, or alternatively, to a courageous mind. These individuals all desire to attain the merits of all Buddhas.
The mind cannot be severed nor can it be broken, being like a vajra mountain; this is called *sattva*.

Furthermore, because this person’s mind is capable of great deeds, is non-regressive and irreversible due to its great heroic resolve, gives rise to great compassion among many sentient beings, establishes the Mahāyāna, is able to practice the Great Path, and attains the state of supreme greatness, they will certainly be able to preach the Dharma and shatter all [obstructions].
Because sentient beings possess great false views, great craving, great self-attachment, and other such afflictions, they are called *mahāsattva*.
The Ācārya says that according to the correct meaning, one should say *bodhisattva*;

here, *sattva* means "one who endures, delights in, practices, and firmly maintains [the path] without abandoning it. However, according to the rules of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), when considering the phonetic characters:
Although the meaning may be correct, if the phonology is not fluid or convenient, one may adopt what is expedient and comfortable;
thus, the worldly masters call it *sattva*, and those who wish to transmit and practice it follow these terms. Within the Yogācāra school, there are briefly three kinds of *sattva*:
first, the ignorant child-like *sattva*, referring to ordinary beings of the six realms who do not understand the reality of cause and effect.
First, because they practice deviant paths, cultivate the causes of suffering, and are attached to the three realms—clinging firmly and refusing to relinquish them—it is named after this.

Second, there are sentient beings with consciousness, namely those of the two vehicles; as soon as they perceive the faults and afflictions of birth and death, they seek liberation for themselves and attain nirvana.
They become stained by attachment to the "transformed city" (the *pariṇāmika-nagara*) and give rise to the notion of extinction and deliverance regarding the merit of the Tathāgata.
Third, because the mind of aspiration has not yet arisen regarding virtue, it is so named.
Bodhisattva-sattva refers to unsurpassed enlightenment that transcends all conceptualizations, frivolous arguments, and various faults; it is exclusively pure, white, subtle, and beyond analogy.
This meaning is precisely the inconceivable mind that is the original nature of sentient beings, which is capable of endurance.
Because he aspires to and joyfully practices such deeds for the realization of the Way with firm and unshakable resolve, he is named *bodhicitta*.
Because among such persons his meritorious achievements are greatest and he is capable of transmitting them to all sentient beings, he is named *mahāsattva*.
Surrounded by this great assembly in front and behind, the World-Honored One Vairocana, with his infinite body, speech, and mind—
Because they made offerings and paid homage for the sake of hearing the Dharma, the text next clarifies the time when the various capacities of sentient beings gathered together to hear the teaching;
this is what the sutra refers to as "the Tathāgata’s empowerment on a day transcending the three times," namely, the dharma-gate of the equal phrases of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, if this sutra were to circulate throughout Jambudvīpa, it would comprise approximately one hundred thousand verses.
When the great assemblies, as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, each extensively expound the Dharma-gates of the distinctions of body, speech, and mind, they are truly limitless.
As for the duration of time during which this Dharma is preached, how could it be measured?

Therefore, the compilers of the canon state that at that time, [the Buddha] dwelt in the Sun of the Buddhas and expounded the Dharma extensively. Just as with worldly divisions of time, there are the past, the future, and the present.

The measures of long and short kalpas vary in many ways; yet, if one calculates them based on the sun’s single circuit around the four continents within a day and night—divided into the initial, middle, and final portions, down to thirty periods (*muhūrta*) and the non-abiding instants (*kṣaṇa*) that succeed one another in constant flux—one observes with the pure eye that the characteristics of the three time-periods (*trikāla*) are utterly unattainable. There is no end and no beginning, nor is there any coming or going.
This reality-mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is a sun that is perfectly bright, eternally abiding, and as serene as empty space; it possesses no distinctions of temporal duration, such as length or brevity.

Nevertheless, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, he causes practitioners of yoga to perceive immeasurable kalpas as being like the time it takes to eat a meal, or to manifest a single meal’s time as immeasurable kalpas.
Thus, through mastery over extension and contraction, he accords with the capacities of all beings, for there is no fixed characteristic.
Because it can be attained, it is called the "Tathāgata Sun. During such a time, whatever Dharma the Buddha teaches is the Dharma-gate of the equality of body, speech, and mind.
This means that the various three karmas of the Tathāgata all reach the supreme, ultimate, and most wondrous realm;
body is equal to speech, and speech is equal to mind, just as the great ocean pervades all places and is one.
Because it has a single salty taste, it is called "equal" (*samapada*). Regarding the term *pada*: in Sanskrit it is called *padma*, which is correctly translated as "foot.

According to the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Phonology), it carries the meaning of "proceeding forward" and the meaning of "place of abiding. Just as when a person walks, they lift their foot and set it down, the trace where that foot abides is called *padma*.
The meaning of the phrases and pauses in speech is also like this; therefore, they share the same name. Now, concerning this...
This school asserts that because one practices such a sequence of the path of training and attains abiding in the three states of equality,
it is called a "phrase" (*pada*). That is to say, taking the secret empowerment of body, speech, and mind as the gateway of entry—
using the secret mudrās of the body, the mantras of speech, and the sublime visualizations of the mind as the means— one thereby attains vision.
The Adhiṣṭhita-Sambhogakāya (the Body of Enjoyment through Empowerment) is precisely the Vairocana-body that pervades all things.
That which pervades all things is the practitioner’s body of equalizing wisdom (*samatājñāna*).
Therefore, for those who abide in this vehicle, to practice by means of non-practice and to arrive by means of non-arrival is called the "phrase of equality" for all sentient beings.
All enter therein, yet in reality there is no one who enters, nor is there any place of entry; therefore it is called the Dharma-gate of Equality.
This is the essential purport of this sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra was the leader, and the various Vajradharas, with the Lord of Secrets as their leader, [were present].

By the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata Vairocana, he manifests with vigorous power the inexhaustible treasury of bodily adornments, even unto the point where the seeds of karma and lifespan among the classes of sentient beings are eliminated, yet sprouts of new seeds continue to arise; this is because he is about to expound this Dharma-gate of equality.
Therefore, first employing sovereign empowerment to stir the great assembly, he fully manifests the secret realm of the universal gate (*samantamukha*).
The inconceivable and unprecedented event of the secret adornment was expounded in response to those questions;
thus, those who hear it will increase their faith and joy, penetrating deeply into the realization of its meaning.

This shall be explained in detail here, as in the *Nidāna-parivarta* and the *Bhūmyutsarpaṇa-parivarta* of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore, O leaders among the virtuous ones, such as the Lord of Mysteries Samantabhadra and others—
This is the Vairocana-body of differentiated wisdom, which has long since attained thorough penetration regarding such realms. Furthermore,
the various spiritual friends manifested through these gates of liberation each lead immeasurable assemblies of beings according to their capacities to enter the maṇḍala of the dharmadhātu,
for the sake of benefiting these bodhisattvas who have newly entered the practice of the Dharma-gate.
This is the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of manifesting the body through vigorous exertion.
Just as a lion king, when about to roar, first exerts his body to display his majestic spiritual power and physical strength before letting out his voice, so too does the Tathāgata;
wishing to definitively proclaim the lion’s roar that expounds the gateway to all-knowledge, he first manifests it through vigorous exertion.
The manifestation of the treasury of immeasurable adornments—what is meant by "adornment" is that from a single, equal body, all modes of conduct are universally manifested;
such conduct is none other than the *mudrā*. From a single, equal speech, all sounds are universally manifested;
such sound is none other than the *mantra*. From a single, equal mind, all original [natures] are universally manifested.
The Honored One is thus the Honored Deity who is none other than samādhi;
yet, because the specific characteristics of each of these various samādhis are boundless and immeasurable, they are called the "Inexhaustible Adornment," the secret wisdom of the Tathāgata.
As the Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, desiring to know the dimensions of the Buddha’s body within the assembly, commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana..."
Searching upward as far as the Brahma palace, he still beheld the Tathāgata as if face-to-face; the Buddha’s physical deportment and the sound of his preaching were no different from before.
Even when he traveled to other buddha-fields by means of his supernatural powers, it was no different than being in the Brahma palace.
At that time, because neither the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin nor Maudgalyāyana could fathom this, [the Buddha] himself...

He went forth to observe the worlds of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, and saw the Tathāgatas in all of them preaching the Dharma without rising from their seats;
even when he had reached the furthest reaches of the ten directions, exhausting the full extent of his supernatural powers, it was likewise so.
Thereafter, as he returned, he saw the goddess Vimatividhvaṃsanī not far from the Buddha, having entered into samādhi.
He formed this thought: "I have heard that this goddess has attained mastery over immeasurable gates of samādhi; I should now observe which concentration she currently abides in.
Furthermore, he exerted all his mental power to observe her, yet he could not fathom the sphere of her mental activity.
Then, immeasurable celestial drums gathered together—each as vast as Sumeru, the king of mountains—and by her supernormal power, they simultaneously emitted sounds, desiring to...

He attempted to emerge from this samādhi but was unable to do so; even until the Buddha said, "When I had not yet resolved upon Bodhicitta, this goddess was already able to abide in this samādhi," it remains thus—this is the meaning of "boundless.

In this way, Vairocana universally manifests throughout all worlds in the ten directions, each appearing as the body sustained by the Buddha's empowerment; each and every one of these bodies is [thus].
In each [assembly], there were great congregations of bodhisattva-vajras equal in number to the atoms within ten buddha-fields.
The faculties and marks of these great congregations were likewise boundless; like oil pervading a sesame seed, they filled the dharma-realm without any intervening space.
Furthermore, it was as if a king possessed a great treasury which, when he wished to show it to others, he could open and display at will.

Because it is spread forth, it is called the "Treasury of Adornment. Furthermore, this great assembly is able to see such an inconceivable realm solely through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
If the Tathāgata were to relinquish his sustaining power, [this realm] would no longer appear before them;
it is not something that can be reached by the limited capacity of their own minds. Just as a practitioner internally cultivates the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* and externally...

Sustained by the protection of spiritual power, one is able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions with one's own physical body born of parents, as clearly as one gazes upon the myriad stars on a cloudless night at midnight. One hears the sounds of the Dharma with perfect clarity and without obstruction.

Now, does this state arise because the practitioner’s mind is pure, or does it arise through the Buddha’s empowerment? If it arises from within the mind itself, then it originates from one's own nature.
If birth were produced by the power of the Buddha, it would arise from an other-nature (*parabhāva*), and thus would not differ at all from the tenets of non-Buddhist schools.
Since neither self nor other exists, their conjunction likewise does not exist. Furthermore, it is not achieved without causes and conditions;
for if either internal causes or external conditions are lacking, [the result] does not manifest. Therefore, one should know that such adornments are thus established.
When its marks manifest, they come from nowhere; when they are concealed, they go nowhere.
Because it is ultimately equal and does not deviate from suchness (*tathatā*), the Sūtra says: "It is not produced from the body, speech, or mind of Vairocana Buddha;
the limits of its arising and ceasing cannot be found in any place. Yet, all the bodily actions and all the vocal actions of Vairocana..."
All mental actions, in all places and at all times, proclaim the dharmas of the mantrayāna syllables within the realm of sentient beings;
this explains why the *Buddhavyūha-kośa* is inexhaustible and without limit, for it is not different from the Tathāgata’s body, which pervades all places and abides eternally without ceasing.
Although it is eternal and without arising or cessation, it is nevertheless able to...
With all three types of karma, throughout the ten directions and across all times and places of the three periods, they proclaim the most authentic teaching of the Way to transform sentient beings,
serving as guides and craftsmen for their minds to lead them to the Buddha-way.

The Sūtra says: Furthermore, he manifests the forms of Vajradhara, Samantabhadra, Padmapāṇi Bodhisattva, and others, universally proclaiming throughout the ten directions the mantra path and the dharmas of pure phrases.

These range from the first production of the thought of enlightenment up to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), whereby the sequence of karma that brings fulfillment in this life, the karma of sentient beings born from the growth of conditions, and the seeds of lifespan are eliminated; yet, there remains the sprout [of future existence].
Regarding the "arising from seeds," this further elaborates on the preceding description, stating that it does not merely manifest the Buddha-body filling all worlds throughout the ten directions;
rather, the bodies manifested as Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattvas and others likewise pervade all places.
This is like the various and distinct seals (mudrās) of body, speech, and mind belonging to the Vajradhara Bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms within ten buddha-fields.

In this manner, each of these classes of principal deities and their retinues fills all worlds throughout the ten directions like Indra’s net, with none obstructing one another; here, for brevity, three holy ones are cited as the foremost:
Vajradhara, who faces the gate of adamantine wisdom and employs skillful means for subduing; and Samantabhadra, who faces... [the gate of] universal excellence.
The gate of the *tathatā*-dharmakāya is the skillful means of quelling calamities (*śānti*), while the gate of Avalokiteśvara facing the lotus is the skillful means of increase (*puṣṭi*).
By citing these three points, all immeasurable and inconceivable wondrous functions are already subsumed within them; therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
As for the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it refers to the various devas, the eight classes of beings, and the five-fold transcendent sages (*pañcābhijña-ṛṣi*) who appear externally.

The representations of the maṇḍala can be understood through such examples. Through various causes and conditions and countless skillful means, the Universal Gate manifests itself to teach and transform all sentient beings.

Although their capacities differ in depth and shallowness, and their manifestations vary between the coarse and the subtle, when one investigates their actual reality, they are none other than secret empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*), each capable of revealing the Tathāgata’s pure knowledge and vision.
If one departs from such a seal of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*), everything else is born of craving and false views;
it acts as a companion to the celestial Māras and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). How, then, could it be called a pure phrase? Next, he explains further:

what is called the "pure phrase" is precisely the vehicle of supernatural powers for attaining Buddhahood through sudden awakening (*tongjue chengfo shentong sheng*). This is unlike other vehicles where Bodhisattvas aspire to seek unexcelled enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Throughout countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there have been those who underwent various hardships and did not spare their own bodies or lives,
yet some attained Buddhahood while others did not. However, if a bodhisattva of this gateway of mantras can practice through skillful means without violating the rules of the Dharma,
they will, even within this very life, attain the vision of the realm of inexhaustible adornment and empowerment— not only that, but...
It is already manifest before one; if one wishes to transcend and ascend to the Buddha-ground, it can be attained just as with Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
Furthermore, when a practitioner first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, they enter the gate of the letter A, whereby a sprout is born from the Tathāgata’s vajra-nature.
One should know that this sprout grows and progresses moment by moment, never regressing, until the attainment of Bodhi.
Because there is no further practice to be increased and one subsequently comes to rest, it is said that "this sequence is fulfilled.
Regarding this sequence, in the Sanskrit original, it carries the meanings of non-abiding, diligence, and universal application.
This means that having first resolved to enter the stage of a Bodhisattva, one practices through the skillful means of these essential mantra teachings and attains the first bhūmi. At that time—

By advancing with a mind that dwells nowhere and never ceasing, one fulfills the second bhūmi; furthermore, by relying on the skillful means of the essential methods of mantra, one attains entry into samādhi.

Proceeding in this sequence until the ten bhūmis are fully perfected, one achieves perfect awakening through a single practice and a single path. Even when the secret intent is revealed through various other doors of skillful means, it is likewise so.

None are apart from such a precious vehicle. Those born through the conditions of karma and afflictions refer to all sentient beings who, due to the causes and conditions of ignorance and craving, create various kinds of false and impure karma of body, speech, and mind.
Riding upon such karma, they take birth in the bodies of the six realms, increasing their cyclic existence and undergoing all manner of suffering.
Now, by cultivating the gate of pure wisdom—the equality of the three karmas—all [suffering] is transcended.
The seeds of the aggregates, the ālayavijñāna, karma, and lifespan are all incinerated, whereby one attains the stainless Great Bodhicitta of space, the seed common to all Tathāgatas.
From within the treasury of compassion, the sprouts of dharmatā emerge, extending through stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits that pervade the entire Dharmadhātu.
Thus, the King of Bodhi Trees flourishes with the blossoming of myriad virtues; yet, by means of the four...

In the contemplation of the meaning of non-arising, there is nothing toward which one tends, nor is there any place of origination; one should know that this very arising is the arising of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
Thus it is said: "Once the seeds of karma, lifespan, and sentient beings are removed, there further arises the sprouting of the seeds.

Furthermore, the various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and gateways of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), equal in number to the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, manifested by the Tathāgata, are all provisional.
If one were to observe and listen to them in succession, they would not be fully exhausted even in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
yet, through the empowerment of the Buddha-sun, they all appear before one in the mere space of a single sitting in this assembly.

This is the manifestation of inconceivable supernatural signs (*prātihārya*) as he prepares to preach this sutra—just as Mañjuśrī beheld that which was illuminated by the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*).

The various causes and conditions through which the bodhisattvas of the eighteen thousand lands all practice the bodhisattva path lead them to know that the Buddhas are about to reveal the provisional to manifest the real by preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. One should know that it is likewise for Vajrapāṇi and others;
they universally perceive the empowerment of the world wherein only the Dharma-gate of equality is taught, and thus they know that the Tathāgata is about to expound the universal [Dharma].
Because this is the teaching that all vehicles achieve Buddhahood through one's own mind, the question posed in the following passage arises from this principle.
At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets, seated within that assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, how does the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha attain the wisdom of all-knowledge, and even such wisdom as this?"
What is the cause? What is the root? What is the ultimate? The Tathāgata’s wisdom of self-realization cannot be shown before others even if sustained by supernatural power (*ṛddhi-adhiṣṭhāna*).
As for what is called the "display of the inexhaustible treasury of majestic manifestations," these are merely traces of external function.
When a wise person perceives the branches and their extremities, they understand the fundamental source, just as one who observes [the branches] [perceives the tree].
The elephant’s footprint surpasses all others; though one does not see its form, one should know that the strength of this elephant’s body must be immense.

Furthermore, when swift thunder and torrential rain cause birds and beasts to die of terror and the hundred rivers to surge forth, overwhelming the mountains and submerging the hills, though one cannot fathom their origin, one should know that the majestic power of these dragons must be immense.
Now this great assembly is likewise so: beholding the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible body, speech, and mind, which can simultaneously respond throughout the Dharma-realm to sentient beings,
perfectly harmonizing with their faculties and dispositions to accomplish the Buddha-work, we know that the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom must, in a single thought-moment,

universally discern the capacities of all beings from beginning to end, their causes and conditions, and their ultimate states, unimpededly illuminating the provisional means for guiding the mundane world.
If even this is so, what then must be said regarding the realm of ultimate, realized wisdom? If phenomena were not thus, there would be some subtle traces to be found;
yet, though I have observed them all, I do not know from whence these phenomena are obtained.
Therefore, Vajrapāṇi, on account of the doubts in the minds of the assembly, asked the Buddha: "How does the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha obtain this?"
It is the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). In the Sanskrit original, *tathāgata* is used:
*tathā* has the meaning of "thus" (*tathā*), *āgata* has the meanings of "come," "understood," "explained," or "gone.

Because the Buddhas have come to achieve perfect enlightenment by following the path according to reality, the Buddha is named "Thus-Come One" (*Tathāgata*). All Buddhas understand and realize the characteristics of phenomena as they truly are.
Having known [this], he also teaches it to sentient beings according to the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;

because the present Buddha is likewise, he is called "One who Knows According to Reality" and "One who Speaks According to Reality. All Buddhas have attained such a nature of peace and bliss that they proceed directly to *nirvāṇa*;
because the present Buddha likewise goes [there], he is called "The One Who Has Gone Thus" (*Tathāgata*). The commentary fully contains these four meanings.
However, ancient translations mostly render it as "Tathāgata" (如來). The *Sīla-sūtra* of the Sarvāstivāda school renders it as "Tathāgata" (如去).
The Master’s intention was that "Tathā" (如) means "as it is" and "gata" (去) means "to go. For now, I shall follow the ancient titles. In the Sanskrit original, it is "Arhat";

here, "ara" signifies afflictions (*kleśa*) and "han" signifies the meaning of "to harm" or "to eliminate. The commentary explains this as "slayer of thieves," for the Buddha has mounted the armor of patience and diligence.

He is so named because he uses the horse of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the bow of concentration (*samādhi*), and the arrows of wisdom (*prajñā*) to externally destroy the army of Māra and internally annihilate the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, "A" signifies "not" and "Arhata" signifies "arising";

thus, it means that the seeds of the Buddha-mind will not give rise to the husks of ignorance in the field of future lives, as they have been stripped away. Moreover, "Arhat" carries the meaning of one who is worthy of receiving offerings.
Because he possesses such merits and is thus worthy of receiving the supreme offerings of devas and humans, this is used as his name.

In Sanskrit, *Samyak-saṃbuddha* means: *Samyak* signifies "correct," *saṃ* signifies "universal," and *buddha* signifies "knowledge"; therefore, it is called "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (*Samyak-saṃbuddha*).
The *Śāstra* states: "If someone asks why it is only the Buddha who speaks according to reality..."

Since his coming is like his going, he should indeed receive the highest offerings. Because the Buddha has attained the wisdom of Right Universal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), "Right" (*samyak*) refers to the fact that the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is immovable and indestructible;
"Universal" (*saṃ*) refers to the fact that it does not consist of one phenomenon or two phenomena.
Because he knows all phenomena completely and without remainder, he is called *Samyak-saṃbuddha*. However, in this school, the term "Buddha" is defined as "Awakened."

This has the meaning of "full blossoming. It signifies that by means of natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), one universally awakens to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*)—like a lotus flower in full bloom, free from any stain—and is also able to cause all sentient beings to blossom; therefore, one is called a Buddha.
In Sanskrit, this is *sarvajña*. *Jña* refers to the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). The commentary states: *Sarvajñatā* is...
"Omniscience" refers to all [phenomena], namely the infinite pairs of dharma-gates such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), each of which encompasses all dharmas.
Likewise, there are infinite sets of three, four, five, six, and so on, up to incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) dharma-gates, each encompassing all dharmas.

Among all these dharmas, there are the single characteristic and the diverse characteristics, the outflowing characteristic and the non-outflowing characteristic, the conditioned characteristic and the unconditioned characteristic, and so forth.

Because of the power of all-encompassing wisdom, one thoroughly and universally knows all phenomena—each with its own characteristics, each with its own power, each with its own causes and conditions, each with its own retribution, each with its own nature, each with its own attainment, and each with its own loss.
This is called *sarvajña* (all-knowledge); what is here termed "the knowledge of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*) is the knowledge within knowledge.

It is not merely that one universally knows all phenomena through all aspects, but also that one knows this Dharma as the ultimate reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), possessing a nature of permanence and indestructibility, neither increasing nor decreasing, like a diamond.
Such a state of self-realization is beyond the words of a speaker and beyond the vision of an observer; it cannot be transferred to another, unlike an *āmalaka* fruit held in the hand. If...
