If that which can be transmitted to others through words were sufficient for enlightenment, then Śākyamuni Bodhisattva should have attained Buddhahood at the very moment he received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Why is this? Is it because one must fully cultivate skillful means and wait until awakening spontaneously without a teacher before being called a Buddha?
Furthermore, when one sees with one's own eyes a person wounded by a blade or a staff, even though one believes they are suffering, there is no room for doubt.

However, although various [teachings] were spoken, one does not realize or know them until one personally experiences and receives them, at which point they become clearly understood. The question is:

how may we attain such self-awakened wisdom? And having attained this wisdom, how can we extensively expound and distribute it for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings, according to their various dispositions, various inclinations, and various natures?
The various paths of skillful means through which he proclaims the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) are as follows:
he establishes immeasurable vehicles, manifests immeasurable bodies, adopts the respective speech and sounds of each, and abides in their respective modes of conduct;
yet this path of omniscience remains of a single flavor, namely, the flavor of the Tathāgata’s liberation. Furthermore, how is this sublime skillful means attained? This...

Regarding the "various destinies" (*nānā-gati*) within the middle [section], the Sanskrit term is *nirya*, which is also called "path" (*mārga*). What is stated below regarding the "Mahāyāna path," etc., has the same meaning.
The *Vibhāṣā* states that there are five destinies, whereas those of the Mahāyāna generally speak of six destinies. Thus they are extensively elaborated;
if even in this world there are already thirty-six *koṭi* of sentient beings in these destinies, how much more so in the ten [directions]?
Regarding those in all worlds who possess desire-natures: "desire" refers to faith, wisdom, inclination, and delight.
For example, Sundarananda delighted in the five desires, while Devadatta delighted in fame and so forth;
even among those who have attained the Way, each has their own particular preference—Mahākāśyapa preferred *dhūta* practices, Śāriputra preferred wisdom, and Revata preferred [meditative] seclusion.

Upāli excelled at sitting in meditation (*dhyāna*), Ānanda excelled at knowing the Vinaya, and others excelled in extensive learning; these matters shall be explained in detail. Regarding "nature" (*prakṛti*):
it is called "accumulated habituation" (*saṃskāra*). Following this nature, desire arises; one acts according to that nature, and sometimes follows desire to constitute a nature.

Habitual desire becomes a nature. As for the term "nature": it refers to a defiled mind engaging in an activity. As for "desire": it refers to arising in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*) regarding that activity. These explanations are fully detailed in the *Śāstra*.

Regarding the elucidation of the various paths of skillful means (*upāya*), Nāgārjuna stated that while Prajñā and Upāya are identical in their essential nature (*svabhāva*), they differ in their application.
For example, just as a goldsmith, through his skillful means, fashions gold into various different objects—each of which is gold yet bears a distinct name—so too is Vairocana; he is able to...

The essence of the wisdom of true gold pervades all places, manifesting as various vehicles. Furthermore, the intent of the inquiry herein is precisely to initiate the Maṇḍala of the Matrix of Great Compassion (*Mahākaruṇā-garbha-maṇḍala*).

Upon the ground of the mind of equality in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one paints the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and even those of the two vehicles and the eight classes of beings, forming a fourfold circular altar of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Each of these—
The seals of the body, speech, and mind of the *iṣṭadevatā* all constitute a specific vehicle (*yāna*).

For example, if there is someone who aspires to the path of knowledge of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), [the Buddha] manifests in the form of a Vedic Brahmin from within the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-vyūha* and teaches the mantra practices of the sage Gautama and others.
If the practitioner applies themselves with diligence, they will before long achieve this sage-body; thereafter, they further transform their skillful means (*upāya*) and...

Thus, one accomplishes the body of Vairocana. In this manner, one may manifest the body of a Buddha to teach various vehicles, or even manifest the body of a non-human being to teach various vehicles;
according to the species, their forms and voices are all mantras and secret mudrās.

Whether for a long or short duration, there is nothing that is not the causal condition of the "poisonous drum. As the Sūtra says: "All are of one and the same flavor, namely, the liberation of the Tathāgata."

As for the reason why this is so: the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the form and mind of all sentient beings has, from the very beginningless limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), always been the equal wisdom-body (*samatājñānakāya*) of Vairocana;
it is not that at the time of attaining *bodhi*, one forcibly empties all phenomena to make them the *dharmadhātu*.
From the ground of the equal mind, the Buddha unfolds the inexhaustible treasury of adornments, the Great Maṇḍala.
Having returned to the use of the syllable A, one opens and develops the inexhaustible treasury of majestic adornment within the equal ground of the minds of sentient beings;

that these wondrous responses and wondrous inspirations do not transcend the gateway of the syllable A—this should be known. The skillful means arising from the conditions of such response and inspiration likewise do not transcend the gateway of the syllable A.
It is, for example, like the waves in the great ocean, which, as they surge against one another, each acts alternately as the agent.
Whatever is burned therein is all of one single taste, namely, the taste of salt.

Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power and desiring to give rise to the secret skillful means of the *Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi* (Great Compassion Womb), further expounds five kinds of metaphors, namely: space, earth, water, fire, and wind. This is the first phrase.
It is said: For example, just as the realm of empty space is free from all conceptualization (*vikalpa*), is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), and is not non-conceptual (*na-avikalpa*);
so too, the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) is free from all conceptualization, is non-conceptual, and is not non-conceptual.
According to the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*, empty space possesses neither faults nor virtues; likewise, the Tathāgata’s body of wisdom is free from all faults and endowed with myriad virtues.
How can the characteristics of accomplishment be illustrated through analogies? One merely takes a small portion of their similarity to metaphorically represent the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
Within this comparison, there are three meanings: first, because space is ultimately pure; second, because it is without boundaries; and third, because it is without conceptual differentiation.
The nature of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) is likewise so. Thus, by means of what is familiar in the world, [the profound is made known].

The "explanation of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-vyākhyāna*) is difficult to understand. First, it says "free from all conceptualization" (*sarva-vikalpa-vivikta*); next, it says "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*).
The reason for stating this twice is that it signifies the arising of further conceptualization upon conceptualization.

This is analogous to the distinction between *vitarka* (initial inquiry) and *vicāra* (sustained investigation): when one briefly observes, it is called *vitarka*, and when one minutely examines, it is called *vicāra*. It is also like the case of the eye.
When consciousness arises, there is coarse discrimination; subsequently, mental consciousness arises, which is subtle discrimination.

According to the old translations, *kalpa* is used as a metaphor for false attachment, meaning that just as space is without the discrimination of false attachment, it is both non-discriminative and non-existent [as a substantial entity].
Furthermore, just as space is free from various manifest colors and shapes, and is devoid of any conditioned activity, [so too is the nature of consciousness].
It can contain all myriad phenomena; all grasses and trees grow by means of it, and the activities of sentient beings rely upon it to attain the wisdom of Buddhahood.

Space is also like this: although it is free from all characteristics and is eternally without arising or activity, immeasurable gates of liberation and various wondrous deeds are all accomplished within it; therefore, it is used as a metaphor. The second line says:
For example, just as all sentient beings rely upon the great earth, so too do gods, humans, and asuras rely upon the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Just as the hundred grains, various medicines, herbs, trees, thickets, and forests—differing infinitely according to their respective natures and portions—all arise from the great earth, and their roots, sprouts, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits are successively brought to fruition; so it is with this wisdom.
It serves as a place of reliance for all sentient beings and nurtures them; yet it does not form such thoughts as, "I now bear the burden of the entire world.
It does not dwell upon their kindness or virtue, nor does it possess any contract of labor. It increases not with joy, nor does it grieve when diminished.
Deep and vast, difficult to fathom, and immovable, the ground of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*) is likewise so; such is the mandala of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-maṇḍala*).
It is that which gives rise to all seeds; it is the locus upon which the immeasurable activities of these various vehicles depend;
its mind is equal toward both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and it cannot be shaken by the eight worldly winds.
Because it possesses such partial similarities, it is used as a metaphor. The third line says: "It is like the element of fire, which burns one..."
Just as there is no satiety in burning all kinds of firewood, so too the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) never tires of burning all the firewood of ignorance.

It is like a spark of fire: even if one were to pile up firewood filling the entire world, each piece as large as Mount Sumeru, and burn them one after another, it would feel no weariness and would not think, "I shall burn only this much wood; I will not burn that."
Just as the fire of fuel burns without ceasing, advancing without weariness until the fuel is entirely consumed and only then subsides, so too is the fire of the Tathāgata’s wisdom:
it burns away the fuel of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) until even their conditions and dependencies are exhausted;
thus, this light of insight has no further basis. Furthermore, just as the fire of the world is used by both the noble and the lowly...
It serves equally as an illumination in the darkness of night for those who are deluded and about to fall, enabling them all to find the correct path;

furthermore, it can accomplish all things. This fire of omniscience exists equally in both noble beings and ordinary worldlings, causing practitioners to see the path of reality within the great night of beginningless time and gradually achieve perfection.
Regarding all Buddha-dharmas, it is used as a metaphor; the fourth line says:
"For example, as the element of wind removes all dust, so too does the wisdom of omniscience remove the dust of all afflictions.

This is like when a great wind arises and smoke, clouds, dust, and mist are all eliminated, leaving the great void clear and vast, the three luminaries shining brightly, and the oppressive heat dissipated.
It brings refreshing coolness to all afflicted sentient beings, causing flowers, herbs, thickets, and forests to bloom, flourish, and grow;

it can likewise destroy all categories of material things. Furthermore, just as the nature of wind is pervasive, has no fixed support, revolves with sovereign ease, and cannot be obstructed, so too is the wind of the Tathāgata’s wisdom:
it sweeps away all veils of hindrance, the dust of afflictions, and causes them to vanish.

It realizes the cool nature of *dharmatā* that is *nirvāṇa*, and furthermore, it causes all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas to increase, destroys the great tree of ignorance by uprooting its foundation;
because this power free from obstruction has no basis whatsoever, it is used as a metaphor. The fifth line says: "For example, all sentient beings rely upon the element of water."
This joy, which is the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) for the benefit and happiness of all gods and humans, is like the great virtue of water:
flowing from high to low, it brings manifold benefit, moistening grasses and trees so that they produce flowers and fruit. Furthermore, its inherent nature is pure, stainless, and unclouded;
it is able to fully satisfy beings who are hungry and thirsty, washing away all dregs and impurities, and cleansing them entirely.
The heat and affliction are deep and vast, difficult to enter and impossible to measure; yet in the midst of these pits and ravines, their nature is entirely equal.

The water of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: flowing from the true Dharma-realm into the world, it moistens all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), gives rise to the factors conducive to enlightenment, and brings forth the great fruit that benefits all sentient beings. Because its essence is free from affliction, it is pure and capable of liberation.

Because it is free from all afflictions, it is stainless; because its single characteristic is not different [from reality], it is unturbid. Since all acquisitions, thoughts, and aspirations regarding existence have been extinguished, one attains the coolness of meditative concentration (*śītalasamādhi*).
Having washed away the dust of worldly toil, one abides in profound stillness that is difficult to conceive, and realizes the nature of equality; thus, these serve as metaphors.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi states that these five metaphors are precisely the meaning of the five syllables that initiate the subsequent text.
The letter A is the gateway to earth; the letter Va is the gateway to water; the letter Ra is the gateway to fire; the letter Ha is the gateway to wind;

and the letter Kha is the gateway to space. Furthermore, just as in the world seeds depend upon the conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind, and only when space does not obstruct them can they grow—yet if even one of these conditions is lacking, they will never increase—so too is the nature of omniscience the seed of the Tathāgata.
The disciple likewise employs the five meanings of the gateway of omniscience as his own conditions to reach the wondrous fruit of eternal abiding in Bodhi—
namely, the inconceivable causes and conditions of neither arising nor ceasing. Vajrapāṇi,
beholding the signs of the Tathāgata’s empowerment within the singular Dharma-realm, reflected in his mind that he would surely know what was to come.
Having spoken this Dharma-gate, he first illustrated its merits to inspire the assembly and awaken their capacity for understanding;
he then asked the Buddha: "What is the cause of such wisdom? What is its root? What is its ultimate consummation?
Thereafter, the Tathāgata’s Seal of Wisdom stabilized their minds and extensively analyzed and explained it, as in the case of Maitreya.
When Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna beheld this auspicious omen of the Buddha’s supernatural power, he was immediately filled with agitation and perplexity, harboring doubts in his mind.

To resolve these, [the Buddha] explained the Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment and conferred upon him the prediction of Bodhi. Mañjuśrī then elucidated its name and essence, pointing to it as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Subsequently, the Tathāgata sealed it with the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and expounded it according to the capacities of sentient beings, thereby causing those who clung to fixed attachments to be moved.
One attains liberation from the net of doubt, just as when the spring sun first causes seeds to sprout and their husks to split open;

stirred by thunderous winds and moistened by timely rains, they emerge from their shells. Likewise, those who lack the necessary capacity cannot give rise to profound benefit even if they encounter such an opportunity.
Vairocana Buddha addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Vajradhara! Excellent, Vajrapāṇi!
You have asked me about such a meaning; listen attentively and apply your mind well, for I shall now explain it.
As for the so-called 'signlessness' of all phenomena, which is the characteristic of space—this, Vajradhara, is because of the secret [nature] of Vajrapāṇi."

The Lord of Secrets, having anticipated the profound intent of the Tathāgata’s empowerment and being able to inspire the assembly to give rise to understanding, and thus fathoming the Sage’s mind without missing the opportune moment, spoke again, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
I observe that among all devas, humans, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and even bodhisattvas of limited practice, none are able [to surpass] the World-Honored One."

As for why he previously posed such a question: it is because within these three phrases, all the secret spiritual powers and profound matters of the Buddha-dharma are entirely subsumed. Furthermore, he praised him, saying: "Excellent, Vajrapāṇi!
You are able to ask me about such a meaning. Then, through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s voice of praise, at that time, Vajra...
Vajrapāṇi’s immeasurable merit increases and becomes doubly radiant; regarding the Dharma he has received, he shall never suffer loss or forgetfulness.
Next, [the Buddha] issues this admonition: "Listen attentively and apply your mind with great care;

I shall now speak of this for the sake of future disciples as a clear instruction on the ritual for receiving the Dharma with a profound heart. Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "If a person's mind is virtuous..."
One who possesses direct faith is capable of hearing the Dharma; if one lacks these characteristics, they will be unable to understand it. As a verse says:

"The listener gazes attentively as if drinking in thirst, Entering single-mindedly into the meaning of the words. Leaping with joy upon hearing the Dharma, their heart is moved by both sorrow and delight.
To such a person, one should preach the Dharma. Furthermore, according to the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra*, there are twenty benefits for listening to the Dharma with a focused mind.
The virtues should be explained extensively.
As the Sūtra says, the Buddha told Vajrapāṇi: "Bodhicitta is the cause, great compassion is the root, and skillful means are the culmination.
This is just as in the world, where a seed relies upon the four great elements and various conditions to produce roots, following this sequence.
Up to the point where the fruition is accomplished, it is called the ultimate;
yet when observed with middle-way wisdom, it is ultimately neither arising nor ceasing, and neither non-arising nor non-ceasing. Therefore, the principle of cause and effect is established.

If phenomena were otherwise—possessing the characteristics of arising and ceasing, or of annihilation and permanence—they would fall into conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and could all be refuted; thus, the principle of cause and effect would not be established.
Now, when a practitioner contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the mind, it is likewise so: it transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), like the pure void.

Within this internal realization of what is practiced, one attains the power of profound faith; the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) becomes firm and immovable, free from the retribution of karma and birth, and gives rise to true nature.
Because the merits of the myriad practices increase from this, it is said that the bodhicitta is [the root].

Regarding the latter two lines: if one considers the roots of goodness planted within the cycle of birth and death as the cause, they are then termed the "fruit," because one beholds the preliminary signs of the Buddha-dharma.
It is like a person who hears a spiritual friend say: "In your own home there is a treasury of inexhaustible jewels;
you should diligently apply skillful means to excavate it, so that it may provide for the entire nation and ensure constant sufficiency."
Being free from lack, once they have heard this, they immediately give rise to faith based on the truth and practice according to what was taught;

continuing thus with unremitting effort, they gradually perceive the preceding signs. At that time, regarding the merits of the treasure-store, they should abandon doubt in their minds and become capable of initiating sublime application (*prayoga*).
Therefore, the bodhicitta is precisely the meaning of pure, white faith (*śraddhā*); so it is also stated in the *Vyākhyā*.
It is said that faith is able to enter the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma. When the Brahma Heaven King requested the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the Buddha spoke this verse:
"I now open the gate to the flavor of ambrosia; those who have faith shall obtain joy.

In this verse, he does not mention generosity, precepts, learning, patience, diligence, meditation, or wisdom—by which people might obtain joy—but speaks only of the person of faith. This was the Buddha’s intention.

Thus, this foremost, most profound Dharma—subtle, immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, unmoving, non-reliant, non-attached, and a dharma of non-apprehension—cannot be understood by anyone who is not an omniscient one. Therefore, faith-power is made primary;
it is not through wisdom and the like that one can first enter the Buddha-dharma, but rather so as to make such a purified mind firm.
The growth of the fetters increases. In the Sūtra, Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is subsequently taught as the root; "root" carries the sense of being able to sustain and hold fast.
It is like the roots of a tree, which sustain the trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruit, preventing them from falling or being uprooted.

In the Sanskrit language, *karuṇā* is analyzed as *kara* (weeding) and *ṇa* (removal); thus, compassion is like weeding. Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is like extensively planting excellent seedlings, while compassion is like the act of weeding.
Because it weeds out the filth [of afflictions], this passage clarifies that compassion (*karuṇā*) simultaneously encompasses great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
For instance, when a practitioner performs an offering— whether presenting a single flower or applying fragrant ointments— they should, by means of the pure bodhicitta that pervades all places,
raise clouds of offerings to perform the Buddha-work universally, engendering the vow of compassion and dedicating the merit to all sentient beings to uproot every suffering.

Bestowing immeasurable bliss through the power of one's own roots of goodness and the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), all performed sublime deeds are brought to fulfillment;
thus, from the ground of universal omniscience down to the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, the roots of virtue are everywhere established.
Whatever myriad practices the practitioner cultivates with a mind free of doubt are, in fact, grounded in the stage of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Because it is sustained by the element of the Great Compassion-Earth, warmed and nurtured by the element of the Great Compassion-Fire, moistened by the element of the Great Compassion-Water,
brought forth and developed by the element of the Great Compassion-Wind, and unimpeded by the space of the Great Compassion; at that time,
immeasurable gateways of liberation spontaneously unfold, like a sprout, root, stem, branch, and leaf, successively adorned.
This is the meaning of the complete causal conditions for all mental phenomena (*cittadharma*).

"Skillful means as the ultimate" means that when the myriad practices are perfected and can no longer be increased, the provisional power that responds to sentient beings reaches its ultimate fulfillment of its function;
this is the sublime fruit of *amṛta* (clarified butter) and the source of the three secrets. Furthermore, the pure bodhicitta is like genuine gold, its fundamental nature being luminous and pure.
Free from all faults and afflictions, he practices great compassion like one training in the arts;

through various medicinal substances, he refines and tempers them until they become as clear as a mirror, supple, and pliable, such that his skillful means are mastered and whatever he creates is accomplished according to his will.
Because his craftsmanship and mastery exceed all other artisans, the subtlety of his attained realization is difficult to fathom.
Bestowing [the teachings] upon others is as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*:
the six perfections, the eighteen emptinesses, the gateways of samādhi, the path-factors, the dhāraṇīs, and so forth—all enter into the category of great compassion.

The fruit of all-knowledge-wisdom (*sarvajñājñāna*), which is accomplished through those myriad practices, is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*). Because one possesses expedient means internally, the activity of expedient means is precisely the benefiting of others.

Because the *upāya* (means) is the Brahma-sound, it is also named "Initiation" (*prasthāna*). It is so named because, just as a fruit arises from a seed and that fruit in turn becomes a seed, [the means and the goal are mutually inclusive].
The Sūtra says: "O Lord of Secrets, what is bodhi? It is the knowledge of one's own mind as it truly is. This is the revelation of suchness.
This is coming to the place where the jewels of merit are found. It is like a person who, though hearing of a treasure trove, resolves to seek it diligently;
yet if they do not know its location, there is no way to proceed toward it. Therefore, he points it out again, saying:
"Regarding the aforementioned foremost, most profound, and subtle Dharma, up to the point that 'no one who is not an omniscient person can understand it'—from where is this Dharma obtained?"
This refers to the practitioner’s own mind; if one can observe it as it truly is and realize it with perfect clarity, this is called the accomplishment of Bodhi.
In reality, it is not realized through another nor obtained from another. Question:
If the mind itself is the Way, why do sentient beings cycle through birth and death and fail to attain Buddhahood? Answer: It is because they do not know it as it truly is.
If foolish, ignorant worldlings hear this Dharma, few are able to believe it; even though those of the Two Vehicles observe for themselves, they do not know it as it truly is.
If one knows it as it truly is, then at the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening.
It is like the impoverished son of an elder: if he recognizes his father, how could he still be a lowly hired laborer?

At that time, because the practitioner correctly knows the true mark of the mind, they see that all phenomena are entirely profound, subtle, immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, unmoving, non-reliant, non-attached, and ultimately unobtainable, being identical to the mark of Bodhi.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "O Lord of Secrets, this is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."

It has already been explained that there is not even a slight portion of that dharma to be found which constitutes the meaning of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Here, the term "slight portion" is rendered in Sanskrit as *anu*, which refers to the atom (*paramāṇu*) composed of seven subtle particles;
it is used as a metaphor because it is the most minute among all forms produced from conditions. As for the phrase "that dharma," it refers to this signless (*animitta*) bodhi.
Focus the mind [on this]: externally there is not a single dharma. The Sūtra next explains the causal conditions, saying: "Why is it that the characteristic of space is bodhi?
Because there is neither one who knows nor one who understands, and there is no one who can explain it. Why? Because bodhi is without characteristics (*animitta*).
It is, for example, like space, which pervades all places; because it is ultimately pure, it is free from all characteristics and is immovable."
Because it is non-conceptual, immutable, and indestructible— possessing such partial resemblances as these—

it is used as a metaphor for the signless bodhicitta; yet herein there are further immeasurable and boundless secret and profound realities that cannot be fully illustrated by the worldly void, and thus we hope that all students will grasp the meaning and forget the vessel.

The ear is also like space, for it is far removed from conceptual proliferation and discrimination; thus, it has no characteristic of knowing or understanding, nor any characteristic of being enlightened.
One should know that the self-realization of *sambodhi* by all Buddhas is likewise so: it is solely the mind’s self-realization of the mind, the mind’s self-awakening of the mind.
Within this, there is no dharma of knowing or understanding, no knower or understander; it is neither something first made known nor is there anything that makes it known.

If one discriminates between the subtle aspects of subject and object as being like motes of dust, then one is grasping at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) rather than the absence of such characteristics (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*);
as long as one does not depart from the notions of self, person, sentient being, or life-span, how can this be called "Vajra-wisdom"?
Furthermore, the Sūtra itself provides its own explanation, saying: "Why is this? Because Bodhi is without characteristics. As the Śāstra states: "The Buddha’s wisdom is pure..."
Because it is pure, it transcends all meditative observations; one does not observe the marks of permanence or impermanence in phenomena,
nor the marks of finitude or infinitude, nor the marks of going or not going, nor the marks of existence or non-existence, nor the marks of outflow or non-outflow,

nor the marks of conditioned or unconditioned, nor the marks of arising-and-ceasing or non-arising-and-non-ceasing, nor the marks of emptiness or non-emptiness— [but rather] they are eternally pure and immeasurable.
Because it is like space, the Buddha’s wisdom is unimpeded. Those who contemplate arising and ceasing cannot contemplate non-arising and non-ceasing;
those who contemplate non-arising and non-ceasing cannot contemplate arising and ceasing. If arising and ceasing were real, non-arising and non-ceasing would not be real;
if non-arising and non-ceasing were real, arising and ceasing would not be real. All such contemplations are likewise so. By means of such purity...
The bodhicitta transcends all contemplations because it is free from all marks; thus, regarding all phenomena, it attains non-obstruction.
It is like the characteristic of space: while it is itself without characteristics, all myriad forms rely upon it, yet space itself has nothing upon which to rely.
In this way, all phenomena rely upon the pure mind, yet the pure mind itself has nothing upon which to rely; these very phenomena are likewise so.

This characteristic of bodhi is what is called the characteristic of pure space; thus the Sūtra further states: "Lord of Mysteries, all phenomena are without characteristics, which means they have the characteristic of space.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, who seeks omniscience? Who is for the sake of bodhi?"
"Who is it that attains perfect enlightenment? Who initiates that omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*)? The Buddha said:
"Lord of Secrets, seek bodhi and omniscience within your own mind. Why is this? Because its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is pure;
thus, even immeasurable merits are all fully accomplished. At that time, Vajrapāṇi, having heard the meaning of what the Buddha had spoken, [realized] that omniscient wisdom is indeed...
From this mind itself, not even the slightest phenomenon exists that transcends it. For the sake of severing the doubts of future sentient beings, he asked the Buddha:

"If the bodhicitta is defined as that which is single-mindedly intent upon seeking all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), and if all-knowledge is indeed the bodhicitta, then within this, who is the seeker and what is the object sought?"
"To whom can awakening belong, and who is the awakener? Furthermore, apart from the mind, there is not a single dharma that exists;

who then could initiate this mind and cause it to reach the sublime fruit? If any dharma could be established without causes and conditions, then all sentient beings should likewise attain Buddhahood spontaneously, without relying on skillful means. Therefore, the Buddha replied: "Lord of Mysteries, it is one's own mind."
One seeks awakening and omniscience because their intrinsic nature is pure.
Although the true reality (*dharmatā*) of sentient beings' own minds is itself awakening—remaining eternally and naturally adorned whether a Buddha appears or not—they fail to know it as it truly is;
this constitutes ignorance (*avidyā*). Because of this ignorance, they erroneously grasp at signs, which gives rise to craving and all other afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because of afflictions (*kleśa*), one gives rise to various karmas, enters various paths, and obtains various bodies, thereby experiencing various sufferings and pleasures.
It is like a silkworm producing silk: without any external cause, it emerges from itself and then entangles itself. It undergoes the suffering of being scorched and boiled;
for example, in the human world, pure water is perceived by devas and ghosts according to their own minds—some take it to be a jewel, while others take it to be fire.
One should know that the mind perceives suffering and pleasure through these [conditions]; apart from the mind, no phenomena exist.
If a practitioner of yoga correctly contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of these three dharmas, this is precisely seeing the true reality of the mind.

The true reality of the mind is the signless (*animitta*) bodhi, also called the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). Although it is free from all causes and conditions, it is not without cause.

This constitutes attainment. Furthermore, World-Honored One, because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know their own minds as they truly are, he further employs skillful means to analyze and explain them.
Why is this so? If one were to say merely that the mind is neither born nor extinguished because it lacks a cause, the meaning would be difficult to understand;
therefore, he first indicates the locus of attachment by stating that the mind does not abide within.
The six sense bases do not exist externally, nor in between the two; the mind cannot be apprehended.

Just as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* enters into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena through immeasurable gateways, I now wish to set forth its essential core: by simply observing the twelve internal and external bases (*āyatana*), one encompasses all phenomena.
Since beginningless time, practitioners have for the most part been attached to the mental characteristics of internal phenomena.

Therefore, first, regarding the six internal sense bases (*adhyātma-ṣaḍāyatana*), one should use skillful means such as the characteristics of identity and difference to contemplate each one with precise discernment (*satya-darśana*).
One finds that the mind is unapprehendable—unborn, signless, and without location—and thus forms this thought: "Could this mind perhaps exist externally?
Then, one contemplates the six external sense bases (*bāhya-ṣaḍāyatana*) according to reality; there too, the mind is likewise unborn, signless, and without location. Just so...
Fearing further error, one should observe that which lies between the two; it cannot be apprehended there either.

Thus, one awakens to the fact that the true nature of this mind is fundamentally without birth or cessation, ultimately and eternally pure. When the clouds of conceptual proliferation are dispelled, it is like the power of a jewel:
because the water becomes clear, the jewel appears. This clarity certainly does not come from any other place.
The Sūtra states: "O Guhyapati, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither blue, nor yellow, nor red, nor white, nor crimson, nor purple, nor the color of crystal;
he is neither long, nor short, nor round, nor square; he is neither luminous, nor dark; he is neither male, nor female, nor neuter.
The preceding section clarified that the mind’s true reality (*dharmatā*) is not any phenomenon (*dharma*); now, furthermore—

In defining the true nature of the mind through the perspective of the *tathāgatagarbha*, this school establishes its doctrine by taking the mind itself to be the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyak-saṃbuddha—namely, the "Great Self" (*mahātman*) within. For instance, there is a class of non-Buddhists who, failing to understand their own minds, speak thus:
"I perceive the True Self, whose color is a pure blue, which others cannot see," or they say: [and so forth].
Some say it is bright yellow or bright red; others say it is pure white or the color of *yan-zhi* (safflower)—in the current terminology, this refers to crimson or purple.
Others say, "I see the true self; its characteristics are extremely short, even resembling the physical features of a man, and only this is real while all else is false.
However, these various characteristics all arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). How [could they be real]?
In response to such various attachments as the notion that there exists a "true self," the Buddha taught that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is not blue and so forth.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of blue is ultimately non-arising, he is therefore not blue;
yet, because the true characteristic of blue is indestructible, he is also not non-blue. One should know that this is the case for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
There is no fixed characteristic that can be described, yet it is not separate from such characteristics either.
It is like when a non-Buddhist teacher leads his disciples before a great elephant on a dark night and tells them, "I shall now show you the true self.
At that time, some among the people observe it with their eyes, while others touch it with their bodies; they gaze upon its form.
When it touches its head, it says, "I have now recognized my true self; its color is exceedingly white, and it is towering and vast.

When it touches its tusks, it says, "My true self is like a halberd. When it touches its ears, it says, "It is like a winnowing basket. When it touches its feet, it says, "It is like a pillar. When it touches its tail, it says, "It is like a rope.
Each, according to what it encounters, forms a different conceptualization based on its own feelings, even as they continue to interact with one another.

Such people will ultimately never be able to recognize its true essence. However, when a practitioner of yoga develops the luminosity of the mind and perceives the Tathāgata who is the sovereign of the mind—
just as one sees various forms with one's own eyes in great light— they will not give rise to such disputes.
Next, it says: "O Lord of Mysteries, this mind does not share the same nature as the desire realm; it does not share the same nature as the form realm;
it does not share the same nature as the formless realm; nor does it share the same nature as the destinies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, up to humans and non-humans.
This is also said in order to demonstrate to those with false attachments that one's own mind is immutable, stating that this mind does not share the same nature as the three realms.

Furthermore, there are various non-Buddhists who reckon that the nature of the self is identical to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, even claiming that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is itself nirvāṇa; or they say that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and other such deities give rise to all phenomena.
Yet, since these three realms are all produced from a multitude of conditions, their own intrinsic nature cannot be found at all—how much less so [for the self]?

Is it that the nature of the mind is made identical to that nature? Next, if one were to analyze and describe in detail each of the infinite realms of sentient beings, none would possess a nature identical to that [of the rain];

it is like the rain of the eight meritorious qualities falling from the sky, which is of a single uniform, pure taste, yet appears as various differences according to the vessels that receive it—whether bitter, sour, warm, or [so forth].

Although turbid, the nature of the eight meritorious qualities does not become identical to that turbidity; when the turbidity subsides, it remains as cool and refreshing as before, never undergoing change.

Furthermore, just as a *cintāmaṇi* jewel has no fixed color of its own but takes on the color of whatever object it encounters, yet the nature of the jewel does not become identical to that object—if their natures were identical, then at the time when the color arises and ceases according to conditions, the nature of the jewel would likewise [arise and cease].

It should arise and cease. Furthermore, because the World-Honored One intends to reveal the Maṇḍala of the Birth from the Womb of Great Compassion, he first correctly reveals the gateway to the true reality (*tattva*) of the mind. Why is this?

It is because, as stated in the *Samādhi of the Practitioner’s Honored Deity*, there are manifested forms such as male and female, as well as bodies manifesting universally throughout the six realms of existence; fearing that [these might be misunderstood as literal], [he clarifies the true nature].
Because practitioners do not understand that the mind arises through causes and conditions, they give rise to conceptual proliferation regarding the true nature of the Jewel King.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "The Tathāgata is neither blue nor yellow," and so forth, up to: "This mind does not share the same nature as the three realms or the six destinies.
If one can observe in this way, it will not obstruct the bodhicitta.
The Sūtra further states: "O Lord of Mysteries, the mind does not abide in the eye-element, nor does it abide in the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;

it is neither seeing nor manifest. Since it was previously stated that the non-abiding of the mind within the three locations already encompasses all phenomena, for those who have not yet realized this, one again analyzes each phenomenon individually:
if the mind does not share the same nature as the various realms of existence, it is said to abide in the eye-element.

Whether it be the perversion of dharmas up to the perversion of abiding in the mind-element (*manodhātu*), if the mind were to abide in the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), then because the eye arises from a multitude of conditions, its nature and characteristics are inherently empty and have no place of abiding; how much less could the true characteristic of the mind abide within the eye?

This should be explained in detail for the eye-element as well as for all dharmas, including the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*). Furthermore, various non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) have already been refuted previously.
Now, the teaching that all phenomena do not abide is for the purpose of destroying the extreme views of the Śrāvakas; as it is said in the *Vātsīputrīya Abhidharma*:
"For example, just as there is the phenomenon of the eye when the four great elements are combined, so too there is the phenomenon of a person when the five aggregates are combined.

This phenomenon of a person is said to exist within the "Ineffable Treasury" (*avaktavyakośa*). The followers of the Sarvāstivāda school say: "The self (*ātman*) and the person (*pudgala*) are among all phenomena."
It cannot be found when sought within the gates [of the senses], like the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise—perpetually non-existent.

Yet the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are said to possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because of such conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one does not recognize the mind.

If one can contemplate the mind so that it does not dwell upon any phenomena, then the mind has no place of movement and all conceptual proliferation is exhausted. That which is neither seen nor manifested is as someone might say:
All sentient beings inherently possess the nature of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is only when the cataracts of ignorance are removed that they can spontaneously perceive the principle.
Some may say that such an eternal principle cannot be contrived, but rather that when the clouds and mists of the aggregates are cleared away, the solar orb naturally appears.
All of this is spoken from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If the pure bodhicitta were something visible...
The phenomena that appear are characterized by signs; whatever possesses signs is entirely false and illusory. How, then, can one perceive unsurpassed bodhi?
Furthermore, the Sūtra itself explains the causes and conditions: Why is this so?
Because the nature of the mind is like space, free from all false attachments and devoid of conceptual discrimination; it is ultimately pure like space, such that no forms or images can defile it.
The nature of the mind is likewise: no conceptual discrimination whatsoever can defile it. If there is no conceptual discrimination, this is precisely to be free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
As the Sūtra says: "Why is this so? Because its nature is identical to empty space, it is identical to the nature of the mind; being identical to the mind, it is identical [to all things]."
Such is Bodhi, O Lord of Mysteries: the mind, the realm of empty space, and Bodhi—these three are non-dual.
With great compassion as their fundamental basis, those who have fulfilled the *pāramitās* of skillful means enter through various such gates of purity;
all these serve to illuminate the meaning of seeking Bodhi within one’s own mind. Now, to conclude: that which is the stainless void is precisely this.
Mind and mind are themselves the fundamental nature of bodhi; they share a single characteristic and possess only three names.
This very dharma-realm mind, although ultimately unborn due to causes and conditions, does not destroy the true reality of causes and conditions.
Because it is unborn, there is no distinction between subject and object; because it is indestructible, it also takes great compassion as its fundamental skillful means (upāya-pāramitā).
The fulfillment of honey is precisely the meaning of the ultimate, inconceivable Middle Way.
The Sūtra says: "O Secret Lord, I have taught all dharmas in this manner so that those bodhisattvas may purify their bodhicitta and recognize that mind.
Thus, the Buddha has already revealed the pure bodhicitta by briefly clarifying three phrases.

The section on the school is concluded. Thus, the entire treatise from beginning to end teaches immeasurable skillful means solely for the purpose of purifying the bodhicitta of all bodhisattvas and making their minds like those described in this sutra.
One should know that the intent of all sūtras is contained herein, just as the Dharma taught by Śākyamuni Tathāgata;
one should know that [this applies to] all [teachings] throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The Tathāgata’s various explanations given through diverse causes and conditions according to what is appropriate are none other than for the sake of this dharma-gate of three phrases;
because they ultimately all return to the same point and do not diverge, he says: "I have taught all dharmas in this way," and so on, up to "knowing their minds."
The Sūtra says: "O Lord of Mysteries, how does one know one's own mind? It is when, whether it be a discrete portion, a manifest color, or a shape;
whether it be an object, or form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; whether it be 'self' or 'what belongs to self'; whether it be the grasper or the grasped;
whether it be purity, or the elements (*dhātu*), or the sense bases (*āyatana*)—if one seeks it among all such discrete portions and cannot find it."
The World-Honored One has already extensively explained the pure *bodhicitta* according to its true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

However, because sentient beings have not yet attained this mind, he employs skillful means to provide a provisional awakening and further explains this "sudden awakening to Buddhahood" as an entry into the gate of the mind’s true nature.

This is also for the purpose of definitively resolving all Buddha-dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Thus, as in various sutras, it is sometimes said that there are the aggregates (*skandhas*).

Within the synthesis [of conditions], a self cannot be found; or it is said that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature, thereby gradually opening the gateway to the true reality (*dharmatā*).
What is called the "true reality of all phenomena" is precisely the true reality of the mind in this sutra;
the true reality of the mind is itself Bodhi, and there is no other principle apart from this. It is merely for the sake of sentient beings with meager merit.
Yet they are unable to have self-confidence that they shall become Buddhas; for those who possess such self-confidence that they shall become Buddhas are exceedingly rare.

Therefore, the World-Honored One first causes them to purify their defilements and obstructions and protects their minds, requiring that the timing and the principle be in accord before he explains the seal of "the mind itself.
This present sutra, however, is not like that; it directly takes the various dharmas as its basis to cause one to recognize the mind. This is why [it is so].
This is a treasury of secret essentials. The first sentence states: "That which is called 'segmented' is a general enumeration of phenomena arising from conditions.
Because phenomena depend upon causes and conditions to be established, they necessarily possess distinct characteristics; therefore, the practitioner should observe them in this way.
Within these segments, what is the mind? When one analyzes and investigates in this manner, it is ultimately unfindable. Thus:

Knowing that this mind transcends all marks and is free from all causes and conditions—because one knows that the nature of the mind is always thus—at that time, all dharmas naturally do not differ from the mind.
"Manifest color" refers to blue, yellow, and so forth; "shape" refers to square, round, and so forth;
"objects" refer to that which is confronted by the six sense organs, namely the six dusts (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). This is for the sake of making it easy for people to understand.
Therefore, one should again examine the phenomena: among these manifest forms and various colors, which is the mind?
Since color itself is fundamentally insentient and lacks the characteristics of cognition, how much less could a mind be found within it, as if it were the manifest form itself?
One should know that all objects of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) are likewise; as with the objects of form, so it is for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*).

The practitioner finds that the mind cannot be apprehended within external objects; furthermore, they observe that the five aggregates of the internal body are likewise like a mass of foam, a bubble, a mirage, a plantain tree, or a magical illusion.
When seeking their essential reality, even these do not exist at all—how much less can there be a mind within them?
Thus, from the coarse to the subtle, and from the broad to the concise, one proceeds until even a single moment of present consciousness is no longer found.
Because that which has no abiding time also arises from various conditions, it is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way;

it is far removed from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and reaches the limit of original non-arising. The limit of original non-arising is the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*);
the intrinsically pure mind is the gateway of the letter A (*akāra-mukha*). Since one enters the gateway of the letter A by means of the mind, one should know that [all things] are one.
All phenomena entirely enter the gateway of the letter A. Having already explained the contemplation of the true nature of all phenomena, we next clarify the contemplation of the mark of self;

therefore it is said: whether it be "I" or "mine," whether it be the grasper or the grasped, or even purity—just as above, when one uses various skillful means to contemplate the mind within the aggregates, it cannot be found; how much less so can a self, a person, or a life-span be found?
These dharmas have, from the very beginning, existed only as provisional names;
yet within them, those who conceive of a mind that can attain purification take what the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) regard as the ultimate state of purity to be *nirvāṇa*.
Just as the brahmin Daṇḍin did not accept any phenomena but accepted this view, so too now one grasps at and adheres to the arising of wisdom through the contemplation of emptiness.

Through wisdom, one gives rise to this perception of purity; within this very perception, one correctly contemplates that one’s own mind has no place of origination, thereby attaining entry into the truly pure bodhicitta.

The above constitutes the extensive treatment of the five aggregates (*skandha*). Next, it further explains that within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and even throughout all segmented phenomena, the meaning of the aggregates, elements, and bases cannot be found upon investigation.
In the Abhidharma, these three dharmas are extensively explained as encompassing all phenomena.

Furthermore, the statement that "even when sought within all segmented [phenomena], they cannot be found" refers precisely to what is extensively clarified through the analysis of phenomena in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā and other texts.

For example, when one analyzes the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas) in search of the mind, the mind cannot be found; one should know that this applies likewise to the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
Even when seeking the mind in various ways throughout the ten thousand practices up to all the doors of *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi*, the mind cannot be apprehended;
because the mind cannot be apprehended, this mind’s characteristics of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as its lack of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, likewise cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, just as when a *śrāvaka* first contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), he seeks [the self] within the aggregates.
When one seeks the self apart from the aggregates (*skandha*), it is entirely unattainable; its characteristics and its location are likewise unattainable.
At that time, within the Eightfold Noble Path, the dust-free and stainless Eye of the True Dharma arises. It is the same for Bodhisattvas of the Mantra Gate:

when they first contemplate the aggregates, elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), they seek the mind within the aggregates and seek the mind apart from the aggregates, yet it is entirely unattainable; its characteristics and its location are likewise not found.
Because it can be attained, one immediately and intuitively awakens to the fact that the essence of one’s own mind is fundamentally non-arising;
within the Great Path of Bodhi—the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision—one becomes free from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.

If one does not employ such skillful means, but instead first observes from the standpoint of attachment and merely says that this mind pervades all places and is ultimately without marks, then [all]...
One should know that for sentient beings who have no other means to awaken and enter [the truth], this contemplation is the most secret and essential dharma-gate.

While other Bodhisattvas who employ various methods of seclusion gradually cultivate ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and contemplate the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—through manifold approaches over immeasurable eons, they are still unable to distance themselves from the mental images [of subject and object]. Now, however, through the practice of *mantra*...

When such a person, at the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, directly contemplates the true mark of their own mind and realizes that it is fundamentally unborn, human and dharma conceptual proliferations are immediately purified like space; they achieve spontaneous awakening without depending on the realization of another.
One should know that this contemplation is also called the "Dharma-gate of Sudden Awakening."
The Sūtra says: "O Lord of Mysteries, this gate of the Bodhisattva’s pure bodhicitta is called the Path of the First Illumination of Dharma.
A Bodhisattva dwelling in this state will, before long, attain the Samādhi that Removes All Veils and Obstructions.
Upon entering the wisdom of the Buddha, there are immeasurable gates of skillful means; however, in this school, one takes pure bodhicitta directly as the gate. If one enters this gate, then..."
This is the initial entry into the realm of all Tathāgatas, which is like Maitreya opening the door of the multi-storied pavilion for Sudhana within;
therein one fully beholds immeasurable and inconceivable matters that are difficult to describe in words, known only by those who have entered.
As for "Dharma-illumination" (*dharmāloka*), it is because one awakens to the fact that the mind is fundamentally unborn; its mind abides in purity and gives rise to the great light of wisdom.
Because it clearly and universally illuminates the infinite *dharmatā* and perceives the path practiced by all Buddhas, it is called the "Path of Dharma-illumination" (*dharmāloka-mārga*).
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this path, all afflictions, karma, and suffering arising from the conditions of false conceptualization are entirely purified, eliminated, and extinguished.
It is like a person who, while in the dark, is wounded by a precious gem and, mistaking it for snake venom, applies poison [to the wound].
Because of this perception, his mind becomes attached and it turns into a poisonous vapor that pervades his limbs.
When he is on the verge of death, a skilled physician examines him, understands the root and the branches of the ailment, and immediately leads him to the site of the wound.
Shining a bright lamp upon it, he sees that the precious jewel which was wounded still bears traces of blood. The man realizes that it is not poison, and the poisonous vapor is thereby dispelled.
Just as one finds joy and delight in various playthings, so too it is with the practitioner:
because they illuminate all phenomena through the pure bodhicitta, they exert little effort yet attain the samādhi that removes hindrances;

by perceiving the true nature of the eighty-four thousand afflictions, they accomplish the eighty-four thousand gates of the treasury of jewels. Therefore, the sutra continues: "The Bodhisattva dwells herein."
If one practices for a short time with diligence, one shall immediately attain the Samādhi that Eliminates All Obstructions and Veils (*Sarvāvaraṇanīvaraṇaviśodhana-samādhi*).
One who attains this dwells on an equal footing with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Within this, there are five kinds of obstructions:

the first is the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which refers to the root afflictions up to the eighty-four thousand grades of superior, middling, and inferior obstructions and veils that hinder the pure mind and arise from...
First, because of habitual tendencies from past lives, they obstruct the capacity for the Way and do not enter the Buddha-dharma. Second, regarding karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*):
this refers to having committed various grave offenses in past and present lives, even to the point of slandering the Vaipulya sutras.

Although such persons possess the causal conditions for attaining the Way, because their prior karmic obstructions have not been eliminated, they encounter various hindrances and do not enter the Buddha-dharma. Third, birth...
The obstacle refers to a person who, had they obtained a superior birthplace free from difficulties, would certainly have awakened to the Way;

however, due to prior karma, they instead receive a body lacking leisure, and thus their very birth serves as an obstacle that prevents them from entering the Buddha-dharma. Fourth is the obstacle of the Dharma:
this refers to a person who has already obtained a birthplace free from obstacles and possesses the potential for awakening to the Way, yet because of [karma] from previous lives...
Fifth is the obscuration of the objects of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):

this refers to a person who, although they have already encountered a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and heard the true Dharma, encounters various causes and conditions such that the two do not harmonize, thereby obstructing the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Deeds of Māra" (*Mārakarmaparivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, it is because in a previous life one may have obstructed the spiritual faculties of others that this hindrance arises with such ease.

Once the practitioner has attained the samādhi of the five purified hindrances, they will constantly perceive the wondrous marks of all Buddhas of the ten directions within their own mind, as vividly as looking into a clear mirror;
even during all postures—whether walking, coming, sleeping, or waking—they shall never [be separated from this vision].

When separated from such causes and conditions of the Buddha’s assembly, the various sages constantly use supreme and wondrous skillful means to awaken their minds, comforting and exhorting them with Brahma-sounds to resolve the net of doubts.
As the practitioner follows each gate and attains awakening, once awakened, the obstacles of the net are removed accordingly;
thus, before long, they accomplish all Buddha-dharmas. Therefore it is said: "If one attains this samādhi, then one is immediately [equal] to all..."
One should know that when a practitioner dwells equally with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they are in a stage identical to Great Awakening (*mahābodhi*).
Because they have awakened their own minds, they receive the name "Buddha"; yet, this is not yet the ultimate stage of Wondrous Awakening (*atyanta-abhisambodhi*) of the Great Muni.
It is like the pure moon: although its essence neither increases nor decreases, its brightness still gradually waxes until it is only on the fifteenth day that it reaches fullness.

It is like stirring the tides of the great ocean. Furthermore, when a practitioner dwells in the same state of equanimity as the Tathāgata, they are able, through the power of skillful means, to give rise to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) without wavering from their fundamental mind.
They travel to the various Buddha-fields, manifesting diverse bodies and engaging in various acts of speech and mind, raising clouds of manifold offerings.
By means of inexhaustible great vows, they extensively cultivate the perfections (*pāramitā*), further purified by the faculty of the mind (*manas-indriya*).
Therefore, next, one attains the various *dhāraṇīs* for understanding immeasurable languages and sounds. For example, within a single world-system, there are thirty-six *koṭis* of destinies (*gati*);
according to their respective superior, middling, and inferior natures and species, there are various local dialects, each distinct.
One understands the purport of them all and employs the appropriate language for each type. As it is with one world-system, so it is with others.
All worlds are likewise so. In the Sanskrit original, *ruta* means "great sound" and *aruta* means "small sound";
*nirghoṣa* refers to a long sound as well as multiple sounds. Thus, these terms are stated in full to reveal that the realm of *dhāraṇī* understands everything without exception.
Because it is difficult to fully translate this into the written characters of this region, [the text] says: "Because one has attained *dhāraṇī*..."
Because of the *dhāraṇī*, one is able to know the mental activities of all sentient beings;

that is to say, one knows that such-and-such a sentient being has a predominance of hatred while their nature of greed is thin, or that such-and-such a sentient being has a predominance of greed while their nature of hatred is thin, and so forth, including the infinite distinctions between the signs of openness and obstruction as extensively explained in the *Śāstra* (Treatise) within the section on the Knowledge of the Paths (*mārgajñatā*). This is not [the case for] the Bodhisattva.
However, the mental faculty (*manas*) is able to perceive [all objects], and even seeing, hearing, smelling, and touching are all mutually employed without obstruction.

Furthermore, one can observe those faculties and their conditions to eliminate hindrances and obstructions; by means of various skillful methods, one brings sentient beings to maturity, adorns Buddha-fields, and performs the deeds of a Tathāgata.
It should be known that practitioners of the Mantra Gate can achieve these accomplishments within a single lifetime.
Furthermore, all sentient beings equally possess, according to their own nature, all the aforementioned virtues;
yet, because they are obscured by the veil of ignorance, they do not realize them for themselves and are unable to manifest such secret power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*).
Now, these bodhisattvas practicing through the gateway of mantras perceive the light of the Dharma.
Because of this path, one immediately attains the samādhi that removes all hindrances and obstructions;

by attaining this samādhi, one is able to dwell together with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and give rise to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). By means of these five supernormal powers, one attains the dhāraṇī of the languages of all sentient beings;
by attaining this dhāraṇī, one is able to know the mental activities of all sentient beings.
Because one performs Buddha-works by being able to extensively carry out such works so as not to sever the lineage of the Tathāgatas,
one is at all times and in all places constantly protected and sustained by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Just as parents’ affection for a newborn infant is exceptionally deep and they never abandon it, one should know that these various phrases are all connected in successive order.
Furthermore, the practitioner, having internally possessed the aforementioned merits and being externally sustained by the protection of all Buddhas,
dwells within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) without defilement or attachment. Just as a lotus flower emerges from the water and is not stained by the mud,
they constantly employ the skillful means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to uproot suffering sentient beings, even unto immeasurable and boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
For *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they constantly remain within the Avīci hell, their physical and mental vigor blazing forth without ceasing, never falling back or succumbing to weariness.
Why is this? Because the nature of the pure bodhicitta is inherently like a vajra;
such extreme solidity is itself the attainment of the unconditioned precepts (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*) without reliance on a teacher—stainless and unturbid.
Regarding the precept that cannot be broken or injured, the Sanskrit term is *śīla*, which carries the meaning of "coolness" or "purity. For example, the nature of water is always cool;
although it may scorch and rot various objects when encountering the conditions of fuel and fire, its own intrinsic nature can never be altered.
Once the fuel is removed and the fire extinguished, it naturally returns to its original state of coolness. In the same way, the practitioner of *mantra* conduct likewise attains this.
At the time of the Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin-samādhi, the fundamental nature of the mind is itself śīla (ethical discipline).

Because it is not a conditioned phenomenon produced by effort and is not obtained from another, it is said that one "abides in unconditioned śīla. For instance, the pure śīla of a śrāvaka must arise only when the conditions—such as the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion and three proclamations)—are fully assembled;
furthermore, it must be guarded through skillful means like one would ward off a sharp thorn for the duration of a single lifetime.

When one's life-span ends, the precepts likewise perish; however, these precepts are not like that. They are born together with one in every successive place of rebirth, requiring no formal reception or maintenance, and are never subject to transgression.
Furthermore, by abiding in these precepts, true wisdom increases and becomes luminous, leading to the vision of the inconceivable, profound Middle Way of dependent origination.
Because it restrains the eight inversions and remains far removed from the two extremes, [it is so called]. Thus says the Sūtra:
Next, it says: "To be far removed from wrong views and to penetrate right view.
Kāśyapa also said: "Prior to this, we were all called people of wrong views. In this context, because wisdom is not correct, it is termed "wrong view.

This is because ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are unable to discern and correctly know the true nature of their own minds; regarding the principle of ultimate reality, they even hold [wrong conceptions] concerning emptiness.

Neither empty nor non-empty, this is called emptiness. Not seeing the path of great enlightenment traversed by the Buddhas of the past, this bodhisattva now, through the illumination of the mind that perceives the Way, immediately gives rise to unimpeded wisdom.
All dharmas manifest before them, and they penetrate them without error, just as one with clear vision beholds all manner of things within the sunlight.

Although the various forms [of Mara] are immeasurable, and all the celestial Māras transform themselves into the bodies of Buddhas, each preaching a semblance of the pāramitās, they are ultimately unable to disturb even a fraction of his mind’s web of doubt. Therefore, the sutra continues:
"Furthermore, O Guhyakādhipati, by the power of faith and understanding of this Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, he will before long, through diligent practice, fulfill one..."
All Buddha-dharmas, through such right view which is like a vajra, constitute the supreme power of firm faith and understanding;

by relying on this to practice and progress with skillful means according to reality, one attains the powers, fearlessnesses, liberations, samādhis, and all other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, fully accomplishing them all.
Nāgārjuna considered this to be like a metal-smelter using various [metals].

Just as various skillful means are used to melt away ore and stone before it becomes gold, so too can those with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) cause substances such as earth and wood to immediately become the substance of gold.
Therefore, it is said that by diligently practicing for no long time, one will soon attain fulfillment;
thus, from the very moment a Bodhisattva first resolves their mind [on enlightenment], they are called a Buddha. Their true merits are immeasurable; even if a Tathāgata were to—
Because even if one were to analyze and expound upon it for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas, one could never exhaust it, the Buddha said:
"To state the essential point, these good sons and good daughters have fully accomplished immeasurable merits."
Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra, Fascicle One.
