The nature of this mind is also like this: whatever thoughts one contemplates or whatever matters one pursues, whether wholesome or unwholesome, they are all profound and far-reaching.
They all desire that others be unable to fathom them; even when living together or working in tandem, they do not recognize their mental conduct.
One should know that this is the "well-like mind. The Dharma-gate of dependent origination and the characteristics of virtuous persons are both clearly manifest and easy to understand;
these are its antidotes. Twenty-sixth: What is the guarding of the mind? It means that only this mind is real, while other minds are unreal.

Just as worldly people, for the sake of protecting their own bodies, wealth, and so forth, employ various defenses such as surrounding walls and multi-storied towers to prevent others from causing them harm,
this mind is likewise constantly guarding the body and mind— just like a tortoise withdrawing its six limbs—
so that they are not harmed by external objects; it considers only this activity to be real, while regarding all other conditioned things as unreal.
All such endeavors are unreal; those who study the Śrāvaka vehicle often give rise to this mind. Furthermore, it is that which is countered by the protection of others:

there are those who preserve their own understanding and do not wish for it to be harmed by the various divergent arguments of others, asserting that all other views are entirely unreal—this is also [an example]. Twenty-seventh: What is the stingy mind? It is said:
To act for one's own sake while not giving the Dharma to others means that whatever this person does is entirely for their own benefit;
they are fond of concealing their wealth, arts, and even wholesome dharmas, rather than bestowing them upon others.

One who possesses these characteristics is known to have a mind of stinginess (*mātsarya*). As an antidote to this, one should constantly maintain mindfulness of generosity and impermanence (*anityatā*).
Regarding wealth, skills, and abilities, when the time of impermanence arrives, there is nothing that follows one into the afterlife;
yet this present body cannot be preserved for even a single moment—how can one begrudge it? (28) What is the "cat-like mind"?
It refers to those who practice the method of gradual progress: like a cat stalking birds, they remain still and silent, waiting their opportunity, rather than striving for rapid advancement.
It is like waiting until one has crossed within the boundary before finally taking [the prize]; such is also the case with this person.

Upon encountering various essential teachings, they merely receive them with their mind and memorize them, yet they do not put them into practice, hoping instead for the convergence of favorable conditions before they might courageously and diligently apply them.

Furthermore, it is like a cat or a wildcat that receives all manner of compassionate care, yet does not recognize its debt of gratitude; so too is it with a person who merely receives [the teachings].
To practice compassion, kindness, and kind speech toward others without thinking of receiving anything in return is also the "cat-like mind.

To act immediately upon hearing the teaching without waiting for the right time or place, while constantly dwelling on the debt of gratitude, is the remedy for this [the cat-like mind]. (29) What is the "dog-like mind"?

It refers to being satisfied with obtaining only a small portion, just as a dog, due to the causes and conditions of its meager merit, encounters only that which is inferior because of its lowly expectations. (30)

When one obtains even a small amount of coarse and inferior food and gives rise to contentment, yet considers anything slightly exceeding this to be beyond what was originally expected—this mind is likewise so.
Upon hearing only a small portion of the sublime Dharma, one takes it as sufficient practice and no longer seeks superior matters;
this arises from the habitual tendencies of the Śrāvaka lineage. It takes the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) as its counteragent.
The thirty-first [practice] is to treat even the mind like the great ocean—neither rejecting the small nor overflowing with the much.
What is the "garuḍa-mind"? It refers to one who accords with those who possess the wings of the Dharma.

Just as this bird always relies upon its two wings to support its body, moving wherever it wills and thereby achieving great power, yet if it lacks even a single feather, it is rendered incapable of action.
This mind is also like this: it constantly seeks to gain many companions and supporters to assist one another in accomplishing its task.

Furthermore, it gives rise to the resolve only after observing the deeds of others; it cannot advance alone. Just as when seeing someone else practicing virtue, one thinks, "If they can do this, why should I not?
One should then contemplate the courageous and robust bodhicitta, which, like a lion king, does not rely on others.
The thirty-first [topic], the mental associate that is the object of opposition: What is the "rat-like mind"? It refers to one who contemplates severing all fetters;

yet, like a rat that sees another's chest or basket tied with ropes and immediately and improperly destroys it, without even thinking, "By severing this, may I obtain such benefit," but simply acts without purpose—such a mind is also [the object of opposition].
Whatever attachments and accomplishments he may have, he seeks out their vulnerabilities to thwart and destroy them.
(32) What is the "chanting mind"? [The Sanskrit text is missing; it is not explained. The Ācārya says: This metaphor refers to the transmission of the sound of the Dharma.
It is like a worldly person who, having mastered the art of adapting melodies from others, subsequently performs them for others. From this... [text continues].
Various exquisite sounds bring joy to those who hear them; yet this mind desires to listen to the True Dharma from others.
I shall, for the sake of sentient beings, analyze and expound it using various phrases and expressions, so that these wondrous sounds may be heard and known everywhere.
Such attachment to sound is a habituation from past lives as a śrāvaka and can also obstruct the pure mind. One should reflect: "I shall..."
Only after attaining the wisdom of internal realization of spontaneity does one universally manifest the form-body (*rūpakāya*) to expound it;

this is the thirty-third counteractive measure. What is meant by "a dancing mind"? It refers to practicing such dharmas with the thought, "I shall ascend and display various supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
Just as when a person's limbs move about and disperse it is called "dancing," so too are these supernatural transformations manifested.

Various unprecedented events that cause the minds of those before you to become pure and their eyes to rejoice are mostly the residual habits of those who possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

If one is biased toward such methods for attaining *siddhi* and pursues them with longing, this will also obstruct the pure mind. One should instead contemplate the Samādhi of Removing Obstacles (*Sarvāvaraṇaviṣkambhin*), maintaining a mind free from distraction and movement;

without giving rise to supernatural powers, one should perform empowerments and miraculous transformations while remaining within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Do not [act otherwise].
Craving for minor worldly attainments is the thirty-fourth [hindrance] to be countered. What is the "drum-beating mind"?
It means that one who accords with this Dharma thinks, "I shall beat the drum of the Dharma. The drum can admonish sentient beings and cause them to attain awakening.
If a practitioner merely forms such a thought as, "Sentient beings have been in a state of long-night slumber; I shall practice various unimpeded [knowledges]," [this is the drum-beating mind].
To strike the great Dharma drum with eloquence in order to awaken others can also obstruct the pure mind.
One should therefore resolve to quickly realize the *dhāraṇī* of immeasurable speech, using the wondrous sound of the celestial drum to universally proclaim [the Dharma] to all sentient beings;
do not allow minor worldly gains to hinder this great causal condition. This is the thirty-fifth counteractive measure. What is it?
The "dwelling-mind" refers to one who practices the method of protecting oneself in accordance with the teachings;
it is like a person who constructs a house to shelter their body, thereby escaping various harmful conditions such as cold, heat, wind, rain, thieves, and malicious insects. This mind is likewise:
"I shall maintain the precepts and cultivate goodness to protect myself, so that in this life and future lives I may remain far removed from the evil realms."

The abundance of various sufferings is the habituation of the śrāvakas; one should contemplate the rescue and protection of all sentient beings rather than focusing solely on oneself—this is the thirty-sixth [antidote] to be countered. What is the "lion-like mind"?
It refers to those who practice all dharmas without cowardice; like the lion king among all beasts, wherever they go, they are victorious and possess no fear.
The weakening of this mind is likewise so: in all matters, one desires to excel all people’s minds;
one is not timid or weak, considering that there is no difficult task and none who can compete with me to determine our relative superiority or inferiority.
If one realizes this for oneself, one should give rise to the mind of the Lion of the Śākyas, causing all sentient beings to be universally surpassed such that no one is superior or inferior.
Regarding the thirty-seventh [topic] to be countered: what is the "owl-like mind"? It refers to one who constantly contemplates in the dark of night.
This bird is incapable of acting during the great light of day, yet at night its six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) become sharp and clear.

Likewise, if a practitioner, though having heard, recited, and studied during the daytime, remains drowsy and confused and fails to attain skillfulness, then at night they will contemplate and recall those [teachings].
When performing a task, deliberate upon it repeatedly until it becomes clear; even when practicing meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*) and so forth, it is superior to do so in a dark place.

However, once one has become aware [of the surroundings], one should maintain equanimity toward both light and darkness, ensuring that the mental application (*manasikāra*) remains without distinction between day and night.
This is the counteractive measure. (38) What is the "crow-like mind"? It refers to being terrified in all circumstances.
Just as a crow or a bird that has been kindly approached and nourished by a person may,
at times, seek an opportunity to strike back, giving rise to a mind of mutual suspicion and fear— a nature that is always thus— so too is this mind:
even toward a good friend who wishes to benefit them, or even toward one who seeks to deceive them, it uniformly suspects and obstructs, harboring doubt and fear until the very end.
When practicing the precepts and cultivating goodness, one may still harbor a sense of fear and dread regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Once this is recognized, one should cultivate a mind of stability and fearlessness; this is the antidote [to that fear]. (39) What is the "rākṣasa-mind"?

It refers to initiating unwholesome states amidst wholesome ones—for example, when people perceive something as a virtuous act, they instead form an unwholesome interpretation of it. The Buddha taught that such constitutes the commission [of an offense].
While various stupas and shrines yield immeasurable merit, one might instead speak thus: "Because of this, countless small insects are needlessly harmed and distressed;
what benefit is there for the donor? They will surely suffer the retribution. Such unwholesome thoughts arise.
In this context, the remedy consists simply in contemplating the merit and benefits while not dwelling upon those faults.
Fortieth: What is meant by "pricking the heart"? It refers to one whose nature is to initiate unwholesome actions in all circumstances.
Just as a thicket of thorns causes much damage and obstruction in every place, making those who approach it feel uneasy, so too is this person's mind.
If they perform wholesome deeds, such as great acts of giving, they immediately give rise to a mind of regret once they have finished; yet if they commit evil, [they do not feel remorse].
When the task is finished, one again reflects upon it and feels shame and fear; therefore, one constantly harbors regret, with a restless mind and no peace.
The remedy for this is: if there is a transgression, one must swiftly strive to confess and eliminate it, without giving rise to agitation or remorse.
Regarding virtuous deeds performed, one should reflect upon them and give rise to a heart of rejoicing. (41) What is the "cave-like mind"? It refers to practicing in accordance [with the teachings].
Regarding the method for entering the caves: it is said that various *nāgas*, *asuras*, and others all reside in deep caves beneath the earth or at the bottom of the ocean.
Within these caves there are many *ṛṣis* and various medicinal herbs capable of bestowing long life and the attainment of sovereign mastery.

Alternatively, one may contemplate that within them there are many beautiful women, as upright and handsome as those in the heavens, such that there would be no anxiety regarding premature death, and one could indulge freely in the five desires. Or...
One should resolve to dwell therein so that one may attain a lifespan of an eon and behold all future Buddhas; this is the "cave-mind.
One should reflect that by practicing according to the Dharma, one may perceive the Path of Dharma-illumination in this very life and even attain Buddhahood;
one should not take detours or linger in hesitation. Remembering the methods of the sages of this world serves as their antidote. (42) What is wind?
The mind, which has the nature of arising and pervading all places, is of the nature of wind and is characterized by distraction because it does not abide;

thus this person’s mind is likewise pervasive in all places, planting roots of goodness everywhere—meaning they cause these roots to take part in the various celestial deities of worldly non-Buddhists as well as in the various practices of the Three Vehicles—and they form this thought: "It is like sowing many seeds."
One should know that when there is success in pervading all places, this is the "wind-mind. One should reflect that a stony field is barren and merely wastes seeds;
one should seek the excellent and fertile fields of merit as the place for cultivation, and by focusing the mind on plowing and tilling, what is harvested will surely be abundant.
This is its antidote. Forty-three: What is the "water-mind"? It refers to practicing purification in accordance with the Dharma.

That which washes away all unwholesome dharmas is like the nature of water, which is pure and clean; though it may be temporarily defiled by various impurities, it becomes clear when stirred, and furthermore, it can wash away filth and grime.
This mind is also like this: it constantly desires to reveal its defilements and evils and to repent for the various transgressions of the three karmas.
To perceive these defilements and this purity, and yet to think, "I am practicing in such a way," constitutes an obstacle.
Regarding the purification of the mind: one should simply contemplate the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the mind and realize that, from the very beginning, defiled phenomena have never arisen;
thus, one is naturally able to eliminate all veils and hindrances. This is the practice of their antidote. (44) What is the "fire-like" mind?
That which has the nature of being blazing and hot is like the nature of fire, which is brilliant and impetuous; this person's mind is also like this. When they perform wholesome deeds...
In an instant, one can accomplish immeasurable merit, yet even a small amount of evil can, in a short time, create extremely heavy karma.

Regarding this, one should contemplate the remedial practice: since a fierce and violent mind causes much ruin and injury, one should use the water of gentleness, kindness, and compassion as a skillful means to extinguish it;
furthermore, one should ensure that the practice of blazing virtues is made constant. This is the fourth remedy.
Fifteenth: What is the "mud-like mind"? (The Sanskrit original is missing; the Ācārya says this is not explained.

This refers to a state of mind characterized exclusively by ignorance (*avidyā*). Because one cannot even discern or remember immediate matters before one's eyes, the Vinaya says it is "like a lump of mud" or "like a muddy quagmire.
Because it is so soft and weak, it is difficult to cross over; one must therefore ensure there is a basis for doing so.
It is said that one can only cross over by means of relying upon bridges and the like;

likewise, if one realizes that this mind exists, one must rely upon virtuous friends to have it skillfully awakened, so that ignorance may gradually depart and the nature of wisdom may arise. (The forty-sixth [section asks]:
What is meant by "manifesting the color-mind"? It refers to those whose nature is categorized as such, for example, being dyed with colors such as blue, yellow, red, or white.
If white silk is dyed, it immediately takes on the same color; the mind of this person is also like this. Upon seeing or hearing wholesome dharmas, one acts accordingly;
upon seeing or hearing unwholesome matters, one likewise follows and trains therein; even with neutral matters, it is the same.

As the practitioner encounters various objects and shifts according to those circumstances, once they have become self-aware of this, they should mindfully and single-mindedly seek personal realization.
This Dharma is not realized through another, nor is it turned by external conditions; it is the antidote to that [fault].
(47) What is meant by "board-like mind"? It refers to practicing the Dharma according to one's capacity while abandoning other virtues.
For example, a wooden board in water can carry various objects only within its own limit; once that limit is exceeded, it can no longer support them and will eventually tip over and cast them away.

The mind of this person is also like this: having discerned wholesome dharmas and performed a single deed according to their own capacity, they immediately say, "From my ancestors until now, I have practiced only this dharma and knew nothing else," and so on, up to practicing the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*).
Thus, they do not abandon it nor do they aspire to practice other virtues, failing to give rise to a vast mind to train in the conduct of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*).
Regarding the forty-eighth [topic], the object of opposition: what is meant by "a deluded mind" where that which is grasped is different from that which is contemplated?
It is like a person who, being confused, intends to go east but instead goes west; this person's mind is likewise so.

They intend to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), yet they instead grasp at signs of purity and say to themselves, "I am now practicing the contemplation of impurity," or if they practice [the contemplation of] impermanence (*anityatā*).

When one is devoid of the notion of self, yet instead acts within the inversion of perceiving permanence and self, thinking, "I am now cultivating impermanence and non-self," this is caused by mental distraction.
To constantly maintain a single-pointed mind, observing with precision, composure, and without error, is the antidote to that.
(49) What is meant by "taking poison"? It refers to the mind’s practice in accordance with the factors of the dharma of non-arising.
"Poison" refers to the venom of dragons and snakes, medicinal herbs, and various other malevolent poisons.

Just as when a person is poisoned they become faint and lose consciousness, turning toward the realm of death with no prospect of rebirth, so too is this person's mind: neither wholesome nor unwholesome thoughts can arise, nor indeed can any state of mind whatsoever be produced;
it merely proceeds spontaneously, gradually entering into a state where there is neither cause nor effect.

Therefore, it is called the "Dharma of the Unarisen Portion. Once the practitioner has personally realized this, they should give rise to great compassion and all manner of wholesome qualities, remaining free from the emptiness of nihilistic annihilation;
this is the sublime medicine that counteracts what is to be remedied. (Fifty) What is the "Lasso Mind"?
It is defined as that which dwells everywhere within the bondage of the self. For example, it is like a person who has been bound by a lasso... [and so forth].
If one cannot move even a limb of the body, such as a hand or foot, this mind has thus fallen into the bondage of the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
This view can bind the practitioner’s mind, constantly constraining it in all circumstances so that it cannot emerge on its own;
it is the most grievous obstacle. Having recognized this, one should swiftly sever it with the sword of right wisdom regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The removal of hindrances and coverings is that which is to be counteracted. [Regarding] the fifty-first: What is the "fettered mind"?
That which has the nature of remaining stationary on two feet is called *nigada*. That which is on the hands is called *kholā*, and that which is on the feet is called *nigada*.

Just as when a person is constrained by shackles, their two feet remain still and they cannot move forward, so too is this mind: it constantly prefers sitting upright or standing in silence while practicing.
The concentrated mind that observes the meaning of the Dharma is called the "shackled mind" because it is bound by this [object]. Regarding its remedy:
one should contemplate and cultivate it at all times and in all places, ensuring that stillness and agitation are continuous. This is the fifty-second [remedy] for what is to be countered.
What is the "cloud-like mind"? It refers to constantly forming the thought of bringing down rain, such as during the three summer months in the West.

During the month of rain, the downpour is particularly severe; because it is often persistent, lingering, and causes distress and confusion, the worldly mind’s anxieties, joys, and discursive thoughts become densely obscured and increasingly abundant.
Therefore, it is said that one should practice "recollection at the time of falling rain.

Once this is realized, one should cultivate the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), depart from worldly sorrow and joy, and accord with the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*). This is the fifty-third [remedy] to be applied as an antidote.
What is the field of the mind? It refers to constantly practicing the cultivation of one's own body.
Just as a person who possesses a fine and excellent field constantly cultivates, plows, and weeds it, employing various skillful means to make it pure;
so too does this person always delight in cultivating and attending to their body, using perfumes, flowers, and flavorful substances to anoint and nourish it, striving to make it radiant.
Having purified oneself and cultivated a state of clear awareness, one should constantly bring to mind the dedication of this merit toward the cultivation of the mind.
By planting seeds in the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) with such articles of offering, one brings about the attainment of the supreme fruit. This is the fifty-fourth [remedy] for that [obstacle].
What is the "salt-like mind"? It refers to the further intensification of one's thoughts; just as the nature of salt is salty, whatever [is thought]...
Just as saltiness increases in whatever place it enters, so too is this person’s mind: regarding the object of thought, they further apply repeated reflection.
When recollecting the desire-realm or form-realm, as soon as this thought arises, they again inwardly investigate from whom this mind is born and what its characteristics are.
While observing this, it remains undecided; they then further consider: "What is the nature of this investigative deliberation?"
When causes and conditions are thus, they are inexhaustible. Having realized this, one should single-mindedly settle the mind in the principle of reality, striving to penetrate it thoroughly.

Furthermore, the nature of the mind is free from thought; it cannot be known through recollection or speculation, nor should one further increase mental factors (*caitasika*) upon the basis of discrimination.
The fifty-fifth [chapter] asks: "What is the 'shaving blade' mind? It means that one should rely solely on such a shaving [of delusions].
Regarding the "removal" (dharma-vinodana): shaving off the hair and beard is the mark of one who has left the secular world to become a renunciant.
This person thinks only: "I have already shaved away the marks of the laity so that evil dharmas may not further proliferate; what more is there to seek?
One should know that this mind is most evil, for by its own act of removal, it is able to shave away all roots of goodness so that they cannot be recovered.
When born, one should reflect upon that which all worthy sages and saints must sever—namely, the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) and the roots of the three poisons.
If one can shave these away so that deluded thoughts do not arise, this is called true renunciation. (The fifty-sixth [question]:
What is meant by a mind equal to Mount Meru? It refers to constantly contemplating that a mind whose nature is loftiness and elevation is like Mount Sumeru.
Soaring high above all peaks, there is nothing that can surpass it; this person’s mind is likewise such that it always takes loftiness as its nature.
Even toward those who should be revered, such as teachers, monks, and parents, they are unable to humble their minds.
They are like a tall banner that cannot be bent or flexed; if one wishes to bend it, it must inevitably break, for in the end, one can never change its nature.
Constantly practicing patience and humility toward all sentient beings, regarding them as one's own teachers—this is the fifty-seventh [remedy] for that which is to be countered.
What is the ocean-like mind? It refers to dwelling in the constant enjoyment of one's own person;
just as the great ocean receives the return of the hundred rivers and swallows them without limit, this mind is likewise [vast], [receiving] all that is superior.
Attributing all matters to oneself and claiming that no one else can compare, one constantly relies on such numerous personal virtues and dwells in the enjoyment of them.
Because the former mind seeks loftiness and this mind seeks expansiveness, it is said to be "equal to the ocean.
Once the practitioner has become aware of this, they should reflect upon the immeasurable great merits of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood.
The ocean of virtue becomes increasingly deep and vast as one progressively disciplines the mind and its conduct; yet, one has never attained even a single drop of it.

Therefore, one should not give rise to a mind of great arrogance. (58) What is the "hole-like" mind? It refers to that which is initially determined to be of a certain nature, but later changes and transforms.
For example, it is like a vessel that is originally solid and strong, but later encounters conditions that pierce it with holes, rendering it incapable of holding anything.
This mind is likewise: at first it can hold much, but later it gradually develops leaks.

Or, when one first resolves on enlightenment and receives the precepts, they are complete and without flaw; yet before long, the phenomena of leakage gradually arise, just like a broken vessel that cannot retain the water of the Dharma.
All such cases are termed "perforated minds. Therefore, a practitioner should ensure that whatever they undertake—

All things have both beginning and end, and one should further know that the nature [of the mind] is subject to many changes and transformations, which are most capable of obstructing the firm bodhicitta;
this is the fifty-ninth [point], its antidote. What is the "mind of taking birth"? It refers to those who cultivate various karmic actions;
their minds of birth are of such a nature. For example, as a person receives good or evil retribution due to white or black karma, so it is according to what has been done.
Because of the various mixtures [of causes], one receives those respective immeasurable and differentiated bodies; this mind is likewise so.
One should know that when dedicating the various practices cultivated toward rebirth, the attainment of the fruit also includes both evil and good.

Therefore, the practitioner should maintain mindfulness to discern between good and evil, eliminate what is unwholesome, and purely cultivate the pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*). Within these wholesome states, one should further use wisdom to...
Removing the coarse dross, one proceeds through these stages in succession until the pure, singular, and sublime fruit of clarified butter (*sarpis*) is attained;
this is that which is to be remedied. Regarding the sixtieth mind, the Sanskrit manuscript is missing the text. The Ācārya says that one *markaṭa-citta* (monkey-mind) is lacking.
By nature, the monkey’s body and mind are distracted and never abide for even a moment; the practitioner is likewise, for his nature is restless.
Because of instability in movement, there is much clinging to objects of perception, just as a monkey lets go of one thing only to seize another;
to speak briefly, all sentient beings are like this—though here the description refers specifically to those in whom this tendency predominates.

Within this context, not following after the signs of movement and distraction, but instead binding the mind to a single object, is the antidote. Just as a monkey, if tied to a pillar, will no longer [wander].
To indulge one’s passions by tossing about, leaping, and bounding is what must be remedied.

Now, these sixty mental states may at times arise because the practitioner’s own nature is biased toward them, or because they are triggered by the habitual tendencies previously cultivated through the application of mind during practice;

they may arise simultaneously in a jumble or sequentially. At all times, one should maintain mindfulness and observe them, whereby one will naturally attain a pure bodhicitta that accords with the Way.
If an ācārya is leveling and purifying the disciple’s mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*), he should likewise eliminate each [defilement] one by one.
As the Sūtra says: "O Lord of Secrets, counting one, two, three, four, and five, there are altogether one hundred and sixty minds.

Transcending the three worldly false attachments, the supramundane mind arises; even when one has reached a quarter [of the path], one passes beyond the stage of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*)."
This answers the characteristics of the various minds and their distinctions. Because of ignorance (*avidyā*), five fundamental afflictions arise within the mind:

namely, greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). The reason the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) are not mentioned here is that they belong to the category of the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), which are mostly included among the sixty mental states.
These five fundamental afflictions are first enumerated as ten, and secondly [as six].
Counting again, it becomes twenty for the third time; counting again, it becomes forty for the fourth time; counting again, it becomes eighty for the fifth time;
and counting again, it becomes one hundred and sixty. Therefore, it is said that by counting one, two, three, four, and five, one reaches one hundred and sixty mental states.
Because the afflictive minds of sentient beings constantly rely on these two extremes and fail to attain the Middle Way, they follow after worldly phenomena.

These various names are immediately divided into two; within these two, they are further subdivided and analyzed in detail, their names and characteristics being fully explained as set forth in the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
If one were to further categorize them according to the nine grades—superior, middling, and inferior—and so on, they would amount to eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*);
if expanded, they are immeasurable. It is like how from a single seed five root-stems arise, and from each of those roots [further branches emerge].
Originally all were broken down into two branches, and by the fifth breakdown, they had become one hundred and sixty minor branches;
from this, if they were further divided and separated, the twigs and leaves would be beyond counting.

It is also like the humans at the beginning of a kalpa, who were all born by transformation, took mindfulness as their food, possessed natural bodily radiance, and lived in peace and unhindered ease; yet, because they did not know the true nature of the mind, they gradually...
Due to their attachment to the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*), as the flavors of what they consumed varied in quantity and quality, distinctions in physical appearance arose accordingly;
from this, the mind of competition—judging right and wrong, superior and inferior—was born. Because of this prideful mind, their merit and benefits declined, and the essence of the earth vanished.

Even the earth-skin, the forest creepers, and the climbing vines subsequently disappeared. Next, they began to eat naturally grown *śāli* rice, at which point the distinction between male and female first appeared, and sexual desire arose.
Theft, killing, lying, and various other unrighteous acts arise in succession; this matter is explained in detail within the Āgamas.

From that time onward, various clans and lineages have arisen in diverse regions and customs, giving rise to various karmas and the web of afflictions, forming the various destinies of sentient beings and creating the various bodies of the five aggregates.
Unless one is an omniscient person (*sarvajña*), one cannot [fully comprehend this].
One who can investigate its underlying threads— the reason the Ācārya employs this analogy— is intended to demonstrate that from a single mind of ignorance,
as it follows various phenomena and becomes differentiated, there arise incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) false attachments.
When one transcends these three worldly false attachments and gives rise to a supramundane mind, if one takes the pure bodhicitta as that supramundane mind, this constitutes transcendence.
Regarding the "three *kalpas* of *yogācāra*": in Sanskrit, *kalpa* has two meanings: first, a period of time; second, deluded attachment.
According to the conventional explanation, one attains perfect enlightenment after passing through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

According to the esoteric explanation, by transcending one *kalpa* of *yogācāra*, one has already passed through the hundred and sixty mental states and so forth, which is termed a single layer of coarse deluded attachment.

Having transcended two kalpas during one asaṃkhyeya-kalpa through the practice of yoga (yogācāra), and further traversing one hundred and sixty mental states and so forth—this being termed the first layer of subtle deluded attachment—one reaches the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.

Furthermore, the practitioner of the Mantra Gate (mantranaya) surpasses one more kalpa and traverses another hundred and sixty mental states and so forth—this being the single layer of extremely subtle deluded attachment—thereby attaining the initial mind of the Buddha-wisdom; hence it is so called.
One attains Buddhahood after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. If one were to transcend these three types of false attachments in a single lifetime, one would attain Buddhahood in that very life;

what need then be said of [long] periods of time? However, at the very moment within the first stage when one initially realizes that there are only the aggregates (*skandha*) and no self, this is called the arising of a supramundane mind.
It transcends the sixty mundane minds and is born from the departure from the inversion of self (*ātman*).
The root of the three poisons is called "transcending the three poisons" through the eradication of false attachments. Furthermore, there are three types of false attachment:

namely, attachment to the faculties (*indriya*), attachment to objects (*viṣaya*), and attachment to the realms (*dhātu*). The "faculties" refer to the six sense organs; the "objects" refer to the six sense fields; and the "realms" refer to the six consciousness realms.
Since the twelve internal and external bases (*āyatana*) constitute both faculties and objects, they are mentioned together. These are the three fruits for those in training (*śaikṣa*).

Because it is the place where one lingers and remains, it is called "prolonged dwelling" (*yanliu*) in the context of spiritual cultivation. Furthermore, there are three types of false attachments (*wangzhi*):

namely, the stumps of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), and the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā*). These are the most difficult points to sever, which are severed by noble ones who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
There are thus three kinds of these three false attachments. For a practitioner of the Mahāyāna who has first attained the supramundane initial resolve:
This is equal to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the Hīnayāna; yet, one does not fall into the fixed position of a Śrāvaka.
The reason for this is that from the very first generation of the mind of awakening, one already knows the nature of the mind, which is merely obscured by the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*).

At that time, one clearly contemplates that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) all arise from conditions and are impermanent and subject to change. Within these, what is there that is a "self" (*pudgala*)?
When I investigate in this manner, I realize that the self (*ātman*) is fundamentally unborn; thus, I transcend the immeasurable nets of views and the clarity of the bodhicitta increases slightly.
Because of the power of having attained the bodhicitta, I do not fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

However, that practitioner still possesses attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*); if they cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and the various perfections (*pāramitā*), [they will proceed further].

Although at this stage one does not give rise to various inversions regarding a self within [the meditative states], the mind remains fixed upon dharmas such as dhyāna and prajñā, lingering and stagnating so that one cannot swiftly reach Bodhi;
because it lacks skillful means for crossing over according to reality, it is called "stagnant cultivation.
Nevertheless, it slightly departs from the three types of false attachments of the lower stages and is able to uproot the seeds of fundamental ignorance, which are the root of karma and afflictions.

One who understands the twelve links of dependent origination realizes that such a profoundly deep Dharma—whether a Buddha appears or not—has a nature and characteristics that are eternally as they are, as previously described.
Various doctrinal tenets, such as establishing purity or not establishing purity, are all inconsistent with this.
Even great masters of treatises, such as Akṣapāda and Brahmānī, sought it for themselves through their own wisdom and sharp faculties.
The true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena likewise cannot be fathomed; the meaning of these twelve links of dependent origination is explained at length in such sūtras as the *Śālistamba-sūtra*.
When it says "profound stillness" (*zhanji*), "stillness" (*ji*) means the sense of non-arising;

because the five root afflictions (*kleśa*) and the one hundred and sixty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are ultimately non-arising, they are called "still. "Profound" (*zhan*) refers to their extreme depth.
The meaning is like a clear pool ten thousand fathoms deep, tranquil and mirror-like in its transparency; those who gaze upon it cannot fathom its depth.
Thus it is said that when the three animals cross the river, each reaches only as far as their respective tracks allow;
only the Great Fragrant Elephant King is able to gradually penetrate to its very source and bottom. Within this, there are those of the three vehicles who likewise rely on the ineffable.

Although one may explain the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, because Śrāvakas enter into the dharma-nature most superficially, they loathe and fear birth and death, claiming for themselves that they have already attained *nirvāṇa* and conceiving the thought of having achieved deliverance.
Because the entry of Pratyekabuddhas differs slightly and is somewhat deeper, they are not as hurried regarding birth and death;
yet, being unable to employ the power of skillful means to give rise to great compassion, they do not awaken like Bodhisattvas.
When such a state of dharma arises, one immediately knows that the defilements of the mind are gradually being removed, and thus the pure mind gradually manifests.

At that time, one attains the power of the bodhicitta; because one can train in various gates of liberation through the path of non-abiding, there are differences in rising and sinking within the same single dharma.
As the Sūtra says: "That which cannot be known by any heterodox practitioners."
In this school, it is taught that there are two kinds of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The "outer-of-the-outer" non-Buddhists are like those who, upon seeing a clear pond, give rise to fear and do not dare to approach or enter it.

Although the "inner-and-outer" non-Buddhists are able to swim within it, removing their impurities and attaining the bliss of coolness, they fail to realize that there are immeasurable jewels and gems therein; thus, they neither enter nor recognize them.
Second, because one enters [this state] without recognizing it, it is said that "no externalists can know it.

When the Buddhas of the past proclaimed that which is free from all faults, they meant that throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, all Buddhas have only this single gate to guide and advance the deluded masses out of the burning house.

In this place, there are no further obstructions and no more engagement in frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); therefore, various causes and logical measures (*hetu-pramāṇa*) are of no avail.
Although none among the various masters are able to point out its faults or defects, it has not yet transcended the obstacles to the Dharma and is not yet called the truly pure Bodhicitta.
It is like a lotus flower that, though already free from the turbid mud, has not yet emerged above the water; thus the Sūtra says:
"That supramundane mind dwells within the aggregates. This is because, although the mind of profound stillness has become manifest within the practitioner's yoga, [it has not yet fully emerged].

However, when engaging with phenomena, although the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses still depend upon the mind— because one feels weary of and fears conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) and thus clings to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)—
by the power of the bodhicitta, there naturally arises such wisdom without depending on the instruction of others.
This wisdom enables one to direct the mind toward the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth to cultivate the skillful means of detachment, contemplating them through five types of analogies.
Examining the emptiness of the absence of intrinsic nature begins with the observation of the mass of foam.

Just as the floating foam upon water may be seen with the eye to have various forms, yet when its substantial nature is sought, it is found to be utterly unobtainable; so too it is with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Whether coarse or subtle, there is nothing that does not arise from a multitude of conditions. That which arises from conditions lacks intrinsic nature, and this is the very essence of form: its original non-arising. Next is the phrase "floating."
"Bubbles" are like the bubbles floating upon the water during a summer torrential rain; they belong only to a combination of conditions.

When viewed through the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*), they have no arising or ceasing. The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is likewise: all feelings of suffering and pleasure arise from the conjunction of the mind and its objects.

Since they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) due to their dependence on conditions, sensation is fundamentally unarisen. The next phrase, "a mirage," refers to the vapors rising from the earth in the springtime.

Looking at the mirage in the sunlight, one who is deluded by thirst gives rise to a longing mind and rushes toward it in vain effort; the further he goes, the more distant it becomes. Sentient beings are likewise:

not knowing that the nature of dependent origination is empty, they give rise to the perception of a self-existent dharma (*dharmasaṃjñā*). If one awakens to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), then this very perception is fundamentally non-arising.
Next, as for the plantain tree (*kadalī*): it is like a person seeking the solid core within a plantain tree, even going so far as to dissect it.

If one analyzes and breaks down [the aggregate of formations] until reaching the level of the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*), it cannot be found; the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is likewise.

A single minute particle entering a realm of movement does not arise without depending on manifold conditions. That which arises through conditions is devoid of intrinsic nature; this is precisely the fundamental non-arising of formations. Next, regarding "illusory phenomena":
it is like the power of worldly spells and medicines that delude the human mind, manifesting all manner of unprecedented things.
The same applies to the *vastu-vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness as objects). From a single moment of the illusory mind of ignorance, the triple world is illusorily produced.

When its ultimate source is investigated, it is entirely devoid of arising and ceasing, or going and coming. One should know that because it arises from various conditions and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the consciousness is fundamentally unarisen.
Although these five metaphors are taught in the *śrāvaka* sūtras, their intent there is to clarify non-self (*anātman*); here, however, these five [metaphors]...

The meaning of this analogy clarifies that the nature of all aggregates (*skandha*) is empty. Just as one contemplates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one should know that the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the six sense-bases, and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) should all be extensively analyzed and explained, as elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

When a practitioner observes in this manner, they penetrate the emptiness of all phenomena through the gateway of "absence of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) and thereby attain liberation from the first layer [of conceptualization].
Having overturned misconceptions regarding phenomena and knowing the nature of the mind to be thus, one is not shaken by the grasper or the grasped within the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases;
therefore, it is called "realizing the realm of tranquility. When realizing this realm of tranquility, one gradually transcends the spheres of the two vehicles.
Just as a lotus flower, though not yet in full bloom, already slightly emerges above the clear stream, so too is the practitioner: their mind no longer [clings].
Because it is not included within the aggregates (*skandha*), it is called the supramundane mind; according to a correct translation, it should be termed the "mind transcending the world.
O Lord of Secrets, that which is free from the net of karmic afflictions and the continuity of the eight types of minds—conformable and discordant—is as previously described:

the seeds, roots, and buds, as well as taking refuge in the Triple Gem, practicing the conduct of the vehicles of humans and devas, observing the fasts, giving alms, and cultivating wholesome dharmas.

The eight minds that accord with the world (*laukika-anuloma-citta*) refer to the period from when one first generates the aspiration for the Path in any of the three vehicles until the extraction of the root of karma and afflictions—the seeds of ignorance—which give rise to the twelve links of dependent origination.

The eight minds that oppose the world (*laukika-pratiloma-citta*) refer to these same stages, or alternatively, they may be divided according to the various levels such as the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), each having its own set of eight minds. A practitioner of the Mahāyāna thoroughly understands all the aggregates (*skandha*).
Because its nature is empty, among all phenomena there is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be abandoned;

one is doubly free from the eight mental states of aversion and favor, as well as the two inversions of self and aggregates and the two kinds of nets of karma and afflictions—this is called the "yogic practice that transcends one kalpa.
*Yoga* is translated as "correspondence" (*xiāngyìng*). If addressed using the feminine form, it is called *yoginī*, which refers to the "characteristic" (*xiàng*).
"Those who correspond" refers to practitioners whose contemplative practice accords with principle.

According to the conventional explanation, a Bodhisattva must pass through one great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* from the initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) before realizing such a realm of quiescence.
However, according to the Secret Vehicle (*Guhyamantra*), merely transcending this single layer of deluded attachment constitutes the leap over the practice of one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
When one has not yet passed this kalpa and is at a level equal to that of a pratyekabuddha, it is called the "Ultimate State Beyond Speech.
At that time, the mind stagnates within the marks of unconditioned dharmas; if one loses the skillful means, one mostly falls to the stage of the two vehicles and realizes a limited nirvana.
However, by the power of the bodhicitta, one can once again give rise to compassionate vows, and from this point onward, the paths of the three vehicles proceed.
At the beginning of the path, although one observes that both persons and phenomena are empty, this does not differ significantly from the various schools such as the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*,

for it merely constitutes this contemplation of equality based on the principle of partial truth (*pradeśa-satya*). Therefore, when the supramundane minds of the three vehicles— superior, middling, and inferior— are discussed together,
it takes one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* to reach the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, at which point one finally diverges from the two vehicles.

The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Guhyapati, regarding the Mahāyāna practice of generating the mind of the objectless vehicle (*anālambana-yāna*) through the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*):

why is this? Just as those practitioners of the past observed the aggregates (*skandha*) and the *ālayavijñāna* to be like illusions, mirages, reflections, fire-wheels, and cities of the Gandharvas—this clarifies the second stage."
This is the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). The Sanskrit term *parā* signifies both "other" and "supreme.

That which is called the "Vehicle of Other-Dependence" (*paratantra-yāna*) refers to the generation of the great vow of equality for the sake of all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*, practicing the path of the Bodhisattva;

even for those who are *icchantikas* or followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) who have not yet entered the stage of correct determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), one should likewise employ various skillful means.

By analyzing and subduing [afflictions] while embracing [beings], causing them all to enter this vehicle together—based on this "objectless great compassion" (nirālamba-mahākaruṇā)—it is called the "other-dependent vehicle" (paratantra-yāna).
Furthermore, as for the "objectless vehicle," it is only upon reaching this asaṃkhyeya-kalpa that one is first able to observe the profound and subtle ādāna-vijñāna;
having realized that the three realms are mind-only and that not a single dharma exists apart from the mind, one mounts this objectless [vehicle].

Because one practices the path to great enlightenment by taking the mind as the object of focus, it is called the "Vehicle Without Objects" (*anālambana-yāna*). This mind of the vehicle without objects is itself the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Since, at the beginning of the first eon when a practitioner cultivates meditative practice, the mind sinks into the aggregates (*skandha*), they observe the selflessness of phenomena through the five gates of emptiness regarding the lack of intrinsic nature.
Nevertheless, in view of the Middle Way of dependent origination, this [practice] belongs to the category of antidotes.

If the *siddhānta* (established tenets) loses the wisdom of *prajñā* and skillful means (*upāya*), one falls into nihilism and is called a "wrong-grasper of emptiness" (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*), thereby conflating with those who follow the *Vaipulya* path.
In the Mahāyāna, even the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) is unobtainable;

although one contemplates that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are non-existent, there is likewise nothing among all phenomena that is empty. Therefore, one must practice the contemplation of the path by remaining free from both existence and non-existence.

The selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is for the purpose of purifying the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). In accordance with the practice of the bodhisattvas of antiquity, one should study the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the *ālayavijñāna*.

That which is explained in the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, and other sūtras regarding the eight consciousnesses, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the three absences of nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) all share this same intent.
When the sūtras speak of "knowing self-nature," it means knowing that the triple world is mind-only (*cittamātra*), like a phantom or a mirage.
The six metaphors—the flame, the shadow, the echo, the whirling fire-wheel, the *gandharva*-city, and so forth—all serve to simultaneously establish both existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, the meaning of the *ālayavijñāna* as the "storehouse" (the literal translation being "chamber")—meaning that the aggregates arise within it—and its specific sense as the dependent origination of the aggregates, differ from the intent of the previous five metaphors regarding the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-śūnyatā*) during the eon.
As for the meaning of *ālaya*, it contains and stores; when translated directly, it is "chamber," signifying that all aggregates are produced therein.

In this context, "cessation" (nirodha) is so named because it is the destruction of the nest of the aggregates (*skandha*). Furthermore, the *ālayavijñāna* has three meanings: first, the meaning of differentiation;
second, the meaning of causal condition (*pratyaya*); and third, the meaning of ultimate reality (*tattva*). As stated in the "Verses on Seeking Ultimate Reality" in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*:
"Because it is free from duality and delusion, it is based on non-existence, beyond verbal expression, and devoid of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)."

One should know that the three natures are all truly real. That which is called "free from duality" refers to the reality of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because the grasper and the grasped are ultimately non-existent.
"The basis of delusion" refers to the reality of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it gives rise to all conceptual constructions.
"Inexpressible and free from conceptual proliferation" refers to the reality of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because its intrinsic nature is free from conceptual proliferation.
In the treatise, following this, the verse explaining the analogies for seeking reality states:

"Just as that illusionist is used as an analogy for unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*), so too are those various magical illusions used as analogies for the two kinds of delusion. The commentary explains:

Just as an illusionist relies on the power of mantras and rituals to transform wood, stone, and the like into causes of delusion, so too does unreal conceptualization rely upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The arising of various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) is the cause of inversion. Just as a magician’s illusions manifest in various forms such as gold and so forth, so too is the nature of the conceptual constructions that arise;
because they consist of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*), these two delusions are constantly manifest.
The subsequent verse says: "Because they lack intrinsic substance, one enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); because they are perceivable, [they exist conventionally]."

To penetrate the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is the intended meaning here: just as that magician and the magical illusions have no substantial reality, so too the two aspects—the dependent (paratantra) and the imagined (parikalpita)—have no substantial reality. By this principle, one penetrates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Furthermore, just as the substance of both the magician and the magical illusions cannot be found, so too is false imagination (abhūta-parikalpa).

It is likewise; by this principle, one immediately attains penetration into the reality of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Furthermore, a verse states: "Because those things lack intrinsic nature, one immediately attains the realm of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);
through such a transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one immediately attains the meaning of ultimate reality. The commentary explains:
"If a person realizes that those illusory things lack intrinsic nature, they immediately attain the equal and real realm. If Bodhisattvas realize those two..."
When delusion, which lacks intrinsic nature, attains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one immediately realizes the meaning of true reality (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, a verse states: "This thing exists there; yet that which has existence also lacks existence. Because it lacks existence, it is said to be an illusion. This verse clarifies that illusory phenomena exist and yet do not exist.
Why? They "exist" because the appearances of the illusions manifest there; however, they do not [truly] exist... [because they lack intrinsic nature].
Some say that because its substantial entity cannot be apprehended, such an existent and non-existent are non-dual;
by this meaning, it is said that it is an illusion (*māyā*). Furthermore, a verse says: "Non-existence is not non-existence, and that which is not non-existence is existence;

there is no duality between non-existence and existence, and therefore it is called an illusion. This verse clarifies that illusory phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, and yet they exist. Why? Because...
Therefore, "non-existence" refers to the fact that those illusory phenomena lack intrinsic substance because they have no real essence;

"existence" refers to the fact that illusory phenomena are not non-existent because they manifest as images. Since this absence of substance and the presence of substance are non-dual, for this reason it is said that they are "illusory.
This illusion serves as a metaphor for the aggregates (*skandhas*); therefore, one should know that while false conceptualization exists, [it lacks reality].
Why is it that they do not exist? Because although those two images appear, their substantial reality cannot be apprehended;
therefore, it is said that the existence of form and so forth is itself non-existence. Furthermore, why is it that false discrimination neither exists nor does not exist?
Because while those two lack any substantial reality, there is the appearance of images; therefore, it is said that form and so forth are both non-existent and existent.

The essence is non-dual; by virtue of this, existence and non-existence are not two. This can refute both reification and denial, as well as the inclination toward the quiescence of the Lesser Vehicle.
Why is this so? Because one knows non-existence through the absence of an essence, one should not establish [reified] positions;

because one knows the conventional truth through the presence of an essence, one should not engage in denial. Furthermore, since these two are not distinct, one should not feel aversion toward the essence.
Regarding entry into small nirvāṇa, that verse further states: "Because of delusion regarding the illusory image and the grasping of the illusion, it is said that there are two;
thus, while those two do not exist, the two are perceived. Because of the skeletal image and the contemplation of the skeleton, it is likewise said that there are two;
though there are no two, the two are said to be perceivable. The meaning of the preceding verse is that the deluded person [perceives] the illusory image and the grasping of the illusion.
Because of delusion, one speaks of the two things—the grasper and the grasped; although these two do not exist, they are perceived because they appear through delusion.
The meaning of the subsequent verse is that the practitioner is likewise:

regarding the image of bones and the grasping of those bones, by virtue of contemplation, one speaks of the two things—the contemplator and the contemplated; although these two do not exist, both may still be perceived because of [delusion].

Having explained that [the nature of things] is observed through manifestation, he asks: "Once one has observed in this way, what dharma serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) and what dharma is the object to be remedied (*vipakṣa*)?
To this, he further states two verses: "One should know that the essence of the object to be remedied consists of those dharmas characterized by delusion;

such an essence is neither existent nor non-existent, neither real nor unreal, like a magical illusion (*māyā*). One should know that the essence of the antidote consists of all dharmas such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)."
The essence is without marks; it is like an illusion, and so it is. The meaning of the preceding verse is as follows:

that which is the essence of the object to be remedied is precisely the delusion regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). This "delusion regarding the characteristics of phenomena" refers to taking such-and-such an essence to be real.

However, while such an essence may be said to exist due to false conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*), it is also said not to exist because of the duality of the grasper and the grasped, and because of their lack of substantiality.
Because there is no distinction, existence is like an illusion and non-existence is also like an illusion; therefore, this characteristic is said to be like an illusion.
The meaning of the subsequent verse is as follows: the essence of the antidote is precisely all phenomena—namely, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth taught by the Buddha.
Because they possess such and such an essence, that essence is also entirely like an illusion. Why? Because it is just as ordinary beings apprehend it.
Thus, because they possess an essence, they are as the Buddhas have taught; and thus, because they lack an essence, this essence is without marks (*animitta*).
Yet, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifests entering the womb, being born, leaving the city, renouncing the world, and attaining perfect enlightenment.
Although it is thus without marks, its reflection appears. Therefore, all phenomena are like an illusion. Question: If all phenomena are identical to an illusion, [how can there be distinctions?]
For what reason is one [factor] the antidote and the other the object to be remedied? That verse answers:
"Just as a powerful illusory king causes another illusory king to retreat, so too do pure dharmas cause defiled dharmas to be exhausted.
For this reason, although a bodhisattva cultivates all practices, there is nothing to be attained. That treatise clarifies the observation of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Since the *ālayavijñāna*’s realization that its own nature is like an illusion accords most closely with this sutra, it is set forth in full.
One should know that mirages, reflections, fire-wheels, and cities of the gandharvas should likewise be explained extensively.

As for the five metaphors from the previous section—foam, bubbles, and the plantain tree—they are not discussed here because these three matters clarify the absence of a substantial self through the analysis of their constituent parts.

Although the nature [of phenomena] is empty, the intent of the metaphors such as illusions and mirages used herein is to clarify that the emptiness of the very essence of consciousness-only—without external objects—is difficult to understand;

thus, it is not discussed here because its coarse aspects have already been transformed and integrated. When a practitioner realizes that the aggregates are mind-only, they know the self-nature of phenomena;

however, as long as they have not yet fully realized this self-nature in its various aspects, they fear falling into the state of grasping at something attainable, and therefore [they do not rest complacently].
One who can thoroughly investigate existence through reasoning fears falling into the view of annihilationism; thus, such a person cannot thoroughly investigate emptiness.

Not only do they fail to clearly perceive existence, but they also perceive emptiness as a finality, failing to exhaust the truth. Now, by means of gates such as "illusory-like," one illuminates that existence and emptiness are non-dual;

since even the marks of the two-fold emptiness of persons and phenomena are not to be grasped by the mind, this is called truly entering the emptiness of phenomena and awakening to the nature of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "O Lord of Mysteries, one who thus abandons the mind of selflessness attains mastery over the realization that the sovereign of the mind is fundamentally unborn.

This sovereign of the mind is the King of the Mind itself. Because it does not linger in existence or non-existence, the mind is without obstruction; thus, its performed wondrous deeds are unimpeded."

Because it can be accomplished according to one's will, it is called the Sovereignty of the Mind-King (*cittarāja*). The clarity of this sovereignty of the mind-king is precisely the pure *bodhicitta*.
When this is further developed through another turning, its illumination becomes twice as superior as that of the preceding eon.

This is because the nature of the mind-king is like the water in a pond, which is inherently pure; the purification of the mental factors (*caitasika*) is like the clearing away of adventitious dust. Therefore, one realizes this inherent purity.
At the time of purification, one is able to self-awaken to the fact that the mind is fundamentally unborn. Why? Because the beginning and end of the mind are both unattainable.
For example, the waves of the great ocean arise from conditions; thus, they are non-existent before and non-existent after. Yet the nature of water is not like this.
When the waves arise from conditions, the nature of the water is not something that was previously non-existent and now exists because of the waves. It is the cause [of the waves].

When conditions are exhausted, the nature of water does not subsequently cease; the mind-king is likewise thus, having neither prior nor subsequent limits because the prior and subsequent limits have been severed.
Although it encounters the winds of objects and arises or ceases according to conditions, the nature of the mind is eternally without arising or ceasing.
To realize that this mind is fundamentally unborn is to gradually enter the gate of the letter A. At that time, one further transcends the hundred [dharmas].
The sixty mental states and the various afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with their single layer of subtle false attachments, are termed the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
Therefore, a sutra states: "To know the nature of one's own mind is the practice of the *yogācāra* that transcends two *kalpas*.

The meanings regarding the causes and conditions of conditioned birth and destruction within this context are explained extensively in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, and the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.
Now, for the time being, I shall clarify the essential meaning and therefore do not explain it in detail; however, tracing the origin and following to the end as discussed above,

from the initial arousal of even a hair’s breadth of goodness up to the transcendence of the two obstacles of persons and dharmas, although the ultimate principle has become brilliantly manifest— becoming increasingly wondrous and profound—
it nonetheless serves only as an antidote to the defilements external to the mind, and has yet to open the various secrets within this very mind.
The esoteric and inconceivable matters will only be explained from this point onward;
if one were not to provide such a preliminary clarification, ordinary people, each clinging to their own prior habits, would be unable to perceive their subtle and profound nature.
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, Guhyapati, those Bodhisattvas who practice the Bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras—
having accumulated immeasurable merit and wisdom over countless, innumerable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas,
and having fully perfected immeasurable wisdom and skillful means— they are intended to clarify that they transcend the third [stage]."
It is merely to inspire faith, joy, and reverence in those who see and hear it that the merits of this kalpa are first extolled.
In other teachings, bodhisattvas practice the path of skillful means as an antidote, gradually removing the defilements of the mind over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
some may reach enlightenment while others do not. However, in this teaching, all bodhisattvas...
The Bodhisattva, however, does not act in this way; rather, taking the mantra as his vehicle, he directly enters the gate of the pure bodhicitta.
When he perceives this path of the luminosity of the mind, the merit and wisdom cultivated by all Bodhisattvas over incalculable eons are spontaneously perfected.
It is like a person of the world who, using boats or carts to traverse dangerous and evil paths, successfully reaches a distance of five hundred yojanas.
Furthermore, there is another person who, directly employing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), flies through the air to traverse his path;

although there is no difference in the destination reached, the vehicle upon which he rides is distinct. Moreover, the reason the World-Honored One previously explained in detail the various characteristics of the mind as described above was to instruct practitioners of the Mantra-gate (*mantramukha*) so that, should they reach such a state, [they may recognize it].
Regarding the element and the time, one must clearly recognize that one has not arrived before actually arriving, nor should one linger along the way.
Furthermore, just as when the crown prince of a Wheel-Turning King is first born, his various marks are complete and lacking nothing;
although he is not yet able to master all arts or govern the four continents, he is already capable of sustaining the seven treasures and accomplishing the succession to the kingship.
What is the reason for this family lineage? It is because he is the very embodiment of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).

Likewise, when a practitioner of mantra first enters the pure bodhicitta, although they have not yet fully cultivated the myriad practices of Samantabhadra or perfected the skillful means of great compassion over countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, all such Tathāgata merits are already accomplished within them.

Why is this? Because he is the very embodiment of the Dharmakāya of Vairocana; therefore, the Sūtra says that throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, his wisdom and skillful means have all been fully perfected.
Furthermore, just as a prince at birth is already the object of veneration for dragons, spirits, and the common people, so too is it with the initial arousal of the pure bodhicitta.

Having become the great refuge for those in the world of devas and humans who have lost their way on the right path, when this mind is realized as it is elucidated in the various conventional treatises, it is then called "Buddha.
Therefore, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, such as Śāriputra and others, cannot fathom it even by exhausting the power of their wisdom. As the Sūtra says: "That which transcends all śrāvakas..."
This is the stage of the Pratyekabuddha. When a practitioner attains this mind, they immediately know that Śākyamuni’s Pure Land is not destroyed;
they see the Buddha’s lifespan as long-lasting, and his body in its original state, together with the bodhisattvas such as Oṣadhiprabhāsa who have emerged from the earth, all gathered in one place.
Although those who cultivate the path of counteractive measures are in their traces close to the stage of the Successor (Ayusmat), they do not recognize even one [of these things].

For this reason, this matter is called "secret. Furthermore, while these Bodhisattvas are able to universally assemble all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-realm in the ten directions within their ultimately pure minds, they are also able to personally travel throughout the ten directions to make offerings to spiritual friends and seek the True Dharma;
yet, they alone clearly understand this, while gods and humans are unable to know it.

For this reason, they are further called "Secret. Although it was said during the previous two kalpas that they had transcended the stages of the Two Vehicles, and although Subhūti and others were able to expound extensively on the emptiness of both person and phenomena by relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they nevertheless felt shock and doubt regarding this secret One Vehicle, not knowing where it leads;
thus, they are termed those who have "directly passed beyond" the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
On that ground, the gods of great majesty and virtue, unable to see the place where the Bodhisattva’s mind was resting, all conceived feelings of reverence and faith.
Consequently, Śakra Devānām Indra made this vow, saying: "This Superior Person will before long attain Buddhahood;
when he attains Buddhahood, I shall offer him the auspicious grass. The Four Heavenly Kings also gave rise to this thought, saying: "If this Bodhisattva..."
"When that Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, I shall offer him a bowl. Brahmā, Lord of the Devas, also had this thought:
"When this Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, I shall request him to turn the wheel of Dharma. Therefore, it says, "I approach and pay homage.
Having thus concluded the praise of the merit of entering the gateway of mantras, by what further method does the practitioner enter this gateway? Therefore, the Sūtra next says: "That which..."
This refers to the emptiness of emptiness, which is the very nature of one’s own mind, equal to space.
As stated above, from "immeasurable like space" up to "the manifestation of perfect enlightenment," these serve as metaphors for this mind.

Having previously realized in past kalpas that all phenomena are mind-only and that there are no phenomena external to the mind, one now observes that this mind itself is the Tathāgata’s spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), and is also Vairocana.

Because the body of Vairocana pervades all things as the mind is thus, so too are all phenomena thus. Since the sense organs and their objects both enter the gateway of the letter A, it is said that they are "free from sense organs and objects.
Because no images arise and there is only the light of eternal quiescence, it is said to be "signless" (*animitta*).
Through the wisdom of the true nature of the mind, one awakens to the true nature of the mind; both object and wisdom are the Prajñāpāramitā.

Therefore it is said that there is no objective realm (*anālambana*). Because these ten types of wisdom within this state, when compared to the preceding ten metaphors, further constitute conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is said that they transcend all conceptual proliferations.

Thirdly, because the seeds of the subtle afflictions, karma, and lifespan—numbering one hundred and sixty—are eliminated, and the sprouts of the Buddha-tree arise once more, it is said that they are equal to space and boundless; all Buddha-dharmas depend upon these characteristics.
Since rebirth does not destroy causes and conditions, it enters the Dharma-realm; likewise, the Dharma-realm is unmoving, which is precisely dependent origination.

One should know that the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions is itself the arising and ceasing of the Dharma-realm, and that the non-arising and non-ceasing of the Dharma-realm is itself the non-arising and non-ceasing of causes and conditions.
Therefore it is said: "Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear," [the nature of] the conditioned and unconditioned realms remains unchanged.
Because all phenomena in the world abide as they naturally do, they are said to be free from all conditioned activity. As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, "All phenomena converge in the eye";
this convergence does not exceed that [reality], just as the hundred rivers flow toward the sea and have nowhere else to go.
Therefore, one should know that the eye is itself the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Within the ultimate reality, even the eye cannot be apprehended, let alone [anything else].
Is it the movement toward or away from [objects]? It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
therefore it is said that one who practices by being detached from eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind attains such subtle wisdom.

At that time, when observing all defiled and pure phenomena—even down to the slightest fraction—one sees that they are like atoms (*paramāṇu*), none of which do not arise from conditions. If they arise from conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If...
