The absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is precisely primordial non-arising (*an-utpanna*); primordial non-arising is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the mind;
and since even this limit of reality of the mind is unapprehendable, it is said that "the mind arises as the ultimate absence of intrinsic nature.

This mind, when compared to the preceding two stages, is like a lotus in full bloom; yet when compared to the subsequent two states of mind, it is itself the fruit that becomes a seed again. Therefore, it is said to be "like [a lotus]."
Because this is the initial mind taught by the Buddha as the cause for attaining Buddhahood, one is liberated from karma and afflictions while yet remaining fully possessed of them.

Regarding the phrase "as taught by the Buddha" herein, the World-Honored One takes the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time as witnesses to state that through this single causal condition, he opens up pure knowledge and vision for sentient beings; the Way is thus mysteriously identical. When the practitioner is liberated, [they realize this].
At the very moment all karma and afflictions arise, one knows that all karma and afflictions are nothing other than the Buddha-work;

they are fundamentally without bondage, so how could there now be liberation? It is like a skilled physician who transforms poison into medicine to eliminate various ailments, or like space, which transcends all characteristics yet serves as the basis upon which all phenomena depend. When one dwells in this inconceivable liberation, [all things are seen thus].
This refers to the true Arhat who, being unattached to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is worthy of receiving vast offerings from all the world;
thus the Sūtra says: "The world honors and reveres him, and he should always be venerated.

Furthermore, because the Ācārya wishes to clarify this meaning of being "worthy of offerings," he provides a comprehensive discourse on the beginning and end of the three *kalpas*, employing the analogy of a precious jewel, as follows:
There is a wish-fulfilling jewel within a mass of rock; because worldly people do not recognize it, they cast it aside upon the road, no different from rubble.
However, one who can distinguish precious gems perceives a slight sign as soon as it begins to manifest on the surface, and immediately recognizes it.
First, using sharp iron, he chips away the dull rock; once he is close to the precious gem, the rock gradually softens, and he continues further with...
Just as various medicines cause the impurities of ore to be digested without damaging its essential substance, so too, when the coarse defilements have been removed, there remain subtle defilements;
these are then cleansed with alkaline water and polished with a fine cloth through various skillful means until they are brilliantly radiant.
Once this luminosity is attained, it is placed upon a high banner, where it can universally rain down all manner of things according to every request.
At that time, the people of the world conceived a sense of wonder and revered this jewel as they would a great deity, because it was able to fulfill all their aspirations.
Yet, at one and the same moment, this precious gem universally accords with the minds of the multitude; according to what each receives, there are various differences.
Now, regarding these various objects: did they previously exist within the jewel, or did they not? If [they] previously...
If these small jewels already exist, how can they suddenly contain all these things? And if there were no objects beforehand, how could they suddenly rain down all these objects?
Since the nature of jewels in this world is already inconceivable, how much more so is the jewel of the bodhicitta of sentient beings!
Therefore, as soon as spiritual friends perceive the eight worldly concerns in sentient beings...
At the very moment they stir, one recognizes them as true treasures and knows the principle that they can be excavated.
Just as those who have long known the name of treasure recognize it immediately upon encountering it, so too do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;

having long since realized this through their own direct experience, they have attained the path of Great Bodhi starting from even a single hair’s breadth of goodness. Therefore, they discern the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.
Using the skillful means of great joy, he entices and encourages them to receive the Three Refuges, as previously explained in detail.

For example, it is like taking a piece of stubborn stone home and first using the three kinds of threefold minds to uproot the roots of karma and afflictions—the seeds of ignorance—just as one uses sharp iron tools to excavate and remove coarse ore;
next, one contemplates the dharma of non-referential cultivation and the selflessness of phenomena.
The nature [of the mind] gradually reaches a state of pliancy, wherein it is digested by medicinal substances without being harmed.

Next, the mind that is utterly devoid of intrinsic nature arises, like ash and water used for polishing, making it exceedingly radiant and pure. At that time, one is born into the family of the Buddhas;
this is called "placing [the mind] upon a high banner" where various jewels rain down. By virtue of these causes and conditions, one becomes worthy of receiving the vast offerings of the world.
If a practitioner directly perceives the jewel of the mind through the gateway of mantras— just as a seer skilled in incantations uses supernatural power to retrieve it—
then although there may be differences in skill or ease, there is ultimately no difference in the path by which the jewel is obtained. Therefore,

this sutra elucidates the characteristics of the mind from the shallow to the profound, extensively clarifying the causes, conditions, and the beginning and end of bodhicitta for the purpose of revealing its essence.
If one were to rely solely on the conventional characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one could not say, "I now fully expound all the great secrets of the Buddhas.
As the Sūtra says: "O Lord of Secrets, through the stages of faith, understanding, and practice, one observes the three minds and the immeasurable *pāramitās* of wisdom."

Regarding the contemplation of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), on the stage of conviction and understanding (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*), there is the establishment of ten minds that are without opposition, immeasurable, and inconceivable, whereby boundless wisdom arises.
This is the core teaching of this sutra: from the pure bodhicitta upward through the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra-bhūmi*), all are within the practice of conviction and understanding;
only the Tathāgata is named the stage of ultimate omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). It is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the bodhisattva of the first stage.

They are able to believe in the Tathāgata’s original practices and the faith therein; they believe in the fulfillment of the various pāramitās; they believe in entering the various supreme stages (bhūmis);

they believe in the accomplishment of powers; they believe in being endowed with fearlessness; they believe in the growth of the indestructible, unique Buddha-dharmas; they believe in the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas;
they believe in the emergence of the Buddha-realm, which is neither middle nor extreme; and they believe in following into the Tathāgata.
The fruit of accomplishing faith in immeasurable realms is such that, regarding these various matters, one's mind is ultimately indestructible and no longer turns according to other conditions;
therefore, it is called the Stage of Practice through Faith and Understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), and is also called the Stage of Reaching Cultivation.
Examining the three minds, they are the causal roots and the ultimate mind; if discussed comprehensively, this refers to the Stage of Faith and Understanding.

When a Bodhisattva of the first stage attains this space-like, stainless bodhicitta, ten great vows naturally arise within the ten inexhaustible realms, eventually fulfilling as many as a million *asaṃkhyeya* great vows;
this is precisely bodhicitta acting as the cause. From the second stage onward, one increasingly cultivates the myriad practices of great compassion, which are themselves inexhaustible.
The great vows take root throughout the worlds of the ten directions and gradually increase until they reach the eighth stage and beyond;

these are all termed the "stages of skillful means" (*upāya-bhūmi*). The *Buddhatva-śāstra* states: "The realms from the eighth stage upward are identical, differing only in that they are categorized as successive stages based on skillful means.
If one contemplates each individual stage, each likewise possesses three aspects of mind, just as there are many sets of ten.

Entering the first stage (*bhūmi*) by means of causes and conditions is called the "cause" (*hetu*). Once one has become established therein, purifying that stage through various great compassionate practices (*mahākaruṇā-pratipatti*) is called the "root" (*mūla*).
Explaining the characteristics of the fruit of purifying the stages and the activity of skillful means (*upāya-karma*) is called the "culmination" (*niṣṭhā*).
All other [stages] should be understood accordingly. In this sutra, the immeasurable *pāramitās* and the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) are precisely the purification of the stages.

Furthermore, when the practitioner transcends all dependence and opposition from this point on, entering the inconceivable stage beyond the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*), ten states of mind and boundless wisdom arise;
this is the sign of the fruit of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:
"Having made the ten great vows, one then attains the mind of benefit, the supple mind, the compliant mind, the tranquil mind, the tamed mind, and the mind of cessation."
With a humble mind, a moistening mind, an unshakable mind, and an unturbid mind, one further accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas that purify the stages (*bhūmi*):
namely, faith; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; being free from weariness; knowing the various sūtras and śāstras; skillfully understanding worldly dharmas;
shame and remorse; and firm power; making offerings to all Buddhas; practicing according to the teachings; and furthermore, dwelling in this stage.

They have thoroughly understood the obstacles to the stages; they have thoroughly understood the formation and destruction of the stages; they have thoroughly understood the characteristics and fruits of the stages; they have thoroughly understood the cultivation for attaining the stages;

they have thoroughly understood the purification of the dharmas of the stages; they have thoroughly understood the progression from stage to stage; they have thoroughly understood what is possible and impossible regarding each stage;

they have thoroughly understood the superior wisdom of each stage; they have thoroughly understood the non-retrogression of each stage; and they have thoroughly understood the purification of all things.
From the Bodhisattva-bhūmi up to the transition into the Tathāgata-bhūmi, there are many such sets of ten minds;
if these were to be analyzed in detail, they comprise one million asaṃkhyeya gateways of transcendence, and for this reason it is said that "boundless wisdom arises.

Furthermore, if one explains the ten minds specifically in relation to the first three minds, then, when considering the stage of faith and understanding (adhimukti-bhūmi) as a whole, the first bhūmi serves as the seed.
The second stage is the sprout; the third stage is the bud; the fourth stage is the leaf; the fifth stage is the flower; the sixth stage is the fruit;
the seventh stage is the enjoyment of the seed; the eighth stage is the basis of fearlessness, which is the fruit among fruits;
the ninth stage is the arising of wisdom that seeks further progress toward the Buddha-stage, which is the most excellent mind; and the tenth stage is the certainty of this mind.
The two minds have no distinct objects; they are merely distinguished as superior manifestations through skillful means within the eighth consciousness itself.

Furthermore, each and every stage (*bhūmi*) inherently possesses these ten minds. For instance, when one dwells in the first stage, the accomplishment of the dharmas that purify all stages and the knowledge of the characteristics of all stages are precisely what was previously understood upon completing the explanation of the first stage. By relying on this...
Based on the increase of wisdom, one should further understand the ten types of mind from the second bhūmi upward by inferring through analogy;
thus, it should be known that the *Avataṃsaka* contains numerous sets of ten dharma-gates, which should likewise be extensively analyzed according to this sequence.
However, because the primary tenet of this sūtra is that one enters the Vajra-Jewel Treasury immediately upon attaining the first bhūmi, each [stage] of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*...
Regarding the names and terms transmitted by the *ācārya*, one must provide two types of exegesis: first, the shallow and superficial explanation;

second, the profound and secret explanation. If one does not comprehend such secret designations and merely explains them according to the literal text, the causal phenomena will often overlap with those in the "Ten Abodes" chapter.
However, if one understands the generation of the sixteen great bodhisattvas from the *Vajraśekhara*, [the meaning is clarified].
This should be understood through the testimony of the sūtras. As it is said: "All that I have spoken is based upon this.

Thus, the entire ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), the realm of inexhaustible adornments (*akṣaya-vyūha-gocara*), and all other immeasurable sūtras praised by the Buddha—none of the fruits of all practices are obtained except through this. Therefore, other sūtras explain this extensively.
Having praised the trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the King of Śāla Trees, this sutra clarifies herein only the seed of this king of trees and the causes and conditions for its growth.
That one could produce such a fruit apart from these causes and conditions is impossible;
is it not for this reason that it is called the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra-king*? The sutra further cites the benefits to encourage practice, saying: "Therefore..."
The wise should contemplate that this stage of faith and understanding (*adhimukti-bhūmi*) of omniscience further transcends one *kalpa* before ascending and abiding in this stage;

this is the initial entry into this stage of faith and understanding. Furthermore, by transcending one hundred and sixty mental states (*citta*), the single layer of subtle afflictions is eliminated, which is termed "crossing over the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
When the practitioner first contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they realize that all phenomena enter [into it].

When the ultimate reality of the mind is such that one does not perceive below any sentient beings to be delivered, nor above any Buddhas to be sought, at that moment all myriad practices come to rest;
this is called the ultimate. If one dwells herein, one retreats from the higher stage of a Bodhisattva and does not fall into the level of the Two Vehicles;
it is termed the arising of "Dharma-attachment" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) and is also called the "indeterminate mind" (*avyākṛta-citta*). Nevertheless, by means of *bodhi*...
Through the power of the mind and the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgatas, one is further able to give rise to compassionate vows.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions appear simultaneously before one and provide exhortation.

Because of receiving these instructions from the Buddhas, one gives rise to a mind of ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), such that even the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the mind cannot be apprehended; thus, although one is liberated from all karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).
Yet, while karma and afflictions remain fully present until this inconceivable stage, it is only here that one is said to truly transcend the stages of the two vehicles.
Within the meaning of the preceding three phrases, the Buddha-ground is further opened as the "supremely superior expedient mind";
when one reaches this fourth mind, it is called the "ground of ultimate omniscience. Therefore, it is said: "These four quarters transcend the stage of faith and understanding."
The Sūtra says: At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, may the Savior of the World expound upon the characteristics of the mind:
how many kinds of bodhisattvas are there who attain the state of fearlessness, and so forth, until they shall attain the self-nature of all dharmas?"
The phrase "the equality of nature and fearlessness" is a response to the previous statement regarding the characteristics of the mind.
Since Vajrapāṇi, having heard this teaching, understood that all bodhisattvas directly ascend to the bodhisattva stages via the gateway of mantras, he asked the World-Honored One:
"When these bodhisattvas practice this path, how many kinds of grounds for attaining fearlessness are there? The Buddha, in turn, explained the distinctions based on the three preceding kalpas.
Regarding "āśvāsa" (明): in the Sanskrit sound it is *āśvāsa*, which in correct translation should be called "reviving.
It is like a person who, when seized by a powerful man and having his throat constricted so that his breath is cut off, is on the verge of fainting; suddenly being released, he returns to life.

Sentient beings are also like this: bound by the karma and afflictions of false conceptualization, they are blocked at every contact with conditions until they reach these six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Just as one who has attained rebirth is called "rested," so too, when crossing a perilous and evil path, the mind is serene and free from fear;

thus it is called the "state of fearlessness. The Buddha said: "O Lord of Mysteries, when those foolish, childish ordinary beings cultivate various wholesome dharmas and eliminate unwholesome dharmas, they shall attain wholesome fearlessness. The meaning of "wholesome" (śubha) applies to both the shallow and the profound.

The meaning intended here is as follows: Just as worldly people drift and sink into the evil realms due to the causes and conditions of the ten unwholesome paths of action without end, they may later attain the eight worldly thoughts and gradually receive the three refuges and precepts.

Thereafter, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, they are born among humans and devas, eventually reaching nirvana to escape the extreme sufferings of the three miserable paths; this is called the "initial" [attainment].

This is the place of rest. If a practitioner of *mantra* enters the *samaya* for the first time and practices the stage of offering to the Buddha through the three mysteries, it is equal to this [stage].
As the Sūtra says: "If one knows me as I truly am, one shall attain fearlessness of body.
This refers to when one practices the contemplation of the body and perceives that this body is a collection of thirty-six impure substances and five kinds of [impurities].
When one observes that the impurities are full and never gives rise to craving for them; furthermore, when one observes sensation, mind, and phenomena and attains detachment from them;

and when one does not observe a self-nature and finds a place of rest from the yoke and fetters of the four kinds of perversions regarding the body—at this stage, the practitioner of mantra practice is equal to the manifestation of the various signs of the deity’s samādhi. As the Sūtra says:

If, regarding this body of mine—which is a collection of the appropriated aggregates—one abandons its own physical form and contemplates that one shall attain the fearlessness of selflessness, it means that when one contemplates that there is only the aggregates and no self, and through various analyses and investigations within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, a self cannot be found;
one who thus abandons this own physical form is like a tree-shadow that appears because of a tree: if there is no tree, there is no shadow.
Since this shadow arises from what cause, and even these present five aggregates arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature, how much more so could there be a self within this collection?
As stated above, until one realizes the mind of profound stillness, free from all faults, one finds a place of rest from the shackles of the self.
For a practitioner of true mantra (*mantra-yāna*) within the sphere of yoga:
Within all segments of the realms (*dhātu*), one cannot find a mind that can be observed; the stage where craving and pride do not arise is equal to this.
The Sūtra says: "If one harms the abiding in the aggregates (*skandha*) and takes the Dharma as the object of focus, one shall attain fearlessness regarding the Dharma.

This means that when the practitioner’s mind abides within the aggregates with the desire to give rise to detachment, they then observe all phenomena by means of metaphors such as illusions and mirages.
The aggregates (*skandha*) are themselves emptiness; by attaining freedom from the eight mental states of attraction and aversion, one realizes the realm of tranquility (*śāntadhātu*).

One is able to leave behind the shackles of the aggregates and find a place of rest within phenomena (*dharma*). "Phenomena" here refers to the ten phrases of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

For the practitioner of *mantra-yoga*, when the state of present realization is like a reflection in a mirror or the moon in water—devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of arising—the temporal stage [of such realization] is equal to this.
The Sūtra states: "If one harms the abiding of phenomena by means of the objectless [state], one shall attain the fearlessness of the selflessness of phenomena.
This means that by observing the nature of the selflessness of phenomena with the mind of the objectless vehicle, one finds through wisdom that no images exist externally to the mind;

having attained mastery over the sovereign mind-king, one realizes that it is fundamentally unarisen. Thus, one becomes free from the yoke and bondage of phenomena and awakens to the selflessness of phenomena.
Regarding the state of cessation (*nirodha*): if a practitioner of mantra-ritual attains mastery within the path of yoga, their stage and timing will be equal to this.

As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, when the emptiness of all aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—whether as the grasper or the grasped, the self, the life-force, and so forth—and the emptiness of phenomena as being without objective support, without intrinsic nature, and without self-nature, arises as the wisdom of emptiness, one shall attain the self-nature of all phenomena."
"Equality of nature and fearlessness" refers to when one contemplates the ultimate emptiness of one's own mind:
the self, the aggregates, phenomena, and the objectless [condition] are all of one single nature, namely, the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

The arising of this wisdom of emptiness is precisely the arising of the mind that is utterly devoid of intrinsic nature. Because there is absolutely nothing to be bound by karma and afflictions, nor anything to be liberated from them.
When one realizes that the self-nature of all phenomena is equal, at that time, one finds a place of rest from the two kinds of yokes—the conditioned and the unconditioned realms.
This is precisely the bodhicitta of the space-like stainless practitioner of mantra.

Yet, whether this mind is within the bonds of affliction (*saṃsāra*) or has emerged from them, it is ultimately without characteristics; even when observed with the five eyes of a Tathāgata, it is not perceived.
If one can perceive the appearance of its image, how much more so for those within the cycle of birth and death?

The reason I have extensively clarified the three kalpas and the six states of fearlessness, as well as the manifold characteristics of the mind, is solely to provide a basis for deliberation regarding external traces, thereby elucidating the depth or shallowness of cultivation and realization.
Above, we have already clearly seen the signs of smoke; from this, one may infer the nature of fire by analogy. It is simply a matter of knowing that the defilements of the mind have been exhausted.
The non-occurrence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) within the [six] bases is itself the sixth ground of fearlessness; how could it be further represented?

The Sūtra says: "O Lord of Secrets, if bodhisattvas practicing the bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras deeply cultivate the contemplation of the ten phrases of dependent origination, they shall attain mastery and realization in the practice of mantra, and even come to know all things as they truly are."
The phrase "examining the characteristics of the mind" is a concise answer to the previous question regarding the section on "practice.

As will be seen below in the section on the "expedient means of the ten thousand practices," there is nothing that does not rely upon these phrases concerning the ten conditions for the arising [of phenomena] to purify the defilements of the mind.

Therefore, one should know that this is the most essential point. Practitioners of *mantra* (true speech) should especially apply their attention to it. However, when considering the ten conditions as a whole within this chapter:

The generation of the phrases is briefly of three kinds: first, for those whose minds are submerged in the aggregates (*skandha*) and who wish to counteract [the notion of] substantial dharmas, they contemplate these ten phrases of dependent origination as previously described—namely, that they are empty illusions;

second, for those whose minds are submerged in phenomena (*dharma*) and who wish to counteract the攀缘 (*ālambana*, objective clinging) toward objects, they contemplate these ten phrases of dependent origination as previously described.

The aggregates (*skandha*) are the illusion of the mind itself, which is the *ālaya*. Thirdly, because the mind has entered into the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the mind and seeks to transcend the realms of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one contemplates these ten phrases of dependent origination as previously explained;
thereby, one is liberated from all karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). Yet, karma and afflictions fully rely upon that which is the inconceivable illusion. This is the Mahāvaipulya.
If the ten intermediate metaphors also encompass these three meanings, then the phrase "profoundly cultivating observation" herein clarifies the third meaning.
For example, when a practitioner within yoga takes their own mind as the "sender" (the cause) and the Buddha-mind as the "respondent" (the condition),
through this causal condition of resonance, Vairocana immediately manifests a body pleasing to behold and speaks what is appropriate for them.
Upon hearing the Dharma, my own mind is ultimately pure, and the Buddha-mind is also ultimately pure.
If I regard my own mind as "self," then the Buddha-mind becomes "other. Now, regarding this state: does it arise from self, from other, from both, or without cause?
When examined through the various gateways of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, arising cannot be found; yet form and sound remain vividly present.

However, this is the discourse on the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the discourse on illusion as illusion, the discourse on the Dharma-realm as the Dharma-realm, and the discourse on illusion as pervading all places;
because it is an illusion that pervades all places, it is called the "inconceivable illusion.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "profound cultivation," it refers to the stage from having attained the pure mind onwards, from the generation of the root of great compassion until the ultimate perfection of skillful means.
Each and every link of dependent origination should be contemplated through ten metaphors; because that which is realized becomes increasingly profound, it is called "profound observation.
For instance, regarding the meaning of the Four Truths, even within the Sahā world alone there are already immeasurable and boundless distinctions of names;
how much more so, then, can the skillful means employed to accommodate the capacities of beings throughout the inexhaustible Dharma-realm ever be fully exhausted? Now, as for practice...

When one penetrates such sands-of-the-Ganges-like Four Noble Truths as empty within a single thought-moment of pure mind, then "emptiness" ultimately does not arise, "existence" exhausts its own nature and characteristics, and the "middle" is entirely eternal.
Because these three dharmas lack fixed characteristics, they are called the inconceivable illusion. As with the Four Noble Truths, so it is for all other dharma-gates; therefore—
Only the Tathāgata is able to exhaustively investigate these ten metaphors and reach their very source;
this is why, following the stainless bodhicitta, this sutra clarifies the ten metaphors—to encompass the beginning and the end, and to synthesize all the stages (*bhūmi*).
Since these are formed through contact with conditions and cannot be explained in detail, I shall now merely clarify their general significance according to the *Śāstra*.

The Sūtra says: "What are the ten? They are: like a magical illusion (*māyā*), a mirage (*marīci*), a dream (*svapna*), a reflection (*pratibimba*), a city of the Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*), an echo (*pratiśrutkā*), the moon in water (*udakacandra*), a bubble (*budbuda*), a flower in the sky (*ākāśapuṣpa*), and a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*). ... [It continues] "... What is meant by 'like a magical illusion'?

It is like how, through the power of mantras or medicinal herbs, various forms—both primary and derived elements—are produced, which deceive one's own eyes so that rare phenomena are seen, arising one after another."
They travel throughout the ten directions, yet they neither go nor do they not go. Why? Because their intrinsic nature is pure.
Thus, when this mantra-illusion is accomplished through recitation, it can give rise to all things. The Buddha taught that the power of medicine is inconceivable:
just as a person, by the power of medicine, ascends into space, becomes invisible, walks upon water, and treads upon fire—these matters are not within the scope of the various masters of logic.
One can establish the causal measures and discern their origins, yet it is not subject to doubt as to whether they must necessarily be thus or otherwise;
such errors arise from conceptualizing objects, whereas only those who personally practice this medicine, uphold it, and apply it can realize its truth for themselves.
Furthermore, although the various forms and images of the primary elements and their derivatives are manifested through the causal conditions of medicinal arts, [they remain as such].
If one seeks thoroughly among all conditions, not a single place of arising can be found; yet they appear clearly before the five senses.
Although they arise from one another and circulate throughout the ten directions, they neither go nor do they not go.
This matter is also not within the realm of calculation or conceptual deliberation. The *Śāstra* says: The Buddha asked the Lady Guṇavatī, "For example, it is like a magician and his illusions."
"What do you think regarding these various things that are produced? Is there anything within them that is produced by illusion? He replied, "No.
Again he asked, "Is there anything outside them, or both inside and outside, or from a previous life to this life, or from this life to a future life, that is produced by illusion?
Is there any real dharma whatsoever that is produced by illusion and subject to arising and ceasing? [He replied,] "No."
They all replied, "No. The Buddha said, "Have you ever seen or heard music produced by an illusion? They replied, "We have both seen it and heard it.
The Buddha said, "If an illusion is empty, deceptive, and without reality, how can music be produced from it?
The woman said, "Venerable One, such is the nature of illusory phenomena; although they lack a fundamental basis, they can still be heard and seen. The Buddha [approved].

It is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise: although it does not exist internally and so forth until the point of being without arising or cessation, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise with ignorance as their condition;
if ignorance is exhausted, the phenomena are also exhausted, and so on, as explained at length.

Now, in this gateway of mantras, the practitioner who maintains the recitation is also like this, as will be explained in detail below: by practicing according to the three secrets, one attains accomplishment.

Although all these extraordinary and inconceivable matters are, when minutely examined within each respective condition, ultimately free from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*), they are nonetheless such by the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and not otherwise;
thus, while the pure mind remains unchanged, the sovereign spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*) appear perfectly and without error.
This matter cannot be fathomed even by great masters of treatises who possess sharp faculties and eloquence; it can only be understood through skillful means (*upāya*).
Only those who have fully attained *siddhi* know this through their own realization.
As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries (*guhyapati*), the nature of a mirage is empty;

it is established based on the deluded conceptualizations of worldly people, and thus its discourse is such that the characteristics of mantras are merely provisional designations. The Commentary explains: "By means of sunlight and wind..."
Because it stirs up dust, it is like a mirage in a vast wilderness; when a person lacking wisdom first sees it, they call it water.

Sentient beings are likewise: the heat of the sun of the fetters and afflictions stirs the dust of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within the wind of false recollection in the wilderness of birth and death.
Those without wisdom perceive one aspect as male and another aspect as female.
Furthermore, if one sees something from afar and takes it to be water, yet upon approaching there is no appearance of water;

likewise, those who are far from the sublime Dharma do not know non-self and the emptiness of all phenomena. Within the phenomena that are empty by nature—the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—they give rise to conceptions of a person and so forth.
If they draw near to the sublime Dharma, they will know the true reality of all phenomena; at that time, all various delusive and false imaginings will be exhausted.

The meaning of this sutra is as follows: Just as when people look from afar, they merely perceive the appearance of these flames and arbitrarily establish provisional names for them, yet no actual substance can be found; thus it is said that "deluded conceptualization establishes what is spoken of.
This is like practitioners of True Word (Mantra) who, within yoga, perceive various extraordinary realms, even up to the Buddhas.

At that time, within the inexhaustible adornment of the ocean-like assembly, one should perform this mirage-contemplation (*marīci-vipaśyanā*). One realizes that [all things] are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti-mātra*) and is free from pride and attachment.
As one draws closer to the stage of the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*), one awakens to the various causes and conditions of empowered transformations (*adhiṣṭhāna-ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*);
these are nothing other than the radiance of the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, it is said: "The characteristics of such mantras are merely provisional designations."

The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, O Guhyakādhipati, just as that which is seen in a dream—such as days, muhūrtas, kṣaṇas, years, seasons, and so forth—appears as various distinct types of experiences of pleasure and pain, yet upon waking one sees nothing at all;
know that the mantra-practice of dreams is likewise. The Commentary explains: "Just as in a dream there is no real entity whatsoever, [it is said...]"

When one awakens from this and realizes it was non-existent, one laughs at oneself; people are just like this. While asleep under the influence of fetters (*saṃyojana*), things are actually non-existent, yet one gives rise to attachment.
Upon attaining the Way and awakening, one then knows they were non-existent and likewise laughs at oneself.

Furthermore, by the power of sleep, one sees phenomena where there are no phenomena: one feels joy where there is no cause for joy, anger where there is no cause for anger, and fear where there is no cause for fear.
The fear of sentient beings is likewise so: because of the power of the sleep of ignorance, one should not give rise to anger, joy, sorrow, or fear when encountering anger, joy, sorrow, or fear.
Therefore, it is now further clarified that this dream-event has an inconceivable dimension:
just as in a dream one sees oneself living for one day, two days, or even for immeasurable years, amidst various lands and species of sentient beings.
Beings may ascend to celestial palaces or undergo various sufferings and joys in the hells; yet upon awakening, it lasts but for a single thought-moment.
Within the causal conditions of the sleeping mind, one cannot find these four states through any investigation, yet the events of the dream are clearly remembered without error.
Thus, a single thought-moment is taken as ten million years, and a single mind is made into immeasurable realms. This is...
This matter is not something that can be fully fathomed through the conjectures, deliberations, or estimations of worldly wise men, nor is it a matter to be doubted;
it is known through the direct personal realization of those who have such a dream. Now, the yogic dreams of these practitioners of *mantra* are likewise:
in a mere moment, they may fully behold immeasurable realms of empowerment, or even without rising from their seats—
Throughout many kalpas, or by traveling through all Buddha-lands to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas for the benefit of sentient beings—
observing within all these causes and conditions that nothing at all arises, yet not departing from a single thought of pure mind, and moreover distinguishing things without error—
who could conceive of this? As for the reason why this is so, it can truly only be personally realized and known.

One who practices the contemplation of the ear-faculty attains such a realm; one should regard it solely through the metaphor of a dream, neither doubting nor being astonished by it, nor giving rise to attachment.
Because one employs the dream of the Universal Manifestation Body (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana*) to create inexhaustible adornments, it is said that "one deeply cultivates the ten phrases."
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, O Guhyapati, one should understand that mantras capable of producing siddhi are like a reflection;
just as a face appears in a mirror when the face is present before it, so too should the siddhi of those mantras be known.

Here, the term "reflection" refers to the analogy of an image in a mirror found in the commentary (*vyākhyā*). That treatise states: "Just as an image in a mirror is not created by the mirror, nor..."
The face does not create it; the mirror does not create it; it is not created spontaneously, nor is it created without causes and conditions.
Why is it not created by the mirror? Because if the face has not reached the mirror, there is no reflection. Why is it not created by the face? Because without the mirror, there is no reflection.

Why is it not created by the one holding the mirror? Because without the mirror and without the face, there is no reflection. Why is it not... [created by anything else]? Because without these conditions, there is no reflection.

It is produced spontaneously; yet, if there were no mirror and no face, there would be no reflection. A reflection depends upon the mirror, and the mirror depends upon the face, only then does it exist.
Therefore, it is also not without cause. If it were without causes and conditions, it should exist at all times;

if it existed at all times, it should appear on its own even apart from the mirror and apart from the face. For this reason, it is not without causes and conditions. One should know that all phenomena are likewise.

Thus, because the self is unapprehendable, because all phenomena produced by causes and conditions lack autonomy, and because all phenomena are dependent upon causes and conditions, they are not self-made;
since there is no self, there is likewise no other, and thus they are not made by another;
if they were made by another, then the power of demerit and merit would be lost; nor are they co-created, as that would entail two faults; nor are they causeless, as previously explained.
The karma of past lives arises from the conditions of good and evil deeds in the present life; from these, one obtains suffering or pleasure.
All phenomena necessarily have causes and conditions, yet because of ignorance, one does not know them. It is like a small child who, seeing a reflection in a mirror, feels joy and attachment;
having lost it, he breaks the mirror and searches for it. The wise laugh at him. To lose happiness and yet seek it further is likewise so.
One who acts thus is ridiculed by the sages who have attained the Way. Now, within this Mantra-gate, one takes the purification of the body through the Three Mysteries of the Tathāgata as a mirror;
the practice of the Three Mysteries of one’s own body is the image within that mirror. Through these causes and conditions, *siddhi* arises, just like a facial reflection.
When the practitioner achieves *siddhi*, they may even give rise to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and abide for a long duration of life.

Beholding the lands of the ten directions and traveling through the various Buddha-fields, one should observe this matter by means of this very analogy: does it arise from oneself, or does it arise from another?

If you claim that the empowerment of the three secrets of others can bestow this fruit, then why, when sentient beings have not yet practiced, does the Great Compassion of the Buddhas—not being partial—fail to cause them to achieve accomplishment? If, on the other hand, you claim that one must act according to what one says...
If one can obtain this fruit [of accomplishment], what need is there to contemplate the body of the pure mirror of the three secrets and seek empowerment?

If they were co-arisen, there would be two faults. Why is this? If you claim that my own mind is the cause and that it only achieves accomplishment by depending on those various conditions, does the fruit of *siddhi* already exist within this cause? Or does it not exist beforehand? If it exists beforehand...

If [the result] already exists, the various conditions would have no function; yet if it does not exist beforehand, what further use would the various conditions have? Nevertheless, the accomplishment of *siddhi* is likewise not without causes and conditions.
Thus, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom), in its verse on the mirror-image, says: "It is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent;
such words are not even accepted. This is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). It should not be understood in the manner of those [Hīnayānists].

Because the child gives rise to false attachments, one should contemplate in this way; thus, because the practitioner’s mind attains nothing and does not produce conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is said:
"One should know it thus. The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, O Guhyakādhipati, the palace of the accomplished *siddhi* is understood through the analogy of a city of Gandharvas."
The *Śāstra* commentary states: When the sun first rises, one sees city gates, watchtowers, palaces, and people coming and going;

as the sun rises higher, these things gradually vanish. Although this city can be seen with the eyes, it has no real existence. There are those who have never seen it before and, believing it to be truly delightful, hasten toward it;
yet the closer they draw, the more it disappears. As the sun grows high, it finally vanishes, leaving them in extreme distress from hunger and thirst.
Seeing a hot vapor like a mirage and calling it water, one again goes toward it; even upon seeking it until exhausted, nothing is seen.
Through contemplation, one awakens to this for oneself and the thirsting desire ceases. The practitioner is also like this:
when, through wisdom, they know there is no self and no real dharmas, at that time the inverted desires cease. In the Śrāvaka sūtras, this [account of] the *gandharva* does not exist.

The analogy of the city of Vārāṇasī further uses a city to represent the body; it explains that while these various conditions truly exist, the city is merely a conventional designation used to refute the notion of a self (*ātman*).
Because Bodhisattvas possess sharp faculties and have deeply entered the emptiness of all phenomena, they employ the analogy of a *gandharva-nagara* (an illusory city).
Here, it is said that the palace of *siddhi* has superior, middling, and inferior levels; "superior" refers to the Land of Secret Adornment (*Guhyavimala*), which transcends [all others].

The three realms are not what can be seen or heard by those of the Two Vehicles; "in the midst" refers to the pure lands of the ten directions, and "below" refers to the palaces of the devas and asuras.
When a practitioner attains the status of a vidyādhara of the three grades, they dwell within such a palace of siddhi;
one should contemplate this through the analogy of how the conditions of ocean mist and sunlight give rise to the magnificent, tiered layers of a city.
The figures on the altar are resplendent and worthy of contemplation; one should not, like those foolish people, give rise to groundless greed and attachment by seeking their physical reality.
By means of these causes and conditions, one’s pure mind will remain unimpeded amidst the various kinds of excellent and wondrous five sensory objects.
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, O Guhyapati, one should understand the sound of mantras through the analogy of an echo.
Just as an echo arises from sound due to conditions, so too should the practitioner of mantras understand it. The commentary explains:

"Whether in deep mountain ravines, in deep and secluded gullies, or within vast empty halls, because the characteristics of vocal sounds strike against one another, sound arises from sound; this is called an echo."
To those who lack wisdom, an echo appears to be something real; however, the wise person reflects that this sound is not produced by anyone, but arises merely through the transformation of sound.
Furthermore, an echo deceives the faculty of hearing. When a person wishes to speak, there is wind within the throat and mouth called *udāna*;
it descends back to the navel, and upon striking the navel, the echo emerges. As the echo emerges, it strikes the crown of the head and the palate.

When [the breath] recedes through the seven locations—the teeth, lips, tongue, throat, and chest—this is called the "linguistic delusion" of the ignorant, who fail to understand it and thereby give rise to the three poisons.
The wise, however, clearly realize that the mind has no attachment; they merely follow the true mark of all phenomena.
Thus, when a practitioner of the True Word hears within yoga the various sounds of the eight winds, whether adverse or favorable, or when the various sages [speak] with immeasurable...
The Dharma-sound manifests before one through instruction, or because the faculty of the tongue is purified, such that one can use a single voice to pervade all worlds.
When encountering these various objective spheres, one should also observe them by means of the analogy of an echo: this phenomenon arises solely from the collective conditions of the three secrets;
it is neither born nor extinguished, neither existent nor non-existent. Therefore, one should not give rise to false conceptions regarding it.
At that time, frivolous conceptualization itself enters the dharma-gate of the wisdom of sound.

The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, O Guhyakādhipati, just as when the moon rises it illuminates clear water and the reflection of the moon appears therein, so too should the mantra be explained by the Vidyādhara through the analogy of the moon in water. The Commentary states:

Just as the moon moves through the void of space while its reflection appears in water, so too does the moon-disk of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) abide within the space of the suchness of reality (tathatā-bhūtakoṭi),
yet to the "water" of the ordinary person's mind, the marks of "I" and "mine" appear. Furthermore,
just as a small child sees the moon in the water and joyfully desires to seize it, while an adult merely laughs at this, so it is with those lacking wisdom.
Because of the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), one perceives a self; because of the lack of true wisdom, one perceives various phenomena.

Having perceived them, one rejoices and desires to grasp at their marks. The noble ones who have attained the Path laugh at this. Furthermore, it is like seeing the reflection of the moon in water: if the water is stirred, the moon is no longer seen.

In the same way, when the mind is agitated by ignorance, one sees the reflections of a self, pride, and the various fetters (saṃyojana); but when the water of the mind is stilled by true wisdom, these are no longer seen.
If one stirs the water of the mind with a staff, one will not see [the reflection]. For this reason, it is said that bodhisattvas know phenomena to be like the moon in water.

Likewise, for the practitioners of vidyā-mantras, because their own minds are clarified and purified through the skillful means of the three secrets, the oceanic assemblies of the Secret Adornments (Guhyasamaya) of all Buddhas appear therein;
or else, by means of their own wish-fulfilling jewel body, they appear within the minds of all sentient beings.
When it appears in water, at that time one should contemplate with clarity: does this present form of Ghanavyūha arise from my pure mind, or does it arise from the pure body of the Buddha?
Since even the true nature of self and other is ultimately unarisen, how much more so could anything arise from discordant causes and conditions?
It is like the moon reflected in all rivers, wells, ponds, and various vessels, large and small.
The pure moon neither comes from the waters nor goes away, yet its single orb can universally enter into all the waters;
I am now likewise thus. The minds of sentient beings do not come from elsewhere, nor does my own mind go anywhere, yet those who see or hear me receive benefit that is truly not in vain.
One should stir them with the staff of wisdom so that they may know there is no reality, and not allow them to grasp at such [appearances].
That infant wishes to employ skillful means to seize it as a plaything;

yet, being able to naturally still his own mind and remaining unmoved in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*), he shall expound it for others. Therefore, it is said that the *vidyādhara* should speak in this manner.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, O Guhyapati, just as rain falling from the heavens produces bubbles, so too should one know that the various transformations of the siddhis of mantras are likewise.

Although the Śrāvaka sūtras use the metaphor of receiving [the rain] as floating bubbles, and the Prajñāpāramitā uses the bubble as a simile because they lack substantial nature, they nevertheless arise truly through causes and conditions; thus, among the ten phrases, there is that which is "like a transformation" (nirmāṇa).
Furthermore, the meaning of the simile of the bubble in this present sutra is also distinct from that [previous explanation].
For example, during the summer rains, as rain falls from the sky, various bubbles arise within the water according to the size of each drop; their forms and types differ from one another.

Yet, the nature of water is of a single flavor, acting as its own causal condition. When sought through the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*), there is no separate entity produced apart from it. Therefore, this bubble—
The entire body arises as a bubble from conditions; when the bubble arises, it is the water arising, and when the bubble ceases, it is the water ceasing.

Therefore, by means of this analogy, one understands the transformations of the mind itself. Just as a practitioner creates a Buddha with their own mind and is in turn graced by that mental Buddha’s skillful means of instruction and awakening, thereby entering immeasurable Dharma-gates, so too does one take the mind as the maṇḍala; this objective realm and the mind [are non-dual].
Because they serve as conditions for performing various inconceivable transformations, the practitioner contemplates them through the analogy of bubbles;

realizing that these do not exist apart from one's own mind, one does not give rise to attachment. The *Śāstra* further states: "Those who cultivate meditative concentration possess fourteen [powers];
even devas, nāgas, and spirits can manifest transformations. These manifested forms were previously non-existent, yet they arise solely through the power of meditative concentration."
When the mind arises, it arises; when the mind ceases, it ceases. Furthermore, this dharma has no beginning, middle, or end;
its arising comes from nowhere, and its cessation goes nowhere. One should know that all dharmas are likewise.
Moreover, like the characteristics of a transformation, they are pure like space, unstained by attachment, and unsullied by either sin or merit. All dharmas are also thus.
The nature of your dharmas is suchness, the limit of reality, naturally and eternally pure.

It is like the four great rivers of Jambudvīpa, each having five hundred small rivers as its retinue; though these waters are variously impure, once they enter the great ocean, they all become completely pure.
This is the same meaning as the analogy of the bubble.

The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, O Guhyapati, just as in space there are no sentient beings and no life-span, and no agent can be found, so too do these various false views arise due to the confusion of the mind. The Commentary explains:
"Regarding 'like space,' it means that there is only a name but no real dharma; space is not a visible phenomenon, for it is seen from a distance."
When the visual faculty turns and perceives a pale blue color, all phenomena are likewise thus: empty and devoid of a person.
Because one is far removed from untainted, true wisdom, one abandons the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and perceives various miscellaneous things such as self and other, men and women, houses, and cities.
The mind clings to them as if a small child looking up at the blue sky were to think there is actual color there, or that a person is flying up to a place of extreme distance.
There is nothing to be seen, and its nature is eternally pure like empty space. People say that the aggregates (*skandha*) are impure, yet all phenomena are likewise eternally pure in their nature.
Because of the "film" of lust, hatred, and so forth, people call them impure.
This sutra says that those whose minds are deluded and distracted are like people whose minds become confused due to various causes and conditions, such as illness or non-human spirits (*amanuṣya*).
In the pure, empty sky of deluded and false views, various forms of persons appear—some terrifying, others enticing.
When one recovers the original mind, one realizes that such phenomena do not defile the empty space when they arise, nor do they return to purity when they cease.
Originally, they do not obstruct the empty space, nor are they different from it. Thus should the practitioner cultivate meditative observation.
At that time, if various demonic activities, karmic conditions, and the objects of affliction arise, one should settle the mind in this analogy:
just as pure empty space remains unimpeded even while dwelling in the hells for immeasurable eons,
so too does the mind— like one who has attained supernatural powers— fly freely within the single manifest color of space, untroubled by the delusions of persons and phenomena.
...that which is defiled by dust and grime.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, O Guhyapati, it is like a firebrand; if a person holds it in their hand and whirls it through the air, a wheel-like image arises.
Just as when a person whirls a firebrand through the air, various forms are produced."
The forms may be square, circular, triangular, crescent-shaped, large, small, long, or short, produced according to one’s will;

the foolish and ignorant perceive them as real entities and give rise to attachment, yet in truth no phenomena are produced at all, but rather the power of swift movement within the hand can manifest a single fire into immeasurable forms.
Thus, when a practitioner of *mantra* follows [these instructions] within *yoga*,...
Whatever the mind directs shall be accomplished without exception; even through the single gateway of the letter A, by revolving without obstruction, one accomplishes immeasurable Dharma-gates.
At that time, one should cultivate this contemplation: it is brought about solely by the power of the swift application of the single essence of the pure bodhicitta.
One should not give rise to various views within this, nor engage in conceptual proliferation by reckoning it as superior or sublime.

Furthermore, the *Śāstra* (commentary) provides a metaphor of a shadow distinct from the metaphor of the fire-wheel, stating: "Just as a shadow can be seen but cannot be grasped, so too are all phenomena;
the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing by the eye-consciousness and other faculties are in reality unobtainable.

Moreover, just as a shadow appears when light shines upon it but is absent when it does not, so too do the fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*) appear as the mark of self (*ātman-saṃjñā*) when they obstruct the light of right view."

The characteristics of phenomena are like a shadow: when the person departs, the shadow departs; when the person moves, the shadow moves; and when the person stands still, the shadow stands still. The shadows of good and evil karma are likewise so:
when one departs for the next life, they depart; while one remains in this life, they remain. Because the retribution is never severed, they emerge when the offenses or merits have ripened.
Yet these shadows are not substantial entities; they are merely phenomena that deceive the eye, like a whirling firebrand.
The rapid transformation of embers into a wheel is likewise not substantially real; the intended meaning of this metaphor is essentially the same.

O Lord of Secrets, you should understand in this way the phrases of the Mahāyāna: the phrase of the mind, the phrase of the unequaled, the phrase of the definitive, the phrase of the perfectly awakened, and the phrase of the gradual arising of the Mahāyāna. In the Sanskrit language, "phrase" (*pada*) has the meaning of *bimba*.

The preceding explanation of these ten metaphors shows that they all pertain to the profound dependent origination of the Mahāyāna practitioners, and are not a place where Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can find footing;
therefore, they are called the "Mahāyāna phrases. The true nature of the mind cannot be displayed by any other dharma, nor can it be transmitted to others;
yet, when one observes deeply in this manner, the clouds of hindrances and obscurations are stripped away.

Because it is that which one must personally realize and know for oneself, it is called the "phrase of mind. Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom has no analogue among all phenomena and nothing surpasses it, it is called "unequaled" (*asama*).
Yet, because the true nature of the mind corresponds to this wisdom like a lid fitting its box, with no interval between them, it is called "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*).
If one understands the locus of the mind through the ten conditions of dependent origination, then...

Because one abides therein, it is called the "Incomparable Phrase. By means of this principle of the tenfold dependent origination, the Buddhas definitively proclaim the lion’s roar of the Tathāgata-nature, the mind, and the seal of the true mark (*dharmatā*).

If there are those capable of faith and understanding, even if all the Māras in the worlds of the ten directions were to manifest as Buddhas and preach a counterfeit *prajñā*, they could not [overcome them].
Because one transforms the mind so that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are no longer as they appear, it is called the "phrase of certainty.

Because one uses this Middle Way of right contemplation to depart from the realms of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and because the ultimate lack of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) gives rise to the manifestation of the Buddha-mind within the very nature of the mind, it is called the "phrase of perfect enlightenment.
Because one practices profound observation, it is like entering the great ocean, where the depths gradually increase further and further.

Because one can only exhaust its source and bottom by means of the highest-of-the-high wisdom (*uttarottara-jñāna*) upon reaching Vairocana, it is called the "phrase for the arising of the gradual Great Vehicle.
One should know that these six phrases thus explain each other in sequence and arise in sequence.
Vairocana adorns this inconceivable *dharmadhātu* of the ten phrases of dependent origination with inexhaustible ornaments.

From the gates of the dharma-realm of all Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds, there constantly emerge the jewels of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, and liberations;
because these are bestowed universally upon sentient beings without ever being exhausted, it is said that they are "endowed with the wealth of Dharma.
Because the wisdom-activities of all Tathāgatas are fully perfected through this, it is said that they "give birth to various great wisdoms of craftsmanship."

If, within a single thought-moment, one clearly perceives the ten meanings of dependent origination, then one reaches upward to the inexhaustible Dharma-realm and downward to the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings;
all mental phenomena therein can be fully and clearly awakened to and known.
Because they all arise from conditions—being simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way—it is said that one "truly and universally knows all mental phenomena," O Ajātaśatru.

Liyan said: "When the practitioner first cultivates contemplative practice and the meditative objects manifest before them, through the power of internal causes and external conditions, the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-jñāna*) arises spontaneously;
this is not like the common approach where one must exert effort in cultivating concentration until, after great hardship, one finally attains thorough penetration.
In the Sanskrit original, it says that following this, the sequence for the recitation of mantras is explained as follows:"
The *Dharmasiddhi* is like the fruit produced according to the Dharma; this is because it was recorded by the transmitters of the Dharma.

Therefore, its general meaning is not set forth in detail within the sūtras. Having already explained the purification of the bodhicitta and the characteristics of all minds, from here below, the skillful means for further cultivation and the arising of the fruit of *siddhi* are clarified.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-tathāgatādhiṣṭhāna-vikurvita-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra, Scroll Two.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-tathāgatādhiṣṭhāna-vikurvita-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra, Scroll Three.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Yi-hang.
Chapter Two: The Mantra Chapter on the Requisites for Entering the Maṇḍala.

Regarding the "Mantra Chapter on the Requisites for Entering the Maṇḍala": In the preceding chapter, the "Supreme Chapter," all aspects of the mind of omniscience were established through various corresponding mental states.
Now, by what skillful means can this sublime fruit be attained? Therefore, [this chapter follows].
This chapter clarifies the ritual procedures for entering the maṇḍala; its various auxiliary conditions, constituent parts, and required mantras are all explained in detail herein.

It is like knowing that milk, curd, and *ghṛta* possess the nature of *maṇḍa*: one is then instructed to prepare the necessary vessels and employ skillful means such as churning and stirring so that [the essence] arises through conditions.
Therefore, it should be understood that this is not different from the ten phrases on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, in the Śrāvaka sūtras, the Vinaya is treated as a secret treasury; it is bestowed only after carefully selecting the individual and screening the assembly.
If one has not yet generated the restraint of discipline (śīla-saṃvara), they are not permitted to hear it. In the Mahāyāna, the vidyā-mantras are likewise treated as a secret treasury;
those who have not entered the maṇḍala are not permitted to read, recite, or receive them. This is identical to the prohibition against eavesdropping.

One incurs grave karmic retribution for this reason: just as when a worldly person compassionately nurtures an infant, even though they have no reluctance in their heart, they would not hand over a sword such as Ganjiang or Moye;
because the child does not know the skillful means of its use, it will surely injure its own body.
This Dharma-gate is likewise: the profound intent of attaining Buddhahood through the very mind is difficult to comprehend, and one fears that [the practitioner] has not yet [mastered it].
Because future sentient beings will treat the Dharma with contempt, they will be unable to seek out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Failing to receive the empowerment of the three mysteries (*triguhyādhiṣṭhāna*), they will instead follow their own arbitrary minds, clinging to the literal text to practice on their own. Though they exert effort for a long time, they will achieve nothing;

instead, they will slander this sutra, claiming it was not spoken by the Buddha. Furthermore, regarding the text of this sutra, there are two interpretations: the superficial and the profound and secret. As for the profound and secret interpretation:
Within this explanation, there are further levels of depth and shallowness. Those who peruse it haphazardly fail to understand the secret designations;
consequently, they give rise to arrogance and contempt based on causal phenomena and conditioned marks, saying, "I practice the True Path—what use have I for incantations and rituals?
Due to such causes and conditions, they incur the karma of obstructing the Dharma and fall into the evil realms for immeasurable kalpas. Therefore, one must cultivate...
Those who study mantras must first enter the maṇḍala. The definition and significance of the term "maṇḍala" shall be explained further below.
The Sūtra states: At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is marvelous, World-Honored One, that you have spoken these..."
The Buddha, having personally realized the inconceivable Dharma-realm of *sambodhi* that transcends the ground of the mind,
manifests the body of a Tathāgata through all its constituent parts for the sake of those sentient beings from their first aspiration up to the tenth stage;
thus he pervades the ten directions and returns to his original position as the Buddha-body, wherein he abides— this is the Golden [Buddha].
Vajrapāṇi, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, understood the preceding passage and first praised the World-Honored One as being most extraordinary,
for it is by virtue of possessing great skillful means that he is able to expound this self-realized *sambodhi* of all Buddhas— namely,
the inconceivable *dharmadhātu* which is self-awakened within one's own mind, transcending all stages of the mind, and being without dependence, just like space.
When ordinary people lift their feet or move them, they all rely upon the earth; the Bodhisattva is likewise thus, for he proceeds by relying on the mind.
Therefore, this mind is called "earth" (*bhūmi*). Because the mind still has something upon which it relies, it is not yet termed "Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" (*samyaksambuddha*).

The Tathāgata has already crossed over this subtle conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and because his forward progress has entirely ceased, it is called "transcending the stage of the mind. Although it is ultimate...
That which is quiescent and ineffable can yet, through various skillful means (*upāya*), expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings according to their natural dispositions and inclinations;
this is precisely the realization of the traces of the inexhaustible adornment of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).
The inconceivable *dharmadhātu* is metaphorically likened to the lotus pedestal, while the various skillful means are likened to the lotus [itself].

In this section on the "Understanding of the Flower and Leaf," although the text is concise, it encompasses the subtle and wondrous principles of the *zongtong* (the penetration of the essence) without exception.

Next, [the practitioner] requests the Buddha: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will next explain the Great Maṇḍala King, the Matrix of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*), which gives birth to the practice of the true words and deeds.
For now, we shall take the *taizang* (matrix) as a metaphor: when a practitioner first gives rise to all...
The wisdom-mind, through the causal conditions of the union of father and mother, first takes refuge in the womb as the seed of consciousness.
At that time, it gradually grows and is fashioned by the skillful winds of karma, until the moment of birth, when all the sense faculties and the hundred parts of the body are fully complete.
Thus one is born into the lineage of one's parents, just like one who trains according to the gateway of mantras.
The pure mind of the ten thousand practices of great compassion manifests; furthermore, this infant gradually acquires the human and dharmic training in various arts and crafts.

Once proficiency in these arts is attained, one engages in worldly activities, initiating skillful means from within the pure mind to cultivate and refine oneself and others, benefiting all according to conditions and delivering sentient beings.
Therefore, it is called "birth from the womb of great compassion. Furthermore, at the beginning...
Entering the gate of the pure bodhicitta, one perceives the path of the illumination of dharmas, like the stage of the *kalala* when the seed of consciousness has emerged;
from the first through the seventh grounds, one is nurtured by the myriad practices of great compassion, as if dwelling within the womb without deliberate effort;
thereafter, one gradually studies the skillful means of the Tathāgata, just as an infant who has already been born practices various arts until reaching the state of a Tathāgata.
The ground of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*) is like a mastery of arts already perfected and applied to governance;
therefore, it is called the "Womb of Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*), which is yet another secret maṇḍala. Now, the meaning of this maṇṇḍala is illustrated by the metaphor of the lotus:
just as the nature of the branches, flowers, and leaves is already fully present within the hard shell of a lotus seed, so too is it here.
The worldly seed-mind gradually increases from this point until the time of the initial emergence of the flower bud;
at that stage, the lotus pedestal and fruit are concealed within the sheath of petals, just as the supramundane mind still remains within the aggregates (*skandhas*).

Furthermore, because it is enveloped by this sheath of petals, it is not damaged or destroyed by external conditions such as wind or cold, and its pure-colored filaments and anthers grow day and night.
Its flourishing is like the Great Compassion Womb Matrix (Mahākaruṇā-garbha-kośa), which, once fully accomplished, manifests and blooms within the light of the sun;
this is like the fulfillment of skillful means. Now, herein lies the meaning of the Maṇḍala of the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma:

the original ground of Vairocana’s eternal mind is the concrete embodiment of the Flower Treasury (Kusuma-alaṃkāra), wherein the four Buddhas and four Bodhisattvas represent the fruit-virtue of the Supreme Essence (Sarpireya).
The multitude of actualities together constitute ten world-systems of atoms of vajra-secret wisdom and various marks of knowledge, like the filaments of a flower;
ten world-systems of atoms of the gates of the ten thousand practices of great compassion and the pāramitās, like the treasury of flowers;
and the immeasurable response-bodies of the three vehicles and six paths, like the roots, stems, branches, and leaves, emitting radiance in alternating patterns. Thus it is.
Because all these manifold virtues are perfectly complete and encompassing, it is called a *maṇḍala*.
Furthermore, through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata, the body of the Central Matrix (*garbha*) with eight petals manifests from the virtue of the Buddha’s self-realized *bodhi*;
from the Vajra-seal (*vajramudrā*), the first circle of inner retinue members such as Vajrapāṇi manifests; and from the myriad practices of great compassion, the second [circle] manifests.

Furthermore, the Mahāsattvas and their great retinues manifest through the skillful means of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) in the third tier bodies that accord with the various types of all sentient beings.
If one were to compare these to the ritual of consecration for a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), then the third tier would be like the sovereign rulers of the myriad nations;
the second tier would be like the various officials of the imperial court; and the first tier would be like the members of the royal lineage.
The central womb (garbhadhātu) is like a sovereign who governs with effortless ease; thus, the Flowered Terrace of Constant Wisdom is the Great Maṇḍala King.
If one considers the descent of traces from the source, then from each individual gate of the central womb, various gates of the first enclosure flow forth;
from each individual gate of the first enclosure, various gates of the second enclosure flow forth; and from the second...
Each of the individual gates of the second level further flows forth various gates of a third level.
If the causal practice reaches its fruition, it is then subsumed by the third level, whereby it can penetrate the second level;
being subsumed by the second level, it can penetrate the first level; and being subsumed by the first level, one is able to perceive the central matrix (*garbha*).
Speaking from this perspective, although the innate dispositions and inclinations of all classes of sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless,
the purpose and benefit of this maṇḍala dharma-gate are likewise exhaustive and leave nothing undone; therefore,
it is said that it is for the sake of fulfilling those immeasurable sentient beings of future ages, and for their protection, rescue, peace, and happiness.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the Bhagavat Vairocana, having surveyed the great assembly, addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries, saying: 'Listen attentively, Vajrapāṇi!
I shall now expound the Dharma-gate for fulfilling all-knowledge through the practice of the maṇḍala. Herein, this great assembly is itself the maṇḍala of the Dharmadhātu.'"

Regarding those sentient beings to be delivered who are encompassed by the *ra* [of *araṇa*], the Buddha now wishes to expound the profound and secret conduct so that their capacity for the Path may not fail;

thus, he observes them universally with the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*). It is through the empowerment of this very eye of wisdom that the sprouts of virtue from previous lives are all brought to full development—just as when good seeds have already been sown in a fertile field, it is then capable of receiving the bounty of the seasonal rain.
Furthermore, this "brahmic sound" (*brāhmaṇī*) is precisely the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*) and the meaning of "path" (*mārga*).

That is to say, from a single thought-moment of wholesome roots until the attainment of Buddhahood, all the dharmas mounted upon during each of the successive stages (*bhūmi*) and the paths traversed therein are collectively termed *yāna*.
Within the maṇḍala, the various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are like those who construct the vehicle, prepare the path, and provide guidance.
Those sentient beings who practice by means of this vehicle are said to be practicing the maṇḍala; this practice is called *caryā* in Sanskrit.

Furthermore, as stated in the subsequent text: "First, for the sake of the disciple, one selects and prepares level ground. If one discusses external matters, it is as explained in the usual commentaries.
However, for the sake of the deluded ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one selects the seed-mind of a single thought that observes the fast (*upoṣadha*) and treats it so as to make it level.

"Correctness" (*samyaktva*) is also called "cultivating the ground" (*bhūmi-parikarman*). This extends even to the stage of a Bodhisattva who is destined for one more birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*), where one selects away and removes the most subtle defilements—the very parents of ignorance—from within the mind; this too is called "cultivating the ground.

From this perspective, how many layers of the meaning of "cultivating the ground" are contained within each phrase of the sutra? For example, the ten phrases on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) all proceed through gradual stages.
It is profound and inexhaustible. Vajrapāṇi made such an exhortation, and each Buddha sealed it with this very mudrā before expounding it;
therefore, it is called the Dharma-gate that fulfills the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
If this ground were not fulfilled, one would be unable to universally provide protection, rescue, and peace for all sentient beings.

The Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana, because he had fulfilled his original vows from the past to liberate the entire realm of sentient beings without exception throughout the inexhaustible Dharma-realm, all Tathāgatas gathered together and gradually entered the samādhi called 'The Arising of the Treasury of Great Compassion.
This was because when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, he established [this vow] as follows:"
