This vow was that I should accomplish all Buddha-dharmadhātus and deliver the entire realm of sentient beings without exception;
now that my vow is fulfilled, yet the sentient beings to be delivered are not exhausted—for the inexhaustibility of sentient beings is itself the inexhaustibility of the dharmadhātu.
There are three kinds of realms: namely, the dharmadhātu, the mind-realm, and the sentient-being realm.

The realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is not distinct from the realm of sentient beings; the realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of phenomena. Apart from the realm of mind, there is no separate realm of phenomena;
the realm of phenomena is itself the realm of mind. One should know that these three are non-dual and without distinction.

To further explain the meaning of the realm of phenomena, it is stated here that there is "no remainder of the realm of sentient beings," because the realm of sentient beings has not yet been attained [as such].
Because all liberations have not yet attained the universal fulfillment of the *dharmadhātu*, the Tathāgatas diligently cultivate their enlightened activities without rest.
Precisely due to these causes and conditions of their original vows, all Tathāgatas assemble together;

it is like when there is a matter of great importance within the Saṃgha—such as the formal demarcation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*) or the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*)—whereupon the assembly of monks gathers.
Having assembled together, they collectively uphold [this teaching] because they share a single precept and a single view; therefore, one should not remain apart from the assembly.
Now, I shall explain the Dharma-gate that fulfills the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), which is also the great causal occasion for the affairs of all Buddhas.
Because they share the same original vow and the same Dharma-realm, they have all gathered together and collectively empower it through their spiritual powers (ṛddhi). One realizes it progressively.
Entering [the mandala] is as follows: the first fearlessness consists of practicing the mandala rite by contemplating sounds and syllables;

the second fearlessness consists of practicing the mandala rite within the contemplation of signs; the third fearlessness consists of practicing the mandala rite within the mind that perceives only the aggregates and no self;
and the fourth fearlessness consists of practicing the mandala rite within the mind that takes phenomena as its object.
The fifth fearlessness consists of practicing maṇḍala rites within a mind free of objective conditions; the sixth fearlessness consists of practicing maṇḍala rites within a mind of equanimity.
From the Vimalā-bhūmi (Stainless Ground) onward, one practices maṇḍala rites by contemplating the mind within each respective stage.
Briefly categorized according to these stages of practice, they are distinguished into sixteen layers of varying depth.

Each of these stages possesses its own seed of bodhi, a mind containing the embryonic matrix (*garbha*) of great compassion, the causal conditions for growth, and the fruit of the enjoyment of wisdom and skillful means, as previously described. From each individual gate, various gates flow forth;

therein, when proceeding from cause toward fruit, the skillful means of the three mysteries (*triguhyaprayoga*) differ successively. *Note: The term "三密" (sānmì) refers to the three secrets of the Buddha-body, speech, and mind.*
Only when one reaches the great ocean of the ultimate mind-king will there be but a single flavor without distinction.
Now, when the Buddhas of the ten directions were practicing the bodhisattva path in their past lives, each followed a single dharma-gate to reach the ground of omniscience.

Having set forth to expound the causes and conditions for the universal gate of all practices, they have together entered this Great Compassion Womb Matrix Samādhi (Mahākaruṇā-garbha-samādhi), which accords with what they have cultivated from the beginning.
As one gradually enters the stages of practice and contemplates each one individually— just as when a Bodhisattva practices dhyāna,

they enter and emerge from the nine successive concentrations in both forward and reverse order, with absorption and dispersion, by skipping stages, leaping over them, and through the display of mastery— all with complete sovereignty;
so too it is with these Tathāgatas’ gradual entry into the samādhi that generates the treasury of great compassion— or [alternatively,]...
Contemplate the inexhaustible Dharma-realm by taking all minds as one mind and all gates as one gate;
or contemplate the realm of sentient beings without exception by taking one mind as all minds and one gate as all gates.
If these sixteen layers of profound meaning are used to comprehensively encompass the twelve divisions of the scriptures both horizontally and vertically, then they will revolve.
It is inexhaustible.
As the Sūtra says: "World-Honored One, all limbs and parts manifest the body of the Tathāgata.

Previously, when the *Vyūharatnakośa* (Treasury of Adornments) was manifested, each individual body of the Universal Gate (*Samantamukha*) pervaded the ten directions, responding to conditions and objects as appropriate. Now, I wish to explain the *Maṇḍala*.
Because the positions within the *cakra* diagram are established according to the Buddha’s own body, they are divided into categories based on its upper, middle, and lower parts.
From the navel downward, the manifested birth-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni appears, demonstrating his conformity to human laws.

Furthermore, the various forms, colors, images, dignified demeanors, speech, sounds, altars, and seats of the three vehicles and the six realms of existence are each distinct; likewise, their respective retinues differ from one another in successive gradations.
Throughout the eight directions, they abide in order according to their original positions within the maṇḍala;

from the navel up to the throat, there appear immeasurable bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), each manifesting the body of the three secrets and accompanied by immeasurable retinues, abiding throughout the eight directions in order according to their original positions within the maṇḍala. Furthermore, herein there are two [aspects].
From the heart downward are the retinues of ten buddha-fields of atoms, who uphold the myriad practices of great compassion;
from the heart upward are the inner retinues of ten buddha-fields of atoms, who uphold the secret wisdom of the Vajra.
These are collectively termed the "Great Mind Assembly. From the throat upward, reaching to the Tathāgata’s cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), appear the four wisdoms and the four [mudrās].
The bodies of the Buddhas who have realized the fruit of their merit consist of these eight bodies; in all worlds, their retinues, buddha-fields, names,
physical actions, and various matters of enjoyment are entirely different, yet they abide in the eight directions according to their respective positions in the fundamental order of the maṇḍala.

The Sūtra says: "For the sake of those sentient beings from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment up to the tenth stage, he goes everywhere throughout the ten directions and returns to abide within the fundamental position of the Buddha-body, and then enters back [into it]. The commentary explains:

"Bodhisattva" refers to when one first generates the pure bodhicitta; having seen this maṇḍala, they pervade the entire dharmadhātu and ascend to the second stage (vihāra), and furthermore transcend it.
Extending further than its depth, it undergoes ten revolutions of clarification, continuing even unto the eleventh bhūmi, after which what is perceived becomes perfectly consummate.
Having thus established these stages of arrangement, one then reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions;
within the gateway of one’s own dharmadhātu, one performs the activities of mantra, manifests the successive stages of cultivation, and instructs sentient beings—this sign appears clearly before one.
The unhindered discourse to be explained below merely opens up this mind to establish names for the sake of circulation.

Furthermore, while it is said that one universally manifests bodies according to the various classes of beings, the statement that one "manifests the bodies of all Tathāgatas" clarifies that both the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku) are inconceivable, and that their sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is non-dual.
How could one wish to cause a single dharma-realm alone to take on various forms? The practitioner should understand it in this way.
At that time, [the practitioner] contemplates that Vairocana’s mind is equal toward ghosts, animals, and others, without any thought of superiority or inferiority;

thus, they enter through any gate at will and perceive the Mind-King (Cittarāja). Having thus performed the Buddha-work, they return to the original position within the Buddha’s body, abide there, and then further enter the "intention" (manas), realizing that all skillful means ultimately converge in the same place.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "At that time, the Bhagavat again addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, saying: 'Listen attentively, Vajrapāṇi!
Regarding the positions in the maṇḍala, first is the ācārya. From this point onward, until the conclusion of the instructions on consecration."
Vajrapāṇi asked, "How much of a mass of merit is obtained? and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"From this day forward, I shall make offerings to these sons and daughters of good family. Why is this? Because those sons and daughters of good family have likewise seen the World-Honored One, the Buddha;
they are clearly entered into the many constituent parts of the maṇḍala, and they are themselves great powerful vidyārājñīs."
Up to the end of the second chapter, it clarifies the mantras required for the ritual procedures at the consecrated altar (*maṇḍala*).

Among the numerous constituent parts [of the ritual], the first clarifies the requirements for the *ācārya* (preceptor). The reason for this is that the Buddha taught that this sūtra must be received from a teacher;
one may not practice it arbitrarily. If there were no enlightened teacher, there would be no basis for the transmission. Nevertheless, because...
Because he understands two kinds of meaning, he receives the title of Ācārya; these are the superficial and the profound.
If one observes that the person before them lacks the capacity for deep understanding, one should explain according to the ordinary path, following the literal text.

If, however, they have already achieved sharp faculties and wisdom, one should then expound the profound and subtle teachings to instruct them. Now, this commentary shall likewise be explained according to these two divisions.

If an ācārya has thoroughly mastered the various components of this maṇḍala, as well as the mantras, mudrās, contemplative practices (dhyāna), and siddhis of all the deities, and has received the empowerment of the transmission of the teachings, he is called an ācārya.
If he transcends the eight mental states of compliance and resistance and realizes the realm of tranquility, he is called an ācārya. If it is his own mind-king...
One who realizes that one’s own mind is fundamentally unborn is called an *ācārya*.
If, having realized that even if it were to arise, it is utterly devoid of intrinsic nature, one is able to enter the ocean-like assembly of the aforementioned maṇḍala, one is called an *ācārya*.
Beyond this, there are ten stages of profound practice, culminating in being the foremost among those who understand the three secrets, such as Vajrasattva; this is called an *ācārya*.

Ācārya, furthermore, Vairocana is called the Ācārya; therefore, when performing the initial activity of an Ācārya, one must immediately contemplate oneself as being identical to Vajrasattva-Vairocana, and through the secret seals (*mudrā*) of body, speech, and mind, perform the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Only then is one said to be well-established in the rank of a master; otherwise, it is not so.
This is what can be accomplished; all other profound practitioners may grasp it through their own insight. Next, to clarify the manifold virtues of an ācārya:

one who should give rise to the bodhicitta must generate a resolute vow, single-mindedly aspiring for the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), and must certainly and universally deliver all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*.
This mind is like a banner or a standard; it is the leader of all practices. Just as...
Just as the seed is the root of all virtues, if one does not give rise to this mind, it is like not having yet conceived the *kalala*;
how then could the Womb of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*) be nurtured? Being unable to establish roots of goodness oneself, how much less can one act as a teacher for others?
One should provide a profound and esoteric explanation for each and every stage (*bhūmi*), until reaching Vairocana, at which point one is first called "Buddha."
This is the ultimate aspiration for the entirety of the Dharma-realm, belonging to those of wondrous wisdom and compassion. There are two kinds of *prajñā*:
*prajñā* conjoined with the six *pāramitās*, and *prajñā* of the true nature (*dharmatā*). Here, the intention clarifies the first phrase;
this wisdom is like a skillful wind that enables the artisan to fashion the embryo (*kalala*) so that the hundred limbs are fully perfected. The practitioner likewise...
Because he possesses wisdom, he is able to skillfully discern the open and the obstructed, and to judge right from wrong;
in all ritual activities within the maṇḍala, his movements accord with the rules and his mind is free from doubt or stagnation. Only such a person is fit to act as an ācārya. To state it in brief:
if one’s wisdom and enlightened activity are perfected like those of Vairocana, such a person is called a "deep-practicing ācārya. [This is] compassion.
This refers to a heart of compassion that penetrates to the very marrow of one's bones;

whatever one does is solely for the sake of establishing all sentient beings, necessarily bringing them to the fulfillment of the inexhaustible bliss of the Dharma-realm and delivering the suffering of the entire realm of sentient beings without exception.
If this mind were lacking, it would be like a fetal sac that fails to form; how then could there be anything nurtured within, even up to the stage of Vairocana?
Abiding in the world of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by virtue of his original vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*), he universally manifests the maṇḍala born of compassion;

this is called the profound and secret *ācārya*. He is one who masters all arts, meaning he is exquisitely skilled in the various worldly crafts and skills—namely, grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), logic (*hetu-vidyā*), the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), the sixty-four abilities, mathematics, medicine, physiognomy, and the arts of craftsmanship.
This is the nature of such things. Since all that is required for the maṇḍala does not depend on others, one will have no fault of deficiency even in sudden or impromptu actions;
only then is one fit to be an ācārya. Furthermore, practicing such dharmas so that they do not contradict the true mark (lakṣaṇa) at all is called "excellent mastery of all arts.
Furthermore, regarding all dhāraṇīs... [the third part]... in the three... [text fragment].

One who attains skillfulness in the gates of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the powers (*bala*), and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) is able to fashion secret maṇḍalas at will; this is called "skill in the various arts.

One who is skillful in the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is one who deeply cultivates the observation of the ten phrases of dependent origination and perceives the profound middle way.
The Path illuminates the emptiness of the unattainable; this matter is explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
If a practitioner thoroughly attains mastery over both words and the mind of contemplation, becoming free from views and attachments, they should then act as a worldly *ācārya* for others.
Furthermore, during the first eon, wisdom still functions in common with the two vehicles, yet it is not [the ultimate].
The profound Prajñā of the second eon is still shared with those of the two vehicles and is not yet the profound Prajñā of the third eon.
The wisdom of the equality of space and the boundlessness of mind cannot be conceived by any of the two vehicles;
this alone is called the profound Prajñā, fit to serve as an Ācārya for secret practices. Furthermore, within these secrets...
Progressively deepening until the Buddha teaches the *Prajñāpāramitā* for those on the tenth stage, the ninth stage is no longer within their domain;

only one who is the Great Vairocana is designated as an ultimate *ācārya*. One who has "mastered the three vehicles" refers to one who is proficient in the textual meanings of the Tripiṭaka teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, capable of both posing and answering difficult questions, and fit to act as a master craftsman.
One who uproots the evil and heterodox views of disciples through the three trainings is fit to be an ācārya;
if one does not do so, they may be defeated by proponents of other doctrines, thereby lacking the power to transmit the Dharma and causing others to lose faith.

Furthermore, the core of this sutra universally encompasses all Buddhist teachings, as it explains that there are only aggregates (*skandha*) and no self (*ātman*), and that the supramundane mind exists.
Abiding within the aggregates (*skandha*) encompasses the various sections of the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna, such as the contemplation of the aggregates;
realizing that the *ālaya* is one's own mind, fundamentally unborn, encompasses the meaning of the eight consciousnesses and the three natures of non-existence found in the various sūtras;

and the phrases concerning the ultimate lack of self-nature and the ten conditions for the arising of the mind encompass all the inconceivable realms of the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*. All are included therein.
Entering therein and knowing one’s own mind as it truly is, as described, is called the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*);

thus, the Buddha-nature, the One Vehicle, and the Tathāgata’s secret treasury are all contained within it. Among the various sacred teachings, there are none whose essential points are not encompassed by this.
If one can maintain this seal of the mind, one will be able to extensively open all dharma-gates; this is called "thoroughly penetrating the Three Vehicles. Furthermore...

Next, regarding the Mantra Vehicle (Mantramukha-yāna), from the practice of the three secrets and seals up to the stage of the Buddha’s threefold equality, it is called "thoroughly penetrating" the shallow and deep levels of the three vehicles;

the enumeration of these stages is as previously explained. One who well understands the true meaning of the mantras [knows that] within the Mantra Vehicle there are various mantras, various bodily mudrās, various deities (iṣṭadevatā), and even the requisite conditions and offering articles, each and every one of which...
The various characteristics of the branches, sounds, syllables, forms, and colors differ according to their respective objects;

one should discern their essential natures and know that such dharmas are for the purpose of pacifying calamities, such dharmas are for the purpose of increasing prosperity, and such dharmas are for the purpose of subjugation.
As explained in detail in the *Vidyādharapiṭaka*, the *Susiddhi*, and other texts, this is the thorough penetration of the true meaning of mantras.
The reason for this is that each and every mantra is the most wondrous and ultimate speech of the Tathāgata. For instance, within a mantra there may be the syllable *citta*;
if explained superficially, it is simply called "mind. However, if explained in its profound and secret sense, *cit* refers to the syllable *ca*, which carries the resonance of *samādhi*.
*Ca* signifies the meaning of being without transition or change; that which is without transition or change is precisely the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Nature is also called Prajñāpāramitā and also called Śūraṅgama Samādhi; therefore, it is the perfection of both concentration and wisdom.
The many syllables signify that all dharmas are suchness, liberation, and ungraspable. To speak in this way is what is called the most wondrous and ultimate speech of the mind.
Furthermore, just as the hand is the seal of the body, the left hand represents the meaning of samādhi, while the right...

The hand signifies *prajñā*; the ten fingers signify the fulfillment of the ten *pāramitās* and also the meaning of the five wheels (*pañcamaṇḍala*) as a metaphor for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), corresponding to the form of the deity.
The female represents meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and the male represents wisdom (*prajñā*).

Yellow signifies the vajra-body; white signifies great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); red signifies great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*); blue signifies the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*); and black signifies... [the ultimate].
Within this Great Power and even within all conditions, there exists the meaning of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*);
how could one possibly produce understanding based merely on the literal text? If one penetrates such true meaning, then one should act as an *ācārya*;

furthermore, one clarifies profound practice by means of the three *kalpas* and the ten stages (*bhūmi*). One who knows the minds of sentient beings is an *ācārya* who skillfully understands the three families (*kula*).

Because he employs various categories of superior, middling, and inferior natures and abides in yoga, he is able to discern the mental activities of sentient beings through the skillful means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
If there is one who comes seeking the Dharma, the teacher should say to them: "You should remain as you are for a moment;
I shall contemplate. Immediately, taking that person's name, he enters a quiet room and maintains it according to the ritual.
Recite [the mantra] and contemplate those causes and conditions; through the empowerment of the *iṣṭadevatā*, you shall see signs.

If a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) intends to come and steal the Dharma, or seeks an opportunity to approach under the guise of a friend, at that time the *iṣṭadevatā* may manifest in the form of a non-Buddhist or similar being.
By carefully observing their appearance and characteristics, they will naturally be recognized. You should then skillfully send them away with this admonition: "O son of good family..."
One who seeks the Dharma should first sever all evil views and the mind of crafty hypocrisy.
Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas seek to deliver sentient beings, they are able to perform various difficult practices and ascetic austerities; can you now truly undertake such difficult deeds?
For now, bring benefit according to your original conditions. If, within the sphere of experience, you perceive the Honored One within the maṇḍala...
The Vidyārāja shall lead his disciples and bestow upon them the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), or hold [the object] and entrust it to them;

when such various auspicious signs appear, one should accept and guide them. Furthermore, if the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) abandons its original form and appears as red in color, that person has much anger;
black indicates much delusion; yellow indicates much greed; white indicates much goodness; and pale blue indicates much [passion].

Furthermore, by observing the neutral signs and the various marks of superior, middling, and inferior quality—namely, the places where the flower falls within the maṇḍala—one may also know whether that person’s mental capacity is a fit vessel or not. Nevertheless, one should not become attached to such signs;

Regarding rivers adorned with geese, swans, and the like, one who intends to construct a maṇḍala born of wisdom and compassion should understand them as follows:

if a famous mountain cannot be obtained, a spring is the next best option. That is to say, at a place where rivers flow constantly without interruption, where melodious birds flock and swim, which is dignified, pure, and far removed from clamor and distraction—one may establish the altar there.
The term *ya-yan* (野雁) is not a direct translation; in the Sanskrit original it is *sārasa*, a bird resembling a mandarin duck that has a loud yet exceptionally elegant and refined call.
Since this species does not exist in this land [of China], the term was coined through a conceptual interpretation (*huiyi*).
Even a worldly maṇḍala must be established by one who possesses wisdom and understands the mantras; therefore, it is said: "One should employ wisdom and understanding to give rise to compassion."
Maṇḍala. Furthermore, water signifies the meaning of flowing without staying;
that mind which does not stagnate but is constantly able to advance is called "water. That the river of merit flows without interruption is called "water.

Although those who can first settle their minds upon the principle of reality are themselves difficult to find, if one allows [the mind] to flow forth from primordial purity and correctly enters into this [state], it is sufficient.
By employing unimpeded wisdom, he establishes the maṇḍala born of compassion.
The adornment of various birds with wondrous voices signifies the ability to proclaim the sound of the Dharma; it also signifies his constant mindfulness of benefiting others.

Thus, all sentient beings who take refuge in him obtain joy, which is a praise of his meritorious virtue and great renown. As the verse says: "The Perfectly Awakened One, the Guide through Conditions."
This region where the noble assembly of *śrāvakas* once traveled and which the Buddha has always praised— such as these mountain springs and blessed sites frequented by the various sages—
belongs to the preceding section. The meaning here is that although this place is not a superior site like those mentioned above,
it is nevertheless a place where the Buddhas, *pratyekabuddhas*, and the disciples of the *śrāvakas* attained the Path and entered *nirvāṇa*.
To dwell in such a place for a long time is the next best option. For instance, in the West, there are many sites such as the eight stupas and the remains of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles;
these are constantly protected by deities of great majesty and power.
Because they are venerated [by them], just as no minor spirits dare to linger where the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is located, spiritual attainments are easily accomplished.
That which the Buddha praised as being like a rishi dwelling in the mountains, as described by the World-Honored One, refers to those places where it is easy to attain the Way.
Furthermore, once a person has resolved their mind on Bodhi, such a place is the birthplace of all Buddhas;
it is also the place for attaining the Way, turning the Wheel of Dharma, and entering Parinirvāṇa, and it is where they dwell for a long time through the four [blessings].

In places where majestic deportment extensively benefits sentient beings, although the secret treasury has not yet been heard, even attaining the common practice of the Three Vehicles is called auspicious.

This refers to observing that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, signless, wishless, and devoid of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span—this is the place where the followers of the Two Vehicles accomplish the Way and enter Nirvana; it is also the place of the various Jātaka-sūtras of the Bodhisattvas.
Having renounced body and life, one may construct a maṇḍala within any place where the pāramitās are practiced.
Furthermore, if one considers oneself to have already attained nirvāṇa and conceives the thought of liberation, that is the domain frequented by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
however, if one does not seek exclusively for bodhi, one should instead level the ground there and draw a maṇḍala born of compassion.
It is *caitya*. The verse says: "And other locations, such as monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) and forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*).

Excluding these sacred sites, wherever in various lands practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) reside—monasteries, which in the Sanskrit sound are *vihāra*, translated as "places of dwelling," meaning places for cultivating merit—laypeople, for the sake of cultivating merit, [establish them] for all those... [comrades].

The Master built these dwellings so that those who maintain the precepts and cultivate meditation and wisdom might find protection against wind, cold, heat, and dampness, as well as various other unwholesome conditions, and settle their minds to practice the Path.
Furthermore, he ensured that the donors would enjoy the merit of their offerings, which flows constantly day and night without interruption;
for this reason, they are called "residences" (*vihāra*). An *araṇya* is called a "place of mental delight," meaning it is the dwelling of those who practice in emptiness and stillness.
In a pleasant place— whether alone without a companion, or with two or three people— in a small, limited hut built outside a monastery, or one provided by a donor,
or even simply dwelling beneath a tree or in an open space— all such places are suitable. Furthermore,
if one practices all virtuous dharmas while separated from the bodhicitta, such as extensively practicing generosity (*dāna*), receiving immeasurable vows (*saṃvara*), and so forth...

Practicing various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), upholding the twelvefold division of the teachings, contemplating their underlying principles, and progressing through the cultivation of compassion and diligence to deliver sentient beings—because these manifold practices lack a guiding leader, they are all termed the "Noble-less" (*anārya*) monastic community.

Nevertheless, as a place where ordinary and noble beings dwell together, it is also a locus for generating merit; it is thus the next best [option]. This excludes the *prajñā* shared with the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). All else...
All the Dharma-gates of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, which seek their own deliverance apart from great compassion, are called "non-sacred sites" (an-ārya-sthāna) and are Aranyas.
One may also, within such places, select and level a plain ground to draw a maṇḍala.
As the verse says: "Flower chambers, high towers, and excellent, wondrous ponds and gardens"—if one cannot obtain such [places]...
One should not remain in a superior sacred site; rather, one should select an excellent location within the secular world.
If it is dignified and pure, one may establish a ritual hall there. Since ancient times, sentient beings have, out of a sense of shame, not wished for their curtains to be displayed prominently;
furthermore, such a structure can protect the body and guard both oneself and others—a multi-storied pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) is a double-roofed building common in the West.
The high, prominent, and level open spaces refer to pure ponds and pools where many water-born creatures dwell, which are cherished by both humans and non-humans alike.
The groves refer to gardens and forests abounding in fragrant, soft grasses and lush, flourishing trees;
they are solemn and secluded, capable of warding off clamor and vexation—all of which rank as secondary to the former. Furthermore, even if one sees a person walking there, though...
Even when not yet having entered other paths of skillful means, its essential nature is fully endowed with shame and remorse, such that it can constantly protect itself and also protect others.
Its mind is clear and bright; possessing great knowledge, it has few obstacles.

Even if one commits an offense, one is able to confess before others to seek personal purification, without any concealment or secrecy; such a person may also transmit [the teachings]. Furthermore, this is like a pond.

The meaning of "thirsting for the water without satiety" is that although this person has not yet attained the flavor of the profound Dharma, they are able to listen and receive it with an open mind, thirsting for it with insatiable longing.
"A place where many people gather for recreation and observation" means that this person possesses great compassion and delights in practicing benevolent salvation;
all look up to them and rely upon their protection. These are all of the Mahāyāna lineage and are capable of being further cultivated and perfected.

Furthermore, the verse states: "At caityas, fire temples, cow pens, sandbars in rivers, shrines of various devas, empty rooms, and places where sages attained the Way—though these are not sacred sites or residences of the Sangha, wherever a caitya has been erected according to the local conditions, one may construct a maṇḍala in its vicinity.
Regarding the fire god (*agni-deva*), he is a Brahmin of pure conduct.
The site of the *agniśālā* (fire temple) is particularly clean, and thus it is suitable for establishing an altar. As for the ox-pen:

in western villages, cattle are gathered together in one place at a distance of ten or fifteen *li* from the village. Since this has been so for a long time, the dung and urine of the cattle have accumulated across the ground;
both Brahmins and laypeople likewise regard it as pure. Nevertheless, it must be moved once the cattle have departed, provided that the cowherds see to it.
"Zhong" (中) also does not mean "in the middle. "Hetan" (河潬) should be translated as "confluence," meaning a place where two or more streams meet;
because this side and the center frequently experience flooding and scouring, they are free from all impurities.
A "temple of the gods" (*devakula*) is a hall for the worship of worldly deities and a chamber for fasting and prayer; it is also generally clean and quiet, yet there are... [omitted].
If those of various heterodox paths and wrong views do not believe, one should not perform [the ritual] in such a place.

A "vacant room" refers to a dwelling constructed by worldly people which they later abandon and depart from; because it is free from all clamor and confusion, it is fit to serve as a place for a Dharma-practicing seer to attain the Way.
It is certainly a place where those in the world seeking the five supernatural powers have long resided and achieved their accomplishments.
Even in places that are not otherwise excellent, one may also construct a maṇḍala there. Furthermore, a *caitya* (stūpa) signifies the sense of establishing what is lofty and superior;
it means that this person is always able to establish the white dharmas (*śukladharma*) with an undaunted resolve.

Although they have not yet manifestly practiced the holy teachings, one should know that because they planted merit in previous lives and possess internal roots of goodness, it is called a *tā* (stūpa). Moreover, fire can...

"Burning away the wild and defiled" means that although this person’s body, speech, and mind have not yet attained purity or transcendence, they possess an internal nature of wisdom, habitually practice pure deeds, and are able to reform their faults;
therefore, it is called "the fire-sacrifice cow. "Cow" signifies the sense of conduct, while "fence" signifies the sense of restraint and protection.
This means that such a person is by nature gentle and pliable, easy to train and guide, and possesses the five sensory faculties that incline toward desire.
Because one is able to restrain oneself and does not fall into negligence, it is called the "cow-pen" (goṣṭhī).
This refers to those whose minds are hesitant regarding the Three Vehicles, not knowing which path they will definitely follow. The *ācārya* should likewise exhort them with the Dharma, saying:
"All these skillful means are the teachings of the Buddha; you should simply choose that which you find most joyful and study it single-mindedly until you reach your goal."
In such assemblies, one should not harbor doubts. If it is difficult to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, one should sever the path of delusion and point out the correct road;
because one is able to maintain faith in both, this indicates that in previous lives one’s mind was already cleansed by the waters of the Dharma—this is also called a "river sandbar" (*sāṅkā*).
As for "heavenly shrines" (*devāyatana*), this refers to those who do not seek the Three Vehicles but instead aspire to celestial pleasures, being granted [the opportunity] for their desires.
Having received the command to depart from the three evil rebirths and be born among the devas of right view, one must receive [their] guidance; this is called a "deva-shrine.
An "empty room" refers to a person who, though dwelling amidst the secular world, is by nature inclined toward emptiness and stillness, and loathes the clamor and vexation of the mundane;

this is a sign that their roots of goodness are about to ripen. Just as when a woman’s pregnancy gradually reaches maturity, her carnal desires naturally diminish, so too is such a person fit for conversion.
If one aspires to seek the path of the formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is also called an "empty room.

Regarding the places where sages attained the Way, it refers to those who merely resolve their minds to seek the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) or the path of the *vidyādhara* sages, or who wish to achieve longevity and various worldly *siddhis*.
One may likewise guide and receive such individuals according to their dispositions and capacities. Furthermore, there are those of various heterodox schools who deeply delight in...

Regarding those who follow the Vedic fire-sacrifice rites with the aspiration to be reborn in the Brahma-world, if they hear that within the Buddha’s secret treasury there are likewise rites for the fire-deities and the methods for the practice of mantras,
and because their underlying intent is profoundly deep, they shall enter the True Dharma through this very gateway. Furthermore,
as for those who serve various worldly deities such as Īśvara, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the Sun, and the Moon— if they hear the Buddha’s secret [teachings]...
Within the *pitaka* there are also the mantra practices (*vidyā-caryā*) of those various devas, even up to the body of the Great Self, Vairocana;

having received them with faith, one enters the True Dharma. Or, for those who aspire to be born among the devas of the three realms, they hear that within the Buddha’s secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*) are contained the mantra practices of the Devayāna, which enable [them] throughout immeasurable lifetimes...
Having been born in that celestial realm, they shall no longer fall back and will ultimately become those who dwell in the ultimate heaven (*paramārtha-deva*).

Because of this profound aspiration and longing, they are able to enter the True Dharma. Furthermore, there are those who practice the worldly methods of the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the *ṛṣis*;

upon hearing that the Buddha’s secret treasury contains various mantras such as those of the great seers Kāśyapa and Gautama, which can cause one to attain the inconceivable, [they too are drawn to it].
Through supernatural powers, even as far as the long life of Vairocana, one leaps with joy and aspires to enter the True Dharma by means of various such gateways;
for this reason, the Buddha taught that maṇḍalas may be constructed in all places, including those of the Fire Deity.
As the verse says: "In the places mentioned above, or wherever one finds delight, for the benefit of disciples..."
Therefore, when one intends to draw a maṇḍala, even if one cannot find an excellent site for it, one must not allow this Secret Teaching to fail to be transmitted.
Rather, wherever the ācārya’s mind finds delight and perceives benefit, there one may construct the maṇḍala.
To explain this more deeply: one need only observe that such a place possesses even a small portion [of these qualities].
Those with virtuous roots who possess right aspirations may all select their own mental ground and cultivate it to be level and upright for the purpose of constructing the Great Compassion Maṇḍala.
Furthermore, even those sentient beings who take pleasure in minor worldly arts such as *cāmuṇḍa* and *naṭakinī* are gathered within this gateway;
when they are able to behold this Honored One, [the result] will be attained naturally.

[The text] states: "One may see immeasurable assemblies of noble ones. It is asked: "In the previous clarification regarding the selection of disciples, it was required that they possess all virtues and be capable vessels of the Dharma before being instructed.
Why is it that in the present explanation of selecting the ground [of the recipient], there is nothing—even a single hair’s breadth of subtle goodness—that is not transmitted?
It is answered: "Within this, there are two kinds of disciples. If one seeks a disciple for the transmission of the Dharma..."
One who is worthy to succeed to the rank of *ācārya* must be such that, were it not for the person, the Way would not be practiced in vain;
as for those who are disciples through a karmic connection (*kṣetra-pratibandha*), there is no good deed—whether raising a hand or bowing the head—that is not encompassed by them.

Furthermore, because a *ācārya* of profound practice clearly perceives the roots and conditions of others, there may be someone whose capacity for the Way has already matured in the past and is fit to be a vessel for the Dharma, yet [remains unawakened] in the present...

Because within this present life one has sunk into the mire, leaving behind only a mere hair’s breadth of roots of goodness, the *ācārya* selects a small portion of level ground from among these and brings forth the secret treasury of the maṇḍala.
Why wait for a person who has attained peace of mind and realized the profound principle before performing the Buddha-work? Therefore, this does not contradict what was previously stated.

The Sūtra states: "O Guhyapati, one should clear that selected site of pebbles, gravel, broken shards, potsherds, skulls, hair, chaff, husks, ashes, charcoal, thorns, bones, rotten wood, and so forth, as well as insects, ants, dung beetles, and venomous stinging creatures.
This next section explains the procedure for purifying the ground: from within the previously selected site, one should select the specific location for the mandala and dig it up.
One should dig to a depth of one cubit and carefully select the soil, removing all unsuitable materials such as insects and the like;
if these are present, they will give rise to many difficulties and create obstacles for the Dharma.
As for stones, sand, and gravel, those that can be easily removed should be selected and discarded; however, if the sand and stones are numerous, this location is considered a thicket.
Furthermore, if there are accumulations in that place which cannot be cleared away or purified, one should abandon them and seek another location.
However, regarding large flat stones, there are sacred teachings stating that one may establish a maṇḍala upon them; it is only the impurities within the soil that should be removed.
According to the common customs of the West, people often eat from earthenware vessels and immediately discard them once they have finished eating.
This is called "defiled contact," and such things are no longer to be used.

This includes various other types of broken vessels, as well as skulls, assorted bones, various forked hair, fur, skin, chaff, dregs, filthy grass, and all manner of ashes, charcoal, thorns, stakes, and rotten wood;
in short, all such various items that are unfit for use do not belong to the original pure land.
All such [beings] should be selected and removed; if there are too many to select individually, they should likewise be discarded and one should seek another location—hence the use of the term "etc.
(ādi). Regarding insects and ants, the Sanskrit term *kṛmi* (pronounced *kilimi*) generally encompasses all small creatures, including those that must be discarded.
The dung beetle (*gonglang*) is among the larger ones; other types, such as earthworms, may be understood by analogy. This also includes venomous insects.
This means that one should employ skillful means to drive away snakes, scorpions, centipedes, millipedes, and the like;
however, if they are too numerous to be removed, then one should simply abandon that place which is beset by such obstacles.
The Sūtra states: "One who is free from such faults... There are many such examples; one who has grasped the underlying meaning should personally discern them according to the circumstances.
This refers to whether the ground is sloping or uneven in height, or whether its color and flavor do not accord with the holy teachings.
Among colors, yellow and white are considered superior; if it is purely black, it is unfit for taking and tasting. As for flavor, sweet and bland are preferred.
If the soil is good, bitter, salty, or astringent, it is not fit for use.
Or, if after digging one refills the pit with the original earth and it does not reach the surface, it is unsuitable; however, if after refilling it overflows, it is excellent.
Furthermore, within that single location, the southern side constitutes the lower ground and is suitable only for performing *ābhicāruka* rites. Next, the Ācārya...

Once it is known that the disciple’s mind-ground is capable of being established as a Great Compassion Maṇḍala, one should immediately abide in profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and examine it with discerning clarity; using wisdom, one should select and remove all that is unfit, impure, and defiled.
Thereafter, one should refine it until it is firm and solid, and then provide it with adornment; otherwise, the residual traces of past karma will be able [to obstruct it].

They constitute obstacles to birth. Just as gravel and pebbles represent those who lack faith in the True Dharma and stubbornly cling to views such as self-attachment and the denial of cause and effect—because they are so difficult to carve or polish and because they are permeated by such [wrong] tendencies—they ultimately cannot produce the sprouts of goodness;

even with diligent effort and refinement, nothing emerges from them. Because their subtle attachments are so numerous and mutually incompatible, they are likened to sand and gravel, or to crushed tiles and broken shards.
If a vessel is like one that has committed the five heinous crimes, violated the four grave prohibitions, or slandered the Vaipulya sutras, its mental vessel is so ruined that it lacks any capacity;
even if the flavor of the Dharma is added, it cannot remain, and it is abandoned by the assembly of the virtuous.
One must first use the hand of wisdom and skillful means to select away and remove such obstacles. Its skull is like something shattered.
The obstacle to the bodhicitta is that which was previously possessed by a person among the various factors of human existence;

having seized the foremost position, because the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) has been severed, the hundred-fold body collapses and becomes incapable of action. Due to this evil habit, even if one were to again give rise to the bodhicitta, it would once more become an obstacle.
Because it causes one to take pleasure in oneself and leads to despondency and retreat, it is especially fitting to wash it away until it is entirely exhausted.
The "remaining breaths and hairs" refers to the sixty mental states and so forth that arise as one essence together with the eight wholesome seeds, as well as those that have already been discerned;
these should be removed and cut away. Since the time before the supramundane mind has been attained, they arise in a confused and disordered manner, making them difficult to organize;
therefore, they are called "hairs. Like chaff and dregs, the mind of ignorance and false conceptualization exists because of its grasping at and attachment to discursive proliferation (*prapañca*).

It is called a "skin" because it retains only names and appearances while losing the rice of true reality; thus, it serves as a metaphor for those who delight in inferior teachings and give rise to the mind of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
If one's roots of goodness are consumed by this, they return to ashes and are severed, failing to produce the sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruits of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
thus, it serves as a metaphor for the "thorns. These refer to having previously performed various kinds of harm toward sentient beings.

Practicing various minor and miscellaneous transgressions of the precepts is called "rotten bones" or "withered wood" because these are the residual obstacles from past lives within the cycle of birth and death;
it refers to those who are indolent and lack the desire [to practice], being incapable of cultivating or completing their work like a craftsman.
Furthermore, the Sanskrit term also carries the meaning of a "stump," referring to the lingering remnants of habitual tendencies toward various afflictions that have persisted since time immemorial.

Deeply rooted and difficult to uproot—because such past karmas are stored within the mind-ground, and because demonic activities easily arise when practicing the Path with single-mindedness—one must exercise preliminary discernment.

If there are too many [obstacles] to discern, one should abandon this site and seek another location suited to other capacities. [One should avoid places infested with] insects, ants, dung beetles, and venomous stingers.
Various types of currently active afflictions are illustrated by metaphors: ants represent delusion (*moha*), dung beetles represent greed (*lobha*), and venomous insects represent hatred (*dveṣa*).

Such categories are numerous; they serve as analogies for the various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Those that are very minute represent immeasurable unwholesome thoughts and reflections (*vitarka-vicāra*).
All these beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*; they should be especially protected so that their life-force is not extinguished, but rather through skillful means (*upāya*).
One should expel them so as not to obstruct the path of practice, merely ensuring that the maṇḍala is not defiled or polluted.
If one wishes to make the site of the ritual (dojō) utterly pure, one must select and remove all one hundred and sixty kinds of subtle, medium, and coarse impurities until none remain;
even within the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka), anything that is not a pure land should be excluded. Only then can it be called ultimate purity.

The Sūtra states: "When one encounters an auspicious day at dawn, having fixed the date, time, and hour, such that the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the *yoga*, and all planetary positions are entirely in harmony;
and when, prior to the meal, one encounters signs of auspiciousness—this explains the selection of the temporal factors (*kāla-aṅga*) in connection with the matter of selecting the site.

For all ritual activities (*dharmakārya*), one must ensure they are in accord with the principles of the timing. Since we are now about to select and prepare this ground, [we do so] on an auspicious day."
One may infer other ritual precedents from this example of alerting the Earth Goddess. Regarding the auspicious morning:

for performing rites, one should use the waxing phase of the moon (*śuklapakṣa*). Among these, the first, third, fifth, seventh, and thirteenth days are all auspicious and suitable for constructing a maṇḍala.
Furthermore, the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days are especially superior; on these dates, one should proceed.

One should also apply diligent effort to constant recitation. Regarding the determination of the date: according to the Western calendar system, one must calculate which day corresponds to a small month (*kṣayamāsa*).
If the small month falls within the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), then the fifteenth day of that month belongs to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) and is unfit for use.
Furthermore, the calendar system calculates the mean degrees of the sun and moon to establish the mean new moon (*madhyama-amāvāsya*), all of which are consistent.
The small and large dimensions of the moon’s orbit relative to the sun involve further variations in speed within its mean motion;

sometimes it exceeds the mean motion, and sometimes it falls short of it. Consequently, the calculated new moon (Śukla-pratipad) may advance or retreat by one day, and the calculated full moon (Pūrṇimā) may occur on either the fourteenth or the sixteenth day.
Generally speaking, when the moon is at its perfect fullness, it is termed "White" (Śukla).
The fifteen days of a month are divided such that when the moon is exactly half like a bowstring, it is also considered the eighth day; by taking this as a standard, one obtains the fixed date.
Regarding the time periods (*kāla*): according to the Western calendrical system, both day and night each consist of thirty periods (*yāma*), and each individual period has its own specific name.
For instance, during the daytime, one calculates the length of the shadow to determine which period a particular task should be performed.

Thus, [if] at such-and-such a time one acts, it is auspicious; if at such-and-such a time, it is inauspicious; if at such-and-such a time, it is neutral. Each of these has its own corresponding category.

What is called "the fixed positions" (*xiùzhí*) refers to the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*). Dividing the circumference of the heavens into twelve houses (*bhāga*) is like the twelve *zī* (lunar stations) here in China;
each station has nine feet, so the entire circumference of the heavens has one hundred and eight feet. Each mansion receives an equal share of four feet.
This means that as the moon travels for one day’s journey over twenty-seven days, it completes one circuit of the heavens.
According to calendrical calculations, the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) in which the moon resides is the "day-ruling mansion" (*tithi-nakṣatra*).

These mansions possess superior, middling, or inferior natures, and differ in being hard or soft, active or tranquil; thus, the ritual acts performed should also accord with these qualities. Those who hold to fixed positions maintain that [these distinctions exist].

The nine [planets] consist of the sun, moon, fire (Mars), water (Mercury), wood (Jupiter), metal (Venus), earth (Saturn)—the seven luminaries—along with Rāhu and Ketu, which together constitute the nine grahas.
Rāhu is the deity of conjunctions and eclipses; Ketu, when translated literally, is *qìdòu* (簱簱); the star *qìdòu* refers to the comet.
Apart from these two grahas, the remaining seven luminaries take turns presiding over each day in succession, and their respective natures and categories are likewise [as follows].

There are good and evil [times] as explained in the *Brahma-calendar* regarding the period before eating: day and night each have three periods. One may perform the rite for pacifying (*śāntika*) during the period before eating;
one may perform the rite for increasing (*pauṣṭika*) in the evening; and one may perform the rite for subjugating (*abhicāruka*) at night.

Entering the maṇḍala and receiving initiation correspond to the rite of pacifying; therefore, it is said that encountering auspicious signs during the period before eating refers to performing the ritual.
At times, whether on the ground or in the air, there appear various extraordinary signs such as forms and sounds.

On the ground, this refers, for example, to suddenly encountering a young girl holding a vessel of the five products of the cow, or a vessel of scented water, or objects held in her hands that resemble the wheel-seal (*cakramudrā*) and similar symbols;
or it may be objects of high esteem in the world, or vessels filled with pure white non-glutinous rice and other such clean items.

Whether it be a state of pure fullness, the wearing of robes that are dignified and brilliantly fresh, or the utterance of various sounds associated with auspiciousness—all these are signs of accomplishment.

Regarding phenomena in the sky: if one suddenly beholds celebratory clouds or auspicious vapors swirling in five colors, or if a vivid rainbow appears out of season, intermingled with brilliant hues, or if it takes on the color of fire and moves as if protected by a guardian—these are likewise signs.
The signs of accomplishment include the appearance of five-colored halos around the sun, or the manifestation of human forms appearing as if dwelling in meditative stillness;

or the hearing of beautiful sounds in the air—such as those of white cranes, peacocks, mandarin ducks, wild geese, and swans—which are clear, harmonious, and elegant, bringing joy to all who hear them. These and others are likewise signs of accomplishment. This is why:

Those who must conform to worldly convention find it difficult even for those with pure hearts and profound faith to believe and accept the subtle, tranquil, and sublime maṇḍala of ultimate truth (paramārtha),
let alone those who harbor doubts and anxieties. This is because when people who have previously studied the Vedas,
sacrificial rituals, arts, and sciences witness the construction of a maṇḍala, they fear that errors in its timing and proportions may lead to inauspicious results.
He immediately gave rise to doubt and wonder, saying: "I have heard that those who possess the wisdom of *dhāraṇī* reach everything without exception;

yet now, observing him, he cannot even select an auspicious star or a favorable time, let alone other profound matters. Because he doubted both the teacher and the Dharma due to this, he lost the power of firm faith and instead incurred grave retribution;
therefore, one must act in accordance with the dispositions and capacities of others. Furthermore, as it is said:
These planetary deities (*graha*) are themselves a gateway to a certain kind of spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) within the maṇḍala.
Those various honored ones (*devatā*) are able to employ skillful means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-upāya*) in accordance with worldly activities;

because the ācārya has skillfully selected an auspicious time, they—being naturally and intrinsically connected to the original vows of those mantras—bestow empowerment so that one may be freed from all obstacles.
Furthermore, all the various gateways of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are the insignia of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

That which is called "an auspicious day at dawn" intends the morning of the sublime assembly of the bodhicitta. The ācārya of profound practice, abiding in yoga, observes those whom he intends to deliver:
whether their planting of roots of goodness was long ago or recent, and to whom they belong by way of causal conditions.

From what causes does it arise? When a practitioner first resolves their mind on enlightenment, they may do so because they have seen the Buddha preaching the Dharma, or witnessed a miraculous manifestation, or observed various objects of pity and suffering; or they may resolve upon the path toward Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas;
or, by making offerings of flowers, incense, and the like to such fields of merit, their hearts become filled with joy, and they immediately resolve their minds [upon enlightenment].
Wishing to aspire for the fruit of Buddhahood, because it is evoked by the interaction of those prior causes and present conditions,
the various capacities for awakening differ; thus, at such times the bodhicitta may possess the power of tranquility,
at such times the power of progress, or at such times the power of majesty, being established in accordance with the various *siddhānta* and skillful means.

Thus, one's merit will not be in vain, nor will obstacles arise. Regarding the fixed days: the sun is a metaphor for the body of the Principal Deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), and the moon is a metaphor for the practitioner engaged in the cultivation of yoga.
Depending on the time, the moon of the practitioner’s concentrated mind may sometimes increase in brilliance and sometimes become faint;
or the practice may be performed too hastily, or too slowly, or it may exceed the middle way, or fall short of it.

The Way brings about the occasion for awakening, yet there are variations in its timing—whether it expands or contracts. According to the constant principle of cultivation, one may reach realization through certain conditions at a certain time;
however, because conditions and environments shift, that which should ripen may do so before the appointed time or place, or it may ripen after that time and place has passed.
One must skillfully understand such transformations; therefore, it is said that "it is an auspicious day."
Regarding the "time-periods" (*kāla-bhāga*): within each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) traversed by the practitioner, there are ten mental states;
each of these ten mental states possesses its own causes, roots, and fruits, totaling thirty mental states. Within these thirty *muhūrta*s, one should carefully discern and select:
at what time is one capable of subduing afflictions (*kleśa*), at what time may one increase meritorious qualities (*guṇa*), and at what time should one act in accordance [with the path]?
To abide with a mind of quiescence in the Middle Way is called the subtle sign within the period of liberation.
"The fixed lunar mansions" refers to the objective conditions encountered during the practitioner’s month of yogic practice;

among all such objective conditions, one perceives the nature of the mind as being like the constellations—their various sizes and forms, though distinct, are all perfectly luminous, just like the movement of the moon.

As the moon passes through twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), the prognostications for the months of the world vary according to the differing auspicious or inauspicious qualities of the mansions it traverses;

for example, when the moon enters the mansion of *Mṛgaśiras* (the Hare), which favors wind, the wind arises, and when it enters the mansion of *Pūrvabhadrapadā* (the Net), which favors rain, the rain falls. The bodhicitta is likewise subject to the power of its encounter with conditions and objects.
It is not the same as the application of skillful means that follows along with the methods of subduing, gathering, and tranquilizing;
if an ācārya can deeply examine the faculties and conditions and clearly understand these matters, it is called "skillfully observing the past roots.

Regarding the nine *grahas*, the Sanskrit term is *kṛtānta*, which carries the meaning of "holding" or "grasping"; the ācārya should observe whether the hand of that person's mental power is capable of holding [the vessel].
What is it that ensures the transmitted secret mudrā does not become fruitless?

It is the Vajra-Wisdom Mudrā of all Buddhas, which only a Bodhisattva with a vajra-mind can grasp. If it were bestowed upon those of lower stages, it would be called "grasping the planets," which is inappropriate.
Among the nine grahas, the sun symbolizes the fundamentally pure bodhicitta, which is Vairocana.
The moon as a metaphor for the practice of bodhi itself; the fifteenth day of the waxing moon as a metaphor for the perfection of all practices, symbolizing the attainment of bodhi;
the fifteenth day of the waning moon as a metaphor for the exhaustion of all practices, symbolizing parinirvāṇa;

and the rising and falling [of the moon] during the intervening period as a metaphor for the power of skillful means—know that these already encompass the gate of the hundred-syllable vidyā-mantra. Saturn sustains the central matrix (garbhadhātu).
The Lotus retinue holds the right side; the Vajra retinue holds the left side; the Tathāgata’s fruit-virtues hold the upper direction;
and the powerful vidyārājas hold the lower direction. Furthermore, these five graspings represent the holding of the five-colored *sūtra*:
earth for faith, wood for diligence, gold for mindfulness, water for concentration, and fire for wisdom.
The other two [planets], Rāhu and Ketu, do not preside over the days because Rāhu acts as an obscuration and Ketu portends inauspiciousness.
The first watch of the day is like the manifestation of a pure mind; the middle watch is like the initiation of various practices;
the final watch is like the completion of all virtues, wherein purposeful activity gradually subsides. The first watch of the night is like dwelling in Great Nirvāṇa on the stage of self-realization.
In the latter part of the night, as he recalls his original vow, he arises through the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and begins his circumambulation once more, revolving without end.
Although the substance of the sun is one, the temporal divisions differ across the four continents;

here, the intention of this maṇḍala is to manifest the sun of the bodhicitta, and therefore it is taken at the time before the meal. To "encounter a virtuous state" means that the mind is signless (*animitta*).
This state of non-objectification is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; even when observed with the five eyes of a Buddha, its characteristics cannot be seen.

Nevertheless, there are various signs of the arising of roots of goodness that can be discerned. If one is an ācārya who has realized the Truths, one will naturally attain direct penetration in the present moment.
If one has not yet realized the Truths, one should examine its objective sphere within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): when one practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), various obstacles and afflictions (*ṣaḍ-kaṣāya*) are unable to hinder them;
they are praised by the various holy ones, and eventually receive the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhy-abhiṣeka*).

Alternatively, as previously mentioned, various seals and signs (*mudrā-lakṣaṇa*) manifest vividly and wondrously within samādhi, differing from the ordinary. By inferring through the analogy of cause and effect, these may be understood through the mind.
Even up to the point where all aspects are universally encompassed, these may likewise be understood.
As the Sūtra says: "First, one should prostrate to all Tathāgatas and awaken the Earth Goddess with such verses.
This means that when the Ācārya is about to awaken the Earth Goddess, he first directs his mind to contemplate the inexhaustible [qualities] of Vairocana.
The bodies of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time throughout the entire Dharma-realm are likewise adorned in this way;

each and every inexhaustible body of adornment pervades the Dharma-realm. From those Bodhisattvas in the tenth stage down to those in the first stage, their partially realized bodies of adornment are immeasurable and boundless, filling the Dharma-realm without any intervening gaps, like [sesame seeds in] a *hū* measure.
One should contemplate that the oil within the hemp reaches everywhere before all the holy ones;
with the three karmas purified and with utmost sincerity, one performs prostrations. By virtue of these causes and conditions, one obtains immeasurable merit.

One should then, with an unerring mind, offer it to those disciples, wishing that there be no obstacles or difficulties and that they may swiftly achieve unsurpassed bodhi. Next, a verse shall be spoken to awaken and inspire the earth deities.
When Śākyamuni Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment, he said to the Māra King:
"Because you practiced an inexhaustible gift in a previous life, you have now attained this body as the sovereign Lord of Devas;
however, since immeasurable kalpas ago, I have cultivated such great gifts in incalculable numbers, even without begrudging my own flesh, limbs, or hands and feet."
"Why do you challenge me to a comparison of our relative merits? Māra said, "The merit I have performed, you have already witnessed.
But who shall bear witness to your own meritorious deeds? If there is no witness, you shall fall into defeat.

At that time, the Bodhisattva extended his right hand and pointed to the ground, speaking these words of truth: "It was upon this very ground that I originally practiced the bodhisattva path in its various forms."
"The earth goddesses who have realized the stage of difficult practices and austerities should know that this refers to the Body Secret Seal (*kāyaguhyamudrā*).
At that time, immeasurable earth goddesses leapt forth from the earth, manifesting half their bodies to bear witness; by this means, the hosts of Māra’s army were dispersed.
Now, because the Ācārya wishes to cause his disciples to succeed to the rank of the Tathāgata before long, he likewise..."
When this seal was used to rouse the Earth Goddess, that goddess gave rise to great joy and thought to herself:
"Now this Son of the Buddha is able to establish the causal conditions for a great undertaking; he has awakened me so that we may be protected and spared from harm and affliction.
I should employ skillful means to protect him and cause him to be free from all demonic activities. With this assembly...
By the power of these conditions, this very ground shall become identical to vajra. The aforementioned *ārya-gāthā* is called the "Mantra of Spontaneous Accomplishment.
When performing the rite, one should recite the Sanskrit original; it is now recorded in full.
Recite it seven times while pressing the five wheels of the right hand against the ground.
*Tvaṃ* (you), *devi* (goddess—note the feminine ending), *śākye* (protector), *durbodhe* (kinsman—at;
the character "at" enters into the following phrase). Translated: O Goddess, you who are the kinsman and protector.
*Sarvabuddhānām* (of all Buddhas—note the plural ending). *Tathā*.
*Nan* (the aspirated vowel indicates "crossing over the world," which carries the meaning of "guide") is translated as "to all the Buddhas, the Guides.
*Śrīye* (a conjunct) (*caryā*) *naya* (practice) *viśeṣa* (excellence) is translated as "practicing supreme conduct. *Bhūmi* (pure ground) *prāptāya*.
*Kāṇa* (meaning "bank" or "shore") *sūtra* (meaning "equal" or "like") is translated as "Pāramitā of the Pure Ground" (the meaning of the word contains the character for "equal").
*Māra* (the celestial Māra) *sainya* (army) *tathā* (thus) *hala* (two syllables, *ha-la*) *na* (to break). Translated: "Thus breaking the army of Māra. *Śākya*.
Saṃghanātha (Saṃgha = lion; nātha = savior). Translated as: "The Lion of the Śākyas, Savior. Tadyathā (tadyathā = thus it is;
māra = Māra; jaya = conquer; kilipta = subdue). Translated as: "I, too, shall conquer and subdue Māra."
*Maṇḍala-likhe-mā-haṃ*. Translated as "I draw the maṇḍala. The meaning of this verse is that one first addresses the Earth Goddess, saying:
"O Goddess, you who personally protect this great earth, you who have already made offerings..."

Having served and drawn near to all Buddhas, the Guides, one cultivates sublime practices, purifies and fulfills the stages (*bhūmi*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*), as well as various other merits.
These are explained extensively through the examination of phenomena in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, it says "and so forth" (*ādi*).

In the current translation, five characters are taken as a single verse-line (*śloka-pāda*), though it cannot be preserved in its entirety; however, this has already been addressed within the section on the Stages and Perfections.
This contains all these manifold virtues. The next verse expresses the intention of providing an exhortation:

"He speaks words of truth, just as when the World-Honored One was formerly in the Bodhi-maṇḍala and subdued the hosts of Māra and the devas; you appeared within that great assembly to act as a witness.
Because of this, the World-Honored One is titled 'Śākyasiṃha' (Lion of the Śākyas), who can stride alone without fear and save [beings]."
O Protectors of the World, I now likewise wish to follow the conduct of the Buddha and succeed to the tasks of the Tathāgata;

for this reason, I draw this maṇḍala. Although I have not yet attained everything equal to the Tathāgata, by means of the empowerment of the three secrets of Vairocana, I am also able to manifest the body of a Buddha and universally assemble the great assembly of all maṇḍalas.
Therefore, you should now likewise manifest as a witness so that the hosts of Māra cannot destroy [this dharma].

Furthermore, the Earth Deity is this female deity who is the meaning of *samādhi*; she is the *samādhi* of the World-Honored One Vairocana for protecting and sustaining the mind-ground of all sentient beings.
Regarding the true nature of phenomena (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), when the World-Honored One was formerly at Bodhi...
When the Maṇḍala subdues the Māra of the Ground of Abiding Ignorance and his sands-of-the-Ganges-like great assembly,
and when the hand of Prajñāpāramitā extends its five fingers to press upon the hearts and minds of all sentient beings,
may you manifest as a witness through your samādhi; therefore, the four kinds of māra-armies of the immeasurable sentient beings who are to be delivered shall thereby retreat and disperse.
Therefore, he is titled the Lion of Silent Action, who is able to rescue the world through his sovereign supernormal powers.
I now also wish to level and cultivate the minds of my disciples and paint the Great Compassion Maṇḍala;
you, too, should act as a witness to this, so that the hosts of the four Māra armies may be subdued. Furthermore, I shall explain this *ariṣa* by means of the letter-gates (*akṣaramukha*).
It possesses immeasurable meanings, yet its essential ultimate principle lies precisely within the syllable *tad*.
In the Sanskrit sound *tad*, the long vowel of the syllable *ta* inherently carries the sound of *a*;

because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, they are, in their true nature (*dharmatā*), neither increasing nor decreasing. It is by means of this meaning that all earth deities are awakened. He recited it.

When reciting the verse, one should kneel with both knees on the ground, extend the hand of wisdom (*jñāna-hasta*), and with the five fingers (*pañca-aṅguli*) spread and the palms level, press them against the earth while reciting this *āryā* verse. Thus, one should seal it seven times;
this is what is called the "correspondence of mantra and mudrā. The Ācārya said: when wishing to perform this rite, first [use] three...
Through the empowerment of the self-nature of the Samaya-dharmadhātu-vajra, one's own body becomes as described in the ritual for making offerings;
having purified the ground of the mind and the site of the practice through the letter-gateway *ra*,
one first generates a half-moon wind-wheel within the yoga and empowers it with the syllable *ha*, followed by generating a water-wheel empowered by the syllable *va*.
Next, visualize the Vajra Earth Mandala and empower it with the syllable *A*. Contemplate this single object with one-pointed concentration until it is clearly manifest.
Skillfully regulate the mind and the breath, reciting the gateway of the syllable *A* continuously and without interruption.
When your strength is exhausted and the breath returns, recite it again—whether for one breath or three breaths—until a sensation of tactile contact is felt. Proceed in this manner.

Because this is a skillful means of single-minded focus, one immediately enters samādhi and beholds the great assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of Secret Adornment, or else perceives within oneself the various faults and transgressions of the internal and external worlds.

As the Sūtra says, "Those who offer offerings such as fragrant ointments and flowers do not merely serve to awaken [the mind]; they should also offer various kinds of incense, flowers, lamps, and light."
This nourishes the Buddhas of the ten directions as well as the earth deities. Now, within this earth there are three kinds [of grounds]:

namely, the ground of one's own mind, the ground of the disciple's mind, and the ground of the path; all of these are purified by means of the letter-gateway *ra* and sustained by means of the letter-gateway *a*, thereby causing them to become adamantine (*vajra*).
If one explains the meaning of "offering" according to the secret interpretation, it is likewise so. If...
The Ācārya dedicates the various merits of the pure bodhicitta toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna);
this is the offering to all Buddhas and the holders of the ground within one’s own dharmadhātu.
By dedicating these merits to the disciple to assist in the causes and conditions for attaining Buddhahood, it is the offering to all [Buddhas] within the disciple’s mental dharmadhātu.
If the Buddhas and the holders of the earth were to use this adamantine *maṇḍala* for adornment, it would constitute a Dharma-offering to all the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Having made this offering, one should further take refuge in all Tathāgatas; the same principle may be understood by analogy.
As the Sūtra says: "Thereafter, one should purify the ground according to the proper sequence and should be fully endowed with all virtues."
This means that whenever one wishes to construct a maṇḍala, one must first perform such rites before excavating the ground and selecting the site for treatment;

this also encompasses the threefold meaning of the ground, including both the exoteric and esoteric explanations, up to the sequence of all constituent parts as described in the sūtra—hence it says, "one should be endowed with all virtues.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, wishing to elucidate the profound and secret [teachings] of the Tathāgata, [proceeded].
With the intent of severing the doubts of future disciples, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and spoke in verse:
“The Buddha-dharma is free from all marks, even not conforming to dharmas;

yet the Way is that which I have personally heard from the Buddha as the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas, far removed from all marks of phenomena. It is where the Buddha dwells, abiding in the station of the Dharma.”

Whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, he is eternally quiescent, inconceivable, and beyond the reach of thought or discrimination; nor can he be expressed through causes, measures, or analogies.

If the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is eternally thus, it cannot be created by any Buddhas, much less could it be produced by the accumulation of conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*). Why is this?

The God among Gods, the Greatly Valiant One, now speaks of these conditioned phenomena—the selection of sites, the construction of mandalas, and so forth—as well as the sequential procedures for mantras, so that practitioners may prepare various incenses, flowers, and offerings;
train the mouth through contemplation and verbal recitation; train the body through mudrās and dignified deportment; and direct the mind toward the color, appearance, form, and status of the deity.
