Since these are conditioned and possess characteristics, how could they truly accord with the unconditioned and characteristicless path of the nature of phenomena?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will reveal the profound meaning therein, so as to eliminate the world’s deluded attachments to words and their feelings of doubt and slander.
At that time, the Bhagavat answered with a verse from the perspective of the World-Honored One, beginning with: "Listen well to the characteristics of dharmas.

Because the characteristics of the true meaning of all dharmas are extremely profound and difficult to perceive, he thus exhorted them to listen well. Indeed, dharmas are eternally without intrinsic nature and arise from a multitude of conditions;
this is precisely the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*), which transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Beyond this, what more do you wish to ask?
Is it that one seeks the signless and unconditioned Dharma? Therefore, the next line says: "The Dharma is free from discrimination and all delusive thoughts.

If one understands the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) in this way, then one clearly perceives the true nature of the mind (*cittadharmatā*), which has been eternally unborn from the very beginning.
At that time, all actions of body, speech, and mind are like empty space.
Because it can be fully exhausted, it is said: "I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment, which is ultimately like empty space.

However, all ignorant, childish, ordinary beings, because they do not know according to reality, falsely and erroneously cling to various objects—namely, time, direction, and various appearances—and are constantly moistened by the waters of craving and shrouded by ignorance. If I were to abandon direction...
If one were to directly preach such a Dharma of self-realization to sentient beings, how could they possibly comprehend it and proceed toward realization?
Therefore, the following verse clarifies the intent behind establishing the teaching: "In order to deliver them, I speak in accordance with skillful means.
The Buddha’s intention is to say that because the characteristics of the profound Dharma cannot be proclaimed directly, he employs expedient means.
Thus, by entrusting this maṇḍala with its complete requisites and constituent parts, the beginner finds a ground upon which to fix the mind;

their practice becomes unfailing. Furthermore, by receiving the Buddha’s empowerment and simultaneously observing the ten phrases of dependent origination, they are able to sport in supernatural powers within the unmoving true reality, universally contemplating all spiritual friends and adorning all things.
The Buddha-land does not desire that practitioners abandon all practices to dwell in signlessness (*animitta*), nor does it desire that they cling to all practices to dwell in signs (*sanimitta*).
Therefore, it is said: "Although time, direction, place, and action are spoken of, in reality there is no time, no direction, no action, and no agent.
All those phenomena (*dharmas*) abide solely in the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If all...
All conditioned phenomena abide entirely within the true mark (*dharmatā*); how could they be like those deluded people who might wish to escape from space or wish to become attached to space?
Furthermore, within this context, the Ācārya extensively expounds the parable of the three carts from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
just as that elder’s sons were young and ignorant, and although he [prepared] various kinds of good things...
When he spoke these words of exhortation, wishing to lead them out of the danger of the fire, they were ultimately unable to do so.
At that time, the elder observed that their deep-seated inclinations were fixed solely upon play; thus, employing a skillful means, he told them:
"Now, outside this gate there are three kinds of wonderful chariots; you should go and take them, and you may amuse yourselves with them. When those sons heard this, they [responded].
Because they were engaged in play according to their own desires, their emotions were all intensely focused and they vied with one another to emerge;
yet when they attained the precious vehicle (ratnayāna) as their equal share—its adornments being supreme—it was not what their original minds had planned.
This Dharma-gate of the maṇḍala is likewise so: the Tathāgata employs worldly causes, conditions, matters, and signs to provide analogies and metaphors for that which is inconceivable.

When one deliberates upon the Dharma-realm to descend and reach the various capacities of sentient beings, if one can receive and grasp it, one will be able to develop faith and understanding through the universal gate (*samantamukha*) and courageously advance in practice.

Furthermore, when one personally perceives the luminosity of the mind through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the three mysteries (*triguhyaka*), one realizes that all various names and phrases are the secret names (*guhyasaṃjñā*) of the Tathāgata; this is not something that can be conceived by ordinary minds. As it is said: "For three months, maintain..."
Reciting [the name] is actually the threefold expedient within the inherently pure and perfect luminosity; how could it be understood merely as a ninety-day practice?
Furthermore, the Buddha Ratnaketu of the East signifies the initial arousal of the pure bodhicitta;
how could it be understood merely as the eastern direction? By analogy with this, all other dharma-gates can be grasped through the mind; therefore, it is said: "And..."
In reality, there is no time or direction; it abides solely in the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, O Bhagavat, out of infinite great compassion and pity for those sentient beings of future ages who possess heavy obstructions and dull faculties, and who are unable to enter the Dharma-realm all at once, you have established provisional skillful means within this profound and secret treasury by means of the *parivarta-dhāraṇī* (the revolving dhāraṇī), while also incorporating superficial and abbreviated methods.
Even if one practices contemplation within the realm of signs (*nimitta*), the accomplishment of worldly *siddhi* will not be in vain;
for through the secret support of the three mysteries (*triguhyasamaya*), one will ultimately attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, the subsequent verse says:

"Furthermore, Lord of Mysteries, in a future age, there will be sentient beings of inferior intelligence who, obscured by delusion and craving, rely solely upon signs and constantly delight in the views of annihilationism and eternalism."

Regarding those who are blind and ignorant concerning the various signs of wholesome and unwholesome actions performed in specific places, and who seek fruits without understanding this path—so that they may be delivered, the Dharma is taught in accordance with their needs.
Therefore, one who transmits the Dharma should skillfully recognize the faculties and conditions of others, as well as the appropriate measure of each Dharma-gate;
one should administer medicine according to the illness without error. If the capacity of the recipient is such that they cling to signs...
If one were to suddenly explain the meaning of the profound emptiness to such a person, it would cause them fear and doubt, increasing their lack of faith;

if one were to suddenly bestow a shallow and abbreviated teaching upon those of sharp faculties, deep roots, and wisdom, they would consider it inconsistent with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) true path and develop contempt for it.
Since this would be of no benefit to others and would cause oneself to violate the samaya, one should first...
Abiding in yogic contemplation, once one has thoroughly understood the causal conditions of that [reality] from its beginning to its end,

one should contemplate the intent within these questions and answers to employ provisional means (*upāya*) to reveal the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*). By instructing others by dispersing this intent into all gates of skillful means (*upāyamukha*),
one will be able to bring great benefit and thus no obstacles or difficulties will arise.
The Sūtra states: "O Guhyapati, within any of the locations thus described, one should prepare a site on a particular ground, making it firm and solid.
One should take *gomaya* (cow dung) and *gomutra* (cow urine) that have not yet reached the earth, mix them together, and smear [the ground].
Next, one should purify it by sprinkling with scented water using mantras, as prescribed in the teachings. In constructing a maṇḍala, one must complete it within seven days."
On the first day, the ācārya should abide in the self-nature of Mahāvairocana;
then, he should rouse the earth goddess (*pṛthivī-devatā*) through the expedient means of adorning her body, as described in the sequence of the *Pūjā-vidhi*.
Having roused her, he should then empower the site with the mantra of Acala. Thereafter, he should dig the ground and purify it according to the ritual rules; he should first dig at the center.
Having measured one cubit (*hasta*) and finished the selection, one should fill it back in again. If there is an excess and it overflows, it is a superior site;

if it is exactly as it was before, it is a middling site; if it does not reach the level, it is an inferior site. Having thus successively eliminated all defects, one should finely treat the excavated earth and fill it back in little by little.
Moistening it with cow’s urine, one should ram it firm and level it until it is as smooth as the palm of a hand. Next—
One uses *gomaya* and *gomutra* mixed together and applies them as an ointment. To explain this in a brief and superficial manner:
it refers to cow dung and its liquid, used for the sake of purification according to the local customs of that region. However, explaining it according to the secret [esoteric] interpretation:

*go* has the meaning of "movement" (*gati*), because by entering the gateway of the letter *A*, all phenomena are without movement; *ma* has the meaning of "I" (*aham*); and *i*... [is the meaning of] *iti*.
As for the meaning of "riding" (yāna): why is it that all phenomena have no movement? Because the self (ātman) cannot be found in any phenomenon;
if there is no self, then there is neither that which is ridden upon nor a rider. This is what is called the Mahāyāna. The meaning of *gum* is the same as explained previously.
*Tāra* means suchness (*tathatā*), the sense of being free from dust and defilement; this is the true mark of the mind. If one practices...
One who can thus purify the ground of the mind will be ultimately pure and free from all obstacles.
Having selected a level site and prepared it, one should ascertain its dimensions;
then, at the center of the maṇḍala, one should dig a pit about one cubit deep, empower five jewels, five grains, and five medicinal herbs with the *Sarvakarmasādhana* mantra, and place them therein.
The removal of impurities and other such matters are all as explained in the *Pūjā-vidhi* (Ritual of Offerings). As for the profound and secret interpretation:
it refers to the five jewels of wisdom established within the *bodhicitta*, which can give rise to the five kinds of wholesome sprouts and eliminate the five kinds of afflictions;
therefore, they are called the "five grains" and the "five medicines. Having thus arranged them, one further cleanses and smears [the ground] to make it perfectly level and even.

One should take the empowerment flask (*abhiṣeka-ghaṭa*), fill it with pure water so that it is not overfilled, insert various flowers and fruits, and place within it the five jewels, grains, and medicinal herbs.

Having placed it at the site where the treasures are buried, from the third day onward after the flask has been set down, one should daily recite the *karmasādhana-mantra* one hundred and eight times during the three sessions of the day to consecrate this flask; thereafter, perform the remaining rites.
On the evening of the fourth day of the ritual proceedings, one next consecrates the perfumed water with the Perfumed Water Mantra, either one hundred and eight times or up to one thousand times;
thereafter, one sprinkles it for purification. That mantra is as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām (1) apratisame gagana-same (2) samatanugate (3) prakkṛti-viśuddhe (4) dharma-dhātu-viśodhani (5) svāhā (6)

The first phrase is "I universally take refuge in all Buddhas. Just as the three bodies (*trikāya*) of Vairocana pervade all places, so too do all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time;

now, having taken refuge in them all with a universal mind, this mantra is further recited so that these World-Honored Ones will not transgress their original vows and will collectively bestow their empowerment.
This is maintained as a proof; the same applies to all subsequent mantras, which will not be explained in detail here.
In the second line, the initial letter-gateway *A* constitutes the essence of the mantra, that is to say, the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
All other letter-gateways serve to adorn this syllable; thus, this letter-gateway is the very source of the bodhicitta.
Now, regarding the Maṇḍala King Born from the Treasury of Great Compassion that is being constructed: first, one sprinkles it with scented water for purification.
This is done to treat such a "mind-ground" (cittabhūmi) so that it may be freed from all defilements. If one discusses external objects, these too are the supported vajra-mind-ground;
therefore, all other syllables serve to perfect this gateway of letters (akṣaramukha). The letter A is the root of all phenomena.
Regarding the meaning of "non-arising," it is next explained as *prā* (*pra*). *Pra* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
*Ra* is called "dust" (*rajas*), because all syllables enter the gateway of the letter *A*; thus, this dust is fundamentally non-arisen.
That which is fundamentally non-arisen is the ultimate truth. The ultimate truth is what is called the pure bodhicitta. Next...
The character *ti* (底) is essentially the gateway of the many characters (*bahudvāra*). Because it carries the sound of *samādhi*, it is transformed into *ti*.
*Ti* has the meaning of "mind" (*citta*) and also the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*). That which is the true aspect of one's own mind is precisely the pure bodhicitta.
This pure bodhicitta, being entirely free from defilement and attachment toward all phenomena, is called abiding in the Lotus Samādhi.
This samādhi is such that even the mark of emptiness of all phenomena cannot be apprehended, because it is the "Great Emptiness" (mahā-śūnyatā) of all Buddhas.
Next, the gates of the syllables *sa* and *ma* are explained; because it possesses the sound of samādhi through the equalization of concentration and wisdom, it is called *samaya*.
Here, the explanation is provided solely by way of the syllable-gates (*akṣara-mukha*), as is done in various Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras according to the four *siddhāntas*.

Through various causes, conditions, and parables, such as the four kinds of non-arising (*catur-ajāti*), the gateway of the letter A (*akāra-dvāra*) is extensively expounded with immeasurable phrases and meanings.
Furthermore, because the sound "A" is present within all speech, every single gateway of letters contains all other gateways of letters.
One who grasps this meaning should be able to explain them by freely revolving [the gates] at will; it cannot be fully described hereafter.

This concludes the detailed exposition. Furthermore, within mantras there are the meanings of syllables (*akṣara*) and the meanings of phrases (*pada*). The meaning of syllables has already been explained as before.
As for the meaning of phrases, this *apratisama* (unequaled) signifies being without equal or counterpart;
it means that this King of Maṇḍalas of the Mind-Ground transcends all speech and metaphors, such that not even a single dharma exists [to compare with it].

Because it can be paired with its counterpart, it is said to be "without equal. Why is this so? It is because it fully encompasses the meanings explained by the aforementioned *dharmamukha* (gateways of letters).
The meaning of the third phrase, "equal to space," is that this ground of mind (*cittabhūmi*) is ultimately pure, non-conceptual, and boundless, being identical to space.
Furthermore, the gateway of the letter *ga* signifies "action" (*karma*); what is that?

The meaning of mastery over phenomena through great emptiness is that, because the gateway of the letter *A* enters the letter *Ga*, all phenomena have from the very beginning been entirely without movement.
The Tathāgata, within these phenomena, has reached the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and furthermore has no further movement;
because he practices by means of non-practice, he dwells in mastery over phenomena through great emptiness by means of the mind of self.
Since the ground is ultimately equal to this great emptiness, one should know that the mental ground of the disciple and the ground of the path are likewise so;
therefore, it is said they are "equal to empty space. Regarding the meaning of the fourth phrase, "equal and conforming":
because the vajra-ground is equal to empty space, it is able to equally pervade all realms of sentient beings and universally manifest bodies that accord with their various types.

Therefore, it is suitable to be depicted as a maṇḍala. Furthermore, *sa* has the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*), *ma* has the meaning of "self" (*ātman*), and *yi* has the meaning of "meaning" (*artha*).

(These characters are retained in both forms because the two meanings of "shallow" and "outflow" have not yet been definitively resolved. Because the realm of all sentient beings is fundamentally unborn, they are all entirely suchness;
therefore, the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings are ultimately equal. *Nu* refers to the Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahā-śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Coming to abide in this Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahā-śūnyatā-samādhi*), there is no practice, no arrival, and no coming or going;
yet, it can manifest in accordance with conditions according to the measure of one's own mind. Therefore, it is called "equal conformity" (*samatā-anuvartana*).

Regarding the meaning of the fifth phrase, "inherently pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*), it further explains the gate of the letter *A* as the pure bodhicitta, as well as the meaning of the fragrant water. The Tathāgata, through the dharma of equal attainment (*samāpatti*), [realizes] the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This fragrance, when blended with the water of the Great Compassion Samādhi, can universally sprinkle the mental grounds of all sentient beings, removing their defilements.

Why is this so? Because its intrinsic nature is pure; just as the nature of water is fundamentally pure and thus able to cleanse all filth, the perfumed water of the Tathāgata is likewise able to purify everything because it is fundamentally pure from the beginning.
Because it concerns the minds of sentient beings, the meaning of the sixth phrase is next clarified: "the purification of the *dharmadhātu*.

Just as scented water is sprinkled on the ground to remove impurities, so too does the Tathāgata, with the fragrance of the naturally pure precepts blended with the water of naturally pure compassion, sprinkle it everywhere upon the naturally pure mental ground of sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*, in order to eliminate all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Because all things are purified and removed, one should also extensively expound them by means of the various *dharmamukhas* (gateways of letters).
Since all Tathāgatas have spoken such great vows in common, they are called *mantras*. Furthermore, the *dharmadhātu* is itself the realm of sentient beings;
the realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of mind; and the realm of mind is itself the primordial purity of intrinsic nature.
Purity is that which pervades all things equally, being equal to space; that which is equal to space is the peerless, equal to the gateway of the letter A.
Just as space is boundless, one should know that the gateway of the letter A is also boundless.
Just as space is unstained, unchanging, and immovable, one should know that the gateway of the letter A is likewise unstained and unchanging.
Unmoving like space, it is free from all marks yet contains all images; it is free from all activity yet the worldly affairs of the world are accomplished by means of it.

The gateway of the letter A is likewise thus: without mark and without activity, yet it is fully endowed with inexhaustible adornments and accomplishes the inconceivable karma of the universal gate. In this way, one should [enter] by means of various gateways oneself.
Although this has been explained, there are furthermore immeasurable and boundless unprecedented qualities that cannot be illustrated even by the analogy of empty space;
therefore, the letter-gate *A* as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of mantra transcends all such analogies.
The final phrase, *svāhā*, carries the meaning of "awakening," for when all Tathāgatas were practicing the bodhisattva path in their past lives, they collectively beheld [this truth].
For this reason, I shall certainly utter a lion’s roar with words of truth:
"I must, by means of this gateway of the letter A, purify the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings everywhere.

If this vow of mine is not false, then for all those sentient beings who recite these words of my sincerity without violating the Dharma rules, I shall fulfill their aspirations exactly as they are. Now, I...
Because this mantra is spoken in accordance with the Tathāgata’s samaya teachings, I pray that you do not violate your original vow;
thus, may my maṇḍala be fully adorned and purified—therefore it says *svāhā*. The meaning of *svāhā* in all subsequent mantras is largely the same.
Whenever one places the five inner jewels, one should immediately pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions as previously described.
Then he makes this request: "I shall perform the invitation for the Dharma tomorrow.

From the third day thereafter, one should gradually determine the size and orientation of the maṇḍala—whether it be four cubits, twelve cubits, or more—and mark the positions of all the noble deities using white sandalwood paste.
If the ācārya is unable to maintain these details in his memory, [he should record them].
One should even paint their images or record them in writing so that each is clearly distinct;
having finished sprinkling pure scented water for purification, one should use white sandalwood to smear a circular maṇḍala measuring twelve finger-widths in diameter.
First, one places the position of the World-Honored One Mahāvairocana within the central womb (garbha); next, in the eastern direction, at the place of Mahavīra, one places all the Tathāgatas.
In the southeastern quarter, place the seat of the *Cintāmaṇi*; in the northeastern quarter, place the seats of all the Bodhisattvas;
in the space before [the central deity], place the seat of the Mother of Buddhas (*Buddhamātṛ*); to the right of Vairocana, place the seat of Padmapāṇi;
to the left of Vairocana, place the seat of Vajrapāṇi; and in the southwestern corner, place the seat of the Noble One (*Ārya*).

The position of Trailokyavijaya is placed in the northwest sector of the moving mandala; the western direction is the location of the main entrance, which is where the ācārya resides and performs the yoga of ritual offerings.
The Sūtra states: First, "the first I-body" refers to the state of Vairocana, who, together with the five Buddhas and others, should be placed upon a single maṇḍala.
Second, "all the World-Saviors" refers to the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who are now divided into two positions.
Third, "those who are equal to them" refers to the Buddha-mothers; the Tathāgata is called the Peerless One, and Prajñāpāramitā...
Because honey is equal to the Peerless (Asamasama), it is said that they are "equal thereto. The fourth and fifth are the lords of the Lotus and Vajra families;
one should know that the sixth, Acala, is Trailokyavijaya. All of these are vidyādharas who accomplish all activities;
one should understand that by citing these six positions, all deities are subsumed. Having performed [the ritual] in this manner, it is completed.
One should first arrange incense, flowers, and offering implements according to the ritual sequence for making offerings.

Then, one should visualize a precious lotus pedestal and a palace of jewel-kings; within it, upon a seat, place a white lotus pedestal and transform the gateway of the letter *A* into the body of the Tathāgata Vairocana, with a color like Jambu-river gold and polished purple-gold, resembling the form of a Bodhisattva.
With a topknot upon his head shaped like a crown, his entire body radiates light of various colors, and he is clad in garments of fine silk and gauze;
these are the insignia of one who has become a Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksambuddha) within the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.

The clothing of the noble devas in that realm is so light and exquisite that it possesses no weight even down to a single *zhū* (liang); its essential nature is pure and refined, such that it requires no external adornments.
The World-Honored One’s appearance conforms to that image. If one were to provide a profound and esoteric interpretation:
the Tathāgata’s wondrously adorned marks are naturally present without diminution, for they are not produced through artificial effort; thus, he does not use external jewels as ornaments.
Even the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power, are able to see his body of empowerment; yet, regarding his eternally quiescent essence, it is as [before].
It is compared to thin gauze because the Jāmbūnada gold is likewise naturally pure in nature and possesses the deepest brilliance;

the essence of the Buddha’s vajra-wisdom is most profound and subtle, emitting various kinds of light from his entire body, which is the universal gate (*samantamukha*) revealing the great wisdom-light.
Next, one should contemplate the Buddhas of the four directions upon the eight petals in the four cardinal directions.
In the east is the Tathāgata Ratnaketu (Jewel Banner), whose color is like the rising sun, a radiant interplay of red and white;

"Jewel Banner" signifies the arousal of the bodhicitta. It is, for example, like a military general who, in leading a great host, must first obtain the banner and standard before being able to deploy the troops in unison to defeat enemy nations and achieve great renown. The myriad practices of the Tathāgata are likewise so.
Therefore, because he took the vow for omniscience as his banner and defeated the hosts of the four Māras beneath the Bodhi tree, it was by this that he was named.
His color is like the morning sun; this is also a corresponding meaning. To the south is the Buddha King of the Blossoming Flowers of the Śāla Tree King;
his physical marks are golden, universally emitting light, as if abiding in the Vimala-samādhi (Stainless Samādhi).
The characteristic signs of this [Buddhahood] begin with the seed of the bodhicitta, which nurtures the myriad practices of great compassion;
now, having attained universal enlightenment, the myriad virtues have fully blossomed, and thus it is so named. "Free from defilement" (vimala) is the meaning of Great Emptiness (mahāśūnyatā).

When this Great Emptiness is realized, it is like pure gold that has been refined a hundred times, such that all impurities are utterly exhausted; the marks and signs of the Buddha’s body are likewise so. This is the worldly [explanation].
If superior gold were compared to Jāmbūnada gold, its color would be pale and somewhat turbid; it could not match the natural, mirror-like clarity and purity of the latter.
This is because the Buddha on the flower-leaf arises from the conditions of mental construction (*citta-mātra*), and thus there are degrees of difference.
Next, in the north, one should visualize Akṣobhya Buddha as dwelling in a state of coolness free from heat, abiding in tranquil meditative concentration.
One should discern that this is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of nirvāṇa; therefore, the meaning is "immovable," though this is not its original name.

Its original name should be translated as "Drum-Sound Tathāgata. Just as a celestial drum has no form whatsoever and yet has no fixed location, yet can produce the sound of the Dharma to awaken sentient beings, so too is Great Parinirvāṇa; it is not like those two [the drum and the sound].
It is used as a metaphor because the vehicle of eternal quiescence possesses no further sublime function. Next, one contemplates Amitāyus Buddha in the western direction;
this is the expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata. Because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, the great compassion and expedient means of all Buddhas likewise have no end;
therefore, he is named Amitāyus. In the Sanskrit language, *amita* means "immeasurable," while *āyuṣ* means "life" or "noble one. Furthermore—
Because he has conquered the four māras, he is called a "Victor" (Jina). Thus, the verse fully translates this meaning, referring to him as the "Benevolent Victor.
These two Buddhas are also of a true golden color; with eyes slightly closed, they gaze downward, assuming the form of the Samādhi of Quiescence.
All Buddhas are like this. At the four corners of the lotus pedestal, there are four bodhisattvas, as described in the following text. The first...
In the position of all Tathāgatas, one should contemplate that a single Buddha is within the golden altar, which is identical to the bodies of all Buddhas;
for the remaining positions according to the various scriptures, one should likewise transform the seed-syllables (*bīja*) into bodies so that each is clearly understood.
Regarding the method of transforming seed-syllables in a maṇḍala, every deity employs its own fundamental seed-syllable, or alternatively, those common to the various families (*kula*).

Regarding the use of syllables such as the three-part *asvā* and so forth: if one fears that an ācārya of shallow practice cannot rotate [the visualization] so swiftly, one should simply contemplate the gateway of the letter *A*.
From this, immeasurable light is produced; wherever that light reaches, the body of the respective deity appears.
This should be followed in all ritual practices during the night. Whenever practicing contemplative cultivation (*vipaśyanā*), one should first, with...
Regarding the method for maintaining the body with the five syllables as explained in the *Pūjāvidhi*: one visualizes one's own mind as an eight-petaled lotus.
The Ācārya says that when ordinary people refer to the "heart" (*hṛdaya*)—this is a corruption of the ancient translation of the Sanskrit term;
the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *hrīḥ* (two-syllable compound), which means "heart," and its form is like that of a lotus bud that has not yet opened.
There are sinews and veins that bind it together, forming eight divisions. The male part faces upward and the female part faces downward;
first, one should visualize this lotus flower so that it opens into an eight-petaled white lotus seat.

Upon this pedestal, one should visualize the letter *A*, the color of a vajra, with the King of Universal Radiance (*Śatasahasraraśmipratimaṇḍita*) placed at its center, and observe it with stainless eyes.
Because this is through self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), one becomes the body of Vairocana.

By means of this expedient, one contemplates that the body of Vairocana is now non-dual and indistinguishable from one's own body; while situated between the two vidyārājas, this is called "dwelling in the Buddha-chamber.
When the drawing of the maṇḍala is completed, the ācārya shifts his seat and emerges from within it.
Outside the entrance of the maṇḍala, one should position at the site of this Buddha-chamber whichever honored deity one prefers;
or place a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra upon a precious golden platter, adorned with offerings; or place one’s own held rosary, vajra, vajra-bell, or other implements.
Furthermore, whenever one intends to select and prepare the ground, one should visualize one’s own mind as a wish-fulfilling jewel upon a lotus flower.
When one observes closely a jewel that is transparent both inside and out, all signs of good and evil appear within it.
The ācārya should then use wisdom and skillful means to select and refine it so that it becomes firm, solid, level, and upright;
the observation of the disciple’s mind is likewise. The profound and secret meaning herein can be grasped through the intent alone; the practitioner should abide therein.
Having completed the aforementioned visualization of the various noble deities within the Buddha-chamber, one should transform the syllable *A* into *Va*.
Then, empowering oneself with Vajrasattva, one should offer incense, flowers, and so forth, according to the ritual; all these offerings are explained in detail in the sequence of the offering rites.
Thereafter, generating a heart of great compassion with utmost sincerity and reverence, one should recite the *Āryā-śloka* verses of invocation.
As in the sūtra text, the Sanskrit is preserved here as follows: *Samvāhalaṃ* (to be mindful),
*dume* (I), *sarve* (all), *īna* (O Noble One, i.e., the Buddhas), *karaṇa*.
Tvaṃ-kāruṇika-bhūme pālaya hūṃ kuru ca putrān śvo 'pi nityam ||
The meaning of this verse is as follows: "O Buddhas who possess compassion, I pray only that you hold me in your mindful regard.

I now request and inform you that the ritual for receiving and upholding the stages (*bhūmi*) shall be performed; together with all the sons of the Buddha, please descend tomorrow to serve as witnesses.
Within the sound of "hold me in your mindful regard" (*dhārayantu*), there is already the intention of requesting their arrival.
This is the position of the White Sandalwood Maṇḍala.
*The Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
*The Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*, Fascicle Four.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Yixing.
Chapter Two, Part Two through Five of the *Mantra-vidhi-sambhāra-maṇḍala*:
On the evening of the fifth day, one should again sequentially prepare all the ritual requirements, properly adorn oneself, and contemplate the eight maṇḍalas.

Having completed each stage of the *caitya* ritual—including the invitation (*āvāhana*) and the protective binding (*rakṣā*)—one should recite the mantra of Acala or Trailokyavijaya in conjunction with their respective secret mudrās one hundred and eight times to consecrate this site. The *ācārya* says:
"From the third day onward, one shall perform recitation at the three sessions each day; at every session, one must recite the Acala mantra."
Recite the mantra one hundred and eight times to consecrate the ground; this is not to be done for this single night alone.
Furthermore, from the first day until the third day, if any obstacles arise, you must withdraw [the ritual] and cease.

Even if the application of white sandalwood has been completed, should various demonic events occur or if there is disharmony between the two parties, you must diligently apply skillful means to ensure that—
The attainment of other [results] is as explained in the *Guhya-samāja*.

On the fifth night, having completed the recitation of the Akṣobhya mantra, one should next recite the Bhūmiparigraha-mantra with the body of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, perform the samādhi-mudrā, and recite this mantra as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām (1) sarvatathāgata- (2) ṣṭhāna-ṣṭhitī (3) ajarī (4) vimarī (5) samalane (6) prakṛtipariśuddhe (7) svāhā.
The first phrase is the taking of refuge in all Buddhas. The meaning of the second and third phrases is that they are empowered by the empowerment of all Tathāgatas;
this signifies that just as that Vajra-maṇḍala was empowered by the combined spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas, so now shall this site likewise be. Furthermore, I have already leveled it...
The purification of the disciple’s ground of purity is completed. This is the site of the Maṇḍala of the Great Compassionate Treasury of the Heart-King Tathāgata.
Now I shall speak words of truth, which are empowered by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas, so that it may become firm and immovable.
The fourth phrase, "A-jo-ri," has the meaning of "immovable. The fifth phrase...
The phrase "Cloud-mi-ma-li" (A-mi-tā-bha) has the meaning of "stainless.

This signifies that through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas, it is made stable and immovable; not only is it immovable, but it is also made free from all stains.
It is precisely with the first syllable "A" of the fourth line that the essence of the mantra is established. By what dharma does the Tathāgata empower it?
Does it mean to cause [the mind] to be ultimately unshakable? It is because of this gateway of the syllable *A* that such power and function exist.

The sixth phrase has the meaning of mindful retention (*dhāraṇā*). Just as when a bhikṣu performs a *karmavācanā*, the assembly of monks unifies their minds in harmony to collectively receive and uphold it, so too is this mantra; it employs the addition of the syllable *A*.
Having completed the upholding, all Tathāgatas are requested to remember their original vows; thus, they collectively uphold it together. This seventh phrase has the meaning of "purity by nature.
This serves as a further explanation of the preceding phrase: for what reason do the Buddhas unanimously remember and uphold [this teaching]?
It is because of purity by nature. If a dharma enters the gateway of the letter A, it is from the very beginning unmoving and unarisen.
Because of this principle, all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time share one and the same precept and one and the same view;

it is for this reason that they collectively bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The final phrase, *svāhā*, is like the concluding seal of approval added at the end of a *saṃgha-karman* (formal ecclesiastical act).
It means: "If the truthful words I have uttered are certainly without error, may the Buddhas please not transcend their samādhi."
Therefore, this causes all that is performed to be perfected. Furthermore, the meaning of all the words herein should be explained in detail.
At that time, the ācārya should go outside the mandala of all Tathāgatas in the east and, facing east, recite and maintain the mantra three or seven times;
this will bring great benefit and virtue. Next, he should go to the south, and then to the west.
Next, proceeding toward the north, one should recite and maintain the mantra while facing away from the white sandalwood seat;
thus completing one circuit, one next proceeds to the position of Ākāśanetra, facing northeast and likewise facing away from the altar, and recites it there.
Next, one proceeds to the southeast, then the southwest, and then the northwest; having completed another circuit, one should once again pay homage with utmost sincerity in various ways.

Having performed the offerings, one sits facing east upon the ācārya’s seat, reciting the root mantra of one's chosen deity and abiding in the samādhi of that deity, all according to what is explained in the sequence of the offerings.
Furthermore, following the sequence, one should recite the mantras of the various deities of the white sandalwood mandala and form their respective mudrās.
The ācārya says: "First, recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family, Mahāvairocana."
Regarding the recitation of one hundred and eight times, for the remaining eight positions, one should contemplate those mantras and maintain them according to their length;

if one is further able to recite, one may additionally maintain the four Bodhisattvas of the second court, the principal deities such as Śākyamuni of the third court, and so forth, up to reciting all positions.
As for the position of white sandalwood, one should merely apply mud and sprinkle it with dry scented water.
Once it is finished, one may perform it; it need not necessarily wait until the fourth day.
After having personally completed the arrangement, one must maintain the recitation according to this method until the night of the ritual, which may be understood by analogy with the above.

On the night of the site-consecration (*bhūmi-parigraha*), the *ācārya* completes the recitation according to the rite, and finally, with the *vajra-chanting*, he extols all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas while remaining in meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*).
When utterly exhausted, one should perform the ritual protection of the body according to the dharma at this very site where the mandala is placed, and lie down facing east.
One should generate a heart of supreme great compassion and pity for the disciple to be initiated.
Furthermore, there is the method for binding the *sūtra* and holding the name of the disciple after the ground has been consecrated (*parigraha*).
When he sleeps peacefully, he should contemplate that within the heart-lotus pedestal, the syllable *ma* signifies that all phenomena (*dharmas*) cannot be apprehended as a self;
this is precisely the unobstructed bodhicitta, and it is also the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
It is further said that this wish-fulfilling jewel is nothing other than the syllable-gateway *a*. That ācārya shall [attain this] within his dreams.

Or they may see immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of great renown manifesting various activities—namely, guiding and transforming sentient beings through the three wheels according to their diverse capacities for liberation; or personally arranging and establishing the maṇḍala born of compassion;
or comforting and exhorting them with subtle and wondrous voices, saying: "You must now take pity upon sentient beings."
Therefore, it is well that you have fashioned this maṇḍala, O Mahāsattva; what you have drawn is most subtle and wondrous.
Such various realms as these, the ācārya should skillfully discern with a mind of wisdom.
One should know that all the holy ones have already together empowered this ground, and one may perform the rites according to one’s will. If there should be any obstacles, one ought to...
One should perform the homa ritual of application as a skillful means to purify [the mind], and must arouse a heart of great diligence so that the task to be accomplished is achieved.
Furthermore, if one encounters a master who has seen the truth (dṛṣṭasatya-ācārya), then within the wish-fulfilling jewel of the pure bodhicitta of the Lotus Samādhi,
one will naturally and clearly perceive the causes and conditions of obstacles and their absence, with an unimpeded mind that is the Buddha.

The face-to-face entrustment is for the purpose of resolving doubts; if one perceives any demonic activity (*mārakarman*), one should employ great wisdom and great skillful means to perform the essential *homa* ritual, ensuring that the mind held in practice remains unmoved and non-regressive, capable of establishing the maṇḍala of the dharmadhātu, after which one may rest.
Furthermore, from the very first moment the *ācārya* was startled and awakened...
From the moment the Earth Deity arrives, one should not abandon this site of the *maṇḍala*;

one should constantly perform empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and recitation therein, observing it with precise discernment. Whenever any part is found to be uneven or incorrect, one should immediately repair it.

Furthermore, one should contemplate that all necessary conditions and constituent parts must be fully prepared in advance, so as not to encounter deficiencies at the time of the rite and thereby give rise to doubt. From oneself...
Once the ritual for taking possession of the site (*bhūmiparigraha*) is completed, one should immediately demarcate the boundaries and establish the cardinal directions;

it is only on the night of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) that one should fashion the various deities. If they cannot be swiftly accomplished, there is no fault in practicing them gradually after the ritual for taking possession of the site.
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, on another day, one should receive those who are to be converted," and so on, down to "granting them scented water to drink for the sake of purifying their minds.

This clarifies the branch of receiving, establishing, and protecting disciples, and because the ritual for disciples must be performed during the clear night of the *dhāraṇī*-ground, it says "on another day. Herein, the qualifications of disciples are extensively distinguished.

The verse on the characteristics of those to be saved states: "If a disciple possesses faith, meaning that the ācārya observes their present faculties or their causes and conditions from long ago, and they believe directly without doubt in these three types of secret skillful means within this inconceivable dependent origination, being incapable of fear, then they are fit to be accepted; the rest is as explained in the section on the qualities of the teacher."
The verse says: "Born into a pure lineage" means being born into one of the four great castes, such as the Brahmins.
If one were born into a *vṛṣala* (outcaste) family or similar status, where the family traditions are inherited and practiced with impure conduct, their nature would be largely corrupt and evil.
If such a person were to receive the empowerment for transmitting the Dharma so as to circulate the Great Dharma, they would incur the contempt of others. Or...

The causes and conditions for becoming deficient in the Dharma are as follows: it is like a bhikṣu who, upon receiving full ordination, excludes those who have brought disgrace upon the Saṃgha or those of extremely low birth;
if one merely establishes a karmic connection to receive the Dharma, that is not what is being discussed here.
Furthermore, if since the distant past there has been the cause and condition of having once resolved to attain bodhicitta, one is born into the lineage of the Tathāgata and is the most excellent.
Regarding the verse on "revering the Triple Gem": this refers to giving rise to a heart of profound sincerity and humble submission toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;

always delighting in drawing near to them, making offerings, honoring, and praising them. One should know that such a person possesses the causal conditions for practicing the Path from previous lives, even as did the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging; this is called deeply revering all sentient beings.
Those who have deep faith in the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and who adorn themselves with profound wisdom— since such qualities as these are boundless like space,

and the Buddha-dharma cannot be contained within the mental vessel of those with inferior wisdom— one should know that it is only for those who adorn themselves with the nature of sharp and keen intelligence that [the Dharma] may be taught.
Those who are patient and free from weariness are those who possess capability and are not subject to defeat.
Tui (退) has a meaning different from *kṣānti* (忍辱) in the Sanskrit original; it refers to being able to endure all manner of hardships for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
Even if one fails once, one should again resolve to advance in cultivation, like vowing to empty the great ocean before stopping.
If a person’s disposition is such as this, they may transmit the Dharma. This is *śīla*.

"Purity without deficiency" means that regarding the precepts of both the householders and the ordained, and even down to the various prohibitions received from one's own family lineage, one guards them with a profound mind according to how they are observed, such that there is no violation or deficiency.

If one possesses such a nature, even if they have not yet entered the samaya—the great vow of equality—they should still be respectful and compliant without opposition; therefore, they are fit to receive the transmission of the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding those who practice patience and are free from stinginess, this is divided here into two phrases.

"Patience" refers to the mind’s ability to remain steadfast and unshakable amidst the eight great winds of internal and external favorable and adverse conditions, as explained in detail in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śīla-pāramitā*.
It should be known that such a person will certainly not violate the grave prohibitions of the vidyādhara, nor will they perform acts that are harmful.

Because they engage in the conduct of sentient beings, they are capable of transmitting the Dharma. Regarding those who are not stingy: this means that with respect to all their wealth and the Dharma, they constantly think of bestowing them upon others;
even when seekers arrive, their minds are free from contempt or parsimony, as explained in detail in the *Prajñāpāramitā* regarding the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
One should know that such a person will certainly not violate the grave prohibitions of the Vidyādhara, and because they are not stingy with the True Dharma, they are fit to transmit it.
Furthermore, those who possess courageous, firm conduct and vows are also divided into two phrases. "Courageous" refers to the quality of the *ācārya*’s virtue;

it signifies that within the lineage of the bodhicitta, even when encountering various terrifying forms and sounds while practicing the path, the mind does not become timid or weak, and one remains free from fear even from birth until death, correctly conforming to the state of a Bodhisattva.
Since this is the practice of the Great Beings (mahāpuruṣa), it should be transmitted. For those who firmly practice their vows, this is the essential core of their aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).

The Sanskrit term differs in meaning from the sense of "seeking" or "petitioning. If one establishes a resolve for oneself to recite it three times every day, then throughout the course of one's life, even if various distracting conditions arise, there shall be no interruption from the very beginning. Such a matter has its commencement.
In the end, even when practicing the bodhisattva path, because one does not fail in one's original vow, one is capable of transmitting the Dharma.
However, regarding the ten virtues of a disciple that have been taught, if these are possessed in their entirety, you should know that such a person is extremely rare;

yet, even if they possess only partial excellence and are capable of being cultivated and perfected, they should still be accepted and guided. Furthermore, it is like observing [the candidate] at the time of receiving full ordination as a śrāvaka.
In examining various obstacles—such as being too young or too old, physical defects, or various illnesses—one would typically exclude such individuals for fear of the reproach of laypeople.
However, this Mahāyāna is not like that; it simply requires that the capacity for the Way (*mārga*) be capable of being saved.
Even if there are other faults, none of them are taken into account. As it says in the verse: "Or ten..."
The figures "eight, seven, five, two, one, four" represent the numerical limits for conferring the *ācārya* initiation within a single-period ritual arena (*maṇḍala*).
Here, the calculation is based on skipping numbers: from one to two; from two skipping to four;
from four to five; from five skipping to seven; from seven to eight; and from eight skipping to ten. This refers to the person.
Therefore, within a single maṇḍala, one may not simultaneously confer initiation upon three, six, or nine persons;

this is indeed the Tathāgata’s secret intention. The ācārya does not explain the underlying reason, as it is similar to the prohibition in the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* against exceeding ten persons.
Beyond this limit, there is concern that the mental capacity of the ācārya might be insufficient.
If the participants are not complete, one must wait for subsequent conditions to perform the ritual separately. Furthermore, regarding those numbering fewer than ten people:
this refers to cases where they simultaneously resolve their minds to renounce all internal and external possessions to make offerings to the Triple Gem and collectively accomplish the maṇḍala;

thus, they may perform the ritual at the same time. If there are individuals who, upon encountering a site for the practice hall, say that such karmic conditions for the Dharma are difficult to encounter and request that the ritual be performed for them as well, [one should grant it].
Regarding those who are to be delivered, it is not appropriate to bestow upon them the *ācārya* initiation.
However, if they merely seek to establish a karmic connection by receiving mantras and mudrās within the dharma of a single-gate *honzon*, then such restrictions need not apply;
the *ācārya* should likewise give rise to great compassion and establish them in the practice for all who can produce even a slight degree of wholesome intent.
Because it is the seed of bodhi, it is said that one may even exceed this number.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One, what should this maṇḍala be named? What is the meaning of 'maṇḍala'? This was because the Tathāgata wished to select individuals and restrict the assembly.

In order to clarify for those who have not yet awakened and who give rise to further doubts, Vajrapāṇi originally requested the World-Honored One to proclaim this realm of empowerment and expound the Great Maṇḍala King born from the Treasury of Great Compassion.
This is the impartial great compassion that is without limit; yet, although there are virtues to be transmitted in what the World-Honored One has now spoken, they do not exceed [this].
Since these ten persons appear to be merely following along through a single gate rather than constituting its specific substance, one asks:
what should this maṇḍala be named? Furthermore, since "maṇḍala" carries the meaning of a complete circle, and the current enumeration is limited and restrictive, it seems incomplete in principle;
thus, one asks again: in this context, what is the meaning of "maṇḍala"? There are two questions in the world.
In the Venerable One’s response, the first part provides the literal definition, while the second part explains its meaning. Within the explanation of the name, he restates his original thesis:
"Now, *maṇḍala* has the meaning of 'generating. This is precisely what is called the 'Maṇḍala that Generates All Buddhas.
One plants the seeds of the Bodhicitta within this ground of the mind of omniscience and moistens them with the water of great compassion."
It shines with the great sun of wisdom and blows with the great wind of skillful means;
unimpeded by the great emptiness, it causes the sprouts of the inconceivable nature of phenomena to grow in succession until they fill the entire dharma-realm and become the king of trees—the Buddha.
For this reason, it is designated as "generating. Just as when thunder and rain break forth, those things that are about to crack open must first sprout before they can unfurl.
The flourishing of herbs and trees differs according to their inherent natures; consequently, even a gift given with impartiality becomes limited.
Next, in the explanation of the meaning, the Sanskrit term *maṇḍala* carries the sense of churning milk and curd to produce ghee (*sarpis*).
*Maṇḍala* refers to the most refined and pure essence that gathers and floats upon the surface, like that refined essence which no longer undergoes further transformation.
Furthermore, it is called the "taste of firm, pure, and wondrous flavor" because it is a harmonious integration that cannot be mixed with other substances;
thus, it carries the meaning of "gathering. For this reason, the Buddha said it is the most incomparable taste and the unsurpassed taste, and is therefore called the *maṇḍala*.
By means of the three kinds of secret expedients, one churns the milk of the Buddha-nature within sentient beings.
Having passed through the five flavors to achieve the wondrous awakening of *amṛta* (the clarified butter), it is pure, refined, and subtle, such that it can no longer be increased;
it is the foremost among all vajra-wisdom seals gathered together within the nectar-flavor of true permanence and unchangeability—
this is the meaning of the maṇḍala.
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, O Secret Lord," and so forth, extensively expounding the meaning of the maṇḍala to eliminate doubts and obstacles. This section is further divided into three parts:
first, it clarifies that the Dharma-realm’s perfect altar is universally accessible and limitless; second, it clarifies the reasons for restricting who may enter and screening the assembly;
finally, the concluding sentence exhorts the ācārya to give rise to impartial compassionate vows. Regarding the first part, [it begins with] "Out of compassion for those who... and so on.
Regarding the broad meaning of the Maṇḍala born from the treasury of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-kośa*) for the boundless realms of sentient beings:
when a practitioner perceives the Central Womb (*garbha*), they immediately know that all sentient beings possess the causal conditions for attaining Buddhahood;
therefore, the Great Compassion Maṇḍala they give rise to also pervades the entire Dharma-realm. For example, it is like the number of atoms in ten worlds, [representing] all the *Vajradhara*s...
When the assembly of Bodhisattvas, such as Vajrapāṇi and others, each takes one gate as the presiding lord of the maṇḍala and the rest as its retinue, a single type of maṇḍala is thus formed.
Such rotations are infinite and inexhaustible, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy;
how much more so when, within these, each employs immeasurable gates and various skillful means to adorn and attract sentient beings.

Furthermore, how could it be fully recorded? If a practitioner, within this single-syllable dharma-gate, subsumes the extensive into the concise and unfolds the concise into the extensive, producing the wealth of the Dharma and bestowing it universally upon all without ever ceasing or exhausting it—this is called being well-versed in the broad meaning of the maṇḍala.
Next, it says: "O Lord of Secrets, the Tathāgata has accumulated [merit] over immeasurable kalpas..."
It is because they are sustained by the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* that they possess immeasurable virtues;
this should be understood in this way. This explains the basis for the extensive meaning:

as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within each of the various gateways through which the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) have attained mastery, the dharmas they penetrate are profound and vast without limit, yet they do not know one another's [realizations].
When the Tathāgata formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, he universally approached as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in such buddha-fields;
regarding each and every treasury of their merits, he attained the supreme, peerless, and unsurpassed flavor.
Because the virtue of such internal realization is immeasurable and boundless, that which is sustained by his empowerment manifests as these dharmas.
The gate and its retinue are likewise immeasurable and boundless; those who practice the gateway of mantras should broaden their minds and form such an understanding.
Having already known that internal virtue is limitless, next we clarify how the *maṇḍala* of the original ground saves beings limitlessly.
Why is this? Because it accords with the fundamental vow of compassion. Therefore, the text of the sutra continues by saying: "O Lord of Secrets, it is not..."
For the sake of even a single sentient being, the Tathāgata attains equal and perfect enlightenment;

nor is it for two or three, but rather out of compassion for the realms of all sentient beings—both those with remainder and those without remainder—the Tathāgata attains equal and perfect enlightenment.

By the power of his great compassionate vow, he expounds the Dharma according to their inherent nature throughout the immeasurable realms of sentient beings. Within this, one generates the bodhicitta...
The meaning of "extracting the essence" (*cittoddhāra*) is explained in detail in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*) and in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Regarding "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*): it refers to when the Buddha, appearing before one, bestows a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), declaring that a certain sentient being will become a Buddha in a certain eon with such-and-such a name, and will possess such-and-such a land, retinue, and so forth; because this is explained with complete clarity, it is called "without remainder."
Regarding predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), there are those that are "with remainder," such as when [the Buddha] addresses sentient beings, saying:

"In the future, at the time of a certain Buddha, you shall exhaust these karmic offenses; a certain Tathāgata will grant you a prediction"—this is an example. Furthermore, as the World-Honored One said:
"Whether I am in the world or after my parinirvāṇa, should anyone hear even a single phrase or a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, I..."
To bestow upon all of them the prediction of unsurpassed bodhi is called the "prediction without remainder.

If one says that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature, and that their production of roots of goodness will continue in succession until they reach unsurpassed bodhi, this is called the "prediction with remainder.
Since I originally came for the sake of such sentient beings to attain perfect enlightenment, how much more so now that my original vow has been fulfilled!
To open the treasure within the minds of sentient beings and bestow it upon them according to their own nature—how could there be any limit?

Furthermore, this is stated as a mere trace of one instance of propagating the sutra through shallow practice during a degenerate age; thus, it says that for a single period of Dharma activity, the number is limited to ten people.
From this point onward, the second phrase explains the reason for limiting the number of people and distinguishing them from the general assembly.

The Sūtra states: "Regarding the secret threefold Great Vehicle, those who have never contemplated the practices of the Mantra Vehicle through past habituation cannot see, hear, or even slightly rejoice in, accept, or believe it.

Furthermore, O Vajrasattva, for the sake of those sentient beings who in the past have already entered and practiced the manifold gateways of the path of the Great Vehicle and the Mantra Vehicle, this limit is established."
Regarding this establishment of names and categories, the intended meaning is as follows:

if sentient beings have not long planted roots of virtue under immeasurable Buddhas of the past and have not already practiced this Secret Vehicle, they will be unable to believe and accept it upon hearing it in a casual manner.
If the person transmitting the Dharma merely explains it according to their own good intentions without discerning the capacity of the recipient, it may instead increase [their delusion].
Because slandering [the Dharma] severs those roots of goodness, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Those who lack wisdom and harbor doubt and regret shall suffer eternal loss.
Among all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions, those who aspire to the vehicle of the Śrāvakas are few; those who seek the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas are even fewer;

and those who seek the Mahāyāna are extremely rare. While those who seek the Mahāyāna may still be considered relatively easy to find, those who can truly believe in this Dharma are the most rare of all.

Because it is difficult [to understand], one observes it with the universal eye (*sarvacakṣus*); those capable of receiving this Dharma are as rare as the dust motes and drops of water in Mount Sumeru and the great ocean. Since one must protect their minds, it is only at the appropriate time that one explains it; how could one not briefly establish its names and numerical categories? What is called "advancing through immeasurable gates" is precisely an explanation of the meaning of the term *maṇḍala*. Now, as for *maṇḍala*: [The text continues: ...it is a term derived from the root *maṇḍ*, which signifies adornment (*bhūṣaṇa*). It refers to the adornment of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind, as well as the adornment of the various dharmas of the Buddha-lands. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is a place where all sentient beings gather and assemble. Moreover, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the locus where the various assemblies of deities reside. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of Bodhisattvas dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of gods and humans dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Asuras, Garuḍas, Kinnaras, Mahoragas, and so forth dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the four classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, and others—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the eight classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and rākṣasas—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the five classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the six classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, and animals—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the seven classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, and hungry ghosts—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the nine classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, and intermediate state beings—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the ten classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, and those who have fallen into evil destinies—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the eleven classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, and those who have fallen into the three evil paths—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the twelve classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, those who have fallen into the three evil paths, and those who have fallen into the three evil realms—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the thirteen classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, those who have fallen into the three evil paths, those who have fallen into the three evil realms, and those who have fallen into the four evil paths—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the fourteen classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, those who have fallen into the three evil paths, those who have fallen into the three evil realms, those who have fallen into the four evil paths, and those who have fallen into the five evil paths—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the fifteen classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, those who have fallen into the three evil paths, those who have fallen into the three evil realms, those who have fallen into the four evil paths, those who have fallen into the five evil paths, and those who have fallen into the six evil paths—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the sixteen classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, those who have fallen into the three evil paths, those who have fallen into the three evil realms, those who have fallen into the four evil paths, those who have fallen into the five evil paths, those who have fallen into the six evil paths, and those who have fallen into the seven evil paths—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the eighteen classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, those who have fallen into the three evil paths, those who have fallen into the three evil realms, those who have fallen into the four evil paths, those who have fallen into the five evil paths, those who have fallen into the six evil paths, those who have fallen into the seven evil paths, and those who have fallen into the eight evil paths—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the nineteen classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, those who have fallen into the three evil paths, those who have fallen into the three evil realms, those who have fallen into the four evil paths, those who have fallen into the five evil paths, those who have fallen into the six evil paths, those who have fallen into the seven evil paths, those who have fallen into the eight evil paths, and those who have fallen into the nine evil paths—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the twenty classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, those who have fallen into the three evil paths, those who have fallen into the three evil realms, those who have fallen into the four evil paths, those who have fallen into the five evil paths, those who have fallen into the six evil paths, those who have fallen into the seven evil paths, those who have fallen into the eight evil paths, those who have fallen into the nine evil paths, and those who have fallen into the ten evil paths—dwell. Furthermore, it is called *maṇḍala* because it is the place where the various assemblies of the twenty-one classes of beings—gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, pretas, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, those who have fallen into evil destinies, those who have fallen into the three evil paths, those who have fallen into the

*Maṇḍala* means "gathering. It refers to the gathering together in one place of the Tathāgata’s true merits, extending even to the various wheels of the seals of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*) as numerous as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions;

these converge like spokes to support the Great Sun Mind-King (*Mahāvairocana-cittarāja*), enabling all sentient beings to advance through the universal gate (*samantamukha*). For this reason, it is called a *maṇḍala*.

To briefly explain the establishment of these names and numbers: it is like using the letter *A* and the five wheels to encompass the Tathāgata’s boundless internal virtues, and using the hundred luminosities of the wheel of letters to subsume the Tathāgata’s universal-eye dharma-gate; this is what is meant by "abbreviation.
Furthermore, it is like employing the skillful means of the atoms of all lands to open the eight-petaled mandala, and establishing the limit of ten persons through infinite great compassion.

This is a brief enumeration of the numbers; yet, for one who aspires to study, if they attain realization by following a single Dharma-gate, this is equivalent to universally entering all dhāraṇī-gates.
It is like seeing a king through a single door, which constitutes universal entry into thousands of doors and ten thousand households.
If one cannot practice according to what has been taught, then even if one were to extensively explain it through various words and phrases, [it would be of no avail].

This demonstrates that there is no benefit [in being limited]. Therefore, the third sentence next clarifies that while the names and numbers are restricted and abbreviated, they do not themselves obstruct the vastness [of the teaching];
hence the Sūtra says: "That ācārya should also, with a mind of great compassion, establish such a vow for the sake of delivering the entire realm of sentient beings without exception;
he should embrace immeasurable sentient beings and act as the seed of their bodhi."

Regarding the causal conditions: establishing this maṇḍala ensures that anyone who sees, hears, touches, or knows it—even down to those who merely raise a hand, lower their head, or feel sympathetic joy for a single thought—will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, even if an ācārya errs by bestowing the full-branch initiation upon one whose faculties are not yet matured, the binding of the jewel [is still effective].
How could the conditions for the "poisonous drum" ever come to an end? Therefore, one should exercise the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and strive to ensure that it is widely disseminated.

Furthermore, just as a person with a secret treasure might fear being spied upon by thieves and thus conceals it with tattered clothing, so too is this maṇḍala dharma-gate; this treasury of secrets must not be proclaimed directly.

Therefore, this intentional reversal is concealed by the expedient means of having signs; what is now said regarding the limitation to ten persons refers only to the maṇḍala of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
However, the ācārya himself should level the ground of his own mind and paint the maṇḍala of Great Compassion, universally measuring out those to be guided—the more, the better.
One must not interpret this according to the literal words. As the verse says:
For the practitioner of the mantra who maintains the branches of the disciple’s requirements, regarding the skillful means for protection and establishment up to the sixth night:

both the master and the disciple shall bathe and purify themselves, don fresh and clean garments, and carrying the articles of offering, proceed to the site of the white sandalwood maṇḍala previously constructed.
There, they should perform the ritual empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon themselves, the path, and the maṇḍala according to the Dharma.

Regarding the methods for protecting the disciples, as explained below in the section on entering the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the *ācārya* should perform the offerings according to the sequential rules.
He should visualize the deities in the position of white sandalwood (*śvetacandana*) and, in conjunction with their secret mudrās, hold their respective mantras.
As the *Guhya-sūtra* states: "Pressing the hands upon the central maṇḍala, recite the mantra."
Recite this once and press [the mudrā] once; repeat this up to seven times, and do the same for the remaining positions.
Next, you should preach the Dharma to the disciples in accordance with their capacities to guide their minds, instructing them in the three refuges and the repentance of prior transgressions.
Once they have repented and their bodies and minds are purified like clear pearls, they will be capable of truly and correctly generating the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Therefore, next, one should cause them to generate the bodhicitta according to what is explained in the *Pūjāvidhi* (Ritual for Offerings).

Next, one should bestow scented ointments, flowers, and so forth, instructing them to direct their minds toward making offerings to the various Honored Ones. Thereafter, one should confer upon them the *Triyadhvānāvaraṇajñāna-śīla* (the precept of unobstructed wisdom of the three times).
This method for receiving the Bodhisattva precepts has its own specific ritual procedures. This is why the Bodhisattva generates the resolve to gather [beings].

The training in the precepts of skillful means is entirely for the sake of accomplishing the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom, so that in a single thought-moment one may penetrate all phenomena of the three periods of time without obstruction.

For those who abide in these precepts, even upon first seeing the clarity of the path of the mind, there arises such inconceivable power; for it is through these precepts that the Buddha-nature can be directly brought forth.

Furthermore, because the discipline (*vinaya*) of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) is limited, [the Buddha] names this [wisdom] the "unobstructed wisdom of the three periods of time" (*tryadhvāsaṅga-jñāna*).

Next, he should provide a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) for the disciples to chew; by means of this, he observes whether those individuals possess the characteristics of being suitable vessels (*bhājana*) or not.
The reason for employing this method is also to accord with the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of local customs.

This is an empowerment performed through secret skillful means. Whenever people of India invite monks for a meal, or even when members of the laity invite one another, they first send a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) adorned with various fragrant flowers and present it [to the guest].
One should know that this signifies an invitation for food and drink on the following day. The reason for acting in this way is to manifest a heart of affection and reverence.

Fearing that he might have pre-existing conditions such as phlegm, indigestion, or residual food, which—if he were to receive my offerings—might be provoked and cause him discomfort, I first protected him with a benevolent mind and alerted him to this.

Having thus purified his physical vessel beforehand, or having him take *harītakī* and other such remedies, he may tomorrow eat and drink as he pleases without committing any transgression, his body and mind remaining peaceful and happy. Now...
The Ācārya is likewise; when bestowing the *yank-chi* (tooth-stick) upon the disciple, he should immediately employ this expedient means to explain the profound Dharma, saying:
"I shall now bestow upon you the Buddha-nature, the supreme and unsurpassed flavor of *amṛta*.
