Having already instructed you to resolve upon Bodhicitta and purify the karmic obstacles of the three activities (*trikarma*) from past lives, I shall, with the unimpeded wisdom of the three periods of time, use the tusks of subduing to bite through all [afflictions]."
The afflictions being ended, you shall now further purify the faults and ailments of body and mind through this secret empowerment.
You must also cleanse the faults of speech; wherever you travel, do not proclaim [this] recklessly. Tomorrow, I shall bestow upon you the nectar of immortality, so that all may be fully satisfied.
He should then take an *udumbara* or an *aśvattha* branch that is straight and upright.
The two pieces should be of good quality, neither too coarse nor too fine, measuring twelve finger-widths in length.

For all methods of measurement, one should use the side of the upper phalanx of the thumb and press them together; this is the correct measurement. These two pieces of wood represent the Bodhi trees of past Buddhas.
If these are unavailable, one should seek wood that has "milk," such as the mulberry or the *śāla* tree, and mark the top and bottom of the wood.
In these distinctions, the branches and tips are considered superior while the roots and base are considered inferior. One should wash them with scented water and further fumigate them with incense.
At their lower ends, one should wrap the flowers with white thread as an ornament and also create a marker so that the upper and lower parts are easily distinguished.
One should press them with the hand and recite the Acala-mantra over them, either a hundred times or more.
Having prepared one thousand tooth-sticks (*dantakāṣṭha*) in their entirety, once the precepts have been received, the master shall take one stick and offer it to the deities;
the remainder should be distributed to the disciples. They shall exit the mandala and, facing either east or north, squat according to the ritual rules and chew the stick.
Having finished chewing, they shall cast it straight toward the direction they are facing to examine its signs. If...
If the chewing end points outward, one’s *siddhi* will not be accomplished; if it points toward the body, *siddhi* will be accomplished.
If, after being thrown far away, it returns close to the body, this is a sign that accomplishment will occur before long. If the head stands straight upward, accomplishment will be even swifter.
If the head points downward, this person shall enter the palaces of the asuras and nāgas. If it is thrown into the air, it shall...
One should know that this person has already achieved success previously. Furthermore, regarding the directions: the north is superior success; the east is middling success;

and the south is inferior success. Even so, if a person first casts [the seed] toward the east and the place where they chew faces east, this constitutes turning one's back to the body, and thus success cannot be attained. The other directions may be understood accordingly. The rest is as before.
As it is taught in the *Guhya-sūtra*, one should next perform the rite of the vajra-thread (*vajrasūtra*).

In making the thread, one should select high-quality cotton fibers, wash them with scented water until they are utterly pure and clean. A pure young girl should twist them together from right to left;
the five-colored threads should be combined, using the mantras of the five Tathāgatas to consecrate each color respectively. Thereafter, with...
The general empowerment of the mantras for accomplishing all activities is likewise applied to the threads for constructing the maṇḍala.

Regarding the colors of the five Tathāgatas: Vairocana empowers the white [thread], Ratneśvara the red, Padmapāṇi the yellow, Amitāyus the green, and Dundubhisvara the black. The ācārya first takes up the thread himself.
Form the three-fold vajra-knot and bind it to the left arm to protect oneself; then, one by one, bind it to the arms of the disciples.
Thus receiving the disciples, they enter the maṇḍala, which is the departure from all obstacles and difficulties.
This method of the vajra-knot cannot be fully described in words; it must be received directly from the face of the ācārya. Furthermore:
The five-colored threads are the five wisdoms of the Tathāgata, which are also the five dharmas of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Because these five dharmas thread together and encompass all gates of teaching, they are called *sūtra*; in ancient translations, they were termed "thread-sūtras" (*tanying*).
If a *darśanajñāna-ācārya* (teacher who has seen the truth) can empower a disciple with the Tathāgata’s five-colored wisdoms, [the disciple is thereby perfected].

The five kinds of roots of goodness within the *bodhicitta* thread together and encompass the myriad practices, binding the arms of yoga so that one may pass through birth and death without ever losing or destroying them.

If one can thus receive and sustain a disciple, it is called "skillfully performing the Vajra-knot. The Ācārya said: "When performing the ritual for disciples on this night, the offerings should be reduced."
At the midpoint of the seventh night, one should further observe their dispositions and capacities, extol the Secret Teaching (Guhyamantra), inspire a longing for it, and stabilize their resolve.
Furthermore, one should analyze the ten types of skillful means regarding the precepts (*śikṣāpada*).
However, those who have established a karmic connection with this unimpeded wisdom of the three times must all first hear the four root samayas; a single verse [of these] is as follows:
One should whisper these instructions to them; those who have received the complete branch initiations are the ones who should hear them.
Furthermore, the two verses of instruction should be recited in the original Sanskrit *āryā* meter, which is beneficial; they are set out below.
Aṇye (from now on), yuṣmābhiḥ (you all), apratimalabha (without rival and without equal), labdha (attained), mahātman (great self), yeṣāṃ (of whom),
sarveṣāṃ jinānāṃ (of all the Victors), yuṣmākaṃ saputrakāṇāṃ (together with your sons, the Bodhisattvas), idam śāsanam.
Nirmāṇa-sarvva-pāri-kṛtya-saṃgraha-jayamāna-mahānaya kṛtyārtha te mahāyāne śvobhūta-he prāptavya. (The mudrā is the teaching; *sarva* means "all";
*pāri-kṛtya* means "to perform"; *saṃgraha* means "to gather"; *jayamāna* means "birth" or "arising"; *mahānaya* means "the Great Vehicle";
*kṛtyārtha* means "to accomplish the task"; *te* means "you"; *mahāyāne* means "in the Mahāyāna"; *śvobhūta* means "at dawn"; *prāptavya* means "to be attained").
The meaning of the verse is as follows: From this day forward, you have already attained incomparable benefit and stand on the same level as the "Great Self" (Mahātman).
The "Great Self" refers to all Tathāgatas who have achieved the eightfold mastery (*vaśitā*), those who possess sovereignty over the Dharma, and the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
It further states that [you are equal to] all Tathāgatas and the Mahā... within this teaching.

The entire assembly of bodhisattvas has already been gathered by you within this teaching—namely, this secret teaching of the Mahāyāna, which includes the ten buddha-fields, the Vajra Bodhisattvas, and so forth.
Next, it says "accomplishing the great task," which means being able to accomplish the great task;
the causal conditions for accomplishing the great task are the revealing, showing, awakening to, and entering into the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.

In the sutra, after expressing the intended meaning, it further states: "On the morrow, you shall attain birth in the Mahāyāna," which means that having entered the maṇḍala of great compassion and received empowerment, you shall be born into the lineage of all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, because one attains the birth of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) by being free from the birth arising from conditions and karma, it is called "birth in the Mahāyāna.
When the *ācārya* has finished thus instructing and empowering [the disciple], he should have him sit in order outside the maṇḍala, facing east.
The *ācārya* should then again make offerings with a sincere heart and invite the various Honored Ones, saying: "I, in the presence of the Vidyā..."

Out of compassion for his disciples and in order to make offerings to the various Honored Ones of the Noble Ones, he established the Mahākaruṇā-garbha-maṇḍala and made offerings according to his capacity, praying:
"I beseech you, out of your compassion, to remember me and to assemble in full within the maṇḍala tomorrow to bestow your empowerment.
The general meaning is as such; the rest is as explained in the *Guhya* [Tantra]. He was thus utterly sincere.
Having requested that the verses of the vajra-words be proclaimed to praise the various deities, one should then dismiss them according to the ritual.
Furthermore, for the sake of the disciple, one should extensively explain the essential points of the Dharma and instruct them to maintain mindfulness and reflection.

Having them lie down facing east upon auspicious grass (kuśa), whatever various experiences they may encounter in their dreams, they should report them all to the master upon waking; then [the master] will know.

This is the sign that the practitioner’s *siddhi* has not yet been accomplished. If one sees a *ācārya* who has realized the Truth (*dṛṣṭasatya*), he shall naturally abide in profound *yoga* and clearly perceive the disciple’s fundamental and derivative capacities and conditions without error;

even if such signs are not manifested or if one acts in accordance with worldly conventions, there is no fault whatsoever. However, if the teacher has not yet realized the Truth, one must then be cautious.

One must not allow this to be deficient or lost according to the Dharma. The Sūtra says: "Seeing a monastery where monks reside in a dream" means that what is seen is pure, subtle, and exquisitely adorned;
one enters therein, prostrates, kneels, and circumambulates, encountering various auspicious and virtuous events.
"Gardens and groves" means that what is seen is flourishing and extraordinary, with flowers and fruits in profusion, or [one personally]...

Gathering flowers, they may ascend to the treetops and walk upon the air; within the halls and pavilions—various flowered chambers with ornate windows, exquisite and magnificent—they dwell at ease, their bodies and minds filled with joy.

As for the multi-storied towers and pavilions—lofty terraces from which one can gaze far out across the four quarters and behold various sublime sights—their spirits are bright and expansive. All such things as these [are enjoyed].
All of these are auspicious; the significance of these dharma-gates within them is as explained in the section on "Selecting the Site.
If they are contrary to these signs—such as seeing stūpas and temples being burned down, collapsing, or falling into ruin and filth—then these are not auspicious dreams.
A "banner" refers to a flag or a precious banner that appears before one, lofty, high, and magnificent, or used to direct the multitude, all of whom obey its command.
The ritual for establishing the Great Bodhicitta forms the image of the myriad practices;

this refers to the five-colored intermingling of peacock feathers and the like, which either shade from above while suspended in mid-air or are bestowed by others to be held while wandering—this is the image of compassionate vows universally covering all.
The mani-jewel is also said to be perfectly luminous and penetrating, or capable of producing various [treasures].
Giving material goods to the multitude is the image of the jewel of pure-mind awakening (*śuddha-citta-bodhi-ratna*), which benefits others through the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*).
The sword is the image of the accomplishment of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva-siddhi*); it is polished, reflective, refined, and sharp, whether bestowed by another or held by oneself.
The "pleasing flowers" (*manojña-puṣpa*) refer to various flowers born of water or land, categorized as superior, middling, or inferior according to their respective natures.

Just as with physical form, where fresh whiteness is considered the superior flavor and sweet醇厚 (rich, mellow) is considered the superior, these are all signs of the auspicious sprouting and development [of virtue];
one should discern them through the mind. A woman is the image of *samādhi*, and a man is the image of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, one should take those who are upright, majestic, and beloved by others; "intimate relatives" refers to parents and the like, while "virtuous friends" refers to those who transmit... [the teachings].
When one sees Dharma masters, spiritual friends, and the like, or herds of cows grazing with abundant milk, whether people are milking them or they themselves are drinking and suckling—
these are all images of the supreme flavor of the *amṛta* (clarified butter) of the Great Compassion Maṇḍala. Or when one sees scripture-cases that are pure white and stainless,
neatly arranged and beautifully adorned, with the colors of the characters distinct and clearly recording various kinds of sublime teachings.
If such matters are auspicious signs—for instance, if one sees that the volumes are soiled or damaged, or that the characters and meanings are incomplete—one should know these are inauspicious.
Alternatively, one may see various Buddhas personally stroke one’s head and bestow a prophecy in their presence, consoling and encouraging one with a subtle and wondrous voice;
or one may see śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, even manifesting immeasurable spiritual powers while dwelling in mid-air.
All such transformations should be carefully discerned according to the specific circumstances to identify their causal conditions and results.
That is to say, rare and wondrous fruits prized by the world, or someone handing them over, or they descending from the sky—these and others are all signs of *siddhi*.
Furthermore, crossing rivers, ponds, or the great ocean, or even dreaming of drinking from them until they are exhausted in an instant—all these are auspicious omens. If...
Those beings who are adrift, submerged, and without anyone to rescue them should know that this is due to their unwholesome deeds;

or perhaps they hear various pleasant sounds in the air—chants of the Dharma, the performance of music, or the praise of the merits of the Triple Gem—which the mind delights in hearing, or words of auspiciousness, or declarations that one shall receive the fruits desired by one's own heart; all such things as these...
Regarding auspicious dreams, one should distinguish them according to the categories of superior, middling, and inferior.

For instance, in the case of temples and the like, there is a distinction between those situated on land and those in the air. Furthermore, the persons seen therein differ as male or female, and as noble or ordinary.
Therefore, the Sūtra states that one should carefully and precisely discern them. If the dream contradicts the aforementioned auspicious signs, or if one dreams that one’s own body...
Being pursued by mad elephants and the like, being in a state of terror and imminent peril, riding upon camels or donkeys,
seeing loathsome and wicked persons whose clothing is tattered and ruined, seeing oneself lying prostrate in green mud or amidst filth and excrement,
or having various impurities fall from the sky— all these are signs of adverse conditions. If one is a master (*ācārya*) of profound practice, one should naturally [recognize them as such].
Within the yoga practice, one should understand the events of the dream and their underlying causes;
when the disciple rises in the morning and reports them to the master, the master should encourage them according to their capacity to sever the net of doubt.

If it is observed that there is no possibility for that person to achieve success, one should not fully transmit the Dharma to them, fearing that they will remain without efficacy for a long time or that doubts may arise.
This is because of slandering [the teachings]. Alternatively, as stated by Ghoṣaka, one should perform a *śāntika* homa to remove all obstacles and only then summon [the deity] to enter.
If various extraordinary visions appear, one should console them with Dharma words to bring about joy.
What is called "abiding well in the precepts" is, in Sanskrit, *suvrata*, which signifies the excellence of the disciple.
The term "gāthā" refers to those such as the verses spoken by the Buddha’s sons. The gāthās mentioned in the sūtras are also *ariṣa*;
it is even better to recite them from the Sanskrit original, so they are preserved here in their entirety on the left.

Oṃ (this) ma-la-ka (path) va-ra (vow) li-man (supreme virtue) ma-hā (great) ya-na (vehicle) ma-hā (great) na-da-ya (mind) ye-na (able) yu-yan (you) yan-mi-sa (that which is manifested) tu (seek) ba-fei (accomplishment) śe-ta (attainment) ta-thā-ga-ta (Tathāgata) sa-tyam (truth).
Bhīṣaṇa-sarva-tathāgata-dharma-labdha-pratibhāna-mana-rājña-sarva-pra... (The term *bhīṣaṇa* means "profound"; *sarva* means "all"; *tathāgata* means "the Dharma of the Tathāgatas";
*labdha* means "attained"; *pratibhāna* means "eloquence"; *mana-rājña* means "incomprehensible to worldly wisdom"; *sara* means "all"; *pra*...)

*Pañca-ra-khe-daṃ* (free from all conceptual proliferation and delusion), *pra-paṃ-ca-la-bha-ra-paṃ-ji-daṃ* (also a reduplication of "proliferation," meaning it is without proliferation and without cause),
*sarva-kriyā-vi-ra-tu-raṃ* (unrivalled in all that is done), *satya-nirvayaṃ* (the truth of nirvana), *saṃ-maśra*.
Yam (rely on), īnam (this), tannaya (vehicle), amala (without thirst), raṃśrī (wishing), śreṣṭha (supreme), rāviśeṣa (attainment), dharmya (the path), satya (abiding).
In general, when the Sanskrit original concludes a verse, it adds the auxiliary phrase *iti*.
The first half-verse praises the excellence of the path of the Secret Vehicle; "aspiration" refers here to the aspiration for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
If one enters this gateway of pure bodhi, one clearly perceives the path of the luminosity of the mind-dharma—this is what is meant by the Great Bodhi of the Ancient Buddhas.
It is called the "Path" because it refers to this supreme path of vows. The meaning of the "Great Mind" (*mahācitta*) is as previously explained in the section on the *mahāsattva*.

Since all beings of the great mind in the past, future, and present ride upon this precious vehicle (*ratnayāna*) directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it is called the "Mahāyāna of the Great Mind. The following verse praises the practitioner for generating the bodhicitta.
The merit consists in the conferral of the prediction of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi-vyākaraṇa*) by means of the Dharma-seal of the certainty of all Tathāgatas;
thus it is said: "You are now able to aspire [to this]; you shall achieve the spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) of a Tathāgata, which is honored by the world like a stūpa, O Great Nāga.
Spontaneous wisdom is the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening and self-realization, which has never before been heard or known.
Because the Dharma naturally manifests with perfect clarity and without any obstruction, it is so named.
*Mahānāga* is an epithet for the Tathāgata, used here as a metaphor for his inconceivable and boundless great functions.
*Caitya* is translated as "accumulation of merit," meaning that all the merits and virtues of the Buddhas are gathered therein; therefore, worldly people seek [this place] to obtain merit.

Therefore, you have fully made offerings to and revered [the Buddhas]; now that you have resolved to attain Bodhicitta, you are likewise able to encompass the immeasurable mass of merit of all Tathāgatas.
For this reason, the world should honor you as one would a stūpa. Next, there is one and a half verses which reveal the seal of the true aspect of the pure Bodhicitta;
it is precisely this that opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, causing them to become clear.
That which completely transcends both purity and impurity is precisely the inconceivable Middle Way arising from conditions;
it surpasses the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, being neither existent nor non-existent, and is a realm where all mental measures do not operate.
Therefore, it is called the "Stainless Vajra-Wisdom Seal Equal to Space. That all phenomena are profoundly deep and mysterious is because the nature of the mind is profoundly deep.

One should know that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), are likewise profoundly deep, because no dharma whatsoever transcends the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the mind. Such true reality can be known only by Buddha after Buddha;
it cannot be reached by conceptualization or discrimination. Therefore, it is called "profoundly deep and mysterious. As for the statement that "worldly wisdom cannot comprehend it": [it means...]
This nature of the mind cannot be conceived by those in the world who are wise or possess sharp faculties;

even if great masters of debate such as the Brahmin Dīrghanakha were to employ various causes, metaphors, ornaments, analogies, and logical measures to evaluate it, it would ultimately not be within their domain.
To contemplate and investigate it with arduous effort would only lead to madness; it can be realized solely through the power of firm faith.

It is only by relying on this secret skillful means that one can enter it. Regarding what is called "difficult to comprehend" by those who lack such containment, it is precisely in this state of non-containment;
for by knowing the aggregates and the *ālayavijñāna* as they truly are—namely, that they are fundamentally unarisen—one has nothing to grasp and no containment.
At that time, all conceptual constructions of mind, thought, and consciousness cease.
All conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are entirely purified within the dharmadhātu, which illuminates perfectly like the autumn moon situated in the sky;

therefore, the next line says, "free from all false imaginings" (*sarva-vikalpa-vinirmukta*). The Sanskrit original reads "free from all conceptual proliferations and false imaginings," but since the phrasing in the verse has been abbreviated for brevity and the meaning remains no different, it is not recorded in full here. The subsequent line states, "conceptual proliferation is fundamentally non-existent."
If the Sanskrit original were preserved in its entirety, it should be stated as "because of the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) within conceptual proliferation.
This is because all conceptual proliferations arise from a multitude of conditions and thus lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); since they lack intrinsic nature, they are primordially unarisen.
Therefore, the preceding phrase is explained as: "this very conceptual proliferation is itself without conceptual proliferation. Now, to clarify the intended meaning: [the text] states...
For this reason, it is said that "fundamentally there is nothing. The following two phrases clarify that this pure *bodhicitta* is the ultimate skillful means;
by transcending all deluded karma, one is able to accomplish the wisdom-karma of the Tathāgata, universally guiding and benefiting others through every gate.
Since there is nothing that is not a great causal condition for the work of enlightenment, all that is performed is peerless. Therefore, it is called "all karma."
It is peerless. Next, the preceding phrase is further explained by summarizing the general outline of the provisional and the real;
thus it says, "Always relying on the two truths," which is what the *Śāstra* means when it states, "The Buddhas always rely on the two truths when preaching the Dharma.

However, the primary tenet of this sutra is that all various expedient means with their constituent parts follow the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). By means of these causes and conditions, one attains the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Thus...
This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); therefore, conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is the cause and ultimate truth is the fruit.

The cause—such as the four flavors—is entirely impermanent, while the fruit—such as *sarpis-manda* (clarified butter)—is eternal. However, when viewed through the ten phrases of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the true nature (*dharmatā*) of conventional truth is itself the ultimate truth.
Thus, the provisional and the real are identical, and both are inconceivable. This...
Although these two lines are concise in wording, they enable the practitioner to have no further doubts regarding the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Tathāgatas;
therefore, one should extend this by analogy so that it penetrates the entire meaning of the text.
Having thus briefly revealed the path to Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), he concludes with the seal of contemplation (*dhyāna-mudrā*), saying: "This vehicle is supreme; may you abide therein."
The "Path" (mārga) also serves to further clarify the meaning of the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
At that time, the Vajradhara who abides in non-conceptualization addressed the Buddha, saying: "I pray that you will explain the precepts of unimpeded wisdom regarding the three times;
if a bodhisattva abides in these, it will cause all Buddhas and bodhisattvas to rejoice. This is because the preceding passage had only spoken of...

Having received the precepts of unobstructedness throughout the three periods of time, their specific characteristics have not yet been revealed; this is a further inquiry to open up the state of abiding in the non-conceptualization (*niṣprapañca*) of the vajra.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, the reason for waiting for a question before speaking is also to clarify the characteristics of the retinue of the Dharma-gate.
Thus, these pure precepts take as their very essence the seal of the wisdom of non-conceptualization (*niṣprapañca-vajrajñāna-mudrā*).
Therefore, I have specifically addressed this venerable one so that the Dharma may be transmitted and preserved in accordance with human practice.
The Ācārya said: "These characteristics of the precepts are also mantras of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
When transmitting them, it is most excellent to first recite and maintain the Sanskrit original, and then explain it through the vernacular language. They are now fully set forth below.
Śrīṇu (Listen! kula-putra (Son of good family!), tvaṃ (You) kula-putra (Son of good family!), kāya-vāk-citta-maya-kṛta-pūṇyam (The merit performed by body, speech, and mind).
Vāgīśvara-sarva-dharma-ākāśa-samatā-nāma-ātma-bhāva-pariṇāmanā-buddha-bodhisattva-vai-pūjā-vidhi. (The mantra: Tadyathā... [followed by the seed syllables]. (Note:

This is a transcription of a Sanskrit title and mantra sequence, likely from a ritual text for the offering of one's own body (*ātma-bhāva-pariṇāmanā*) to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, performed through the equality of all phenomena with space (*sarva-dharma-ākāśa-samatā*). The specific mantra provided appears to be a condensed or abbreviated form.)
Svāhā (tadyathā). Rūpe ātmabhāve pātre yadi tyajet tathāgataḥ svāhā.
Tadyathā | pṛthivī kṣetra-pati-kṛta-maś-citta-tanva-s-tūtra-yam | yan-nu-tka-ya-vajra-mana-iti | tathāgata ||
Tad (therefore), Kula-putra (son of good family), kāya-vāk-manas-saṃvara-samādāna (undertaking the restraint of body, speech, and mind),
bodhisattva-veṇī (O Bodhisattva), bhaviṣyasi (you shall become), tat kasya hetoḥ (for what reason?).
*Kṣaṇikāyāvartamāna-saṃprati-tyajya* (having abandoned that body, speech, and mind); *śikṣā-kāraṇāt* (one should train);
*kuryāt* (should perform); *bodhisattvo mahāsattva idam* (the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, this). (*Idam* is an auxiliary particle.)
Regarding the first phrase, "O Son of the Buddha, listen attentively": *kula* (in Sanskrit) means "clan" (*jāti*) or "lineage" (*varga*); *putra* means "son" (*puruṣa*).
If explained according to worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), those born among the four castes are all called "great clans," and are thus termed "sons of noble lineage" (*kulaputra*).
Now, having been born into the family of the Tathāgata, one is the most eminent among all lineages.

Because it is preeminent, he is called a "son of noble family" (*kulaputra*). The term *ācārya* should be understood according to its intended meaning as "Buddha-son," which is appropriate in this context.
The Sūtra states: "If a son of noble family abides in these precepts, he should unify his body, speech, and mind into one.
These precepts are called *trivara* in Sanskrit; they are formed through common conditions and are collectively accomplished.
The meaning of this is that it is the integration of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*);
whereas *śīla* (ethical discipline) carries only the sense of purity. Furthermore, *trimaṇḍala* signifies equality.

The Buddha said that to unify body, speech, and mind into one is precisely to abide in the Dharma-gate of the three equalities; therefore, it is named "unobstructed wisdom of the three periods of time."

Regarding the precepts: just as the Buddha briefly taught the instructions for the śrāvakas by saying, "The purification of these three paths of action is the path of the Great Sage," and subsequently elaborated upon their meaning over twelve years to establish various codes of discipline (*vinaya*), so too is the meaning of these brief precepts for the Vidyādhara.
If the practitioner’s skillful means of the three actions are all entirely correct and compliant with the Three Jewels, [then they are pure].

One should know that the state of equality is itself the possession of the ethical discipline (*vinaya*) of all Buddhas. Furthermore, "tearing apart the net of conceptualizations" is the meaning of *tribhava*.
This refers to the net of various views of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), which is called a "net" because its warp and woof are mutually established and intricately interlaced.
Now, when the practitioner contemplates the actions of body, speech, and mind, they find no separate essence; by tracing back from the branches to the root, [they realize they are unified].
Fundamentally, this is but the one mind, and the true reality (*dharmatā*) of this mind is eternally the equal *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, abiding in this precept, all various actions of body, speech, and mind are of a single characteristic, and the infinite nets of views are entirely purified.
For this reason, it is called "abiding in the Vajra Seal of Non-conceptual Elaboration. As the Sūtra says: "One does not perform any..."
The Dharma consists of the various five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which depend upon afflictions (*kleśa*); these afflictions depend upon karma.

These various types of karma all arise from body, speech, and mind. When categorized according to body, speech, and mind, they are divided into ten kinds of wholesome and unwholesome paths of action (*karmapatha*).

If one traces their detailed ramifications, they are immeasurable and boundless. Therefore, whatever is practiced through the three types of action (*trividha-karman*) possesses a progressive advancement toward liberation.
One who loses the progress of practice does so because of inverted perceptions; due to these inverted perceptions, immeasurable perceptions arise.

Obstructed by these various perceptions, one cannot attain the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom. Now, when the practitioner deeply contemplates the ten phrases of dependent origination and realizes that the three karmas are ultimately non-arising and that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently and eternally without activity, this is called "dwelling in non-existence."
Such is the nature of the precepts. If even pure morality is not something created by the Tathāgata, how much less could one who abides in these precepts create any phenomena?
The Sūtra asks: "What is meant by morality? It refers to observing and relinquishing one's own body to offer it to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because if one relinquishes one's own body, one relinquishes those three things. What are they?

Third, regarding body, speech, and mind: next, it clarifies that by maintaining the precepts of non-action (*avijñapti-śīla*) and being fully endowed with wisdom and skillful means, the practitioner contemplates the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the body and realizes that the body is ungraspable; this is itself the liberation of the Tathāgata. Therefore, one completely relinquishes this body to offer it to all Tathāgatas.
From this point forward, whether moving or stationary, in whatever actions one performs, they are all for [the sake of...]

The liberation of the Tathāgata is not for his own sake; although he adorns the Buddha-lands and brings sentient beings to maturity through various blazing myriad practices, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently so, and is not something produced by effort.

One who can practice and cultivate in this manner is said to possess a boundless accumulation of merit and a river of inexhaustible merit; with every single drop of roots of goodness they create, they cast them [into that river].
Because it is within the ocean of the *dharmadhātu*, even reaching to the limit of the realm of sentient beings, it is likewise inexhaustible.

The Ācārya said that in the Sanskrit original of this treatise there is a verse which says: "If there is one who has attained liberation and, holding this dharma of liberation, makes an offering to those who have attained liberation, this merit is the most supreme.
If a practitioner of mantras does not understand such pure precepts, then even though their mouth [may recite them]...

If one recites mantras, maintains secret mudrās with the body, dwells in the samādhi of the deity with the mind, and fully performs the successive ritual procedures to make offerings to the various honored ones, this is still called "constructing all phenomena" and one has not yet escaped the net of self and person. How, then, can such a person be named a Bodhisattva?
Therefore, the sutra continues: "For this reason, son of good family, by receiving the precepts of body, speech, and mind, one attains..."
Why is it called "Bodhisattva"? It is because they are detached from those [faults] of body, speech, and mind. A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should train in this manner;

herein one should train. What was termed *śikṣāpada* in the old translations—just as the fifth section of the Vinaya, the *Vinayakṣudraka-vastu*, comprehensively encompasses the rules for dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*)—likewise should those who study the Mahāyāna uphold these.
This precept serves as the skillful means for universally entering into all mantra practices;
were the precepts to be deficient, it would be impossible to accomplish the conduct of a Bodhisattva. As the Sūtra states:
"On the following day, one should empower oneself as Vajrasattva and pay homage to the World-Honored One Vairocana"—this refers to the day immediately following the reception of the precepts.

This refers to the completion on the evening of the seventh day. When performing various tasks for the construction of the maṇḍala, one should always empower oneself with Vajrasattva; that is, one should visualize oneself as Vajradhara.
The methods for this are explained in the text of the lower fascicle and within the sequence of offerings. As for the ācārya who has seen the truth (dṛṣṭasatya), he is as follows:
Abiding in the mind of Vajrasattva— that is, the peerless bodhicitta—
one is empowered by this secret empowerment such that no one can obstruct or destroy whatever actions are undertaken. Next, as before,
one should direct the mind to pay homage to the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, and then recite the Trailokyavijaya mantra to empower the purification flask.
This is also the mantra for accomplishing all activities. First, one should take a ritual vessel according to the rules and fill it with pure water, filtering it according to the rite.
Within it, place the five jewels and the five grains. Then, take various scented waters and various exquisite flowers and fruits, inserting their branches into the vessel.
Adorn it in various ways and tie fresh, clean cloth around its neck; all of this should be performed according to the sequence of offerings.
First, one should remove impurities and purify [the site] by means of the *dharmadhātu-citta* syllable, and then perform the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Generally, there is no fixed limit for the number of recitations for mantras; they should be calculated by the number of syllables, as explained in the *Susiddhi*.

Furthermore, therein, when constructing the maṇḍalas of the three families, one should respectively use the family-heart mantra (*kula-hṛdaya*) or the family-mother mantra (*kula-mātṛ*) for the consecration. Now...

In this sutra, the mantras for accomplishing all tasks are universally employed; as these mantras include both extensive and abbreviated versions, their specific recitation counts are not fully detailed here and should be determined according to one's own judgment.
For the most significant rites, one should recite up to one hundred times; for intermediate ones, five hundred times;
and for minor ones, up to one thousand times. Once the empowerment is completed, the object should be placed upon white sandalwood.
For those who intend to enter the maṇḍala outside the planned entrance, one should first sprinkle them with this [water] to purify their latent obstacles;

only then may they behold the maṇḍala. Furthermore, one should prepare scented water in a separate vessel using various exquisite fragrances such as turmeric, camphor, and sandalwood, and having empowered it with mantras, bestow it upon them.
Have them drink a small amount of this, which is called "Vajra Water. Because it is empowered by secret *adhiṣṭhāna*, even the heavy obstructions of the hells will be entirely eliminated;
being purified both internally and externally, they become fit vessels for the Dharma. The Ācārya says:
"This is also called 'Water of the Vow. It accords with worldly convention, like a binding oath, so that [the disciple] may be made to abide in the presence of all the noble ones."
Previously, by partaking of this fragrant water, one made a vow to oneself that the mind would never retreat from the aspiration for Great Bodhi.

Furthermore, when the pure water of the mind is blended with the fragrance of unimpeded precepts and the gateway of the syllable *Vaṃ*, all who drink or touch it will certainly achieve unsurpassed Bodhi; with such a purified mind, one is fit to enter the Secret [Teaching].
This is the *Guhyamaṇḍala*.
At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets questioned the Buddha with verses concerning the constituent parts for constructing a maṇḍala.
Within these verses, he first praised the Buddha, saying: "I pray only to the Omniscient One, the foremost among all who preach the Dharma."
This refers to that specific period of time; this period of time extends from the initial drawing of the maṇḍala until its completion.
Next, it is asked: "At what time do the great assembly gather universally and manifest auspicious signs? This means:

at what time do all the universal gateways of the various bodies within the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha* (Great Compassion Womb) gather universally at the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and appear before one?
This is the manifestation of majestic efficacy through the empowerment of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-adhiṣṭhāna*).

If a disciple’s faculties are pure and sharp, and their capacity for liberation is profound, they may at that very moment personally behold the boundless assembly of sages as if sitting together at the Vulture Peak assembly;

they will see the three transformations of the Pure Land and the Buddhas of the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) exactly as they appear without distinction. One should know that at such a time, this is itself the maṇḍala.
Because the Ācārya upholds the words of truth and performs the deeds of the Tathāgata, it is said that he "diligently maintains the mantra.
Having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One then addressed the Holder of Vajra-Wisdom, saying:
"One should always construct the maṇḍala during this night; that is to say, one should bring the ritual matters to completion within this seventh night."
Within this context, the period from after sunset until the appearance of the morning light is collectively termed "night.

At the very beginning of the night, one should immediately prepare the various positions for the deities and arrange all the ritual offerings; these must be completed and the deities dispatched before the morning light has appeared.
If one violates this rule, obstacles will arise, even affecting the dwelling place where the practice is maintained.
This is also not auspicious. However, in the profound secret interpretation, "time" refers precisely to the auspicious convergence of the conditions for the Way;
or, through the skillful means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one may condense a hundred kalpas into a single night, or expand a single night into a hundred kalpas.
Whether long or short depends on conditions and has no fixed limit. If it is a *ācārya* of shallow practice, they must fully conform to the ritual rules.
During the daytime, one should delineate the boundaries and establish the positions and divisions for the various deities using white sandalwood paste and other materials.
When the sun is about to set on the following day, all items such as incense, flowers, and lamps must be prepared in advance.
According to the *Guhya-tantra*, in a certain location on the northern side of the maṇḍala, one should delineate the area with white powder while reciting the mantra for the removal of obstacles.

"It is difficult to arrange all the ritual implements. The Ācārya said, "If you cannot complete the painting of all the Venerable Ones within a single night, there is no logical impediment to proceeding gradually from the fifth day after receiving the site-consecration (bhūmiparigraha).
Furthermore, there are three other expedient means—venerated forms, mudrās, and seed-syllables—as explained in the subsequent text."
The Sūtra states: "The Dharma-transmitting Ācārya, having recognized the proper time, shall clearly establish the ritual procedures.

When the sun has set, the Ācārya and his assistant disciples shall each bathe according to the Dharma, don new and clean robes, arouse the mind of great compassion, and carrying offerings, proceed to the site of the maṇḍala;
first, one should perform the preparatory rites for each [deity] in accordance with the Dharma."
The manner of holding [the vows] is as explained in the sequence of making offerings. Next, one should protect oneself according to the Dharma;
call the disciples to be initiated and act as their protector, sprinkling them with scented water and having them all sit together in order.
Then, the ācārya goes before the entrance of the maṇḍala, universally extending his mind to pay homage and prostrate to all those in the ten directions.
The Buddhas are also as described above. Then, taking a five-colored thread, one stands facing the position of the maṇḍala and wears it upon the crown of the head.
Next, one visualizes oneself as Vairocana—what the Sūtra calls Mahāvairocana—and performs self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).
The reason for this is that the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana is this very Great Compassion.
Therefore, when a practitioner performs the duties of an ācārya within the Garbhadhātu, they should regard themselves as Vairocana;
when performing various tasks related to the maṇḍala, they should regard themselves as Vajrasattva.
The methods for such empowerment are explained in the subsequent sections and in the *Pūjāvidhi*.
Furthermore,
the practitioner should know that in the eight directions of the protective enclosure, whatever maṇḍala is constructed follows this orientation:
Indra in the east, Yama in the south, and Varuṇa in the west.
Rūṇa is in the north; Vaiśravaṇa is in the northeast;
Īśānī is in the southeast for homa; Nairṛtī is in the southwest; Vāyu is in the northwest;
as for the deities above, most rely on the left of Śakra, while those below mostly rely on [the right].
To the upper right of the Naga Lord refers to the celestial dwellers (ākāśavāsin), and to the lower [part] refers to the terrestrial dwellers (bhūmivāsin).

Furthermore, within the circular *garbhadhātu*, the threefold realms are all marked with the character "Yü" (豫) as a signpost, ensuring that the cardinal directions and intermediate points are equalized.

When determining the positions for this diagram, the *ācārya* must first ensure that the position of Mahāvairocana coincides with the center of the fivefold heap of jewels (*pañcaratnakūṭa*). At the time of drawing these various features of the diagram, the *ācārya* first...
Having performed the ritual prostrations according to the rules toward the direction of Indra, one next stands facing north in the direction of Agni.
The assistant disciple holds the *sūtra* in opposition at the direction of Īśāna to fix the outer boundary.
Next, the disciple should circumambulate to the right until reaching the direction of Nairṛti; the master likewise circumambulates to the right, facing west in opposition.
The Ācārya holds it and then circumambulates to the right, proceeding to the Vāyu direction; the disciple also turns to the right and faces north while holding it.
The disciple again circumambulates to the right, proceeding to the Īśāna direction; the Master also turns to the right and faces east while holding it.
Having completed one full circuit, he ensures that [the object] remains level with the navel, suspended equally in the space of the void.
Once the ground has been leveled, proceed to the second circuit as before, marking the lines for the boundary paths by drawing them clockwise in sequence.

Next, following the established measurements for the four intermediate directions (*vidiś*), the *ācārya* should again circumambulate to the *nairṛti* direction, while the disciple, who was previously at the *aiśānī* direction, faces him and holds [the cord] while turning clockwise. The disciple then likewise turns clockwise.
Having circumambulated until reaching the Vāyu direction, the master turns to the right toward the homa direction;
the disciple likewise turns to the right and faces him, holding [the object] so that it is level with the navel and fixed in mid-air at its proper position.
The disciple then again circumambulates to the right until reaching the Nairṛti direction, while the master turns to the right toward the Īśāna direction.

The preceptor aligns the cord facing [the disciple] at the northeast; the disciple then circumambulates clockwise and reaches the southeast, where he faces the preceptor as the latter turns clockwise to that direction and likewise aligns the cord facing him. The *ācārya* says:

"Although the sūtras do not explicitly state it, the principle dictates that there must necessarily be a cross-shaped boundary for the four cardinal directions; one must also determine these by aligning the cords facing each other while circling clockwise."

Having thus completed the determination of the outer boundary and the characteristics of the eight directions, one next enters the interior. First, one determines the outer boundary of the central womb;
this is also marked by rotating lines to form a square, as before, though its eight directional characteristics need not be determined again.
One first determines the outer boundary of the first layer, and then determines the outer boundary of the second layer, which is identical to that of the central womb.
According to the principle, the dimensions of their breadth and width should all be halved successively;
for example, if the central *garbha* measures eight feet in length and width, the first layer should be four feet, the second layer two feet, and the third layer one foot.
The Ācārya said: "The fundamental method is thus; however, if one fears that the sizes will be so vastly different as to be disproportionate,"
One should gradually adjust it with the mind so that there is no deviation from the principle.
Having thus completed the division, one should again divide each successive layer into three parts. The innermost part is the circumambulatory path for the Buddha’s disciples;
hence it is called "the path traveled by the Buddha’s sons. The next part is the place for arranging the various offering articles. The outermost part is...
Because these two sections are the seats of the noble deities, one next establishes the surrounding boundary lines outside of them.

Within this space, one should mentally visualize and observe, inviting and making offerings to all the deities who correspond to their respective positions and divisions according to the directions. This is done for the following reason:

If the Ācārya, when facing the ritual, should happen to err or make a mistake in arranging the various deities, or if there are those who should be invited but for whom no specific position has been assigned, all such cases should be addressed by directing the mind toward this central area for making offerings.
Regarding the method for dividing these three sections of the boundary: first, from within the outermost of the three layers, take a small portion to serve as the boundary-mark.
The dimensions of width and breadth should be determined by one’s own judgment, ensuring that the layout is sufficiently spacious for the seating arrangement.
Within this boundary, divide it into three equal parts. First, determine the inner boundary for the seats of the various deities;
next, determine the middle boundary for the circumambulation path and the offerings. Thus concludes the first layer. Next, regarding the second layer:
Furthermore, proceeding from the outside toward the inside, one divides them gradually; the third layer is likewise as described above.
The light emitted from below the navel of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata constitutes this third layer;
the light emitted from the navel upward to the throat constitutes the second layer; and the light from the throat upward to the crown of the head [constitutes the first layer].
The radiance of these marks constitutes the first stage; within it, the matrix (garbha) is the eight-petaled lotus of Vairocana’s own mind.
The maṇḍala established therein must be thoroughly understood by the vajra-disciples through the essential points of the mantra-dharma.
By drawing near to the teacher, they will be able to assist one another without any omission. If not...
If one finds such a person, one should simply take someone who has already received empowerment according to the Dharma and instruct them to perform the rite when the occasion arises.
Furthermore, if such a person is unavailable, one should drive stakes into the ground as a preliminary measure:

first, drive a stake beneath the master’s position in the southeast (Agni) direction, and next, place one in the northeast (Īśāna) direction. Having stretched the cord, the master first mentally notes the stake in the southeast; this is the master’s [position].
Once the positions are established, one draws the line from Īśānī to the direction of Nairṛti; the rest may be understood by following this procedure accordingly.

The Ācārya further states that when intending to draw the lines together, one must first take the disciple who is to receive the empowerment, sprinkle them with consecrated scented water, and perform the ritual activities together with them regarding the mandala sites and so forth that have been drawn. For now, [one should proceed] thus.

Cover the objects so as not to let them be seen. Regarding the four gates of the Vaipulya [mandala]: this refers to the three-tiered enclosure (triple court) where all four gates are established to be centrally aligned and symmetrical.
One gate is opened facing west for the purpose of entry and exit; the remaining gates are demarcated by horizontal lines drawn across them. Guhyapada states:
"In all cases where gates are opened toward various directions, their width and narrowness should be determined according to the specific orientation of that quarter."
Divide the nine parts into sections; take one part as the entrance, while the remaining eight parts are divided such that four parts are obtained on each side of the entrance.
Make the entrance slightly wider than the other doors. Close the remaining doors by drawing them with white powder.
The Ācārya says: having completed the demarcation using the vajra-line, it should be like a vajra that cannot be severed.

"Transgressing the transgression" refers to violating the *samaya*. Furthermore, although the scriptural text generally prescribes facing west, if there is a specific cause or condition for facing another direction, it is permissible according to principle and carries no fault.
Other details are as explained in the text below. One should proceed with a sincere and reverent mind to manifest the various honored ones of the sages;
that is to say, when first undertaking the painting, one should abide in *yoga* and contemplate this maṇḍala.
In this great assembly, every single form, color, appearance, deportment, nature, category, seat, and mudrā shall all manifest before one, being fully and clearly understood.
Thereafter, with a heart of immeasurable earnestness and reverence, one should paint them;
even the measurements of large and small, or sparse and dense, must be made uniform and proportionate. Therefore it is said: "Thus create the various marks so that they are all equal."

It is well-discriminated and harmonized. That which is the "wondrous white lotus within the mind" is the *puṇḍarīka* flower of the wondrous Dharma of the fundamental mind of sentient beings, the secret emblem.
The eight petals of its calyx are perfectly full and equal, in the shape of one fully blossomed;
this lotus calyx is the natural wisdom of the true aspect (*dharmatā*), and the lotus petals are great compassion and skillful means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, this very treasury constitutes the essence of the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala;
the remaining three layers are merely the gateways to the Dharma-realm through which various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) emerge from the merit of one’s own self-realization.

The four petals at the cardinal directions represent the four wisdoms of the Tathāgata, while the four petals at the corners represent the four practices of the Tathāgata; in terms of their manifestation, these constitute eight [petals].
Because each of these types of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) maintains the seal of adamantine wisdom (*vajraprajñāmudrā*), it is said that they "pervade and emerge from between all the petals.

Thus, each of these sixteen dharmas is equal to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); since there is not even the slightest portion that is unequal, their manifesting signs also correspond in secret harmony with it.
Briefly summarizing the ten thousand virtues of the Tathāgata, they are taken as sixteen fingers; when extended, [they reach]—
If extended, it is immeasurable and boundless; therefore, this maṇḍala has a minimum dimension of sixteen finger-breadths, while its maximum is limitless.
The filaments are all the gates of samādhi, the gates of dhāraṇī, the six perfections, the eighteen emptinesses, and so forth, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
From each of these filaments, one should perform empowerment through divine power.
By the power [of the Buddha], there appears within the triple maṇḍala a single kind of majestic retinue.
This is the secret transmission of the Tathāgata; it cannot be expressed in ink and brush, and thus it is entrusted to images to be shown to practitioners.
Those who grasp its profound meaning shall naturally recognize it in silence. From this lotus pedestal of the true nature (dharmatā), then—
This represents the signs of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Vairocana Tathāgata; its meaning has already been explained as previously stated.
The remaining eight secret mudrās will be described in the subsequent chapter along with their diagrams.
Next, within the eastern inner court, directly above Vairocana Tathāgata, one should draw the mudrā of Sarvavit (the All-Knowing One).
Form a triangle with its apex pointing downward, encircled by pure white light and flames, resting upon a white lotus;
this is the Great Vajra Fist Seal (*mahāvajramuṣṭi-mudrā*) of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time, also known as the Heart Seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas.
The triangle signifies the subduing and removal of demonic obstacles, representing the Buddha’s majestic and fierce power while sitting beneath the Bodhi tree.
Having subdued the four māras through his power and attained perfect enlightenment, the pure white color is the manifestation of great compassion.

It is precisely for this purpose that the Tathāgata exerts the great power of the lion’s springing forth; by means of these causes and conditions, he emits the light of great compassion which constantly pervades the entire Dharma-realm—hence it is said to be "universally pervasive."
Next, proceeding from the Great Diligent Hero (Mahāvīra) to the northern direction, one places Ākāśanetra, who is the Mother of the Buddha Vairocana.
The meaning of "Mother" is explained at length in the "Mother Chapter" of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

As for "pure gold," it is the essence of the suchness (*tathatā*) and the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the ultimate term of purity; because it serves as the external ornament for that teaching, it is called "white silk."
When all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) have ceased for the sake of clothing [the world], the sunlight of the mind shines upon everything without exception;

therefore, it is called "Pervasive Illumination" (*Samantaprabhā*). Just as the sun's light is seen only by those whose single mind is tranquil and serene, its iconographic representation is like that of a celestial maiden abiding in the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Next, to the south of Mahāvīra, in the southern quarter, one forms the Cintāmaṇi seal of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is the accumulation of the boundless practices and vows of the pure bodhicitta;
it can constantly rain down all mundane and supramundane wealth and treasures, for all World-Saviors emerge from the naturally pure lotus pedestal.
Because such jewels appear within it, it is said that [the practitioner] "dwells upon a white lotus. The Ācārya says: "This is the seal that pervades all;

it may also be placed on all sides. Even for those sūtras of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas that do not mention the specific characteristics of the seals to be held, one may likewise grasp this priceless jewel, and in all cases it will be effective. Generally, this is the foremost."
Above, representing the Buddha-body adorned with all virtues, is the Vajra Family; below, representing the Buddha’s vidyādhara messengers, is the Tathāgata Family.
To the right, representing the Tathāgata’s great compassion and samādhi which can nourish and flourish all wholesome qualities, is the Lotus Family.
To the left, representing the Tathāgata’s great wisdom and power of function which can shatter the three obstructions, is the Jewel Family.
The Vajra Family is likewise; therefore, entering the gateway of the letter A signifies that all phenomena are unarisen, which is the meaning of the Dharmakāya.
Entering the gateway of the letter Va signifies that all phenomena are free from defilement and attachment, which is the meaning of the Lotus.

Entering the gateway of the letter Ba signifies that all phenomena transcend verbal expression, which is the meaning of the Vajra. As stated in the "Chapter on the Wheel of Letters," these three letters govern [the entire system].
The intent of the "Hundred Illuminations" is subsumed herein. As the Sūtra states: "To the right of Mahāvairocana is placed Mahāvīra Avalokiteśvara.

This refers to the Lord of the Lotus Family; because the Tathāgata has attained this Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) through the ultimate contemplation of the ten phrases of dependent origination, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
In terms of the Tathāgata’s practice, he is called a Bodhisattva, and in terms of his crown, he is called the "Bodhisattva-Crown."
The manifestation of Amitāyus clarifies that the ultimate fruit of this practice is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of universal gateways (*samantamukha-upāya*).
The countenances of this image and the Bodhisattvas all assume expressions of joy and smiling serenity while abiding in the bliss of the present dharma (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
The body of Avalokiteśvara is colored like the pure moon, or like a *śaṅkha*—that is, a supreme and exquisite conch shell—or like a *senāpa*... [text fragment].

That flower blooms in the west and is also exceedingly fresh and white; one should understand these three metaphors collectively to signify that its radiance is fresh, lustrous, and the very pinnacle of pure whiteness.
Next, to the right of Avalokiteśvara, paint the Bodhisattva Tārā; all such holy beings face toward Mahāvairocana.
Now, when it is said that the right side of Avalokiteśvara is toward the west, all other instances should be understood accordingly.
This is also because he manifests in the form of a woman through the samādhi of Avalokiteśvara. [Ā] means "eye," and the blue lotus signifies "pure and stainless.
Because he thus embraces all sentient beings with his universal eye, he acts neither before nor after [the proper time]. Therefore, he is made [in this form].
The middle-aged woman appears neither too old nor too young. Her blue color signifies the power of subjugation, while her white color signifies great compassion;
since their excellence lies in the union of these two functions, the two colors are blended together. For this reason, she is neither purely blue nor purely white.
The image has its palms joined, holding this blue lotus within them, with both hands and faces turned toward Avalokiteśvara.
He has a smiling expression and a halo surrounding his entire body, which is like pure gold in color.

He wears white garments and has a topknot on his head in the shape of a celestial crown, which differs from the hair-crown of Mahāvairocana. To the left of Avalokiteśvara is situated the noble Bhṛkuṭī;
her body has four arms, one of which on the right side hangs down holding a rosary garland, while another performs the varada-mudrā (gesture of granting boons). To the left [of her],...
On one side he holds a lotus flower and in the other hand grasps a *kamaṇḍalu*; he has three eyes on his face like the image of Maheśvara.
On his head he wears a hair-crown in the shape of a topknot (*uṣṇīṣa*) like that of Vairocana.
As for what is called "holding," it is like saying that the earth "holds" all things, which carries the meaning of supporting and sustaining. His body is pure white, surrounded by a halo of light.
Within it are the three colors—yellow, red, and white—and because they are not purely white, purely red, or purely yellow, it is said to be "without a master.
Generally, yellow is the color of enrichment (*puṣṭi*), white is the color of pacification (*śānti*), and red is the color of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
Since these three powers are all contained within the light of this samādhi, it is therefore used as its emblem (*cihna*).
Next, to the left of Vighnāntaka, one should paint Mahāsthāmaprāpta. He is so named because his majestic power and sovereignty are like those of a worldly king or great minister;
he is called "Great Power" (*Mahāsthāma*) because this noble being has attained such a state of sovereign mastery through great compassion.
The reason he holds an unopened lotus is that it is like the *dharmadhātu-jñāna* (wisdom of the expanse of reality) of Vairocana.

Once the fruit has been realized upon the lotus pedestal, one again takes such seeds and scatters them universally throughout the waters of the minds of all sentient beings, where they give rise once more to unfurled lotuses. The traces of this Honored One are identical to this place;

he is also able to universally protect the latent sprouts of goodness in all sentient beings so that they are not damaged or destroyed, causing them to increase in every thought-moment. This is the Vidyādhara of the Lotus Family.

The King. To the left of the Enlightened King (Vairocana), paint the Consort Yaśodharā—translated as "She Who Holds Renown"—her body of true golden color, adorned with various necklaces and ornaments so that she appears exceedingly beautiful like a celestial maiden; her right hand...
He held a long branch of fresh, white, and exquisite flowers, interspersed with fruits and leaves, lush and beautiful;
among the blossoms were some still in bud, some about to open, and some in full bloom—five, ten, or even dozens in number.
With his left hand he held a bowl, and the *utpala* flower he encountered was likewise a superior flower of the West, for it is presided over by the Great Powerful Vidyārāja.

She establishes the seeds of bodhi for all sentient beings, and since this Vidyārājñī contains and gives birth to these various merits therein, her garments and insignia are all consistent with this meaning.
To the right of Tārā, one places Paṇḍaravāsinī, translated as "White Dwellress."
This Honored One is named for her constant presence within a white lotus flower; she wears a crown of celestial hair-tufts and robes of pure white silk, holding a blossoming lotus in her left hand.
Because she is born from the place of supreme purity and possesses the Universal Eye, this samādhi is called the Mother of the Lotus Family.
Next, below Avalokiteśvara, place Hayagrīva (translated as "Horse-Head").
His body is neither yellow nor red, but the color of the newly risen sun. He adorns his body with white lotus flowers as necklaces and other ornaments.
His flames are all fiercely blazing and radiant; his mane and claws are long and sharp, and two fangs protrude upward.
The hair on his head is like the mane of a lion, manifesting the form of an extremely roaring and wrathful state; this is the Wrathful Vidyārāja of the Lotus Family.

Just as the precious horse of a Cakravartin King traverses the four continents at all times and in all places with an unceasing mind, so too is the great power of diligence of the Bodhisattvas. This is why he is able to [attain it].
That such a fierce power disregards body and life to extensively subdue the heavy obstacles of birth and death is precisely because of the pure and great compassionate heart;
therefore, he adorns his own body with a necklace of white lotuses.
Thus, the formal establishment of the various retinues of Avalokiteśvara is complete.
Next, to the left of Mahāvairocana, one should place the Lord of the Vajra Family, known as Vajrapāṇi, the Fulfilled One of All Wishes.
His color is like that of the *pāṭala* flower—a pale yellow—or like an emerald (*marakata*), which is a green gemstone;
his manifest color is like space, due to the pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Because form is in union with the essence of Vajra-wisdom, his body is yellowish-white.
This wisdom-body is like space, indestructible, and such that no one can subdue it; therefore, he uses the color of space as his emblem.
The meaning of this is that if even a minute portion of a phenomenon were obtainable, such as an atom, [it would not be so].
That which is subject to impermanence and the transformation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is therefore ultimately empty;
among all solid natures, the wisdom of ultimate emptiness is supreme. The secret mudrā maintained therein is the five-pronged vajra.
Since the wisdoms of the five Tathāgatas all encompass both the provisional and the ultimate functions, and because the hand of Vajraprajñā holds it at its center, it is called "right."
Holding the *vajra*, this mudrā should be universally encircled by a garland of light; hence it is said that "light-flames arise all around.
On his head he wears a three-peaked jewel-crown, its shape like the letter *śa*. Between the peaks are forms like those of upward- and downward-facing crescent moons.
His body is adorned with various subtle and exquisite mixed jewels and all manner of necklaces. This signifies:
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* transforms into the name "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*) upon reaching the mind of the stage of fruition,
it is said that "the head is crowned with a crown of various jewels. Because this wondrous wisdom extensively traverses all phenomena,
revolving with mastery to give birth to the adornments of the infinite *dharmadhātu*, it is said that they are "interlaced and mutually adorned in vast abundance."
Their number is immeasurable.

Next, to the right of the Lord of the Vajra Family, one places Mañjuśrī—also known as the Mother of the Vajra Family—who likewise holds the vajra of wisdom and whose body is adorned with various necklaces and ornaments; she is the source from which vajra-wisdom arises.
The *Baladhararāja-samādhi* is what is called the *Vajra-samādhi*.
Next, to the right of the Mother of the Family (*Kulīśvarī*), place Mahābalavajrasūcī; Sūzhi translates this as *Vajrasūcī-dhara*.
She takes a single-pronged *vajra* as her emblem (*cihna*). This *vajra* represents a single characteristic and a single object-condition (*ekalakṣaṇa-ekālambana*).
The wisdom of firm penetration uses this to thoroughly penetrate all phenomena without anything remaining uncomprehended; therefore, it is named the "Vajra Needle.
Below [the needle], there are two messengers, both in the form of women, kneeling with one foot on the ground and smiling as they gaze up at it.
Their appearance is small yet full, of a pale yellow color, and they bear the vajra as their insignia. This is the samādhi that destroys heavy obstructions.
Furthermore, to the left of Vajrapāṇi, place Vajraśṛṅkhala (translated as "Vajra Chain").
His mudrā consists of holding a chain with both ends fashioned in the form of a *vajra*; beneath the chain [is also...]
There are two female messengers who are no different from the messenger Vajrasūcī;
they are so named because they sustain all stubborn and difficult-to-transform sentient beings through this wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*), ensuring that they do not regress from unsurpassed bodhi.
Next, below Vajradhara, one should place the wrathful vidyādhara known as Candramaṇḍala, who subdues all great obstructors of the three times.
He has three eyes and four fangs, his appearance is like a cloud during the summer monsoon rains, and he manifests a form of great laughter.
He wears a necklace made of vajra-jewels; this is the Vajradhara who, by means of non-... [is the one].
The Samādhi of the Great Power and Fierce Majesty that Protects and Sustains Sentient Beings through the Gate of Measurement.
Surrounded by an immeasurable retinue, all of whom are humble yet fill the space, they manifest wrathful forms;

even a single body may possess hundreds of thousands of hands, brandishing various implements in a dense, formidable array that seems inexhaustible. When painting these, one should depict at least one or two.

The messengers, numbering up to five or six, should all abide upon lotuses; this indicates that within the heart of these lotuses, the power of all-courageous and great heroic diligence is naturally accomplished by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), having not come from any other place.
Thus, the assembly of Vajrasattva’s retinue has been fully established.
Next, proceed to the western direction and paint the Tathāgata’s vidyādhara messengers and the assembly of vajradharas.
Their various forms, colors, natures, and classes, as well as their various secret mudrās and insignia, should all be brought forth within the diagram.

This is because each and every honored one possesses the great wisdom-light that pervades the entire dharma-realm; since the secrets of their body, speech, and mind also pervade the dharma-realm, it is so described.
He universally emits perfect light for the sake of all sentient beings.
Below this, in the direction of Nairṛti, one should paint the Tathāgata messenger Acala in the form of a youth;
his right hand holds the seal of the Great Wisdom Sword, and his left hand holds a noose. On his head is a topknot of hair with locks hanging down.
With the left shoulder slightly drawn back and the left eye closed, one bites the upper lip on the right side with the lower teeth;
the lower lip on the left side is slightly turned outward. Wrinkles appear on the forehead like ripples on water.
Seated upon a stone, the body is low yet full, robust and flourishing, assuming a posture of fierce wrath and an expression of extreme indignation—this is the characteristic mark of its secret mudrā.
Furthermore, this Honored One attained Buddhahood long ago upon the lotus pedestal of Vairocana;

yet, by virtue of his samaya and original vow, he manifests the form of one who has newly resolved upon the Great Mind, appearing incomplete in his various marks as a servant and attendant to the Tathāgata, performing all manner of tasks.
Thus, he holds a sharp sword and a lasso, desiring to exhaust [all afflictions] by receiving the command of the Tathāgata’s wrathful power.
To slay all sentient beings: the noose is the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) within the mind of bodhi;

by binding those who are not subdued with these, one uses the sharp sword of wisdom to sever their karma and their endless life-span, thereby causing them to attain birth in the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
If the seeds of karma and life-span are eliminated, then the winds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) will also be extinguished. Therefore...
Sealing his mouth and gazing with a single eye, he intends to clarify that the Tathāgata, with his impartial gaze, observes all sentient beings as having no one who may be pardoned;
thus, whatever deeds this Honored One performs, they are solely for the sake of this one purpose.
He stabilizes their heavy obstructions like massive boulders so that they shall not move again, thereby establishing the wondrously lofty Bodhicitta of purity.
Therefore, it is said that Śailendra resides upon a flat rock.
Furthermore, in the lower northwestern corner, one should visualize the wrathful Vidyārāja Trailokyavijaya as the principal deity;
he wears a jeweled crown and holds the five-pronged vajra mudrā, gazing up at Vairocana as if receiving his instructions.
Regarding its form, the verse says: "One who disregards one's own life" means that one should assume an expression of ultimate wrathful fury, disregarding even life itself.
This signifies the desire to summon all sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu* and cause them to comply with the majestic command of the Dharma King;
it is also the mantra for accomplishing all activities (*sarvakarmasādhana*). For this reason, it is the great sovereign of the wisdom of these five Tathāgatas.
All that is washed away and destroyed by power reaches the stage of fruition and is adorned;

it is not merely the realization of emptiness alone without any obstacles. Therefore, holding the five-pronged seal and wearing a jewel crown within the wind-circle, one causes all that is enacted to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, as stated in the Lotus Sūtra.
The intention of purity having been established, the foremost of the first maṇḍala is completed.
Next, one proceeds to the second enclosure to paint Śākyamuni Ācārya.
It is said that "this second [enclosure]" is a term of esoteric meaning; from the center toward the outside, one should [depict] the retinue of Śākyamuni.
Regarding the third court: now, the retinue of the Vairocana-dharmakāya is established as the first; the retinue of Śākyamuni’s *janmakāya* (birth-body) is established as the second;
and because the various bodhisattvas seek the supreme above while transforming those below, situated between compassion and wisdom, they are established as the third.
The reason for such alternating textual arrangements is that this is the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, intended to prevent [misunderstanding].
Because those who possess pride and do not receive [teachings] from a teacher will distort the scriptural texts, it is necessary to transmit them orally.
Within the first gate of the eastern quarter, one should first place the body of Śākyamuni, golden in color and endowed with radiant brilliance and the thirty-two marks;
his saffron-colored (*kāṣāya*) robe should be the color of *gandha*, and he should be seated upon a white lotus, performing the act of preaching the Dharma.
The description states that he holds the corner of his *kāṣāya* with his left hand, as in the image of King Aśoka;
his right hand has its fingers extended upward, held in the *śūnyatā-jala-mudrā*. This is his insignia. This white lotus is the Womb of the Pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-garbha*).
In order to cause this teaching to spread widely, the World-Honored One used this insignia of his birth-body.
Since the act of preaching is non-dual and inseparable from the body of the fundamental Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is said that he dwells therein while preaching the Dharma.
Next, the Buddha-Eye (*Buddhalocanā*) is installed to the north of the World-Honored One; she is also the mother of Śākyamuni Buddha, and in this region—
She is translated as the Mother Śāntamātṛ. Her form is of incomparable beauty, pleasing to behold by all in the world;
her entire body is surrounded by a halo of light, and she smiles with joy. This is the Tathāgata’s Samādhi of Manifesting Forms According to the Capabilities of Beings.
This samādhi has Great Compassion and the Universal Eye as its essence; it observes sentient beings who are ready to be saved and guides them toward their benefit.
Because the light of the compassionate eye pervades everywhere without exception, it is called the "all-pervading, perfectly pure light.
Next, to the north of the Buddha-mother, one should paint the seal of the Tathāgata’s white ūrṇā-kośa, abiding upon a lotus flower.
His body is the color of a conch shell (*śaṅkha*), he possesses a halo, and his hand holds a lotus flower in the form of a half-blossomed bud, within which is a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
This is that which has been accumulated through the Tathāgata’s boundless meritorious deeds, as extensively explained in such sūtras as the *Buddhānusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra*;
therefore, it is able to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings.
Next, to the south of the Lion of the Śākyas, place the five *uṣṇīṣa* of the Tathāgata: first, the White Parasol *Uṣṇīṣa*;

second, the *Śveta* *Uṣṇīṣa*, translated here as "Victorious Crown" (*Jaya-uṣṇīṣa*); third, the *Viśveta* (this is pronounced with a plural suffix) translated as the "Supreme Buddha-Crown" (*Paramajaya-uṣṇīṣa*);
fourth, the *Tittira-śi*, translated as the "Fire-Mass Buddha-Crown" (*Jvālana-uṣṇīṣa*). As the Sūtra says:
"Multitude of Virtues" (Zhòngdé) should be correctly translated as "Great Portion" (Dàfēn), which carries the meaning of being endowed with great virtue.
