The fifth, "Subtle Kīlaṇa" (Wēijílúoná), is translated as "Discarding the Buddha’s Crown" (Shěchú Fódǐng); this carries the meaning of abandoning all afflictions (*kleśa*) and also signifies "crushing.
This is the crown of the five wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*) of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, which, among all merits, is like—

The Universal Monarchs possess great majesty and power; their forms all take the shape of a *cakravartin* king, meaning they have a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) on the crown of their heads, upon which there is further a topknot—that is, a double topknot.
All other physical characteristics are like those of a Bodhisattva, making them exceedingly dignified and pleasing. The secret mudrā held by them is as shown in the diagram.
Next, to the east, closest to the northern edge, array the assembly of the Five Śuddhāvāsa deities:
first, the Devaputra Īśvara; second, the Devaputra Samantakusuma; third, the Devaputra Prabhāmandala; fourth, the Devaputra Manomaya;
and fifth, the Devaputra Yaśaskīrti. They should be arranged in this order. Their mudrās and physical forms are fully detailed as described in the diagram. Ajita.
Li said: "These are the five *anāgāmin* devaputras. Beyond this, there are those who have attained the rank of Bodhisattva and are called the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) deities;
these are mostly Bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*). They are included within the second precinct and are not what is being explained here.
To the south of this heaven, to the right of the *ūrṇā-kośa*, one should further paint three *buddhoṣṇīṣas*."
The first is the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa; the second is the Extremely Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa; the third is the Boundless Sound Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
The physical forms of these are all identical to the five uṣṇīṣas, which are the crowns of the meritorious virtues of the three families of Tathāgatas.
These five kinds of Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas possess five colors, namely: true gold color and emerald gold color.

Pale yellow, extreme white, and pale white are the [colors of] true gold; the two colors of *uragasāra* (turmeric) are similar, yet true gold is luminous and pure while *uragasāra* is somewhat heavy in color.

As for the three *uṣṇīṣas*, there are three colors—namely white, yellow, and red—which correspond respectively to the colors of pacifying (*śāntika*), increasing (*pauṣṭika*), and subjugating (*abhicāruka*). These are the eight types of Buddhas.
The crowns of their heads and their entire bodies are radiant with light that is exceedingly vast and thick; they adorn their bodies with various necklaces and ornaments.
Because of the power of the Tathāgata’s original vows, they are able to fulfill all aspirations. In the southeast corner, the hosts of the Fire Devas (*Agnideva*) are arrayed, dwelling amidst flames;
on their foreheads and both arms, there are three lines of ash drawn, which are the same as those used by Brahmins.
He takes ashes with his fingers and smears them upon his body, appearing entirely deep crimson in color. At his heart is a triangular seal within a circle of blazing flames.
His left hand holds a rosary, and his right hand holds a ritual water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*). This is one manifestation of the Universal Gate (*Samantamukha*) body;
it is displayed as a skillful means to attract and guide the fire-worshipping *Veda*-brahmins, thereby revealing the Buddha’s own *Veda* teachings.
This is the insignia of the Great Wisdom Fire Mandala for the purification of the Brahma-faring life.

Next, to the right, south of the Great Sun, one should depict Yama, the Dharma King, holding a *daṇḍa* seal in his hand that resembles a staff; atop it is a human head, assuming an expression of extreme wrath.
Seated upon a water buffalo, his body is a deep, dark black. The Ācārya said: "In my youth, once when I was exhausted and unconscious from a severe illness, I went before the Lord of the Underworld.
There I beheld this Dharma King conversing with his consort; their countenances were exceedingly compassionate and forbearing.
Yet, this *daṇḍamudrā* assumes a wrathful form to examine the transgressions committed since birth, and from its mouth it utters [the words of judgment]."
The firelight was most severe and intense; yet, when the deeds performed after his renunciation were examined, they were thus tranquil and no longer subject to verbal expression.
King Yama and his queen immediately descended from the steps, praising him with kind words and respectfully paying homage as they earnestly requested to receive the precepts of refuge.
Having released him, he returned; by the time he reached the *sū* [the city], the cords bound to his two arms remained held fast.
The site still bore the scars of the wound, which only healed after ten days and ten months. To the west of Yama, one should fashion the consort of Yama (Yamī) and the deceased mother;

she is likewise the consort of Yama. To the east, one should fashion the goddess of Night (Rātri) and the seven mātṛs—translated as the "Seven Mothers"—who are all female spirits. Their forms are entirely black.
Next, in the southwest corner, one should paint the ghost-king Nṛti, holding a sword and appearing in a terrifying form;
this is the directional guardian Rākṣasa king Varuṇa, the western directional guardian nāga king,
who holds a noose as his mudrā.
To the south of the Five Peaks in the eastern direction, one should paint Indra, the lord of the Śakras, seated upon Mount Sumeru and surrounded by a host of celestial beings;
he wears a jeweled crown on his head and is adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, holding a *vajra* and other implements, together with his retinue,
namely the lady Śacī and the deities of the six heavens of desire, all as depicted in the illustration.
To the south of the retinue of Śakra-devendra, one places the assembly of Sūrya-deva within an eight-horse chariot,
with his two consorts on either side— namely, Jayā and Vijayā, translated as "Victory" and "Unconquered.
The various planetary deities (grahas) belonging to the retinue of Sūrya-deva are distributed [therein], while Aṅgāraka is situated in the west.
Śukra is in the east; Budha is in the south; Maṅgala is in the north;
Śaniścara is in the southeast; Rāhu is in the southwest; Ketu is in the northwest;
and Jupiter is in the northeast. Furthermore, [Jupiter] is situated to the south of the latter.
To the south is placed Nirgrantha, which refers to the heavenly dog-star (Tiangou); furthermore, to the north of the northern latitude is placed Ulkāpāta, which refers to the falling fire-star.
To the north of the retinue of Śakra Devendra, near the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, is placed Mahābrahmā, wearing a topknot crown and seated upon seven [lotuses].
In the *haṃsa-ratha* (goose-vehicle), there are four hands on each of the four sides;
one hand holds a lotus, one holds a rosary, one grasps a water jar (*kuṇḍikā*), and one forms the *oṃ-kāra-mudrā*. This is the left hand:

one should slightly bend the index finger, extend the remaining fingers straight, and press them against the side of the hand while reciting. This is called the *Śubhakarī-śrī-mudrā*. The remaining four [hands] are in *dhyāna*.
All the devas are arrayed to his left, while the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens, such as Avṛha, are arrayed to his right.

What is called *vinaya* refers to observing the ritual protocols for the attire of those in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; it is the discipline of wearing the three robes and inner garments in a neat and orderly manner.
Next, to the west near the gate, place the assembly of Earth Deities (*bhūmideva*).

his body is of a golden-yellow hue, he has five topknots on his head, he appears in the form of a youth, and in his left hand he holds...
The *nilapadma* is a blue lotus with slender petals;
upon its flower is a vajra seal, and he sits smiling joyfully upon a white lotus pedestal—this is his secret insignia.

The Ācārya says that *uraga* (saffron) represents the color of Jambūnada gold, used to symbolize the profound wisdom of the Vajra; as for the five topknots on his head, they serve as a symbolic representation.
The Tathāgata has long since accomplished the five wisdoms; yet, by virtue of the causal conditions of his original vows, he manifests in the form of a youthful Dharma Prince.
This blue lotus represents the samādhi of non-attachment to all phenomena. Because the mind abides nowhere, one directly perceives the true mark (*dharmatā*).
The Vajra Wisdom Seal is able to universally illumine the entire Dharma-realm with the light of eternal quiescence; for this reason, he sits.
The white lotus signifies that its meaning is no different from the Central Womb Treasury (*garbhadhātu*).

To the north of Mañjuśrī, one should paint the Bodhisattva Kūṭāgāra-kumārabhūta, his body golden in color, holding a precious net and adorned with various necklaces, seated upon a jeweled lotus. Mañjuśrī holds the wondrous signlessness (*animitta*).
With wisdom as a net of light, one upholds the adornment of myriad virtues as described in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Just as salt harmonizes various foods, increasing their flavor so that they cannot be eaten in vain, so too does the practitioner who loses *prajñā* and relies solely on skillful means fall into nihilism, while one who cultivates merit alone falls into the state of grasping at attainments; therefore, one contemplates the Buddha.
The "eldest son" refers to this very point.
Next, the five messengers of Mañjuśrī are listed: first, Keśinī;
second, Upakeśinī; third, Citrā; fourth, Bhūmimati; and fifth, [the fifth name].
They were summoned and arranged in succession on either side of Mañjuśrī, for each of them upholds a single wisdom of Mañjuśrī.
*Keśinī* means "one with beautiful hair"; *upā* signifies "a subordinate.
Because Mañjuśrī symbolizes the five wisdoms by means of his five topknots (*pañca-keśa*), these messengers are likewise named after their fine hair. *Citrā* means "variegated color."
Each of the five messengers below assumes the form of an attendant who, kneeling toward the messenger, appears as if receiving a proclamation;
these are all manifestations of Mañjuśrī’s samādhi, for the Sūtra says: "He is attended by those of invincible wisdom."
Next, on the second tier to the left of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, one should paint the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
According to the worldly convention of the West, he faces east; thus, the east is considered the primary direction, the south the right, the west the rear, and the north the superior direction.
Since the entrance of this maṇḍala altar faces west, this position corresponds to the left side of Mahāvairocana. [Illustration]
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin holds a lotus flower with his left hand, upon which rests a maṇi jewel;
his right hand forms the mudrā of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*). This bodhisattva and all his retinue are great beings of compassion who uproot suffering and remove obstacles;
through this very mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), they bestow the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) and fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
This fulfills their aspirations.

The Sūtra states that "at the two secondary positions, one should paint eight Bodhisattvas," meaning that beside Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, one should place two messengers, and then, according to the proper sequence, position the eight Bodhisattvas; in all listings of retinues, this is the case.
He places the first on the right and the second on the left; the third again on the right and the fourth again on the left.
In this manner, one by one, left and right, they are arranged in succession.
Now, among these eight bodhisattvas, he first places Vyapagataśaṅkita to the right of Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Sarvābhayapradātā to his left. Next, he again places...
All the deities of the evil destinies are placed to the right of Vimati-cchedaka; to the left of Abhayam-dada is placed Citta-trāṇa.
Next, to the right of Vimati-cchedaka is placed Karuṇāmaya, and to the left of Citta-trāṇa is placed Maitreya.
Next, to the right of Karuṇāmaya is placed Sarva-jvarāpanayana, which is inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva Prajñā (Wisdom) is positioned to the left of Maitreya; all other placements should be modeled after this.
Next, in the northern direction, paint the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha upon a ground adorned with various interspersed precious jewels.
His lotus throne is made of the four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and should be rendered with the utmost skill and beauty.
The Bodhisattva sits upon a lotus throne, his body surrounded by a pervasive radiance as if within a womb; thus it is said he "dwells in a womb of flames.
This holy being upholds the treasury of boundless jewels arising from the nature of the *cittabhūmi* (the ground of the mind) through the King of Jewels;
therefore, his insignia is adorned with a variegated array of all manner of rare and wondrous treasures. As for his other attendants...
The same applies to the meaning of the Bodhisattvas.
One should place the Bodhisattva Ratnākara to the right of Kṣitigarbha and the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi to the left of Kṣitigarbha.
Next, one should place the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara to the right of Ratnākara and the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta to the left of Ratnapāṇi.
To the right of Samantabhadra, one should place the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati;
in this manner, these and other principal deities are each surrounded by their respective retinues, painted on both their left and right sides.
Next, in the western direction, paint the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, clad in fresh white garments, holding a lotus flower in his left hand upon which is the seal of a great sword;
from the sword, flames and light radiate everywhere. He and all his retinue sit upon upright lotuses.
This Bodhisattva maintains the wisdom of the Tathāgata that is equal to space; as for why he holds a great sword, it is because it represents sharp wisdom.
The insignia and the wearing of white robes, pure and stainless, are the external adornments of this teaching’s gateway.
Just as space is without discrimination and without accumulation, yet the myriad phenomena of the world arise in dependence upon it, so too is this Dharma-gate:
from within ultimate emptiness, it gives birth to inconceivable and sovereign functions.
Because it is inexhaustible and is extensively elucidated in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-gaganagañja-sūtra*, it is named "Gaganagañja" (Space-Treasury).

The retinue of this dharma-gate consists of the Bodhisattvas Gaganāmala (Stainless Space), Gaganamati (Space-Wisdom), Viśuddhamati (Pure Wisdom), Cāritramati (Conduct-Wisdom), and Suvimalaprabha (Peaceful Wisdom); they are likewise arranged in order to the left and right as previously described.
The reason they are all described as "equal" is to clarify that these principal deities each further possess boundless retinues;

their physical forms and characteristics are all as explained in the diagrams. At the end of this verse, it says, "The arrangement of the Maṇḍala of the Treasury of Great Compassion is briefly explained.
These two lines were added by the transmitter to conclude the meaning and are not the original text of the sūtra.

As stated above, that which takes bodhicitta as its cause, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as its root, and skillful means (*upāya*) as its culmination is precisely the blooming of the flower-pedestal of the true nature of mind and the womb-matrix (*garbha*) of great compassion.

By manifesting through the skillful means of great compassion as the three-tiered assembly of universal gates (*samantamukha*), it is for this reason called the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-maṇḍala*. As it is said:
Within a single world-system, they universally manifest bodies corresponding to each of the six destinies according to their respective types;
it is likewise so in all world-systems. Among the various classes of beings in each of those places, they are the most preeminent leaders.

The Dharma they preach is also the most subtle and supreme among all such teachings. Furthermore, by means of this principle, they are able to universally embrace and sustain inexhaustible sentient beings.
Therefore, Vairocana is named the King of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhāturāja*). Now, these foremost deities have gathered together to seal and uphold this Dharma.
All those sentient beings of a similar kind will each give rise to a sense of wonder, saying:
"The one whom I revere as peerless is also present within this assembly. You should know that this Dharma is most profound.
Because they gave rise to a sense of rarity by regarding this as something marvelous, they planted roots of goodness within a single gateway of the Dharma-realm.

Even those who, throughout the long night, had cultivated unwholesome roots with the intent to destroy the True Dharma, upon reaching the site of enlightenment, saw Mahādeva—the one whom they themselves had venerated—and received the gift of the inconceivable food of the Dharma; their evil minds were immediately extinguished, and they abandoned Māra.
If, regarding any matter, one gives rise to even a single thought of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), because that single thought of pure mind has been produced,
one can thereby manifest the *Mahāvairocana-mandala* (Great Compassion Womb Mandala) therein. Furthermore, although the various dharma-gates of this mandala are of one and the same *dharmadhātu*,
their functions possess respective differences in depth and shallowness, just as in the case of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Although they all grow and are moistened by a single rain, the natures and capacities of the various medicinal herbs differ.
If a King of Physicians examines them, he knows that such-and-such a medicinal herb is not a suitable remedy for a particular disease, yet it possesses superior power for another disease.
If one distinguishes each of these universal gateways of skillful means without error, [one attains this knowledge].

Thus, one is fit to become a Great Ācārya. Within the great compendium of one hundred thousand verses, those various Honored Ones each proclaimed the gateways to the Dharma-realm through which they themselves had attained realization—various diverse expedient means.

This present abbreviated version merely sets forth the essentials for the general path of practice. If a practitioner cultivates according to the Dharma without violating its principles, [they will attain the fruit].
When one receives inconceivable empowerment, the expedient means will naturally be revealed in detail, such that there is nothing through which one cannot pass.
The Ācārya said: "Generally, a practitioner who does not abide in yoga is unfit to establish a maṇḍala for others.

The Ācārya said: "In the first enclosure, from the Tathāgata Hook in the east up to the Tathāgata Nail, all are forms of Vairocana’s samādhi, each appearing in the form of a goddess according to the square or circular layout of the maṇḍala.
They sit upon white lotus pedestals, holding lotuses in their hands, upon which various symbolic images are depicted."
They are used as identifying marks; such as the wheel, sword, spear, conch, bell, *pāśa*, armor, and so forth—all these should be depicted according to their original forms.
The *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance), the *ūrṇā* (hair-treasure), the mouth, tongue, teeth, and lips may be understood by analogy with these examples.
On the navel of the Tathāgata, one should depict a lotus upon which is drawn a perfectly circular, continuous ring. The waist of the Tathāgata is also somewhat curved and rounded.
The rosary is the form of the Tathāgatagarbha; the wheel-like form is the appearance of the non-manifestation of the Cakravartin’s horse-treasure.
The Tathāgata grants boons with the hand that bestows wishes. The Dharma and eloquent exposition are sometimes held as the Sūtra-piṭaka, or made into the hand of preaching the Dharma.
The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), and so forth, are all dharmas corresponding to *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, forming the third [aspect] of tranquility.
Regarding the appearance of *samādhi*, one should assume the form of the Buddha’s uṣṇīṣa; this uṣṇīṣa-form of the Tathāgata fully encompasses all merits.
If there is no object in the hand that can serve as a *cihna* (emblem), one should leave it empty.
If, in the maṇḍala, a deity is not depicted in anthropomorphic form but is represented solely by a secret mudrā, then upon the vajra-seat one should fashion a lotus pedestal, and upon that pedestal—

As previously described, one should draw the insignia (*cihna*). Regarding the creation of a maṇḍala with written characters, if there is a seed-syllable (*bīja*) for it within the sūtra, it should be placed according to the ritual rules;
if it is not recorded in the sūtra, one should take the first letter of its Sanskrit name as the seed-syllable, or one may generally use the syllable *A*.
As for the various deities of the Lotus Family (*padmakula*) facing north, if their forms and characteristics are not explained in the sūtra—
This [deity] is generally depicted with the color of a red lotus or a pure white like gold, as in the case of the Honored One [Vajrasattva] and others;
thus, the characteristics of the mudrā held are also as described in the Buddha Family section.
However, using the lotus as its emblem, one should fashion a lotus-wheel image with four lotus petals arranged in the shape of a cross to serve as the spokes of the wheel, outside of which...
One should fashion a lotus encircling a blade; the sword should be placed upon the lotus, and the tip of the blade should likewise be marked with a lotus as its insignia.
The vajra, trident, and other implements are all treated in this same manner. For the lotus-noose, the lotus serves as the two tassels;
for the bell, the lotus serves as the binding garland; and for the chain, it is threaded through the lotus.
Adorning the body, one may place it upon a held flower; placing a stūpa upon the crown of the head as a mark of auspiciousness, or placing a *stūpa* upon a held flower;
the Lord Padma-śrī (Lotus Glory) is placed upon that flower, and upon that lotus is the Jewel-Virtue Lord (*Ratna-guṇa-śrī*), the King of Vidyās who can grant all vows and fulfill all hopes.
May his form be exactly like that of Avalokiteśvara holding a lotus, upon which a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) is placed;
according to the rites of pacifying, increasing, or subjugating, he should be situated within the corresponding maṇḍala.
Mahāśrī holds a lotus in each of his two hands, or water emerges from the lotuses, or water flows from his hanging hands; the Honored One is clad in a deer skin.
Adorning the body with deerskin like the image of Brahmā, their mudrās and maṇḍalas are to be understood according to the examples previously explained;
the syllable *sa* is universally used as their seed-syllable.
As for the various deities of the Vajra Family on the southern side, those whose names are listed at the beginning of the sūtra may all be installed there in their entirety.
According to the shape of the maṇḍala—whether square, circular, triangular, or crescent-shaped—the color of its body should be likewise.

Alternatively, one may hold a single-pronged *vajra*, or hold various types of vajra insignia such as those with three prongs, five prongs, or two points above and below, as described in the sūtras, placing them according to one's preference.
As for the sword, axe, hook, needle, and so forth, all of these take the *vajra* as their emblem.
The blade, edge, hilt, and ornamentation of the sword are all fashioned in the form of a *vajra*, with its tip being sharp and pointed;
the *pāśa* consists of linked chains, both ends of which resemble a three-pronged *viśvavajra*; the wheel has spokes and a rim formed by a cross-shaped *vajra*, surrounded by a ring of sharp blades;
and the bell has a single-pronged *vajra* at its top, with a cross-shaped *vajra* serving as its tongue.

The rest may all be understood by analogy. Regarding the mudrās and maṇḍalas, one should likewise place white lotuses upon the vajra-throne, with each [deity] represented by its respective object atop the flower.
If a maṇḍala of letter-mudrās is constructed, the *vaṃ* syllable is used as the seed-syllable for the retinue governed by Vajrapāṇi;
for other Vajras, the *hūṃ* syllable is generally used as the seed-syllable. Chapter [Number].

Regarding the various assemblies of bodhisattvas in the two assemblies (*dvimandala*): if their physical forms are fully described in the sūtras, they should be depicted exactly according to the original teachings.
For those not explicitly mentioned, the Cintāmaṇi seal is used universally: one should hold a lotus flower with a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) placed upon it, surrounded by a wreath of flames.
Alternatively, their forms may be represented according to the meaning and significance of their respective names, as in the case of [the Bodhisattva] Ratna.
The Bodhisattva Makuṭa placed a precious crown upon the flower; the Bodhisattva Ratnajāla placed a precious net upon the flower;
the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi held a jewel in his hand; and the Bodhisattva Citta-utpāda-cakra-pravartana held a wheel in his hand.
In all vacant positions, the Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa were placed. Their messengers who had received their instructions and so forth all performed [their respective duties].
Their humble appearance and the messengers they employ—wielding knives and clubs as if guarding a gate—follow the instructions of those who serve;

some hold painted seals, while others gaze upon their honored masters. Those who receive commands and instructions for protection act like gatekeepers conveying messages, each according to their respective class, reporting whatever they have to consult. This is the passage concerning the descent of the Honored One Yama.
He is accompanied by an extraordinary retinue and possesses great majestic power. His body has six faces, six arms, and six legs, with a water buffalo as his seat.
Each face has three eyes, and his color is like dark clouds; he manifests in an extremely wrathful form.

While the features of the six-faced deity are largely the same, there are variations such as having four arms and six legs, or two hands and two legs. One should consult the Sanskrit manuscript of Mañjuśrī for a complete illustration.
Regarding all such deities, if their physical forms are fully described in other sūtras, they may likewise be depicted according to those descriptions and admitted into the maṇḍala.
As for these deities whose mantras and mudrās are not recorded in the Vairocana Sūtra but are separately set forth in other sūtras,
one should grant the mantras and mudrās according to those respective sūtras, and cause them to rely upon this [maṇḍala].

This is the sequence of ritual practice for making offerings according to the Sūtras. As for the Buddhas of the ten directions in the third enclosure, each should be depicted according to their usual characteristics.
If one is to form mudrās, they should be done with the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown-protrusion) of the Tathāgatas; as for the seed-syllables (*bīja*), they are the letter *A*.
For the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it is entirely the same as the ritual protocol for Bhikṣus. The slight difference regarding the Pratyekabuddhas therein is that, alternatively—
Regarding the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa), such as the uṣṇīṣa, if one employs mudrās, one should use [implements] such as the alms bowl, the saffron robe, and the mendicant’s staff.
The seed-syllables are as described in the mantras within the sūtras. One may place the goddess Mārīcī before the Sun Deity in the east, as it appears in the *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha*;
however, she is omitted from the diagram of the Eight Great Yakṣa Generals in the north.
The younger ones are for the most part similar in appearance; they all wear armor and hold the gadā-mudrā, their physical forms being perfectly complete and upright.
Because they travel from that place to this one, their desires are never lacking, and they always experience joy and self-indulgence.
Those with ears like sheep, horses, or elephants are all the retinues of the kumbhāṇḍas; their forms differ from those of the yakṣas.

They have exposed bodies with hanging hair, appearing like non-human beings, resembling beasts and animals; the illustrations label them as "vidyādhara sages," yet these are all *siddhi-vidyādharas* produced by the power of medicinal herbs and the like.
Those who are *vidyādharas* through the exclusive reliance on incantations are those who attain *siddhi* solely through mantra arts;
those simply called "various sages" are all those of the Vedic fire-worshipping class who have achieved [their state] through diligent practice of asceticism.
Furthermore, there are ṛṣis possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and yakṣas who are holders of vidyā-mantras;
those among them whose merit is most preeminent are subsumed within the realm of the gods (*devagati*), and thus they differ from worldly ṛṣis.

As for the deities of mountains, seas, rivers, lakes, forests, trees, grains, medicinal herbs, cities, towns, and roads, each is marked by its own original name as its insignia. For instance, the mountain deity is seated upon a mountain, and the river deity [is seated upon a river].

Regarding those who sit by rivers, trees, medicinal herbs, and so forth—whether holding them in their hands or relying upon them—one should infer [the corresponding deities] according to their respective categories.

Within the *Avataṃsaka*, there are further "foot-traveling spirits" (*pādacārin*) and "host of body spirits" (*kāyika-deva*), which protect those with physical disabilities such as lameness, as well as "body-protecting spirits";
these may also be listed in their proper order. As for the non-human realms (*amanuṣya-gati*) in the West, one should know that they are [governed by] Vairocana.

Within the body of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), all miscellaneous classes of spirits, ghosts, and animals that have no distinct names or characteristics in the diagrams are mostly subsumed therein;
these are the most numerous. Those with red complexions are mostly *rākṣasīs*, those with yellow complexions are mostly *piśācas*, and those with black complexions are *kṛtyas*.
Those with blue complexions are also included among them. If one follows the conventions of this region:
Regarding the clear meaning, each should be depicted individually. The *Kṣobha* are white and all belong to the same class of nāga kings;
they should each be painted according to their respective colors. If the prefix *Upa-* is added, their color is slightly lighter.
*Suna* and *Upasuna* are also great nāga kings who guard the gates; both hold a sword in their right hand and a noose (*pāśa*) in their left, and they are the presiding lords.
The deities of the years, months, seasons, and divisions of time all assume the forms of celestial maidens, holding flower branches and the like as their identifying marks.

If they preside over auspicious matters, their flowers are made to possess perfect color and form; if they preside over inauspicious matters, they hold withered flowers, shriveled fruits, and the like.
The deities who preside over the six periods of the day may likewise hold flowers of six branches, according to the specific time.

The imagery of flourishing and falling represents the affairs of the Lord of Day and Night; one may also apply this to the blossoming and closing of flowers, and all other cases should be understood accordingly.
To the south lies Bhilingkilila, who is known as the son of Maheśvara.
His body is extremely withered and exhausted, for he constantly subdues his enemies; even if his flesh and bones were to waste away entirely, he would still insist on doing so.

Because he attained victory, he assumed this form. In my private opinion, this is precisely what is referred to in the *Prajñāpāramitā* as one who "constantly practiced asceticism, cut his own flesh to offer to the fire, and thereby caused various evil deities to be born.
This is why his station is located in the south. In the *Sūtra of the Twelve Fire Deities*, a brief description of his iconography is provided;
there is one deity whose name is missing, which simply follows the general characteristics of the various fire deities.

The Sūtra says: At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries, amidst the entire assembly, gazed intently upon Mahāvairocana.
When the Tathāgata, whose eyes do not blink for even a moment, had finished expounding the positions of the various deities as manifested in the Universal Gate Maṇḍala,
the Lord of Secrets, observing each and every deity with his universal eye, saw that none possessed a fundamental basis nor any place of abiding;
they were all bodies of the true reality (*dharmatā*) within the Lotus Treasury, manifesting in various forms.

The skillful means are inexhaustible. At that time, he rejoiced deeply within himself and gave rise to a rare and marvelous mind, conceiving a sense of the extreme difficulty of encountering this Dharma even more intensely than before.
Desiring to further inquire into its profound meaning, he first spoke these verses. The intent of the first verse is as follows:
"The All-Knowing One appears in the world only once in a great while, just like the auspicious *utpala* flower, which manifests but rarely. Thus spoke the Buddha.
Although the udumbara flower is difficult to encounter, this essential dharma of the mantra exceeds it even further. Why is this?

This is the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, guarded through the long night and not bestowed upon people indiscriminately; if one lacks the capacity for sudden awakening, it shall not fall into their hands.
When the World-Honored One was still in the world, there were already many who harbored resentment and jealousy—how much more so in these final ages? Furthermore...
Next, the sutra itself explains the causes and conditions for why it is difficult to encounter [this mandala]:

"If a sentient being sees this mandala even once, the heavy obstructions of evil karma from beginningless time will be destroyed without remainder, and they will certainly receive the prediction of great bodhi;
therefore, it is not something that can be encountered by those of dull faculties or meager merit. If it is difficult even to see it once, how much more so to practice it in successive stages?"

One should know that such a person is even more rare and marvelous, constantly praised within the ocean-like assemblies of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), their fame reaching throughout the ten directions;
furthermore, because they possess various names and titles identical to those of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, they are called "Immeasurable Renown."
The Sūtra states: "One who practices this unsurpassed phrase is practicing the phrase of unsurpassed bodhi.
This gateway of the letter A is the king of all mantras, just as the World-Honored One is the king of all dharmas; therefore, it is called the "Mantra Savior of the World.
The next two phrases clarify the activity of saving the world: they enable the practitioner to become [like] gold.
The firmness [of this practice] brings about the cessation of all evil destinies and the non-arising of all suffering. As the Sūtra says:
"If one cultivates such a practice and possesses a wondrous wisdom that is profoundly immovable," according to the authentic original text, it should state:

"possessing a wisdom that is extremely profound and immovable, like the mind of the great ocean, because it is extremely deep and vast, and because it is utterly remote from the two extremes, even when great winds arise."
At that time, they cannot be shaken; likewise, when a practitioner enters the heart of this great ocean of mantras,
they too are thus unshakable by all phenomena, because their sublime wisdom is profound, immeasurable, and utterly remote from the two extremes—
just as when the Dragon King Sāgara sends down rain upon the six heavens, his three karmas within his own palace are entirely [unmoved].
If one understands this meaning—that there is no activity—then one knows that all the various skillful means (*upāya*) of the maṇḍala abide entirely within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the entire great assembly and all the Vajradharas, with a single voice..."

Regarding those who praise Vajrapāṇi: when that great assembly had heard the Buddha extensively expound the layout and positions of the maṇḍala, they wished to inquire about the symbols of the dharmadhātu therein and the vajra activities. Out of reverence for the World-Honored One, they did not dare speak;
however, because Vajrapāṇi was able to perceive the minds of the assembly and would surely know how to resolve their doubts by speaking verses according to the occasion, [they praised him].
To resolve the net of doubt for the universal benefit of immeasurable sentient beings, he praised, testified to, and exhorted them to pose their questions.
Furthermore, it is said that a multitude of beings equal to the atoms of ten buddha-fields, with a single mind and a single flavor, caused one person to praise and recite this Dharma-sound;
this does not mean that every individual spoke separately at the same time. As the verse says: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Diligent Hero! You have already..."
"Those who practice the mantra path and are able to inquire into the meaning of all mantras—we all intend to contemplate this—namely, that the mantra path is the Dharma-gate of the three equalities.

Because you are the foremost among those who uphold the three secrets, you are able to inquire of the World-Honored One regarding the profound meaning of the Universal Gate. Whatever you wish to ask the Buddha, we likewise [desire to ask]."
All of them had this thought: "Now we shall all with one mind desire to quickly set forth [our testimony]. Next, it says:

"O you who are currently present as witnesses for you, relying upon the power of the practice of mantra—[we say] that when we first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), by dwelling in these unsurpassed words, we were even able [to enter] the profound ocean of Vajra-wisdom."
Therefore, I shall now roar the lion’s roar before you as a manifest testimony for the verses you have spoken:
"Whatever we do is entirely due to abiding in the power of mantra practice; it is by relying on the force of mantra that we attain accomplishment.
If you inquire about the secret skillful means of the Tathāgata, all those who seek the Mahāyāna should [rely] upon mantra."
All who practice the Dharma will attain thorough penetration; because they have attained such penetration, they will not long require diligent cultivation and will be no different from us.
Seeing such benefits and meanings, we use a single voice to encourage and assist them with one mind.

At that time, having been exhorted by the great assembly, the Lord of Secrets (Guhyapati) immediately spoke a verse, extensively inquiring of the Blessed One with the first stanza regarding the meaning of colors.
This stanza consists of four lines: the first line asks what the meaning of "colors" is;
the second line asks with what colors [one should paint]; the third line asks how these colors are to be arranged, and first, where they should be placed.
Is it internal or external? This fourth question concerns what color should be used first when laying out the colors;
this is one component of the time for constructing the maṇḍala. Next, the verse asks about the characteristic signs of the various gates in three parts:
the first part asks about the shape and dimensions of the gate banners; the second part asks about the shape and dimensions of the gate corridors; and the third part asks...
The dimensions and forms of the various gateways and ritual procedures, as well as these diverse secret insignia (*mudrā*), the *ācārya* must thoroughly master;
this is yet another branch [of the practice]. Next, there are two verses comprising approximately eight questions.
The first line asks: "How does one offer food, flowers, incense, and so forth? The second line asks about the precious vase (*ratnaghaṭa*).
According to the Dharma, one should know that all implements for offering are contained therein;
the Ācārya should, in accordance with the specific circumstances, distinguish their respective natures and categories—this is yet another branch [of the ritual].
The third phrase asks: "How does one summon the disciples into the maṇḍala? The fourth phrase asks: "How does one perform the rite of consecration (abhiṣeka)? The fifth phrase...
Question: How does one offer veneration to the Honored One? Furthermore, within this, there are two types:
for a beginner practitioner relying on the mundane mandala, how does one summon [the deity], confer initiation, and offer [veneration] to the ācārya?
And for one who has already practiced yoga and performed the secret initiation, how does one summon [the deity], confer initiation, and offer [veneration] to the ācārya while performing it correctly?
All empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*), instructions (*avavāda*), and skillful means (*upāya*) pertaining to the time of the Dharma are subsumed herein; this is yet another branch [of the teaching].

The sixth phrase asks about the locations for *homā* (fire rituals), which also have two explanations—the exoteric and the esoteric—as well as various distinct skillful means such as those for pacifying (*śāntika*), increasing (*pauṣṭika*), and subjugating (*abhicāruka*).
The seventh phrase asks about the categories of mantra sections, the meaning of the syllables, and the meaning of the phrases, and so forth.
The eighth question concerns the characteristics of the differences in depth between the various gates of samādhi.
Generally, an ācārya who has not yet attained thorough mastery of such dharmas should not establish a maṇḍala; furthermore, this constitutes three types of constituent factors.
Having thus finished the questioning, the Great Sage, the Dharma King, addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying: "You should listen with single-minded attention."
Next, the verse says: "The most supreme mantra-path gives birth to the fruit of the Mahāyāna.
The fruit of the Mahāyāna is the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha; it must arise only through such skillful means (*upāya*).
Because you have been able to question me with these excellent words, I shall now universally reveal and expound this for all the Mahāsattvas. The first verse answers the nature of form (*rūpa*).
The meaning is as follows: it refers to dyeing the realm of sentient beings with the flavor of the *dharmadhātu*, as proclaimed by the Buddhas of antiquity;
this is what is meant by "form" (*rūpa*). The meaning is like the dyeing of worldly cloth, which can color a clean fabric so that it becomes of a single flavor.
Thus, one explains "form" through "flavor" (*rasa*); for example, the "flavor of the *kāṣāya*" refers precisely to dyeing the robe into the color of the *kāṣāya*. Now, regarding this *maṇḍala*...
The meaning of the syllable *ra* is likewise: because the inconceivable form of the *dharmadhātu* dyes the minds of sentient beings, they become of one flavor with pure bodhi.

Furthermore, just as a garment dyed in the world must first be washed clean with lye-water so that it easily receives the dye, now, by means of the *ra*-gate, the defilements of the disciple’s mind are incinerated until they are reduced to ashes; thereafter, with...
The gate of the syllable *va* is great kindness and great compassion; it washes [the mind] clean with water so that it becomes purely white and free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Thereafter, one paints the Dharma-realm maṇḍala, causing the various bodies of the universal gates to all be identical in color to the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Next, there are two verses that provide a general answer to the three questions. Among those questions, it was asked: "With what color should one [paint]? This is now the answer.
Within this, the five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—are employed. A verse states: "First one arranges the internal colors;
it is not the external colors that are arranged. This answers the question: how are the colors arranged? Where do they first arise, and where do they arise later?
With pure white as the first and red as the second, yellow and blue subsequently manifest in gradual succession. One.
That which is entirely internal, profound, and mysterious is called the "priority" of form (*rūpa*). This is the answer to the question: "What is the first of these forms?
White is the color of Vairocana’s pure *dharmadhātu*; since it is the source of all sentient beings, it is the foremost.
Red is the color of Ratnaketu Tathāgata; having already generated the bodhicitta, he subdues Māra within the path of the luminous mind.

The second yellow represents the color of the King of Śāla Trees; because it eliminates enmity and removes hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), it signifies that at the time of attaining perfect enlightenment, the ten thousand virtues blossom and all reach the adamantine limit of reality (*vajra-bhūtakoṭi*). The third blue represents the color of Amitāyus;
since one has reached the adamantine limit of reality, one employs the skillful means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-upāya*) to universally manifest the Great Compassion Maṇḍala.
Because the pure void contains all myriad phenomena, the fourth black [circle] represents the color of the Tathāgata Drum-Sound (Duṇḍubhisvara).

Thus, the manifestation of the traces of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) is entirely for the purpose of revealing the Original Source. This "Original Source" is the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, abiding in Great Nirvāṇa.
If one were to relinquish the sustaining power of *adhiṣṭhāna* (empowerment), then all sentient beings who are merely mental constructs would not be within his sphere of experience.

Therefore, its color is profound and dark, and it occupies the very last position. Furthermore, just as in the world a clean white cloth first receives dye, black is the initial stage and the ultimate limit of dyeing;
because it is the deepest, nothing further can be added, and thus it occupies the final place.
The significance of the colors in the maṇḍala is likewise: white signifies the transcendence of the one hundred and sixty mental defilements. This...
The first is red because it signifies the color of faith and the meaning of Great Diligence (*mahāvīra*);

the second is yellow because it signifies the color of vigor (*vīrya*) and refers to the time when mindfulness is associated with a single thought-moment, wherein concentration and wisdom are equal and the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) blossom; this is called the color of mindfulness.

The third is blue because it signifies the meaning of the Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahāśūnyatā-samādhi*) and is called the color of concentration (*samādhi*). The fourth is black, which refers to Great Nirvāṇa.
The meaning of "pan" (pari) is the ultimate wisdom of the Tathāgata; because it is called the "color of wisdom," the fifth [element] is so designated.
Alternatively, some say that white is the first, yellow is the second, red is the third, blue is the fourth, and black is the fifth.
This is based on the sense of the depth of defilement (*kleśa*), the capacity for receptivity, and the presence of superiority. Furthermore, white is the color of faith, being supreme.
First, yellow is like a vajra, indestructible; this is the meaning of "advancement. Second, red refers to the purification of mental obscurations and the manifestation of radiant illumination;
this is the meaning of "mindfulness. Third, the remaining colors are explained as above; the specific dharmas symbolized by each are distinct.
Furthermore, white is the color of the pacification of calamities and represents the meaning of the Tathāgata family. Therefore, it is supreme.

First, yellow is the color of increase, representing the meaning of the Lotus Family (*padmakula*). Second, red is the color of subjugation, representing the meaning of the Vajra Family (*vajrakula*).
Third, blue is for the accomplishment of all activities, as it also produces forms according to their respective types.
Fourth, black is the meaning of summoning, referring to the various tasks performed by the messengers and wrathful deities (*krodha*) who carry out instructions. Fifth...

Furthermore, just as the colors used in worldly painting do not exceed five, yet through their mutual interpenetration they produce various degrees of lightness and depth, which a skillful artist can distribute so as to give rise to myriad images without end;
so too it is with the inconceivable colors of the Dharma-realm. To summarize, they do not exceed the five letter-gates, yet furthermore—

Furthermore, do they mutually manifest and give rise to various differentiated wisdom-seals (*jñāna-mudrā*)? The Tathāgata, through his universal skillful means, has depicted the Maṇḍala Born of Compassion;
yet even if he were to produce forms corresponding to every class of being as numerous as the atoms within all worlds, he would still not reach the limit.
If a practitioner of Yoga can skillfully grasp the underlying meaning herein, they should touch upon one category and extend their understanding to all others.
Within the true suchness (*tathatā*) of quiescent activity, one should abide in what sequence?
As stated in the verses, this merely presents one path of the Dharma to provide a general outline.
The Sūtra says: "First, one should arrange the internal forms, not the external forms. Regarding all methods of painting, one must first establish [the foundation].
Having completed the establishment of the inner mind-secret Lotus Treasury, next construct the first tier: the three points of the letter *I* and all the inner retinues.
Next, construct the second tier: the four Bodhisattvas and other great retinues, as well as the third tier:
the retinues of all worldly deities. Furthermore, the center of each realm-path and the first tier should be endowed with the five colors.
First, having completed the perimeter with white, next arrange a red boundary outside of that; next, arrange yellow outside of that;
next, arrange blue outside of that; and finally, arrange black on the outermost edge. For the second layer, likewise arrange the three colors—white, red, and yellow—in the same sequence as above.
For the third layer of the perimeter, arrange only a single color, pure white.
Ensure that all are perfectly even, straight, and arranged in a gradual clockwise rotation.
Regarding the outer borders of the path for practice and the area for offerings, apply a single solid color; according to the *Guhya*, it says simply to use white.
The reason for first using white from the center toward the outside is to clarify that the five faculties and powers of this bodhicitta increase gradually.
Extending even to abiding in Great Parinirvāṇa, it pervades all places and is nowhere absent; therefore, the black color occupies the outermost position.

If one proceeds from the shallow toward the deep, returning from the traces to the source, then the World-Honored One condescends to accord with the six realms of existence as the initial gateway, and his retinue develops the pure bodhicitta. If sentient beings enter this gate of illumination, they transcend...
At the time of the one hundred and sixty minds, because one has already transcended the mundane world and ascended to the stage of a Bodhisattva, the third maṇḍala uses white alone as its boundary.
As for the second maṇḍala, upon the white mind, red and yellow are further added:
red represents the diligent and courageous bodhicitta in which one cultivates the myriad practices, and yellow represents suchness (tathatā).

When the ten thousand virtues bloom through the recollection of the *smṛtyupasthāna*, one then enters the gate of the "Twofold Mystery" (*chongxuan*) and dwells in the Land of Quiescent Light (*jiguangtu*).
Even when manifesting as a successor to the Buddha’s position (*puchu*), one still fundamentally does not recognize a single person;
therefore, the second layer uses only three colors as its boundary. Upon these three colors of the first-layer maṇḍala, blue and black are further added—blue being...
This is the Great Emptiness Samādhi, which is the inexhaustible empowerment of the Tathāgata’s secrets of body, speech, and mind;
therefore, it manifests as the color of the great void, black. This refers to the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding body of immeasurable lifespan.
Because such a wondrous body is ultimately formless, it appears as a profound, dark hue. These two phrases constitute the secret treasury of the Tathāgata and are not intended for everyone.

Because they are sentient beings, they are called "inner retinue. Furthermore, when entering this profound and mysterious color, it is precisely the *garbhadhātu* (womb-realm) of the *padma* (lotus) realized within the Tathāgata’s self-attestation.
At that time, one sees that the colors of the five wisdoms are all of one identical *dharmadhātu* color;

how could there be any distinction between shallow and deep? Nevertheless, among sentient beings, there are those who enter gradually, those who ascend by leaping over stages, and those who enter instantaneously. However...
Because that which they pursue ultimately returns to the same destination, it is said that "all are internally profound and mysterious.
The Sūtra states: "The construction of gates and insignia is equal in measure to the central Womb Realm (*garbhadhātu*); the surrounding enclosures are likewise so.
Regarding the sixteen sections of the flower pedestal, the gates of the maṇḍala all have banners and flags erected as markers; these are called "gate insignia" (*dvāra-lakṣaṇa*).
Measure the distance between the two markers using a ruler so that it is exactly equal to the central *garbha*; place a horizontal crossbeam upon it, its width being likewise the same.
On top of the banner staff, place an inverted crescent moon (*ardhacandra*), and beneath the moon, place the image of the insignia. Take silk cloth and cut it into perfect squares;
break them at the corners to form two banners, each attached to the exterior of the banner staff, tapering to a point at the top and hanging downward.
At the four intermediate corners, one should also place flagpoles and crescent moon banners; these insignia are placed facing both ways at the gate of Mahāvīra.
Upon each of the crescent moons at the gate of Vajrapāṇi, one should place a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*); upon each of the crescent moons at the gate of Padmapāṇi, one should place a *vajra*;
and upon each of the crescent moons at the gate of Śaṅkhapāṇi, one should place a conch shell (*śaṅkha*). Furthermore, upon all four intermediate corners, one should likewise place jewels.
Furthermore, at the flanking pavilions and guard stations of the gates, which are shaped like the letter "A," vajra-kīlas are placed at every bend of the central passage;
the heads of these kīlas are shaped like single-pronged *viśvavajras*, while their lower ends are sharp and pointed.
There are six kīlas on each side of one pavilion, totaling twelve for both sides. Including the four gates and the four corners, there are fifty-eight in total, arranged in three tiers.
Prepare five-colored threads as examples; empower them one hundred and eight times or one thousand and eighty times with either the *Acalamantra* or the *Trailokyavijayamantra*.

When the Ācārya has correctly performed the ritual and the maṇḍala is finished being drawn at night, he first examines the central womb (*garbha*) and the first enclosure (*prathama-krama*) to ensure nothing is missing, and then lays down the vajra.
One should surround the vajra-wedges with vajra-thread, stopping at the location of the gateway without cutting it across;
this should be done in this manner for all three tiers. If one is unable to do so, the third enclosure must certainly be established according to this method without omission.
Upon reaching the gateway, one should lift the thread and follow the curvature of the gate markers.

Furthermore, one must not obstruct the head [of the boundary], and once the *sīmā-bandha* (demarcation of the boundary) is completed, one should enter and exit strictly through the designated gates and must not arbitrarily cross over other areas.
Each time one enters or exits, one must recite the Acala-mantra. If one is a Yoga-ācārya, it is also permissible to enclose the perimeter with thread;
when it is necessary to enter or exit, one should visualize lifting this thread and passing beneath it.
Once the time has passed, one returns to the original state. Alternatively, if one must enter or exit urgently while far from the gate, one should visualize oneself as Vairocana;
with an unimpeded body, one should not give rise to the thought of crossing the boundary lines, and may enter or exit at will without fault.
At the curved points between the six stakes, ensure that all measurements are equal by the cubit, and there must be a passageway for travel.

Since the side chambers and guards of the outermost gate of the Āyatanakula (Realm) court are also equal in size to those of the central womb [maṇḍala], it is said that "the side chambers and guards are likewise.
The flower pedestal is the place for consecration (*abhiṣeka*); the layout of the lotus altar is largely identical to the eight-petaled treasury of the central womb.
Its smallest dimension is sixteen finger-widths (*aṅgula*), the further implications of which shall be explained below; however, it opens as one.
Open the gates so that they face the great maṇḍala. A verse states: "One should know that the first gate is equal in height to the inner maṇḍala," meaning it corresponds to the first tier of gates.

Based on the ninefold division, ensure the width and breadth are perfectly aligned so that the central axis of the gate falls exactly upon the heart of the Flower Treasury (Kusuma-alaṃkāra). The remaining second and third gates should also follow this same standard.
These divisions naturally expand in gradual succession, each finding its proper place.
Within the second tier of gates and corridors, two nāga kings, brothers, are placed: Nanda in the south and Upananda in the north.

Their remaining adornments of various jewels are largely the same as those described in the chapter on the "Arrangement of the Secret Maṇḍala. The Ācārya says: "If one provides a profound and esoteric interpretation..."

The four sides, being square, upright, and perfectly equal, signify the meaning of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). The four gates are the four dhyānas and also the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*).

The main hall signifies the four divine abodes (*catvāri brahmavihārāḥ*). The curved corridors signify the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*). The four corners signify the four noble truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*).
The vajra-line is the *sūtra* (scripture), by which it holds together the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad bodhipakṣadharmāḥ*). Thus it is constructed.
This defines the dimensions of the Dharma-gates; thus, the measurements of the external gates—their lengths, heights, widths, and depths—are all exactly equal to those of the central womb.
This clarifies that every single Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata accords with the Dharma-realm, without the slightest increase or decrease.
Furthermore, it causes the Middle Way practiced therein to be perfectly aligned with the mind of the true reality (dharmatā) of the lotus pedestal.
Because the traces of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) extend far and become increasingly vast, it is said that the wise one gradually increases [the mandala] from the outer enclosure outward.
The verse says: "Briefly stated, samādhi is the mind dwelling single-pointedly upon its object. From this point downward, the maṇḍala is explained.

Regarding the factors of the middle *samādhi*: if one has not yet cultivated yoga, one may not act as an *ācārya*, for because of the deficiency in these factors, the ritual (*dharmakarma*) will not be accomplished.
In the Sūtra, first there is a brief explanation of the name and meaning of *samādhi*, followed by a profound and extensive exposition.
As for the brief explanation: it means that the mind is bound to a single object (*ālambana*) without wandering; this is the meaning of "equipoise" (*samāhita*).
The verse states: "Briefly explained, samādhi is the one-pointed mind abiding upon its object. Now, regarding yoga with signs (*sanimitta-yoga*), there are three types:
superior, intermediate, and inferior. The superior refers to contemplating the bodies of all Tathāgatas, such as Vairocana;
the intermediate refers to contemplating the bodies of all Bodhisattvas, such as Mañjuśrī; and the inferior refers to contemplating those who correspond to various categories, such as Indra.

Each and every body, appearing with the colors, forms, postures, secret insignia, mudrās, or syllables as shown in the maṇḍala, dwells with single-minded focus upon its object without further distraction;
this is precisely the samādhi-gate of that honored one. To state the essential point:
just as in the oceanic assembly of the maṇḍala, each and every spiritual friend, numbering as many as the atoms within a buddha-field, is but a single [manifestation].

Entering the samādhi-gate of the Dharma-realm: if one contemplates this entire assembly of the universal gate as being single-mindedly abiding in its object without distraction, this is the samādhi-gate of the Universal Eye, also called the samādhi-gate of the Universal Gate World.
As for "one gate and all gates," it may refer either solely to entering the samādhi-gate of the division of the Truly All-Knowing One, or solely to...
One enters the samādhi-gate of the Lotus Family, or perhaps only the samādhi-gate of the Vajra Family, or takes the universal assembly of Mañjuśrī’s retinue as a single samādhi-gate;

it is the same for the other three Bodhisattvas, as these vary according to the different capacities of practitioners' minds. When the practitioner cultivates yoga, whether visualizing the deity or...
When contemplating secret mudrās or mantras, if various visionary experiences manifest that do not accord with the original visualization, these are all instances of erroneous contemplation.
For example, within meditative concentration, one might see the sun, moon, and various stars with brilliant and magnificent radiance;
or see great lotus kings filling the entirety of space; or see jewel trees and pavilions of extraordinary splendor.
The visions may be as magnificent as celestial palaces or various pure lands; or they may suddenly vanish, such that the marks of body and mind no longer appear.
One may see immeasurable assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, hear various extraordinary sounds, or see precipitous cliffs and sheer abysses extending down to the Avīci Hell.
Because these do not accord with one's original object of focus, none of them should be grasped; rather, one should simply remain as usual and unified.

Although mental attention may correspond with the object of concentration, one must deeply cultivate the observation of the ten phrases of dependent origination and should not become attached to their flavor.

If one perceives a different object as extraordinary and grasps at it with attachment, this is called the "concentration of self-conceit" (*māna*) and also the "concentration of stingy attachment" (*mātsarya*).
However, when in accord with right contemplation, one naturally perceives *koṭi*s [of phenomena].
Regarding "Buddha-fields" herein, "Buddha" refers to the hundreds of thousands of assemblies, and "fields" refers to pure abodes.
When one is thus in accord with reality, one immediately knows that the various phenomena and characteristics from the past onward do not arise without causes and conditions;

rather, through such and such causes and conditions, there exist such and such phenomena and characteristics. This is realized without depending on another for awakening, and is free from all obstructions. Furthermore...

Next, regarding the profound and secret explanation: it means that within the true mark of the body of each and every dharma-gate of the spiritual benefactors (*kalyāṇamitra*), one dwells in the object of focus without giving rise to deluded thoughts or conceptual proliferation; this is the meaning of *samādhi*. It is like entering the gate of the letter *A*, wherein in a single thought-moment one enters the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
this is the Samādhi of Vairocana. To remain with a single mind undisturbed within the seal of the Lotus of the Dharma is *vipaśyanā* (insight).
The sovereign samādhi consists of remaining single-mindedly without distraction within the seal of adamantine wisdom; O Lord of Mysteries, this is the samādhi [of the Tathāgatas].
Furthermore, from Brahmā and Śakra down to all the various honored ones, each attains sovereignty within a single gateway of the dharma-realm.

If one remains focused on a single object without distraction within that body of liberation, it is called the samādhi of the pure divine eye. If one [remains so] within the ocean-like cloud-mass of the treasury of great compassion...
"One-mindedness without distraction" is named the Samādhi of the Universal Eye and is also named the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Form Body.
Even if the Tathāgata were to expound its extensive meaning for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, it would still not be exhausted.

Now, wishing to encompass it within two verses so that it may be thoroughly understood without remainder, it is said: "The extensive meaning is further extraordinary, and the great assembly of sentient beings..."

Listen attentively! Within this, there are further two parts: first, the elucidation of the Tathāgata’s seal of samādhi; second, the elucidation of the seals of differentiation within the path of samādhi.
The verse says: "When the Buddha speaks of all things as empty, this is precisely the entry into the gateway of the letter A, up to the point where not even the slightest dharma exists."

That which can be attained likewise lacks any fixed characteristic that could be named "abiding in samādhi. This single-mindedness within the dharma-realm is called the samādhi of perfect enlightenment.
Why is this so? If, outside of this nature of mind, there were a realm to be taken as an object, it would not be a permanently abiding realm;
since the realm is transmuted by the four marks [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing], the mind that dwells upon and takes that as its object would likewise be subject to change.

Furthermore, how can that which flows according to objects be called "concentration" (*samādhi*)? Therefore, the Perfectly Awakened One’s *samādhi* awakens to the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn;
they are merely the mind’s self-realization, and the mind itself knows the mind.

Since time immemorial, this mind has always been like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), without change or alteration. Because the mind thus abides by itself within such conditions, it receives this name.
This is for the sake of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is precisely the inexhaustible treasury of adornments manifested by the Honored One Vairocana;
nor is it separate from such a Honored One. For those who perceive otherwise, all are termed "erroneous views. Therefore, next, the words of the *Mudrā of Certainty* are spoken:
"Samādhi is the realization of the mind itself; it is not obtained through external conditions. According to the Sanskrit original, to speak of its essential nature:
The statement that "there is nothing else from which one can obtain this intended terminology" means that it cannot be obtained from any other source. Next, it says:
"Such a realm as this is the samādhi of all Tathāgatas. As clarified in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
this Buddha-nature is precisely what is called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and is also named the Vajra-samādhi.
It is also called Prajñāpāramitā; the Way of all Buddhas is the same, and there is no other path.

If a practitioner, at the very moment they first resolve their mind [for enlightenment], can thus correctly contemplate the nature of the mind, they are immediately said to have entered the Tathāgata-samādhi.
Why then trouble oneself with gradually transcending the four stages before reaching the ultimate? Furthermore, if a practitioner of Yoga receives the majestic power of the Buddhas...

By virtue of divine empowerment, one comes to clearly perceive within samādhi the three types of secret mudrās of immeasurable holy masters, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, without any confusion among them;
or again, with a single undistracted mind, they transform into one's own body.
Although this is marvelous and inconceivable, because it still involves signs and conditions, it is called "worldly" (laukika).

When this samādhi manifests before one who is thus immersed, the practitioner contemplates the ten phrases of dependent origination, purifying all conceptual proliferation and becoming in accord with emptiness and stillness.

They then realize that this oceanic assembly of the maṇḍala arises entirely from manifold conditions—like reflections in a mirror, the moon in water, or a city of gandharvas—and is utterly devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics. This is called...
Even supramundane samādhi is still not called "Great Emptiness" because the sickness of emptiness has not yet been emptied;
however, when one sits at the site of enlightenment and personally realizes the nature of the mind, one knows that such realms of empowerment are all the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the mind.
At that time, the mind does not dwell in signs nor does it rely on emptiness, yet it clearly perceives both emptiness and non-emptiness.
Because it is ultimately signless yet possesses all signs, it is called the Samādhi of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā-samādhi*).
One who dwells in this samādhi dwells in the unimpeded wisdom of a Buddha; the Buddha has said that such a person’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is ultimately perfected.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "It is therefore called the perfection of Great Emptiness and *sarvajña*."

The beginning of the second fascicle of the Sūtra states: "At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana, together with all the Buddhas, assembled and each proclaimed the path of samādhi for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
The Tathāgata has already expounded the seal of the ultimate threefold emptiness (trīṇi-śūnyatā) samādhi, so that those who advance through the universal gate may do so without hindrance."

Therefore, it is further taught that within the path of samādhi, the various forms displayed in the threefold maṇḍala of the *viśeṣa-mudrā* are all the single body of the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata; for this reason, they are all named "Buddha.
Each of these Buddhas, within their own respective Dharma-gates currently in circulation, personally expounds that path of samādhi, whether manifesting as a celestial being of the present age...
If he manifests in the body of a celestial being, he teaches the path of the samādhi of those devas;
if he manifests in the body of a śrāvaka, he teaches the path of the śrāvaka’s samādhi; if he manifests in the body of a pratyekabuddha, he teaches the path of the pratyekabuddha’s samādhi;
if he manifests in the body of a bodhisattva, he teaches the path of the bodhisattva’s samādhi; and if he manifests in the body of a Vajradhara, he teaches the [Vajra]...
Regarding the path of the adamantine samādhi, one should know that the verses herein cannot be fully recorded in the volumes of scriptures compiled by worldly beings;

rather, when practitioners enter deeply into the realm of yoga, they will hear them with perfect clarity, no different from when they are being correctly expounded. For this reason, it is called the "Day of the Buddha’s Empowerment."
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "At that time, the Buddha entered the Samādhi of the Swift Power of the Single Essence of All Tathāgatas.
This means that upon entering this samādhi, one realizes and knows that all Tathāgatas are of one and the same essence, which is the wisdom-body of the single Dharma-realm. In this [state],...
Within mindfulness, they are able to sequentially observe the gateways of samādhi as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable oceans of worlds;
they know that such-and-such numbers of sentient beings should enter the Path through this or that gateway of samādhi,
and they know which virtuous friends have already created various causes and conditions for certain beings, while for others they have not yet done so.

Sentient beings act as the causal conditions for the seed; some sentient beings enter such a Dharma-gate that they may transcend and attain Buddhahood, while those who enter other Dharma-gates remain delayed for a long time and do not attain Buddhahood.
Such various differences in root-natures and the corresponding expedient means of progress are likewise diverse, even unto the successive cultivation within these playful manifestations.
By practicing the entry and exit that transcends the world, one attains the ability to accomplish the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings through each and every gateway;

therefore, it is called the Samādhi of the Single Essence and Swift Power. At that time, the World-Honored One, having observed everywhere and fully understood that the various paths of samādhi all converge into a single essence and are entirely the Buddha Vehicle, further spoke to Vajrapāṇi regarding everything.
Within the path of samādhi, the seal of attaining bodhi is established. The first two verses clarify the external traces of becoming a Buddha:
"When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, by the power of this single essence and its swift momentum, I subdued the hosts of Māra’s celestial armies.
Yet within this, there remains an even more difficult place to subdue, namely the māras of the afflictions (*kleśa*), which possess neither form nor location.
Furthermore, there are no footprints left, making them difficult to perceive; since they are all utterly extinguished within a single thought-moment, it is said that he has "subdued the four māras.
Regarding the phrase "with the voice of great diligence and valor," it means that the Buddha addressed Māra Pāpīyas with truthful words, saying:
"Throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, for the sake of taming sentient beings, I have sacrificed my body and life; this cannot [be undone]."
"The number [of those to be saved] has now been fully accomplished, for there are beings with the capacity to enter the Path.
Therefore, I shall realize Bodhi and open the pure eye for those sentient beings; how could your power possibly obstruct this?

As soon as these words were spoken, the fear of all sentient beings was entirely removed, and the celestial Māras, overcome with confusion, fell to the ground and immediately retreated and dispersed."

If there are sentient beings who receive and uphold this triangular seal, it can even eliminate the immeasurable terrors within the Avīci Hell, let alone the fears of devas, māras, ghosts, and spirits;
therefore, it is said that with the voice of Great Diligence and Valor, it removes the fears of sentient beings.
At that time, the earth deities rejoiced and proclaimed it from one to another, until the sound reached the Pure Abodes.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King and the other beings of the eight classes of spirits perceived only these external traces of the subduing of Māra;
therefore, they gave rise to a reputation and titled him "The Great Hero of Diligent Effort. However, the actual place where I attained Buddhahood is beyond their power to measure.
Thus, there follow two verses clarifying the true meaning of Bodhi: "I have awakened to the original..."
"Non-arising" means realizing that one's own mind is fundamentally unarisen from the very beginning;
this is itself buddhahood, yet in reality there is neither realization nor attainment. All sentient beings do not understand this mark of eternal quiescence;

through recollection, conceptualization, and deluded thoughts, they undergo the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence and cannot escape on their own. Even though they have now heard the True Dharma...
If one seeks and calculates within the various conditioned phenomena, hoping to attain Buddhahood, what principle of attainment could there possibly be?
That which transcends the path of language—from this point downward—is entirely an exegesis of the gateway of the letter *A*.
Awakening to original non-arising is itself Buddhahood; it is the Dharma realized by the Buddha himself, not something accessible to thought, deliberation, or discrimination.
The capacity to reach [this state] cannot be transmitted to others; the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) refers to that place where all speech comes to an end and no longer functions.
That which is called "liberation from all faults" means that all conceptual constructions and discriminations are termed "faults.

These are the various frivolous proliferations (*prapañca*), such as arising and ceasing, permanence and annihilation, coming and going, identity and difference, and so forth, which arise because one does not know the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
All of these can be shattered and overturned; yet, if one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally without the limit of arising, then one attains liberation from all such faults.
Therefore, the vajra-body is far removed from the hundred negations. As for being far removed from causes and conditions:
if the essence of the dharma-realm possessed the characteristics of arising and ceasing, then causes and conditions could be proclaimed.
It is taught that all phenomena now arise from conditions and thus lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If they lack intrinsic nature, they are fundamentally unarisen;
when causes and conditions assemble, there is nothing that arises, and when causes and conditions disperse, there is no exhaustion.
Therefore, like the pure void, they are eternally immutable. A Great Sūtra also says: "Only the Tathāgata is free from all causes."
Furthermore, one who knows that emptiness and so forth are equal to space understands that they are fundamentally unarisen; this is the meaning of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

Because their intrinsic nature is pure, boundless, and non-discriminative, they are identical to the great void. Therefore, the emptiness of the inconceivable is illustrated by means of the emptiness of the world, which is easily understood.
As for the arising of the wisdom of the true mark (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa-jñāna*), the true mark of the mind is precisely Vairocana.

When Vairocana, who pervades all places, sits at the site of enlightenment and understands according to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), all various modes of unreal seeing are extinguished without remainder. Therefore, the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) is equal to space.
