That which has already departed from all darkness—namely, the failure to know the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are—is ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, awakening is fundamentally... [not ignorance].

At the very moment of arising, there is the manifestation of light pervading the entire dharma-realm; through all modes of cognition, one contemplates all phenomena such that nothing is unseen, unheard, untouched, or unknown.

That which is "supremely real and stainless" refers to this most ultimate reality beyond which nothing higher exists, called the "ultimate limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*), namely the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*), because it is free from all darkness—the very knowledge and vision of the Buddha.
The statement that "there is no further defilement" means that all things are transformed into the sense of being fundamentally unborn (*anutpāda*). Next, there are two lines which conclude:

"The various realms of existence are merely conceptual names; the marks of the Buddha are likewise so. This means that the sentient beings of the six destinies and Vairocana are fundamentally non-dual in essence;
it is only according to the various deluded thoughts of sentient beings that various names are established. The Buddha is also like this.
All those in the world merely see the traces of my skillful means in subduing Māra, attaining the Way, and delivering sentient beings;
they speak of them according to their own mental dispositions, calling me either "the Great Śramaṇa" or "the Great Vīryavanta," and so forth.
Even as described in the *Avataṃsaka*, there are infinite different names throughout all worlds, yet these do not correspond to the reality of the Dharma realized within myself.
That which is spoken can be expressed; the following verse further explains and clarifies how the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) serves as the basis for the arising of the teaching.
Thus it says: "This first ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), by the power of its empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), speaks through words and letters in order to deliver all worlds.
This means that when viewed with the Buddha-eye, these various names and expressions likewise do not transcend the ultimate.
Although the *bhūtakoṭi* is such, the causes and conditions for sentient beings to enter the Path are diverse and not uniform.

If there are those who should be delivered through written characters and spoken language, the Tathāgata, without moving from the *bhūtakoṭi*, empowers various sounds and syllables through his sovereign spiritual power (*vibhutva-ṛddhi*) and proclaims them.
If sentient beings practice in accordance with the Dharma, they will attain correspondence with the three mysteries (*triguhyasamaya*).
At that time, one knows that the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is not different from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As the Sūtra says: "Then the Virtuous One, the Vajradhara, having attained what was unprecedented, with eyes wide open, prostrated to the All-Knowing One and spoke these verses.
Here, "Virtuous One" means being fully endowed with the secret adornments of all Tathāgatas.
His virtue is like a lotus flower that, when fully grown and matured, naturally blossoms upon being struck by the light of the sun—beautiful, majestic, and lovely.
Vajradhara is likewise: when the eye of his mind-lotus encounters the radiance of the Bodhicitta-seal, it opens wide and bright;
all myriad virtues are complete, flourishing within and manifesting outwardly in his countenance, which possesses the blossoming eyes of a blue lotus.
Regarding these characteristics, he spoke in verse to comprehend the preceding intent. The initial statement, "The Buddhas are most rare;
their skillful wisdom is inconceivable," when fully preserved in the Sanskrit original, should read: "The rare wisdom of all Buddhas and their inconceivable wisdom of skillful means.
This refers to comprehending the realization of the non-arising of the fundamental [nature] within the preceding verse; "skillful means" refers to comprehending the preceding verse.
Next, regarding the empowerment of the center (*madhya-adhiṣṭhāna-śakti*): "Wisdom" refers to the lotus pedestal of the mind; "expedient means" refers to the unfolding of its petals and filaments.
Because these two types of endowments are inconceivable, they are called "marvelous. Next, it says:

"The Dharma that transcends all conceptual proliferation is the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*). This is a broad praise of the inconceivable wisdom, which he then fully expounds for the sake of the world.

The multitude’s rare aspirations are a vast praise of inconceivable skillful means. If a dharma is obtained by relying on a teacher and arises from various causes and conditions, it is born of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and possesses the characteristics of arising and ceasing; it is not the true nature (*dharmatā*).

The Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is such that if it were a spontaneous wisdom, it could not be reached through cultivation and study, nor could it be transmitted to others, just like the celestial nectar tasted within oneself.
The flavor of dew, even if explained through various skillful means to one who has never tasted it, can ultimately not be understood;

yet, by the Buddha’s power of great skillful means, he employs the signless Dharma-body to manifest as various names and signs through empowerment, enabling all sentient beings to realize the dharma that is neither cause nor effect by means of the dharma of cause and effect. Therefore, both the provisional and the ultimate wisdoms are beyond conceptualization.
Next, it says: "The characteristics of mantras are thus always based upon the two truths.
This concludes the section on the inconceivable twofold wisdom and explains the intent behind the provisional establishment of the two truths mentioned in the preceding text.

Because one knows that names and characteristics are identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one is able to empower names and characteristics by means of the limit of reality; because one knows that what is shallow and superficial is itself the profound secret.
Therefore, one is able to take what is profound and secret as being shallow and concise, according to the benefits realized by sentient beings; all such meanings are real and not false.
If one can understand this conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one will naturally penetrate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus it is said:

"The Buddhas always rely upon the two truths when teaching the Dharma. Next, there is a verse which clearly explains that by understanding the seal of the Buddha's Bodhi, one obtains immeasurable merit.
Because it is an accumulation, it is said: "If there are sentient beings who know this Dharma teaching, those of the world should make offerings to them, just as they revere a *caitya*.
A *caitya* is that upon which the bodily relics depend; therefore, all gods and worldly people who seek blessings and protection make offerings to it.
If a practitioner believes and accepts this meaning, that is the relic of the *dharmakāya*."
It is the basis capable of receiving all worldly offerings and veneration.
Furthermore, the *brahma-svara-caitya* and *citta* (mind) are identical in essence; the secret meaning herein is that the mind is the *caitya*.
As in the third maṇḍala, taking one’s own mind as the foundation, one gradually increases [the layers] until the color of *nirvāṇa* occupies the central womb.

For this reason, this caitya is exceedingly high. Furthermore, from the central womb, it increases in stages through the eight petals, reaching even to the third level, the Universal Gate Body (*samantamukhakāya*), which pervades everywhere without exception; therefore, this caitya is extremely vast.
The lotus pedestal is the *dharmadhātu*, which is to say, the *dharma-kāya* relic. If sentient beings understand this, it is the seal of the Bodhicitta of the mind.
Because he is identical to Vairocana, it is said that the world should make offerings to him, just as one honors a *caitya*.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, after Vajradhara had spoken this verse, he gazed intently at Vairocana without blinking for even a moment and remained silent.
At that time, having heard the Seal of the Ultimate Samādhi (*atyanta-samādhi-mudrā*), Vajradhara desired to inquire about that samādhi.
Regarding the seals of differentiation within the Path: had he voiced these words to the Buddha, it might have deviated from the ultimate principle;
therefore, he remained silent, contemplating the Buddha with single-minded focus—this itself constitutes a profoundly deep inquiry.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi’s silence signifies the Tathāgata’s illumination of sentient capacities, as is traditionally taught in the constant instructions: "The Buddha, during the day..."
Observing transformable sentient beings during the three periods of the night to deliver them—this is merely spoken according to the mental capacity of the śrāvakas.
If one observes with the Buddha-eye, then one sees; if one does not observe, then there is nothing seen.
When observing, wisdom arises; when not observing, wisdom does not arise. Thus, the realms of arising and ceasing, or light and darkness, cannot be attained.
It is named "Great Wisdom of Equality" because the Tathāgata’s signless and non-conceptual wisdom is, by the very nature of reality, unimpeded and constantly illuminates the dharma-realm;
its engagement with faculties and conditions is like the tide of the great ocean, never overstepping its limit.
Therefore, Vajrapāṇi, as soon as there was a receptive capacity for transmission, the Tathāgata immediately expounded it, answering without waiting for a question. Furthermore...

Next, Vajrapāṇi realized that the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is none other than the sphere of activity of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and that their final state is not different;

therefore, he remained silent and spoke no word. The Tathāgata, however, realized that the ultimate truth is none other than the conventional truth, and that their final state is not different from the sphere of activity [of the former];
therefore, he explained it in detail through extensive analysis in order to enable sentient beings to attain thorough penetration.
Because the two truths are mutually illuminating through their characteristics, they ultimately converge in a single consistency. As in the Tathāgata’s response, there are briefly four statements;

the first states: "Furthermore, Secret Lord, a Bodhisattva in his last birth who dwells in the samādhi-path of the Buddha-ground is free from fabrication, yet he knows the characteristics of the world and dwells firmly upon the ground of karma."
As for the "Buddha-ground" (*buddhabhūmi*), because it is the stage of the supreme empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), it is explained first.

As clarified in other sūtras, this refers to a Bodhisattva bound by one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*); from this point, they will ascend to the Tuṣita heaven and subsequently succeed to the position of a Buddha, which is why they are called "one who is to fill the place [of Buddhahood] after one birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
Now, according to the primary intent of this sūtra, the term "one birth" (*ekajāti*) means "born from one."
When one first attains the pure bodhicitta, immeasurable and boundless gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī arise from the ground of single reality;
it should be known that they likewise increase sequentially within each successive ground.
This continues until the tenth ground is fulfilled, yet before reaching the eleventh ground, at which time [the qualities] are fully developed from the realm of single reality.

Having brought forth all adornments, with only one stage—that of the Tathāgata—remaining before they attain realized wisdom, there is yet one further turning of the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) through which they are born and succeed to the Buddha’s place;
therefore, they are called "those who will be born into Buddhahood in one more life" (*ekajātipratibaddha*). This is the ultimate generation of the bodhicitta;
because it is the most firm and powerful among all paths of samādhi, and because one enters the path of the Buddhas through such diligence, it is said that they "dwell" [in this state].

The path of the Buddha-ground is the samādhi that is free from all conditioned activities. "Activity" refers to the cultivation of the deeds of the stages, up to the adornment of the Buddha-fields and the maturing of sentient beings;
because these involve the conceptualizing mind of wisdom, they still possess the characteristics of the mundane world.
Now, this Bodhisattva correctly practices the Great Emptiness Samādhi, remaining far removed from the subtle conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of phenomena produced through conditions.

It is said that "detachment from activity" means knowing the characteristics of the world as they truly are—that is, knowing that the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the world is ultimately no different from the limit of *nirvāṇa*.
While remaining unmoved from the limit of reality, one is able to fully perceive the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) that give rise to the world.
Therefore, dwelling within this path of samādhi, one advances moment by moment toward the stage of a Tathāgata, abiding in the stage of karma. This is expressed in pure Brahma-sounds.
Regarding this, it should be said that "creating the ground" (*bhūmi*) means practicing the Tathāgata’s vajra-activities and attaining skillfulness in the *ratnāvalī* (jewel-garland).
It is also called "entering the gate of the profound mystery" (*chongxuan men*), which is training in the Buddha’s majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).

To "firmly abide in the Buddha-ground" means to remain steadfast and immovable within the stage of the Tathāgata; this is termed "abiding. Its meaning differs from the previous instance of the word "abiding," just as a person suffering from thirst seeks [water].
Having already spent a long time [in practice], one suddenly beholds the gate to the Cool Lake (śītalahrada) without any further obstacles;
by advancing with single-minded focus and no longer following divergent conditions, this is called the Samādhi of the Stage of the Successor (kṣāntipratilabdha).

Having reached the Cool Lake, all aspirations for further attainment cease, as this is the stage of Buddhahood itself. Although it shares the same name as the Great Emptiness Samādhi (mahāśūnyatā-samādhi), there is a distinction in its meaning.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "O Lord of Mysteries, the Bodhisattva of the Eighth Stage who possesses mastery, through the path of samādhi, does not perceive any phenomena as having birth;
he knows all things to be like illusions. For this reason, the world calls him 'Avalokiteśvara' (The One Who Observes with Sovereignty)," as has been explained above.
If one were to explain the ten stages of the path in their sequential progression, one should speak of the Buddha-stage;
if one were to descend gradually, one should speak of the ninth stage. Why, then, is the eighth stage mentioned?
It is because when all Bodhisattvas first transcend the seventh stage, they see no Buddhas above to be sought and no sentient beings below to be saved; this is called abiding in Great Nirvana.

When one rests from the myriad practices, at that time the Buddhas of the ten directions use this path of samādhi to inspire their minds, enabling them to cross over the difficult terrain of the bodhicitta.

For this reason, it is explained separately; because from this point onward one enters the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*) where there are no further distinct hardships, it is not necessary to explain a separate seal of practice.
From the initial generation of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*) onwards, one has deeply contemplated the ten...

When entering this stage through the phrase of dependent origination, one attains the further shore of the emptiness of nature; thus it is said that one does not grasp at any phenomena and remains detached from birth.

Furthermore, by means of skillful expedients, within the immovability of suchness, one gives rise to the infinite great utility of the ten modes of dependent origination, and through the illusion-like samādhi, one reaches all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions to draw near to the various [Buddhas].
The Good Spiritual Friend universally studies the infinite gateways for delivering sentient beings;
according to whatever form, category, speech, or sound by which a being may be delivered, he immediately manifests them all and preaches the Dharma.
Therefore, because those in the world witness such deeds, he is titled Avalokiteśvara—this is another name for his initial entry into the Lotus Samādhi.
Furthermore, in this context, "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*)—according to the correct Sanskrit translation—is the meaning of "prosperity.
Just as a person who has attained a position of great power and possesses abundant wealth naturally accomplishes whatever they desire according to their will, so too it is with this Bodhisattva.
Even if all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions were to seek various mundane and supramundane requisites, according to their respective dispositions and desires...

Although various different things can be bestowed simultaneously through the Illusion-like Samādhi so that each may fulfill their respective wishes, it is still not yet able to sever the traces of the arising of activity, such that all that is performed becomes like a vajra;
therefore, they are divided into two seals. Furthermore, herein one should explain the path of the samādhi of the first Dharma-illumination gate within the superior grade.

Since this has already been explained, it is not stated again. Furthermore, as previously mentioned, the descriptions of those in their "last birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*) and the samādhis of the eighth stage are merely spoken of in this way according to the dharma-gates of the path of formal teaching.

However, for those of the Secret Vehicle who are able to penetrate the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), they possess the practice of the Great Emptiness Samādhi from the very moment they first resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*).
If one is ignorant and thinks it is not so, then within a single lifetime one will be unable to suddenly fulfill all the stages (*bhūmi*).
As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, O Guhyapati, when the Śrāvakas dwell on the stage of having conditions, they eliminate the arising and ceasing of consciousness;
through the wisdom of ultimate observation, they attain non-conforming practice. For this reason, it is called the path of Śrāvaka samādhi. Thus it is said.

In the Abhidharma, it is explained that the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight recollections (*aṣṭasmṛti*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the three samādhis, etc., are all termed "dwelling on the ground of objects.

By relying on these samādhis as skillful means, one’s mind becomes tranquil and still, enabling correct observation and the realization that all mundane and supramundane phenomena possess causes and conditions. Regarding the mundane: [text continues]
Taking accumulation as the cause and suffering as the result is the supramundane; taking the path as the cause and cessation as the result is likewise supramundane.
As extensively clarified in the Āgamas and stated in summary in the Vinaya: "All phenomena arise from conditions; the Tathāgata teaches their cause.
When those phenomena and their causal conditions are extinguished, this is what the Great Śramaṇa proclaims. This is because one knows that [phenomena] arise from causes and conditions.

Because [ignorance] ceases, existence ceases; by abandoning the views of existence and non-existence and distancing oneself from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, one attains the knowledge of the true reality (*tattva-jñāna*).
It is called "the wisdom of ultimate observation" because it observes to the utmost. Because it is neither inverted nor erroneous, it is termed "truth" (*satya*).
From ignorance through old age and death, because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises, and so on until the limitlessness of saṃsāra.

If one turns in accordance with this ignorance, it is called "conformity. Once the Four Noble Truths have been seen, one turns away from the flow of birth and death and proceeds along the Noble Path until one can personally declare:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.
This is called "non-conformity. Such various forms of non-conforming conduct are [the result].
Because one must take samādhi as the cause, it is said that one attains the cause for practice that is not in accordance with [ordinary] śrāvaka samādhi.
Although various schools offer diverse and differing explanations, anyone who possesses such a Dharma-seal is termed one of right practice;
if one lacks such a seal, they are termed one of wrong practice.
The Sūtra says: "O Lord of Mysteries, the Pratyekabuddha contemplates cause and effect and abides in the teaching that is beyond verbal expression;

he does not turn back from that which is beyond verbal expression, and regarding all phenomena, he realizes the ultimate cessation of linguistic expression—this is called the path of the Pratyekabuddha-samādhi.

As for "cause and effect," this refers to the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). Just as the Śrāvaka uses the wisdom of ultimate observation to understand that there are only the aggregates (*skandha*), [the Pratyekabuddha likewise contemplates the causal chain].
Because they possess a mind of intense revulsion and dread toward the self, they swiftly sever the afflictions and personally realize *nirvāṇa*.
However, they are unable to analytically investigate the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the twelve links of dependent origination.

Because the wisdom of the *pratyekabuddha* is profound and sharp, they are able to deeply observe it through both general and specific characteristics, seeing that all phenomena of accumulation (*saṃudaya-dharma*) are phenomena of cessation (*nirodha-dharma*). This is what distinguishes them from the *śrāvakas*.
The Āgamas state that the dharma-position (*dharmatā*) of the twelve links of dependent origination remains eternally constant whether a Buddha appears or not.
Nāgārjuna also says that this "dharma-position" is another name for *tathatā* (suchness).

Because this is the most difficult point in all the world to understand, it was for this reason that the World-Honored One did not wish to preach the Dharma immediately upon attaining enlightenment; such was his intention regarding the stage of the Pratyekabuddha.

Because one enters ever more deeply, it is said that one "dwells in the teaching of wordless dharma. That "words do not turn" means that when dwelling in this ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there are no sounds or syllables;

thus, they cannot be turned to be transmitted to others. The World-Honored One, having attained unimpeded knowledge and vision and possessing mastery over all dharmas, is able to provide names and designations within the teaching of wordless dharma to cause sentient beings to enter it.
The wisdom of the Pratyekabuddhas is obstructed; therefore, they are unable to expound it.

Furthermore, because the Pratyekabuddhas contemplate all phenomena of origination as being identical in nature to nirvāṇa, and because within the various conditioned realms the winds of conceptual proliferation have subsided such that they no longer know what to say, they are said to have realized the ultimate samādhi of the cessation of language and to have cultivated yoga.
That which accords with this is called the Samādhi of the Pratyekabuddha. These two kinds of samādhi are both difficult points regarding the bodhicitta;

however, they are merely one type of mental characteristic within the path being practiced, and it does not mean that the inconceivable nature of the bodhicitta can possess such fixed characteristics of the three vehicles. Therefore, the practitioner [should] by means of this Dharma-seal...
If one recognizes [the seal] through knowledge, one shall pass straight through without obstruction; if one does not skillfully recognize it, one will be hindered and obstructed.
The Sūtra says: "Lord of Mysteries, the causes and effects of the world, as well as karma—whether arising or ceasing—are bound to another master.
That which gives birth to the samādhi of emptiness is called the worldly path of samādhi. This means that all worldly samādhis, in brief, [are so designated].
When discourse reaches its ultimate point, it all results in the destruction of cause and effect, as well as the functional activity involved in producing an effect from a cause.
These three matters—whether arising or ceasing—are all dependent upon another; that "other" is the *ātman* (the self).

This is because if a practitioner does not understand the meaning of correct causal conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) yet practices and realizes the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), [they will inevitably fall into error].

When one becomes attached to one's own mind as an internal self, seeing that the myriad phenomena of the world exist because of the mind, one then claims they are produced by a divine self (*puruṣa*).
If one does not rely on an internal self, one must necessarily rely on an external self, such as Īśvara or Brahmā.
If one seeks deeply into the ultimate subtleties within this, one naturally discards causes, karma, and conditions, asserting that only the nature of the self alone exists.
To maintain [the mind] until not even a single dharma enters the heart and one realizes the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) is the ultimate principle for the world;
therefore, though one may exhaust the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*), one falls back into the three miserable paths (*tri-durgati*).

Even if, within meditative concentration, one gives rise to various kinds of worldly superior wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), possesses the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhijñā*), and investigates their essential tenets, they ultimately all return to this very state. For this reason, it is called "this single seal."
This universally encompasses all worldly paths of samādhi; when a practitioner enters this mind, they should realize it for themselves.
In the sutras, the Buddha spoke a summary verse concerning these five types of paths of samādhi, which are broadly divided into two categories:
those of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas—these four are called supramundane samādhis—whereas those of the various devas and others [are mundane].
The teachings on the methods of mantra recitation belong to both mundane samādhi and supramundane samādhi; because both possess actual benefit, it is said that they "subdue and destroy all faults.
Mundane samādhi possesses only provisional benefit, which is why it is said, "for the sake of benefiting sentient beings," as explained in other sūtras:
those who seek the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) should develop deep faith in the mundane teachings.

Those who feel weary of cyclic existence and seek the Mahāyāna, yet harbor deep fear toward the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle—all such cases are explained through these skillful means for those who have not yet realized the secret treasury.
According to the fundamental tenet of this sutra, all five kinds of samādhi are gateways that reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the mind;
thus, when a practitioner first dwells in yoga with signs (*sanimitta-yoga*), they are still at the mundane level.
Samādhi that merely understands within this [state] that there are only the aggregates (skandha) and no self is the samādhi of the śrāvaka;
if one contemplates all aggregates as being without intrinsic nature and without arising by means of the ten phrases of dependent origination, this is the samādhi of the bodhisattva.

The rest is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Abiding in the Mind" (*Zhu xinpǐn*). It differs from other teachings because the principle of the nature of mind has not been clarified therein; thus, the five vehicles are distinct.

Their interpretations do not harmonize. If one were to provide yet another profound and esoteric explanation—claiming that within the threefold maṇḍala, the samādhis of the five positions are all the secret empowerment of Vairocana, such that those who correspond with them can all attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime—then what distinction could there be between "profound" and "shallow"?
The explanation given in the present verse is based on their own [perspectives].
This refers merely to the Dharma teachings that have been transmitted.
As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, the World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, saying: 'Lord of Secrets, you should listen attentively.
These characteristics of mantras are the mantra-constituents within the requisites for the maṇḍala. This is the great [section].
The classification of mantras is briefly of five kinds: those spoken by the Tathāgata; those spoken by Bodhisattvas or Vajradharas;
those spoken by the followers of the Two Vehicles; those spoken by the various devas; and those spoken by the earth-dwelling devas, such as nāgas, birds, and asuras.

Furthermore, the first three types are collectively termed "mantras of the noble ones" (ārya-mantra); the fourth is termed "mantras of the assembly of devas"; and the fifth is termed "earth-dwelling [mantras]."
These mantras may also be collectively termed "mantras of all deities.

Just as the mantras of the Noble Ones are said to consist of the letter *A* or the letter *Ra*, and so forth, those of the worldly devas, down to the earth-dwelling spirits and ghosts, are likewise spoken in such a manner.
What difference is there between their characteristics? The Ācārya replied: "If they are spoken by Buddhas or Bodhisattvas, then within a single [syllable]..."
Within a single syllable, immeasurable meanings are contained; for now, I shall explain them briefly. The syllable *A* inherently possesses three meanings:
the meaning of non-arising, the meaning of emptiness, and the meaning of existence. According to the Sanskrit original, the syllable *A* possesses the sound of the primordial beginning.

If there is a primordial beginning, it is a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions, and is therefore called "existence. Furthermore, *A* signifies the meaning of non-birth. If a phenomenon depends upon causes and conditions...

Since that which is established lacks an intrinsic nature of its own, it is empty; furthermore, that which is unarisen is the realm of the single reality (*eka-tattva-viṣaya*), and this realm of the single reality is precisely the Middle Way.
Thus, Nāgārjuna said: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are empty, they are provisional, and they are the middle.
Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that *sarvajña* (omniscience) has three types of names: first, "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*), which is shared with the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*).
The knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) is shared with bodhisattvas, whereas the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the unique quality of a Buddha.
Although these three knowledges are actually attained within a single moment of mind, they are designated as three types for the sake of easy understanding by means of differentiation;
this is precisely the meaning of the syllable *A*. Furthermore, the syllable *Ra* also has three meanings: first, the meaning of "dust" (*rajas*); second, the meaning of "entering."
Because it is the gateway of the letter A, it signifies the meaning of being free from dust (*araja*), and it also carries the meaning of *pāramitā* because it reaches the ultimate further shore.
It is thus the primordial non-arising; one should know that it likewise possesses the three points (*bindu*).
These three points encompass all phenomena, just as it is with the letters A, Ra, and so forth—the same applies to the meanings of all other letters. Furthermore, within all speech...
Those mantras containing the sound *a* are all subsumed under the gateway of the letter *a*; those containing the sound *ra* are all subsumed under the gateway of the letter *ra*.
The same applies to other letters. This interpretation is identical to that provided in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and other such texts;
therefore, it will not be explained in detail below. If a bodhisattva’s mantra contains the letter *a*, one should know that, in each case, it pertains to its own respective [object].
Within the gateway of penetrating the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), all meanings are fully present; it is not that all meanings are present within the universal gateway of the Dharma-realm.

If the mantras of the two vehicles contain the syllable *A*, one should know that this refers solely to the meaning of non-arising as explained through the wisdom of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*) and the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*. If the mantras spoken by Brahmā contain the syllable *A*, this refers to emergence.

The meaning of "detachment from the five desires" and "the non-arising of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*)" is that if the mantra of Śakra or the World-Protectors contains the syllable *A*, it signifies the non-arising of the ten unwholesome paths of action and calamities; the rest may be understood by analogy.
All that has been explained above is speech according to the intentions of others, clarifying only the shallow and abbreviated meaning. If one proceeds according to one's own intention...
The speech clarifies the profound and secret meaning such that entering through a single gate encompasses all gates of the Dharma-realm;
even all the worldly devas and others are none other than Vairocana—how could there be any distinction between shallow and deep?

If a practitioner can understand the meaning of differentiation within non-differentiation, and understand the meaning of non-differentiation within differentiation, it should be known that this person has attained universal penetration.
One who has realized the meaning of the two truths also understands the characteristics of mantras.
Furthermore, the sūtra itself explains the characteristics of mantras; the first verse states:
"The mantra of the Perfectly Enlightened One is established through the nature of names, just as Indra is [established] by his various functions. This clarifies the mantra of the Tathāgata.
This is the general characteristic. Now, for the time being, let us explain this based on the initial *samaya-mantra*.
It means that each individual syllable is a gateway for entering the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). For instance, regarding the words "A-sa-me": the syllable "A" is the gateway of non-arising;
"Sa" is the gateway of non-truth; and "Me" is the gateway of Great Emptiness. This is called "forming a single [unity] through these gateways of syllables."
"Ā" is named as "non-existence," and "ma" is named as "equality. If these are further combined, it is "non-equal.
To establish this means that by means of these various names, from beginning to end, they collectively form a single meaning.

As in the first phrase, which says "non-equal," the second phrase says "threefold equality," and the third phrase says "samaya"; when these are mutually established, it is "non-equal threefold equality."

Samaya. Furthermore, just as multiple names are combined to form a single phrase—such as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*) and so forth—and these multiple phrases are further integrated to form a single verse, whereby the meaning becomes complete; thus, statements such as "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, they are of the nature of arising and ceasing;
when arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityā utpādavyayadharmāṇaḥ / utpadya hi nirudhyante teṣāṃ vyupaśamaḥ sukham*) are all formed by means of mantras.

The establishment of these characteristics is followed by all others accordingly. For example, regarding those who follow the school of Indra: Indra is an alternative name for Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
Śakra himself composed a treatise on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*), and because he was able to encompass manifold meanings within a single word, he is cited here as proof.
If even worldly wisdom is like this, how much more so is the Tathāgata’s mastery over all phenomena? Such are the various meanings.
Regarding the accomplishment of benefit: it means that within each and every syllable of the Tathāgata’s mantra, there is the capacity to accomplish all aims and benefits;
likewise, within each and every name, there is the capacity to accomplish all aims and benefits;
and even within each and every established characteristic, there is the capacity to accomplish all aims and benefits. To illustrate this, we shall first cite the samaya-mantra.
Because the letter A signifies the meaning of primordial non-arising (*anutpāda*), it possesses the function of pacifying (*śāntika*);

because it is primordial non-arising, all merits are fully present without deficiency, thus it possesses the function of increasing (*paustika*); because it is primordial non-arising, immeasurable faults are extinguished without remainder, thus it possesses the function of subjugating (*vaśīkaraṇa*);
and since not a single phenomenon exists apart from this primordial non-arising, [it possesses the function of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*)].
There is the function of summoning; thus, within this primordial non-arising (*an-utpanna*), there is nothing that cannot be accomplished, and one is able to bring all matters to fulfillment.

Just as it is with the letter A, so it is with each and every other letter. Just as it is with each individual letter, so it is likewise with each individual name, phrase, and established characteristic. Therefore, one should know that this is contained within this very mantra.
Having fully explained all the functional applications, the general characteristics of mantras have now been concluded.
Next, in order to clarify the specific characteristics of mantras, it is said that there is a method for augmenting the phrases of the original name;

this refers to the correspondence with practice. That is to say, whenever one performs a ritual activity involving a mantra, one should contemplate the original name established within that mantra and its intended purpose.
One should distinguish their categories and differences, and employ them according to what is appropriate for their respective natures and characteristics.
If the names and meanings within a mantra do not correspond to its intended application, one should augment the phrasing in accordance with the ritual rules (*vidhi*).

For instance, regarding the various distinct designations such as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) found within mantras, these correspond to the Tathāgata’s...

One should know that mantras corresponding to the realization of the true essence belong to the Buddha Family; even if they belong to other families, they may also be employed for the purposes of the Buddha Family.
If there are names and meanings corresponding to great compassion, the universal eye, non-attachment, and so forth, one should know they are for the use of the Lotus Family.
If there are names and meanings corresponding to indestructible vajra, the absence of conceptual proliferation, and so forth—
One should know that such meanings as these regarding the applications of the Vajra Family are immeasurable and boundless;
practitioners of yoga should infer them through their own minds, for they cannot be recorded in detail.
Furthermore, the Sūtra itself speaks of what is called the application corresponding to practice (*caryā-yoga*), which refers to when these [mantras] are present within various vidyā-mantras.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ khaṭ khāhi, etc.— one should know that these syllables are the names and titles of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣas.
If there is *kṛtāntaka* (the meaning is "seizer"), *khādaka* (the meaning is "eater"), *bandhaka* (the meaning is "destroyer"),
*hanaka* (the meaning is "summit" or "top"), *māraka* (the meaning is "slayer"), *pātaka* (the meaning is "striker")— such are the categories.
It should be understood that the mantras of these wrathful deities and other attendants may be employed for the purposes of subjugation (*abhicāra*) and summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*).
Regarding the meaning of "consuming" as it is described: "consuming" means causing the wrathful deities and others to swallow and destroy all classes of *vināyakas*.
As for the statement that the Buddhas would incur the sin of killing sentient beings, this point is clarified by our own school’s doctrine.
That which is called Vināyaka is that which is capable of creating all obstacles; these obstacles all arise from the mind of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
If one can devour such heavy obstacles so that the eyes and mind are opened and enlightened, know that this is truly named the "Wrathful One" (*krodha*).
By means of this gateway of the letter *Kha*, one devours the obstacles of all sentient beings; this is the teaching of the Tathāgata.
The performance of the Tathāgata’s activities may be understood by inferring other cases according to this principle.

Furthermore, if within a mantra there are words such as *namaḥ* (meaning "homage" or "taking refuge") and *svāhā* (meaning "to take up" or "consecration"), one should know that it is a mantra for practicing samādhi and corresponding with tranquility; or if there is the word *śānta* (meaning "tranquility").
One should know that the syllables beginning with *viśuddha* (meaning "purified") are mantras for fulfilling all aspirations. Furthermore, this *śānti* has the meaning of pacifying calamities;
it corresponds to the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*). Other details are explained extensively in the *Susiddhi* and other texts.
All that has been described above constitutes the characteristics of the mantras of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Next, it says: "If one were to arrange every single word spoken by a śrāvaka, because the śrāvaka attains understanding through another and has not yet deeply entered the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they cannot encompass all virtues within a single word.

For example, regarding the four-line verse 'All conditioned things are impermanent,' it must be arranged in its proper sequence with neither deficiency in text nor meaning for it to truly constitute a mantra."
By means of the gate of syllables (*akṣaramukha*), the meaning is clarified and names and phrases are augmented;
thus, although the Pratyekabuddhas have no verbal discourse, they can manifest mantras through their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). All who receive and uphold them obtain benefit and profit.

In this regard, there is a slight difference: namely, that the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas are identical in the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), yet differ in their meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
There are differences of depth and shallowness; [the Buddha] is able to benefit sentient beings through supernormal powers, causing all their aspirations to be fulfilled.
This is something that none of the other śrāvakas—excluding the four great disciples—can achieve by their own power.

Furthermore, because these mantras expound only the principle of the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination, it is said: "By means of the differentiation of the samādhi portion, one purifies karma and birth."
The Sūtra itself subsequently explains the mantra according to its true nature, stating:
"Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries, this characteristic of the mantra was not created by all the Buddhas, nor was it caused to be created by others, nor was it approved [by them].
Why is this? Because such is the nature of these dharmas, whether Tathāgatas appear in the world or whether Tathāgatas do not appear."

All phenomena abide as such by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*); that is to say, because the mantras are established by their own nature, and because the body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata are ultimately equal, the characteristics, sounds, and syllables of these mantras are all eternal, non-flowing, and without change.
They are established by nature in this way, not produced through artificial construction; for if they were produced through construction, they would be phenomena subject to birth.
That which arises is subject to destruction; the four marks [of conditioned phenomena] are in flux, impermanent, and without self—how can such things be called true speech?
Therefore, the Buddha does not create them himself, nor does he cause others to create them; even if there were one capable of creating them, he would not rejoice in it.
Thus, the characteristic of this mantra remains whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, or whether [the teaching has already]...
Whether already taught or not yet taught, whether manifest or not, the teaching of the Dharma abides in its own position; its nature and characteristics are eternally constant.
For this reason, it is called the Seal of Certainty (*niyata-mudrā*). The paths of all the sages are identical.

This very Great Compassion Maṇḍala and the characteristic of each and every mantra therein are all *dharmatā* (the natural order of phenomena) in this way; therefore, they are stated repeatedly. If it is thus, then these are the various mantras.
It is said that because the characteristics of phenomena are ultimately quiescent and cannot be transmitted to others, why is it that they sometimes appear and sometimes disappear?
The sutra further explains the reason for this, saying: "O Lord of Secrets, having attained perfect enlightenment, he is the All-Knowing One and the All-Seeing One."
When such a one appears in the world, they teach various paths according to this Dharma, following various inclinations and even the sounds of various destinies;
yet through empowerment, they teach the Mantra Way. This Mantra is the self-realized essence of the Tathāgata;
it was not created by the Buddha himself, nor is it a creation made by other devas or humans. It is the eternally abiding Dharma-nature, which is empowered [and taught].

Possessing supernatural powers, he appears in the world to benefit sentient beings; this secret body, speech, and mind of the gateway of mantras is itself the equal body, speech, and mind of the Dharma-Buddha. Nevertheless, by the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it appears in the world to benefit sentient beings.
The Tathāgata’s unimpeded knowledge and vision reside within the mental continuums of all sentient beings.

The nature of phenomena is spontaneously accomplished and without deficiency; yet, because one does not realize the essence and characteristics of this mantra as they truly are, one is called a person within saṃsāra.
When one is able to know and see for oneself, at that time one is called the All-Knowing One and the All-Seeing One.
Therefore, such knowledge and vision are not something created by the Buddha himself, nor are they transmitted by another.
After the Buddha had sat at the site of enlightenment and realized this Dharma, he fully understood that all worlds have, from the very beginning, always been the Dharma-realm.
Immediately, he gave rise to great compassion, thinking: "How is it that sentient beings, though the path of the Buddha is so near to them, cannot awaken to it themselves?
For this reason, the Tathāgata appears in the world and again employs such [teachings].
The inconceivable *dharmadhātu* is divided into various paths and revealed as various vehicles;
according to the diverse inclinations, faculties, and natures of beings, it is taught through the sovereign empowerment of various phrases and dialects as the Way of Mantras (*mantranaya*).

Although it arises from the conditions of responsive resonance with sentient beings and does not stir from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and although it employs skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to act in every way, it is nonetheless not the Buddha.
Although the various teachings of the universal gate differ, they are intended solely to reveal and awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If a practitioner, amidst these ten metaphors of the mantra, falsely perceives conditioned arising and ceasing and thereby further increases the defilements of the mind,
this is not the original intent of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, because sentient beings of future ages will have dull faculties and be deluded regarding the two truths—
failing to know that the conventional is itself the ultimate— the Tathāgata has earnestly pointed to specific instances, saying, "Lord of Secrets, what is the Tathāgata’s Way of Mantras?
It is said that by empowering these written characters, worldly letters and speech are no different from the reality of the mantras."
For this reason, the Tathāgata empowers [this teaching] with the true meaning of mantras.
If there were worldly words existing apart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they would be but the deluded views of a false mind, and no real substance could be found therein.
That the Buddha empowers them through his spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) would then be a fallacy, not a mantra. This has already been understood.
Regarding the locus of empowerment, by what dharma does the Tathāgata empower? Therefore, the Buddha next said:

"Lord of Secrets, it is through the true speech accumulated and practiced over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas—the Four Noble Truths, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four bases of psychic power, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the six pāramitās, and the seven jewels of enlightenment."
Regarding the Brahma-abodes and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, Secret Lord, to speak briefly:

it is by means of the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom, the power of his own merit, the power of his own vows, and the sustaining power of the entire dharma-realm, that he reveals the teachings of the mantra-methods to sentient beings in accordance with their various dispositions. This is what is meant by "by the Tathāgata."
The merit accumulated over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas serves as a universal empowerment (*sarvatragata-sāmānya-mukha-adhiṣṭhāna*).
Therefore, within the establishment of each and every word and name, all purposes and benefits are accomplished without exception, just as in the system of Indra.
Furthermore, each of these individual merits is identical to the nature of the mantra; such is the self-nature of the *dharmatā*.
It is not produced through conditioned effort; for now, let us briefly discern its meaning by means of the single syllable *A*.
When a practitioner realizes their own mind, they understand that the causes and effects of both the mundane and supramundane realms are fundamentally unborn.

Thus, there is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path, yet there exists one true reality (*satya*). Having seen this truth, one will certainly roar the lion’s roar and extensively explain it for the sake of sentient beings.

This is called the accumulation of the practice of truthful speech. Furthermore, because one knows that the eight inversions are fundamentally unarisen, one achieves the Tathāgata’s foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Because one knows that the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) are fundamentally unarisen, one achieves the supernormal knowledge of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-abhijñā*).

Because one knows that the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*), and so forth, are fundamentally unarisen, one achieves the Buddha’s natural power of wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna-bala*). Because one knows that the six obscurations are fundamentally...
Because they have given birth [to these qualities], they reach the further shore of the six perfections;

because they know the seven factors of enlightenment are fundamentally unborn, they accomplish the seven kinds of jewel-like self-awakened wisdom without a teacher; because they know the four Brahma-abodes are fundamentally unborn, they accomplish objectless loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity;
because they know the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are fundamentally unborn, they therefore transcend the mind-measure and do not associate with any sentient beings.
One shall freely expound upon these various Dharma-gates.
Furthermore, as for the meaning in the first chapter of this sutra, once one understands that there is only the aggregates and no self, up until the realization of the realm of tranquility,
one should clarify the various Dharma-gates by means of the fact that the self, persons, sentient beings, and life-span have been fundamentally unarisen from the very beginning.

When one observes the emptiness of intrinsic nature by means of establishing five similes, one should clarify various Dharma gates based on the fact that the aggregates (*skandha*) are fundamentally unarisen;
when one observes that the aggregates and the *ālayavijñāna*, up to the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), cannot be found at their prior or posterior limits,
one should clarify various Dharma gates based on the fact that the mental image of the mind is fundamentally unarisen, such that the arising of the mind is utterly devoid of self-nature.
At this time, one should explain various Dharma-gates based on the principle that the originally unborn Bodhicitta is fundamentally pure, up to the entry into the stage of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, one should explain various Dharma-gates based on the ultimate meaning of non-arising within the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala;
for instance, such gates as the "A" syllable gate of non-arising and the "Ka" syllable gate of non-action should all be explained in detail.
Each individual syllable, even down to each individual name, is established as such; all these should be explained in detail.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One possesses mastery over the Dharma: he may subsume various single dharma-gates, such as the bodhicitta, within a single syllable;
or he may subsume various dual dharma-gates, such as śamatha and vipaśyanā, within two syllables; or he may subsume [various triple dharma-gates] within three syllables.

Various triads of dharma-gates, such as the three emptinesses, are subsumed by three characters; various tetrads of dharma-gates, such as the foundations of mindfulness, are subsumed by four characters;
various pentads of dharma-gates, such as the faculties and powers, are subsumed by five characters;
various hexads of dharma-gates, such as the six perfections, are subsumed by six characters; or various heptads, such as the seven jewels of enlightenment, are subsumed by seven characters.
Dharma-gates may be subsumed by eight characters to encompass various eightfold dharma-gates such as the Eightfold Noble Path;
or by nine characters to encompass various ninefold dharma-gates such as the Nine Meditative Concentrations; or by ten characters to encompass various tenfold dharma-gates such as the Ten Powers;
and so on, up to being subsumed by immeasurable characters to encompass immeasurable dharma-gates—all such names and phrases are likewise [to be understood].
This is because, according to the general characteristics of mantras, when a practitioner holds even a single *akṣara-dvāra* such as the letter *A*,
they may, in accordance with their own dispositions, desires, and capacities, realize either the four foundations of mindfulness or the four supernormal powers,
each case being different. Nevertheless, as soon as one understands a single dharma-gate, all other dharma-gates and various jewels of the Dharma are spontaneously present without being sought.
Regarding the distinct characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is the method of subsuming the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) by means of four characters.

When practicing according to the Dharma in this manner, although one has never previously correctly contemplated the body, sensation, mind, or phenomena, one spontaneously awakens to the gates of the foundations of mindfulness and enters the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The conventional names and meanings of these various dharma-gates are explained extensively in such works as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Furthermore, because the Tathāgata cannot exhaustively enumerate all the various dharma-gates, he again summarizes them by stating the essentials.

First, the term "Omniscient Wisdom" (sarvajñajñāna) is a general designation for the adamantine wisdom-seals (vajrajñānamudrā) of all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time;
through their collective empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is nothing that is not pervaded. Moreover, this refers to the original practices of all Tathāgatas.
The boundless accumulations of merit gathered while practicing the bodhisattva path give rise to inexhaustible great vows that reach ultimate fulfillment within *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

Therefore, they all attain the designation "wisdom. By means of such power of merit and vows, as well as the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the intrinsic nature of the entire *dharmadhātu*, they act in accordance with the world, performing empowerments according to the specific types [of beings].
For this reason, one is able to reveal the teachings of the mantra-dharma for all the various bodies, speech, and minds of all sentient beings.
As the Sūtra says: "O Lord of Mysteries, what is the teaching of the mantra-dharma? It refers to the gateway of the letter A and so forth."

Although the characteristics of the Mantra teachings do not differ from their essence, nor does the essence differ from its characteristics, these characteristics are not something produced through artificial cultivation and cannot be demonstrated to others;

yet they are able to manifest without departing from the characteristics of liberation, appearing as sounds and letters, wherein each individual sound and letter is itself a gateway for entering the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, it is called the "Mantra Dharma-teaching. When discussing the Mantra Dharma-teaching, one should...
Although names and terminology throughout all directions and realms of existence follow accordingly, these are merely traces of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world;
since the transmission of the Dharma began in India, I shall here clarify the meaning by following one approach based on the Sanskrit texts.
The Sūtra states: "The letter A is the gateway because all phenomena are fundamentally unborn.
The letter A is the root of the teaching on all phenomena; for whatever sound is first uttered when opening the mouth, it contains the resonance of A.
If one were to depart from the sound of A, there would be no utterance of any speech or sound whatsoever. Thus, it is the mother of all sounds—the speech of the entire triple world.
It is said that all speech relies upon names, and names rely upon syllables; therefore, the letter *A* of the Siddham script is also the mother of all letters.
One should know that the true meaning of the gateway of the letter *A* is likewise thus, pervading the meanings of all phenomena (*dharma*). Why is this?
Because there is no phenomenon that does not arise from a multitude of conditions, and that which arises from conditions [is empty of intrinsic nature].
All things have a beginning and a source; now, observing this very condition that gives rise to them, we see that it too arises from a multitude of causes and conditions.

As these conditions arise one after another from further conditions, who can be called their ultimate source? When one observes in this way, one knows that the limit of non-arising (*anutpāda-koṭi*) is the source of all phenomena.
It is just as when one hears any speech, one is simultaneously hearing the sound "A. Thus it is.
To see the arising of all phenomena is to see the limit of their original non-arising; to see the limit of their original non-arising is to know one’s own mind as it truly is;
and to know one’s own mind as it truly is is the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Therefore, Vairocana employs this single syllable alone as his mantra. Yet, worldly ordinary beings do not contemplate these...
Because the source of all phenomena is thus, they falsely claim that there is birth; consequently, they follow the stream of birth and death and cannot escape it on their own.

Just as an ignorant painter, having himself applied various colors to create the form of a terrifying yakṣa, looks upon it and feels such fear that he suddenly falls to the ground, so too do sentient beings:
having themselves projected the fundamental nature of all phenomena, [they become terrified by them].
The Source paints the three realms and yet sinks back into their midst; his own mind blazes forth as he undergoes all manner of suffering.
Once the Tathāgata—the wise painter—has fully understood this, he is then able to freely establish the Great Compassion Maṇḍala.
Speaking from this perspective, that which is called the profound secret treasury is merely what sentient beings conceal themselves; it is not something the Buddha possesses.
It is hidden.
Regarding the gateway of the letter *ka*, it is said that "all dharmas are free from karmic action" (*kriyā*); this is because the Sanskrit term *kaliya* has the meaning of "karmic action.
Just as the various non-Buddhist schools (tīrthikas) postulate an agent (*kartṛ*) and a cause of action (*kārayitṛ*), so too do the masters of the various [Buddhist] treatises.
It is taught that there is fruition because of the conjunction of three factors: the action, the agent, and the instrument of the action.

If one relies on wisdom and skillful means and asserts that there is a fixed certainty, one falls into the view of causelessness. If one falls into the view of causelessness, then all phenomena would lack cause and effect.
That which can produce is called the cause; that which is produced is called the fruit. These two dharmas are without deliberate agency.
Furthermore, there would be no action, no agent, no dharma to be performed, no retribution for sin or merit, and no path to nirvana; everything would be non-existent.
Moreover, since the action and the agent arise in mutual dependence upon one another, if the action were definitively existent, then the agent would necessarily be definitively existent.
All of this would not differ from the arguments of the non-Buddhists, as explained at length in the "Examination of Action and Agent" chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
Now, when one correctly observes that the action, the agent, and so forth all arise from a multitude of conditions, one enters the limit of primordial non-arising (*an-utpāda-pada*).
This limit of primordial non-arising is such that whether a Buddha appears or not, the Dharma-nature remains as it is; who could have created it?
Therefore, if one sees the letter *ka*, one knows that all phenomena are merely names established through conditioned construction; this is called the "characteristic of letters" (*akṣara-lakṣaṇa*).
If one is a practitioner of ritual action (*kriyā*), one should know that ultimate non-action is what is called the true meaning.
Regarding the gateway of the letter *kha*: because all phenomena are equal to space and are unapprehendable;

for in the Sanskrit language, the letter *kha* signifies the meaning of "space," and it is universally acknowledged in the world that space is unborn and a state of non-action. If [one realizes] this...
All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and free from all activity; they are ultimately like the characteristic of space. Now, even this characteristic of space cannot be apprehended. Why?
Because in the world, that which has no form is called the characteristic of space. Form is a conditioned phenomenon and is impermanent.
If form has not yet arisen, then because it has not arisen, there is no cessation. At that time, the characteristic of space does not exist as a cause.

Because of form, there is the formless realm; the name "formless realm" is explained at length within the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* in the chapter on the contemplation of the six elements, and the meaning herein is likewise.
If form were originally unarisen, what could be called the formless realm?
Since the formless realm cannot be described, there would be no fixed characteristic of empty space. Furthermore, all phenomena have a nature like that of empty space.
This is the characteristic of non-deception. As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the meaning of *nirvāṇa* is that when the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) cease, no further five aggregates arise.
If the five aggregates were originally unarisen, what would there be to cease now that one calls *nirvāṇa*?
Therefore, like the characteristic of empty space, it is also unattainable; this is the true meaning of the letter-gateway *kha*.
Regarding the statement that "the gateway of the syllable *o* (Sanskrit: *oṃ*) is because all phenomena and all formations (*saṃskāra*) are unattainable": the term for "formation" is *saṃskāra*.
It refers to the meaning of going and coming, advancing and retreating, and non-abiding. Now, by explaining this through the gateway of the syllable *a* in a successive manner:
because all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, they are without action; because they are without action, they are [unattainable].

That which is dependently opposed and can be described as "emptiness of emptiness" is precisely the state of non-activity; since even the state of non-activity cannot be apprehended, how much less so the state of activity?
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the chapter "Examination of Going and Coming," clarifies the meaning of activity and cessation:

it is called "activity" by virtue of continuity, such as the production of sprouts, stalks, and leaves from a grain seed, or the arising of formations conditioned by ignorance; it is called "cessation" by virtue of interruption.
Cessation is like the cessation of the sprout and stalk when the grain seed ceases; because ignorance ceases, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth cease.

If a dharma has already been performed, there is no performing, because it has already been performed; if it has not yet been performed, there is also no performing, because the dharma of performing does not yet exist;

and at the very time of performing, there is no performing, because one cannot be separated from what has already been performed and what has not yet been performed. One should investigate to the ultimate through such various gateways as these.

Because there is no practice and no non-practice, there is nowhere to rest. Because there is no practice and nowhere to rest, there is neither coming nor going among the various realms of existence, nor is there anyone who dwells in nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, if a person does not move from their original place and that itself is the destination, one should know that such a person has neither practice nor arrival; therefore, it is said that all practices are non-existent.
It can be understood thus:

regarding the statement that "the gateway of the letter Ga is because the single composite mark (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena cannot be apprehended," the Sanskrit term for *ga* is *gaṇa*, which carries the meaning of "close union.
This is like how various subtle particles combine to form a single minute dust mote, or how the various aggregates (*skandha*) combine to form a single body.

In the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the chapter examining "Union" (*saṃsarga*), various masters of treatises state: "Because of the three things—the seeing, the object seen, and the seer—there is that which is seen;
one should know that there is union. This applies to hearing, the object heard, and the hearer, and so on, up to the defilement, the object defiled, and the defiler;
all such afflictions are likewise. The respondent says: "All things have union because they are distinct from one another; however, in this case, all [three]..."

The distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena (*dharma*) cannot be apprehended; therefore, there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*), as has been explained at length. By means of the gateway of syllables (*akṣaramukha*), they explain one another in succession;

thus, let us clarify this through the meaning of "practice" (*caryā*). Whatever is practiced must be understood as necessarily involving three factors: the practice itself, that which is to be practiced, and the practitioner.
Now, because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen (*anutpanna*), there is nothing to be practiced. If there is nothing to be practiced...
What is the practice, what is the practitioner, and how can they be joined? Furthermore, if all phenomena possess distinct characteristics, there will never be a time when they join;
yet if one reaches the limit of original non-arising, there are no distinct characteristics and thus they cannot be joined.
Therefore, all phenomena are ultimately without conjunction.
The letter-gateway *Cha* (Sanskrit: *cyuti*) signifies that all phenomena are free from all transition and change;
*cyuti* is the term for transition and change. Furthermore, the Sanskrit sound *carya* signifies conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

Just as when one sees the letter *Cha*, one immediately knows that conditioned formations are subject to transition and do not abide, the "Examination of Formations" chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Formations are named the five aggregates."
Because they arise from conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all false and illusory, lacking any fixed characteristic.
From the physical form of infancy up to the physical form of old age, there is no moment-to-moment stability; a determinate nature cannot be found.
That which is called "determinate existence" is unchangeable, like pure gold that does not alter. Although all phenomena (*dharma*) now arise, [they are likewise unstable].
Because they abide in their own nature, one should know that they are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), as explained extensively therein.

That which is without intrinsic nature is primordially unarisen; that which is primordially unarisen is the body of the Tathāgata, eternally abiding and without change—hence it is said to be "free from transition and transformation.
Furthermore, if all phenomena were composed of a combination [of parts], then...
Since all phenomena are now subject to transition and change, yet are without arising, without action, and even without any range of activity, there is no combination;

because there is no combination, one is free from all transition and change. All gateways of letters should be explained through mutual rotation in both direct and reverse order so as to be without obstruction; for now, I have merely followed the sequential transmission.
Regarding the gateway of the letter *Cha*: all phenomena (*dharmas*) are unobtainable as images. In the Sanskrit language, *chaya* means "image.
Just as a person’s reflection depends entirely upon their own body, so too the myriad phenomena of the triple world are merely the consciousness-mind;
through the conditions of causes and effects, they manifest as various objects. This matter is explained at length in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*, even for those who practice yoga.
There are various inconceivable matters, such as being able to see face-to-face the Buddhas of the ten directions who universally manifest their form-bodies;
these too are all reflections of the mind. Since the mind is fundamentally unborn, one should know that reflections are likewise without arising.
Because they do not arise, even the mind undergoes no transition or change, and because it undergoes no transition or change, reflections likewise undergo no transition or change.
The reason for this is that, just as a shadow has no inherent nature of its own and its movement follows that of the body, so it is with the mind;
because the mind moves through conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there is not a single moment when it abides. Thus, the myriad phenomena of the world also flow and turn along with it.
When one realizes the mind according to its true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), the shadow likewise accords with its true mark and cannot be apprehended.
Regarding the gateway of the syllable *Ja*: it is because the arising of all phenomena cannot be apprehended. In Sanskrit, this is called *jāta*, which carries the meaning of "arising.
For example, a jar arises through the conjunction of a lump of clay, a wheel, a cord, and a potter;
a cloth arises through the conjunction of thread, a loom, a shuttle, and a weaver; and [a house arises] through the earth, the foundation, beams, rafters, mud, straw, and human labor.

Through combination, there is the production of curd from milk; through the combination of a vessel, a churning rod, human effort, and so forth, there is the production of clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Through the combination of seeds, earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, and other factors, there is the production of sprouts. The causal conditions for internal phenomena are likewise:
ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and the rest each produce their respective causes, which in turn produce further effects. Therefore, if one sees the letter *ja*:
The Gate immediately knows that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are none other than those produced from conditions, as stated in the verse:
"That which arises from various causes and conditions has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); if it lacks intrinsic nature, how can such a phenomenon exist?
Therefore, arising cannot be apprehended. The non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika-ācārya*) speak of various false causes and conditions, or claim that all things arise without any cause at all.
Within the Buddha-dharma, there are also those who, due to a lack of skillful means (*upāya*) regarding Prajñā, grasp at the characteristics of arising and ceasing produced by causes and conditions;
this is extensively refuted in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. Furthermore, the letter-gate "A" is the original nature of all phenomena, which is non-arising.
The letter-gate "Ja" is to contemplate arising through ten similes: although arising exists from conditions, it cannot be apprehended. If arising is ultimately non-existent...

If it can be attained, it is not different from the limit of non-arising; furthermore, since these ten metaphors are reflections of the mind, and reflections do not transcend the dharma-realm, arising likewise does not transcend the limit of non-arising.
Regarding the gateway of the letter *Ṣa*: because the "enemy" (*śatru*) of all phenomena cannot be apprehended. In Sanskrit, *ṣamaḷa* means "enemy.

If one sees the letter *ṣa*, one knows that all phenomena have enemies—just as in the world there are wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, those that flow against the stream of birth and death and those that flow with the stream of birth and death, such as generosity versus stinginess, and ethical discipline versus breaking it.

From morality up to wisdom, and from ignorance and so forth, they exist in mutual dependence and opposition, characterized by victory and defeat and impermanence, even unto the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world who, by the power of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), destroys the four armies of Māra—this too is called "battle.

However, since the notion of a "self" (*ātman*) is not established within any phenomena (*dharma*), to whom ultimately do wisdom and afflictions belong? It is in this sense that one speaks of *vipaśyanā*.
Can it destroy the afflictions? If you say it is called "destroying" because darkness ceases when light arises, does it destroy what has already arisen or what has not yet arisen?

If it destroys what has already arisen, there is no longer darkness; what then remains to be destroyed? If it destroys what has not yet arisen, then that which has not yet arisen lacks its own substance;
how then could it be destroyed? If it is said to be "arising," this is called being half-arisen and half-unarisen; therefore, it is light.

Darkness and ultimate reality can never meet; furthermore, because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and even lack any semblance of form, they share a single characteristic that does not transcend suchness (*tathatā*).
How, then, could the suchness of the Buddha-realm and the suchness of the realm of Māra contend?

When the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, he simply realized the suchness of all phenomena as being without opposition; yet, in accordance with worldly conventions, it is said that he established himself as victorious in battle.
This is merely a name.
Regarding the statement that "the letter-gateway *ṭha* is because pride (*māna*) is unattainable in all phenomena": in the Sanskrit sound, *ṭhakāra* has the meaning of pride;
it refers to viewing those phenomena as inferior while regarding this phenomenon as superior, such as the various distinctions among the three realms and the six destinies.
The various distinctions of the conceit that arises from inferiority are immeasurable; briefly stated, there are seven types, as explained in detail in the Abhidharma.
Even those seeking the three vehicles still harbor views of inequality regarding higher and lower stages.
Now, by contemplating that all phenomena are unarisen and even devoid of mutual dependence, one realizes Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Bodhi is equal toward all phenomena, with no distinction of high or low;

therefore, the Tathāgata is also called the "All-Vajra Bodhisattva," is also called the "Sages of the Four Fruits," is also called "Ordinary Beings and Heretics," is also called "Sentient Beings in Various Evil Destinies," and is also called "Persons of the Five Heinous Crimes and Wrong Views. The Great Compassion Maṇḍala precisely represents this meaning.
Regarding the statement that the gateway of the syllable *Ṭha* is because the nourishment (*puṣṭi*) of all phenomena cannot be apprehended:

in the Sanskrit sound, *vithapana* has the meaning of "nourishing. Just as in the world seeds act as the cause and the five elements and the seasons act as conditions for gradual growth until the fruit is produced, so it is with internal phenomena;
the seed of consciousness is sown in the field of karma through ignorance.
Covered by the waters of craving and moistened by them, it grows and flourishes, as explained in detail in the *Śālistamba-sūtra*.
Therefore, in this present sūtra, the eight mental states that conform to and oppose the world continue in succession and grow, each having its own causes and conditions;
