even up to the pure bodhicitta, which takes the five syllable-gates (*pañcākṣara-dvāra*) as its condition to give rise to the root of great compassion, causing the Buddha-śāla tree to grow and spread far and wide.

It pervades the entire dharma-realm; yet all dharmas, by virtue of these five letter-gates, are fundamentally unarisen, beyond verbal expression, pure in their intrinsic nature, devoid of causes and conditions, and like the characteristic of space—thus, they cannot be grasped as being nourished or increased.
Furthermore, from the syllable *a-ka* onwards, through successive mutual explanations, it is shown that all dharmas are ultimately equal and without distinction.
Because there is no high or low due to the absence of high and low, one should know that there is no increase.
Regarding the gateway of the letter *ṇa*, it is said that "all dharmas are such that their adversaries (*pratipakṣa*) cannot be found.

In the Sanskrit original, this is *ṇamara*, which carries the meaning of "adversary. Just as in the world, enemies retaliate against one another, they are thus called "adversaries" (*pratipakṣa*). Furthermore, previously...
To speak of "waging war against an enemy" implies mutual confrontation; here, "hostility" (*vaira*) carries the sense of avoiding enmity. The Sanskrit terms for these are distinct from one another.
In the *Vinaya*, the Buddha taught: "Requiting enmity with enmity never brings it to an end; only by being free from enmity does enmity cease.
Furthermore, regarding women as a source of hostility for those practicing the holy life (*brahmacārin*), the *Anantavaraṇīya-sūtra* also speaks of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Enemies naturally disperse and perish as one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), which is half of the jewels of a Buddha-land;
therefore, when a practitioner sees the gateway of the letter *Na*, they know that all phenomena have their opposites, and this is termed "understanding the characteristics of letters.
Furthermore, because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and even their growth cannot be apprehended, one should know that their opposites are likewise fundamentally so.
Because they do not arise and so forth, up to being without nourishment, the Tathāgata is ultimately without any adversary;
this is the true meaning of the "gate of letters" (akṣara-mukha).
Regarding the letter *ḍa*: because the grasping of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) is unattainable, it is called *taṅka* in the Sanskrit language, which means "grasping."
Regarding the meaning of the character *ṭa* (荼), by placing a dot (*bindu*) above it, the sound shifts to *taṅ* (湯); thus, their essential nature is the same.
Furthermore, *graha* (蘖哩訶) is also another name for this. The sutras state that being possessed by ghosts and spirits, or being held by non-human beings (*amanuṣya*), refers to this.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that "being afflicted by decline" (*śīla-graha*) is all caused by the *graha* spirits, as they do not abandon those whom they possess.
Because they are separated, they are given their names; likewise, the sun, moon, and the five planets follow one another through their cycles of beginning and end.

In the Sanskrit language, this is called *graha*, which is translated as "the nine graspers" (*jiuzhi*). When they truly assemble in one place, it is designated in the Indian calendar as the time of "true conjunction.
This meaning of "grasping" (*zhi*) is different from that of *dhāra*. Upon seeing this gateway of the letter *ṭa*, one immediately understands all things.
Sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been possessed by the four māras and have been unable to abandon them; this is the characteristic of names and signs.
Now, by means of various gateways such as the letter A, one contemplates all dharmas in succession and finds that they are all unattainable.
Therefore, one should know that all dharmas are without enmity, because enmity is fundamentally unarisen, and thus it can never be pacified.
Because one realizes the equality of the dharma-realm through non-attachment to the dharma-realm, it is said that "the grasping and maintaining of all dharmas is unobtainable.
Regarding the gateway of the syllable *ta*: because the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas is unobtainable. In the Sanskrit, this is *tathatā*;

the term *tathatā* carries the meaning of "suchness," and within the flow of the language, it also includes the sound of "attainment" (*prāpti*). Thus, the realization of suchness is precisely the meaning of liberation.

As it is said: when the various false conceptualizations regarding the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) are extinguished through non-illusory vision, that which is eternally such as its own original nature and indestructible is realized.
If one perceives the "gate of the letter *ta*," one knows that all phenomena are the mark of *tathatā* (suchness);
this is called the "mark of the letter. However, there is a class of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who posit a nature of *tathatā*; if one understands and perceives [this]:
This is what is called "liberation. Although this is said, it is merely a different name applied to the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*).
Nāgārjuna considers that when the Śrāvaka sūtras speak of the "abiding of dharmas" (*dharma-sthiti*), this also refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.

Because their entry [into the truth] has not yet been deep, they conceive the thought of "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*), thinking they have realized *nirvāṇa*. However, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are... [the two are non-dual].

If one understands that the phenomena of mutual dependence (pratītyadharma) have been eternally identical to the characteristic of nirvāṇa from the very beginning of saṃsāra, with what else could they be dependent?
Therefore, it is said to be "nirvāṇa. For this reason, all phenomena are ultimately neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* also states: "The limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) of nirvāṇa and the limit of the world—these two limits..."

There is not even a hair’s breadth of distinction because there is no differentiation; because all phenomena are without differentiation, they are without opposition, and because they are without opposition, there is no grasping;
and because there is no grasping, there is likewise neither suchness nor liberation.
Regarding the statement that "the gateway of the letter *ta* is because the locus of all phenomena cannot be apprehended":
in Sanskrit, this is *sthāna*, which carries the meaning of "locus" as well as "stage.

Just as when a person ascends from one place to another, the basis upon which they stand is called a "stage," so too are the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) established in relation to those who practice the path through various conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Because it is the basis and the place of rest for the traces of the mind, various names are spoken.

When one sees another character (*akṣara*), one immediately knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without exception established in dependence upon conditions; thus, one should know that they all have a basis and a place of abiding—this is the characteristic of a character (*akṣara-lakṣaṇa*).
However, all phenomena are originally unarisen, and even suchness (*tathatā*) and liberation (*vimukti*) are ultimately unattainable.
Thus, there is no going and no coming, no proceeding and no abiding. Within such a mark of quiescence, what stages or positions could there be?
Furthermore, when entering the gateway of the letter "ma" (mā), one realizes that all phenomena are like [space] (tathatā);
therefore, one does not abide within saṃsāra. Since even this very suchness (tathatā) is ungraspable, one does not abide within nirvāṇa. At that time, this is the sphere of practice.
The complete cessation of all states, which is entirely pervasive and without any basis, is called "abiding in the Great Abiding of the Tathāgata by means of the dharma of non-abiding.
Regarding the gateway of the syllable *Na*, it is because all dharmas cannot be apprehended as "giving"; in Sanskrit, *dāna* means relinquishment (*tyāga*).
The meaning of "giving" (dāna) is such that if one sees the letter Na, one immediately knows that all dharmas are characterized by being relinquishable. Why is this?
Because all dharmas arise and cease in dependence upon conditions and possess no fixed stability. If one becomes attached to them and gives rise to craving, one will surely be consumed by it.
This applies even to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages regarding the pure and wondrous merits produced within their own respective stages.
Because their virtue has not yet reached the further shore of relinquishment (*tyāga-pāramitā*), they still possess inconceivable retrogression and thus cannot be called the state of supreme bliss.
Now, because one contemplates that all phenomena are unarisen, the giver, the recipient, and the gift are all fundamentally unarisen from the very beginning;
even unto all phenomena, there is no place of abiding. Because there is no place of abiding, these three things as well do not exist.
Because this is the dwelling place, when the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he attained nothing and relinquished nothing.
Within the treasury of empty space (ākāśagarbha), there is no accumulation, yet it flows forth through universal gates to bestow gifts upon all living beings;

this is called seeing the true mark of giving (dāna-satyalakṣaṇa) and is also called being fully endowed with the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). Furthermore, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata is entirely the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
That which is called "that which cannot be bestowed upon others" is merely brought forth from within the mental chamber of sentient beings when it is given to them.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The gift of all dharmas, which cannot be named, is called the 'Gate of Letters' (akṣaramukha) in its true sense."
Regarding the gateway of the syllable *Dha*: because the *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena) of all dharmas cannot be apprehended.
In Sanskrit, *dharma-dhātu* is called the "realm of phenomena" (*dharmadhātu*). "Realm" (*dhātu*) has the sense of "essence" (*tattva*) and the sense of "division" (*vibhāga*).

The relics of the Buddha are also called the *tathāgata-dhātu*; here, *dhātu* refers to the constituent parts of the Tathāgata. If one perceives the gateway of the syllable *Dha*, one immediately knows all dharmas.

All possess a substance, namely, taking the *dharmadhātu* as their substance. Why is this so? Because if one were to depart from the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, the meaning of the substance of all phenomena would not be established. Now, the *dharmadhātu* is precisely the *cittadhātu*;

since the *cittadhātu* is fundamentally unarisen, one should know that the *dharmadhātu* is also fundamentally unarisen, and even that the *cittadhātu* is without acquisition and without relinquishment.

Therefore, one should know that the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is likewise without acquisition and without relinquishment; since there is not even a single dharma to be relinquished, how could there be anything to be acquired?
If the dharma-realm were a characteristic that could be acquired, it would arise from a multitude of causes and conditions.

If it arises from a multitude of causes and conditions, one should know that it has no intrinsic essence of its own; how much less could it serve as the essence of all dharmas? Thus, the dharma-realm is solely self-... [nature].

The realization of the eternal mind is not a separate dharma. Furthermore, that which is called the Tathāgata’s Great Bestowal—the Great Compassion Maṇḍala and the Dharma-realm—is the Universal Gate of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Since such a true mark cannot be demonstrated to people through the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), no dharma can be apprehended.
Regarding the gateway of the syllable *pa*: because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
In Sanskrit, this is called *paramārtha*, which is translated as "ultimate meaning" (*dìyīyì*) or "supreme meaning" (*shèngyì*). *Satya* is translated as "truth" (*dì*).

The characteristics of the meaning of "truth" are explained in the gateway of the syllable *sa*. Here, the gateway of the syllable *pa* specifically clarifies the characteristics of the ultimate meaning. This was taught by Nāgārjuna.
The Tree says: "The term 'ultimate truth' (*paramārtha*) refers to the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), because it is neither broken nor destroyed.
Furthermore, among all phenomena, the foremost is called *nirvāṇa*. As the Abhidharma states: 'What is the unsurpassed dharma?

It is the cessation through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Cessation through wisdom is precisely *nirvāṇa*. If one sees the character 'pā', one immediately knows that all phenomena are not separate [from this]. "
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) does not depart from the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*); this is the characteristic of words (*akṣara-nimitta*).
If one knows the true meaning of the gateway of words, even the ultimate truth cannot be apprehended. Why? Because there is neither craving nor attachment.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further states: "Because sentient beings are attached to the sounds of 'nirvāṇa,' they engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), [asserting] either 'it exists' or 'it does not exist.'"
Because it destroys attachment, one speaks of the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*; this is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
It does not destroy that which is attained within the minds of the noble ones (*ārya*), for the noble ones do not grasp at signs (*nimitta*) among any phenomena (*dharma*).

Furthermore, since all phenomena enter the equal Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is neither high nor low; how could one wish to establish superiority or inferiority within the dharma of non-arising?
Because they are thus characterized, the ultimate truth (paramārtha) cannot be apprehended.
Regarding the gateway of the syllable *pha*: all dharmas are not solid, like a mass of foam. In Sanskrit, this is called *phenapinda*, which is translated as "mass of foam.
It is like when the waves of a great body of water surge and collide, forming a mass of foam of various kinds.
Through mutual production and even through firm binding and mutual support, there comes to be a solid function;
yet, if one observes each stage from the coarse to the subtle, it is merely a condition. Furthermore, since these conditions cannot be grasped or touched, they possess no substantial reality.
Reaching their ultimate limit, the entire body is seen to be water, with nothing produced at all. Now, the various five aggregates of the world are likewise thus.

Now, if one gathers the branches back to the root and reduces the fathom to the cubit to observe them—even down to the point of a single strand of silk or a fleeting instant—any slight movement whatsoever is all a successive arising from conditions.
If it arises from a multitude of conditions, it has no self-nature (*svabhāva*). If there is no self-nature, one should know that this arising is non-arising.
Reaching the limit of fundamental non-arising, there is only the ocean of the mind-nature (*cittatva-samudra*).
By listening and following the deluded sentiments of the six realms, there subsequently arises what is termed a "world.
That which is the ocean of the mind-nature is itself the Dharma-realm; that which is the Dharma-realm is itself ultimate nirvana.
If one can see it in this way, then even though vast waves surge and toss about, manifesting various universal form-bodies, they do not destroy the nature of limpid clarity.
Regarding the statement that "the letter-mā gate is because the bondage of all phenomena cannot be apprehended": in Sanskrit, this is *bandha*, which is translated here as "bondage.
For example, when a person is caught in shackles or fetters, they cannot move or turn; this is the meaning of "bondage.
If one uses skillful means to untie these knots, it is then called "liberation. Apart from the body or the rope, there is no separate phenomenon of bondage or liberation.

Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, binds the Asura King with subtle fetters and places him atop the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, such that when the thought arises to return [to the underworld], the five fetters are already upon his body, yet when he ceases that thought, the fetters spontaneously dissolve;
if even the snares of Pāpīyas are a hundred thousand times more powerful than this, how much more so are the fetters of karma and afflictions? How could they not bind one whose mind is unconditioned?
Regarding birth, bondage, and so forth—to state it briefly: if one is apart from all causes and conditions and does not fall within the category of dharmas, this is called "unbound.

This is the meaning of the term. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If there were a sentient being existing separately from the five aggregates, then the five aggregates would bind that sentient being.
However, in reality, there is no sentient being apart from the five aggregates. If [one were] apart from the five aggregates..."
If there were afflictions, they would bind the five aggregates; yet in reality, apart from the five aggregates, there are no separate afflictions.
Through such various causes and conditions, one should know that there is neither bondage nor liberation.

Because there is neither bondage nor liberation, nirvana is precisely birth-and-death, and birth-and-death is precisely nirvana, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on Contemplating Bondage and Liberation."

Furthermore, if all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and are like a mass of foam, then within this, who is the one capable of being liberated and who is the one bound? Therefore, no bonds can be apprehended.
Regarding the gateway of the letter *ba*: because all phenomena (*dharma*) and all existents (*bhava*) are unattainable.

In Sanskrit, this is called *bhava*, which is translated here as "existence. Existence refers to the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) and even up to the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
If one sees the letter *ba*, one immediately knows that all phenomena possess causes and conditions; it is because they arise from the conjunction of manifold conditions that they are so designated.

This is because existence and non-existence would possess a fixed nature. Why is this so? If one were to say that existence possesses a fixed characteristic, then there would ultimately be no characteristic of non-existence;

this would constitute eternalism (*śāśvata*). As it is said regarding the three periods of time: if a dharma-characteristic exists within the future, and that dharma arrives in the present and transitions into the past without relinquishing its original characteristic, then one falls into the view of eternalism. This is also the case if one asserts that non-existence is fixed.
If that which previously existed must now be non-existent, this constitutes the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Because of these two views, one distances oneself from the Buddha-dharma.
As explained at length in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* in the chapter refuting existence and non-existence, we now observe that all phenomena arise from conditions;

this is precisely the meaning of being fundamentally unarisen (*anutpanna*). Because they are fundamentally unarisen, there is no action and no activity, up to and including neither bondage nor liberation. Therefore...
The letter-gateway *ba* (va), because it arises from conditions, is fully endowed with all letter-gateways;
being fully endowed with all letter-gateways, it is the King of Samādhis, which can destroy the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
For this reason, Śākyamuni is called the Dharma-King who Destroys Existence.
Regarding the gate of the syllable *ya*: because the vehicle (*yāna*) of all phenomena is unattainable.

In Sanskrit this is called *yāna*, which is translated here as "vehicle" (*cheng*) and also termed "path. Just as when a person mounts a boat or a carriage they can carry heavy loads and travel great distances to reach their destination, so too, upon seeing the gate of the syllable *ya*, one knows that all sentient beings proceed toward [liberation] by means of various causes and conditions.
Those who are headed toward the retribution of birth and death, as well as those who are proceeding toward nirvāṇa, each have their respective vehicles;

yet one knows that all immeasurable vehicles are in fact the Buddha-vehicle—this is called the characteristic of letters. Now, observing that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen, they are thus without practice, without abiding, unmoving, and non-retrogressive.
Within this, who is there to be a rider of a vehicle, and what dharma should one ride? Furthermore:
This vehicle departs from the three realms of existence and dwells within *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). If one perceives the true mark of the three realms of existence, that itself is *sarvajñā*.
Since there are no five hundred *yojanas* that are not places of treasure, by which path would one wish to travel, and to what place would one go?
Therefore, because all vehicles are unattainable, it is called the Mahāyāna path.
Regarding the statement that the letter-gateway *ra* signifies that all phenomena are free from all defilements (*rajas*): in Sanskrit, *rajas* means "defilement.
Defilement refers to the sphere of activity of deluded sentiments; thus, it is said that the six sense organs, such as the eye, engage with the six objects, such as form.
If one perceives the letter-gateway *ra*, one knows that all phenomena which are seen, heard, touched, or cognized are merely defilements.
The marks are like a clean cloth stained by dust and grime, or like drifting motes of dust that stir up the great void, causing it to become turbid so that the sun and moon are not bright.

This is the discourse on the marks within the analysis of letters. When one seeks with various methods, if one sees that phenomena have no seer, then if there is no seer, who could employ seeing to differentiate external forms? How could there be seeing or the seen?
When one sees that dharmas are non-existent within dharmas, the four dharmas of consciousness, contact, sensation, and craving are all absent;

because craving is absent, the twelve links of dependent origination are also equally absent. Therefore, when the eye perceives form, this is itself the mark of nirvāṇa; the same applies by analogy to the other sense objects.
Furthermore, by means of the gateway of the letter A, one successively examines all sense objects, for they are fundamentally unarisen.

Therefore, because there is no conditioned activity, and so forth, up to the absence of any vehicle or one who rides it, you should know that all phenomena which are seen, heard, touched, or known are entirely the pure *dharmadhātu*. How could the pure *dharmadhātu* defile the six sense faculties of the Tathāgata?
The *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states that with the Buddha’s eternal eye, complete and without deficiency, he clearly perceives eternal forms, and so forth.
The mind and mental phenomena (*dharmas*) are also like this; this is the true meaning of the syllable-gateway *ra*.

Regarding the statement that "the syllable-gateway *la* [indicates] that all phenomena and all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are unattainable," in Sanskrit it is called *lākṣa*, which is translated here as "characteristic.
Some say that there is no difference between nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristic, just as it is said that the nature of fire is itself [heat].

Regarding the characteristic of heat (*uṣma-gata*), some say there is a slight distinction between its nature (*svabhāva*) and its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Its nature refers to that which can be cognized;

for example, when a son of the Śākya lineage undertakes the prohibitive precepts, these constitute its nature, while shaving the head, cutting the hair, and dyeing the robes constitute its characteristic.

If one sees the letter-gateway *la*, one knows that all phenomena possess characteristics. Furthermore, characteristics are of two kinds: first, the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which is [the realization of] non-existence (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The characteristics of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self are distinct from one another;

that is to say, although all phenomena are impermanent and devoid of self, they each possess their own specific characteristics, such as the solidity of earth, the moisture of water, the heat of fire, and the motion of wind. Generosity has the characteristic of relinquishment; ethical discipline has the characteristic of being without regret or affliction;
patience has the characteristic of the mind remaining unchanging; diligence has the characteristic of exerting effort; and meditative concentration has the characteristic of gathering the mind.

The characteristic of non-attachment to signs is the characteristic of wisdom; the characteristic of being able to accomplish tasks is the characteristic of skillful means; the characteristic of consciousness producing birth and death is the characteristic of the world;

the characteristic of the absence of consciousness is the characteristic of nirvana. Now, when one contemplates that the essential nature of both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is empty, with whom would these characteristics function as characteristics?
This is explained at length in the "Chapter on the Three Characteristics" and the "Twelve Gates" of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
It is said: Furthermore, within the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the various characteristics such as the one hundred and sixty mental states are fundamentally unarisen;
being thus unarisen, there is no volitional construction (*abhisaṃskāra*). Because there is no volitional construction, there is ultimately no objective dust (*rajas*);
because there is no objective dust, all characteristics are transcended. Because all characteristics are transcended, it is called the self-realized *sambodhi* of all Buddhas.
Regarding the gateway of the syllable *va*: because all phenomena (*dharma*) are cut off from the path of speech, it is called *vāk-patha* in Sanskrit, meaning "speech.
When one sees the syllable *va*, one immediately knows that all phenomena do not depart from the ground of speech;
for there is not a single phenomenon that does not possess causes and conditions. If a phenomenon is fundamentally unarisen, it is then free [from speech].
For these reasons, the path of language is cut off. Furthermore, if a phenomenon possesses the characteristic of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it can be expressed;
but that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has its path of language cut off. If the characteristic of space were a [definitive] characteristic, it could be expressed;
however, since the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena is like the characteristic of space and is likewise without characteristics, the path of language is cut off. If a phenomenon...
That which possesses activity, transformation, and reflection can be explained;
if there is no activity, no transformation, and no reflection, then the path of language is cut off. Even so, if all phenomena possessed characteristics, they could be explained;
however, since all phenomena are now devoid of all characteristics, they cannot be indicated and cannot be transmitted to others. Therefore, [this is] language.
The path of speech is cut off. Furthermore, one should know that the signless is also without fixed characteristics;
all dharmas are thus characterized, yet without characteristics, and neither characterized nor without characteristics. Just as those three eyes are inconceivable, the path of language is cut off;
other dharma-gates may be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the gate of the letter *śa*, it is because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent (*śānti*). In Sanskrit, this is called *śānti*, which is translated here as "quiescence.

Just as ordinary worldly beings who attain a slight degree of tranquility and still the clamor and agitation are said to have attained "quiescence," so too are those of the Two Vehicles, who have eternally severed the various formations of saṃsāra and realized nirvāṇa, said to have attained "quiescence."
Quiescence is not the nature of things; it is eternally quiescent. Why is this so? Because all phenomena have, from the very beginning, been characterized by constant self-extinction.

Among the three realms and the six paths of existence, what is not itself *nirvāṇa*? When untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises, how does it differ from that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?
Yet, now you alone conceive the notion of extinction (*parinirvāṇa*) within this state—is this not a perversion? Furthermore, if [it were as you claim], then regarding all...

Regarding the fact that the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is quiescent: among the forty-two stages (*bhūmi*), which is not the stage of a Tathāgata, and which is not the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?

If Maitreya Bodhisattva has attained the prediction of birth in one more life (*ekajātipratibaddha*) because his intrinsic nature is quiescent, then all sentient beings should likewise attain such a prediction.
If all sentient beings [do not attain it] within the quiescence of their own intrinsic nature...

If Maitreya Bodhisattva must also practice the affairs of ordinary beings—those which obstruct the cultivation of study—and yet he still forms conceptual distinctions between them, is this not frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*)?

When one enters the gateway of the letter *Śa*, one knows that these dharmas are equal, without high or low, eternally unmoving, and yet there is nothing they do not accomplish; therefore, it is called liberation.
That the Great Parinirvāṇa can contain much and establish great meaning is all due to this.

Regarding the gateway of the letter *sa*—"all dharmas are dull by nature"—if the Sanskrit original were preserved in its literal form, it would say "their nature is identical to that of the insentient.
"Insentient" (*wa[n]*, *mūḍha*) means, for example, like wood or stone, having no capacity for cognition and no sense of touch or sensation. This is what is meant.

The statement that they are "the same" is a figurative expression; it does not mean they are unilaterally identical to that [object]. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Prajñā has no cognition because its self-nature is dull.
This accords with the meaning of this syllable-gateway (*akṣara-mukha*). Thus, the one who embellished the text preserved the terminology of the ancient translation.
Now, that which is "dull by self-nature" is precisely the mind of ultimate non-discrimination—neither deluded nor wise.
Without consciousness, without wisdom, without delusion, and without awakening—even all dharmas cannot shake it;

it is nothing other than a single, pure, and solid adamantine ground. Why is this so? Because worldly people, due to their failure to forget grasping and rejecting, still cherish wisdom and cast aside folly, honoring nirvana while despising birth-and-death; whereas here, it is all of one uniform essence from the very beginning.
If from the beginning there is no arising, and even the slightest trace of inherent nature is quiescent, then who is sharp and who is dull?
It is like a diamond blade: because it encounters non-solid objects and is applied unilaterally, it is called "sharp.

If one were to direct it toward places where everything is entirely diamond, such that its entire body is perfectly rounded and cannot be applied unilaterally, then the quality of sharpness would likewise be subsumed [within that totality].

"It is dull. Regarding the statement that "the gateway of the letter *sa* is because all dharmas and all truths (*satya*) are unattainable," in Sanskrit this is *sattya*, which is translated here as *di* (truth).
"Truth" means knowing the true nature of all dharmas as it is, without inversion or error, just as it is taught.
The sun may be made cold and the moon may be made hot, but the Buddha taught that the Truth of Suffering cannot be made otherwise. Accumulation (*samudaya*) is truly the cause;
there is no other cause. When the cause ceases, the fruit ceases. The path for the cessation of suffering is the true path; there is no other path.
Furthermore, Nirvana is the understanding that suffering is non-existent; therefore, because suffering does not exist, there is the True Truth (*satya*). There is nothing else.

The same applies to the three [truths], up to the analysis of the four truths, which possess immeasurable characteristics as well as the single ultimate truth, as explained in the "Chapter on Noble Practice" (*Āryacaryā-varga*).
This is the characteristic of the "gate of letters" (*akṣara-mukha*).

However, because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, ultimately signless, beyond the reach of language, quiescent by nature, and dull by their very essence, one should know that there is no [discerning] vision.
There is no abandonment, no realization, and no cultivation; seeing it thus, abandonment, realization, and cultivation are all the inconceivable Dharma-realm.
It is both empty, provisional, and the Middle Way; it is neither real nor false, for there is no fixed characteristic that can be demonstrated. Thus it is said that the Truths cannot be apprehended.
This meaning is also extensively analyzed in the "Chapter on the Four Truths" of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
Regarding the statement that "the gateway of the letter *ha* is because the cause (*hetu*) of all phenomena is unobtainable": in Sanskrit, this is called *hetu*, which carries the meaning of "cause.
There are six types of causes, as well as twenty-five types of causes within the context of the meaning of causal conditions (*pratyaya*), as explained in detail in the *Abhidharma*.
If one perceives the gateway of the letter *ha*, one immediately knows that there are no phenomena whatsoever that do not arise from causes and conditions.
This arising is termed the "characteristic of letters" (*akṣara-lakṣaṇa*), for all phenomena are established through mutual dependence on causes;

one should know that because there is ultimately no basis, non-abiding is taught as the root of all phenomena. Why is this so? As the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* observes through various gateways that the causes and conditions of all phenomena are entirely non-arising, one should know that the myriad dharmas are nothing but mind, and the true nature (*dharmatā*) of that mind is precisely...
This is the knowledge of all modes; this knowledge of all modes is the dharma-dhātu of all buddhas; and the dharma-dhātu is the essence of all dharmas, which cannot function as a cause.
Speaking from this perspective, the cause is also the dharma-dhātu, the conditions are also the dharma-dhātu, and the dharmas produced by causes and conditions are also the dharma-dhātu.
What was previously stated regarding the letter-gateway *a*—that it proceeds from the fundamental back to the derivative—applies here as well.
Ultimately reaching such a state, the present *ha*-gate likewise proceeds from the root to the branch, ultimately reaching such a state.

The letter *a* is unborn from the very beginning, yet gives rise to all phenomena; now, by taking the absence of causal dependence as the cause of all phenomena, the beginning and end converge, and thus the intermediate significance may all be understood.
Furthermore, herein, the characteristic of the wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) of the *Pratibhāna-dhāraṇī* refers to: explaining the meaning of all syllables by means of a single syllable;
explaining the meaning of a single syllable by means of all syllables; establishing the meaning of all syllables through the meaning of a single syllable;
establishing the meaning of a single syllable through the meaning of all syllables; and subverting the meaning of all syllables through the meaning of a single syllable. By means of one...

The meaning of all syllables is resolved within the meaning of a single syllable; in this way, one should understand that all syllables—whether rotated in forward or reverse order—are to be known by this same principle.

How is it that a single syllable explains all syllables? For instance, when explaining the syllable *Śa*, one simply contemplates its fundamental non-arising through various causes and conditions, and thereby perceives the meaning of "non-action. This applies even up to the explanation of the syllable *Ha*.
By contemplating primordial non-arising through various causes and conditions, one sees the meaning of causelessness. How so?
Just as when explaining the single letter "A" (A-kāra-mukha) through various causes and conditions, one contemplates the absence of fabrication and thereby sees the meaning of primordial non-arising;
likewise, by contemplating that all phenomena are without cause through various causes and conditions, one sees primordial non-arising.
The meaning of non-arising applies to all other syllables as well; this shall be explained in detail. How do all syllables establish a single syllable?
It is because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, due to being without activity, like space;
due to being without marks, without formations, without conjunctions, and so forth, up to being without causes. How does a single syllable establish all syllables? It is because all...
Dharmas are without action because they are fundamentally unarisen; even all dharmas are without cause because they are fundamentally unarisen.
How, then, can one dharma be refuted by all words? It is like a person who clings to the notion that all dharmas have a basis and an arising;
such a claim must be refuted. If it is said that dharmas arise while being devoid of conditioned activity, this meaning is not tenable.
Furthermore, if one claims that phenomena arise when their causes cannot be apprehended, this meaning is untenable. How so?
Just as a single word can refute all words, so too must the claim of "volitional activity" (kriyā) be refuted for one who clings to its existence.

Since the principle that phenomena are fundamentally unarisen is already established, to claim that there is volitional activity is untenable; this applies even to those who cling to the existence of causes.
This also refutes their statement: "If the meaning that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen is already established, then to claim they have causes is incorrect.
Why? Because of the reversal and turning [of the argument]: if a phenomenon is fundamentally unarisen, then there is no volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*);

if there is no volitional activity, then it is like space, being without characteristics (*animitta*); and if it is like space, being without characteristics, then there is no conditioned action (*saṃskāra*).
If there is no activity, then there is no conjunction; if there is no conjunction, then there is no transition or change.
Furthermore, if there is no cause, one should know that phenomena are fundamentally unarisen—this is called "conformity. If a phenomenon has no cause, then truth cannot be apprehended;
if truth cannot be apprehended, then its intrinsic nature is inert. If its intrinsic nature is inert, one should know that its fundamental nature is quiescent.
If it is quiescent by nature, one should know it is signless; even if it is fundamentally unarisen, one should know it is causeless.
In this way, he speaks by means of various approaches, turning them with mastery. Furthermore, what is now called "all phenomena" is merely their general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*);
if one relies on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, from form (*rūpa*) up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), [they are all such].

The meaning of explaining each [aspect] individually is immeasurable; furthermore, within each gate, one should distinguish the successive stages of the shallow and deep characteristics according to the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra* (Juzhixinpin), for as the gates of syllables (*akṣaramukha*) revolve, their meanings also differ.
By this principle, one is able to give birth to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇīs*. Furthermore, the Tathāgata...
Since all verbal expression is nothing other than mantra, one should universally enter into all sūtras by means of the meaning of these syllables.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If a bodhisattva hears the syllable 'A' within any speech, they immediately understand its meaning as follows:
that all dharmas have been unarisen from the very beginning (*ādita evānutpanna-lakṣaṇa*). 'Ādi' in the language of Qin means 'beginning'; 'an-utpanna' in the language of Qin means 'unborn'."

If one hears the syllable *ra*, one immediately understands according to its meaning that all phenomena (*dharma*) are characterized by freedom from defilement (*raja*; "ra" in the language of Qin means "defilement").
If one hears the syllable *pa*, one immediately knows that all phenomena enter into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*; "paramārtha" in the language of Qin means "ultimate truth").

If one hears the syllable *ca*, one immediately knows that all conditioned activities (*caryā*; "caryā" in the language of Qin means "activity") are in fact no-activities. If one hears the syllable *na*, one immediately knows...
All phenomena are neither gained nor lost, neither coming nor going—as explained at length in the "Chapter on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness" (*Catur-smṛtyupasthāna*) of that treatise.
Furthermore, among all names and expressions, those containing the sound *a* all enter the gateway of the letter *a*;
those containing the sound *ka* all enter the gateway of the letter *ka*, and so on, up to those containing the sound *ha*.
The letter-gateway *ha* is such that within this single gateway are contained immeasurable meanings;
it is not that the letter-gateway *ha* possesses only the meaning of "causelessness. One should know that the other letter-gateways follow this same principle.
For example, *satya* means "truth"; therefore, the Sūtra says: "The letter-gateway *sa* is that in which the truth of all phenomena cannot be apprehended. Furthermore, *satya*...
This "sa" (娑) signifies attachment; therefore, in the *Pūjāvidhi*, it says that the gate of the letter "sa" is that all phenomena are without attachment.
Furthermore, "ba-ba" (婆縛) signifies existence; therefore, the Sūtra says that the gate of the letter "ba" is that the existence of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Moreover, "ba-va-na" (婆嚩娜) signifies contemplation; therefore, in the *Pūjāvidhi*, it says that the gate of the letter "ba" is one—[and so forth].
All phenomena are free from all phenomena; observe that the rest follows this same principle.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Syllables of Nirvāṇa," the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā Sūtra*, and the "Dhāraṇī-īśvara-rāja" chapter of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* each explain the Siddham alphabet in a manner consistent with what is taught in this sūtra.

The meanings of these [teachings] may differ or be identical; if one grasps this intent, then all sūtras will clearly and spontaneously accord with one another, without any contradiction or obstruction.

Furthermore, since every single gateway of syllables (*akṣaramukha*) speaks of "unobtainability" (*anupalabdhi*) in order to clarify the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), we shall now temporarily use the syllable *ca* (the letter for "car") to explain it.
It is like observing the reflection of a face in a mirror, which takes the actual face as its cause.
With the pure mirror as a condition, an image appears; this is the "arisen phenomenon. Because the appearance of its beauty or ugliness manifests before one without error, it is called "existence.
Yet, when sought through various skillful means, it is entirely unobtainable; this is called "emptiness.

This existence and this emptiness both do not transcend the substance of the mirror. That substance is "oneness," while the three characteristics [of existence, emptiness, and oneness] differ in name.
It is neither identical nor different, yet it is both identical and different; therefore, the world’s philosophers are unable to conceive of it. Now, the gateway of Mantra is likewise:
because the oceanic assembly of the universal gate manifests before one through the cause of contemplating the mind and the conditions of the three mysteries without error, it is called "existence.
Because it cannot be found at all when sought through various methods, it is called "emptiness. This is existence.
Since all emptinesses do not transcend the Dharma-realm, they are said to be the Middle Way. While the three truths are distinct, they are identical; while they are identical, they are distinct.
Those who follow the various provisional vehicles cannot conceive of this; other dharma-gates are all like this, and it is impossible to cite them all exhaustively.
The Sūtra states: "O Guhyapati, *aṅgana-maṅgu*, you who possess mastery over all samādhis and can swiftly accomplish all tasks;
whatever aims and benefits you undertake shall all be fully realized.
Within the five classes of sounds—ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa—there are likewise five syllables each; of these, the first through the fourth syllables are all...
The gateways of wisdom have already been explained as before; now, the fifth syllable is a gateway of realization, which shall be explained here together with them.
In the Sanskrit script, these five syllables all share the same circular dot (*bindu*).

For instance, when the four syllables *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *gha* are extended through to the eleventh vowel, a dot is placed above the initial letter; if one wishes to remove this dot, [the following method applies].
Furthermore, when the character *yaṅ* (仰) is successively added above the subsequent characters, those preceding characters become no different from those with a dot (*bindu*).
Moreover, among the twelve vowels of the Sanskrit script, the first is the fundamental essence and is therefore called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*);
the second character is "formative activity" (*saṃskāra*); and from the third onwards, all those that increase by means of strokes are called "samādhi," the eleventh.
The dot placed upon it is the realization; the two dots placed alongside it are parinirvāṇa.
Because this syllable *yaṃ* is the sound of the samādhi of all-pervading wisdom, one should know that its meaning is Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).

For this reason, it is explained separately and not discussed in conjunction with the preceding syllables. As in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, these five syllables also fully clarify the meaning of the syllable *ma*.
Now, the Vairocana school relies upon these five characters to clarify the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*).

Since this Great Emptiness is the locus of realization where no dharma can be spoken, it is represented solely by the circular dot (*bindu*). Furthermore, although this circular dot has no gates within its own essence, it pervades all dharma-gates;
like space, it is free from all characteristics yet contains the ten thousand forms. Therefore, all [dharmas]...
If the letter-gate is provided with the bindu (the dot of emptiness), it possesses the function of mastery and is able to accomplish all matters.
For instance, the wondrous wisdom of non-arising within the letter-gate *A* is that which all sentient beings equally possess;

yet, because they do not personally realize it themselves, they are like a poor woman who has a treasure storehouse in her house but cannot access its power. When the time comes for practice to arise, it is as follows:

When one enters realization through skillful means, it is like a treasure trove appearing before one; at that time, one may enjoy whatever is desired, and all that is sought will certainly be obtained.
Therefore, it is said that by adding this great bindu of emptiness (*mahābindu*), all purposes and benefits are accomplished.

Next, regarding the verse spoken by the World-Honored One concerning the "Mantra Samādhi Gate that Perfectly Fulfills All Vows," the Sanskrit original contains the word *mārga* (path) beneath the term *mantra*;
thus, one should add the character for "path" (*dao*). When a practitioner dwells with single-minded focus upon the syllable *A*, it is called the "A-syllable Samādhi.
This samādhi is precisely the gate of the path of illumination that opens the mind; all other syllables are likewise so.
Furthermore, "all vows" (Sanskrit: *sarva-āśā*) refers to the aspirations of the mind;
that is to say, for all sentient beings who practice this gate of samādhi, whatever they seek with their resolve shall be fully accomplished.
When these vows are fulfilled, it is precisely the inconceivable fruit of the Tathāgata—the fruit of eternal abiding and the wisdom that requires no teacher. It is as follows:
It is able to bestow [attainments] upon sentient beings, let alone the worldly *siddhi* that they desire.
Furthermore, because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the sounds and syllables of each and every gate of samādhi of the Tathāgata remains thus whether a Buddha exists or not, it is eternal;
being non-fluctuating, it is the original ground of the Tathāgata, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Desiring to universally bestow this Dharma-body upon all sentient beings, [the Tathāgata manifests].
Therefore, by means of the empowerment of sovereign spiritual power (*vaśitā-ṛddhi*), such naturally occurring sounds and syllables are sustained;

these sounds and syllables are themselves the empowerment-body (*adhiṣṭhāna-kāya*) of all Buddhas. This empowerment-body universally manifests as bodies corresponding to the various classes of beings, being omnipresent.

One should know that the empowerment of sounds and syllables is likewise so. For this reason, the practitioner should simply, with single-minded attention, clearly take these sounds as the object of contemplation.

The syllables themselves shall naturally manifest the Buddha’s body of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-kāya*). If one sees the body of empowerment, one immediately sees the Dharma-body of the original ground (*mūla-dharmakāya*).
When the Dharma-body of the original ground is seen, it is none other than the practitioner’s own self;

therefore, each and every gateway of these syllables is the inconceivable fruit of the Tathāgata, which does not come from any other place. This is the definitive mantra that fulfills all supreme vows.
Regarding the definition: according to the extant Sanskrit manuscript, it should be stated as "the definitive realization of the true meaning of the mantra possessing all supreme aspirations.

Here, "supreme aspiration" (vara) in Sanskrit signifies being endowed with various merits—namely, the powers of samādhi, dhāraṇī, and fearlessness—and carries the sense that what was wished for has been fulfilled and all that was sought is complete. This is the meaning.
The preceding syllables have distinct Sanskrit pronunciations; as for what is called "definitive," take, for example, the gateway of the syllable *A*.
Whether as a sound or as a letter, its entire substance is non-arising. The meaning of the sound and the letter is that their entire substance is non-arising.
When one realizes this, one realizes only this non-arising; in the interim there is no intermingling, nor is there any alternative path. If one perceives this true meaning, [one enters the gateway].

At that time, even if the Buddhas of the ten directions were to appear simultaneously and speak various similar *pāramitās* in an attempt to change their minds, they would still not give rise to doubt or confusion; therefore, it is called "decisive.
Furthermore, "being endowed with all supreme vows" refers to the Tathāgata’s internally realized merits, numbering as many as the atoms within ten worlds, which are established through decisiveness.
Therefore, each and every one becomes a vajra-mudrā; from this self-realized body, there again arises the body of empowerment. Thus it is said:
"Transcending the three times, stainless and identical to space. This refers to the purification of the inconceivable ground of the mind, which is free from stain.
Because the mandala of the Universal Gate is drawn upon this ground by means of great compassion and skillful expedients.
The sutra continues: "Abiding in the inconceivable mind, one gives rise to and performs all activities.

The Sanskrit original fully reads "the ground of the mind" (*cittabhūmi*), but since five characters form a single verse-line, it cannot be written redundantly; however, because the "ground" is the very essence of the mind, it is simply stated as "abiding in the inconceivable mind.
Although such inconceivable fruits and virtues exist within the gate of mantra-samādhi, [it is here expressed thus].
It is capable of providing for an entire nation and bestowing gifts equally upon all sentient beings.

If sentient beings are unable to conceive the thought that [the Dharma] is difficult to encounter, and thus fail to make offerings and practice, then even if various foods like those of a king’s banquet were placed before them, they would have no intention to drink or eat; what could the Buddhas do in such a case?
Therefore, the sutra continues: "If one reaches the stage of cultivation, one receives the inconceivable fruit. This stage of cultivation is precisely...

This is the first Dharma-gate of the purification of the bodhicitta; it is analogous to how a śrāvaka, after attaining the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), subsequently enters the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Within this Dharma-gate of the hundred syllables, this bodhisattva perceives the world-ocean of the Lotus Womb Maṇḍala (*padmagarbha-maṇḍala*), the characteristics of whose adornments are all distinct from one another.
First, from the gate of the syllable *kha*, the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*)—
Within the center of the wheel, by means of the syllable-gateway *ha*, a great wind-wheel arises; next, upon that, by means of the syllable-gateway *va*, an ocean of fragrant water arises;
next, upon that, by means of the syllable-gateway *a*, the vajra-ground and the mountain of the vajra-wheel arise, as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Within each of these hundred lotus-womb worlds, there is a bodhi-maṇḍala.
Each *ra* (direction) contains ten worlds, with various Bodhisattvas, Vajradharas, and others as their retinues;

this practitioner of Yoga is able, without rising from his seat, to reach all such assemblies of Buddhas and is likewise able to successively seek out and inquire of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Therefore, it is said that a Bodhisattva of the First Ground transforms and returns to the lands of a hundred Buddhas; it is not merely a matter of seeing them, but...
Furthermore, one is able to transform these hundred lotus-treasures into one’s own body;

from the stage of the sprout through the bud of the first bhūmi, when the ten minds are fulfilled, ten gates of liberation open within a single gate of illumination, such that a thousand worlds all receive inconceivable fruits according to their respective capacities.
Upon reaching the eleventh bhūmi, [one perceives] the ocean of clouds of illumination within empty space.
Within each and every gate, one perceives the nature, characteristics, and forms of the Lotus Treasury World (Padmagarbha-lokadhātu), which differ from one another in their successive manifestations;
using these as one’s own body or the bodies of others with sovereign non-obstruction—this is called the fulfillment of the inconceivable fruit.
Next, there are two lines of verse that encourage faith and serve as a seal of authentication, stating: "This is the foremost reality, revealed by all Buddhas. Within this [context]:
The "revelation" (*kaishitsu*) is identical in meaning to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) as found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The subsequent half-verse states:
"If one knows this Dharma teaching, one shall attain all *siddhis*. This cites the path of all Buddhas and likewise exhorts faith in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If a practitioner of *vidyā-mantra* clearly understands the sequential methods within this Dharma teaching, they will certainly believe it and practice according to the instructions.

One shall attain the accomplishment of all *siddhis*. If one were to say that this teaching is not so, then one would incur the sin of violating the original vows of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, thereby deceiving sentient beings. The next verse exhorts faith in the True Truth (*satya*):
"Even young children and cowherds recite and uphold these *Siddham* syllables; as for [their application in] *homa*, offerings, and so forth... [The text continues with the syllables].
The ṛṣi Dāśa and others all practiced together [in this way], yet this gateway of mantras alone has achieved the state of secrecy because it is empowered by the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*).
If one merely recites mantras orally without contemplating their meaning, one may only achieve worldly benefits;
how could one possibly achieve the dharmatā of the vajra-nature? Therefore, the verse says: "Supreme..."
The practitioner who contemplates with focused attention the mantra of the supreme true sound attains the indestructible state.
This sound is the essence of the gate of mantras and the secret of speech; within the sound "A," it signifies the foremost ultimate truth, namely, primordial non-arising (*an-utpāda*).
Initially, the term "mantra" is pronounced with a plural suffix in the Sanskrit original, which serves as the general designation for them all.

This refers to the characteristics of the hundred-syllable gate, the wheel of letters of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). Next, regarding what is called "the characteristic of the mantra," this refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of this mantra;
because it is contemplated through the truths, each and every syllable enters the phrase of the lotus pedestal, which is the place where the traces of thought cease.
The Sūtra says: At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One!
Regarding the path of the Dharma of the inconceivable characteristics of mantras spoken by the Buddha, it is like the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, wherein there are no words within liberation;
yet Vimalakīrti explains the characteristics of liberation without departing from words. Therefore, it is called the characteristic of inconceivable liberation."

Now, this wheel of syllables is likewise: it takes the signless Dharma-body and produces various sounds and syllables, and by means of these various sounds and syllables, it constitutes the signless Dharma-body. Therefore, it is called the inconceivable characteristic of mantra.
It is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor is it for all sentient beings in the general sense; rather, this sutra is for the Dharma King alone.

This secret treasure is not shown recklessly to those of lowly status; for example, although Śākyamuni appeared in the world for over forty years, it was only after Śāriputra and others had made earnest requests three times that he finally briefly expounded the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Since this body of the original ground is the most profound and secret aspect of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the "Life Span" chapter states that [the Buddha] is eternally present.

That the Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and all other dwelling places—even my own Pure Land—remain undestroyed while the multitude perceives them as being consumed by fire, is precisely the intended meaning of the Yoga of this school.
Furthermore, it was only after the Bodhisattva who is next in succession had made three earnest requests that [the Buddha] finally taught it;
since those lacking the capacity for sudden awakening would not enter its grasp, it was not universally taught to all beings.
Birth also refers to receiving the inconceivable fruit upon reaching the stage of practice as mentioned in the preceding verse.
Furthermore, it is said that this constitutes two verses for receiving the understanding and encouraging faith to provide authentication; thus it says:
"If one has faith in this Way of True Mantras, all dharmas of merit shall be declared fulfilled. When they are fulfilled, this is the complete possession of all supreme vows. Thus ends the above.
The detailed explanation of the branches of the mantra is concluded.
Vajradhara again follows upon the preceding text and requests the Buddha to next explain the sequence required for entering the maṇḍala.

Within the verses spoken by the World-Honored One, he first answers the two lines concerning the offering of incense, flowers, and so forth, as well as the various precious vases, summarizing them as a whole.
This is called the branch of the offerings. Regarding the various implements of offering, first clarify the presentation of flowers:
for whatever is offered, one should carefully distinguish each according to the nature and category of the respective deities, as well as their positions within the maṇḍala.
One should ensure that the color, fragrance, taste, and texture are pleasing to the human mind. As for any inauspicious flowers from water or land, they may only be used for cutting.

I humbly submit this report: among the three colors—white, yellow, and red—the Tathāgata family should employ white for its lotus retinue, yellow for its vajra retinue, and red for its [other] retinue.
Furthermore, according to the orientation of the maṇḍala, a circular altar should be white, a square altar yellow, and a triangular altar red. Furthermore...
All Buddhas use white [fragrance], all Bodhisattvas use yellow, and all worldly devas use red; other fragrances should also be applied according to this principle.
Furthermore, one may consult the *Susiddhi* and *Guhya* texts for their application, as they cannot be recorded in full here.
*Padma* refers to the red lotus; in general, all water-born flowers such as blue, yellow, red, and white lotuses may be used.
This is offered universally to all the Honored Ones. Regarding the *nāgakeśara* flower: this *keśara* is the flower of the *nāga* tree;
under this tree, the World-Honored One Maitreya will attain Buddhahood. To refer to it simply as the "Nāga Flower" means it is the flower most esteemed among *nāgas*.
Its species exist quite commonly in the West, such as the *ketaka*, *mallikā*, and *tagara* flowers.
The *campaka*, *aśoka*, *tīrajana*, *pāṭala*, and *sāla* flowers are all found in India;

they cannot be fully identified here in this land. When the sutra speaks of these "fresh and exquisite flowers," the Sanskrit original includes the particle *vā*, which means that these various flowers may all be used interchangeably; thus, they are cited as examples. However, some...
Whatever exists in other regions but is absent in this one—provided it is pleasing to the human mind and regarded by the world as auspicious—all such things may be used for offering.
One should attend to each item with care and distinguish them well, collecting them to form a garland.

This means they are interspersed and adorned, either strung together or tied in knots; because this causes the practitioner’s mind to become earnest, pure, and profound, it will bring about [the desired result].
May all the Honored Ones joyfully protect and mind us.
Next, regarding the description of scented unguents: sandalwood, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, and *kuṅkuma* are all available in this land.
As for the herb named *sarpis* in Sanskrit, it is similar to the *kapūra* of today; the *durvā* grass of the present day is of the same category as *kapūra*.
The sweet flag (*mushukakhāra*) of the Western Regions differs slightly from that found here;

as do other exquisite unguents such as aloeswood (*agaru*), spikenard (*tagara*), clove (*lavaṅga*), cinnamon heart (*citraka*), the Western nutmeg (*jātīphala*), and costus (*kuṣṭha*), as described in the Susiddhi and Guhya scriptures.
Furthermore, it is said that among these unguents, one must not use the bodily parts of sentient beings, nor purple [safflower].
Regarding minerals, insects, and other such substances, one should select those that are pure and excellent and grind them with water.

If making an offering to the Buddha, one should use fresh, high-quality *uraga* (turmeric) or black *agaru* (sandalwood) mixed with *karpūra* (camphor). For the retinue of Padmapāṇi, one should use white sandalwood;

for the retinue of Vajrapāṇi, one should likewise use white sandalwood. For all other deities, one may combine the ingredients as desired according to the specific requirements. As for the [respective]... [text ends].
In all blended incenses (*saṃyukta-gandha*), camphor (*karpūra*) is always included.
Next, regarding the burning of incense (*dhūpa*), one should use agarwood (*agaru*), *gandha-māṃsī*, *vālaka*, camphor, and white sandalwood (*śveta-candana*).
In the West, this is called *mālayu*; it is the name of a mountain, namely the "Māli" mentioned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (translated as "removing Māli").
The mountain where there is no longer any source for producing sandalwood is this very place. *Guggulu* is the resin of the *sāla* tree.
*Śrīvaśaka* incense resembles the *kunduruka* incense of this region;
"śrī" signifies auspiciousness and excellence, and it is so named because even the devas all take delight in this fragrance. It also includes other types of burning incense that are fragrant.

Regarding fragrances praised by the world, it is as explained above: Guhyasamāja states that one should use white sandalwood and *agaru* (aloewood) mixed together to make incense for making offerings to the Buddha Family;
the resinous incense of the tree [sandalwood] for the Lotus Family; and black *agaru* and *guggulu* (bdellium) for the Vajra Family.
Alternatively, one may prepare a general blended incense according to those methods to present to all the Honored Ones, as appropriate.
Regarding the "Dharma teachings," this refers to the removal of defilements through mantras, mudrās, and empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*), as explained in the sequence of offerings;
other items such as unguents and flowers may be understood by analogy with these.
Next, regarding the statement "offering various foods according to the teachings": as in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtras*, each of the food offerings and so forth has its own methods of preparation;
however, their profound and secret meanings correspond individually to specific dharma-gates.

Since these have not been fully transmitted here [in this land], one simply follows the *Susiddhi* and other such texts to fashion the offerings according to the rules, performing the rites of binding, protection, and empowerment—this is what is meant by "relying [on the teachings]."

Regarding the "milk gruel" (*kṣīrayaṣṭi*) mentioned in the teachings: in the Western regions, there are many varieties of porridge, some made with sesame juice, others with various beans and medicinal flavors, as explained in detail in texts such as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-bhaiṣajya-vastu*. Nevertheless, milk gruel is considered the most superior.
Whenever offering food, one should further add ghee, sugar, and so forth to ensure it possesses both color and flavor, and thus present it first.
Furthermore, in the western regions, there are many varieties of rice, among which rice mixed with curd (*dadhi*) is considered the most excellent offering.

When serving this food, it should be accompanied by flavors such as granulated sugar, salt, and ginger. One should also present soup, prepared according to the culinary methods of that region or following local customs.
As for the *modaka* (joy-balls), one should boil various cakes in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and mix them with a variety of seasonings.
The *maṇḍaka*—variously adorned with the three kinds of pungent spices and other ingredients—is a type of thin pancake from this region (China).

As for the hundred-leaf cake (*śatapattraka*), it is a culinary method of Western India: flour is mixed with sugar, honey, and various flavors, then boiled in vinegar and oil until it becomes extremely sweet and delicious.
Regarding the "sugar cake," this sugar is called *khaṇḍa*, and its appearance is like that of the sugar produced in Yizhou (Sichuan).
This substance is extremely white and crumbles upon touch; it is used by mixing with water, first soaking several flour cakes within it, and then eating them.
"Pure and exquisite" means making them particularly refined and clean so that both color and fragrance are fully present.
*Pulikā* is translated as "stuffed cake," which is made by combining various superior flavors and hollowing out the center while preparing it.
There are two kinds of cakes: some are pierced with holes, while others are shaped like tangled threads with layers of perforations and enriched with various flavors.
*Mṛdvīkā* cakes are also coated with honey and smeared with molasses and sugar.
*Paiṇḍolika* cakes are made from leavened flour, fried in clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and resemble lovely bubbles floating upon water.
There is also no "you" (yǒu); these are rolls, sugar cakes, and *pātra* (bōpózhā) snacks, which are not made of flour and satisfy hunger.
Such various delicacies and cakes are also referred to as whatever superior flavors and rare, exquisite fruits exist in various regions, offered according to one's inclination.
As for the white sugar, rock honey, granulated sugar, clarified butter, and honey, each of these is set out separately.
Regarding those who drink various syrups, the methods for Western syrups are extremely numerous; they are all mixed with fragrant medicines to make them delicious and effective for curing illnesses.
There are also various non-time-appropriate syrups (*vikāla-pāna*), such as those made from grapes, as described in the Vinaya.

Furthermore, when consuming milk and curd, one uses *pi-p'o* (pippalī) or *lung-lao* (kakkola), following the dietary prescriptions of medical science. In general, this is the manner of preparing food and drink in the West.

Regarding the sequence of priority, it is largely based on the art of medicine; because there is the merit of nourishing one's nature and preventing disease, most people complete their natural lifespan and rarely suffer the calamity of premature death.
Whenever food is placed, one should smear fragrant ointments all over the area.
Within the food container, lotus leaves, lotus petals, or plantain leaves, etc., should be spread out to surround it completely; if these are unavailable, [one should use whatever is appropriate].
Using a new, clean white cotton cloth or a clean piece of cloth, wash it thoroughly with pure water and smear it everywhere with fragrance.
When arranging the food, one should increase the number of deities for the presiding honored ones:

specifically, Vairocana of the Central Womb Matrix (Garbhadhātu), Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi of the second court, the four bodhisattvas beginning with Mañjuśrī of the next court, and Śākyamuni of the outer court.
Regarding the placement of the principal deities and others whom one worships: even if other [deities] are assigned one part, the principal deities should be assigned two parts;
or if others are assigned two parts, the principal deities should be assigned three parts. Guhyapati said:
"The Lord of the Maṇḍala should be increased by a multiple of those numbers. Although there are such differences in these gradations, from the Buddhas above—
Down to the worldly spirits and deities, one should offer them with an impartial mind, ensuring that the offerings are abundant and equal.
Even for those who cannot afford this, one should simply make offerings to the Lord of the Family or place food within the inner courtyard;
by extending the mind to offer to all the honored ones, the same principle applies to the incense, flowers, and other offerings presented. Thus it should be understood.
Next, regarding the offering of lamps and light: there are many types of fragrant oils, such as *campaka* oil, *sumana* flower oil, and so forth.
As for the method of preparing these fragrant oils and the like, one should take fresh flowers and string them according to the method for making garlands.
Hang them in the sun and place an oil vessel beneath them. Using an implement, draw up the oil from above and pour it onto the flowers, causing it to drip back down.
Once the oil has been used, take more oil and pour it in; thus one proceeds in cycles from sunrise until sunset, at which point one stops.
On the following day, one again takes fresh flowers and performs the rite as before, continuing until the fragrance of the oil is equal to the fragrance of the flowers, and only then ceasing.
As for the vessels for the food offerings, the lamps, and so forth, they are made of various precious gems.
Regarding the superior [arrangements]: if one cannot afford silver, copper, or the like, even new and clean earthenware vessels will suffice for the purpose.
As for the silk banners and canopies on the four sides, if one has the financial means, it is best to place them separately before each individual image;
furthermore, using various precious gems is superior. If one cannot afford these, one should use various colored silks, or even paintings.
At that time, one must use pure materials and may not use glue or similar substances. If one cannot construct it extensively, one should at least place a canopy on each of the four sides;

as for the gate markers, bells, and so forth, these should all be fashioned according to one's means with various adornments, while also conforming to the characteristics shown in the "Chapter on Entering the Secret Maṇḍala Positions."
The Sūtra states: "Alternatively, one may perform all offerings with the mind alone. As the World-Honored One has taught, among all forms of offering, the mind is supreme.

As previously explained for each individual offering substance, one should direct the mind to pervade the entire Dharma-realm and sustain it with mantras and secret mudrās, as detailed in the section on the sequence of offerings; or alternatively, one may visualize the Great Jewel Tree King.
Pervading all worlds, it is fully adorned with the characteristics of the Bodhi-tree King of the Avataṃsaka;
from within it, every requisite for enjoyment emerges in inexhaustible abundance.
Reaching before all worthies and sages, one performs vast offerings and universally delivers all sentient beings. Having cultivated such a mind, one should then...
By means of the empowerment of the Queen of Mantras of the Ākāśagarbha-Parivarta, accomplishment is spontaneously achieved according to one's wishes.
Next, the method for the auspicious vase (*śrī-kalaśa*) is explained: it should be made of gold, silver, or other precious materials;
if none are available, it should be made of porcelain or clean clay. It must be perfectly round and well-proportioned, and it must not leak, following the skillful means prescribed in the Vinaya.
Filter pure water and fill [the vessel] with it; place within it the five jewels, the five grains, and the five medicines—these are explained in the *Guhya* [Tantra].
However, these five medicines all originate from the Five Indias and cannot be found everywhere in this land.

Furthermore, take the various ointments and powdered incenses mentioned previously, mix them with water, and together with camphor and bezoar, place them in the flask and insert [the medicinal herbs] therein.
Using precious flowers, or whatever famous flowers exist in the local region, select those with flourishing blossoms, fruits, branches, and leaves that are complete and perfect;
have them interspersed and hung down so as to be extremely magnificent. Wrap their necks with colored silks and tie flower garlands upon them, anointing them with various fragrances.
The methods for binding, protecting, and purifying them are also as explained in the sequence of making offerings within the *garbha* (womb-palace).
One should place five vases within the mandala; the central Vairocana vase is placed upon the flower pedestal (*padma-kośa*), while the others are placed among the outer petals.

When offering the food of the *garbha-maṇḍala*, the four Buddhas and four Bodhisattvas each occupy their respective seats within the flower pedestal, while those offered to Vairocana are placed before the flower pedestal.
If one has the capacity, [offerings] should be made at the location of each individual deity.
Place one flask; if that is not possible, place them according to the internal or external directions at the locations of the principal deities.
Place two flasks at each of the four gates and one flask at each of the four corners. Outside the gates, there is another flask separately;
empower it with the mantra and mudrā of Trailokyavijaya. When entering or exiting, use it to sprinkle oneself for protection and for summoning.
When the disciples enter, they should likewise sprinkle [water] at the site of the homa. Furthermore, one should set aside another flask—approximately one hundred flasks in total.
The Sūtra states that six flasks is the minimum limit; one should place one in each of the four directions of the central womb and one outside the gate.
This flask outside the gate must certainly not be omitted. If eighteen flasks are used, [the arrangement is as follows]: the center...
Place one flask at the center; in the second courtyard, place one flask each for Mahāvīra, the Lord of the Lotus-Vajra Family, and the gates—making four flasks in total.
For the four great bodhisattvas of the second courtyard, such as Mañjuśrī and the others, place one flask each.

As for those used at the four gates and four corners of the outer courtyard, as well as outside the gates, use as many as desired for the recipients of initiation; if there are many, [use accordingly].
One should have as many jars prepared as there are people, ensuring that none are omitted.
Just as with the incense-water jar, the same applies to all *argha* vessels. These bowls should be made of gold, silver, white crystal, and so forth;

alternatively, one may use conch shells, wrought copper, stone, wood, tree leaves, or new earthenware to hold various perfumed waters and place famous flowers within them, just as was done with the previously mentioned jars.
At each location, one should also place [an offering]; furthermore, at the positions of each deity, one should present pure garments as previously described.
Since the method for presenting food for the principal deities is to be doubled, it is said that "each shall be presented along with garments.
If one is unable to provide these, one may simply place them at the positions of the principal deities, or use boxes or baskets according to what one possesses.
