Within the Garbhadhātu-maṇḍala, one should direct the mind to make offerings to all the deities. Generally, when presenting the offering implements of the Garbhadhātu, they should be placed within the first layer of the empty space surrounding the central womb.
Furthermore, when making offerings to the nameless deities, they should be placed inside the perimeter of the three-layered boundary.
Moreover, at the time of worship, one should first present arghya water, followed by the offering of fragrant ointment, and then...
The sequence of the scriptural text—flowers, incense, food and drink, and finally the offering of lamps—is not in its proper order.
Furthermore, if one provides a profound and esoteric interpretation: "unguent" (vilepana) signifies purity;

just as worldly unguents can cleanse filth and alleviate the torment of feverish affliction, so now the practitioner uses the *argha* vessel, equal to space, to wash and purify the one hundred and sixty [defilements] within the bodhicitta.

The stains of various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are removed by dwelling in the unconditioned precepts (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*), whereby the heat and affliction of birth and death are extinguished and the nature of coolness is attained;
therefore, it is called "unguent" (*vilepana*). That which is called "flower" signifies arising from compassion;

that is, these seeds of the pure mind blossom as the myriad practices within the matrix of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*), thereby adorning the Bodhi-tree of the Buddha; thus it is so described.
To burn incense for the flowers signifies the meaning of pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
Just as when the king of celestial trees (*devadruma*) blooms, its fragrance naturally spreads everywhere—both against and with the wind—so too is the fragrance of Bodhi.
As each individual merit is consumed by the fire of wisdom and fanned by the wind of liberation, it turns freely through the power of compassionate vows, universally perfuming all.
Therefore it is said that burning incense and offering food and drink is the supreme nectar, the flavor of neither birth nor death.
If one partakes of this flavor, the fruit and virtue are accomplished; since there is no flavor superior to this, it is then called "entering realization. Thus it is spoken of as "food.
As for what is called a "lamp," it signifies the Tathāgata’s light that destroys darkness. When one reaches the stage of fruition, the mental hindrances are entirely...
Because they transmit the inexhaustible wisdom to its ultimate limit and universally illumine all sentient beings, they are called "lamps.
If explained vertically, each of the stages (*bhūmi*) possesses these five meanings; if explained horizontally, each of the gates (*mukha*) likewise possesses these five meanings.
This is, for example, as clarified in the preceding text: although various foods differ, their suitability for the palate is one and the same, depending on the person who prepares the meal.
Just as the body and hands possess various distinct flavors that differ from other fragrant flowers and the like, one should know that all such cases follow this same principle.
If a practitioner is skillfully able to perform the Vajra dance through the five-gate syllables (*pañcākṣaramukha*), universally responding to sentient beings— just as one blends the five flavors,

arrays the five colors, harmonizes the five tones, and compounds the five medicines— then although their essential components do not exceed five types, they manifest in a thousand transformations and ten thousand variations.

Their skillful transformations are inexhaustible; one should know that such a person understands the meaning of the Samādhi of Ointment Incense, as well as the meanings of the Samādhis of Flowers, Burning Incense, Food and Drink, and Lamp-Light. They also understand the meaning of these five kinds of dhāraṇīs.
By means of such various Dharma-gates and ritual offerings, they are able to make offerings to the Tathāgata Mind-King.

This causes all the Honored Ones to rejoice and ensures that whatever is sought will certainly be obtained. If one understands the underlying intent herein and contemplates the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),

one will naturally know that the nature and portions of those forms, fragrances, flowers, and so forth, as well as their respective applications, arise through immeasurable skillful means in contact with all things.

Chapter Two, Part Four: The Chapter on the Mantras for Entering the Maṇḍala with All Requisite Conditions.
The Sūtra states: "Having thus performed the offerings, one next leads in those to be initiated," and so forth.

This clarifies the section on empowerment and instruction (*adhiṣṭhāna-śāsana*) as well as the section on *homā* at the time of the actual ritual procedure. Within the empowerment and instruction, there are generally three [parts] that respond to Vajrapāṇi.

Question: Regarding the three phrases—how to lead the disciple, how to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and how to make offerings to the master—once these have been asked, one then asks about the site for the *homa*.

In this response, first the leading of the disciple is explained, followed by the clarification of the *homa*, and then the remaining two phrases are answered. However, the *homa* applies to all ritual matters and is not limited to [these alone].
Since this concerns only the empowerment of the disciple, it is appropriate to treat it as a distinct branch [of the ritual].

This was already clarified in the previous fascicle during the explanation of the seventh night, the actual time for performing the rite, where the specific branches required were explained separately within the layout of the maṇḍala.
Because the flow of the text was interrupted there, I shall now continue from that preceding passage and explain the sequence once more. The Ācārya...

Once the mandala has been completed by Li, he observes it thoroughly; having ascertained that it is perfectly complete, he goes outside and performs ritual sprinkling for purification according to the rules.
As before, he directs his mind to universally prostrate to all Tathāgatas, confesses his transgressions, and takes refuge, thereby purifying his own three karmas.
Thereafter, following the ritual of offering, he binds the samaya-mantra and so forth to protect his body. As for those various articles of offering:
Furthermore, one should remove impurities and perform the ritual of expulsion using the *Amogha-mantra*, ensuring that all preparations are pure and in accordance with the Dharma.

One should also don the *Vajra-armor* (vajrakaṅkaṭa), performing each action according to the instructions of the *ācārya*. When manifesting as the body of a Tathāgata, one should use the *Tathāgata-armor*;
when manifesting as a Vajra-body, one should use the *Vajra-armor*. These should be employed by alternating between them as appropriate.
Furthermore, according to the Susiddhi and other texts, it is especially excellent to adorn one’s own body with the marks such as the *uṣṇīṣa* and the halo of the Tathāgata;
alternatively, one may perform this using the *Sarvakarmasādhana-mantra*.
Having done so, one then proceeds to the position within the maṇḍala and sits according to what is appropriate, abiding in yoga and first employing the syllable-gateway *ra*.
Purify the mind thoroughly. Next, purify the site of the maṇḍala, completely removing all afflictions until it is identical to empty space.
Then, by means of the syllable *HA*, give rise to a great wind-circle; upon that wind-circle, by means of the syllable *VA*, give rise to an ocean of fragrant water;
and by means of the gateway of the syllable *A*, give rise to the vajra-ground and Sumeru, the King of Mountains. One should know this to be the maṇḍala.
The syllable *ra* is then positioned upon it; according to the method for the sequence of offerings, one skillfully visualizes various adornments and sustains them with the *Ākāśagarbha* [mudrā].
Next, upon each of the positions of the deities within the individual maṇḍalas, one visualizes their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).
From these syllables, they all transform into the bodies of the deities, provided that the Ācārya’s path of visualization is such.
If you fear that the visualization will not be integrated and time will be wasted, simply contemplate the letter *A* on the lotus pedestal within the central womb;
from this gateway of the letter *A*, immeasurable light radiates, pervading the seats of all the honored ones. At that moment, the honored ones immediately appear.
Then, through skillful means, one turns the contemplation to see that these honored ones and one’s own body are non-dual and indistinguishable—these are the Buddhas.
The Venerable One is right within one's own body. The Ācārya says: "If a practitioner has not yet established themselves in yoga, how can they construct such a maṇḍala ritual?
Even at the time of its initial establishment, one must first visualize [the deities] within one's own body, and only then draw them.
Furthermore, for a master of profound practice, he is always accompanied by such a holy assembly from the Great Compassionate Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha)."
Realize that this very mind of mine is identical to those ten phrases of dependent origination, which are ultimately unfindable.

Having visualized the deity, next further direct the mind to create various jeweled vehicles, consecrating them with the mantra and mudrā of Acala to welcome the assembly of sages and purify the path. Next, perform the invocation; as for Gaurī, say: "Each of you should..."
One should invite each deity using their respective root mantra, or invite all the deities collectively using the mantra of the Maṇḍala Lord;
or, according to what is taught in one's own specific tradition, one may employ the mantras and mudrās for summoning and inviting as extensively or concisely as desired.
Furthermore, according to the tenet of this sutra, the invited deities receive the invitation at their original seats and, by means of the "non-coming" aspect, arrive here at this ritual site.
In the intermediate state of coarse preparatory means, once the great assembly has gathered, one should employ the Immovable Vidyā to dispel obstacles;
then, having revealed the three types of samaya, one performs the empowerment.
Next, one should offer argha water and prepare a seat, speaking these words: "Welcome, Bhagavān! Welcome, Bhagavān! By the power of your original vow..."
Please descend and arrive; we pray that you grant your empowerment and accept this request and our humble offering. Out of great compassion, please deign to accept it.

At this time, the Ācārya, wishing to perform the Vajra rites, further uses the sword of immovable wisdom to remove his own bodily obstructions, transforming himself into Vajrasattva to subdue the activities of Māra, and furthermore binds the various [mudrās] with the sword of wisdom.
Furthermore, one should again bind the perimeter of the square boundary using the Tathāgata Great Boundary mantra and mudrā;
protect each of the four directions with the four Great Protectors, and universally protect them all by holding the Unbearable Great Protector (*Akṣobhya-mahārakṣa*). The Ācārya says:

"In the construction of a maṇḍala from the very beginning, one should employ either the Immovable Honored One (*Acalanātha*) or the World-Subduing Honored One (*Trailokyavijayanātha*) for protection."
In the space between these grounds, whenever one performs the recitation, one should perform the ritual boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) according to the rules and then release it;
when the night for the ritual arrives, one should again measure with a vajra-thread and fully establish the boundary within.

At the site of the initiation and homa altar, one should further use thread to form a perimeter outside the maṇḍala so that it connects with the inner boundary, and place the [ritual] implements therein.

If, at the time of entering, the outer perimeter of the maṇḍala is completely enclosed by vajra-lines, then when performing the homa offering, one should likewise direct the mind toward the gate of passage and lift the upper vajra-line so that the various deities may pass through.

Furthermore, when binding the boundary (sīmābandha), one should simply perform the ritual as usual at one's own seat; however, if one wishes to perform a circumambulation, [the line must be adjusted].
If one circumambulates once and binds the boundary, all [rites] will likewise be accomplished.
Should the boundary be broken due to a sudden thought of delusion, or if various demonic obstacles arise, one should immediately maintain the mindfulness of the Great Protection of Akṣobhya.
If one wishes to remain free from obstructions at all times, one should first protect the perimeter boundary, the offerings, and so forth with this Great Protection.

At a later time, when obstacles arise, one should again employ [the ritual]. Next, one should perform prostrations and offer *argha* water, sprinkling all the offering implements thoroughly with the Great Wisdom Sword. One should purify them with the mind of the inconceivable *dharmadhātu*.
When presenting scented ointment (*vilepana*), one should abide in the *vilepana-samādhi* and maintain it with the *vilepana-mantra*. Furthermore, during the sequential offerings...
To each [offering], add the mantra of that respective deity—whether general or specific, or one personally maintained;
other offerings should be treated accordingly. Furthermore, perform the mental offering (*cittapūjā*) by reciting the *Gaganagañja* mantra and the *vajrāriṣa* chant in praise.
Next, go outside and offer food to the *Kṣetrapāla* (Field Protector) spirits according to the diagram.
Outside the eastern gate, offer to Vināyaka; outside the southern gate, offer to Kṛtyā, who is a malevolent spirit that possesses people;
outside the western gate, offer to Graha, who causes epidemics; and outside the northern gate, offer to Ḍākinī.
On both sides of each gate, place four positions. Furthermore, according to Gūhī, these include Rākṣasas and Piśācas.
The bhūtas who consume flesh and blood, various non-human beings— whether dwelling on the earth or in forests—
and those with whom one has a mental connection, shall each be summoned from their respective directions and offered food everywhere.
All the food for the offerings to the maṇḍala’s retinue shall be gathered together in one place, along with various incenses.
The flowers and other offerings should also each be set aside individually and then placed together in one location.
The Ācārya, having aroused a mind of great compassion and the intent to bestow the Dharma-gift infinitely, should, within the yoga, visualize these as various articles for enjoyment;
he should then empower them with the *Gaganagañja-parivarta-vidyā* and scatter them as gifts. When these spirits and deities receive the food, they do not form a maṇḍala.
The *rājavāraṇa* (obstacle-warding) should first be performed from the east; then proceed to the south, west, and north, completing one circuit in this manner.
Next, perform it in the northeast, then proceed to the southeast, southwest, and northwest, completing another circuit.
Returning to the east of the altar, offer food to the spirits of the upper realm; then proceed to the west of the altar to offer food to the spirits of the lower realm.
Generally, when offering food three times during the various ritual procedures, this particular rite is especially difficult.
At that time, there may appear various extremely terrifying forms, or one may hear loud sounds such as the crashing of thunder or the howling of jackals;
amidst such various extraordinary signs, the ācārya must remain well-composed and at ease. Furthermore, before wishing to bestow [the offerings], he should first further protect himself.
One should serve each person according to the Dharma; if their food is exhausted and they seek more, one should give it to them again, ensuring it is abundant so that they may be joyful.
If the material is scarce, one should simply provide whatever is available.
Furthermore, when making offerings within the maṇḍala, one must do so with a mind of equanimity, without any omissions or deficiencies. Guhyaka said: "When serving the food..."
If there are errors or omissions, they should be rectified; furthermore, I pray that you accept with joy whatever food items have been offered.

If the types of food are not complete, they should be supplemented with other substances to ensure the full count. Once the offering of food to all directions is finished, wash the hands and sprinkle water for purification.
Then, burn incense at the entrance as an offering, and next enter within to present *argha* water, burn incense, and mentally offer garments.
Having performed the preparatory offerings (*kṣuṇa-dāna*), one then takes the seat of yoga (*yoga-pīṭha*). With the five-syllable wheel, one sustains the body and head;
placing the King of Universal Radiance (*Śataraśmi-prabhāsa-rāja*) at the crown, one gazes upon the lotus pedestal of one’s own mind with stainless eyes.

Since the syllables are originally unborn, one then performs the universal-gate recitation (*samantamukha-japa*). First, the mantra appears vividly within the moon-disc of Vairocana’s heart, and then one recites it. Furthermore—
Having shown the pervasive *guhyamudrā* within the central *garbhadhātu*, one proceeds next to the deities of the second enclosure and so forth until the end.

One may perform the recitation while visualizing each [deity] appearing before oneself, or one may manifest as that very *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) and visualize the syllables of the mantra upon the moon-disc in one's heart while performing the recitation,
or even suddenly manifesting the body of the maṇḍala itself while performing it.
The practitioner who performs the recitation should contemplate the power of their own mind;

if they are unable to do so, they should recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family one hundred times with a single-minded focus, and for each of the remaining principal deities, recite seven times while forming their respective mudrās, as explained in detail in the sequence of offerings. Once the Ācārya has completed these rites, he further...
With a sincere heart, prostrate to all the Honored Ones. Then, summon each of the disciples one by one and lead them inside.
Purify them by sprinkling scented water, and give them unguent to apply to their hands.

Next, bestow pure flowers and briefly proclaim the true meaning of bodhicitta from the "Chapter on Abiding the Mind," so that they may know their place of refuge and generate the authentic resolve with utmost sincerity and devotion.

One should repeatedly bring to mind all the Buddhas; for it is because the practitioner is able to give rise to the Buddha-mind that they become a child of the Buddha (*jinaputra*) and shall receive the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of a Dharma Prince, being born into the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
Therefore, in every movement, pause, or action, one must not forget the Buddhas. Now, in this sutra, whenever it is about to expound any mantra, it invariably states:
To universally take refuge in all Buddhas is precisely this meaning.

Regarding the term "Pure Buddhas" (*viśuddha-buddha*): in the Śrāvaka teachings, even Arhats are called "Buddhas," and other Mahāyāna sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) also contain the sense of attaining Buddhahood;
however, they cannot be termed "Universally Pure. Here, we are correctly elucidating the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*).
Because he is the eternal Buddha, he distinguishes him by means of the pure syllable. In the Sanskrit original, this is correctly translated as "Buddha Family" (*buddhakula*);

"family" (*kula*) carries the meaning of a lineage or class. At that time, the Ācārya contemplates the disciple’s body as the five wheels (*pañcacakra*), sustains it with the five syllables, and further places the syllable *Aṃ* and others within the lotus pedestal of the heart, thereby causing [the disciple] to become identical with the essence of Mahāvairocana.
Seal their crowns with the Buddha-samaya-mudrā; next, seal their hearts with the Dharmadhātu-janma-mudrā;
and again, form the Dharma-cakra-pravartana-mudrā and seal the navel region. Recite the respective mantras three times for each.
Next, transform the letter *A* at the heart into the letter *Va*; then, seal all the limbs with the Vajrasattva-mudrā.
This means that the reason for these five stages is to accomplish that vajra activity;
at that time, the ācārya should also further protect and sustain himself by means of the samaya and other practices.
Next, take a new, clean white cotton cloth or other silk fabric;
first purify it according to the ritual using the Acala mantra, and then apply it three times with the Mantra King of the respective family.
If one is constructing a Mahāvairocana maṇḍala, one should use the Vairocana mantra; for Padmapāṇi and Vajrapāṇi, the same should be applied accordingly—using this purified cloth.

If one wishes to cast [the ritual items] again, one should perform *homā* (fire oblation) and only then cast them; the rest is as explained there.
Next, one should perform the *śāntika-homā* for the disciples; this is the *śāntika* rite, which may also be translated as "pacification.
This is one of its constituent parts, and here, in the Tathāgata’s response, it is presented according to the sequence of the ritual procedure.
The exposition of the branch of empowerment-instruction (*adhiṣṭhāna-avavāda*) being unfinished, it is precisely at this juncture that the *homā* is taught;
alternatively, it may be combined with the methods of initiation (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth as a single branch. The Sūtra states: "Perform the tranquil *homā*;
for one who abides according to the *homā* ritual," where the preceding mention of *homā* refers to the performance of this *homā* method, followed by the subsequent mention of "guarding" (*rakṣā*).
The term "homa" (ma) refers to one who performs the ritual of *homā*; since one must abide according to the Dharma when performing *homā*, it is stated twice for emphasis.
Within this, from the empowerment of oneself through the yoga method up to the invitation and the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), all are based on the skillful means of recitation;
therefore, it says "one should abide according to the Dharma. This begins from the central matrix (*garbha-maṇḍala*) and extends to the second outer [circle].
Regarding those who maintain a mind free from doubt within the maṇḍala, the aforementioned secret terminology explains that the courtyard of Śākyamuni’s retinue constitutes the second great maṇḍala,
which is made to correspond with the central Garbhadhātu; furthermore, the ācārya stands outside of this,
facing the maṇḍala, and between these two positions, he establishes the fire altar (agnikuṇḍa), as indicated by the Sanskrit text.
The esoteric instruction states: "When constructing a homa altar within the ācārya maṇḍala, if one does not receive it from a teacher, one will often lose its essential meaning;
therefore, one should construct it within the precincts of the maṇḍala.
Now, since this must also be aligned directly with the central womb (garbha) of the consecration altar, one may shift this altar slightly toward the south or even the southwest.
From the time of the *koṇa* [corner] onwards, these three positions are mutually related; in principle, there is no error.
A mind free from doubt and hesitation is precisely the intent of *śāntika* (pacification). One should perform it with single-minded focus and without distraction.

If the practitioner abides in the gateway of the syllable *ŚA* and contemplates all phenomena as eternally quiescent, then doubts and regrets will naturally be exhausted forever, and obscurations and coverings will be purified and removed; this is the silent *homa*.
The original intent also prescribes the *maṇḍala* rite: take the measurement of one’s own forearm (*hasta*) for both length and width, making it one cubit;
its depth shall be half that. A border (*pradeśa*) four finger-joints wide is placed all around, with the height being the same.

Generally, *homa* altars may be square, circular, or triangular according to the specific ritual activity (*karman*), but for the rites performed herein, one should use a square altar. [It is to be smeared with] cow dung (*gomaya*).
Regarding the *gomatratuṣā* (the *gomatratuṣa* offering) with scented water, the "marking with the Vajra seal" means that one should draw a *vajra* within the hearth.

The reason for this is that *homa* is the fire of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which can burn away all calamities and misfortunes born of karmic causes and conditions, sweeping them utterly clean until nothing remains. A square altar is called "Great Indra."
*Ra* signifies the meaning of the King of Mind; it clarifies this seal of the fire of wisdom, which exhausts the very source and bottom [of existence].

Because it arises from the nature of vajra, it is identical to vajra and indestructible. As for the causes and conditions, the World-Honored One will explain them in detail later in the "Chapter on Mundane and Supramundane Homa.
If a practitioner of true mantra merely performs mundane homa without understanding [this], [it is ineffective].
In this context, does the underlying intention not risk being confused with the Vedic fire sacrifices?

Therefore, the translator included the name "Wisdom" (Jñāna) so that both the shallow and deep interpretations might be presented together, allowing their respective functions and meanings to be fully conveyed.

The Sūtra states: To the right of the Master’s position, for those possessing the various requisites for *homa*, even if the gate of the Great Maṇḍala opens toward the west, the fire altar (*homa-kunda*) should be situated to the west of the main altar. The Ācārya, moreover, should sit to the west of the fire altar facing east.
All the requisite implements and materials used for the *homa* should be placed to the south of the Master’s position. Protection [is thus established].
The firewood for the ritual should consist of milky trees, such as those of the *śamī* or *udumbara* species, or alternatively, the stems of *gojihvā*.

These should be cut to a length of twelve finger-widths (*dvādaśāṅgula*) and must be fresh and moist. One should select branches that are straight in their grain and observe that they are uniform from top to bottom;
these should be placed with their roots facing toward oneself after being purified by sprinkling them with scented water. When one wishes to kindle the fire, it should be done as follows:
Dip both ends [of the thread] in milk, curd, ghee, and honey, and cast them into the furnace;
or, take agarwood four finger-joints long and as thick as a thumb, dip it in storax, and use it one hundred and eight times—this is especially excellent.
Furthermore, regarding the various foods, incense, flowers, and so forth offered within the maṇḍala, each should be taken individually.
Using the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-mantra*, perform the ritual purification according to the rules and place [the vessel] to the right of your seat. The *argha* vessel should be placed on the left side.
As for the various foods to be offered, they should be prepared by mixing them with ghee, curd, and so forth, and placed together in one vessel;
likewise, the five grains should also be moistened with clarified butter, oil, and so forth, combined in a separate vessel. All of these must be prepared in advance.
Regarding this profound and esoteric explanation: this branch of *homa* (fire sacrifice) signifies the meaning of manifold causes and conditions.

By means of these causes and conditions, the calamities of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*) can arise; now, conversely, by taking these very same factors as the fuel for the fire of wisdom, one makes offerings to the universal body (*sarvadvāra-kāya*) to increase its inconceivable power. As the Sūtra says: "Afflictions are the fuel, and wisdom is the fire. It is because of this.
The meaning is this: by means of causal conditions, one prepares the meal of Nirvana so that all disciples may partake of it with delight.
Furthermore, when performing the ritual for the disciples, one should spread fresh *kuśa* grass on the northern side of the *ācārya*, and have them sit in a squatting posture (*utkuṭuka*).
The *ācārya* himself must likewise sit upon a seat of *kuśa* grass; he must not use items such as couches or cushions. However, regarding the reception...

The use of fresh *kuśa* grass has, in brief, three meanings: first, its nature is pure and free from all pleasant sensations, whereby it can eliminate the practitioner’s mind of dullness, indolence, and arrogance;

second, this is the auspicious grass upon which the World-Honored One sat to realize *bodhi*, and therefore it can remove all karmic obstacles and hindrances; third, by means of this auspicious [grass]...
The *máo* grass symbolizes the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). This plant has many sharp thorns on both sides;
if one sits, lies down, or handles it without skillful means (*upāya*), one will be injured by them. However, if one follows its direction and protects oneself accordingly, it cannot cause harm.

All phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise: if one contemplates them in accordance with the principle of truth (*satya*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) possess the function of inherent purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
If one loses the skillful means, it can damage the wisdom-body; therefore, it is used as a symbolic representation of the dharma-gate.
If one cannot dig a hearth upon a large rock or atop a multi-storied pavilion to construct a maṇḍala, one should instead use colored powders to paint it, making it extremely clear and magnificent;
this may then be employed for practice. This is called the abbreviated method of performing homa.

If one constructs a maṇḍala within a room that is cramped or narrow, one should go outside and construct it according to the ritual rules at a location where the site of the maṇḍala can be seen from afar.
On all four sides of the hearth, one should spread fresh *kuśa* grass in a continuous circle, ensuring they all turn to the right;
their tips should be pressed down against one another and their bases should extend outward, as further described in the *Homa-paṭala*. Furthermore, one should surround [the area] on all sides.
Make it wide and thick so that no part of the ground is exposed, and sprinkle it everywhere with scented water.
One should use the aforementioned mantra for sprinkling the ground, which is empowered to accomplish all purposes (*sarvakarmasādhaka*). Regarding the ritual procedure for the *homa* here:
first, the *ācārya* completes the offerings and recitations within the maṇḍala, and subsequently, he shall go outside to perform the fire rite to the east.
First, having taken firewood and dry fuel from the auspicious *kuśa* grass seat and placed them in the hearth, sprinkle clarified butter (*ghṛta*) over them and ignite them.

Then, place wet wood and recite the mantra for accomplishing the task. After performing the rites of removing impurities, expelling obstacles, and sprinkling for purification (*prokṣaṇa*), one should abide in yoga.

Namaḥ samantabuddhānām (1) Aghnayai (2) Svāhā. The meaning of the first phrase, "taking refuge in all Buddhas," is as explained previously. The second phrase, *aghnayai*, has the meaning of "fire.
In this context, the initial syllable *a* serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen (*anutpanna*).
This is identical to the essence of Vajrajñāna; it is the meaning of "practice" (caryā).

Because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, although one is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices, there is nothing to be practiced. Therefore, it is called "self-awakening without a teacher.
If it is self-awakening without a teacher, it is identical to the Great Emptiness that pervades everywhere and in all places; thus, it is of the same essence as the letter NA.
Because all dharmas are without activity and because they pervade all places, one neither moves nor emerges from the triple world to reach *sarvajñā* (omniscience);
therefore, there is neither vehicle nor rider—this is the reason for the name "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle). The character "so" (爾) is added with the sound of *samādhi*;
its meaning clarifies that this vehicle is the equalization of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). When all Buddhas practiced the bodhisattva path, they all...
Because this fire of wisdom burns away all mental impurities and kindles the radiant light of the True Dharma, it is therefore spoken of as it truly is, becoming a mantra.

take various grains, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), curd (*dadhi*), and other substances, and perform *homa* as an offering to the Fire Deity by reciting the aforementioned mantra three times.
Whenever performing *homa*, one should first fill a large ladle with pure clarified butter and burn it, followed by burning wood, and then protect the site.
Following the rice and other grains, one may burn milk porridge, or again lotuses and so forth, as desired.
During these intervals, all that is offered should be done with a small ladle; thus the Sūtra says: "One should hold a vessel full and offer it in worship.
Having completed the offerings, one should sprinkle scented water again and pour out argha water, just as one uses [water] after a meal.

Having rinsed the mouth with water, one should further offer incense, flowers, and so forth as an offering. One should then direct the mind to escort the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*) and place him upon his original seat.
Next, one should invite the various deities; first, taking a flower and reciting the *Siddhi-mantra* to remove impurities and purify it, one should empower both hands with the *Kulapati-mantra*.
Holding them together with palms joined, one should mentally and verbally say: "I pray that all the deities will bestow their grace."
Holding this at the place where you receive my humble offering, you should immediately cast it toward the maṇḍala from across the incense burner.
According to its distance, when about to cast it, first contemplate that this flower reaches everywhere to the seats of all the honored ones, forming a seat corresponding to each deity's type.
Furthermore, using the *Sarvakarmasādhana* [mantra] within the burner to remove impurities and purify it, you may then invite the honored ones. Or...
One should invite each of those Honored Ones individually by their respective mantras, or according to the retinue of a particular section, or even invite them all at once using the King of Mantras.

Furthermore, since this fire altar is identical to the Great Boundary (*mahāmaṇḍala*), when inviting [the deities], one should simply visualize that all the Honored Ones descend from their original seats;
when the ritual is completed, they likewise return to their original places without the appearance of departing.
For the homa of a single deity, take scented water and sprinkle it upon the hearth, as well as the water for rinsing the mouth;
recite the Mantra for Pacifying Calamities seven times to make offerings in this manner. When each [deity] has been completed, perform the homa one hundred and eight times again.
Once more, offer clarified butter from a full vessel once; if one is unable to do so, one should instead make a total of one hundred and eight offerings.
Alternatively, one may recite one thousand and eighty times while thinking: "In accordance with all that exists here, I pray that all Honored Ones will likewise accept this offering.
Next, one should universally solicit their joy, perform offerings according to the Dharma, repent through skillful means, dedicate the merit, and form the vajra-mudrā.
Recite the hymns while burning incense so that it does not cease, and then offer *arghya*.
Next, prostrate before the deities and summon the disciples as described above, performing rites such as scattering flowers until the instructions are fully concluded.
Only then lead each disciple one by one to the site of the *homa* ceremony, to the left of the *ācārya*, with a mind of reverence.
Squatting, the master grasps the right thumb of the disciple with his left hand and recites the *Śāntikara-mantra*.
With each recitation, he offers one portion of fire-oblation (*homa*). This is done twenty-one times, and each disciple performs the rite in this same manner.
According to Ghuṇika, one should further smear the hands with incense and place them upon the disciple’s chest, holding them there as desired.
Recite this and dispatch [the deity]. Now, I shall explain this mantra for pacifying calamities: *Namo samantabuddhānām. Amoghaśānti-karapraśamadharmānilaya-apavasa vaḥ*.
*Vadha dharma-samanta-pāripātra svāhā*. This mantra takes the initial *a* (pronounced with an abrupt, rising tone) as its essence.
*A* signifies that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally unarisen; it is the essence of the vajra-wisdom fire.
By adding the bindu (*am*), it represents the practice of fundamental non-arising, which is the vajra-intelligence fire.
The two dots flanking the *samādhi* [symbol] signify *nirvāṇa*. This means that by entering this gateway of the letter *A*, one’s wisdom and practice become fully perfected;
thus, one is able to incinerate and eliminate all hindrances and obscurations, attaining the great tranquility of *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, the true meaning of the *Śāntika-mantra* lies precisely in this. Furthermore, when performing the ritual, one should visualize this letter surrounded by a garland of light radiating from fire.
Emerging, it is fully endowed with three colors: its fundamental body is yellowish-white;

its samādhi-form is red like Jāmbūnada gold, with two black dots beside it like the fire of the kalpa-ending eon. Because its intrinsic nature is pure white, it has the function of pacification (śāntika);
combined with yellow, it is the function of increase (puṣṭika); red is the function of subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa) and incineration; and black is for crushing and overcoming (abhicāruka).
It serves both as a great obstacle and for the function of summoning. Furthermore, this syllable-form is a gateway of skillful means;

one should know that it is identical to the color of the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) and possesses various ritual activities. Moreover, regarding the twelve fires mentioned below, the letter *A* is the fire of wisdom;

when combined with the stroke of samādhi, it is the fire of perfected practice, which possesses the meaning of summoning; and it is the fire of wind-drying, which possesses [the power of]... [omitted].
The meaning of "subduing" (dāruṇa) is the *lohita* fire, which is a blend of yellow and red; the *mṛtyu* fire is a blend of red and black;
the *krodha* fire is a blend of all colors; and the *jvalana* fire, to speak briefly, encompasses all twelve types of applications, which shall be explained in detail.
The subsequent phrases below all explain one another in turn. First, *mahāśānti* means "great tranquility," and *gautama* means "gone.
It is said that because the Tathāgata possesses the meaning of this single syllable, he has gone to and reached the great *nirvāṇa* of the eternally quiescent original nature.
The essence of the syllable *A* is inherently quiescent; because it is marked by *samādhi*, the Sugata is fully endowed with pure elimination.
For this reason, Nirvana is immovable; this very place is the path, and reaching it is identical to the Great Void, as there is nowhere it does not pervade.
Therefore, it is called "Great Quiescence. The next phrase, *saṃdhi-kāra*, has the meaning of "making quiescent.

This gateway of syllables signifies that because skillful means (*upāya*) are perfected, one constantly and universally pervades the ten directions and the three periods of time, universally performing the activities of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha-karman*) to bring all sentient beings to fulfillment.
Because it causes one to go to the midst of great quiescence (*mahā-śama*), it is called "becoming quiescent" (*śamī-karoti*).
Next, regarding *praśamadharmānirjāta*: *pra* means "supreme"; *śama* means "to realize this quiescence. This reiterates the previous phrase;
because one "becomes quiescent," it is the quiescence within quiescence. Why is this? Because quiescence is ultimately ungraspable.
Because it is attained, it is eternal; because its activity is ultimately unattainable, it is eternally quiescent.
Because it cannot be conceived by any world, it is called "supreme. *Dharma* means "phenomenon" (*dharma*), and *nirvāṇa* means "extinction.
From what could birth arise? It arises precisely from this inconceivable, quiescent activity. Because movement and stillness are ultimately equal, it has been so from the beginning.
Within the phrase "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), the roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are complete, forming the king of Bodhi-trees.
Just as the fire-element can both burn and nourish, so too does the vajra-wisdom-fire; its function is to purify by burning the *tilaka* (mark) and to nourish the *samādhi-tilaka*.
Next, it says *apavaḥ sarvabhāvāḥ*, which is a further explanation of the preceding phrase, meaning that there is no self-nature (*svabhāva*).
The nature of all things is quiescent by its very essence, yet arises from conditions; therefore, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which arises from conditions is inherently quiescent; for this reason, it constitutes the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svabhāva*).

By virtue of this principle, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise, and Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) emerges. Next, it says *dharma-samanta-prabheda*, which further explains [the preceding].
For this reason, as stated in the preceding sentence, the Tathāgata regards all phenomena as equal, meaning he has realized unexcelled *bodhi*.
*Prāpti* (attainment) here signifies "to obtain," yet because there is nothing to be obtained, he attains this state of equality.
The remainder is explained as above.
Whenever performing a homa, various signs may appear: sometimes the fire burns but does not flare up; or it is extinguished quickly without becoming very intense;
or smoke arises without flames; or the smoke is extremely turbid; or it emits sounds like those of donkeys and other such animals, which people find unpleasant to hear;
or it says things such as "it is not accomplished. One should know that these are signs of obstacles and failure.
Alternatively, if within the smoke and flames there appear various wondrous forms such as jeweled vases, jeweled nets, lion chariots, and vehicles;
or if there are sounds like those of bells, gongs, conchs, and chanting, resembling the resonance of musical instruments;

or if the sound of auspicious accomplishment issues forth—one should know these to be the signs of unimpeded *siddhi*. Furthermore, one who is skilled in performing *homa* should receive special grace therein.
Having been clearly instructed, one fully understands the signs of penetration and obstruction.

For all *homā* rites, one should act according to the specific task at hand—whether it be through a mind of tranquility, joy, or ferocity. Regarding the clothing worn, there are white, yellow, and red;
one should sit facing north, east, or south. Furthermore, the *maṇḍala* may be circular or square in three forms.
The different colors of the prongs may also indicate their use: for pacifying (*śāntika*), one should use the upper branches of trees suitable for *homa* fuel;
for increasing (*paustika*), the middle branches; and for subjugating (*abhicāruka*), one should use the roots.
For pacifying rites, one should use ghee, milk, barley, honey, milk-rice, sprouts of *kuśa* grass, *muñja* flowers, white sandalwood, and *aśoka* wood.
For rites of augmentation (*puṣṭi*), one should use milk-rice, curd-rice, honey, milk-curd-rice, sesame, *devadāru*, *tagara*, *śatāvarī*, *nāgakeśara*, various grains, and so forth.

For rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should use red or white mustard seeds, or mustard oil, poisons, bones, hair, thorns, and thorny wood; although these are not fully detailed in the sūtras, they should be employed accordingly.

One should infer accordingly: for each subsequent ladleful of clarified butter (*sarpis*) burned, the number of sesame seeds is likewise the same; for the remainder, one may act according to one's preference as to quantity.
At both the beginning and the end, one must fill the ladle with clarified butter for the *homa*; all other ritual procedures are similar to this.

Generally, when performing a *śānti-homa* (pacification rite), one must first perform the method of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*); if the mantra employed contains the sense of subjugation, it is used directly.

Recite according to the root text; if its meaning is absent, one should increase it according to the ritual manual using substances corresponding to subjugation, such as *sarṣapa* (mustard seeds), performing the *homā* offering seventeen or twenty-one times.
Next, visualize the phrases and meanings corresponding to enrichment (*puṣṭi*) along with their respective offerings, performing them once, twice, or seventeen times;
only then is the rite for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*) fully accomplished, just as when performing [the other rites].
For the *puṣṭi-homa* (enrichment homa), one must first perform the *abhicāra* (subjugation) rite before it can be fully accomplished as an enrichment rite.
However, the single method of the *abhicāra-homa* is directly effective without requiring preliminary preparations. One should know that this maṇḍala possesses these three types of ritual procedures.
Ghuhyaka states: "After the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is completed, one should again perform the homa according to the ritual rules. First...
Recite the mantra of the Maṇḍala Lord one hundred times while burning ghee; next, recite the Śāntika mantra one hundred times over rice mixed with ghee, honey, and curd;
then, recite it one hundred times over sesame seeds. Only after this should you extensively display the maṇḍala.
When the ritual is nearing completion and you are about to disperse, the master should sprinkle himself with water and further offer arghya, making offerings to each [deity] in succession.
Next, perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings for each of the deities using the Maṇḍala Lord mantra; then, one hundred times with the Śānti mantra;
then twenty-one times with the Family Heart (*kula-hṛdaya*) mantra; then seven times for each individual deity mantra using cow’s ghee.
Thereafter, perform *homa* as desired with the root-holding (*mūla-dhāraṇī*) mantra, and only then perform the ritual release (*visarjana*).
Regarding the methods for dismissing the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth, or alternatively, one may perform them according to the general procedures previously described.
In this sutra, the three syllables *a-sva-vaḥ* are the heart-mantras (*hṛdaya-mantra*) of the three families, as explained in the "Chapter on the Wheel of Syllables" (*Akṣaracakra-paṭala*).
If it is another occasion involving these three types of ritual activities, once the recitation within the maṇḍala is completed, one should immediately depart and perform the protection (*rakṣā*).
When performing the *sādhana-homa*, one must align five points in a straight line: first, the primary deity; second, the fire pit; third, the object to be accomplished;
fourth, the vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*); and fifth, the seat of the *ācārya*. Prior to this, the object to be accomplished should be covered with pure leaves;
each time one takes up the clarified butter and other substances, they should be added using a ladle over these leaves.

If one wishes to incinerate [the object] from above, it shall be done when sentient beings are to be brought to accomplishment; one should draw its image at the place where the object is kept, as described above.
If performing a homa for the protection of humans, one should call out each name individually before casting [the offerings] into the fire.
If there is no maṇḍala and one performs only the homa rite, one should construct a single-layered maṇḍala around the hearth and place all [the items] therein.
Regarding the seats for the honored ones, one may invite them for offerings according to one’s preference, whether extensively or briefly. The Susiddhi states:
"Once the homa is completed, one should always take pure water, empower it with the root mantra, and sprinkle it around the hearth three times while circling it with the hand.
Then, again invite the Fire Deity to receive the remaining offerings, and finally visualize the residual grains returning to their original seats."

Combine ghee, honey, curd, and so forth in one place, and perform *homa* by reciting the *Tattva-mantra* three times while maintaining protection through the repeated performance of the seals for protecting the body,
protecting the directions, and so forth, until the boundary (*sīmā*) is released, at which point you may dismiss [the deities]. Furthermore,
Guhyasamāja states that when the rites for the disciples are completed on the sixth night, one should first perform the *homa* of subjugation (*abhicāra*) in order to eliminate obstacles.
Next, for the sake of one's own increase, perform *homa* with the Family Heart Mantra (*kula-hṛdaya-mantra*).

Then, perform the *śāntika-homa* with the Peaceful Mantra (*śānti-mantra*). When the time for the ritual procedure arrives, if there are frequent inauspicious signs, one should perform the *śāntika-homa* with the Family Mother Mantra (*kulamātṛ-mantra*) one hundred times each using *kaṇḍu* and firewood during the performance of the rite.
Because one must fulfill all deficiencies on the following day, one should further perform one hundred and eight *śāntika* homas.

Furthermore, this fire ritual is a difficult matter among the ancillary rites; since it removes calamities and obstacles and increases the majestic power (*tejas*) of the True Dharma, those who create hindrances and difficulties will all seek an opportunity within this very process. Therefore, if one does not clarify each point individually...
One must realize that self-inflicted harm is not to be committed by acting recklessly according to one's own whims.
As the Sūtra states: "When the practitioner has completed the homa, they should be instructed to offer a respectful gift (dakṣiṇā) as follows.

This response to the question posed by Guhyapati regarding "how to make offerings to the master" still belongs to the branch of empowerment and instruction; therefore, it is taught [here] for oneself.
As for the disciple’s act of making a supplementary offering, it is not done out of attachment to material things or for the sake of seeking them;
rather, it is for the purpose of generating the roots of goodness in others and accomplishing the merit of empowerment.

If the disciple can offer all their various internal and external resources for the sake of this great causal condition, without any stinginess or regret, they shall reverently and sincerely present these as a report to the lineage.

One who practices the Dharma is able to destroy immeasurable karmic obstructions from past lives; furthermore, seeing the benefits of giving (*dāna*), they give rise to a heart of profound joy and gratitude, thinking:
"I now renounce this worldly wealth, which is beloved yet shared by the five families [of calamities] and fraught with many afflictions, to purchase the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma.
This wealth of the True Dharma I bestow universally upon all sentient beings, never to be exhausted."
Having reflected thus, because his mind is joyful and gladdened, he becomes free from doubt and regret; being free from doubt and regret, he dwells in inner tranquility and bliss.
Thereafter, by bathing him with the water of the Dharma, he is able to be forever freed from dust and defilement.
If one possesses nothing else, one should even offer one's own body as a gift to the teacher, meaning that one serves him by offering this very body.
In serving the ācārya, he did not shrink from weariness or hardship, never abandoning his quest for the True Dharma even to the point of disregarding his own life for the sake of seeking the Way.
At that time, the ācārya, moved by his earnest devotion, conceived a heart of compassion and instructed him in profound and secret expedient means,
until the practitioner’s cultivation of the mantras he had received was nearly complete on the Path.
The ritual performed within this site is employed for the sake of bestowal; by expending little effort, one attains great accomplishment.
This is the supreme among all forms of giving. Guhyaka said: "The disciple, at the place of homa, with a heart of utmost sincerity, should prostrate before the ācārya.
First, one should offer two pieces of cloth, and thereafter relinquish other wealth. Furthermore, he said this:
Once the consecration is completed, the characteristics of the maṇḍala are extensively displayed; the instructions on mantras and mudrās are then offered.
This differs from other scriptures, as it may be employed according to one's needs.
The scripture states: "Having already performed the empowerment, one should summon [the deity] and address them. This refers to the period from the initial invocation and entry onwards.
All of this is through the power of his sustaining grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and skillful means (*upāya*), intended now to inspire their minds; furthermore, he instructs them, saying:
"This supreme field of merit is taught by all Buddhas for the sake of extensively benefiting all sentient beings.
This means that the World-Honored One perceives that sentient beings have been constantly impoverished of both internal and external things since beginningless time.
Because they lack mastery over their wealth and all that they do, by these causes and conditions they fall into the states of no-leisure and cannot swiftly reach unsurpassed bodhi;
for this reason, through the power of empowerment, [the Buddhas] together proclaim this unsurpassed field of merit.
Within this treasury of great compassion, there is no great ocean of all universal gateways that is not fully assembled here now.

Because they have extensively planted infinite roots of goodness, from this present life until the end of the future, they constantly manifest as wish-fulfilling jewel bodies and space-treasury bodies, able to fulfill all the aspirations of both themselves and others; thus it is said that they "extensively benefit all sentient beings.
Furthermore, they have already completed the bestowal upon the Sangha of the ultimate truth and those who transmit the Dharma.
Furthermore, he instructs them to make offerings to the Saṃgha of conventional reality;
for when one gives to the Saṃgha of harmony, all the monastic assemblies of ordinary and holy beings throughout the ten directions share in the merit.
Therefore, this merit is like the clouds and oceans of space—inconceivable—and shall result in a great fruit, which is ultimate benefit. To plant merit within this [Saṃgha] is like eating gold.
Since the adamantine [resolve] ultimately does not diminish and must reach the limit of the adamantine ground before coming to rest, Master Sengsheng said:

"Even a single hair’s worth of goodness all tends toward the fruit of Buddhahood. Next, to clarify the rare aspirations of the world, he further explains the meaning of worldly benefit, namely, inexhaustible great wealth.
Because the worldly say it is always present at birth, this is the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the world-accepted standpoint).
It is said in the world that because Bakula offered a single harītakī fruit to the Sangha,
he has remained free from illness for ninety-one kalpas and has never met an untimely death; likewise, because Aniruddha offered a single meal to a pratyekabuddha,
he has been born together with treasures throughout immeasurable kalpas, as is explained in detail in the Jātaka-sūtra.

It is said that [merit] constantly arises in accordance with [the recipient]. Furthermore, it is stated in the Vinaya of the Sarvāstivāda school that among the four great disciples—Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Subhūti—who are like precious vases, if a person makes offerings and shows reverence with a pure mind while seeking worldly rewards in the present life, they will not fail to have their wishes fulfilled;
how much more so for one who gives to the entire Saṃgha? One should know this.
All such virtuous persons throughout the worlds of the ten directions, including even those who have attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa),
rely upon the power of the Saṅgha when they wish to prolong their lifespan and remain in the world. Therefore, now that you desire to attain the fruit of siddhi,
you must ensure that the practice of dāna you perform is complete and without deficiency, and you should do so with a joyful mind.
One makes offerings to the *saṃgha* present before one according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because it is impossible to assemble the *saṃgha* of the ten directions;
by bestowing gifts upon those who have gathered within the boundary (*sīmā*) as they happen to be present, one thereby gives to the entire *saṃgha*.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana again addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets...
Below this, the *vidyā-abhiṣeka* (wisdom-consecration) is explained; it belongs to the section on empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and instructions (*avavāda*).
However, this consecration also applies generally to other ritual matters, or it may be treated as a distinct subsidiary branch (*aṅga*). The *ācārya* shall then construct the second maṇḍala. When...
Facing the central maṇḍala and two cubits from the great maṇḍala is the second, which signifies the "next smaller" [maṇḍala];
this is stated in terms of relative proximity. Generally, the fire hearth should be situated in the center of the womb [of the maṇḍala].

If the location is inconvenient, it may be gradually moved toward the south, even as far as facing the southwest corner; this is the consecration altar (abhiṣeka-maṇḍala), and it is also located within the fire altar.
To the north, one should likewise ensure that the four sides are equal, establishing only a single gate facing the mandala.
On the four corners of the mandala, one should draw four Vajrapāṇis: in the southeast (Agni) place Akṣobhya; in the southwest (Nairṛti) place Gaganāmala;
in the northwest (Vāyu) place Vimalanetra; and in the northeast (Īśāna) place Citravastradhara. In the center of the mandala...
One should fashion a great eight-petaled lotus king complete with a central stamen; within four of the petals, one should place the four companion Bodhisattvas:
in the direction of Indra (East), the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja; in the direction of Yama (South), the Bodhisattva Smṛtidhara;
in the direction of Nāga (West), the Bodhisattva Hitacitta; and in the direction of Yakṣa (North), the Bodhisattva Kāruṇika. As for the four intermediate corners:
The leaves placed in these directions are as follows: in the southeast (Agni), they are called *Catur-śikṣā-dhara*; in the southwest (Nairṛti), they are called *Vicitra-vastra*;
in the northwest (Vāyu), they are called *Pūrṇa-manoratha*; and in the northeast (Īśānī), they are called *Vimukti*.
The Sūtra states that "in the center, the inconceivable color of the Dharma-realm is displayed" refers precisely to this syllable *laṃ*, which is made pure white;

it is the emblem (*cihna*) of the inconceivable Dharma-realm. Furthermore, according to the profound and secret interpretation, the square altar is the essence of the Great Indrākṣa-cakra-vajradhātu, abiding in non-conceptualization (*niṣprapañca*).
The primordial purity of the unimpeded wisdom of the three periods of time arises from this very precept; therefore, all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is stilled.
Because conceptual proliferation is stilled, one attains the great wisdom that is teacherless. When the dust and obscurations are entirely exhausted, it is like the pure void;
thus it is called "stainless as space. Just as when there are no stains or obstructions in space, one gazes across the ten directions without limit.
Not seeing Prajñā is likewise so, because it is free from all marks (*nimitta*).
Since there is nothing whatsoever that is not seen, heard, sensed, or known, it is called the "stainless eye" (*vimalacakṣus*).

Just as one with clear vision can freely perform all manner of activities, so too, having universally observed all faculties and conditions through unobstructed compassion, one shall immediately manifest the form-body (*rūpakāya*) everywhere to provide guidance.

For the sake of benefit, one wears robes of various colors; if these four kinds of vajra-wisdom seals are fully present and without deficiency within a single mind, one is then able to stabilize this ground of the mind and sustain the body of wisdom resulting from empowerment, just as the area beneath the Bodhi tree from the vajra-ground upward has been entirely solid and firm.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, [he was established therein].
"Neither tilting nor sinking" refers to the four companions, which are the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*). These are the companions of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

It is said that when this pure *dharmadhātu*—the mind-king—accomplishes these four dharmas, it is able to perform the four kinds of Tathāgata activities and is thus fit for consecration (*abhiṣeka*) to receive the rank of Dharma King.
The initial mention of the "Sovereign King of Dhāraṇī" refers precisely to the mastery of the letter *A*.
When one encounters this King of Mantras at the gateway, one attains mastery over all dharani-gateways; therefore, it is so named.
Furthermore, because of its sovereign power of total retention (*dhāraṇī*), it becomes like the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels for the Tathāgata’s mindfulness and awakening.
It can sustain the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, just as the secret treasures within a dragon palace sustain the great ocean, preventing it from overflowing. It is also able to...
Because one maintains it so that it is never exhausted, it is called "mindfulness-maintenance.

Having obtained such a treasure of mindfulness, one then recollects one's original vow to universally rain down the wealth of the Dharma to fill the entire Dharma-realm and bestow it upon all sentient beings; therefore, it is named the "beneficial mind.
Having produced inexhaustible resources and performed boundless great acts of giving, yet inferior sentient beings have no intention to receive and enjoy them, nor do they wish to accept them.
Seeking this end, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and, through various skillful means (*upāya*), disciplines the impoverished sons;

thus it is said that "the compassionate one" refers to these four. Those who follow the teachings are those who, from these four gates, perform the deeds of the Tathāgata by means of analysis, subduing, and gathering in.
One should know that wearing robes of variegated colors is the work performed by the Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs (*dhāraṇī-īśvara-rāja*) to fulfill all vows.
This mindfulness maintains the activities of the King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels without any obstruction; it is the activity of the Dharma-gift of great compassion which brings liberation;
it is the activity of the skillful means of great compassion which uproots suffering for sentient beings;
therefore, they are called the "Four who Uphold the Teachings."
Furthermore, regarding the vases made of the four jewels: these are the jewels representing the four virtues of Vairocana, which are placed at the four corners of the central womb as described above.
Having performed the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by means of Acala Vidyārāja, one then uses the mantras of the four Bodhisattvas, each holding one vase:
Samantabhadra represents the jewel of inexhaustible vows and conduct, and Maitreya... [is]... [the jewel of compassion].
The Jewel of Infinite Benefit for Sentient Beings is the removal of the hindrances; the Jewel of Infinite Pure Knowledge and Vision is the removal of the evil destinies;

the Jewel of Infinite Great Compassion and Skillful Means is, furthermore, Samantabhadra, who is the pure bodhicitta pervading the entire dharma-realm, and Maitreya, who is this pure mind generating roots, sprouts, stalks, and leaves within the womb-treasury (garbha), as well as the removal of the hindrances.
This King of Pure Awakening Trees, with its wondrously adorned flowers and fruits manifesting in full bloom, eliminates the evil realms;
having gathered these fruits, they are sown again within the fields of all sentient beings.

Thus revolving and producing one another in an endless succession, these four precious jars are filled to the brim with various precious medicines and grains, soaked in water of intrinsically pure nature.
By using this to consecrate the inconceivable mind of the Dharma-realm within the center of the lotus pedestal, one is thus named a son of the Dharma King.
It should be known that a single precious flask corresponds to a single Bodhisattva, a single Vajra, and a single messenger;

through the application of skillful means (*upāya-dvāra*), this resonance between the stimulus and the response can be understood. Whenever one intends to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), these are used to accomplish the task.
Having consecrated the seat with mantras and placed it upon a lotus pedestal, the ācārya again performs the ritual protection of the disciple’s body according to the dharma:
first, he employs Acala Vidyārāja to eliminate all obstacles; next, he employs the three types of samaya to consecrate the three places;
and finally, having consecrated the limbs with Vajrasattva, he causes [the disciple] to assume the auspicious posture (*śrī-āsana*).
Seated therein, all the ointments, flowers, lamps, and *argha* water should first be consecrated according to the ritual, as described above.
The *ācārya* should first offer that scented water, then use the ointment to smear his entire body, and adorn him with flower garlands and crowns as necklaces.
Next, he should offer incense to fumigate him and present the various lamps.

Arrange these before him and present various foods; these offering articles comprise thirteen seats in total, namely those for the four Vajras, the four Bodhisattvas, the four Messengers, and the Disciples.
The offerings for the Disciples should be made most abundantly, as if making offerings to the Principal Deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
Alternatively, one may also arrange their positions within the Great Maṇḍala and perform the offerings there. Up to...
At the time of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should merely hold their names and request their empowerment for the disciple.

One should place those four bodhisattvas, each in a different direction within the first enclosure (*prathama-maṇḍala*). As for the messengers, they are placed below the Tathāgata, flanking the doors on both sides.
Furthermore, prepare a new, clean white parasol with flower garlands and white silk suspended above it; first, employ Acala to remove stains and eliminate obstacles.
The Ācārya himself should hold it while reciting the mantra of Mahāvairocana to cover its top;
furthermore, he should have others hold a pure yak-tail whisk, a fan, and an incense burner, all consecrated with the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna* mantra.
Inside the chest, one should place garments along with auspicious objects, namely: a golden probe, a bright mirror, a wheel-jewel (*cakraratna*), and a conch shell (*śaṅkha*).
Together with these [attendants], one should hold vases made of the four jewels to offer them, while performing the *Saṃgrahitamanas* music;
this melody is fully contained within the *Yoginī-mahātantra*. When offering scented unguents (*vilepana*), there is likewise a specific melody for the offering of unguents.
The same applies to flowers, lamps, food, and drink; each song is a mantra, and each dance performance is [accompanied by] no [other sound].
Regarding those secret mudrās that no one understands, the ācārya should perform them himself; if he cannot do so, he is not said to be "comprehensive in all arts.

As for what is called "gathering the mind": just as when worldly people see beautiful forms or sounds, their bodies and minds become intoxicated and their emotions are focused upon them such that they no longer attend to other objects, so too can this Vajra music evoke [such a state].

The human mind is also like this. It is just as when the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa himself performed the *Rādhavāṇī* melody, and upon hearing it, five hundred princes simultaneously renounced their homes to enter the Path; this is precisely that meaning.
In the *Guhya*, it merely says that if one has the means, one should perform music.
The Sūtra states that "the extensive and exquisite words such as the *maṅgala-gāthā*" refers to three types of verses:
first, the *mangala* (auspicious); second, the *maṅgala* (blessing); and third, the *parama-maṅgala* (supreme blessing).
These are all *āryā-gāthās* used to console and gladden the mind, and they possess the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The Ācārya should recite them himself; next, [he should...]
The following section sets forth one type of auspicious rite currently employed in this region, which is already roughly complete.
When reciting these verses, one should personally hold a white whisk (*śveta-vālavyajana*) and sweep over one’s own body.

Upon finishing the recitation and praise, the *ācārya* should again prostrate to all the deities of the maṇḍala for the sake of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Having made this sincere petition, he should then take up the jewel.
Having slowly circumambulated the maṇḍala three times with the vases, he again performs the empowerment according to the ritual rules and proceeds to the disciple.
First, using the syllable RA as fire, he incinerates the disciple’s body until it is entirely reduced to ashes. Only then does he consecrate him in succession with the four vases.
Having performed the consecration, he visualizes the syllable VAJRA appearing within these ashes, its color pure white, from which the five [wisdoms] are born.
Regarding the seed-syllables—namely A, VAṂ, RAṂ, HŪṂ, and KHA—one should contemplate their five wheels in succession.
One should visualize the syllable AṂ upon the crown of the head, which transforms into the Central Womb Realm (Garbhadhātu). Furthermore, from this syllable, three layers of light-flames arise;
one layer encircles the throat and above, and wherever it shines, the various deities manifest accordingly, thereby accomplishing the first [stage].
A second layer of light radiates and encircles the heart, where the various deities manifest accordingly, forming the second layer of the maṇḍala.
Next, a third layer of light radiates and encircles the navel, where the various deities manifest accordingly, forming the third layer of the maṇḍala.
At that time, the disciple’s body becomes entirely the maṇḍala. To explain this more deeply: it is the Universal Gate (Samantamukha).
Following the Body of the Dharmadhātu, one should next lead [the disciple] to a single location where the Ācārya personally dresses him in garments and crowns his head with a white silk turban.
He should anoint his body with incense, adorn him with flower garlands, and make offerings according to the ritual using burning incense and lamps.

Furthermore, he should wrap his upper arm with a *vajra*-cord and place a bracelet and finger-ring upon it; the method for their manufacture is as described in the section on *siddhi* offerings. Moreover—
The Ācārya first consecrates the golden probe with the syllable RAṂ, the clear mirror with the syllable MAṂ, and the Dharma-wheel and Dharma-conch with their respective mantras.
He should then, before the disciple, polish the disciple’s eyes with the golden probe and recite this verse:
"One should contemplate the letter-gateway RAṂ to purify the defilements and obstructions within the eyes. Next, he manifests [the following]:
Previously, he showed him a bright mirror and spoke this verse: "One should contemplate the gateway of the syllable *maṃ* to purify the defilements and obstructions within one's mind.
Next, he placed the Wheel of Dharma between his two feet and bestowed a conch shell upon his right hand, speaking verses for each while empowering them with their respective mantras.
The reason for doing so is that if the practitioner is able to purify...
The mirror of the mind, which is directly perceived before the eyes, is itself the attainment of great bodhi; having attained great bodhi, one shall turn the wheel of Dharma.
To turn the wheel of Dharma is not merely to set limits for a certain number of sentient beings, but rather to awaken all sentient beings.
For this reason, one blows the great dharma-conch. All within the Secret Mantra tradition relies upon this.
Because the causal phenomena and characteristics are used as metaphors for the profound meaning, the transmission is conducted in this manner.
Next, the Ācārya shall hold a parasol to cover [the disciple] from above and lead him to circumambulate the maṇḍala three times:
first circling the first processional courtyard, then the second processional courtyard, and finally the third processional courtyard; thus he performs the circumambulation.
At that time, the Ācārya should recite verses such as the *Maṅgala* and *Paramamaṅgala*, or otherwise recite auspicious Sanskrit texts;
having completed these, he should proceed to the western gate where the two nāgas stand in attendance and cause them to perform reverent prostrations.
He should hold the parasol over their bodies, raising and lowering it as they move, and then shall explain for them the *samaya-gāthā*, which is as follows:
Regarding the four kinds of grave prohibitions within the Secret Treasury (*Guhyakośa*), these shall all be explained below under the *āryā* verses.
Ghuṇe states: "After the disciple has performed prostrations at the western gate, the *ācārya* should address the deities, saying:
'I, [Name], have already conferred the initiation upon [Name]. I now entrust him to the deities so that he may uphold the Vidyādhara-piṭaka. Having spoken thus—"
Having spoken thus, one should have the disciple set aside the parasol and rise. Facing the maṇḍala, one should proclaim the samaya precepts:
"Now you have completed the accomplishment of the maṇḍala vidyā-ācārya. All Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, the Lords of Mantras, and all devatās know you.
If you see sentient beings who are fit vessels for the Dharma, you should feel compassion for them."
Out of compassion for them, one should establish a maṇḍala and instruct them; for within this sūtra itself there is a verse for the transmission of the Dharma conch.

Just as when people of the West receive the empowerment ritual, they take the waters of the four great oceans and all the rivers within the realm, together with precious medicines, grains, and so forth, to create a map of the realm and cause this—
The youth sat upon the lion throne, adorned with various kinds of precious jewels; his retinue, according to their respective ranks and sizes, stood in order to attend him.

The Vedic Brahmin teacher sat upon the elephant-treasure behind him, taking this precious water and pouring it over the tip of the elephant's trunk so that it fell upon the youth’s crown, after which he proclaimed these words to inform the multitude.
Furthermore, he sighed and spoke of the methods by which ancient and former sage-kings governed their people and saved the age, saying:
"One who practices in accordance with these teachings shall attain a long life, see the flourishing of their own lineage and branches, and be able to inherit the karma of a Wheel-Turning King.
If one does not perform such deeds, they shall naturally lose their position, perish, and leave no heirs. Thus he instructed them one by one.

Now, this consecration of the Dharma Prince is not like that; rather, he is seated upon the lion-throne of sovereign spiritual powers within the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma, amidst the great map of the Dharma-realm of the Ghanavyūha Buddha-field.
With the water of innate purity—wisdom and compassion—containing all myriad virtues, his mind is consecrated. At that time, the assembly of Bodhisattvas... [proceeded].
When all eight classes of sentient beings were filled with joy, offered praise, and gave rise to reverence, the Ācārya instructed them using the bequeathed teachings of the Dharma King.
From that time forward, they would constantly be born into the family of the Tathāgata and would certainly succeed to the rank of Buddha;
had it not been for this, they would not have understood the respect due to the True Dharma.
