Namo bhagavate śākyamunaye tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya | tadyathā | oṃ śāntikara tvaṃ dya || (The eleven verses)
Bearing auspicious and manifold virtues, possessing the radiance of a golden mountain of marks,
the Teacher of the three times who has eliminated the three defilements and opened the eye of perfect enlightenment— like a lotus leaf,
he benefits all sentient beings; this is the foremost of blessings.
The above first clarifies that all auspicious and celebratory occurrences arise solely because the Tathāgata has appeared in the world.
In Sanskrit, this is called *lakṣmī* (pronounced with the three-syllable combination), which is translated as "auspicious signs" (*śubha-lakṣaṇa*).

It may also be rendered as "possessing signs," which carries the meanings of "excellent celebration," "auspiciousness," "joy and consolation," "majestic virtue," and "excellent appearance. One should know that this name encompasses all meritorious qualities.
Because of its virtue, it is expressed through a compound meaning; the second phrase, "blooming," also carries the sense of awakening.
"Water-born" is a synonym for the lotus. Since it possesses such meanings, the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world brings great benefit;
thus it is called "the foremost auspicious celebration," or "auspicious celebration," or "excellent celebration," or "joyful celebration"—in essence, they are the same.
And that which he has proclaimed—the supreme, immovable Dharma—has been revealed for the sake of the humans and devas of the three realms;
it is worthy of their offerings. This sublime Dharma can bring about the eternal peace of all sentient beings;
this is the world’s second great blessing.
The above refers to all that the World-Honored One has taught, which ultimately reaches the supreme limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); therefore, it is called the "Unmoving Dharma.
In the Sanskrit original, *khyā* (pronounced *qiè*, with the second tone) primarily carries the meaning of "proclaiming" and also the meaning of "revealing.

Here, the term "three realms" (*tridhātu*)—according to the Sanskrit text—is correctly rendered as "three times" (*tryadhvan*), meaning it encompasses the past, present, and future, as well as the three states of existence (*tribhava*). This is because it is able to reveal [these] universally.
Because it is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) supreme in the world, all humans and devas should make offerings to this Dharma as a way of repaying its great kindness.
In Sanskrit it is called *śāntikara*, which is translated as "making peace. Here, "making" (*kara*) carries the sense of that which causes, enables, or brings about.
This Dharma can cause sentient beings to realize that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is eternally quiescent, both internally and externally.
Because hindrances will ultimately never arise, it is said to be "eternally quiescent"; the subsequent examples are likewise so.
Because the Tathāgata appears in the world and is thus able to proclaim this Dharma, it is called the second "auspicious celebration."
Those who are in accord with the sublime True Dharma and have attained the blessing of great learning;
the Sangha of monks worthy of offerings by humans, devas, and asuras; those endowed with wealth, auspiciousness, and a sense of shame and dread of blame;
this assembly of beings of preeminent merit—this is the third blessing in the world.
The term "Right" (Dharma) is, in Sanskrit, *saddharma*, which is translated as "True Dharma" or "Sublime Dharma. It is preserved here in its entirety for the sake of completing the verse.
Within this context, "correspondence" (*yukti*) is, in Sanskrit, *yukti*, meaning "to be joined together" in this manner;

it carries the sense of being in accord and in profound resonance, and differs slightly from the meaning of *yoga*. The next phrase, "due to having heard much of this Dharma," [is explained as follows:]
When one’s practice accords with the principle, it is a great cause for celebration; thus it is said that "much learning is a cause for celebration.

According to a correct translation, this should be rendered as "rich in learning," but here I follow the old translation. Furthermore, the Sanskrit name for this "Arhat" (one worthy of offerings) differs from that of an *arhant*.
This "one worthy of offerings" carries the meaning that gods, humans, and others should offer worship to him in order to seek merit. This is the beginning of the second verse.

The term "wealth" (*bhoga*) mentioned previously and the "wealth" referred to here have the same meaning; they both signify being fully endowed and lacking nothing—namely, the wealth of auspiciousness (*śrī*), the wealth of shame and dread of blame (*hrī-apatrāpya*), and the wealth of merit (*guṇa*).
The final phrase, "the multitude" (*gaṇa*), is merely a designation for a large number; its Sanskrit name differs from *saṃgha*.
While *saṃgha* carries the additional sense of "harmonious assembly," when the treasury of the True Dharma (*saddharmapiṭaka*) appears in the world, [it is established].
Because there are those who practice and are oriented toward the fruit [of the path], it is called the "Third Auspicious Celebration.
Just as when he was dwelling in the treasury of the Tuṣita Heaven palace, there was celebration;
and likewise, when descending from heaven to benefit all sentient beings, Śakra and the host of devas followed him like attendants.
Now you have attained equality with them; this is the sublime joy of tranquility.
To the right of this, the Sanskrit term for "garbha" (center) is *garbha*. It refers to the center of the center, the matrix of the matrix (*maṇḍala*).
Its meaning differs from that of *piṭaka* (basket), *kośa* (treasury), and so forth. For example, as when a Bodhisattva is within a celestial palace...
When descending from the heavens, there were immeasurable and boundless auspicious events in all worlds, as explained in detail in scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka*.
Asuras are essentially members of the celestial hosts; however, to distinguish them from the gods (*deva*), they are called *asura*.
Treatises such as the *Lokasthāna-śāstra* refer to them as "non-gods" (*asura*). Furthermore, *Tathāgata* is translated as "Thus-Come One."
Furthermore, it is said that "Tathāgata" (Thus-Gone) refers to having gone from the path of suchness to enter into nirvāṇa, where one is no longer reborn; thus it serves as a name.
This is used to explain the occasion of descending from heaven, as it is more convenient in meaning for that context, and therefore the phrasing is reciprocal.

If there is a Bodhisattva in the position of succession in Tuṣita Heaven, then the seed of the Buddha in the world will not be severed. If a person receives [the teaching] within the Secret Treasury...
Regarding the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), because one may attain perfect enlightenment within a single lifetime, it is said that this rejoices equally with that [attainment].
Just as when there was celebration in the supreme palace-city of Kapilavastu, the gods of great majesty praised and prostrated;
it is truly inconceivable, like a "welcome" according to reality.
Now you have attained equality with them; this is the sublime joy of tranquility.
(In the Sanskrit original, the sense of "time" is contained within that very "joy"; hereafter it shall be the same.

This refers to the time when the Bodhisattva was dwelling in the womb, at which time there were immeasurable auspicious and celebratory events throughout all worlds, just as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm.
In the "Chapter on the World," it is explained in detail that even the assembly of infinite great Bodhisattvas from the ten directions gather within his womb for the sake of hearing the Dharma;

therefore, as for the meaning of "coming" (*āgata*) in the preceding verse, which is inconceivable, it is now explained by means of "attaining perfect enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), as this is also convenient for the logical flow of the meaning. For example, although a Bodhisattva is within the womb...
There are no gods of great majesty who do not praise you and pay homage; you have now likewise entrusted your holy embryo within the Matrix of the Mother of Buddhas, the Eye of Space.
Therefore, the eight classes of beings, including the nāgas and spirits, all revere and honor you. Thus it is said that you share in their celebration.
Just as in a flower garden, where light and glory are everywhere adorned,
and where the Venuvana grove is filled with the joy of immeasurable hosts of devas; so too, when the Guide was first born,
you have now attained that same state— this sublime celebration of peace, the final body at the end of existence.

In Sanskrit, *kīśalaya* refers to flowers on trees that still possess their stalks and leaves; *puṣpa*, which follows, specifically denotes the substance of the flower itself, such as those used for flower garlands or scattered blossoms—all of which employ this term.
Therefore, the preceding phrase uses "flower garden" (*puṣpavana*) to distinguish it [from other types].
Furthermore, at the time of the Bodhisattva’s initial birth, there were likewise immeasurable [such gardens] throughout all worlds.
The auspicious celebration of these omens has reached such a point that immeasurable hosts of devas have gathered at the Lumbinī Grove for the sake of making offerings;
furthermore, immeasurable and inconceivable Bodhisattvas of liberation, like clouds enveloping the moon, have simultaneously descended to be born.
Now, you too have first attained birth within the secret *garbha*. All!

The retinue of this Dharma-gate has already begun to sprout; if one can courageously advance in practice, that too is the final body of birth and death, and thus it is said that one shares in their celebration.
Just as there is joy when the various sufferings of household life are extinguished, so too, with a heart full of gladness in the middle watch of the night,
you have gone to the place of ascetic practice; like the hosts of devas who pay homage and surround him,
you now share in that same state— this is the sublime joy of tranquility.

This refers to the time when the Bodhisattva first left the household life; in the Sanskrit original, it simply says "extinguishing various sufferings," which implicitly contains the meaning of leaving the household.
This refers to abandoning the various sufferings of attachment and the bonds of affection inherent in the household life.

Regarding the "place of ascetic practice" (*duṣkaracaryā*), the Sanskrit term should be translated literally as the "place for cultivating the body" (*kāyabhāvanāsthāna*). For example, when the Bodhisattva initially crossed the city wall and proceeded toward such cultivation.
At that time, throughout all worlds, there were immeasurable and boundless auspicious events, as described at length in the *Avataṃsaka* and other scriptures.
Then, the hosts of Śuddhāvāsa deities, down to the World-Protectors (*Lokapālas*), were all filled with great joy;
knowing that the *udumbara* flower of the Perfectly Awakened One would soon blossom, they all prostrated themselves, circumambulated him, or personally attended upon his feet.

And as they were escorted away, you now likewise depart from the parents of ignorance within the Secret Treasury and proceed to the place where one cultivates the body on the path of the primary illumination of the Dharma.

You should know that the gods of the Pure Abodes and others also rejoice and pay homage, knowing that before long you will become equal to the World-Honored One; thus it is said that "one attains such celebration."
Furthermore, just as that Dragon King was honored and celebrated when he paid his respects, and as the flocks of birds on the riverbanks circled him in formation,
so too have you now attained that same state— having reached the rare and peaceful meaning and being about to destroy all realms of existence— you bring forth the sublime joy of tranquility.

This was when the Bodhisattva, having reached the very depths of ascetic practice and realizing its lack of benefit, accepted the milk-rice from the cowherd woman and bathed in the river, his physical marks becoming perfectly complete.
At that time, as he drew closer to the path of Buddhahood, there appeared the auspicious omen of immeasurable blue jays;
as explained in detail in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, these birds are properly named *caṭaka* and resemble [the following description].

The small green parrot is what is commonly called the "Immortal Bird" (Sennin-chō) in local dialects. After the Bodhisattva had finished bathing, he contemplated that all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent;
with a clear mind, he clearly beheld the path to Great Enlightenment and gave rise to a sense of wonder.

He knew for himself that he would surely be able to destroy all states of existence through his great power. At that time, there were furthermore immeasurable and boundless auspicious and celebratory events.

Having appeared in the world, you now likewise, within this Secret Treasury, have cast aside the various exhausting practices of body and spirit belonging to the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths—
practices that yield neither purpose nor benefit— and instead have increased your constant life-force, physical strength,
and vitality by consuming the milk-rice of the single flavor of the letter-gateway *A*, and have bathed your body with the pure water of the Dharma, clearly discerning the King of the Mind.
Because the Great Way is about to proceed to the place where Vairocana sits at the site of enlightenment, it is said that one attains a celebration equal to his.
It is like the celebration when the Bhagavat was beneath the King of Trees; by the power of the mind of compassion, he shattered immeasurable demonic armies.
In various forms according to their kind, [he] pervades the worlds of devas and humans.
You have now attained equality with him; this is the sublime joy of attaining tranquility.

When the World-Honored One sat at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, subduing the celestial Māras and attaining Perfect Awakening, all manner of mundane and supramundane auspicious and virtuous events occurred, like the King of Celestial Trees fully blossoming in the month of high spring.

Having fulfilled all the aspirations he formed while practicing the bodhisattva path in former lives, he has now attained his wishes and manifests his form-body throughout all worlds to transform and enlighten sentient beings.

In whatever direction they reside, that place becomes one where the Buddha dwells and performs the work of a Buddha.
This is just as it is said in the Śrāvaka sūtras: wherever Śāriputra travels, in that direction [the Buddha is present].
Facing me, there is nothing further to be done. The reason all sentient beings make offerings to and draw near to the Tathāgata is that he is able to give birth to inexhaustible merit and wisdom;
now, the mass of merit possessed by these good men and good women is exactly equal to that of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, out of great compassion, the World-Honored One entrusts this to all sentient beings.
If those born in this world desire to make offerings to the Buddha, they should make offerings to these sons and daughters of good family;
if they wish to see the Buddha, they should immediately contemplate them. The mass of merit possessed when first entering the worldly maṇḍala is equal to that of the Tathāgata;
so too is the mass of merit possessed when first entering the profound and secret yoga maṇḍala.
Furthermore, the accumulation of merit produced when entering each individual stage and maṇḍala,
as explained at length, is entirely equal to that of the Tathāgata; herein there is both distinction and non-distinction,
because by seeing such a Vajradhātu, one is named Vajrapāṇi, and by seeing such a Dharma.

Because he belongs to the realm [of Samantabhadra], he is named Samantabhadra. Thus, this foremost of holy lords, together with the entire assembly of Vajra Bodhisattvas, spoke with one voice, saying:
"From this day forward, we shall respectfully honor and make offerings to these good men and good women. Why is this?
Because they have seen the Buddha, the World-Honored One, just as the ministers and attendants of a Wheel-Turning King do."
Because they recognize the lineage of the Wheel-Turning King, they see that his appearance in the world brings manifold benefits;
desiring that the seven treasures never again be obscured, they all pay homage with utmost sincerity and protect the Prince within the womb—not with words of mere pretense.
As for Ghuṭika, having performed the homa as described above, he says: "O Ācārya..."
Sprinkle pure water upon the heads of the disciples and extensively show them the positions within the maṇḍala.

Instruct them in the great mudrās and the mantras of the vidyārājas, and have them sit in one place to recite them. Next, instruct them to make offerings of incense and flowers to the principal deity and the other deities;
once this is finished, they shall sit in order while the master himself recites the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for them to hear. Then...
I shall now fully explain the samaya precepts for you: from this day forward, you must daily revere, honor, and make offerings to the Triple Gem, all bodhisattvas, and all mantras;
maintain constant faith and understanding toward the Mahāyāna sūtras;
whenever you see anyone who has received the samaya, you should feel affection and joy; and you must always show respect toward the abodes of the venerable ones.
One should not harbor resentment toward the various Honored Ones nor place faith in the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths;
one should give to all who come seeking according to one's ability, constantly arouse compassion for all sentient beings, diligently cultivate all meritorious virtues,
always delight in the Mahāyāna, and never become lax or negligent regarding the mantra practices and all secret dharmas.
One who lacks the samaya should not be taught; such is the general outline. The remainder is explained in detail in the first chapter on the *pūjā-vidhi*.

Having thus provided these instructions, one should individually show each disciple the mantra and mudrā of their respective tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) along with the corresponding family (*kula*), and then explain the primary maṇḍala. Thereafter, perform the final homa; once the homa is completed, furthermore—
Having protected the body according to the Dharma and completed the offering of food to the various directions, wash the hands and sprinkle water for purification.
Then, together with the disciples, make successive offerings of incense, flowers, and so forth to all the honored ones, prostrating with a sincere heart and requesting their joyful acceptance.
Next, holding *argha* vessels, dismiss each deity according to the ritual using their respective root mantras, either following the specific original teachings or by means of the *maṇḍala*.
The *Rāja-mantra* is dispatched at once according to the ritual for invitation. All food offerings should be given to the poor;
one should not give them to dogs, crows, or similar creatures to consume. All wealth and possessions should be taken by the *ācārya* and used as he sees fit.
If he cannot use them, they should be offered to the Triple Gem; parasols and fly-whisks should be offered to the Buddha, as well as unguents and incense.

Dharma robes, water jars, bowls, and other such items should be offered to the Buddha or to the Sangha of the four directions; if there is no Sangha present, they should be given to the seven classes of people.
The disciples, even to the smallest degree, must not use them; if they do so, they violate their samaya, as explained in detail therein.
At that time, Vairocana again surveyed the entire assembly and addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries and the others:
"Since the Ācārya must understand the mantra components required for the ritual activities of the maṇḍala, I shall now explain them.
Furthermore, in order to reveal the treasury of the Tathāgata’s secret speech, he again surveyed the assembly universally."
The Great Assembly empowers him as if he were the Buddha in his physical body.
When he is about to utter words of truth, he may display the mark of the broad and long tongue, covering his entire face, and address those who are ready for deliverance, saying:
"Have you ever seen in the scriptures such a person as this who utters false speech? Or, as in the Mahāyāna, he may display the mark of the tongue, covering [his face].

In this trichiliocosm, because the World-Honored One is now about to proclaim the Tathāgata’s impartial speech, he clarifies that this wheel of speech pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* both horizontally and vertically;
therefore, it is called the mark of the broad and long wheel of speech (*prabhūtarucira-vāk-cakra*). Regarding this term "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*), in the Sanskrit original it is correctly termed *maṇḍala*.
Previously, the universal-gate body *maṇḍala* was revealed; now, once again, the universal [gate]... is manifested.
The Gate of Speech Maṇḍala is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*): it is tranquil and without mind, and yet it lacks no fixed form;
it is able to respond universally to all beings, causing them all to find satisfaction in their own hearts. Therefore, it is named the "Skillful-Colored Maṇi.

From the body of the Skillful-Colored Maṇi issues the speech of the Skillful-Colored Maṇi, which reveals the mind of the Skillful-Colored Maṇi, raining down the wealth of the Dharma everywhere to fill the entire Dharma-realm.
The various aspirations of sentient beings are thus met through traces that correspond to their needs, constantly pervading the ten directions and the three periods of time.
By means of immeasurable gateways, they plant the roots of all virtues without end.

Abiding at such a time in conduct that cannot be harmed, this signifies that within all undertakings, nothing can obstruct or destroy it; therefore, it is called "the unobstructed throughout the three periods of time."
The mantra syllables of the *Bilaka* (Power) are a general exposition of the source from which all mantras arise.

As for the "Great Power" (*Mahābala*) and "Great Protection" (*Mahārakṣā*) explained in the subsequent text, these are the functions manifested according to the capacities of sentient beings, emerging from the wish-fulfilling jewel wheel (*cintāmaṇi-cakra*).
At that time, the entire assembly realized that their own mental vessels were pure and received the inconceivable empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata.

Because they were able to uphold [the Dharma], they were capable of receiving the Great Dharma; immediately, through immeasurable gateways, they all together with one voice entreated the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, now is precisely the right time; Sugata, now is precisely the right time.

According to the Sanskrit original, the former term *kāla* refers to a long duration, such as a year being divided into three parts and so forth; the latter term *samaya* refers to the midst of that time.
"Small" refers to periods such as the six divisions of day and night, or even smaller fractions thereof. It is like someone saying:
"Now is precisely the time for spring cultivation; having encountered this fertile rain, you should hasten to sow the seeds so as not to miss this opportunity.
Thus, it is stated repeatedly. At that time, the World-Honored One, having accepted the invitation, was about to expound the Great Power and Great Protection.
The Consort dwells in the Samādhi of the High Peak of the Pure Dharma Banner, which fulfills all vows and emits the mark of the broad and long tongue that completely covers all Buddha-fields.
Here, the word "emits" (*niḥsṛta*)—according to a direct translation from the Sanskrit—should be rendered as "arises.
The older translations may say "exertion" (*visphurita*) or "emergence"; this broad and long tongue-mark is precisely the Tathāgata’s exertion.
This is spoken with intentional meaning because it manifests great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Among the universal applications of the "Universal Gateway" (*samanta-mukha*)—such as the Tathāgata’s mark of the broad and long tongue that pervades all Buddha-fields and the exquisite-colored *maṇi* jewels—this samādhi is the foremost, like the banner of a great general;
therefore, it is called the "Pure Dharma Banner. In Sanskrit, it is called *dhvaja*.

The *dhvaja* is translated as "banner" (*ketu*); this is translated as "flag. Its appearance differs slightly from that of the *dhvaja*, being adorned merely with various multicolored streamers and insignia.
The appearance of the *ketu* is largely similar, yet it further adds hanging streamers and banners.

Its secret designation is like that used by military strategists who depict various forms such as tortoises, dragons, birds, and beasts to serve as signals for the three divisions of the army. There is.

Since *sthāna* (place) is also translated as "banner" (*dhvaja*), these are combined in the translation; if the Sanskrit original were preserved in its entirety, it should be rendered as "the banner of the pure Dharma.
This is like a great general who, having erected a banner atop a high peak, clearly perceives the terrain, the advantages and disadvantages of the ground, and the dispositions of the enemy;
he commands a host of millions such that their movements are unified and their joining or parting follows his will as he wages war.

If one must conquer in order to attack and must seize what can be taken, yet the general is clumsy and ignorant of the situation, and furthermore loses the battle banner, then each person’s mind will become disunited and defeat will follow before long.
In this way, the pure bodhicitta serves as the banner for the myriad practices;
it is likewise established firmly and immovably upon the mountain of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way through the samādhi of vigorous progress.

Universally observing the ten directions, he clearly perceives the immeasurable gateways of liberation, the superior or inferior nature of their constituent materials, the specific applications for which they are suited, as well as the various stages, their permeabilities and obstructions, and the causes and conditions that hinder the Path;

therefore, he is able to sustain immeasurable merit and universally protect all sentient beings, such that whatever he undertakes cannot be thwarted. At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought: "I, from [the beginning]..."

Since first resolving my mind upon enlightenment, I have constantly used this courageous and steadfast bodhicitta to protect and uphold the True Dharma and all sentient beings amidst various difficult and painful practices, remaining as unyielding as a vajra without ever retreating.
This was precisely for the sake of accomplishing such a samādhi to universally protect the Buddha-fields of the ten directions; now, all my vows have been fulfilled.

"It is precisely now, when all that ought to be done has been fulfilled, that I shall emit a voice pervading the entire *dharmadhātu* of all Tathāgatas—a sound of compassion for the realm of sentient beings without exception—and speak these mantra-words of the Vidyādharas.
If what I have spoken is truthful and not false, let whoever maintains and recites them possess power no different from my own; therefore, this is called the 'Name'."
"Great Power" and "Great Protection. The *ācārya* says that "Wisdom" (*vidyā*) has the meaning of the light of great intelligence. As for "Queen" (*rājñī*), in Sanskrit it is *rājñī*;
it is the character for "king" (*rāja*) pronounced with a feminine suffix, and thus those who transmit the teachings explain its meaning as "queen.
"Queen" here carries the meaning of *samādhi*, namely the *samādhi* of the Womb of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*). This *samādhi* is [the essence] of all Buddhas.
This mother of the sons of the Buddha—namely, the Bodhicitta, the banner of the pure Dharma—is like a womb;
from the very stage of the *kalala*, it contains and protects [the embryo], ensuring it is not harmed by various conditions.
It gradually increases until after birth, when she continues to protect and nourish it with steadfast diligence. Therefore, it is said:

The mother’s kindness and virtue are most profound and difficult to repay. Those who arise from this samādhi—whether entering, abiding in, or emerging from it—all do so within the inconceivable dharma-realm;
it is not like worldly meditative concentration, where movement and stillness obstruct one another, leading to decline, loss, or intervals of distraction.
Namo sarvatathāgatebhyo (1) sarvavidyebhyo (2) viśvamukhebhyaḥ (3) svāhā (4) rakṣa mahāmāle (5) sarvatathāgatapūjite (6) namaḥ.
(Jingyin) Jaḥ (protracted) te (7) hūṃ hūṃ (8) traṭ traṭ (9) apratihate (10) svāhā. The first phrase is the taking of refuge in all Tathāgatas;
the second phrase is able to eliminate all obstacles, terrors, and the like.

This praises the Tathāgata’s qualities of all-pervading great power and great protection; furthermore, the subsequent phrase praises the *Viśva* (All) of immeasurable Dharma-gates, which carries the meaning of "skillful means.
That is to say, the immeasurable gateways of skillful liberation are the high peak of the *Dharmadhvaja* (Dharma-Banner) contemplation-samādhi and its universal gateways of activity.
Now, wishing to explain this *Vidyārājñī* (Wisdom Queen), he first pays homage to all the Tathāgatas.
"Come" (*āgaccha*) refers to such merits. Next, "sarvathā" is a general reference to the merits of all Buddhas, intended to cause them to enter the single-gate (*ekākṣara-mukha*).
Following this are the two syllables *haṃ* and *khaṃ*, which constitute the very essence of the mantra and are also called the "seed-syllable" (*bīja*).
All subsequent phrases are successive explanations of these two gates. The syllable *ha* signifies the meaning of "cause."

That which is called the cause of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) is the bodhicitta; because all causes are fundamentally unarisen and even devoid of causes and conditions, it is named the "pure bodhicitta.

This pure bodhicitta is the true cause for attaining Buddhahood and the seed of the banner of the True Dharma (*saddharma*). The addition of the nasal dot (*bindu*) above signifies the meaning of entering into realization;

thus, the sound is transformed as follows: [The Sanskrit term *bodhicitta* becomes *boṃdhi* with the *bindu*. (Note: The final sentence provides a phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit *bodhicitta* modified by the *bindu*, resulting in *boṃdhi*, to indicate its realization.)
*Haṃ* and *kha*: This *kha* is the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) with the vowel *a* and the nasal bindu (*anusvāra*) added above; when the sound is transformed, it becomes *khaṃ*.
This is the realization of this great emptiness, which is named Prajñāpāramitā, the Mother of Buddhas; it is precisely the meaning of the Consort (*vidyārājñī*).
Within this empty space, one nurtures the seeds of the true cause; this is the meaning of "Great Protection" (*mahārakṣā*). Furthermore, the syllable-gateway *kha* is like space, ultimately [empty].
That which is pure and wherein nothing is absent is the object of knowledge for the "High Peak" contemplation (*kūṭāgāra-vipaśyanā*).
The syllable *HA* is the seed of the Bodhi-banner and is also the power of mastery; because these two syllables are conjoined, they are like a great general who can defeat enemies.
Furthermore, the gateway of the syllable *HA* is the jewel of the bodhicitta, which, through its union with the gateway of the syllable *KHA*, is identical to space.
It is attained as a *maṇi* jewel of exquisite color capable of fulfilling all hopes and desires;
this missing syllable is absent here within the mantra but is present in the subsequent text. The next phrase says *rakṣa*, which has the meaning of "protection.

Just as a person who is terrified by calamities or misfortunes feels secure when relying upon a powerful great man, or when possessing the strength of a high city and deep moat, so too [is one protected].
One need not worry that those various enemies, despite their manifold expedients, can do anything about it; the practitioner is likewise so.
Relying upon the King of Bodhicitta and taking the matrix of Prajñā as his citadel, he is like space, indestructible.
This is a further explanation of the preceding meaning. The next phrase, *mahā-māri*, is translated as "Great Power" (*mahā-bala*). *Ha* [is the suffix].

The syllable *Bodhi* is inherently endowed with all the powers of the Tathāgatas; now, because it is joined with the syllable *Kha*, it is liberated from all fetters and is no longer subject to obstruction.
Like the wind revolving with sovereign freedom within empty space, it is therefore called "Great Power" (*Mahābala*).
Furthermore, there are seven phrases that explain the origin of this Great Power, stating: "It arises from the merits of all the Tathāgatas."
It is said that this Great Firm Power originally arises from the vajra-lineage of all Buddhas;
furthermore, since immeasurable kalpas past, it has constantly cultivated the ten thousand virtues of the syllable *kha* by means of the true cause, the syllable *ha*.
Each of these is like a vajra, indestructible and unbreakable. Now that all virtues are fulfilled and all powers are complete, one shall further [proceed] with this Dharma-banner.
Gazing at the high peak in samādhi, he greatly crushes the enemies of the dharmadhātu and universally protects all sentient beings.

He then utters words of truth, namely the syllable *HŪṂ*. *HŪṂ* is a sound that terrifies them; the reason it is repeated is that one [instance] crushes external obstacles and the other crushes internal obstacles.
Furthermore, the external refers to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), while the internal refers to the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). If one were to explain...
Regarding the letter-gateway: by what dharma does the Tathāgata terrify all obstacles? It is precisely by means of this letter-gateway *ha*.
Below, the three *samādhi* strokes represent the complete cultivation of the ten thousand practices; above, the great *bindu* of emptiness represents the perfection of the ten thousand virtues.
The letter *ha* is the banner of the Dharma-pinnacle; because it is conjoined with the *samādhi-bindu* of emptiness, it is the contemplation of the high peak.

The syllable *Maim* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of all Tathāgatas: the upper dot (*bindu*) is the Mother of the Vidyārājñīs, and the lower stroke represents the embryonic stage (*garbhāvasthā*) increasing day by day;
for this reason, as soon as its sound is uttered, the armies of Māra are defeated and dispersed.
Next, *Taraṭa* signifies the meaning of rebuking and subduing, just as when a lion roars with fierce fury, the various beasts [are struck with fear].

"Nothing is not subdued" and the repetition of the word "also" refer to the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and even the afflictions within the realms (*dhātugata*) as well as those outside the realms. The final phrase, *apratihata*, means power that is unimpeded and peerless;
it summarizes the preceding text, meaning that by virtue of these causes and conditions, it is called "Great Power" and "Great Protection."
“Vidyārājñī svāhā. This [mantra] awakens all Buddhas to act as witnesses; it also carries the meaning of mindfulness and upholding, as has already been explained previously.
The Sūtra says: “At that time, when all Tathāgatas and the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples had spoken this vidyā, immediately and universally...”

Regarding the sixfold trembling of the Buddha-fields: when the Tathāgata Vairocana utters this sound that pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—by virtue of their non-dual realm—speak it together with one voice, so that the power and majesty of these empowered phrases may be fully realized.
Furthermore, by the power of the Tathāgata’s words of truth, at that very moment...
The ten directions of Buddha-fields tremble in six ways to clarify that the fundamental vows of the Buddha are true and not false.
While the meaning of these six types of trembling is explained in detail in other sutras, here, within this secret interpretation of our school,
the "six" refers to the six root afflictions— greed, hatred, delusion, views, pride, and doubt— which constantly reside within the minds of all sentient beings.

Held fast by heavy defilements, they were unable to rise on their own; now, moved by the sincere truth of the World-Honored One, they have all cracked open and scattered like buds, and the seeds of the Buddha-nature have sprouted—hence it is called the "sixfold earthquake.

At that time, all the bodhisattvas, seeing these two kinds of causes and conditions for the earth’s trembling—the superficial and the profound and secret—had their minds and eyes opened without exception.
It is unprecedented that the Great Sun World-Honored One is praised with such subtle and wondrous verses;
as for the scripture stating "before all Buddhas," it means that when this mantra was spoken, the bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions each saw their respective Buddha also reciting it.
Therefore, with a single voice, they all simultaneously attained understanding. This very passage serves as proof that the Great Protection is accomplished.
This is the majestic power [of the mantra]. Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas are most extraordinary" within the verse of realization, the Sanskrit original should actually read:
"How marvelous! All Buddhas have spoken this Great Power Protection (Mahābala-rakṣā).
This means that in every single world-system, all Bodhisattvas simultaneously realize and understand the mantras spoken by all the Buddhas of the ten directions. By means of these ten...
Because all Buddhas together protect and uphold it, it is like a vajra city—solid, high, and impossible to ascend;
furthermore, it is encircled by a boiling moat, deep and impossible to cross. For this reason, no obstacles whatsoever can invade or oppress it.
Those who abide with that protective mind enable practitioners to guard their body and mind through these mantras and secret mudrās.
Because one dwells in this [syllable], all obstructors, such as the Vināyakas and the hideous Rākṣasas, naturally retreat and disperse.
Furthermore, if one follows the Sanskrit pronunciation, this syllable *vra* (or *vraḥ*) is also called "to suppress"; it is placed upon the heart.
To provide a profound interpretation: it means that a person of pure bodhicitta protects their mind by means of the true meaning of this consort (*vidyā*).
Because they abide in this, the three kinds of heavy obstacles and all the evil rākṣasas are utterly dispersed and unable to harm their roots of goodness;
even when they merely give rise to a thought of recollection, they possess such power and majesty. Therefore, the final sentence further confirms this.

The Sūtra states: "At that time, the Bhagavān, through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the vast Dharma-realm, at that very moment abided in the Samādhi of the Matrix of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-garbha-samādhi*).
Arising from this meditative absorption, he spoke of entering the Buddha-samaya-vidyādhara.
The Sanskrit term *vipula* has the meaning of 'vast'—that is, profound and boundless, immeasurable; such is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all these dharmas."
It is called the *Vipula* Dharma-realm; the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all Buddhas, the true reality of sentient beings, and the true reality [of phenomena] are all the *Vipula* Dharma-realm.
Because they mutually empower one another through this, it is called the empowerment of the Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, just as when the causal conditions of the union of a man and woman cause the seed to be entrusted to the womb without being lost or destroyed, this is the meaning of "mutual empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*);

so too, when the Buddhas, kings, and vidyārājñīs consort with their consorts to co-create the *Vairocana* seed, it is sustained by the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha* (Great Compassion Womb) without undergoing loss or destruction. Therefore, it is named the *Dharmadhātu*.
The World-Honored One performed an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), universally empowering all sentient beings so that they all became seeds of equality.
Having completed this, he immediately entered the Samādhi of the Womb-Treasury Pervading the Dharma-Dhātu.
He beheld that each and every seed was the infinite adornment of the Universal Gate retinue of Vairocana upon a lotus pedestal, and was also identical to the Great Compassion Maṇḍala.

Although there is no difference between the *catura* and so forth, because sentient beings have not yet been able to realize this for themselves, it is called being within the "sage’s womb" (*āryagarbha*) in the *Abhidharmakośa*.

When one emerges from this treasury, it is the liberation of the Tathāgata. Having thus observed in this manner, the World-Honored One immediately arose from samādhi and spoke the *Buddhasamayasamādhi-vidyāsamaya*, which is the state of equanimity.
The meaning of "equality" (samatā) is the meaning of the original vow, the meaning of removing obstacles, and the meaning of awakening.
To speak of "equality" means that when the Tathāgata realized this samādhi, he saw that the various bodies, speech, and minds of all sentient beings were entirely equal to those of the Tathāgata;
their meditative concentration, wisdom, and the body of the true mark (dharmatākāya) are also ultimately equal to his, just as they were at the moment of his first aspiration for enlightenment.
When the pāramitā of the ground is perfected, it is likewise ultimately equal; therefore, one utters words of truth to inform sentient beings:

"If what I have said is certainly not false, then at the moment all sentient beings utter these words of truth, may they also receive the empowerment of the three secrets, attain inexhaustible adornments, and become equal to the Tathāgata. By virtue of this causal condition, one is able to...
It is called *samaya* because it performs vajra-activities. Regarding the "original vow":
when the Tathāgata witnessed this *samaya*, he saw that all sentient beings possess the potential for Buddhahood; therefore, he immediately established the great vow:
"I shall now, through the universal gate and by means of immeasurable skillful methods, cause all sentient beings to reach the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment]."
As long as the realm of sentient beings to be awakened has not been exhausted, my activity shall never cease.
If there are sentient beings who, in accordance with my original vow, utter these words of truth, I shall cause all their activities to become entirely of a vajra nature;
therefore, it is called *samaya*. Regarding the "removal of obstacles," the Tathāgata perceives all...
All sentient beings possess the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata; yet, due to a single thought of ignorance, they constantly fail to perceive it even though it is ever before their eyes.

Therefore, I utter these words of truth: "I must now employ various skillful means to universally remove the cataracts from the eyes of all sentient beings. If this vow of mine is certain to be fulfilled, may all sentient beings..."

When I spoke these words of truth according to my skillful means, from that moment until the end of one's life, one attains the stainless eye and all obscurations and veils are completely exhausted; therefore, it is called *samaya*. Regarding the meaning of "awakening":
because all sentient beings are asleep in ignorance, they do not themselves realize such qualities; for this reason, the Tathāgata— [...employs skillful means... (as the preceding context implies).

These sincere words shall move them to awakening; likewise, they shall startle and awaken all Bodhisattvas, causing them to arise from the cave of profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and learn the lion’s stretch.
If there are practitioners of mantras who proclaim this samaya, we Buddhas shall likewise remember our original vows and not transgress them, just as a king restrains himself.
Because one has already returned to personally revere and accord with the Dharma by practicing it, it is called *samaya*.
"Vidyādhara" is in Sanskrit *dhāraṇī*, meaning "to hold" (total retention) of all gates of vidyā and vidyā-practice;
because from the time this *samaya* vow was first undertaken until its end, nothing is ever lost or leaked, one is thus called an "Entrant into the Buddha’s *Samaya*-vidyādhara."
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām (1) asame (2) tulyasame (3) samaye svāhā (4). The first phrase is the taking of refuge in all Buddhas, as explained above.
The second phrase means "unequaled" (*asama*). The third means "equal to the equal" (*tulyasama*).
When taken together with the subsequent phrase, this constitutes the "Incomparable, Triple Equality Samaya Phrase.
Furthermore, *a* signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn; this is the essence of the Dharmadhātu. *Sa* signifies truth (*satya*). *Mi* signifies samādhi.
*Ma* signifies self-realized great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), as well as the meaning of "I" (*ātman*). When the World-Honored One realized this samādhi...
Contemplate clearly that within the mind of each and every sentient being, the universal mandala is equal to oneself;
therefore, there is nothing further with which it can be compared or matched, and thus it is called "inequalled" (*asama*).

The three types of equality—equality of the three times, equality of the three causes, equality of the three paths of action, and equality of the three vehicles—are the further explanation of why it is "inequalled" as stated in the preceding sentence.
*Itatari* means that the mind, according to its true nature, is such that all defilements have never arisen from the beginning;
it is for this great causal purpose that the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time employ their various skillful means. This is precisely the meaning of "removing obstructions.
It is concluded that *samaya* refers to the definitive lion’s roar that explains the equality of all dharmas.
Having established the great vow to cause all beings to attain [realization] just as I have, and desiring to universally open the pure knowledge and vision for all sentient beings,
and thereby to startle and awaken all beings as well as the Buddhas— for this reason, this samaya is called the Vajra Vow of All Tathāgatas.
If one does not first recite and maintain it, one shall not perform any of the rites of the *maṇḍala*.

This refers to the Dharma-activity. After the World-Honored One had proclaimed this samaya by means of the wheels of body, speech, and mind that pervade all buddha-fields, there was not one among the assembly of all the sons of the Buddhas who did not hear it.
Having heard it, they dared not transgress any of the mantra-dharmas. The reason for this is that if a bodhisattva, regarding sentient beings and all phenomena...
To harbor various views of inequality within [the practice] violates the samaya dharma; to maintain a mind of various limitations regarding this vow of equality also violates the samaya dharma;

to perform any actions merely for the sake of worldly fame and profit, rather than for the sake of the great causal conditions, also violates the samaya dharma; and to be negligent or indolent [is likewise a violation].
If one cannot reverently awaken the mind, one also transgresses the samaya dharma;
because of this transgression of the samaya, various obstacles arise, resulting in harm to oneself and others, and no benefit whatsoever.
Therefore, bodhisattvas and others uphold this samaya as they would protect their own lives, not daring to violate it.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, the Bhagavān again spoke the mantra for generating the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
When the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of the Matrix of the Dharma-realm, he beheld that all sentient beings possess the seed of Bodhi and are equal to all Buddhas;
therefore, he taught the entry into the Buddha-samaya-vidyā. By means of this vidyā, one attains entry into the equality of the Buddha's precepts."

This is the meaning of entrusting the holy embryo (*garbha*). At that time, the World-Honored One again observed with the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*) and saw that all sentient beings were fully endowed with the holy embryo and born into the family of the Buddha.
At that time, Anantavyūha was also equal to the Tathāgata. Having arisen from this samādhi, he immediately spoke the Mantra for Producing the Dharma Realm, and with the Universal Eye...

When one observes clearly that each and every sentient being is fully accomplished in the vajra-activity, at that time the Inexhaustible Ornament (Akṣayavyūha) likewise becomes equal to the Tathāgata. Having arisen from this samādhi, he then utters the mantra of Vajrasattva;
thus these three are all called samayas. Furthermore, it is by virtue of entering the Buddha-samādhi that...

Because he is born from the *dharmadhātu*, he is not caused to perish prematurely within the womb; because he is born from the *dharmadhātu*, at the moment of first emerging from the womb, he is free from all obstacles.
Because he is Vajrasattva, he is able to manage household affairs and master all arts and crafts.
Furthermore, through the empowerment of the secret *garbha-maṇḍala* of the Buddha-samaya, he is empowered by the *Vajrabodhisattva* born from the *dharmadhātu*.
The two groups of retinues of the *sattva* [mantras], through the empowerment of Vajrasattva, enter into various forms according to their respective types;

they arise from the Buddha-samaya like the Dharma-realm within a lotus treasury, unfold like a blooming lotus, and—like the fruit of a lotus—Vajrasattva is accomplished and returns once more as the seed. Thus, these three kinds are all termed *samaya*.
Namo samantabuddhānām (1) dharmadhātuḥ (2) sarvabhāvaguhya-dharmadhātuḥ. This "dharmadhātu" signifies the realm of phenomena;
"sarvabhāva" refers to self-nature, also called the "essence-phrase" (*prakṛtipada*).
The meaning of "I" (*aham*) in this phrase is that "I" is the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*. This is the sense of equality expressed through the definitive lion’s roar:
"I and all sentient beings are equally the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. The meaning of "I shall" is the sense of my original vow:
"I shall employ various skillful means to cause all sentient beings to fully realize and know this. Thus it is known.
Because I am the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*, I am able to eliminate all conceptual discrimination and open up pure knowledge and vision; this is the meaning of "removing obstructions.
May all Buddhas, by virtue of their original vows, cause this body of mine to become identical to the *dharmadhātu* nature of Vairocana;
this is the meaning of "awakening. This should be explained extensively through the gateway of syllables (*akṣaramukha*).
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ vajratrama kuṭaṃ.* The first phrase, "Namo samantavajrāṇām," is spoken because it introduces the mantra of Vajrasattva;

it is a taking of refuge in all Vajras, which means causing those who possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s vajra through immeasurable gateways to remember, uphold, and protect it. The next phrase is *vajra*.
*Vajratama-ku-haṃ* means that my own body is identical to the vajra. The vajra is the self-nature of the dharmadhātu;
because it has accomplished great, firm power and cannot be dismembered or destroyed, it is referred to by an alternative name as Vajra Tathāgata.
With the universal eye, one observes that the essence of vajra-wisdom in all sentient beings is no different from oneself; this is equanimity.
Because sentient beings do not realize this equality for themselves, one performs various vajra activities through the gateways of immeasurable vajra-wisdom;
the essential purpose is to destroy such great obstacles and lead them to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is the meaning of the original vow.
Thus, this limit of reality is called the "Stainless Eye Vajra," which is the very meaning of removing obstacles. By means of this lion’s roar:
The shaking of the Buddha-fields of the ten directions signifies the meaning of awakening; therefore, it is called *samaya*.
Furthermore, by means of the first *samaya*, the practitioner of mantra attains a body equal to the secret body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata;
by means of the second *samaya*, they attain equality with the Honored One of the Dharma-realm Palace who is sustained by the Tathāgata’s empowerment.
By means of the third samaya, his own body causes both this body and its environment to become like vajra, surrounded by an immeasurable host of Vajradharas.
The Buddha taught that the first samaya is for the sake of self-enjoyment;
the second samaya is for the sake of accomplishing the dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya) for all bodhisattvas; and the third samaya is...
In order to subdue and gather sentient beings according to their respective types, the Buddha taught the first three samayas:
the first is for the purpose of establishing the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala; the second is for performing the activities of the Vairocana Ācārya;
and the third is for performing the activities of the Vajradhara disciple. Thus, the first three...
The first samaya is for the purpose of empowering the retinue of the Tathāgatas; the second samaya is for the purpose of empowering the retinue of the Padmas;
and the third samaya is for the purpose of empowering the retinue of the Vajras.
Therefore, the Buddha taught the three samayas.
Next, regarding the explanation of the Vajra Armor Mantra: in order to adorn the body of Vajrasattva, the practitioner has already made the vajra vow;
because they wish to destroy all obstacles for the sake of all sentient beings, they don the armor of vajra through firm and powerful diligence.
Furthermore, just as each of the six pāramitās is, in accordance with reality, like [the nature of phenomena], so too is this.
The vajra is indestructible; furthermore, each one fully possesses the five perfections. Therefore, its entire body is dense and compact, without any gaps.

Just as with the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen emptinesses, the one hundred and eight samādhis, the five hundred dhāraṇīs, and so forth, shall all be explained in detail.
Because one is clad in such vajra armor, one transmigrates through the six [realms].
The Way transcends birth and death, and cannot be harmed by any afflictions, karma, or suffering. To explain this in a brief and general sense:

because the practitioner empowers themselves with this mantra, all devas, nāgas, and other beings perceive them as identical to the body of Vajrasattva, their entire form clad in adamantine armor that is firm, dense, and boundless in its radiance.
Like a fierce flame, therefore none who act as obstacles can harm it.
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ vajrakavaca hūṃ*.
*Vajra* is the Vajra-kavaca (Vajra Armor), which is the Tathāgata named Kṣa.
With the vajra-eye, he universally observes all sentient beings so that none are without this vajra armor; therefore, it is expounded through words of truth.
Taking the initial syllable *vaḥ* as the essence of the mantra, *vaḥ* signifies that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression. If one were to play...
The treatise states that all objects of verbal expression can be refuted and overturned, as they lack any inherent solidity;
therefore, the syllable *va* is taken as the essence, and the subsequent syllables are explained through its transformation. Why are all phenomena beyond verbal expression?
Because their arising cannot be apprehended. Why can their arising not be apprehended? Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is pure. This intrinsic purity is precisely...

This is the body of Vajrasattva. Next, the meaning of "armor" (*kavaca*) is clarified: if a phenomenon were produced through artificial construction, one should know that it possesses only a provisional name;
since it undergoes transformation according to conditions, it cannot even maintain its own nature, let alone serve to shield against the sharp arrows of the six sense-objects.
Now, observing this vajra-body of inexhaustible adornment, it is entirely free from all artificial construction.
Therefore, it is firm and indestructible, such that the hundredfold negations cannot disturb it; for this reason, it is called the "Vajra Armor.
The final syllable *HŪṂ* is the sound of fearlessness, and it also carries the meaning of sovereign power as well as the meaning of joy.

When one realizes this gateway of the syllable *HA* through the perfection of meditative concentration and wisdom, one knows for oneself that one will surely be able to shatter all obstacles. Universal...
Because he protects all sentient beings, he experiences great joy.
Next, regarding the explanation of the Tathāgata’s Eye mantra: it is like the King of Golden-Winged Birds (Garuḍa), who is endowed with majestic power and possesses complete and firm wings;
furthermore, having attained eyes of extreme clarity and sharpness, he gazes down upon the great ocean from the midst of the void as if looking at a reflection in a mirror.
Just as one who is able to capture dragons at will with sovereign power, it should be known that the practitioner of mantras is likewise so;

because they empower themselves with these Tathāgata-pure eyes, the ocean-like assembly of the maṇḍala constantly appears before them, allowing them to fully perceive all faculties, conditions, and the methods for removing obstacles.
Because all such vajra-activities are accomplished according to their will, [the following section] follows.
Recite the mantra:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatākṣayavaiyavalokāya svāhā.
Within the meaning of the phrase, *tathāgata-cakṣu* refers to the Tathāgata’s eye; next, *vyavalokana* means "to observe.
Thus, it means to observe by means of the Tathāgata’s eye. It takes the initial syllable *ta* as its essence.
*Tathatā* (Suchness) is the meaning of the many phenomena (*tathā*), because all phenomena are fundamentally unborn; therefore, this Suchness itself is also not [born].
Because this can be attained, the Tathāgata contemplates all phenomena as ultimately neither identical nor different; though they are invisible, he perceives them clearly.

As it is with the Buddhas, so it is with the eyes of all sentient beings. When a practitioner utters these words of truth, they receive the empowerment of the inconceivable Buddha-eye and gradually attain the purification of their own vision.
Next, there are six mantras for unguents and so forth; because they are required when entering the maṇḍala to perform offerings, they are explained in this chapter:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ viśuddha-ghana-dhūpa-vāsane svāhā*.
In this compound term, *viśuddha* has the meaning of "pure," *gandha* means "fragrance," and *janmabhava* has the meaning of "arising.
Thus, it signifies the arising of pure fragrance. Its essence is the initial syllable *vi*;

by adding the stroke of the vowel *i* to the syllable *va*, the sound is transformed into *vī*, which represents the syllable *va*. This *va* signifies "vajra" and the meaning of "transcending verbal expression."
Samādhi has the meaning of "abiding. Thus, the equality of concentration and wisdom is itself abiding in non-conceptualization (*niṣprapañca*).

O Vajradhara, the wisdom of unimpeded knowledge throughout the three times is such a precept. This fragrance of the precepts is by nature fundamentally quiescent, without coming or going, yet it constantly and universally pervades the *dharmadhātu*;
therefore, it is called the "pure ointment. Although all sentient beings equally possess it...

However, because [the Bodhisattva] had not yet generated the aspiration for enlightenment, this incense had not been produced; now that I have already applied this fragrance of the precepts (*śīlagandha*) to smear the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), this pure fragrance universally perfumes all things.
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām (1) mahāmaitrīya (2) vigatāghātāya svāhā (3). Regarding the meaning of these phrases:
*mahāmaitrīya* means "great loving-kindness" (*mahāmaitrī*), and *vigatāghātāya* means...

The meaning of "arising" refers to the arising of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). Taking the syllable *ma* as the essence of the mantra—specifically the letter *ma* with the stroke of samādhi—one pronounces it with a shifted vowel (*mā*).
Here, *ma* signifies "mind" (*citta*) and "self" (*ātman*), and is also called "great emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).

It is said that this lotus of the mind was previously entangled by the false notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*) and thus could not grow; now, because one has personally realized the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the mind, [it flourishes].
Because the eight petals and stamens unfold in succession from within the treasury of compassion, it is said that [the Buddha] is "born from great compassion.

Furthermore, because the seed of the king of trees, the pure bodhicitta, grows and flourishes from the ground of compassion, blossoming the flowers of the ten thousand virtues and, through skillful means, bearing fruit, it is said that [the Buddha] is "born from great compassion. One should understand this by means of the gateway of syllables (*akṣaramukha*).
To explain this in detail:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām* (1). *Dharmadhātunuge te* (2). *Svāhā*. Regarding the meaning of these phrases:
*dharmadhātu* signifies the "dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*), and *anugate* signifies "following after" or "reaching unto. It is also...

This meaning of "pervasive arrival" (*pari-gata*) also carries the sense of "going forth" (*gati*) and "advancing without dwelling. It is translated as "the Dharma-realm pervasively arrived at" (*dharmadhātu-parigata*).

Taking the character *da* (達) at the beginning of the phrase as its essence: because the realm of sentient beings is fundamentally unborn, even the defining characteristics of the Dharma-realm cannot be apprehended.
Thus, this Dharma-realm is profound and vast, boundless and immeasurable; yet, one practices yoga within it.
Because people constantly and exceptionally advance without ceasing, their physical, verbal, and mental activities pervade this entire Dharma-realm;
even when offering a single flower to the Buddha, it likewise pervades this entire Dharma-realm—this is the meaning of "incense."
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām (1) Arara (2) Karara marīndare marīndane (3) Mahāmarī (4) Svāhā. Regarding the first phrase,
"Arara" means a sound that is unpleasant to hear, an unwholesome sound, like the cry of a person in distress.
Noisy sounds clamor and disturb the minds of those who hear them; next, "kara-kara" signifies the cessation of such unwholesome loud noises, carrying the meaning of tranquility and serene detachment.
Herein, the meaning is that the food consists precisely of the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna;
therefore, it is expressed by means of these words. Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the syllabic wheel (*akṣara-cakra*), "A" signifies the sense of primordial beginning.
When this primordial ground exists, there are two kinds of defilements, namely the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Due to these two kinds of defilements, there is conceptual proliferation and clamor; because of this conceptual proliferation and clamor, there is the sound of conceptual proliferation and clamor.
Now, because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, these two kinds of defilements are also fundamentally unarisen.
This is the opening of the gate of ambrosia (*amṛta*) and the preparation of the meal of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called *A-ra-ra*.

Furthermore, if a person diligently cultivates the ten thousand practices in the hope of attaining such a flavor of the Dharma, because there is still the element of conditioned activity (*abhisamskāra*), the two obstacles will arise again;
this is not the true ambrosial flavor of constant life, color, and strength. Now, because all phenomena are without conditioned activity, one internally realizes it.
"Flavor is not obtained from another," meaning that once one has consumed the milk-rice porridge, there is nothing further required; thus it is said to "cease previous unwholesome sounds.

Regarding *phalaṃ nandāmi*, generally in the Western regions, the food offered during sacrificial rites—presented upward to the Buddhas and downward to the spirits—is collectively termed *phalaṃ*. The meaning of the phrase is: "I offer this food. Next, it says *phalaṃ*...
*Nirṇāmayati* means this: having accepted the food offered by me, you should in turn bestow upon me excellent food.

Just as people in the world offer delicacies to the *puṇyakṣetra* (field of merit) so that they may lack nothing in terms of food and drink in both this life and future lives, so now, through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the inexhaustible Dharma-food, the offerings presented to the World-Honored Ones shall be returned to fulfill [my needs].
My wish is that there may always be an abundance of the flavor of neither-dying-nor-arising. Next, regarding "Mahā-phala" (Great Fruit):
this refers to being doubly vast, expansive, and exquisite among all foods. By means of this analysis, it is said of the preceding phrase:
"That which I now offer and that which I pray for, all exist within a flavor that is utterly incomparable and unsurpassed; I do not seek [anything else]."
This is food of limited measure.
NAMAḤ SAMANTABUDDHĀNĀM (1) TATHĀGATA-RAÑJA-SAPARAṆA-VYAVASĀNA (3) GAGANAUDĀRIYE (4) SVĀHĀ.
In this phrase, *tathāgata* means "Tathāgata"; *arciḥ* means "flame-light"; next, *sapharaṇe* means "pervasive";
*avabhāsana* means "all darknesses"; and *gaganodare* means "limitless like space.
The intended meaning is that the Tathāgata’s flame-light pervades all darknesses, being equal to space.
There is no limit to this mantra; it takes the many syllables of its opening phrase as its essence.

Just as the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the mind is the great wisdom-light of Vairocana, which universally illumines the world and pervades everywhere without exception—whereas what are called "all darknesses" are simply ignorance (*avidyā*), and because ignorance is fundamentally unarisen, its very essence is light—therefore:
The Tathāgata’s radiance pervades all darkness and is said to be equal to space because ignorance and so forth are as immeasurable as space;

thus the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is also immeasurable like space. This extends even to old age and death, which are as immeasurable as space, and thus the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is also immeasurable like space, just as all things are in accordance with the twelve links of dependent origination.
All dharmas are likewise explained according to this definitive meaning; therefore, it is called the Lamp-Light Mantra.
To empower a lamp with this mantra and offer it to the Buddha is the supreme among all offerings.
Namo samantabuddhānāṃ gaganasamāsama svāhā. In this phrase, *gagana* means "space";
*sama* means "equal," and *asama* means "unequaled. That is to say, it is equal to space and yet unequaled.
Because the fundamental nature of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is pure, it is without division.
Because they are distinct and because they are boundless, they are equal to empty space;
yet, furthermore, they possess immeasurable, limitless, and inconceivable merits that cannot be illustrated by that empty space, and are therefore said to be "unequaled.
Furthermore, *asama* means "unequal"; that which is unequal refers to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). Now, since [these merits] are equal to empty space, they are also equal [to them].
Because this is peerless, it is said to be "equal to the peerless void.

Since even the characteristics of coming and going within the realm of sentient beings cannot be apprehended, and the characteristics of coming and going within the dharma-realm also cannot be apprehended—because the Tathāgata’s suchness (tathatā) cannot be apprehended—it is called the "Great Emptiness" (mahā-śūnyatā). Because this Great Emptiness is pure by nature, it is equal to the peerless void.
Using water to bathe the stainless body is the true meaning of *argha*.
Next, there are four mantras which are also taught in this chapter because they constitute the marks of the adornment of the maṇḍala-ācārya.
First, the mantra of the Tathāgata’s Uṣṇīṣa:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ, gagana-ananta-spharaṇa-viśuddha-dharmanirjāta svāhā.
In this phrase, *gagana-ananta* means "infinite space"; *sarvatra* means "universal"; *viśuddha* means "pure";
and *dharmadhātu-ja* has the meaning of "born from the realm of phenomena" (*dharmadhātu*). This statement signifies that the Tathāgata’s cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) is like space:
it transcends all measure, is universal, and is pure; one should know it to be thus.
The uṣṇīṣa is born from the matrix of the *dharmadhātu*, not from the matrix of worldly parents.
This mantra also takes the letter *ga* as its essence; it says that the mark of the Tathāgata’s uṣṇīṣa has no marks of coming or going, being identical to the great void.
Yet, all sentient beings perceive it through the marks of coming and going; therefore, they are unable to traverse the ten directions [to reach it].
When one perceives its limit—if a practitioner, with a mind of certain resolve, knows that the mark on the crown of their own head is likewise so—it is called the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-mantra.
When the ācārya himself manifests as Vairocana, he should loosen his topknot and re-bind it;
if he is a renunciant, he should form a fist with his right hand and place it upon his crown.
After first reciting this mantra to empower it, none of the various devas and other celestial beings will be able to see the mark on the crown of his head.
Next is the Tathāgata-kavaca-mantra.
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vajrajvālāviśapuṣpa hūṃ. Regarding the meaning of this phrase:
*vajrajvālā* means "adamantine light," and *viśapuṣpa* has the sense of "pervasive.
This signifies that the light of adamantine wisdom pervades all things, capable of removing the darkness and obstructions of birth and death, such that none can [resist it].
That which outshines all else is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s armor. This mantra takes the final *hūṃ* syllable as its essence and is endowed with the three gates of liberation:
the *na* syllable above it, together with the nasal dot (*bindu*), signifies the Great Emptiness, which is the gate of liberation through emptiness;
its fundamental essence is the syllable *ha*, which, being free from causes and conditions, is the gate of liberation through signlessness.
Below is the syllable *U*, which represents the samādhi; because it is primordially unborn (*an-utpanna*), it is the gate of liberation through non-action (*an-abhisamskāra*).
These three gates cannot be entered by any obstacles. Because this light of wisdom universally adorns the body, it is called the "Tathāgata Armor.
Upon examining the *Guhyamudrā-paṭala*, the Sanskrit manuscript appears to have some omissions; I suspect this refers to the *Vajra* [armor].
The mantra of Vajrasattva’s Circular Halo should further be sought in other Sanskrit manuscripts.
Next is the mantra of the Tathāgata’s Circular Halo: Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ jvala-m-ariṇi tathāgatārci...
*Svāhā*.
In the meaning of the preceding phrase, *jvala* signifies "blazing light" (*jvālā*) and *mālīna* signifies "garland.
Because the garland of blazing light forms an uninterrupted circle, it is called the Tathāgata’s "perfect halo" (*prabhāmaṇḍala*). The next phrase says: *tathāgata-ṛṣi*.
The meaning of *jñāna* (旨) is the light of the Tathāgata; this is the light of clear understanding (*vidyā*).
Although its name differs from the Sanskrit term for the light of the *Jvālāmālā*, it is precisely this character *jñā* (旨) that constitutes the essence of the mantra.

The *ra* sound above signifies defilement (*rajas*), while the base *cha* (遮) below signifies change and transformation (*vikāra*). Because it enters the gate of the syllable *a*, it is the primordial source itself.
Being free from dust and defilement, and being subject neither to transition nor change, this is the Tathāgata’s light of eternal quiescence.

Furthermore, accompanied by the sound of the *ī* syllable, it signifies that this light of eternal quiescence is fully endowed with both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, it is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, and illuminating yet ever-quiescent.
Through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the *ācārya* upon his own body, all the celestial deities and others behold the Tathāgata.
A wreath of flames completely envelops his body; his majestic and fierce splendor is difficult to behold, like the orb of the sun.
Therefore, those who would create obstacles find no opportunity against him.
This is the Tathāgata’s tongue mantra.
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ mahāmahātathāgatairhavadharma-pratiṣṭhitāya svāhā. Regarding the meaning of these phrases:
*mahāmahā* means "the Great, the Non-Great" (the Great that is not great); *tathāgatairhava* [is derived from] *tathāgata-īrṣyā*.
*Vaḥ* signifies the tongue of the Tathāgata; because this tongue possesses the characteristic of being broad and long, pervading and covering all Buddha-fields, it is called "Great" (*mahat*).
Since this greatness has nothing superior to it, nothing with which it can be compared, and even the characteristic of greatness cannot be apprehended, it is called "Non-great" (*amahat*).
Next, *sattya* means truth (*satya*), *dharma* means phenomenon (*dharma*), and *prati-* [means...]
*Śatruṃjaya* is translated as "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*), referring to the dharma of accomplishing the True Reality (*satya*).
Because the Tathāgata has constantly cultivated truthful speech throughout immeasurable kalpas, he has attained this accomplishment of the dharma of the Wheel of Equal Speech.
Since the sincere words he utters are invariably without discrepancy, the final syllable *ta* constitutes the essence of the mantra, clarifying the nature of the Tathāgata.
All languages are eternally like the true mark (*dharmatā*): non-deceptive and non-different.

By means of this empowerment of the body, the *ācārya* turns the wheel of the Dharma teachings so that they are all like vajra; even to the point of being able to pervade all Buddha-fields with a single sound.
All such mantras and the like should be extensively explained by means of the "gateways of letters" (*akṣaramukha*).
