However, the Ācārya takes "indestructible" (*abhedya*) as the correct meaning.
It is like a person in debate who has fallen into a position of defeat from which he can no longer recover; yet another person is able to emerge from that fault and overcome the opponent.

That which cannot be overcome by opponents is called "indestructible" (*abhedya*) in the Sanskrit language. By the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata is non-artificial and indestructible;
likewise, the characteristics of all mantras are also by nature non-artificial and indestructible.

Because they are empowered by their own intrinsic characteristics, it is said that they are "empowered by the indestructible nature of reality" (*dharmatā-adhiṣṭhāna*). As for the term "purifying," it refers to the removal of various [defilements].
When the stains of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the conscious mind are removed, the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) is itself the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
in reality, there is nothing to be removed.
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva immediately abided in the Buddha-realm Adornment Samādhi and spoke of non-existence."
The Mantra of Obstructive Power refers to this Buddha-realm, which is the adornment of the inconceivable, equal ground of mind realized by all Buddhas themselves.
That is to say, from the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala, the Universal Manifestation of Form-body pervades the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm,
simultaneously practicing the Bodhisattva path to adorn various Buddha-lands and achieve the One.
Because every single sentient being, by giving rise to even one kind of root of goodness, possesses all myriad virtues, they are named Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
this is precisely the perfect cause of Mahāvairocana, and the Buddha is the fruit of that perfect cause.
The mantra now being explained correctly clarifies this meaning.
Namo samanta-buddhānāṃ | Samantanugata-viraja-dharmanirjāta-mahā-maha-sa-...
The first word is *vāha*; the second word is "taking refuge" (*namas*); the third word, *samantam*, has meanings such as "all.

*Nugate* has the meaning of "progressing," or it is called "going," or "departing," or "setting forth"; when connected with the preceding vowel *ā*, there are also instances where the sense of "progressing" is absent.

This means that body, speech, and mind are ultimately equal. Because one traverses the bodhisattva path through all places by means of such an excellent cause of equality and thereby attains perfect enlightenment, it is called "Equal Gait" (*samagati*). One should know that such a gait is characterized by neither going nor coming;
therefore, it is said to be "without progression. Regarding the third term, *vīraja*, it carries the meaning of being free from dust and defilement.
*Dharmamegha* (Dharma-cloud) means the arising of the Dharma.
Because one has not realized the three types of action (*trikarma*) and so forth as they truly are, there arise the sixty mental states and various defilements.
Now, because one knows that such defilements are ultimately equal [to the Dharma], all obscurations and veils are naturally purified; this is the single perfect cause of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
The merit of all Tathāgatas is by its very nature (*dharmatā*) without deficiency; therefore, when one is free from all obscurations, it is called the "seed for the adornment of the Buddha-realm.
From this seed, which pervades all places, there arise stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits, forming the Great King of Medicinal Trees with unimpeded power;
hence it is said that "the Dharma arises," just as a lotus grows within a great pond.
Gradually spreading and flourishing, it is able to fill the great pond; likewise, these seeds originally arise from within the equal Dharma-realm and return to fill the equal Dharma-realm.
Therefore, the next phrase says "Mahā-mahā," which refers to the greatest among the great. Furthermore, as for what was previously called "Mahā":

Regarding the "Greatness of the Place of Birth" (*janmasthāna-mahattva*): that which follows is called the Greatness of the Accomplished (*siddha-mahattva*), while that which precedes is the Greatness of the Cause (*hetu-mahattva*) and that which follows is the Greatness of the Fruit (*phala-mahattva*).
Furthermore, that which precedes is the Greatness of Wisdom and Vow (*jñānapraṇidhāna-mahattva*), while that which follows is the Greatness of Practice (*caryā-mahattva*).

Moreover, the intermediate [term] also includes the sound of "attracting" (*ākṣepa*), which signifies the Greatness of the Great (*mahā-mahattva*). This is because within the Great there is no further "greatness" to be contrasted with it; thus, even the characteristic of greatness (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended. As it is said: [omitted].
When the yogin contemplates that the mind is perfectly luminous and pervades all places, even this mark of perfect luminosity cannot be apprehended;
therefore, it is called "the Great Non-existence of the Great. Furthermore, *ma* signifies the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*), and *ha* signifies the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*).
This cause is the pure bodhicitta, which is precisely Great Emptiness. Great Emptiness is the Buddha-realm and the Adornment Samādhi; it is also named *sa*.
The reason *prajñā* (wisdom) is mentioned repeatedly is that this mind is perpetually sublime and advances, increasing and expanding from moment to moment;
therefore, it is great and yet greater. Furthermore, the initial mind is not different from the subsequent mind;

the great emptiness at the time of first entering the *dharmadhātu* is the same as the great emptiness at the time of reaching the ultimate *dharmadhātu*. Thus, the fruit is identical to the cause, and the cause is, moreover, no longer a cause.

Furthermore, the syllable *Ha* also carries the meaning of "joy," because when a bodhisattva first attains the realization of Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), they are born into the family of all Buddhas and give rise to the ten inexhaustible vows with great rapture. Therefore, this mantra takes the syllable *Ha* as its very essence.
When a practitioner contemplates and contemplates within the gateway of the syllable *Ha*, they immediately attain equality with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

This is the Samādhi of the Adornment of the Buddha’s Sphere wherein the Bodhisattva abides; here, I shall briefly clarify the meaning of the phrases, each of which shall be extensively explained through the gateway of syllables (akṣaramukha), as is the case with all subsequent examples.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva dwelt in the Samādhi of the Universal Arising of Great Compassion and spoke the mantra of his own mind.

Just as the previously mentioned Samantabhadra Bodhisattva dwelt in the realm of all Tathāgatas and brought forth inexhaustible adornments, so too did he now pervade the realms of all Tathāgatas and give rise to great compassion according to each seed."

Although it is said that one attains mastery within a single Dharma-gate by bestowing the joy of the True Dharma according to the various dispositions and desires of sentient beings, in reality, one is fully endowed with all gates of the Dharma-realm.
Because one expounds the essential heart of the mind according to what one has personally realized, it is called the "Heart of Mantra" (*mantrahṛdaya*). *Arthāñjaya* translates as "Incapable."
"Victorious" (*jaya*) is an epithet for the Bodhisattva Maitreya within the Yoga school.
According to the meaning of that sutra, because there is no subtle or profound aspect of the various vajra-activities that he does not thoroughly investigate, he is called "The Unconquerable One.
This present mantra takes the letter *A* as its essence; it is by means of this that one knows all phenomena are originally unarisen and arise only from...
Because of dependent origination, although one transmigrates through the cycle of birth and death, one does not depart from Suchness;
by relying on this Suchness, one attains perfect enlightenment throughout all realms of sentient beings. For this reason, he is called "The Invincible One.
The subsequent phrase further explains the causes and conditions for being invincible: *sarvasattvāḥ* means "all sentient beings."
*Aśaya* means "the nature of the mind" (*citta-svabhāva*). *Nirjñāti* means "to reach," "to know," or "to go.

It refers to thoroughly understanding the mental natures of all sentient beings and acting in accordance with them; it means clearly perceiving all faculties and conditions, as well as knowing various crafts and skills.
Because one can thus pervade all realms of existence and fulfill them according to their inclinations, it is so named.
It is the Samādhi of Universal Great Compassion. Furthermore, the correct Sanskrit pronunciation of Maitreya is *Maitrīye*.
This means "Kindly One" (*Maitreya*). This name itself is the mantra; the initial syllable *Mai* serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
*Ma* is the mind and also the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). By adding the sound of *samādhi*, it signifies self-realization.
This mind is precisely the Great Emptiness Samādhi; because it contains all phenomena within itself, it is able to universally manifest great compassion.
If there are sentient beings who can cultivate this gateway of letters (*akṣaramukha*), they are identical to the Bodhisattva Maitreya. The Ācārya said:

"If one follows the original name, the syllable *Tṛ* (pronounced with the *dviḥ-svāra*) serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*). This refers to the 'Suchness' (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), which is non-existent."
Defilements are the obscuration of compassion.
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha entered the Samādhi of the Pure Realm and spoke the mantra of his own mind.
This means that upon entering this samādhi, one immediately knows that the realm of all Buddhas is ultimately pure, just like...

Because space is thus, the Universal Gate Maṇḍala is entirely free from all characteristics; it is solely the Buddha’s self-realization of mind, which can only be realized by oneself and cannot be shown to others.
Yet, through sovereign spiritual power, its giving and receiving, its bestowing and taking, provide for sentient beings exhaustively and without end.
Furthermore, it is precisely because space possesses nothing that there is nothing it does not contain. Thus it is said: "A."
*Kāśa* is space; *samudra* is that which is equal to it; *nirveda* is thorough knowledge.
It is also called "proceeding" (*prasthita*), meaning that because one knows the mind to be identical to space, all phenomena are entirely equal to space.
At that time, by means of the dharma of non-abiding, one fully cultivates the ten thousand practices (*sāhasrikā-caryā*) through non-attachment.
That which is attained for the sake of skillful means is likewise identical to empty space;
thus, this mantra takes the initial long syllable *Ā* as its essence. The long *Ā* signifies the meaning of initiating practice;
it means that one cultivates the myriad practices by means of the stainless bodhicitta that traverses empty space, thereby producing various stalks within the great void.
Since [the preceding] refers to leaves, flowers, and fruits, the subsequent phrase further explains it:
*vicitra-raṅga* means various wonderful colors; *vastra* means clothing; and *dhāra* means wearing.
Thus, "wearing garments of variegated colors" refers to the Dharma-body adorned with myriad virtues, and is also depicted as a great painting.
The adornment of the pure ground of the Compassion Maṇḍala also signifies the meaning of the universal manifestation of myriad images within the mirror of the great void.
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin entered the Samādhi of the Power of Compassion," which is like the universality of great loving-kindness (maitrī).
One should know that the power of compassion (*karuṇā-bala*) is likewise produced from the gateways of all *dharmadhātus* to bring about various benefits and joys;
it purifies all veils and obstacles through the gateways of all *dharmadhātus* and uproots the suffering of sentient beings.

Furthermore, just as when thunder resounds in the month of spring, those who are hibernating all emerge from their shells, it is therefore called the power of compassion. This mantra begins with the letter *A*.
The sound drawn out and urgently called is the essence; the Sanskrit pronunciation is the sound of subduing, which is the thunderous roar of great compassion.
The syllable *A* is the fundamental mind of all sentient beings, fully endowed with the nature of all-knowledge.
However, because they do not know it as it truly is, it is termed various "coverings and obstructions. The two dots on its side signify the meaning of purifying and removing them.
What is called "removing the hindrances" (āvaraṇa-vinivartana) is simply opening this gate of the letter A to purify the Buddha-eye.

Because the drawn-out sound of the letter A carries the meaning of samādhi, and because its movement merges with the bindu of nirvāṇa, it is the complete fulfillment of the meaning of skillful means (upāya).
It is said that when the hindrances and veils of this mind are removed, all the skillful means of the myriad practices are fully perfected.
This signifies the blossoming of the Lotus-womb Treasury (Padmagarbha). For this reason, these syllables are also used as the mantra for the Tathāgata’s seat.

Next, it says *sattvārthāya vyutthānāya*, which means "for the benefit of sentient beings" (*sattvārtha*) and "for the purpose of arising" (*vyutthāna*), the latter signifying origination. This clarifies the reason why [this mantra] eradicates hindrances and obstructions.
The intent [of this] is precisely to give rise to the merit of the myriad practices and benefit sentient beings;

just as the lotus seed attains freedom from its hard husk, gradually emerges from the mud, flourishes and thrives, and remains unstained by dust or water, it enables those who partake of it to experience joy in body and mind.
Therefore, the next phrase clarifies the fruit of such benefit. In Sanskrit, *tāla* refers to its essence.
The "many sounds" refer to the consciousness-mind of sentient beings; furthermore, there is the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness), which is the mind as it truly is (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*).
The reason it is linked with the syllable *ra* is to express that the true nature of the mind is eternally pure by its very essence (*svabhāva*), devoid of any dust or defilement.
The circle above [the letter] signifies that it is identical to the great void (*mahā-ākāśa*); even while abiding in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), it remains thus, and likewise enters into *nirvāṇa*.
Because it is likewise when turning back, it is stated again; because it is likewise when abiding in the two extremes, and likewise when practicing the Middle Way, it is stated again;
because it is likewise when not yet having finally emerged from the entanglements, and likewise when already having finally emerged from the entanglements, it is stated again.
Hereafter, there shall be further detailed explanations according to one's mastery of discernment.
The syllables *talaṃ talaṃ* signify the traces of the path of instruction for dispatching [delusions];

they directly clarify the state of realization, stating that within this very mind, even the mark of suchness (*tathatā*) cannot be apprehended, being nothing other than the solitary, inconceivable Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As for the repetition of other meanings, it is the same as explained previously.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara entered the Samādhi of Universal Contemplation (*Samantadarśana-samādhi*) and spoke the mantras of his own mind and its retinue.

This is precisely the Samādhi of the Universal Eye (*Samantanetra-samādhi*). As explained above, within the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala (*Mahākaruṇā-garbha-maṇḍala*), there are immeasurable Dharma-gates;
furthermore, within each individual gate, there are immeasurable roots and conditions, and immeasurable directions.
It is like the void or the great ocean, immeasurable and unfathomable. Furthermore, upon entering a single dharma-gate, one immediately possesses all gates of the dharma-realm;
thus they are neither different nor identical, yet they are both different and identical—only the wisdom of a Buddha can know this.
When entering this samādhi, one is able, in every thought-moment, to universally observe with the universal eye (samantacakṣus) in its full perfection.
Because it is characterized by clear comprehension, it is called the Samādhi of Universal Contemplation (*Samantadarśana*).

At that time, from within this samādhi, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara spoke the mind of the Universal Eye (*Samantanetra*) and the associated dharma-gates such as Mahāsthāmaprāpta in words of impartial truth.
This is because they all belong to the Lotus Family (*Padmakula*). The initial phrase "Sarvatathāgata" refers to all the Tathāgatas.
*Vairocana* (the long vowel is drawn out): this is a term for "observation," because it is that which is observed by all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
therefore, it is called the "Observation of All Tathāgatas" and is also named the "Equal Observation. In the *Vajraśekhara* school, it is called the "Vajra Eye.
The next phrase says *karuṇā*, which means "compassion," and *maya*, which means "essence"; it is said that this is universal...
Because the eye has great compassion as its very essence, it is called the "essence of compassion. It is like casting pure gold into the form of a person;
because its own substance is entirely gold, it is called a "golden person. This essence of compassion is likewise so; therefore, Avalokiteśvara is named the "Compassionate One.
Furthermore, the eternally quiescent Dharmakāya has meditative concentration and wisdom as its two hands, and likewise possesses both compassion and wisdom.
Because there are two hands, the Secret Holder holds the Vajra-Wisdom Seal and Avalokiteśvara holds the Lotus Seal.
If viewed in relation to the Three Truths, this is the wisdom that enters the provisional from emptiness; if contrasted with the three dots (*bindu*), it is the Tathāgata’s virtue of liberation.
Thus, he bears the name "Avalokiteśvara, the Compassionate One. This is the meaning established regarding these three eyes within the *Vidyādharapiṭaka*.
It is divided into three sections; Avalokiteśvara is the lord of the Lotus Family (*padmakula*).
The next phrase, "ra ra ra," precisely clarifies the meaning of this lotus samādhi as being free from dust and defilement.
Because the syllable-gateway *ra* is fundamentally unborn, and because even causes cannot be apprehended, the compassionate eye of the Tathāgata is eternally free from the cataracts of defilement.

It is spoken in turn because it opposes the stains of the three poisons, the stains of the three paths, the stains of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, and the stains of ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas;

because the stains to be remedied by the three eyes and the three wisdoms are originally unarisen and their causes cannot be found, it is spoken in turn. Next, "HŪṂ" signifies that which is capable of terrifying.
Fearing that meaning because his own mind was free from the three stains, he knew that the minds of all sentient beings were likewise free from the three stains.
With great compassion permeating his heart, he thought: "Why is it that sentient beings cannot, even for a moment, observe and realize this for themselves?
Therefore, he uttered the lion’s roar, desiring to cause all sentient beings [to realize it] through the power of Avalokiteśvara.
One is born free from these originally non-existent defilements. Furthermore, the essential nature of the syllable *HŪṂ* is the gateway of the syllable *HA*.
*HA* signifies the meaning of "cause," which is the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*). Below it is the sound of *u*, representing the filaments of the myriad practices;
above it is the great dot of emptiness (*bindu*), by which it is fully blossomed. By means of this very word of truth, one terrifies all obstacles.
In the Padmakula, this signifies wrath. Next, it says "ja," which carries the meaning of "arising.
With two dots (bindus) on its sides, it signifies the arising that purifies the three stains, causing the lotus lineage to arise. This mantra primarily clarifies the meaning of increasing merit;
thus, this syllable constitutes the essence of the mantra, or alternatively, the initial syllable *sa* may serve as its essence.
This is the meaning of being free from defilement and attachment. Furthermore, this *Mahāsthāmaprāpta* mantra is a repeated utterance of the syllable *ṣṇī* belonging to the Lotus family.
Its fundamental essence is the letter-gateway *ja*, which signifies "arising.

That which is to be remedied—the arising of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the arising of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—is now shown to be fundamentally non-arising in both cases, even down to their causes.
Because it is unattainable, the two obscurations do not arise, and true great emptiness (*tattva-mahāśūnyatā*) is produced; therefore, a circular bindu is added.
Next, there is the syllable *sa*, which constitutes the essence of the mantra and signifies "immovable.

Whether phenomena are considered existent or non-existent, or whether they are moving or immovable, all are signs of decay and instability. Now, because arising is unattainable, [the syllable *sa* is established].
By adding two dots to the side of the syllable *sa*, this Lotus Samādhi is made identical to Nirvāṇa—supremely firm and immovable.

This is the sovereign rank (*aiśvarya*) of the Tathāgata; because this King of Mantras holds the unopened lotus so that it does not fall away, and ensures that one shall likewise attain such a great rank, it is called Mahāsthāmaprāpta (He Who Has Attained Great Power).
The mantra of the Bodhisattva Uṣṇīṣavijayā is also a member of the Lotus Family.
*Karūṇa* means "compassion" (*karuṇā*); *nava-vai* signifies "born from compassion," which is to say, born from the eye of Avalokiteśvara.
Next, *tārā* has the meaning of "eye" and also the meaning of "to deliver."
Now, this mantra takes many syllables as its essence; for the most part, it expresses the meaning that all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*).

Because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and even their causes cannot be apprehended, one should know that they possess no real characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Since they are without characteristics, suchness itself cannot be apprehended;
this is precisely what is meant by "suchness" regarding the real characteristic of all phenomena. Alongside this, there is the samādhi of the painted image. This is...

The myriad practices are all suchness; "ra" signifies the meaning of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Because all phenomena are neither identical to nor different from suchness, the six sense objects are all suchness.
The true mark (*dharmatā*) is the original nature; being free from sense objects is called the purity of seeing reality as it is, the stainless eye.
Furthermore, the six faculties and the six sense objects are called the great ocean of birth and death, and all sentient beings are entirely...

Sunk therein, they could not find its limit; now, because he perceives the true mark of the six sense-objects as they are and has reached the further shore of the Buddha-eye, he is called "Crossed Over.
The term *tāraṇī* is translated as "thoroughly crossing over":
having himself attained liberation, he is further able to universally deliver all sentient beings; having himself attained the Universal Eye free from dust, he causes all others to do so as well.

The Universal Eye of sentient beings is free from dust; this is the "Many Voices" [chapter], which, according to the *Mahāmūla*, states that five hundred Tārās were all born from the eye of Avalokiteśvara, and that their secret yogic mantras constitute the sisters of Amitābha Buddha.
The above is Bhṛkuṭī, a member of Avalokiteśvara’s retinue, as described in the *Vidyādharapiṭaka*.
Once, when Vajrapāṇi manifested an immeasurable host of fierce attendants within the Buddha’s assembly, the entire great multitude was struck with terror.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara manifested this Bodhisattva from the wrinkles upon his forehead, just as a person manifests a frown upon the forehead when angry.
Because the waves and ripples are called *vikṛti* in the Sanskrit language, he is named after them.
When Vikṛti appeared, all the Vajradharas were greatly terrified and entered into the body of Vajragarbha;
he, in turn, approached Vajragarbha in his wrathful form, and Vajragarbha likewise became terrified and entered [into another].
Standing before the Tathāgata, she spoke these words: "May the Buddha protect me. The Buddha said to Bhṛkuṭī, "Sister, you must remain there.
She immediately stood there and addressed the Buddha, saying, "I shall carry out whatever the Buddha instructs me to do.
Thereupon, the fears of all the Vajradharas were dispelled, and they all rejoiced greatly, saying, "This one of great compassion is truly able to..."
The manifestation of this majestic and powerful majesty is most rare. Why is this so?
Because the retinue of Vajradhara, employing the wisdom of ultimate emptiness, has utterly destroyed the delusions and inversions regarding persons and phenomena without remainder;
yet, they now seek to damage the merit of great compassion by means of this same fierce power. Therefore, Avalokiteśvara manifests as the Protector of the Lotus Treasury.
Therefore, by means of the *Vijayā* (Pi-ju-ti) samādhi, one subdues and breaks it;
yet, because this great compassionate wrath reaches the middle way, it should also be brought to rest. Thus the Buddha said: "Sister, you must stay!
First he says *Sarva-pāyā*, translated as "all terrors," and next he says *Tara-sani*. Furthermore—
The syllable *hūṃ* at the end of this [mantra] is also a sound of terror; it possesses three layers of meaning regarding terror.

Just as all sentient beings in this world, amidst the great terror of the perilous path of birth and death, remain unaware and ignorant, yet further erect the banner of *māna* (pride) and rely upon it for self-sustenance, they are therefore terrified by the initial phrase of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
At that time, all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) were extinguished, and they entered the adamantine true nature (*vajra-bhūta-svabhāva*).
They perceived neither sentient beings below who could be converted nor Buddhas above who could be sought; they claimed to have realized *nirvāṇa* and relied upon this as their own security.

Even when seeing the Tathāgata’s various and inexhaustible adornments, they likewise regarded them as false and wished to eliminate them. Therefore, [the Buddha] subdued them with Great Compassion (3).

When the obscured [mind] is made supple and submissive, the adamantine true nature is already like pure wax refined a hundred times, which may be shaped as one desires; yet if one continues to temper it without ceasing, one will harm the Great Wisdom of Equality. Therefore, by means of the majestic power of the Tathāgata, it is restrained. "Destroying" (tsan-hai) is a further explanation of this *hūṃ* syllable, meaning that the three stains and pride are brought to ultimate completion without remainder.
This mantra takes the syllable *ta* as its essence; it is like [the principle of] the Middle Way, wherein one must neither allow for increase nor allow for decrease.
All remaining "gate-syllables" (*akṣara-mukha*) should likewise be explained through transformation. For instance, take the following syllable *ra*:
This is the meaning of "defilement": first, having marks (*sanimitta*) is defilement; next, being markless (*animitta*) is defilement;

third, not relinquishing the state where existence and non-existence are equal is defilement, because it conforms to the Middle Way. Thus, one is able to depart from these three defilements, and others should all follow this example.
The above is the mantra of Sitātapatrā. She is the Mother of the Lotus Family; "white" signifies that she is the primordially pure bodhicitta.
Because she is the locus wherein the seed of the lotus is contained and from which all adornments of myriad virtues arise, she is given this name.
The initial phrase, *tathāgataviṣaya*, means "the realm of the Tathāgata," for the first syllable, *ta*, constitutes the essence of the mantra.
The phrase "the essence is like the true mark of the mind" refers to the primordially pure bodhicitta.
The next line, *sambhava*, has the meaning of "arising from," signifying that it arises from the realm of those Tathāgatas.
The final line, *padma-mālī*, means "lotus-garlanded"; *mālī* refers to a garland, which signifies the gathering together of various flowers.
To regard this as solemn adornment signifies the meaning of the many retinues of the Lotus Family (*padmakula*). This, in turn, further explains the preceding phrase:
from what does she arise within the realm of the Tathāgata? It is because the Lotus Garland arises from that [realm] that she is the Mother of the Lotus Family.
Furthermore, since this White Realm (*śvetadhatu*) is the samādhi of the primordially pure bodhicitta, she manifests in the form of a female deity. If...
The wisdom of primordial purity is none other than Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
The mantra of Hayagrīva on the right is that of the wrathful vidyārāja of the Padmakula;
just as Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva attained his present state by universally surveying all dharmadhātu-gates with the universal eye, so too has Hayagrīva now attained it.
By this power of Avalokiteśvara, through the gateway of all *dharmadhātus*, he utterly crushes the three obstructions and uproots the suffering of sentient beings;
thus, Hayagrīva (Horse-Head) signifies the meaning of great *vīrya* (heroic diligence). The initial syllable *HŪṂ* has the same meaning as explained previously.
*Khāna* means "to devour," and *praṇāśana* means "to destroy. *Sphoṭaya*... [The text continues with further mantric syllables].

*Ṭa-ya* signifies the meaning of "shattering until nothing remains. This is an alternative explanation of the syllable *hūṃ*, which means that by means of this Lotus Wrathful One (*padma-krodha*), one devours the three impurities (*trimala*) and destroys the three obstructions (*trāvaraṇa*) so that they are crushed without remainder.

If it were from the perspective of the single Dharma-realm gate, the obstructions would not be entirely destroyed; however, since this is from the perspective of the entire Dharma-realm gate, they are utterly extinguished.
Furthermore, this mantra takes the syllable *kha* (pronounced with a long vowel) as its essence. This *kha* is the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*);
it is called with a long vowel because all myriad practices take the emptiness of non-apprehension as their skillful means (*upāya*).
It is like space, which cannot be destroyed; except for the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it devours everything else.

Next, the syllable *na* signifies "giving" (*dāna*); its meaning is that of expelling defilements and obstructions, intending precisely to universally bestow [benefits] upon all sentient beings by thus removing those defilements and obstructions.
The remaining letter-gates (*akṣaramukha*) shall be explained in detail and at length.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva dwelt in the samādhi of the adamantine, indestructible realm of practice.
This is like the adamantine wheel of the earth, which, being extremely firm and indestructible, is able to sustain all things so that they do not collapse or move;
it is also like the great earth, which gives birth to various treasures and hidden stores without end, containing them within itself.
Just as all seeds are prevented from decaying and gradually flourish, so too is this samādhi:

it can sustain the seeds of the roots of goodness of sentient beings within the dharma-realm, so that throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas they never perish, giving rise to the qualities of true nature without end.
Furthermore, it is like a diamond, for such is the essential nature of this ground. Therefore...

It cannot be broken or wounded; likewise, this firm bodhicitta is also the foremost reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), and even if one must endure all manner of sufferings for the sake of all sentient beings while constantly remaining in the Avīci Hell, it is not harmed by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is used as a metaphor. The initial character "He" (賀) signifies the meaning of the cause (*hetu*); just as there are seeds in the world, although they exist...

There are no natures—superior, middling, or inferior—that do not arise from a cause; although the seeds of the myriad virtues of all sentient beings differ according to the three vehicles, there are none that do not arise from this Vajra-ground. Therefore, to state it thrice is precisely the meaning of the causes for the three vehicles.
Furthermore, just as worldly seeds, though they grow through conditions, [are nonetheless rooted in their own nature].
Just as all various forms and shapes, when analyzed down to the element of earth, are found to be neither arising nor ceasing, so too are these seeds of the three vehicles.
Since the phenomena produced cannot be apprehended, one should know that the cause is itself no-cause;
when analyzed down to its substantial reality, it is but a single Vajradhātu. Next, it says *sutanu*, which means "good son. Because—
This firm bodhicitta bears the burden of the world and cannot be shaken;

because it is able to succeed to the family business of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, it is named accordingly. Furthermore, because its lineage is authentic and true, it is called a "virtuous son.
One observes that every iota of goodness in all sentient beings arises from the lineage of the Tathāgata Ratnarāja; this is the ground.
The most authentic speech of the Bodhisattva of the *Zang* [Tibetan] tradition takes the syllable *Ha* as the essence of this mantra.

As for the passage in the Sūtra stating that Mañjuśrī dwells in the samādhi of the Buddha’s sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the meaning of "sustaining power" has already been explained in the first chapter.
This Bodhisattva thoroughly penetrates the profound *prajñā* of the Tathāgata; he is solely a Buddha among Buddhas.
Self-realization cannot be transmitted to others; if separated from the skillful means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it is beyond the reach of all those who rely on mental constructs.

Therefore, by employing the conduct of an infant, he manifests in the body of a youth and expounds the non-self of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*) to eliminate the dharma of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). This is a stage with traces, not the ultimate state of non-practice.
Because they abide in secret empowerment (*guhyādhiṣṭhāna*), practitioners of the path are enabled to realize the intended meaning beyond the literal words by means of these verbal expressions.
Were such skillful means not revealed, sentient beings would become attached in every instance and fail to know the profundity of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Furthermore, each and every one of the various samādhis mentioned above pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Gate, this empowerment-samādhi is likewise: though its inexhaustible adornments pervade the entire Dharma-realm, it is yet the Tathāgata’s intentional display of the traces of childhood, descending to reach all sentient beings.
He desires to cause them to rely upon this vessel until the time comes to set aside the raft;
he takes that which cannot be grasped as the place of realization, and regards shards and rubble as bright pearls.
The initial *kīṭi kīṭi* has the meaning of summoning; *kumāragā* means "youth";
*vimuktibhūtasthitāḥ* refers to those who abide in the path of liberation; *smara smara* means "remember, remember."
*Pratijñā* (the vow) refers to the previously established aspiration; its intended meaning is as follows:

"May the Dharma Prince Kumārabhūta, who abides in the path of liberation, remember his original vow and, through the empowerment of universal gate mastery (*samantamukha-vaśitādhiṣṭhāna*), cause me to swiftly awaken to the spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata. Liberation is the liberation of all Buddhas, the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Nirvana is this path of liberation; it is the path practiced by the sons of the Buddha, which consists of the contemplation of the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*).
Therefore, this mantra takes the fourth syllable, *ma* (pronounced with a long vowel), as its essence, for it signifies "self.

Since all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, the self is also fundamentally unarisen. Furthermore, since there is no one else against whom to speak of "selflessness," [the syllable *ma*] signifies the self.
Not observing self or non-self, and fully seeing both emptiness and non-emptiness, is called the Great Self and also called the Great Emptiness.
These are spoken of in this way through the skillful means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); however, at the time of ultimate liberation, it is truly not as it has been described.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, Vajrapāṇi, abiding in the Great Vajra Invincible Samādhi, spoke the mantras of his own heart and his retinue, saying:
'O Wisdom! The *Mahāvyutpatti* explains that the Sanskrit term *mahā-vijaya* has three meanings: great (*mahat*), much (*bahu*), and supreme (*vijaya*).
Because this Vajra Wisdom Seal held by the Lord of Secrets is both lofty and vast, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm."
Because it possesses both the center and the periphery, it is called "Great"; because it has as its universal retinue atoms of world-systems, it is called "Many";
because it is the most supreme among all vajra meanings, it is called "Victorious.
It is able to reveal the faults and afflictions of saṃsāra through every gateway of the dharma-realm; yet, as for the essence of this wisdom, there is no one capable of describing its faults.
It is named "Unconquerable" because it utterly shatters the hosts of the four māras across all gateways of the dharma-realm and cuts off their lineage;
yet, as for this essence of wisdom, there is no other dharma capable of destroying it, and for this reason it is called "Unconquerable.
If it possessed only the function of a single gateway, it would not be called "Great. Furthermore, O Mahāmati, such great wisdom is equal for all sentient beings.
Because it is now fully endowed with samādhi, it is called "Unconquerable" (Ajita);
thus, abiding in this samādhi, he speaks the mantra. The first phrase is a universal homage to all the Vajras;
the second phrase says *Canda*, translated as "Extremely Fierce," meaning one who is violent and even capable of devouring the entire Dharma-realm.
Sentient beings and all the worthy sages are left without remainder;
next, "Mahāluṣaṇa" signifies great wrath, even to the point that it is like the fire of the kalpa-conflagration which, having already incinerated all things, further extinguishes even their ashes.
Furthermore, "raṇa" signifies that all phenomena are free from transition and change.
*Na* signifies that all phenomena are free from enmity and opposition; therefore, the essence of Vajra-wisdom is invincible.

*Ma* signifies the four māras, the meaning of ego-clinging (*asmimāna*), and the meaning of mind and mental objects—all of which lack intrinsic nature because they arise dependent upon various conditions.
Thus, they are primordially unborn, eternally free from defilement, and by nature insentient, like the great void.
Therefore, it is called *mahā-rūṣaṇa*; this further explains the meaning of being indestructible.
Furthermore, the essence of Vajra-wisdom is free from all transition and change;

because it is without opposition, without self, without intentionality, free from defilement, and without cognition, it is identical to the great void. This is the verse for its extensive explanation.
The syllable *maṅku* is the essence of the mantra; *ha* signifies the meaning of "cause. If a phenomenon were established in dependence upon a cause, it would be subject to change and transformation;
being not free from opposition, it could all be destroyed or altered.
However, because this cause is fundamentally unarisen, its nature is eternal and constant, indestructible, and possesses firm power like the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Below this is the sound *u*.
This refers to the fact that because there is an empty dot (bindu) upon the *anuttara-samādhi*, it pervades all places;

therefore, it is called the Great Vajra. Specifically, within the Vajra Family, it carries the meaning of "wrath," being capable of [subduing] the four Māras at the great terror beneath the Bodhi tree.
Regarding the mantra *Mamukī*: *Ma* has the meaning of "mother" (*mātṛ*), and *muki* has the meaning of "many" (*bahu*).

This refers to the mothers of all the Vajradharas, as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds; since the wisdom-seals (*jñānamudrā*) of all Tathāgatas arise from them, she is called "Many Mother" (*Bahumātr̥*).
The mantra's essence consists of the initial syllable *Tṛ*, and the syllable *Ta* is... [the remainder of the sentence is missing from the source].
The mind, in its true mark, is by nature pure; all defilements have been fundamentally unarisen.
The sound "I" above [the seed syllable] signifies the meaning of samādhi.
Within this, the nature of wisdom is the Vairocana-vajra seed-syllable, which likewise arises from this samādhi. Regarding the meaning of the word, *taraṭa* means "to shatter."
The meaning of "destruction" (bhaṅga) is contained within the half-body of the syllable *ṭha*, which also carries the sense of death.

First, one slays those dwelling in the four stages (*catur-vihāra-bhūmi*), and subsequently, one slays those dwelling in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*). This is stated emphatically because it involves not only slaying all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) but also slaying all noble ones (*ārya*).
If translated according to the *Yan-di* [tradition], it is called "Superior Birth" (*jaya-janman*) and is also named "Amṛta-Birth. This is it.
Because she is the mother of all those who are invincible, she is named "Victorious Birth" (*Jaya-janman*);
because this birth is itself the state of immortality, it carries the meaning of "Nectar" (*Amṛta*).
To the right, the Vajra-śṛṅkhalā mantra takes the initial syllable *ma* as its essence; this has the meaning of "binding," and this binding is fundamental.
Because its essence is unarisen, it is like a vajra; its connection with the letter *baṅ* signifies the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).

It is said that because this vajra-binding is due to Great Emptiness, whatever is performed will necessarily be accomplished. Because it universally binds sentient beings such that none can release them, it is called the "Vajra Lock.
Regarding the meaning of the term *pūrṇa*: it signifies "binding and protecting" (*bandhana-rakṣaṇa*).
Because it is conjoined with the Great Emptiness, all places are universally and firmly bound by the vajra-chain;
even if there were a single hair’s breadth of a possibility for binding, one would never let it go. Next, it says "mudrā," which signifies firmness.
Furthermore, this explains the preceding phrase by clarifying that it is not like worldly bondage, as worldly things are subject to impermanence, change, and transformation.
The term "dispersion" (*vikiraṇa*) is repeated twice, its meaning being the same as before.
The subsequent phrase says *vajranarbha-ve*, which is translated as "born from the vajra.
*Sarvatrāpratighāti* means "that which is entirely incapable of being harmed"; this further explains the sense of being firmly bound and solidly established.
The meaning is that this chain arises from the adamantine true nature;
it is of the same substance and is so dense that there are no gaps, nor is there any form to be grasped, nor any subtle trace to be sought or seen; therefore, it is ultimately indestructible.
Furthermore, regarding the mantra of the Vidyārāja Candramaṇḍala from the Vajra Family: its mantra essence consists of the initial syllable *hrīḥ*.
Because this represents the pure bodhicitta conjoined with the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), it achieves sovereign power;
moreover, by sharing the same substance as the syllable *ra* and adding the nasal bindu (anusvāra), its intrinsic nature is free from defilement and is thus able to cleanse away all things.
Because the sound of samādhi exists above the defilements and obscurations, there is the perfection of power through the equalization of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Within this single syllable are contained bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the skillful means of the myriad practices;

therefore, the categories within this Vidyārāja division are most numerous, even including those with hundreds of thousands of hands wielding various implements. *Hrīḥ* has the meaning of "summoning" or "invoking. That is to say:
Having summoned all the people within the realms of the four Māras, one next terrifies them with the great, heroic sound of the syllable *HŪṂ*.
This is for the sake of universally accomplishing all vajra activities, because it is through immeasurable gateways that all Buddha-dharmas are fully perfected.
Next, the word *PHAṬ* is used; it has the meaning of "reproach. Since the great heroic sound has already been emitted, there remains a sense of firmness.
Because even those sentient beings who are most difficult to subdue do not yet consent to obey his commands, he further subdues them with a voice of great wrath.
Furthermore, the Vajrasūcī mantra is also a member of the Vajra retinue; the emblem of this wisdom-mudrā is shaped like a [needle].

"Gvajra" (Vajra) signifies being extremely sharp and keen; it refers to a wisdom that is single-mindedly focused and acutely penetrating, which pierces through all phenomena via the gateway of the entire *dharmadhātu* without exception, reaching directly to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Therefore, this is its name.
Taking the initial syllable "Sa" as the essence of the mantra, because it represents the ultimate truth, one is thereby able to enter deeply into the Dharma.
If one’s nature is such that they give rise to attachment in every place, by what means could they attain this?
Therefore, when a wise person hears the name of the fundamental principle (*su-śāstra*), they immediately understand it according to its meaning.
The gateway of the syllable *ba* (*ba-dvāra*) is established therein; *sarva-dharma* refers to all phenomena, and *nirvedha* refers to piercing through.
The *Yìcì* (義次) states: "Vajrasūci" refers to the essential meaning of the Vajra-needle;
"Varade" means supreme vow (*varapraṇidhāna*). This signifies that by means of the supreme-vow vajra-needle, one pierces through all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Just as a person suffering from thirst seeks only water without any other thought, one is thus able to penetrate through even the highest [obstructions] without regard for the labor or effort required.
One should know that this Vajrasūcī is precisely the meaning and function of bodhicitta; therefore, wherever one goes, one will surely pass through without any obstruction.
Furthermore, all the mantras of the Vajradharas are the ten [mantras] listed above, such as Gaganāmala and so forth.
Those who hold the seal of the Tathāgata’s differentiated wisdom, as numerous as the atoms of the world-systems, together entered the Great Vajra Invincible Samādhi.
From within their own hearts, they emitted inconceivable light, and within that light appeared these mantra syllables of the full moon.
From within the syllables, a great sound issued forth, which all the great assembly heard universally, just like Vajrapāṇi.
One should know that it is likewise when all other Honored Ones proclaim their mantras. The mantra-body consists of the initial syllable *HŪṂ*;
within it, the syllable *HA* is the body of Vajra-wisdom. Below it is the sound *U*, which signifies the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
Because this body of wisdom is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices, there are various distinctions known as mudrās. Furthermore, the sound of the syllable *U* is also [so designated].
The meaning of these samādhis is that because there are various modes of practice, there are various "Vajra Unconquerable Samādhi Gates.
The addition of "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*) above [the title] clarifies that each of these individual samādhi gates pervades all places.
The three [aspects] signify the sense of multiplicity, clarifying that although the secret gates of all Vajradharas undergo various transformations and distinctions, [they ultimately converge].
The meaning of these characters is entirely consistent with the Way; therefore, they are spoken three times. *Phaṭ* (撥吒) has the meaning of rebuking and scolding.

Furthermore, this is explained by turning back to interpret the preceding phrase: these various gates of wisdom are all for the sake of universally responding to sentient beings and greatly crushing the two kinds of birth-and-death.
Moreover, it is further explained by turning back to clarify why the life-force of the two kinds of karma and afflictions is severed.
Because one attains the arising of two kinds of great emptiness, the character *nī* (髯) is repeated.

Furthermore, all those who follow instructions— mantras being like the attendants and servants of a noble person in the world who carry out various tasks according to the commands and directions of their master—
are called "those who follow instructions" (*ājñākārin*) or "messengers" (*dūta*).
Alternatively, those known as the "Guardians" and others all receive their mandates through distinctions of activity;
these are likewise expounded by Vajrapāṇi while abiding in the Great Vajra Invincible Samādhi. The messengers of the three families are universally applicable.
Taking the initial syllable *he* as the essence of the mantra, its original sound is the letter-gateway *ha*, which is the Bodhicitta.
The Vajra lineage is also the activity performed by the wind-mandala (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), due to the addition of the sound of the syllable *kṣi*.
This refers to the samādhi of the ten thousand vajra-practices. The repeated term *he he* signifies that the practitioner performs the ultimate concentration within concentration.
To explain the meaning of the words: *he he* is a sound of invocation, followed by *kiṃjirā*.
The translation by Yeshé Dé states: "Why not hurry? This has the sense of an exhortation, like a person giving instructions to a servant;
thus, one first calls out the name and then admonishes them, saying, "Why do you not hurry with this task? Why do you delay so long?
It is intended to urge them toward urgency so that the opportunity is not lost. Next, it says *hṛīḥ hana*, which means "seize."
"Upādāna" (holding) means to cause [beings] to swiftly go forth and grasp by means of the power of Vajra-sovereignty;

the repetition of the term signifies the sense of "guarding. Having grasped and guarded them, one must further maintain them with firm diligence, so that they do not become lax or negligent and are subsequently coerced or snatched away by those who create obstacles. *Khana khana*.
This meaning of "eating" (*khādan*) further explains the preceding phrase: having grasped it, one should eat it;

furthermore, one should eat it thoroughly until it is entirely consumed, so that not even a trace of a remnant remains. Moreover, because there are two sets of three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) and four māras regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the terms "summoning," "grasping," and "eating" are all stated twice.
*Pṛ* means "to fill"; *svapratijñā* means "one's own original vow.

You originally established a wrathful vow, desiring to devour all sentient beings in order to nourish the body of merit and fulfill this great greedy aspiration; therefore, you must act swiftly. Furthermore, as...
The great elder instructed those in charge of managing household affairs to open the storehouses and bring forth various kinds of rare treasures to bestow upon those who came seeking alms,
so that all might return with their hopes fulfilled and without any lack; thus it is said that he has fulfilled his original vow.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha entered the Jewel-Abode Samādhi and spoke the mantras of his own mind and its retinue.
Because of this samādhi, the Tathāgata appeared in the world;
and because the Tathāgata appeared, immeasurable and boundless Dharma-jewels of the five vehicles all came forth, just as when a Wheel-Turning King ascends to the throne."
At that time, various hidden treasures of the world spontaneously open up, just as there is nothing that does not exist within the various jewel mountains;
according to sentient beings who possess the hand of faith, they are able to take whatever they desire at will.
This shall be explained in detail here in the "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. *Sarva-giri-śe*—this [removes] all afflictions.
*Nir-āsrava* means "free from outflows"; *sarva-dharma* means "all phenomena";
*vaśitā-prāptaḥ* means "attained mastery. The intended meaning is that one has subdued all afflictions and attained sovereignty over all phenomena. By the first... [end of fragment].
The syllable *sa* constitutes the essence of the mantra. *Sa* signifies "outflow" (*āsrava*) and is also called "solidity.

It refers to how all contaminated and conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*), which lack power and solidity, are nevertheless perceived by sentient beings as having a real, intrinsic nature; thus they cling to them with firm attachment and do not relinquish them.
Therefore, when these phenomena—which are impermanent and subject to decay—perish, one immediately sinks into the great ocean of craving and suffering. Now, entering into *A*...
Because of the gateway of letters, one knows that all outflows (*āsrava*) are fundamentally non-arisen; how much less could there be anything that dwells with solidity?

Therefore, by means of this Dharma-King Samādhi, one can universally shatter the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), universally close the gates of all evil destinies, and transform immeasurable dust-like afflictions (*kleśa*) entirely into a place of jewels.
Thus, it is called "the Dharma-King who shatters existence," being sovereign over all dharmas.
The final phrase says: *Ākāśasama-samādhi*. "Equal to space" (*ākāśasama*) is translated as "equal to the void.

"Without equal" means that this samādhi does not merely attain mastery within a single trichiliocosm, but attains mastery throughout the infinite realms of all sentient beings; therefore, it is vast and boundless.
It is equal to space; yet, just as space, while being all-pervasive, contains myriad images of diverse kinds, it is said to be "without equal.

Furthermore, just as the nature of jewels is one, yet their functions differ—some ward off evil spirits and dispel poison, some cure diseases, some preserve wealth, and some can accomplish various illusions—so too is this [nature].
Among practitioners, there are those capable of universally raining down all manner of objects, even to the point of conversing with them and commanding their service;

there are those capable of revealing to sentient beings their past lives and karmic actions, such that the great assemblies of worthies and sages all appear therein. For this reason, it is said that they are "equal and unequal."
Furthermore, the mantra of the ūrṇā-kośa (the hair-treasure) is the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits;
it is a kind of wish-fulfilling jewel within the Ratnakoṭi-samādhi. The first part, *vara-de*, is translated as "granting wishes";
the second part, *varaprada*, means "attaining wishes," just as one obtains them for oneself.
Wealth and treasures are able to provide for and relieve all people; that which I have long desired is now entirely fulfilled.
I shall now bestow upon all sentient beings their various aspirations. The final *hūṃ* syllable constitutes the essence of the mantra.
*Ha* signifies cause and joy; "cause" refers to the aspiration for omniscience, and "joy" refers to its initial attainment.
This vow reaches the stage of cultivation; therefore, upon the sound of the "myriad practices" (*sādhana*) of samādhi, the dot of great emptiness (*bindu*) is added.

This signifies that by refining such a jewel of a vow through the skillful means (*upāya*) of the myriad practices, its mirror-like clarity penetrates the void and its majestic power becomes fully perfected.
Thus, it is able to produce all manner of treasures to bestow universally upon sentient beings. By means of this sound of courageous giving, one subdues [all obstacles].
Causing those who are poor and lowly to attain mental composure and serenity is the meaning of the syllable *HŪṂ* within the *ūrṇā-kośa* (hair-treasure) dharma-gate.
Furthermore, the mantra of all Buddha-uṣṇīṣas takes "the crown" (*mūrdhan*) as its primary meaning of supreme excellence;

it is a synonym for the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Tathāgata, and it is the most difficult place to reach within the *ratnakośa-samādhi* (jewel-treasury samādhi), like the topknot of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).

The secret treasures within are not for ordinary or inferior persons to behold. Taking the initial syllable *praṃ* as the essence of the mantra, *va* signifies the realm where the mind and intellect do not function and where language cannot reach;
furthermore, by adding *mahāśūnyatā*, it becomes that which pervades all places without limit.
It is the ultimate destination and point of convergence for the myriad practices of the three vehicles.

Therefore, it is recited three times; furthermore, because it is the most supreme among the three families, because it is the most true reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) among the three truths, and because it is at the summit of the three virtues, it is recited three times.
Next, the syllable HŪṂ is the sound of fierce and great power; all those whom no holy ones can subdue are entirely subdued by it. All holy ones... [are subdued].
Because he severs all that cannot be severed by the wise, he is like a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) among the lords of mantras, able to augment their majestic power and remedy their faults;
furthermore, because he returns to the two types of birth and death, the term is stated twice.
Next, the explanation of *phaṭ* as a transformation clarifies the meaning of the Tathāgata’s wrath through the use of two *hūṃ* syllables.
It utterly destroys the two kinds of afflictions without leaving a single remnant, causing the heavy obstructions of the two extremes to become ultimately pure;
because it is the most sublime among the eight types of Buddha-uṣṇīṣas of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, and because they all converge therein,
it is called "the Uṣṇīṣa of All Buddhas."
Furthermore, the *Ajita* mantra is the wrathful vidyārāja among the retinue of Śākyamuni. "Invincible" (*ajita*) signifies that which cannot be destroyed;
it refers to the universal crushing of all obstacles and the subduing of sentient beings through various dharma-gates adapted to their respective types throughout all worlds.
Its mantra essence is the syllable *laṃ*, representing the first stage (*bhūmi*).
*Ḍa* signifies the meaning of the *dharmadhātu*; *ra* signifies the meaning of defilement, obscuration, and dust-like taint.

Because it is conjoined with the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) of *samādhi*, the sound is transformed into *dharī*. The syllable *ra* is the fire-wheel, which serves the purpose of incinerating and subduing;
because it is the *dharmadhātu*, there is nothing to which it does not pervade; because it is the great emptiness, it possesses immeasurable gateways; and because it is *samādhi*...
By means of the skillful means of the myriad practices, expressed through two turns of speech, one is able to eliminate the two major obstacles;
therefore, its vast and majestic power is such that nothing can subdue it. Next, regarding the term *ling-ling*:

when the obstacles of the world are purified, there is likewise nothing left to confront or oppose, which is described as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); thus, it is named the "One True Dharma-realm" (*ekavyūha-dharmadhātu*). Therefore...
Removing superfluous characters, only the syllable-gate *ra* remains. *Ra* is the fundamentally pure *dharmadhātu*;

because it is joined with the sound of *samādhi*, it possesses the meaning of liberation. Because it is augmented by the dot of great emptiness (*bindu*), it possesses the meaning of the inconceivable.
In contrast to the previously mentioned immeasurable gates for removing obstacles, these are all gates of inconceivable liberation. Furthermore, the syllable *ra* is wisdom.
The Buddha-wisdom herein is precisely this samādhi; as it faces the Buddha-eye, it is called "seeing," and as it faces wisdom, it is called "knowing.

Because of the Great Emptiness, it is ultimately pure, as indicated by the preceding two characters. The reason for universally taming sentient beings through the Universal Gate is precisely for the sake of these current two characters.
That the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are ultimately pure is what follows next, described as the "sunlight."

The syllable *ja* (jña) is the essence of the primary body and signifies "arising. The two syllables of the first phrase eliminate all faults and afflictions, leading one to the second phrase, the equal dharmadhātu.
Now, these two syllables of the final phrase again arise from that equal dharmadhātu to produce all meritorious qualities;
therefore, the syllable *ra* is taken here as the seed-syllable of the pure bodhicitta.
The samādhi is depicted as the Matrix of Great Compassion (*Mahākaruṇā-garbha-vyūha*); the great void dot (*bindu*) constitutes the inexhaustible adornment of the Universal Gate (*Samantamukha*).
Because of the syllable *ja*, the sprouts, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits unfold in succession; this is precisely the arising from the Great Void.
Furthermore, by means of the first two syllables, one possesses all the functions of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*);

by means of the next two syllables, one possesses all the functions of pacifying calamities (*śāntika*); and by means of the final two syllables, one possesses all the functions of increasing prosperity (*puṣṭika*).
Each contains two *ra* syllables, which correspond to the three provisional functions and the three actual functions respectively. Within each *ra* syllable, [the following is contained]:
Because it is primordially pure, it is white and possesses the function of pacification (*śāntika*); because its essence is wisdom, it is yellow and possesses the function of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*);
because it is the fire-wheel, it is red and possesses the function of subjugation (*vaśya*). This is the glorious wrathful one;
therefore, he is able to subdue all, and there is none who can overcome him.
Furthermore, Aparājitā (Invincible) is also spoken of within the Ratnasthiti-samādhi;

however, while the Vidyārāja is wisdom (*prajñā*) and the Vidyārājñī is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because the union of concentration and wisdom gives birth to all the Invincible Sons (*aparājita-putra*), she is given this name.
*Aparājite* means "O Invincible One," and *jayaṃti* [means] "she is victorious."
"Jaya" is another name for "victory," meaning the victory of triumph that has the sense of subduing.
"Tathāgata" means one who has subdued and conquered the supreme objects of experience. By means of this word of truth, I have manifested it as a verification;
through the power of this samādhi, I have utterly destroyed the two kinds of four māras. You, sons of the Buddha, if..."
One who can practice in this manner shall surely restore the legacy of the Dharma King; do not harbor doubt or regret.

Taking the second syllable *pa* as the essence of the mantra, it is called the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and also the Supreme Truth (*agryārtha-satya*), because through all its functions it reaches the state of supreme perfection.
It universally surpasses all sentient beings; this is precisely what is meant by "supreme."

Furthermore, because the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are fundamentally unarisen and thus cannot even be apprehended, how could there be any phenomenon capable of surpassing them? For this reason, it is called "supreme" (*parama*).
Moreover, regarding the mantra of the Earth Deity: the earth is the place upon which all things rely and dwell; all beings depend upon it to come into existence.
The ground of the Tathāgata’s mind is likewise thus: it is the locus upon which all sentient beings rely, and by means of it, the seeds of goodness grow and flourish;
therefore, it is called the Samādhi that Sustains the Root, and also the Samādhi of Universal Support (*pṛthivī*).
*Pṛthivī* is the name of the Earth Deity; here, the third syllable, *thi*, is taken [as the basis].
The true essence of the mantra is the *dharmadhātu* (the letter *a*), which signifies that all phenomena have a basis upon which they abide;
thus, the Tathāgatagarbha is like the great earth. Now, because all phenomena are fundamentally unborn (*anutpanna*), the basis upon which all phenomena abide cannot be apprehended.
Above this is the letter *i*, which is the sound of *samādhi*. Following this is...
The syllable *va* is augmented by the sound *e*; this *e* is both the meaning of "samādhi" and the sound used for pointing at an object, signifying the essence of the mantra.
This place transcends the realm of language and cannot be demonstrated; it is solely the sphere of internal realization for the practitioner.
*Ye* has the meaning of "vehicle," just as in the world a vehicle must rely upon the ground to function.
The Tathāgata has advanced beyond all stages of the mind-ground and no longer relies upon them; thus, he proceeds by transcending all vehicles (*yāna*).
This aforementioned mantra of Viṣṇu is that which is venerated in the world as King Nārāyaṇa, and it has many variations.
The name is now correctly pronounced *Vaiśravaṇa*. This is Viṣṇu, who takes the initial syllable *vai* as the essence of the mantra.
By adding the vowel *i* to the syllable *va*, it becomes what is called the "Samādhi of Vajra-Mahābala.
Furthermore, because it transcends verbal expression, it is named "Ultimate Emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). *Śravaṇa* has the meaning of "progression" and the meaning of "arising."
Just as this celestial vehicle, the garuḍa bird, travels through the air with sovereign unimpededness, so too does Śakra-Nārāyaṇa;

likewise, riding upon the Greatly Powerful and Fierce King of Golden-Winged Birds, he flies throughout the ultimate void to cut off the flow of saṃsāra and to deliver those who are to be saved. Therefore, his name and title are words of truth.
Furthermore, the mantra of Rudra is that which is venerated in the world as Maheśvara;
he also has many other names. Rudra is a type of Īśvara who takes the initial syllable *ru* as the essence of his mantra.
Because of the samādhi of being originally free from dust and defilement, his mind [abides] in all phenomena.
Because it is attained through mastery and is naturally accomplished as such, it is called Maheśvara. *Nara* has the meaning of "bestowing.
If one explains this by means of the gateway of syllables (*akṣaramukha*), it is the vehicle of the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Since there is nothing in all the worlds that is not the pure dharma-realm, one should know that such jeweled vehicles are infinite in number.
Therefore, one is able to take and give at will, bestowing [benefits] universally upon all sentient beings.

Furthermore, regarding the wind-deity mantra *vāyave*, this is the authentic phonetic form of "wind. Taking the initial syllable *vā* as the essence of the mantra, because it enters the *a*-gate (*akṣaramukha*), it is fundamentally non-existent;
thus, *va* signifies "binding" (*bandhana*). Because it enters the *a*-gate, it is originally non-existent.
Because there is neither bondage nor liberation, it is true liberation; that which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.

This is the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*), and it is also a type of wind-deity vehicle (*vāyu-deva-yāna*). The final syllable *ve* signifies the wordless samādhi and also the meaning of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
It is said that this wind-vehicle of liberation revolves without obstruction within ultimate emptiness.
Therefore, she travels with divine swiftness and is able to universally deliver all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the mantra of Gītamati-devī is also named Mahāprajñā-devī and Vāgīśvarī-devī;
among all the devas, she is the one whose songs and chants are most exquisite, much like Viśvakarman who is skilled in the arts, and is not a Gandharva.
*Bhaya-sarasvatyai*: this is its name; in its correct phonetic transcription, it constitutes a mantra and is also a type of wondrous sound-vehicle of the gods (*deva-yāna*).
Taking the initial syllable *sa* as the essence of the mantra, it carries the meaning of "firmness" (*sāra*).
It is like Aśvaghoṣa himself playing the *lāṭa-vaira* music, while five hundred princes contemplate the world.
Just as those who leave the household life simultaneously transcend worldly faults and afflictions, so too is this mantra:

it is able to cause all sentient beings to realize through Vajra-recitation that the three realms are impermanent and lack any stable abiding; by diligently cultivating the steadfast Dharma, they shall achieve a solid and adamantine body.
Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra says: "His speech is gentle and soft, pleasing to the hearts of the multitude, and he teaches all dharmas in accordance with [their capacities]."
Causing them to attain joy is also the intended meaning of this dharma-gate.
Furthermore, the mantra of Nairṛti is that of the Rākṣasa King;
its correct phonetic form is *rākṣasādhipataye*, which means "to the lord of the rākṣasas. This is indeed the mantra of the rākṣasa.
*Sa* has the meaning of "to devour"; taking the first syllable as the seed-syllable, it signifies "defilement-obstruction.

Just as a *rākṣasa* constantly devours sentient beings without ever being satiated, so too does the Tathāgata constantly consume all sentient beings who possess defilements and obstructions without ever being satiated.
*Dha* has the meaning of the "dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*); by adding the vowel *i*, it is transformed into the sound *dhi*, which means "earth" (*bhūmi*).
It is called "Abiding" because it is frequently named as such; by means of the Samādhi of Abiding in the Dharma-realm, it is termed "Sublime Abiding.

When one abides thus sublimely, one sees that all sentient beings who are defiled and obstructed have entirely entered into the treasury of the Dharma-realm. This carries the meaning of being able to swallow them into one's own belly.
One who rides upon such a vehicle is swift beyond compare; it is therefore called the Rākṣasa Vehicle.
Furthermore, the mantra of Yama is *vevasvata*, which is its original name and constitutes the mantra itself.
*Veva* signifies "firmly established," and taking the initial syllable as the essence of the mantra, it carries the meaning of "unfettered.
This refers to the samādhi of firm establishment and non-binding; thus, through this principle, one eliminates the multitudes [of afflictions].

He binds not by means of what is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*). "Sa" has the meaning of truth (*satya*), for he is eternally in accordance with the marks of reality (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) by being free from the conceptual proliferation of verbal expression (*prapañca*);
thus, in his adjudication of right and wrong, there is no error. For this reason, he is called the Dharma King (*dharmarāja*). It also has the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*):
by mounting this suchness (*tathatā*), one proceeds to the station of the Dharma King; this is called the Yama Vehicle.
Furthermore, the Mantra of the King of Death is the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka, who seizes the life-faculties of all sentient beings.
Therefore, those born from the karma of ignorance and mental formations are unable to escape his realm. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"Even the Unsurpassed World-Honored Ones, along with the Pratyekabuddhas and the assembly of Śrāvakas, must relinquish their impermanent bodies; how much more so for ordinary worldlings?"
The majesty of this King of Death is supreme. *Mṛtyu* means "death";
taking its initial syllable as the essence of the mantra, *ma* signifies "I.

Because all sentient beings do not contemplate the impermanence of all phenomena moment by moment, they give rise to two kinds of self-conceptions; thus, they are subject to the King of Death and cannot attain autonomy.
For this reason, the Tathāgata awakens all sentient beings by means of the phrase "impermanence," so that they may know all phenomena are without self (*anātman*).
If there is no self, who would belong to the King of Death, and who would undergo various sufferings? Next, it says: *tīrthya* (heretics).
By means of this vehicle, and because of the true reality (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of these two selves, one is able to sever the karma of all sentient beings.
To preserve one's life-span without being constrained by the two types of death is called "the vehicle of the King of Death.
Furthermore, the mantra of the Night Goddess (Rātridevī) is as follows: the attendant of Yama is named Kālī;
"Kālī" means black, and "rī" means night. This "Night Black One" is the mantra itself; she is the dark night, the darkness that is all ghosts.

In places frequented by *piśācas* and *kiṃnaras*, where living beings generally harbor much fear and experience decline and affliction, this deity alone possesses sovereign power within the black of night;
he is also able to govern his retinue so that they do not unlawfully harm or distress the world.
Likewise, the black night of ignorance is likewise a state of terror and insecurity for the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the three realms.

In this world, various demons of affliction roam at will; now, by means of the Mantra of the True Night, one dwells securely therein and attains inconceivable liberation. Therefore, the initial syllable *Kaṃ* is used as the essence of the mantra.
It is said that all sentient beings, due to ignorance, create illusory karma, lose their way on the correct path, and fall into the cycle of birth.
The dense forest of death—now, observing that this karma is fundamentally unarisen, it is signless and stainless.
Therefore, the dark night is no different from the great radiance; if one abandons darkness to seek light, that light again becomes an obstruction.
Abiding in this unobstructed samādhi, one attains perfect enlightenment within the dark night; this is called the "Vehicle of the Dark Night."
Furthermore, the mantras of the Seven Mothers belong to the Yama-kula; they are the seven sisters among all classes of malevolent spirits and ghosts.
Their names are: first, Cāmuṇḍā; second, Caṇḍālī; third, Vaiṣṇavī;
fourth, Kāmarī; fifth, Indrāṇī; sixth, [the sixth name]...; seventh, [the seventh name]...
Lau-na-li (7), Ma-la-ra-he-mi (7)—these seven names are all mantras; what is now called *mātṛ-viyoga* refers to the general application of the Seven Mothers (*sapta-mātṛ*).
*Mā* signifies "mother," and the inclusion of the particle *ca* within the phrase conveys the sense of plurality rather than singularity.
Since the class of mothers is numerous, they further represent a multitude of spirits.
The Mother is thus named for this reason; furthermore, the syllable *ma* constitutes the essence of her mantra. It signifies non-self and the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
Just as space, being devoid of marks (*animitta*), does not obstruct sentient beings, so too the Great Emptiness does not obstruct any afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because it can give rise to various modes of illness to benefit sentient beings, she is called the Vehicle of the Ghost-Mother (*bhūtamātṛ-yāna*).

The above is the explanation of the mantra of Śakra-devānām-indra. "Śākya" has the meaning of "one of a hundred blessings," because by performing a hundred great assemblies of unobstructed giving (*vaiśvāsika-mahādāna*) during the causal stage, he attained this fruit; thus it is named as such. It is now called "Śākyara."
This is the correct pronunciation. Taking the initial syllable as the essence of the mantra abandons the meaning of "intrinsic nature" (prakṛti) as being quiescent;

furthermore, *śamatha* also carries the meaning of "cessation. Next, it is further explained that because the defilements of all karma are fundamentally unarisen (*anutpanna*), various activities arise from the ground of the mind of intrinsic nature, as well as the various pure and wondrous objects of the six sense-fields.

This is the meaning of purifying Buddha-lands and adorning the Dharma-body; because it possesses the merit of a hundred syllables within a single syllable, it is called the "Wheel-Treasure of a Hundred Blessings.
Riding upon this Wheel-Treasure of a Hundred Blessings is what is known as the "Vehicle of Śakra."
The above is the mantra of the Naga King Vāruṇa; he is a nāga of the great ocean, and this may also be used universally for all nāga kings.
*A-paṃ* has the meaning of "water," and *pa-da-ya* has the meaning of "lord";
the sound *e* is an auxiliary. Because he has attained mastery over the dharma-gate of the water of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), he is therefore named [Vāruṇa].
The Lord of Waters takes the initial syllable *A* as the essence of his mantra; because this water is originally unborn and eternally unmoving,
and because it is like the syllable *Haṃ*— having neither this shore nor the other shore, being all-pervasive and omnipresent, identical to the great void—
it is named the Heart of the Tathāgata’s Great Ocean of Wisdom, the Sovereign Dragon King.
Abiding eternally therein, he manifests miraculous transformations and empowerments, raining down the Dharma from the Universal Gate to moisten all beings;
because the final syllable is *ye*, it is called the Vehicle of the Lord of Waters.
Furthermore, the first phrase of the Brahmā-mantra says *pra-ja*, which is translated as "all beings.
The next phrase says *pati-svāmi*, where *svāmi* is the substantive and *pati* is the auxiliary sound; thus, it means "Lord of all beings.
For example, at the beginning of a kalpa, when the Brahma-palace was silent and devoid of people, as soon as Brahmā conceived a thought, a deity whose life had ended descended.
Furthermore, because they do not perceive the beginning or end of the Brahmā King, they conceive this thought: "We were born from the Brahmā King;
