because he is able to give birth to all sentient beings, he is called the Lord of All Beings. Yet, in reality, the prior limit of these beings is beginningless, and they were not born from the Brahmā King.
The Tathāgata is likewise so; by means of even a single hair’s breadth of worldly merit...
Because all the sons of wisdom are born from the mind of the Buddha, and because the Tathāgata is seen to have neither beginning nor end, he is called the Father of the World;
yet, in reality, the buddha-nature of sentient beings has no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and is not produced by the Tathāgata.
Taking the initial syllable *pra* as the essence of the mantra, *pra* signifies the supreme meaning (*paramārtha*).
*Ra* is the pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), unstained by defilements; it is the womb of the lotus (*padmagarbha*).

All sons of the Buddha are likewise born from this most supreme womb; therefore, they are called "supreme sons" (*jinaputra*). Because the syllable *ye* is added at the end of the phrase, it is named the "Vehicle of the Brahma King."
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the mantra of the Sun Deity (Sūryadevatā) as being identical to that of Mahāvairocana, it has already been explained in the first chapter.
*Āṇi-ti-ya-ya* is its name; therefore, the Sun in the world, which constantly benefits sentient beings, takes the initial letter *Ā* as the essence of its mantra.
This letter is pronounced by drawing out the sound; it is the very first [syllable] of the Jewel Buddha’s own nature.
The practice of "Birth" (*janman*) is also called the *Sūryodaya-samādhi* (Sunrise Samādhi) and the *Tamo-vidhamana-samādhi* (Dispelling Darkness Samādhi).

Next, regarding the syllable *ni*, it explains the meaning of *bodhicitta*: having personally opened this sun of wisdom, one vows to transmit it to all others for the universal benefit of sentient beings;
by proceeding toward the state of Vairocana Mahāvairocana through this suchness (*tathatā*), it is called "the Sun."
This is the celestial vehicle (*devayāna*). Furthermore, the mantra of Candradeva signifies the pure moon of yoga;
since *candranātha* is the name for the moon, and because it is able to pacify the heat of affliction for all the world and bestow the bliss of coolness, it is called "sweet" (*madhura*).
The tradition of the *Luk-tsao-li* (the Expositor of the Calendar) states that this nectar consists of sixteen portions;
having bestowed fifteen portions universally upon all sentient beings, the remaining single portion is now brought forth.

Taking the initial syllable *Cana* as the essence of the mantra—where *cana* signifies "immortality"—there is nothing among all the flavors of nectar that surpasses the Samādhi of the Pure Moon (*Vimalacandra*). Its consumption [is as follows]:
That which is [denoted by] *na* is free from all transition and change, neither dying nor being born;

next, *na* signifies the meaning of bestowing upon sentient beings, while *ra* is "dustless" and also serves as the function of the pure moon. Because the sound *e* is added, it is called the vehicle of the Moon Deity (*Candradeva*).
Furthermore, the mantra for all nāgas is "Megha-śani-ye. Here, *megha* means "cloud"; *śani* means "to devour" (*atti*);
and *ye* is an auxiliary particle. In the West, nāgas are called "devourers of clouds" (*meghāda*).

A cloud signifies that which provides various obstructions and coverings, causing sentient beings to become drowsy and dormant so that the sun of wisdom does not shine clearly; yet a nāga can [cause it to rain] in an instant.
Exhausting all [obscurations] so that the great void becomes clear and vast, and the myriad phenomena appear with clarity.
Furthermore, just as the various dragon kings not only remove all clouds but can also produce all clouds, so too is the inconceivable and wondrous function of this Dragon King of Bodhicitta:
it can give rise to clouds of inexhaustible adornments that universally cover the Dharma-realm, just like Sāgara.
Because it causes rain to fall from the six heavens at its place of origin, this mantra takes the initial syllable *ma* as its essence;
by knowing that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*), one attains the samādhi of the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*).
Next, *ga* signifies "union," *śa* signifies "quiescence," and *ni* signifies "great emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*), which is densely gathered by various clouds of coverings (*chāyā*).
Since all marks are fundamentally quiescent, they are free from hindrances and identical to the great void;

within this primordial purity, clouds of Buddha-transformations arise once more, merging in essence and pervading the Dharma-realm. Because of the sound "kāśyapa," they are called the Vehicle of the Various Dragons (Nāgas).
Furthermore, regarding the mantra of the two Dragon Kings who guard the gate: *Dānū-harṣi-pa*.
The syllable *pa* is joined with the preceding sound and pronounced as *uppa*, which carries the meaning of "near" (*upa*) and "subordinate" (*ya*).
Upānanda is the name of the second dragon king. Just as the Great Dragon King rains universally upon the world to bring benefit to all sentient beings, so too do these two.
To observe one’s own power and thereby give rise to joy is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gate of Joy. Regarding the two dragons:

the first is the power of wisdom (*prajñā*), and the smaller one is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Furthermore, the first is the power of the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), and the smaller one is the power proximate to the Buddha-stage.
The first is the power of the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), and the smaller one is the power of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*).
Within the secret treasury, the power of the initial thought-moment (*ādikṣaṇa*) is no different from that of the final thought-moment;

yet, because there is also a slight distinction, it is called "next small" (*kṣudra-anantara*). Furthermore, taking the initial syllable *Na* as the essence of the mantra, by adding the bindu and shifting the vowel, it becomes difficult to pronounce repeatedly.

That which is called "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*) is the Great Emptiness of emptiness itself. Moreover, it corresponds to various categories such as merit and wisdom, the provisional and the real.
Because these two types of Dharma-gates are both identical to the Great Emptiness (mahā-śūnyatā), they achieve inconceivable power;

since this is universally bestowed upon sentient beings, it carries the meaning of a great cloud raining everywhere. Therefore, the syllable *gha* is added, and because there is the sound *yu* at the end, it is called the "Vehicle of the Two Dragon Kings.
All of the above are within the Jewel-Abode Samādhi (*ratnasthiti-samādhi*), which is the retinue of Śākyamuni.
Regarding the remaining portions of the single gateway of the *dharmadhātu* that have not yet been exhausted, they shall be explained further below.

The Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana desired to proclaim his own teaching-trace, the *Amoghasiddhi*, the Mother of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the *vidyārājñī* Ākāśadṛṣṭi. As previously [stated], each of the great deities..."
Having explained the gateways of the *dharmadhātu* through which he himself has attained realization, he taught the mantras of his own mind and its retinue,
desiring to attract and gather immeasurable sentient beings according to their respective natures and lineages, so that they might attain mastery in those various *dharmamukhas*. Now,
Vairocana further desires that all those who advance toward and practice these gateways of the *dharmadhātu*, even down to a single...
Because even the slightest virtuous deed is never in vain, all that is undertaken is accomplished without exception, as revealed in the first chapter of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, from each and every gate, there arises the Tathāgata’s body of universal-gate great wisdom;
therefore, the teaching of the self-realization of the Mind-King is further expounded—namely, the *Mahāprajñā*, the mother of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The Vidyārājñī explains its meaning as set forth in the "Buddhamātṛ-parivarta" chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
because the teaching of the Tathāgata’s empowerment is originally unborn, no trace can be found. Therefore, the traces of the *Amogha* (Non-empty) teaching pervade all places;
if there were any trace to be found, it would be a locus of arising and ceasing, and not a trace of the self-teaching. Furthermore, this...
The mantra takes the syllable *ga* as its essence; *ga* has the meaning of "action" (*gati*), which signifies "coming and going.
Because all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, and even because their causes cannot be apprehended, there is no action whatsoever in any phenomenon.
That is to say, one does not act upon form, nor upon sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one does not act upon the permanence of form, nor upon the impermanence of form.

One should extensively explain that one does not practice [the notions of] form as suffering or form as pleasure, self or non-self, purity or impurity, emptiness or non-emptiness, with marks or markless, with activity or without activity, conditioned or unconditioned, tranquil or non-tranquil, and so forth, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is likewise.
Furthermore, one neither practices nor does not practice. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are neither originally existent nor now non-existent, they possess the characteristic of non-deception;
since even nirvāṇa cannot be apprehended, it is said that *gagaṇa* signifies the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*). To further explain these two characters:
because the two extremes do not operate, it is named "Great Emptiness. Within this context, the term *ākāśa* is translated as "empty space."
*Vara* means supreme vow; *lakṣaṇā* means mark. This supreme vow has a mark like empty space.
That mark is the mind of pure bodhi, because it is ultimately pure, because it is boundless, and because it is free from conceptual discrimination.
Therefore, it is compared to the great empty space. Nevertheless, within it there are immeasurable merits that even empty space cannot illustrate.
Because one contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the mind in this manner, it is called the "Eye of Space" (*ākāśacakṣus*).

Within this very Eye of Space, the Lotus Womb (*padmagarbha*) unfolds and the Buddha of the Mind (*cittabuddha*) appears before one; for this reason, it is called the "Lotus Mother," the Mother of all Buddhas.
The subsequent phrase, *gaganasamaye*, indicates that the "Mind" was already explained in the preceding phrase.
The Master now further clarifies that the essence of the mind is all-encompassing and vast, equal to empty space;
next, he says *sarvatra*, translated as "in all places," and *anuttara*, translated as "unsurpassed.
This means that this wisdom of emptiness aspires to reach the most sublime and ultimate state within every gateway of the Dharma-realm; therefore, there is nothing [beyond it].
It serves as a metaphor for that which nothing can equal; only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it. It also carries the dual meaning of "mother" and "son.
Next, *āveśvara* means "firm and indestructible," signifying that this wisdom is born from the nature of the vajra-jewel and is therefore indestructible;
furthermore, it is the Mother of the Buddhas of Space (*ākāśa-buddhamātṛ*).
Because it is that which nurtures and sustains, it cannot be destroyed. Next, "tribhava" means "arising from.
Just as when the fetal parts of a person are fully formed, they emerge from the womb, so too is it with the Tathāgata:
when the pure bodhicitta reaches ultimate perfection, it transcends all meditative observations and natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) arises. Such is the manner of its arising.
Because it arises from the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), it is said to arise from the Indestructible (*akṣaya*).
*Jvalana* signifies the meaning of radiant illumination; just as when the Mahātejas-born deity is born, light spontaneously appears and illuminates all worlds, so too does the Tathāgata:
at the very moment he descends from the Buddha-Mother, the majestic radiance of Vairocana pervasively illuminates the Dharma.
At that time, when Vairocana’s vows were fulfilled, he had this thought:
"Now, my body has been manifested through the universal gate, arising entirely from the Eye of Space; therefore, this kindness is difficult to repay.
From this, he uttered words of truth, taking refuge in Prajñāpāramitā, saying: *Namo Amogha*.
"Namaḥ" (Nan) means "to take refuge in the Unfailing One" (*Amogha*). This meaning is all-pervasive; therefore, the plural form is used to address Him.
The reason for this is that just as worldly people, even if they possess complete intelligence and sovereign power and status, always make offerings to their mothers, so too is it with the Tathāgata:
although He is the King of Dharma, honored and peerless, [He is likewise revered].
One should always revere the Prajñāpāramitā and abide by it; this is the meaning of the Brahmajāla Sūtra’s teaching that filial piety toward one’s parents constitutes the essence of the precepts.
The Sūtra further states: "Moreover, the Bhagavat, in order to extinguish all obstacles, dwelt in the Tejovatī Samādhi and spoke..."
This mantra of the Noble Immovable Lord, the Great Destroyer of Obstructions, has Hayagrīva as its wrathful vidyārāja among the lotus family;
Candavajrapāṇi as its wrathful vidyārāja among the vajra family; Aparājita as its wrathful vidyārāja among the Śākya family;
and now, within the scriptural tradition of Vairocana himself, [Amoghasiddhi].
The Noble Acala Trailokyavijaya acts as a wrathful vidyārāja;
because he is the Vairocana who pervades all dharmas, one should know that the Honored One Acala universally accomplishes all activities and utterly crushes all obstacles.
The syllable-gateway *ra* is the great wrathful fire of Vairocana, which can incinerate all worlds.
With not a single ash remaining, the Immovable Honored One (Acala) now arises from within this fire, just as the Honored One Kuṇḍalī arose from the fire of Vajrapāṇi.
Therefore, the Tathāgata abides in the Samādhi of Fire-Birth. Briefly stated, there are two kinds of obstacles herein:
those arising from various external conditions and causes are all termed "external obstacles. From the seeds... [text truncated]

All things produced by internal causes and conditions are termed "internal hindrances," and so on, up to the subtle signs of frequent disharmony within this state, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Demonic Deeds" (*Prajñā-mārakarmaparivarta*).

Furthermore, those produced by the causes and conditions of the four stages of abiding (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) are termed "external hindrances," while those produced from the stage of beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikā-avidyāvāsabhūmi*) are termed "internal hindrances. This...

The mantra of Acala is capable of destroying all such obstacles; therefore, this Vidyārāja possesses great majestic power and can universally protect all practitioners of mantras, ensuring that their bodhicitta never wavers and causing all the virtuous deeds they undertake to be accomplished according to their wishes.
Furthermore, just as one who serves as a messenger for the Buddha cannot be harmed by any sentient being, so too is this Vidyārāja invulnerable.

Yet these [demons] have long obscured [the truth]. Now, because this enlightened king upholds the majestic mandate of the Buddha and carries out the deeds of the Tathāgata, even those such as Padma and Vajrapāṇi cannot restrain him, let alone the likes of Pāpīyān.
Therefore, practitioners should keep in mind that the three obstacles are heavy in Jambudvīpa; they should always maintain mindfulness and practice. Furthermore—
The first phrase reads *caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa*. Its etymological explanation is largely identical to that of the Vajrapāṇi mantra, though the meanings differ slightly as follows:
whereas the preceding [explanation] clarifies immutability through the gate of Vajra-wisdom, the present [explanation] clarifies it through the body of eternal wisdom upon the lotus pedestal.
Regarding transformation and change, there is the gateway of the letter *ṇa*: even a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood still possesses one death;
thus, he has not yet escaped from adversaries. Because the Tathāgata’s body of wisdom is fundamentally unborn, it is without death and is forever free from adversaries.
Therefore, Acala Vidyārāja can slay the coarse and heavy body of an anointed Bodhisattva and sever its subject to change.
How much more so for the beings of the other three realms, who are the most extreme among the violent and evil—this is the meaning of *ma* (I) and *ha* (cause).
Even the various Bodhisattvas still possess subtle forms of birth;
thus they remain subject to manifold conditions, impermanent, and non-self, unable to attain autonomy. Now, the Tathāgata’s eternal wisdom is free from these.

Through various causes and conditions, the eight forms of mastery (*aṣṭavaśitā*) are accomplished; because I possess the power of being incapable of being harmed, this syllable *Ha* is called the wind-wheel (*vāyumaṇḍala*) and is also named the noose seal (*pāśamudrā*).
Next, there is the syllable *Ra*, to which the sound of samādhi is added; it is precisely the essence of the samādhi from which fire arises.
When it unites with the wind-wheel, its fierce majesty blazes intensely; this is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s great wrathful manifestation (*mahākrodha*).
Next, there is the syllable *sa*. Because its intrinsic nature is dull, it is the seal of the Great Wisdom Sword (*mahāprajñā-khaḍga-mudrā*).
Since all obstacles are, by means of the gateway of the syllable *ra*, the pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), illusory appearances are fundamentally non-arising;
thus, there is no phenomenon to be destroyed. Since the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is fundamentally non-arising and ultimately indestructible, this sword of wisdom is entirely non-existent.
That which is to be destroyed. Next is the syllable *ṇa*, which refers to the Great Emptiness Samādhi;
it signifies that this violent and blazing power pervades all places through immeasurable gateways. Next is said to be *sphoṭaya*, meaning "to destroy";
this further explains the preceding phrase to clarify the efficacy of the wrathful one. *Sa* means "firm."
The meaning is as follows: all sentient beings each cling tenaciously to the dharmas they have acquired, refusing to let go and giving rise to the notion that they are indestructible.
Now, by entering the gateway of the letter *pha*, one sees that all dharmas arise successively from a multitude of conditions, like a mass of foam that is easily crushed and subdued.
Therefore, next the letter *ṭha* is explained; it signifies the meaning of "base pride," like a lion king.
Because he wished to battle with the jackal and relied upon his own physical strength, he considered himself insufficient to match him;
therefore, this is taught as the Vajra Pride (*vajramāna*). By adding the syllable *ya*, it is named the Wrathful Vehicle (*krodhayāna*).
Next is the syllable *hūṃ*, which expresses words of truth and utters the roar of a lion. *Ha* signifies the meaning of the Tathāgata’s sovereign power.
Because it is united with the great emptiness of samādhi, it is fully endowed with the myriad practices of the universal gate (samantamukha), pervading all things without exception;
this is the meaning of the syllable *HŪṂ* within the central matrix (*garbha*). The next phrase, *tāraṭa*, signifies "firmness," clarifying the intent of the great destruction of all obstacles;
it is precisely for the purpose of protecting and sustaining the Buddha-field, causing the seeds of the Path to be firm and immovable throughout.
Because there is no regression, the meaning of the middle character here refers to contemplating all phenomena as they truly are;
this is precisely the Pure Dharma-realm. Whether a Buddha exists or not, the Dharma-nature remains thus, free from all conditioned activity.
Therefore, the King of the Sumeru Throne cannot be shaken, and those held by this lasso cannot be released again. The final phrase is *haṃ* (or *mu-han*).

The two characters [“A” and “Hūṃ”] constitute the essence of the mantra; that is to say, although the various skillful means for accomplishing all matters differ, they ultimately lead to the same realization of the eightfold self-mastery, which returns to a single principle. This shall be analyzed in detail according to each phenomenon.
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, the one who expounds the mantra of Trailokyavijaya is also the wrathful vidyārāja who accomplishes all tasks.
In this regard, there is a slight difference between him and Acala: Acala is the sword of the fire of great wisdom, whose primary function is subjugation;
Trailokyavijaya is the sword of the wind of great wisdom, whose primary function is summoning."
The preceding mantra arises from the syllable *ra* because it burns all fuel of ignorance;
this mantra arises from the syllable *ha* because it removes all dust of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, just as in the world internal and external seeds do not rot or decay and reach fulfillment because they are sustained by the fire element, so too [they are sustained] by the wind element.

Therefore, it grows, flourishes, and unfolds in accordance with the seasons; thus, the Trailokyavijaya mantra is able to subdue all stubborn and difficult-to-transform sentient beings, causing their minds to become supple and giving rise to the myriad practices—this is its distinction.
As for what is called the "three worlds," "world" (loka) refers to greed, hatred, and delusion; from these, all [afflictions] come to exist.
It is called "world" (*loka*) because it is the world itself, and because it is the nature grasped by the world.

Furthermore, because one has already planted the roots of these three poisons in past lives, they give rise to the causes and conditions for karmic actions; subsequently, one sows such seeds within the field of future lives.
For this reason, it is called the "three times. Moreover, the three times are called the "three realms" (*tridhātu*); the Tathāgata has added [this designation].
By virtue of his supernatural power, having attained perfect enlightenment for the first time among the Śuddhāvāsa devas, he descended by the majestic power of mantras into the fourth dhyāna.
At that time, his physical form, radiance, the dharmas known and seen, and all his retinue were entirely similar to those devas,
yet they surpassed them by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond all comparison, even compared to those in the fourth dhyāna.
The gods were overcome by a mixture of joy and fear; finding it unprecedented, they thought to themselves:
"This place is now the most honored in the world, yet there is one who has surpassed our own realm. We do not know from where he comes, nor what he is called.
They immediately gathered together and asked the Buddha: "Great Lord, what dharma do you follow such that your majestic power is like this? At that time, the World-Honored One—
He taught and guided them by means of the three wheels of conversion according to the Dharma each was fit to hear;
once they were subdued, he then descended in succession throughout the triple world.
For the sake of taming the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, he descended from Tuṣita in the form of one in his final birth and turned the wheel of Dharma, even manifesting great [powers] in Śrāvastī.
Through divine transformations, he subdues various difficult-to-convert sentient beings, such as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the spirits of the wilderness, and Hārītī;
this is explained in detail in the *Vajraśekhara*. Therefore, he is called Trailokyavijaya (Victor over the Three Worlds).

The initial syllable "Ha" precisely represents the mastery of the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*), for there is not a single sentient being who does not depend upon causes for their formation. Thus, it follows accordingly.

Karmic activity flows through the three periods of time without attaining sovereignty; only Vairocana reaches the ultimate limit of the first non-arising, and thus, being free from all causes, he possesses sovereign spiritual power that revolves without obstruction, manifesting throughout all times and places to awaken immeasurable sentient beings.
This is stated thrice to correspond to the meaning of the three periods of time.

Therefore, it is also because he eternally uproots the great trees of the three paths for the three types of sentient beings—those who are foolish, those who are children, and those with conscious awareness—and opens the flowers of the three virtues;

furthermore, "ha" has the meaning of joy, as described in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and is also the sound of the Tathāgata’s great laughter, intended to bestow the extraordinary prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon all sentient beings; thus, he transforms his majestic deportment at all times.
Next, regarding "mi sa ma yu," it means "how marvelous! or "how extraordinary!
As the Buddha’s constant teaching states, the five *sthāpana-citta* (five methods of settling the mind) each have their respective gates of remediation;
now, this mantra uses the power of the three great poisons to subdue the three poisons of the world—namely, using greed to subdue greed, and using hatred to subdue hatred.

It is called "strange" because it abandons the affliction of delusion. Furthermore, it is like a disease that has already been terminal for those of the Two Vehicles, which various excellent medicines could not cure;
now, by using three kinds of poisonous drugs to rescue them and cause them to arise, it is called "strange.
Furthermore, the nature of the Vajra-seed is originally unarisen, yet through skillful means it is planted and causes various roots to grow.
Because it possesses stems, flowers, and leaves, it is called "strange"; because the final phrase includes the word *āyate*, it is named "Great Crusher of Vehicles" (*Mahā-vāhana-saṃhara*).
The second line, *sarvatathāgataviṣayam*, refers to the realm of the Tathāgatas;
*saṃbhava* means "arising," which explains the preceding [term].
From where does such sovereign power of the phrases arise? It arises from the realm of the Tathāgata.
Herein, the syllable *vi* is the point where the path of verbal expression for all phenomena is severed; it is the Dharma realized within the Tathāgata’s own mind.
*Śa* has the meaning of "dullness," referring to the limit of generosity (*dāna*) being no different from the limit of stinginess (*mātsarya*), and so on up to wisdom (*prajñā*).

The limit of wisdom (*prajñā-koṭi*) is not different from the limit of ignorance (*moha-koṭi*); therefore, there is no fixed characteristic that can be described, nor is there anything upon which one rides.

This is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s sphere of activity (*tathāgata-viṣaya*). Because it arises from such a sphere, although one remains within the various realms of existence (*bhava*), one is neither defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*) nor bound by karma.
Just as a great wind encounters objects without obstruction, it is called *svabhāva* (the intrinsic nature).
The *Bodhicittavivaraṇa* states: *tad* (transliterated as *tad*) and *loka* (transliterated as *lokiya*). Translated, it means "the three times" (*tri-kāla*).
Furthermore, it explains the preceding phrase by stating that for this reason, one is able to universally conquer and subdue the three times.
This mantra takes the syllable *tad* as its essence; this is translated as "three."
The true mark of the three poisons in the world is precisely the pure dharma-realm; the word "samādhi" signifies the skillful means of the myriad practices.
It is like a skilled trainer who tames the unruly nature of a wild horse to serve as a well-broken steed of gentle utility.
Therefore, when it has not yet been tamed, its physical strength is fierce and magnificent, charging wildly among the herd; once it has been tamed, [it becomes useful].

Afterwards, one will be capable of traveling a thousand li in a single day; it depends entirely on what one’s spiritual disposition (*gotra*) is like—how could one easily change one's nature and then govern it?

It is the same with the Buddha, the Tamer: he can tame those who are stubborn and fierce, taking the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) as the function of the universal gate Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);

he also tames those who are stubborn and fierce, taking *nirvāṇa* as the function of the universal gate world. Therefore, the Tathāgata’s three karmas and the three poisons are universally victorious.
In the world, the subsequent syllable *HŪṂ* is the fierce sound of this Great Tamer;

the final syllable *JRAK* (or *JRA*) is the sound of summoning and awakening, and it also carries the meaning of "arising," signifying that all sentient beings are no different from oneself and are born from the realm of the Tathāgata. This is the wind of Trailokyavijaya, which performs various activities.
Karma is precisely that which causes the tree of the Buddha’s Bodhi to blossom and grow;

therefore, it adds purity and removes stains, transforming those stubborn and turbid natures so that they may all flourish. When a practitioner utters this sound with words of truth, it can penetrate the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to attain awakening.
Furthermore, the mantras of the śrāvakas are the retinue of Śākyamuni and were also taught within the Ratnasthiti-samādhi;
it is merely that the text as transmitted has been copied out of order. It begins by stating:
*hetu* (cause) is *pratyaya* (condition), *vīrya* (diligence) is *karman* (action).
*Nirjāta* (born) refers to the self-realized Dharma of the *svabhāva-vidyā* (innate wisdom), which is free from all causes and conditions.
Because it is free from causes and conditions, it is able to eternally destroy the arising of karma; therefore, the syllable *HŪṂ* is added.
The meaning of the six causes and four conditions should be explained here in detail. As a verse in the *Vinaya* states: "All phenomena arise from conditions; the Tathāgata has taught their cause."
The exhaustion of the causes and conditions of those phenomena was taught by the Great Śramaṇa in this verse, which subsumes the meaning of the Tripiṭaka and also subsumes the meaning of this mantra;
therefore, it is traditionally transmitted in India as a "Dharmakāya Relic. The first syllable-gate, *ha*, signifies the cause;
it refers to the fact that the root of all suffering is craving (*rāga*), and because the sound of the "ten thousand practices" is added to this, [it is established].
This refers to the various paths for extinguishing suffering; because these causes are extinguished, there is no further basis of dependence, which is termed *nirvāṇa*.
The character "du" (都) signifies the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.

Within the Śrāvaka teachings, the Four Noble Truths are regarded as the four kinds of true suchness, and the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise regarded as "abiding"; that which abides is precisely suchness. Next, [the text] says "pra" (鉢羅).
Because the six sense-faculties do not cling to the six sense-objects, all cravings are extinguished and there is no longer any nesting place;

this is that which is most profound and difficult to understand in the world. Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* takes the nirvāṇa attained within the minds of the sages as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This vehicle is in accordance with the meaning of "thusness" (*tathatā*); it refers to the path that leads to the cessation of suffering and proceeds toward [enlightenment].

Because it is within *nirvāṇa*, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*). Following this, there is the syllable "ma," which signifies the *nirodha-vāk-patha-samādhi* (the samādhi that extinguishes the path of speech).
Thus, Śāriputra said: "Within liberation, there is no verbal expression; I do not know what can be said regarding this.
*Gati* has the meaning of "no coming or going"; one who rides upon this vehicle does not return again to the six realms of existence.

*Karma* means non-action and non-self; *nirvāṇa* (the "ni" being pronounced as in *ning-yi*) means the Great Emptiness, for in the *Śrāvaka* sūtras, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is termed the Great Emptiness;
thus it is said: "Who is aging and dying? Aging and dying are also all false views. *Jña* means non-arising;
that is to say, one can personally declare: "My births are exhausted... and shall not arise again."
For this reason, the word "more" (*bahu*) is added once again. In the final phrase, the syllable *hūṃ* signifies that because one is separated from all causes, the mind attains mastery;
because there is the sound of samādhi below, one achieves both types of liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*);

and because there is the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) above, one attains the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), thereby achieving unimpeded liberation. This is called a Śrāvaka of Great Power; therefore, he is able to use this lion [roar].

The roar of his voice subdues the three obstacles as he turns the wheel of Dharma following the Buddha. Furthermore, because he enters the gateway of the letter *A*, all sentient beings are from the beginning free from all causes;
since he knows that all phenomena are eternally quiescent and extinguished, even the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*) is extinguished.
When one is thus without doubt or regret, this is called the definitive understanding of the Śrāvaka-dharma. It means that one is able to [realize] this through *HŪṂ*.
Because his voice causes all to hear universally;
furthermore, the mantra of the Pratyekabuddha is also a member of Śākyamuni’s retinue.

"Va" signifies the severance of the path of speech, for because the wisdom of the Pratyekabuddha is profound and sharp, they perceive that all phenomena of origination (*samudaya*) are phenomena of cessation (*nirodha*). Therefore, it is so named.

When one realizes the realm of tranquility and dwells in this samādhi, observing all phenomena as having the characteristic of nirvāṇa such that they cannot be expressed in speech, it is called the "Samādhi of the Ultimate Extinction of Language. For this reason, one does not delight in preaching the Dharma;

yet, in order to fulfill the vows of sentient beings, one simply employs the power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhibala*) to empower this single syllable as a mantra. Furthermore, regarding the nature of letters:
Because detachment is itself the characteristic of liberation, this syllable *va* is the gateway to the vajra speech of all Buddhas;
it can pervade the world with a sound that is beyond words. To know that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma is what is called being fully endowed with great learning;
this is termed the definitive vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, this is the entry into the Dharma for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Because the realms and vehicles differ, the use of the letter-gates clarifies their meaning; however, if it is a mantra proclaimed by the noble ones of the two vehicles themselves, it merely clarifies the meaning of the phrases and lacks the meaning of the letters.
Furthermore, the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is the Cintāmaṇi,
which is universally applicable for the activities of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It begins with "Sarvabuddhabodhisattva-hṛdaya," translated as "The Heart of All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."

The Bodhisattva’s mind, by means of this jewel-king of the pure bodhicitta, is such that there is no one among those who have realized it throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time whose realization is not identical.
Furthermore, this *hṛdaya* is the pivotal heart, not a mere *jñāta*-heart.
The next phrase, *nija-vaiśānya*, has the meaning of "entering"; it enters into all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The mind of the Bodhisattva is precisely that which enters the universal gate of the Dharma-realm; therefore, this mantra takes the syllable *niṃ* as its essence.
This syllable is connected to the long stroke and the sound of *a* within the preceding character.

*A* is the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the mind, while the syllable *niṃ* is identical to the circle (*bindu*), signifying the meaning of entry into realization and also the meaning of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). The mind itself...
At the time of realization, it is identical to the great emptiness; therefore, it is free from all marks while endowed with all marks of inexhaustible adornment.
Because of the inclusion of the character *jia* (加), it is named the Universal Gate Vehicle (*Pumen Cheng*).
The next phrase, *namo sarvavidye*, means that Vairocana utters words of solemn truth, universally returning [homage].
O Bhagavān, this jewel of the bodhicitta is like the precious horse of a universal monarch (cakravartin); though it travels throughout the four continents, its resolve does not cease.
The Tathāgata is likewise; although he has already perfected the ten thousand practices, he does not rest because of his mind of reverent service toward all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Furthermore, O Bhagavān, [the Buddha] reflected upon his own past conduct when he was practicing the path of a bodhisattva, and he constantly received...

Thus, by virtue of the grace of all Buddhas, when Bodhisattvas first dwell upon the stages (*bhūmi*), attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), receive the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), or ascend to the stage of the Tathāgata, they rely entirely upon the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and establishment provided by the Buddhas of the ten directions.

This is also the meaning behind the invocation "Namo to all Buddhas" as chanted in the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta* (The Chapter on Expedient Means) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. *Sarva...* [omitted].
Vinitaruci translates this as "Bestowing All Wishes. Because he fulfills himself through the vow for all-knowledge, he is able to bestow upon all sentient beings their various rarefied wishes;
by means of these causes and conditions, he attains the fulfillment of the great bodhi-vow.
Therefore, because Vairocana Buddha desires to universally rain down all manner of jewels from the universal gate, he first pays homage to such a reality.
Furthermore, the syllable *sa* signifies firmness and non-attachment; *rava* signifies the heart of the dharmadhātu, which is free from suffering and bondage;
*vi* signifies the sound of the samādhi of the water of great compassion, which is beyond language and thus the objectless (*anālambana*) samādhi; *ni* signifies bestowal upon all sentient beings.
May I always be self-sufficient and alone capable of bestowing such gifts; may this boundless giving provide for the entire kingdom without ever being exhausted.
Furthermore, the mantras of all the world-protectors and devas are also the retinue of Śākyamuni, though they are not listed here in their proper order. First...
The phrase *lokāloka-kara* is explained as follows: *loka* is translated as "the world.
Next, because the syllable *loka* is joined with the sound *a*, it is called *aloka*, which has the meaning of "illumination. *Kara* has the meaning of "to do" or "to act."
"To become an illuminator of the world" means that by means of this illumination, one universally shines light upon the world to dispel its darkness.
The reason for this is that "world" (*loka*) carries the meaning of "darkness," because since darkness is fundamentally unarisen, it is itself the radiance of Mahāvairocana.
Therefore, the initial syllable *lo* constitutes the essence of the mantra; *la* signifies the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because this mark is originally without marks, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);

therefore, the Buddha is able to universally manifest various worldly bodies by means of his body of true mark. Next, it says: all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas... [and so forth].
Regarding *ghulakaṇi*, the syllable *ṇi* carries such meanings as these:
it refers to all the various immeasurable and boundless classes of beings and realms of existence beyond these eight groups;
this single, signless illumination (*vidyā*) is used to unify them all. Next, *hrīḥ naya* signifies "mind" (*citta*), and furthermore, it is accompanied by—
*Anītyaka-karṣaya*: this is the summarized meaning, which means that by means of such a single point (*bindu*), one gathers the pivotal mind of all worlds.
The final phrase, *vicitrāṅga iti*, means "various activities" and also signifies "skillful form"; in the West, this is called brocade (*kambala*).
It is embroidered as *citra*; this name for the practice of brocade signifies the body that all sentient beings joyfully behold.
It is also called the *dhāraṇī* of the speech of all sentient beings, and it is also called the *dhāraṇī* of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of revolutions.
This is because all various skillful fields of knowledge revolve forth from the sun of formlessness and return to the state of ultimate subtlety.
It is named the "Vehicle that Universally Illuminates the World.
Furthermore, the mantras of all Buddhas situated in the position of the Great Vīra (Mahāvīra) in the eastern direction are universally applicable to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
it begins with *sarvatha*, which is translated as "comprehending all" (*saṃgraha*).
*Matī* is translated as "lack of wisdom" (*amati*). Because of this lack of wisdom, various doubts and regrets arise; therefore, this term is correctly translated as "doubt.
*Vijrmbhita* has the meaning of "casting off" or "removing," just as people use this same name for the clearing away of filth and excrement.
It refers to the moment of attaining vast and perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.
In the midst of all modes of omniscient knowledge and vision, doubt and regret are forever exhausted, and the wisdom of the true nature (*dharmatā*) arises;
this body of the true nature is precisely the Dharmadhātu-body of Vairocana.
Therefore, the next phrase says *Dharmadhātunirjāta*, translated as "born from the Dharma-realm. Within this—

The syllable *Nye* (pronounced as before) is named the Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahāśūnyatā-samādhi*). The prefix *ja* has the meaning of "arising. It carries the sound of *ra* above and the sound of *ha* below;
*ra* is the mind of the pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and is also the great fire of wisdom of the Tathāgata’s triangle.
The syllable *ha* is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata; therefore, when this wisdom arises, it arises from Great Emptiness.
The final phrase says: "Sammai Kō. These three characters are all seed-syllables (*bīja*) that constitute the essence of the mantra.

The character *sa* is precisely the heart of the lotus. Because all phenomena (*dharma*) cannot be apprehended through ultimate truth, it is called "knowing and seeing as they truly are" (*yathābhūta-jñāna-darśana*).
Because all phenomena are without attachment, it is called the "Buddha's untainted wisdom" (*anāsrava-jñāna*), which is free from outflows.
Because it is eternal, it cannot be destroyed; thus it is called the "first limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Because it is augmented by the *bindu* (the point of emptiness), it pervades all places like the blooming of a lotus flower. Therefore, the central tenet of this sutra is that the Buddha is the one whose awakening-wisdom has blossomed as a flower.
This is because it corresponds to the sublime cause and the sublime fruit, corresponds to the two functions of the provisional and the real, and corresponds to self-realization and empowerment.
Because of the meaning of the fundamental and the manifest, and because of the meaning of awakening oneself and awakening others, it is for this reason that these words are repeated.

The character *he* (賀) signifies the Tathāgata’s power of mastery; precisely by means of such power of mastery, from these two layers of lotus-flower displays (*phenyū*), there is manifested the inexhaustible treasury of adornments.
Through the broad meaning of the Great Compassion Maṇḍala, all sentient beings are universally gathered.
Furthermore, the mantra of Nattadraśa is one who constantly guards the inner gate of the maṇḍala as a follower of the Dharma-Buddha’s instructions, stationed on the right side;
translated, he is called "Difficult to Grasp" or also "Difficult to Subdue.
By virtue of the great, unimpeded power of the void of Vairocana, there is no one at all capable of grasping or subduing him. Moreover—
The translation says "untransgressible" (*anatikramaṇīya*) and also "unviewable" (*anavalokanīya*).
Because one constantly upholds and proclaims the Tathāgata’s *samaya* teachings, its majestic power is so august that none dare to overstep it.

Furthermore, its radiance is so intensely brilliant—as if a hundred thousand suns were gathered together—that the eyes of any infant cannot gaze upon it directly. It is because one wishes to embody all such meanings [that this name is given].
Therefore, its Sanskrit name is preserved; the first phrase is *nṛtyarāsa*, which is the correct pronunciation for *mahā-ruṣaṇa*, meaning "Great Wrath," as explained previously.
*Khādaya* means "to devour"; the syllable *kha* itself constitutes the essence of the mantra, and by means of all...
Because the Dharma is like space and likewise ungraspable, it is called "the emptiness of the ungraspable.
Because all sentient beings do not understand this emptiness, they constantly allow the four Māras and others to act as they please, violating and plundering the palace-city of the Dharmadhātu.
Now, by employing the power of this very emptiness, one expels and devours them until nothing remains; furthermore, one can freely summon and gather them all.
It causes all sentient beings to enter this dharma-gate that is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, so that they may universally behold the Buddha within their own minds.

Next, regarding the syllable *Na*: it does not merely summon them in, but can also open up and bring forth the secret treasures of the Tathāgata through immeasurable gateways and bestow them [upon them].
This is the activity performed by those who revere the teachings of the Dharmakāya. Next is the syllable *Ya*.
The gate signifies the meaning of "no vehicle" because there is nothing to be mounted; within a single thought-moment, it performs a complete circuit throughout the ten directions.
If the mind has something upon which to rely, it can act in such a way.
Next, it says *sarvatathāgatajñānakūṭa*: here, the syllable *jñā* is drawn out with a protracted sound.
Therefore, it is said that *ajñā* has the meaning of "instruction," while *kuru* has the meaning of "to act.

Furthermore, this explains the preceding phrase by extending it to mean that one is able to act in accordance with the instructions of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Moreover, it conveys the intent of respectfully proclaiming the instructions of the Dharma King, thereby causing [them] to...
One must act exactly as instructed and may not transgress it. The mantra *Abhimukha* is translated as "Facing One Another" (*xiāngduì*).
Furthermore, because this follower of the Dharma Buddha stands facing *Nattarāśa*, always on the left side of the gate, he is given this name. The initial syllable is a vocative used for summoning.
The *Arthakrama* states that *mahāpracaṇḍa* is translated as "extremely great and violent";
because it is contrasted with the preceding mantra, it also carries the meaning of "extreme wrath.
Furthermore, the *Arthakrama* explains the meaning of *abhimukha*: because of the initial syllable *A*, it is capable of slaying the twenty-five forms of self-clinging (*ātman*).
Because the syllable *kha* overturns sentient beings, it further slays the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). It overturns the notion of a self in sentient beings.

Furthermore, "having a self" is the characteristic of the accumulation of the two kinds of birth-and-death, while "not having a self" is the characteristic of the cessation of the two kinds of birth-and-death.
Because it is without transition or change and because it has no counterpart, it is able to destroy everything; therefore, it is called "extremely violent and evil."
Furthermore, it is said that *ghṛṇa* has the meaning of "seizing," while *khādaya* has the meaning of "devouring.

Moreover, the syllable *kha* constitutes the essence of the mantra; this clarifies the reason why the Tathāgata issues the summons—to cause those two types of obstructors to be seized and then devoured.
Furthermore, as for the majestic power (*prabhāva*) of this Honored One...

They are all equal to the previous Honored Ones; because they are distinguished as having "emptiness of non-apprehensibility" (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*) as their seed and their characteristic, they are designated by names corresponding to these [qualities].

Furthermore, because this meaning of the emptiness of non-apprehensibility universally protects all doors of the *dharmadhātu*, this Honored One is also named "Extremely Fierce Vairocana" and is also named "Extremely Fierce Jewel."
Dhvaja-buddha is also named Pracaṇḍa-kusumavikāśana-buddha, also named Pracaṇḍa-dundubhisvara-buddha,
also named Pracaṇḍa-aparimitāyus-buddha, also named Pracaṇḍa-mahāvīra, also named Pracaṇḍa-gagananetra,
also named Pracaṇḍa-cintāmaṇi, and also named Pracaṇḍa-vilokita.
Īśvara is also named the Extremely Fierce Vajrapāṇi; the others are all to be spoken of by analogy in this manner.
Thus, each individual gate pervades all gates, and because they relate to one another as being neither identical nor different, it is called the "Inconceivable Dharma-realm Palace Gate.
The next phrase says *kiñjalkāya tse*, which is translated as:
"Why not proceed quickly? Having thus explained it, the subsequent phrase "samayam anusmara" is translated as "recollect the samaya. This also corresponds to the meaning of the preceding section;
whereas the previous mantra concerned what should be done according to the instructions given, here the phrasing serves to cause one to recollect the *samaya*.
Furthermore, the mantra for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) was also spoken by Vairocana while dwelling in the samādhi of "Beholding the High Peak of the Pure Dharma Banner.
It is like a skilled general commanding a threefold army; according to the strength and capacity of each soldier, they each fulfill their function.
Therefore, when the entire earth is guarded [by this mantra], none can transgress it. One who enters this samādhi likewise [attains such power].
One should know that these are capable of organizing all dharma-gates such that, like pulling the main ropes and shaking the collar, every hair and eye is raised.
The two Vidyārājas, the two Command-followers (ājñākārin), and the four Great Protectors are all, within this context, instruments for repelling aggression and resisting insult.

Thus, when the city walls and moats are strictly fortified, none dare to trespass; likewise, if a practitioner of mantras employs these to bind the perimeter boundary (sīmābandha), [the same result follows].
Even the various venerable noble ones cannot destroy it because they do not transgress the samaya;

likewise, when a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya has performed the formal boundary-marking (*sīmā-bandha*) and the various *karmas* according to the Dharma, even if the entire Saṃgha were to assemble outside the boundary, there would be no means whatsoever to invalidate that ritual act. First, [the mantra] says: *Sarva*.
*Tara-nu-ge-te* is translated as "pervading all" (*sui-i-qie-bian*), meaning it thoroughly pervades all locations throughout the ten directions.
Next, *man-da-ya-tsi-mu-han* is translated as "binding the boundary" (*jie-jie*);
this means binding the boundary throughout all directions and locations. *Mahā-samaya*.

*Nirjaṭi* is translated as "arising from the Great Samaya. For example, just as when a community of monks formally establishes a boundary (*sīmābandha*), for as long as that boundary has not been relinquished—whether it be for a short or long duration—the dharma of the boundary constantly arises;
one should know that the Great Samaya is precisely the vajra-activity (*vajrakarma*) of all Buddhas. Therefore, once the boundary has been established according to the rite, the Vajradhātu arises.

*Samaraṇe* is translated as "recollection and retention. Just as when the boundaries for a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) are proclaimed, one first instructs the assembly of monks to focus their minds in harmony and collectively recollect and retain [the matter], so too here is it likewise:

a universal proclamation to the vast assembly of atoms, commanding them to recollect their original vows and together provide empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Furthermore, according to the profound and secret interpretation, this is [the state of] being together...
Within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) of the minds of those who practice the vows, from this point forward, all shall become the Vajradharmadhātu-palace;
the hosts of Māras and followers of heterodox paths shall no longer be able to enter, and all sublime activities shall be accomplished according to one’s will.
Since this realm is fundamentally unborn, it can never be relinquished. *Apratihata*.
This means "incapable of being harmed," "incapable of being destroyed," and "unobstructed. *Dhaka* means "majestic radiance";
it is repeated to signify "supreme majestic radiance," such that even the fierce flames of the kalpa-fire cannot approach it.
This is the inherent nature (*dharmatā*) of the *dharmadhātu*, not something produced by artificial effort. Next, *cara* means "conduct."
The meaning is stated repeatedly as follows: it refers to the ultimate practice; because it is the ultimate practice, it is pervasive, swift, and rapid, reaching everywhere without exception.
Furthermore, "left" (vāma) signifies "non-extinction" (*aniruddha*), and "ra" signifies "unobstructed" (*anāvṛta*).

This indicates that this realm is not only firm and indestructible, but also possesses fierce and blazing majestic light that spreads in all four directions, such that it cannot be concealed or extinguished. This is the next phrase.
The phrase "cloud-heavy" (yun-chong) signifies *pūrṇa*; "extreme knot" (*ji-jie*) means *bandhana*.
*Namośanika* is the meaning of the ten directions. Because the syllable *pūrṇa* is fundamentally without bondage, the essence of this realm is identical to great emptiness;
since there is no knot of bondage that can ever be untied, it is called the "extreme knot. Furthermore, within a single atom (*paramāṇu*), one establishes the boundary (*sīmā*).
Because it also pervades the ten directions, it is called the "Ultimate Bond" (atyanta-bandhana).
The next phrase is *sarvatathāgatānugīta*, translated as "Chanted by All Tathāgatas.
*Pravāra* is translated as "that which is realized," and *dharma* is named *dharmalakṣaṇa*.
*Ḍha* means "to obtain," which also carries the sense of "attainment. *Vijaya* is translated here as "victory" (*śeṅ*) and is also called "the Invincible" (*mi nus pa*).

Because one establishes the boundary in this manner, one attains the self-realized Dharma of the Tathāgatas according to the samaya teachings of all Buddhas; since no obstacles whatsoever can thwart its efficacy, it is called "Invincible."
"Vijayā" means "victorious. Next, "bhagavatī" is the general title for this virtuous name, which is the principal mantra.
Then, "vikurvi vikurile" both carry the meaning of "removal":
the first, "vikurvi," exhorts one to purify and remove; the second, "vikurile," indicates that [the purification] has already been accomplished.
"Removing" (*chud*) means first removing all impurities; "further removing" (*chud yang chud*) means subsequently purifying all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
The next line says *līlupuri*, which has the sense of a palace (*kūṭāgāra*) or a dwelling place (*sthāna*).

This means that within this consecrated boundary (*sīmābandha*) is the palace of all the Blessed Ones, free from defilement and devoid of marks. Because the purpose of establishing the boundary lies in the boundary itself, [it is so called].
The syllable *li* constitutes the essence of the mantra; the syllable *la*, joined with the sound of samādhi, signifies that all myriad practices are entirely without marks (*animitta*).
This is the palace of the self-realized mind of all Buddhas, for it is not the domain of those who possess a mind of mental construction (*cittamātra*).
Therefore, it is further stated: *vikuṭi*, which clarifies ultimate purity. From this point onward—
This explains the Seed-Syllable Mantra.
Furthermore, the Gate of the Letter *A* in the Bodhicitta Mantra is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the mind;
because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, this mind is itself primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Since it is the very essence of the sun, it constitutes the Dharma-gate of Vairocana.
Furthermore, the true essence of the mantra of the *Bodhicaryāvatāra* is the letter Ā (āḥ), which is the pure bodhicitta. When this is joined with the sound of samādhi—
namely, the myriad practices— it is called the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, for these myriad practices take the sun of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their banner.
Furthermore, regarding the mantra for accomplishing Bodhi, the letter *A* is the seed-syllable of the bodhicitta;
because it is augmented by the bindu of great emptiness and pervades all places, with its myriad virtues in full bloom, it is called the Buddha "Flowering King of the Śāla Trees."
Furthermore, the two dots (bindus) flanking the *nirvāṇa* mantra signify the meaning of purification.

When the delusive conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of sentient beings' own minds is purified, that itself is *nirvāṇa*. Although it is ultimately without any basis, it gives rise to all sounds and syllables;
therefore, it is called the Tathāgata Drum-Sound (*Duṃdubhisvara*). The above are the mantras of Trailokyavijaya and Acala, both of which [employ these].
The sovereign wind (*īśvara-vāyu*) constitutes its essence; it is called by means of a long vowel.

Being endowed with the ten thousand practices, it is marked with the *nirvāṇa-bindu* to manifest the power of the Tathāgata’s liberation; it is marked with the *buddha-bindu* to manifest the power of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom.
Wisdom and abandonment support one another like two wings, both capable of accomplishing all tasks.
Furthermore, regarding the *Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin* mantra, the letter *A* represents the Buddha’s nature of knowledge and vision inherent in all sentient beings.
When combined with the samādhi of painting, it is the sprout of the myriad virtues within this very ground of mind (*cittabhūmi*).
Now, by means of the power of compassion-samādhi, one resolves its cataracts and breaks its husks; therefore, it is named "Remover of Obstructions" (*Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin*).
Furthermore, regarding the *sā* syllable of the Avalokiteśvara mantra: it is the heart-lotus of the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣu*).
By means of this, one universally contemplates all worlds; this is the empowerment of Sovereignty (*vaśitā-adhiṣṭhāna*).

Those who receive this empowerment likewise have their embryonic treasury (*garbha*) blossom, such that they cannot be defiled by the mud of the outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, the *nirvāṇa-bindu* is added.
Furthermore, regarding the syllable *vaṃ* in the mantra of Vajrapāṇi, it is the seal of vajra-wisdom (*vajra-prajñā-mudrā*).

Because the path of verbal expression is severed in all phenomena, it is indestructible and irreversible; all manifold conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are extinguished, and phenomena are like nirvāṇa.
Because one desires to purify all sentient beings with this wisdom, the point of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-bindu*) is added.
Furthermore, regarding the mantra of Mañjuśrī, the syllable *ma* signifies the meaning of "mind" (*citta*) and is called "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*).

By means of this mind of Great Emptiness, one personally realizes the Great Emptiness of the mind; therefore, it is further augmented with a nasal bindu (*anusvāra*). Because there is no virtue therein that is not complete, he is named Mañjuśrī.
Furthermore, regarding the Mantra of the Eye of Space: because the gateway of the syllable *ga* involves no movement within phenomena, it is called "walking the path as it truly is.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time have come from this path to achieve perfect enlightenment; therefore, the syllable *ga* is named "coming.
When the bindu of emptiness is added above it, it becomes the phrase for "attaining Bodhi. The remainder is explained as before.
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma-dhātu mantra, the syllable *ra* serves as its heart because all defilements are fundamentally unarisen and thus ultimately and eternally pure;
the addition of a circular dot (*bindu*) above it signifies that within this, the illusory manifestations of dependent origination are omnipresent and non-existent nowhere.
Furthermore, regarding the syllable *kha* in the mantra of Mahāvajra, it is named "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It is said that even Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage do not possess its domain; for when I sat at the site of enlightenment, I realized that emptiness is equal to space.

Thus, it transcends the path of language and is free from all causes and conditions. Nevertheless, worldly beings merely perceive the traces of the subduing of Māra, yet this Vajra [mantra] is far greater than that.
This is his title.
Furthermore, the mantra of the Honored One Water-Svayambhū (Water-Self-Existent) also upholds a single virtue of the Dharma-body;
it is named as such because he attains mastery over the dharma-gate of the "water of the mind. *Jña* signifies the meaning of non-arising, like a great cloud that rains everywhere.
Although the birth of the myriad things is of one flavor and equal, they nevertheless receive nourishment according to their respective capacities, resulting in various differences;
therefore, the *bindu* (dot) of great emptiness is added, for this dot also signifies sovereignty (*īśvara*).
Furthermore, the mantras of the Venerable Tārā are for the most part the meaning of "all phenomena as they truly are" (*yathābhūta*), which is also the meaning of "the eye.
Because she contemplates all phenomena as their true nature (*dharmatā*) such that nothing remains unpenetrated, the vowel *am* (the great dot of emptiness) is added.
By virtue of this dot, one attains mastery over the dharma-gate of the eye and is able to perceive the Buddha-fields without dualistic characteristics.

Furthermore, regarding the mantra of Bhṛkuṭī, the syllable *bhaḥ* signifies the meaning of "existence" (*bhava*) combined with the sound of *samādhi*, thus being named "Samādhi of Mastery over Existence.
Since all existences are fundamentally unborn, there is nothing to be abandoned; therefore, by means of the skillful means of great compassion, one abides therein.
One merely remedies the affliction of impurities and does not abandon the Dharma; if one were to eliminate the affliction itself, that would constitute a diminution of the Dharma.
This is the gateway of syllables.

Furthermore, the Mahāsthāmaprāpta mantra is formed in conjunction with Avalokiteśvara; by adding the *nirvāṇa-bindu* (anusvāra) to the preceding syllable, it brings about the accomplishment of the fruit of liberation from all defilements.
Therefore, this syllable has the *mahā-śūnya-bindu* added to it to cause [the fruit] to flourish.
Because the unimpeded flower stamens are in full bloom, the remainder is as explained previously.
Furthermore, regarding the *bha* in the mantra of Sitātapatrā, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), namely *nirvāṇa*;

because the ultimate truth is ungraspable, one gives rise to the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the myriad practices (*sarvacaryā*) without realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). All lotuses [are thus].
Because its retinue is all born from this and it can exercise various sovereign functions through *nirvāṇa*,
it is augmented with the *bindu* (the dot). Furthermore, the *HAYAGRĪVA* mantra corresponds to the Lotus Samādhi.
Because the function of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) Sovereignty is slightly different in meaning from the Immovable (Acala) mantra, it is invoked using only short vowels.
Furthermore, the mantra of Yaśodharā is the vidyā-queen of the Lotus Family; regarding her adornment—
Because one attains mastery by adorning the Dharma-gate of the Jewel Vehicle, the syllable *ya* is used as its seed-syllable;

because it is augmented with the great empty dot (*bindu*), it pervades all places and provides for all sentient beings universally. This is called the Universal Contemplation Vehicle, and it is also called the Universal Gate Vehicle.
Furthermore, the Sanskrit name for the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi is *Ratnapāṇi*, which is identical in meaning to the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi found among the retinue of Kṣitigarbha mentioned below.
Since there is no separate position for him in the diagram, it is suspected that there is a redundant error; one should consult other editions to verify this.
Furthermore, the mantra of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha is a member of Mañjuśrī’s retinue.
In the Sanskrit language, *jālinī* translates as "net" (*jāla*); therefore, the first syllable is used as the seed-syllable.
Because this Net of Light is ungraspable in its arising, it is called the "Eternally Quiescent Light. This light is neither form nor mind, yet it possesses all manner of inconceivable forms.

Each and every one pervades the entire Dharma-realm, identical to the great void; because they attain mastery in this gateway of delivering sentient beings through the net of light, a circular dot (bindu) is added.
Furthermore, in the mantra of Śākyamuni, "Bha" signifies existence; by means of the Samādhi of the Dharma King, it universally manifests both...

The fifteenth [syllable] contains a dot (*bindu*) attached to its side; this signifies that all bodies corresponding to the various realms of existence are purified and harmonized, causing them to enter the secret treasury.
Furthermore, the meaning of the *hūṃ* syllable, which is commonly used for the three *uṣṇīṣas*, is as previously explained. *Ṭha* has the meaning of pride (*māna*).

Because he has purified the defilement of pride throughout immeasurable kalpas, and because he has realized that the *dharmadhātu* is equal and devoid of high or low, he has attained this mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*). The circular dot upon it signifies the meaning of being as limitless as space;
it is also the summit of all virtues, endowed with the sovereign power and majestic authority of a Dharma King. Therefore, [it is so].
It is also the Great Emptiness.
On the right is the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa; "White" signifies the meaning of great compassion.

Entering the syllable-gateway *la*, because the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended, it is ultimately and eternally pure. This is the crown of the Tathāgata’s manifold marks, being white and pure.
Because compassion pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*, it is augmented with the *bindu* (the great dot).
On the left is the *Uṣṇīṣavijaya*, which enters the syllable *śa*; because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent, this is the pinnacle of great quiescence.
Thus, its name signifies "Victorious Great Emptiness," as explained previously.
Furthermore, the "Uṣṇīṣa" (Buddha-crown) of the Most Victorious One is so called because it possesses the sound of the *dharmapuṇḍarīka-artha-garbha-samādhi*;
as it is the crown of the Tathāgata’s secret supernormal power regarding the measure of his lifespan, it is named "Most Victorious."
Furthermore, the *Tāra* of the *Uṣṇīṣa-jvālā-buddha* signifies the stainless nature of suchness (*tathatā*), and it also signifies the "wheel of fire.
This is the crown of the Tathāgata’s radiance of meditative concentration and wisdom; it is so named because it is able to eliminate the obscurations of darkness.
Furthermore, the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-vighnāntaka* is named "Free from All Causes and Conditions" (*hetupratyaya-vinirmukta*) and is also called "Power of Sovereignty" (*vaśitā-bala*).
This is the crown of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and supernormal knowledges; it can subdue the karmic defilements of all sentient beings and cause them all to become pure.
Therefore, the syllable-gateway *ka-ra* has the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*), as explained previously.
Furthermore, the Mantra of the World-Mother (Lokamātṛ) is the seed of all worldly deities;

for the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Tathāgata is precisely the suchness of the world, because he has attained mastery over causes and conditions, because ultimate nirvāṇa is unattainable [as a fixed entity], and because the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) are fundamentally unborn (*anutpanna*). Thus, within the triple world, all vehicles...
Because it is immovable and unborn, one abides in the *ratnasthāna-samādhi* (Jewel-Abode Samādhi) and manifests various bodies according to the types of beings.
If the bindu (dot) of emptiness is added, it signifies the meaning of being all-pervasive; it signifies the accomplishment of all benefits through various forms.
Any worldly deity may take a single syllable as its seed-mantra (*bīja*).
Furthermore, the *huṃ* syllable of the Unconquerable Mantra is the sound of the wrathful lion’s roar of Śākyamuni Tathāgata;
its meaning is as explained previously.
Moreover, regarding the mantra of the Earth Goddess, in the Sanskrit language the Earth Goddess is called *Pṛthivī*.
Therefore, taking the final syllable as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) signifies the meaning of the Vajra Samādhi;
it can sustain this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), making it like a vajra.
Furthermore, the Śānti mantra is called "Auspicious" (*śiva*) because all phenomena are free from all conditioned activities.
The syllable *ra* represents the samādhi of auspicious and wondrous karma; it is the body of signless wisdom (*animitta-prajñā*).
Because the function of the samādhi of empowerment manifests from this body of wisdom, the sound of the syllable *i* is added.

Furthermore, the mantra of Upakeśinī is called the Samādhi of the Wish-Fulfilling Gift of Mañjuśrī and the Signless Empowerment Samādhi because all dharmas are unobtainable; it is explained as before.
The mantra of the youth Citra mentioned above is the Great Emptiness Samādhi of Wondrous Auspiciousness;
because it is adorned with ten thousand virtues and is able to accomplish all meaningful benefits, it is named Citra. The remainder is as explained previously.
Furthermore, regarding the mantra of the youth Vasumati: because all phenomena are free from causes and conditions, it is called the "Samādhi of the Sovereign Power of Wondrous Auspiciousness.
The remainder is explained as before. The Ācārya says that each of the five deities who are attendants of Mañjuśrī has one who receives their instructions;
all of them take the second syllable *ri* as their seed-syllable, as their function is identical to that of the messengers (*dūta*).
Therefore, fifth is the mantra for summoning the youth (*kumāra*). The Sanskrit text is missing;
the transliterated sound is *ākarṣaṇī*. This name for "summoning" is itself the mantra.
By inferring from its meaning, one should take the initial syllable *ā* and pair it with the letter *ri* to form the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Furthermore, regarding the removal of doubt and wonder, from this point onward is the section on the meaning of the "removal of obstacles" within the *karuṇā-bala-samādhi*.
In the commentary on the meaning of the *parivāra* (retinue), *hasana* signifies joy;

that is to say, by means of the power of compassion (*karuṇā-bala*), one pulls all sentient beings out of the net of evil, heterodox views, doubts, and regrets, causing them all to abide in true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) through initial vision.
One should leap for joy because of the Dharma; this should be extensively explained by means of the "gateways of letters" (*akṣaramukha*). This is the mantra of the *sūkṣmacitta* (subtle mind).
One should take the initial letter as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), or employ a single letter according to the requirements of the meaning.
Furthermore, in the commentary on the meaning of the mantras for bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings, the term *rasana* signifies "taste.

This means that by the power of compassion and samādhi, one opens the gate of nectar (*amṛta*), uproots the seeds of the dark night of birth and death, and causes fearful sentient beings to see the right path and attain their own refuge; this is the final *na*.
The syllable itself is the true nectar-like flavor of the syllable.
In the commentary on the meaning of the mantras for eliminating all evil destinies, the term *tromaṣaṇa* specifically carries the sense of "crushing";
it means that by the power of compassion and samādhi, one destroys the obstacles of the evil destinies for all sentient beings.

The syllable *ḍha* signifies the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is the fundamental mind of sentient beings. This mind is bound by the accumulation of karma, becoming dense and firm so that it cannot emerge on its own.
Now, because one contemplates that the Dharma-realm is fundamentally unbound, it naturally emerges beyond the constraints of karma;
therefore, it is designated as "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).
Furthermore, regarding the general meaning of the *Uṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī*:
"By means of various skillful expedients (*upāya-kauśalya*), one causes [beings] to attain peace and happiness. This explains the intent of compassionate protection within the *Karuṇā-bala-samādhi*.
If one lacks wisdom and expedient means, one cannot even liberate oneself, let alone liberate all sentient beings; therefore—
To universally study various skillful means with a mind of compassion is called the wisdom that rescues the intention.
Furthermore, the seed-syllable *Ṭa* of the Great Compassion Mantra has the meaning of "nurturing";

because it enters the gate of the syllable *A*, it represents the ground of omniscience where the various sprouts of goodness exist within the hard husks of the three obstructions, nurtured by the sunlight of craving.

That which was scorched and burned cannot now grow; however, from within the samādhi of the power of great compassion, a great cloud of loving-kindness arises, universally raining down the rain of Dharma so that all may grow according to their respective capacities. Therefore, it is named "The Arising of Great Loving-Kindness."

Furthermore, the mantra of being bound by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-saṃvṛta*) is like a great tree entwined by creeping vines, which become firmly interlaced and knotted so that they cannot be separated.
The pure bodhicitta is likewise: because it is bound by the power of compassion, one dwells within the prison of the triple world as if in one's own home, having no intention to seek escape;
for this reason, it is named "Flame" (*jvālā*), which should be understood as various vehicles (*yāna*).

The matters of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the burning house are clarified therein; however, because they are used as provisional names to guide all sentient beings, various vehicles (*yāna*) are ultimately unattainable.
Furthermore, the mantra that removes all feverish afflictions is the letter *I*, which is called the Samādhi of Ultimate Non-arising. That is to say:
It is named thus because it is a pool of the pure dharma-nature of the water of omniscience, a place where all noble beings (ārya) joyfully congregate like sārasa birds;
for now, by the power of the Samādhi of Compassion, it leads sentient beings suffering from the heat and afflictions in the wilderness of saṃsāra to enter therein together.
Furthermore, the *mantra* of inconceivable wisdom, the syllable *U*, is also the samādhi of ultimate non-arising; there is merely a slight difference in the dharma-gate.
Because one knows that all dharmas are ultimately equal, one is able to take various afflictions and evil karmas as the work of a Tathāgata.
Since one experiences the bliss of the third dhyāna even within the Avīci Hell, it is called "inconceivable liberation."
Regarding the gates of liberation: if one enters such gates of liberation, one will be able to dwell long within birth and death without ever becoming weary or disheartened.

Furthermore, from this point forward is the mantra of the "Jewel Place" (*ratnasthāna*), which belongs to the retinue of dharma-gates within the Samādhi of the Vajra-Indestructible Conduct of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva; in Sanskrit, it is called *Ratnaka*.
"Lo" (pronounced with urgency) is translated as "Jewel-Maker" (*Ratnakāra*) or "Jewel-Born" (*Ratnasaṃbhava*); "Jewel-Abode" (*Ratnasthāna*) is taken as the correct [reading].
The *samādhi* of Śākyamuni is the place where these various jewels manifest in the world. Now, the name of this Bodhisattva is the place from which all these jewels are produced and nurtured.
It is like the earth in this world: wherever there is a nature of jewels, various jewels constantly arise.
Now, because the *ratnagotra-citta* (the treasure-nature of the mind-ground) constantly gives rise to the treasures of all the myriad virtues of sentient beings,
the syllable *Na* is used as the mantra; since its meaning of "bestowing" (*dāna*) is identical to the great void, it pervades all places and there is nothing it does not produce.
Furthermore, the Ratnapāṇi mantra is like a wish-fulfilling jewel held in the hand, which can provide for all seekers according to their requests;
this is the Dharani-dhātu of fulfilling vows within the Samādhi of Kṣitigarbha.

"Sprinkling" (sa) signifies that the nature of these dharmas is dull, just like a perfect sphere that has no mind, no intention, and no discrimination, yet is able to respond and accord with sentient beings individually.
If one acts with appropriateness and possesses a sense of strategic timing within this, then despite exhausting oneself all day long, what ought to be accomplished will not be incomplete.
The meaning of "Great Emptiness" (Mahāśūnyatā) is as explained above.
Furthermore, the mantra of the Earth-Holder (Dharaṇīdhara) is like the great earth that sustains and supports all things; its vajra-like realm is likewise indestructible.

Furthermore, this is the source from which the roots of the ten thousand virtues arise, the locus where various activities are established, and that which ensures not even a single hair’s breadth of merit shall perish throughout immeasurable eons.
It is the addition of a circular point upon the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (mahā-śūnyatā);
it is Great Emptiness because the mind realizes the mind itself. Therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Great Emptiness. Within this Great Emptiness...
