That there is nothing which does not exist therein is precisely the meaning of the Earth-Holding (Dharaṇīdhara) sustaining all things.

Furthermore, although the name of the Bodhisattva is absent from the Sanskrit manuscript of this single mantra, when one examines the various chapters above and below, the retinue of Kṣitigarbha consists of only five bodhisattvas;
thus, this mantra seems to be a redundant repetition.
The mantra of the Right Jewel-Seal Hand (Ratnamudrāhasta) is largely based on the meaning of all phenomena being like a mass of foam.
Just as worldly foam and bubbles are merely water acting as its own cause and condition, possessing no self-nature at all, so too are the jewels of all merits:

they are likewise merely the waves of the water of the mind acting as their own cause and condition, ultimately never emerging from the gate of the letter A (A-kāra-dvāra), for it is able to illuminate them.
Because he knows the nature of jewels and possesses mastery over their function, he is named Ratnamudrāhasta (Jewel-Seal Hand).
The mantra of the right [hand], the Firm Resolve (*dṛḍhamati*), uses the seal of the pure *bodhicitta*;
because its nature is eternally firm, it is precisely the essence of the indestructible Vajra realm of practice. The syllable *ṇa* augmented with the great dot of emptiness (*bindu*) is the mind.
The self-realized mind accomplishes all the purposes and benefits intended herein; this is precisely what establishes sentient beings within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Furthermore, from here on, the "Stainless Space Mantra" is the third [section], which is the pure realm of Ākāśagarbha.
The "Dharma-gate of the Family of Latency" (*maimō*) signifies the meaning of cause; it is also the pure *bodhicitta*.
Because all causes are unobtainable, it is like the pure void, free from all characteristics.

Furthermore, because it is augmented by the *bindu* (the dot of great emptiness), it pervades all places and revolves with sovereign mastery, like the wind moving through space without any obstruction.
Furthermore, because all defilements are fundamentally unarisen within the *ra*-gate of the Ākāśamati mantra, it is called the "Light of Innate Pure Wisdom.

Moreover, by adding the great void-point (*bindu*) of samādhi, it is named after the autumn sky when the myriad phenomena are clear and serene, not a single speck of dust stirs, and the full moon shines upon the void, pervading everywhere. Thus, this name is established.
Furthermore, the Mantra of Pure Wisdom enters the gateway of the syllable *kṣa*;
it does not engage with any phenomena, for all phenomena are their true reality (*dharmatā*). Because it is augmented by the bindu of great emptiness, it likewise neither engages nor discriminates.
Since this mind of wondrous wisdom is unattached and universally purifies the universal mandala, it is given this name.
Furthermore, the *ḍa* syllable-gateway of the Mantra of the Practice of Wisdom signifies the meaning of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
By entering the mind of the Dharma-realm through this, one is like the youth Sudhana, who personally approached all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and fully cultivated all bodhisattva practices;
therefore, the addition of the term "samādhi" signifies the meaning of the ten thousand practices. The syllable *ra* is the wisdom of the pure Dharma-realm.
It is named as such because it expands the points of emptiness and, within a single thought-moment, embodies the path of Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, regarding the mantra of Wisdom-Settled (*An-hui*), "An" signifies immovability, non-retrogression, and fearlessness;
because this mind of stainless wisdom regarding space is fully endowed with all powers, it strides alone without fear and utters the lion’s roar. Thus it is named.
The syllable *go* constitutes its essence because it universally extinguishes all the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of sentient beings.
Furthermore, for those who follow the teachings, the mantra syllable *dhiḥ* signifies the meaning of the pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
*śrī* signifies the meaning of auspiciousness and the possession of merit; and the syllable *haṃ* signifies the accomplishment of all activities.
The term *Mahāsāmanta* (Great Sovereign) signifies being everywhere unbound and stainless; this shall be explained in detail.
Any of the messengers may be taken as a seed-syllable according to the instructions, or used according to its corresponding meaning and function.
Furthermore, because the nature of karma is fundamentally quiescent, because all phenomena are free from opposition, because suchness is ungraspable,
because the dharma-realm is free from defilement, because there is nothing to be mounted, and because it is detached from all conditioned activities,
the mantras spoken by Bodhisattvas take even a single syllable from among the multitude of Bodhisattvas— as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields— as their mantra.
The term "or" (*vā*) signifies that it corresponds to the application according to its meaning.
Furthermore, the mantra of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika devas should be recited as explained in the section on the Jewel Samādhi above; it is merely out of sequence in the original scripture.
Regarding the etymological interpretation of the word *manorama*, *maṇḍala* is translated as "pleasing to the mind."
*Dharma* means "Dharma" (the teaching), and *sambhava* means "arising.
This signifies that these deities are born through transformation from the pure Dharma, unlike worldly deities who are born from the causes and conditions of karma and suffering.
Furthermore, in the Western language, anything that is perfectly adorned, subtle and wondrous, and pleasing to the human mind is collectively termed a *maṇḍala*. Moreover—
Because the palace of the pure *dharmadhātu* has the meaning of "Pure Abode" (*śuddhāvāsa*), and because it is born from the womb of the lotus, it is called "Delightful Arising of Dharma.
The next phrase, *tathābhavakaṇa*, translates as "speaking";

this should be placed at the beginning of the sentence, as it refers to the one born from the transformation of the Dharma who is able to speak these skillful means for the sake of the world. Next, it says:
"Saṃsaṃ" constitutes the essence of this mantra. "Sa" signifies the lotus and also the sense of "birth.

Because it is adorned with the bindu (dot), it is fully perfected; that is the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha). It is stated twice because it corresponds to the meaning of the two layers of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa).

Furthermore, the Heart Mantra of the Rākṣasas is spoken according to the linguistic sounds of their respective realms. The Ācārya does not explain the meaning of the phrases, but rather, based on the *dharmamukha* (gateways of letters), there are two layers of addition: the syllable *ra* (Rākṣasa). It devours the two layers of karmic defilement and enters the belly of the pure Dharmadhātu; this is the meaning of "Rākṣasa. Using the initial syllable as the essence of the mantra: *RĀKṢA HŪṂ PHAṬ* This is the mantra body. It is taught that by reciting this mantra, one can subdue all malevolent spirits and obstructive demons. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing oneself as a Rākṣasa, one will attain mastery over all Rākṣasas. Furthermore, it is taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity, one will be able to summon them and command them to perform various tasks. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the belly of the practitioner, all karmic obstacles will be purified and one will attain the state of a Vidyādhara. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the heart of the practitioner, one will attain the power of clairvoyance and clairaudience and be able to perceive the thoughts of others. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the crown of the practitioner's head, one will attain the power of flight and travel through the air. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the soles of the practitioner's feet, one will attain the power of invisibility and be able to move about unobserved. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the palms of the practitioner's hands, one will attain the power of transformation and be able to manifest various forms at will. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's entire body, one will attain the power of longevity and live for a kalpa. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's speech, one will attain the power of eloquence and be able to expound the Dharma to convert sentient beings. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's mind, one will attain the power of wisdom and be able to penetrate all phenomena. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's life-force, one will attain the power of immortality and never again undergo birth and death. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's merit, one will attain the power of inexhaustible wealth and be able to provide for all sentient beings. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's name, one will attain the power of invincibility and be able to withstand all enemies and obstacles. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's lineage, one will attain the power of lineage protection and be able to ensure that one's descendants are always safe and secure. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's dwelling, one will attain the power of dwelling security and be able to protect one's home from all calamities. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's possessions, one will attain the power of possession protection and be able to guard one's wealth and goods from being stolen or lost. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's activities, one will attain the power of activity protection and be able to ensure that all undertakings are successful. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's intentions, one will attain the power of intention fulfillment and be able to have all one's wishes granted. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's vows, one will attain the power of vow fulfillment and be able to accomplish all great aspirations. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's compassion, one will attain the power of great compassion and be able to universally save all sentient beings. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's wisdom, one will attain the power of great wisdom and be able to discern the nature of all phenomena. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's liberation, one will attain the power of great liberation and be able to transcend all bonds and afflictions. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's enlightenment, one will attain the power of great enlightenment and be able to realize the supreme, perfect awakening. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's nirvāṇa, one will attain the power of great nirvāṇa and be able to enter the state of ultimate peace and bliss. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's dharmakāya, one will attain the power of the dharmakāya and be able to manifest in accordance with the needs of sentient beings. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's sambhogakāya, one will attain the power of the sambhogakāya and be able to enjoy the bliss of the Dharma. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's nirmāṇakāya, one will attain the power of the nirmāṇakāya and be able to manifest in various forms to benefit sentient beings. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's three secrets, one will attain the power of the three secrets and be able to integrate body, speech, and mind into the state of non-duality. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's ten directions, one will attain the power of pervading the ten directions and be able to manifest throughout all worlds. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's three times, one will attain the power of penetrating the three times and be able to know the past, present, and future. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's six sense bases, one will attain the power of purifying the six sense bases and be able to transform the six consciousnesses into the six pāramitās. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's five aggregates, one will attain the power of transforming the five aggregates and be able to realize the five bodies of the Buddha. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's twelve links of dependent origination, one will attain the power of cutting off the twelve links and be able to escape the cycle of birth and death. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's eighteen elements, one will attain the power of purifying the eighteen elements and be able to realize the eighteen emptinesses. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's twenty-two faculties, one will attain the power of perfecting the twenty-two faculties and be able to fulfill the capacity for enlightenment. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's four foundations of mindfulness, one will attain the power of the four foundations of mindfulness and be able to observe the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's four right efforts, one will attain the power of the four right efforts and be able to abandon evil and cultivate good. It is also taught that if one recites it while visualizing the Rākṣasa deity entering the practitioner's four bases of psychic power, one will attain the power of the four bases of psychic power and be able to master
Furthermore, the Naṭakinī mantra belongs to the yakṣa-gati; it is traditionally said in the world to belong to Mahākāla.

Those who receive its incantations are empowered by him, and because he delights in eating human hearts, this refers to those such as the *kiñjalka* or *manuṣya-kiñjalka* mentioned in the Lotus Sūtra. This applies to ordinary human beings.
There may be yellow medicinal substances such as ox-gall (*gorocanā*) and the like;

if one encounters and consumes them, one will immediately attain the highest accomplishment and be able to travel throughout the four quarters in a single day, performing whatever one desires. However, that rite must not be performed without cause;
one must know when another's life span is about to end, and only within six months of that time may one take [the substance].
An illusionist secretly steals his mind and replaces it with other substances;
although he loses his ordinary nature, he remains firmly alive until the time of his destined death arrives, at which point he finally dissolves and perishes.
Vairocana, descending with the Dharma-gates of the three periods of time, transforms himself into the Great Black Deity, possessing great majestic power, and smears his body with ashes.
In the midst of a wilderness, he performed a rite to summon all the Nākinīs and rebuked them, saying, "Because you have constantly killed people, you shall now eat [me].
Using skillful means, he manifested himself as being swallowed by that host. They were struck with terror and all took refuge in the Buddha;
only then did he release them. He established a precept forbidding killing. He said to the Buddha, "If I..."
To those who do not eat meat, [the Buddha] said: "I allow you to eat the hearts of humans who have died. They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a person is about to die, various great yakṣas and others vie with one another to seize them; how can they be obtained? The Buddha said:
"I allow you to empower them with dhāraṇī-mantras for six months; when their lives come to an end, I allow you to take and eat them."
This mantra is spoken in order to discipline those multitudes and lead them into the Buddha’s wisdom. *Ha* signifies the meaning of "cause," because all phenomena have the mind as their cause.
Now, by means of the syllable-gateway *ra*, which is named "eating," it devours the minds of people;
furthermore, by adding a nasal dot (*bindu*) to it, the defilements of the mind are forever exhausted, and one abides in Great Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the mantra syllables of the yakṣiṇī: because one who holds the yakṣiṇī vidyā addresses her with a feminine voice, she is called "Dāri.
Because all vehicles are fundamentally unarisen, one does not move from their original place and immediately arrives at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Therefore, the dharma-nature of this vehicle is inherently such that it is free from all conditioned activity; its original nature is eternally quiescent, and thus it is named "Yakṣa" (Medicine).
Regarding the meaning of *yakṣa*: those who ride this vehicle are hidden and secret, beyond all analogy; therefore, it is called the *Yakṣa-yāna*.
*Darī* refers to the samādhi of the pure *dharmadhātu*, for it can extinguish the various stains of the mind; thus, it devours the remaining worldly *yakṣas*.
These mantras are not for those who merely hold them, as they are explained in the chapter on seals (*mudrā*) within the *Vidyādhara-paṭala*.
Regarding the mantra of the Piśāca, its essential meaning is its original name; it has become corrupted and abbreviated because it follows the phonetic expressions of that particular realm.

"Piśāca" carries the sense of extreme suffering and torment, as they belong to the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) and are constantly oppressed by the afflictions of hunger, thirst, and heat; thus, this serves as its name. If one examines the meaning through the gateway of its syllables: *Pi* signifies *pīḍana*, meaning "to oppress" or "to cause pain. *Śā* signifies *śamana*, meaning "to pacify" or "to extinguish. *Ca* signifies *ccheda*, meaning "to cut off" or "to sever. Thus, the compound *pi-śā-ca* implies that which "pacifies and cuts off" [suffering]. Furthermore, *piśāca* can be analyzed as *piśita* (flesh) and *āca* (eating), meaning "flesh-eater. Alternatively, it may be understood as *piśāca* derived from *piśācaka*, signifying those who "consume" or "devour" their victims. Therefore, the term denotes both the infliction of pain upon others and the state of being tormented by one's own afflictions.
This refers to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) in the sense of being free from transition and change; it is stated twice in contrast to the two kinds of death.

By adding the term "samādhi," it means that through the power of great compassion, one does not abandon suffering sentient beings, but rather enters and abides in inconceivable liberation. This is the true speech of the Vaiśravaṇa.
The aforementioned *Yugamdhara* mantra is likewise of the yakṣa class; it is a mantra formed according to the phonetic expressions of that particular realm.
The meaning of "going" (*ga*) is the sense of attaining mastery within the secret treasury of nirvāṇa—the three virtues—by means of "non-going" (*aga*).
It is stated twice to signify the ultimate meaning. This should be explained extensively by means of the "gateways of letters."

The Ācārya said: "In general, regarding mantras that do not explicitly state a seed-syllable (bīja-akṣara), one may take any single syllable from the beginning, middle, or end, or take whichever syllable is appropriate according to the meaning; either way is acceptable."
Furthermore, regarding the mantra of the asuras: the term *asura* is called "heavenly" (*deva*) because it contains the sound *ā*;

yet, because it is named "non-heavenly," it is called an *asura*. Briefly stated, there are four kinds of heavens: namely, the heaven of birth, the worldly heaven, the pure heaven, and the heaven of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because they enter the gate of the syllable *A*, all of them are unobtainable. Furthermore, [this] accomplishes the supreme...

Because he possesses a great body, he is Vairocana; the meaning of "asura" also follows the vocal expressions of those realms as mantras, which shall be extensively explained through the gates of syllables.
Furthermore, regarding the mantras of the mahoragas, their phonetic expressions follow the speech of those realms;

thus, the gateways of syllables (*akṣaramukha*) can be understood. In general, when explaining the mantras of the eight classes of beings, one should cite from the "Chapter on the Pure Eye of the World" (*Lokanetra-parivarta*) for each individual syllable, providing an extensive analysis according to the ten gates of mastery (*vaśitā*) within those respective realms. All other cases should be modeled after this.
Furthermore, regarding the mantras of the kinnaras, *hasana* has the meaning of "joy," while the subsequent phrase has the meaning of "causing others to rejoice.

Thus, by means of the vajra music, the Tathāgata universally delights all sentient beings, causing them all to deeply delight in the sound of the Dharma and to leap for joy; this extends even to Mahākāśyapa and others who firmly abide in reality.
If even those at the limit [of existence] can still be raised up, how much more so those within the cycle of birth and death;
this is called the *kiṃnara* spiritual friend within the treasury of the *dharmadhātu*. The meaning of the name is explained as before.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has taught this mantra for all people who desire to be constantly born among humans; it is the vehicle for the human realm.

If sentient beings recite and practice it, they will forever leave behind the various unfavorable states of the evil realms, as well as the long-lived states of the higher heavens where there is much negligence and difficulty. Thus, within the gateway of the human realm, they shall attain mastery.

Therefore, it constitutes the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala. Furthermore, because all aspects of the Tathāgata’s birth-body manifest as being identical to the human dharma, this vehicle is able to establish great benefit within the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*).
Ācārya [desires that] sentient beings of various dispositions and inclinations may attain understanding according to their respective types; thus, he does not explain the phrases [literally].

In principle, one should contemplate those to be delivered by means of the eighty-four thousand dharma-treasuries corresponding to their needs through the extensive exposition of the gates of syllables (*akṣaramukha*).
Thus, each individual syllable serves as a seed-syllable (*bīja*), as clarified by the meanings of the phrases in all the mantras mentioned previously;
this is merely an illustration based on the dharma-gate of a single disciple. However, in reality, within each and every syllable there are immeasurable meanings that cannot be fully detailed.
It is my intention that you should extend and expand this by applying it to various categories, revolving it with mastery so as to enter universally into all *sūtras*.
If one merely measures what has been heard and remains fixed without progressing, it cannot be called the "Inexhaustible Dharma Gate.

Furthermore, this Inexhaustible Dharma Gate cannot be understood through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination; it can only be realized by a practitioner who cultivates according to the teaching.
When one practices until reaching the time of seeing the path of the luminous mind, it occurs spontaneously, just as the youth Sudhana, within a single moment of mind,
universally beheld as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in the world, comprehending all the Dharma-treasuries of the three mysteries without anything being unpenetrated.
The Sūtra says: "O Lord of Mysteries, I have thus proclaimed all these mantras;
you should listen attentively to the heart of all these mantras, which is as follows: the gateway of the letter A.
This heart of all mantras is the most unsurpassed; it is the abode of all mantras, and through this mantra one shall attain certainty."

In this samādhi, as described in the sūtra, there were assemblies of vajra-bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms within ten worlds, along with immeasurable and boundless bodies conforming to various types.

Within each gate, there were root mantras, heart mantras, and随心 (anucara) mantras, etc., which, like the Universal Eye Dharma-gate, could not be fully recorded; the Tathāgata, by means of his universality...
Having explained the various distinctions of the gates and the body, they are again subsumed within the gate of the letter *A*.
If it were not thus, those sentient beings who enter the secret treasury would not know that this heart of mantras is vast and boundless, penetrating deeply to the limitlessness [of reality].
It is like the universal manifestation of all things from the single thought-moment of the signless mind of Vairocana.
Each of the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) upholds a gateway to the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-mukha), the treasury of the three mysteries.
Now, observing that each of these gateways is fundamentally unborn (anutpanna), they ultimately do not emerge from the Tathāgata’s single thought-moment of signless mind.
For this reason, one should know that this mind is the most supreme and the source of all mantras.
Just as the abodes of the ten directions all dwell in empty space, yet empty space has no basis of its own,
so too, if one realizes that the letter-gateway *A* is the heart of all mantras,
then one realizes that all letter-gateways are the heart of all mantras and the dwelling place of all mantras— all of which are most supreme.
In order to provide a detailed analysis that facilitates easy understanding, the practitioner should explain the meaning of all the aforementioned mantras by means of this gateway of the letter *A*.
Because the gateway of the letter *A* does not obstruct any phenomena, as they arise from conditions,

and because arising from conditions is itself the meaning of being fundamentally unborn (*anutpanna*), one should know that the mantra of Mahāvairocana and all other mantras likewise possess this same nature.
There is neither differentiation nor non-differentiation; it is neither real nor false, neither suchness nor different.

When one clearly perceives this without obstruction within the single mind, that is precisely seeing one's own mind; the path of clarity is attained right here, and through this mantra, one achieves definitive certainty.
