Chapter Five: Attainment in the World.
Regarding this "Attainment in the World" chapter at the beginning of the third volume: previously, the Lord of Secrets asked, "How does one hold the mantras?
How does one achieve their results? Thereupon, the Blessed One extensively explained the mantras to be held from this point forward.
The following clearly elucidates the ritual procedures for receiving and upholding the mantras, as well as the methods for accomplishing siddhi.

Since the Tathāgata’s profoundly deep secret treasury cannot be demonstrated to people through verbal expression, he employs the conventional, conditioned phenomena of the world as metaphors to illustrate the profound dependent origination within the treasury of the *dharmadhātu*. If there are sentient beings who penetrate this...
The middle conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is that which, by the power of natural empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), transcends to realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
When one realizes the ultimate truth, the true nature of worldly phenomena becomes twice as clear; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Worldly Accomplishment" (*loka-siddhi-paṭala*).
Furthermore, because the practitioner first relies on yoga with signs (*sanimitta-yoga*) to achieve worldly accomplishment, they gradually purify the six sense faculties.
I see the Buddhas of the ten directions who, by means of this wondrous function of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), sport in divine transformations (*vikrīḍita*) to extensively benefit sentient beings;

yet they still take pleasure in worldly *siddhis*. Now, observing that such *siddhis* arise solely from a multitude of conditions, they are devoid of arising and ceasing, permanence and annihilation, coming and going, or identity and difference—all are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, reflections in a mirror, or the moon in water, and are but empty echoes.
Vasubandhu: Since all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) have ceased at that time, it is because this is the *Sarvāvaraṇanīvaraṇaviśodhana* Samādhi;
therefore, one should not seek supramundane accomplishment apart from this. As stated by the Buddha in the verses regarding the attainment of the fruit according to the mantra teachings:
"In performing any accomplishment, one must first prepare all the constituent parts as the preliminary practice (*pūrvayoga*)."
The sequence of rituals for the rites of offering and service is largely identical to what is commonly taught in the *Vidyādhara-piṭaka*;
however, in this system, all material requisites are established as symbols of the *dharmadhātu*, and every activity performed is permeated by yoga.
Therefore, it is only through the definitive interpretation of this school that the essential meaning of the *Susiddhi* and other such sūtras can be fully realized. This, then, is...
This differs from the usual tradition. The holy one who transmitted the Dharma produced these three thousand verses of scripture because he intended to preserve both the concise and the detailed.
Within this chapter, those matters that are commonly understood by all ācāryas and others are no longer set forth in full;

rather, only the summary verses (*uddāna*) from the scripture are cited, stating: "Just as the fruit is accomplished through the teachings of the mantra-dharma," and from here on, the mind [is described].

The contemplative recitation of the Dharma and other methods previously kept secret are now fully explained here. The *Ācārya* composed the *Vairocana-pūjā-vidhi-krama* in the land of Uḍḍiyāna; this is precisely the essential text for this chapter.

As it is extensive and cannot be recorded in its entirety, it shall be explained separately. However, that work contains briefly five sections: 1. The section on the preliminary preparations (*pūrva-saṃskāra*).

2. The section on the ritual of the maṇḍala (*maṇḍala-vidhi*). 3. The section on the ritual of the homa (*homa-vidhi*). 4. The section on the ritual of the initiation (*abhiṣeka-vidhi*). 5. The section on the ritual of the subsequent service (*paścāt-karma-vidhi*). [End of first section]
First, one should fully maintain the samaya precepts; second, one should increase the protection of pure conduct, which means:

three times each day, according to the yoga method, prostrating to the Buddhas of the ten directions, confessing all transgressions, taking refuge in the Triple Gem, offering up one’s body as a gift, generating the bodhicitta, rejoicing in merit, requesting [the turning of the wheel of Dharma], and so forth, up to the dedication of merit.

The third ritual for performing the offering, which is the method for purifying demonic activities through the Great Protection and other rites of purification of the Tathāgata Samādhi-trimandala-vajra-kavaca-viśuddha-dharmadhātu-citta, is as follows:
First, one should purify the mind-ground and this defiled land by means of the syllable-gateway *ra*; next, one should visualize the arising of a great wind-circle and an ocean of fragrant water.
By means of the gateway of the syllable *A*, one creates a vajra-ground, fully adorned and purified with great jewels;

thereafter, by means of the seed-mantra, one transforms [the ground] into the assembly of Great Sages such as Mahāvairocana, as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, and duly invites them, reveals the samaya, offers arghya water, and presents lotus seats. Next, one purifies the interior with the sword of immovable wisdom.
Having subdued the māras by means of the empowerment of Vajrasattva upon oneself and having bound the perimeter boundary, one again offers argha water.
Having purified the offerings with the sword of wisdom of the Dharmadhātu-citta, one makes offerings according to the rite.
By means of the Vajragarbha-vidyā, one transforms and sustains great clouds of offering ornaments, chanting the true qualities of the Tathāgata with vajra-speech.
The Venerable One contemplates the Buddha’s transformation-clouds pervading all places to guide and benefit all sentient beings.
Having thus completed the Dharma-offering, the fourth [step] is to arouse a mind that benefits inexhaustible sentient beings and to recite according to the Dharma.

Within this chapter, from the words "each word shall correspond" (*zì zì xiāng yìng*) onwards, the expedient means are fully explained; I shall now explain them following the text. Generally, when a practitioner wishes to practice...
When performing the visualization, one should first take one's place upon the yoga-seat and empower one's own body with the five syllables *a-vā-ra-ha-ka*,
as described in the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Siddhis" and the "Ritual Sequence for Offerings. This is because,
although the supreme enlightenment of all Buddhas is indeed quiescent and signless, it must nevertheless be realized through...
Seated upon the adamantine ground within the adamantine body, one may enter into realization; other illusory bodies and lands lack the power to sustain this.

It is likewise for the yoga practitioner: desiring to enter the subtle yoga and perceive the boundless realm of the Tathāgata, one must protect one’s own body and mind through these skillful means, and furthermore, observe with the stainless eye.
Upon the heart-lotus pedestal, at the crown of the gateway of the letter *A*, one places the letter *Am*.
By means of this self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), one becomes identical to the state of the Conqueror (*Munīndra*) who is universally illumined by a hundred rays of light.

Thus, one is fit to perform vajra-activities (*vajrakarma*), just as a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) is qualified to participate in the communal rites of the Saṃgha. Furthermore, it is said that one should practice...
First, one should single-mindedly practice the method of mental recitation until it is clear, precise, and spontaneously mastered, in order to achieve accomplishment within this very life.
One should set a time limit for oneself by relying on the expedient means of counting, time, signs, and manifestations, and perform the practice according to the Dharma.
Having first performed the recitation, once one can personally realize that hindrances and obscurations have been eliminated, only then should one proceed to the full ritual.
Furthermore, having personally realized the preliminary signs of *siddhi* through the practice of recitation (*japa*), one should then arise to accomplish the maṇḍala.
Now, from the passage "the correspondence of each syllable" up until "having purified those [obstacles]," this scriptural text generally explains the method for practicing and reciting;
when it comes to the time of performing the rites for accomplishment (*sādhana*), one continues to hold the mantra according to this same method.
Furthermore, for all who practice the mental recitation (*manas-japa*), one first follows the preceding method to transform the seed-syllable (*bīja*) into the body of the deity.
One’s physical appearance, demeanor, and qualities such as tranquility, joy in the Dharma, and majesty should all correspond to the mudrās of the Body Secret (*kāyaguhyaka*) without any error.

Nevertheless, these may be transformed according to the specific rite; for instance, when performing a recitation for the pacification of calamities (*śāntika*), one should visualize the deity accordingly.
If one performs the recitation for enrichment (*puṣṭi*), one should visualize the deity as having the color of white jade, abiding in an expression of serene silence.

If performing the recitation for subjugation (*abhicāra*), one should visualize the deity as having the color of blazing fire or the radiance of the sun, or like an emerald or a dark blue cloud, abiding in a fierce and majestic expression. Now...
That which is discussed here is precisely that, at the time of constant recitation, one should follow each [deity] according to its original form in the maṇḍala.
One should visualize a perfect luminosity upon the heart of this honored deity, like a pure full moon disk— empty, bright, and translucent— with the seed-syllable appearing within it,
or else with the syllables from *namas* through *svāhā* appearing in succession, with a single-minded focus.
Because one dwells within the conditions (*ālambana*), it is called "the correspondence of syllables" (*akṣara-saṃyoga*).
Alternatively, when these syllables combine to form a phrase, they manifest all at once like the image of a wheel or the shape of a garland—luminous, stainless, and circling to the right.

Because one likewise dwells with a single mind within the conditions, it is called "the correspondence of phrases" (*pada-saṃyoga*). When a practitioner first begins their practice, they may fear that the mind...
If the mind becomes distracted, one should simply contemplate the seed-syllables; once they have become thoroughly matured after a long time, one may gradually increase the practice.

One should visualize each individual syllable of the mantra as being like pure milk or like a string of bright pearls, pervaded by garlands of light that flow in succession and enter the practitioner’s mouth, or else enter through the crown of the head.
The Ācārya says that it is also permissible for them to arise from the practitioner’s face and proceed from one [syllable] to the next.
As the flow enters, it is virtuous to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

When the flow enters in this manner, one should visualize it pervading the body, filling and saturating it, bringing internal serenity and joy as if sprinkled with nectar (*amṛta*), which can gradually eliminate the defilements and obscurations of body and mind from beginningless time.
One may visualize the seed-syllables (*bīja*), or the mudrās, or the deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
One should know that it likewise flows into the body of the practitioner.

Having seen this mantra-wheel, one should immediately regulate the breath, join the lips and teeth, and recite it mentally; with the tongue not touching the palate, one moves it slightly within the mouth without producing sound.
Therefore, in the Yoga school, this is called "Vajra-speech free from sound. One should maintain this.
"Completing one *lakṣa*" means maintaining it with vajra-speech until it reaches one hundred thousand recitations.
This "one" is the mother of all numerical counts; all other numerical counts for dharmas are contained within it.
If one has not yet attained realization after completing one *lakṣa*, one must perform another *lakṣa*, ensuring accomplishment within a period of one or two months.
It is all like this. To explain it according to the profound secret [tradition], *lakṣa* has the meaning of "vision.

This means that when the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) appears before one, one contemplates it with the mind's eye; because the single object-condition is undisturbed, it is called "single vision" (*ekadṛṣṭi*).

When abiding thus in a single object-condition, even if various difficulties arise—such as the manifestation of terrifying forms—even those with distracted minds who behold them may be driven to madness.
Or, even if a great sound were to arise that could shatter the King of Mountains itself, at that time the mind would neither be startled nor terrified, nor would it waver;
therefore, it is called "abiding well" (the first "seeing"). Furthermore, it is not merely a matter of seeing, but also of hearing, as described in the following verse.
Thus, the *Preface to the Nien-fo Samādhi* by Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu says: "The resonance of the profound sound..."
Listening with the mind is identical to this meaning; it is not merely hearing, but also touching. That which was previously characterized by many ailments is now entirely healed;

that which previously had an excessive increase in the fire element is now attained to clarity and coolness; that which previously had an excessive increase in the water element is now attained to warmth and nourishment.
Even when entering the mouth, it has a flavor like nectar (*amṛta*), and so it is with respect to objects of perception.
Within this, one naturally attains realization; that the ten phrases of dependent origination are themselves the meaning of "realization and knowledge" is stated in the Sūtra:

"The first letter is *bodhicitta*, the second is called 'sound' (*śabda*). This means that when one first contemplates the letter within the perfect luminosity, this letter is metaphorically like *bodhicitta*, for it arises through the wondrous function of the mantra. The second [letter] follows from this.
These syllables emerge from the sound of the mantra just as the myriad practices of great compassion arise from the bodhicitta;
when one hears the sound of the mantra, one immediately accords with its meaning, just as one attains the realization of bodhi by relying upon the myriad practices of great compassion.
Furthermore, the Brahma-sound *akṣara* is translated here as "syllable" (*zi*). Because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, this is the meaning of the bodhicitta.
*Akṣa* refers to the suchness of the nature of things (*dharmatā*), which is not something created by any Tathāgata, for it is uncreated;
thus its nature is quiescent. *Ara* means that this mind is fundamentally pure and free from defilement.
It is called "Pure Bodhicitta" because from this Pure Bodhicitta emerges the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s boundless wheel of speech;
thus it is called the second, "Sound. This is the profound and esoteric interpretation.

When a practitioner first engages in cultivation, having already perceived the characters within the perfect luminosity, they subsequently hear the sound of mantras emerging from those characters and phrases, like a gentle breeze harmonizing with the chimes of bells.
It is also like striking a bell or a chime: once the initial sound has emerged, it gradually fades away; as the subsequent sound follows, it immediately arises.
In this way, they circulate without interruption, flowing into the body with a refreshing and sublime bliss that is beyond comparison.
Just as a clear breeze fanning objects dispels the veil of darkness, the meaning of "abiding well" (*susthu-sthita*) is also as previously explained.
The Sūtra states: "One should visualize the phrase as the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) within its own locus. Here, "phrase" (*pada*) has the meaning of a dwelling place;

it is the point of ultimate convergence for the true meaning within the sound of the mantra. It is like the myriad rivers flowing toward the ocean, or like the ten thousand practices of great compassion all tending toward *nirvāṇa*;
therefore, it is called a "phrase" (*pada*). That the phrase itself constitutes the body of the *iṣṭadevatā* is because, like the Tathāgata, it is one.

Just as each of the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) is complete with an accumulation of immeasurable merit, and these marks together constitute the Buddha-body, so too is the meaning here:
each sound of a mantra possesses immeasurable meanings, and the collection of these various meanings constitutes the mantra-body.
For example, the mantra *dharmadhātu-svabhāva-koṭi* [is explained thus].
Each of these ten syllables is itself a gateway to a mantra, and each gateway inherently possesses manifold meanings. Now, these syllables are combined to form various names:
first, *dharma* is "Dharma"; next, *dhātu* is "Realm"; next, *svabhāva* is "Self-nature"; next, *gahanam* is "I. Furthermore, through these various names—

Taken together as a single phrase, it says: "I am the self-nature of the *dharmadhātu*. Because the meaning of this phrase collectively clarifies the body of the single *dharmadhātu*, the phrase and its conceptualization are said to be the *bhaṭṭāraka*.

If explained according to the perspective of the practitioner’s contemplation (*śikṣā-darśana*), it means that first the person perceives the forms and colors of each individual syllable of the mantra as vividly manifest;
next, sound issues forth from these various syllables; and now, one again unifies these sounds and syllables.
One should transform into the samaya-body of the deity and abide profoundly within the perfect luminosity; one should know that this deity possesses the three secrets:
because of the forms and colors of the various syllables, it is fully endowed with the secret body; because of the sounds of the various syllables, it is fully endowed with the secret speech;
and because of the meanings and intentions of the various syllables, it is fully endowed with the secret mind. Since these three matters are equal, [one should abide therein].
The practitioner who knows how to act, with a single-pointed mind undisturbed, dwells well within the contemplation of the three secrets;
next, they contemplate this Honored One’s body without forming notions of internal or external. At that time, seeing the body of the Honored One as being one's own body—this is the second turning.
Within the single-phase mind, one dwells well in the method of one *lakṣa*; among all gateways of mantra recitation, this is the most supreme.
Therefore, it is said above: "One should know that the second phrase is the supreme phrase of all Buddhas.
Because one enters this supreme phrase, within the universal mandala (*samantamukha-maṇḍala*), various bodies and lands transform according to one's wishes as they appear;
if one desires to hear the sound of those mantras, they emerge in accordance with one's thought; and if there is something in the mind not yet understood that one wishes to inquire about...
The questioner asks: Since the Principal Deity (iṣṭadevatā) explains matters according to whatever is asked, one can achieve all accomplishments (*siddhi*) as desired.
However, those in the world who cling to the *Susiddhi-tantra* and other such scriptures do not understand the secret instructions and remain bound by the literal text;
they expect that by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, the *Susiddhi* will manifest within them—when could this ever be attained? Furthermore, regarding the scripture...
Furthermore, because it explains the supreme and wondrous skillful means therein, it says: "The practitioner visualizes abiding within that most perfectly pure lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*);

therein, with sincere contemplation, one visualizes the various syllables, placing the words and phrases in their proper sequence, and visualizes the purification of the *jīvajīva*, which is to say, the wind (*vāyu*), following the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.
Once these have been purified, one performs the preliminary method of recitation (*pūrvasevā*)."
The practitioner, as before, contemplates the single object and single mark until, within the perfected clarity, the central deity transforms into his own self.
At that time, the practitioner perceives only himself within this pure lunar disc, identical to the central deity without distinction.

Furthermore, upon his heart, he possesses a perfect circle of clarity; within this clarity, he contemplates the various syllables with a mind of sincere truth, whether they be single syllables or otherwise.
Each character is linked to the next like beads strung together; if one places a phrase, it likewise proceeds in a clockwise sequence, radiant and perfectly clear.
Furthermore, each individual character is surrounded by a wreath of flames, pure and exquisite beyond compare.
Beyond this circular brilliance, there is also light, like the cool moon shining clearly through a cloudless autumn night. He employs this [in such a manner].
The mantra constitutes the inhalation and exhalation of the breath. When the breath goes out, this syllable follows it out; when the breath comes in, the syllable likewise follows it in.

As the breath is regulated and becomes tranquil, it pervades the entire body. At that time, one no longer perceives any distinct act of breathing, but takes the mantra itself as the inhalation and exhalation.
By means of this expedient, one is able to extinguish various discursive thoughts, conceptualizations, and mental distractions.
Regarding the gradual purification of the six sense faculties, when contemplating in this manner, one should also apply the distinctions according to their specific meanings:
if one desires to internally quiet the mind, one should use white; if one desires to increase merit, one should use yellow; if one desires to subdue internal obstacles, one should use red.
White signifies the meaning of original purity; yellow signifies the meaning of indestructible vajra, as well as the meaning of the radiance of wisdom.
Just as the physical body of worldly beings maintains its life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) without interruption because it is sustained by the winds of the breath,
and because of the movement of these breath-winds, one performs various activities of body and speech— the practitioner is likewise so.

By means of this secret empowerment (*guhyādhiṣṭhāna*), one purifies that life-force, causing all stains of karma and lifespan accumulated since beginningless time to be entirely eliminated, thereby accomplishing the fundamental state.
The life-force of the unborn mantra sustains this body of merit so that it does not perish;
only then can one engage the three secrets to accomplish all siddhis. To speak of the specific phenomenon: this "life-force" is the vital wind (*prāṇa*).
Just as a lamp in the wind cannot illuminate its function perfectly, so too does this vital wind cause the mind to scatter and waver. Now, perform this [practice] accordingly.
Through the skillful means of breath-control, one stills the winds of distraction until the inhalation and exhalation become so subtle as to gradually fade away and cease.

At that time, the wisdom-mind becomes perfectly luminous like a lamp in a sealed room; it ascends serenely and directly, such that demonic activities cannot enter and its illuminating function is impartial.
If one can achieve this, one may then seek *siddhi* in this very life, having first performed the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "abiding well in the mantra" according to the Dharma, this refers to the recitation performed for one month.

When a practitioner first begins to practice recitation, they may also externally visualize the words and phrases of the mantra appearing clearly and radiantly upon the heart of the Honored One (Bhagavat), as previously described.
Thereafter, they should follow the inhalation and exhalation of the breath; when the breath enters, these syllables enter the practitioner's own body from the heart of the Honored One.
When the breath goes out from within, follow it as it exits until it reaches the heart of the deity; thus, cycle through this sequence in succession without interruption from moment to moment.

Thereafter, one no longer perceives a separate inhalation or exhalation, but follows the syllable, which gradually becomes more profound and subtle—until there is neither sound nor syllable, and one simply breathes in and out spontaneously. At that time, the body of the deity is no different from one's own.

One's own body is not different from the deity. Furthermore, when a practitioner first practices visualization, although they may briefly attain correspondence—like a flash of lightning seen and then instantly extinguished—even if it becomes clear and bright, one should not become attached to it or give rise to arrogance.
Even if it should fade and vanish, one must not dwell on it with regret or self-reproach; rather, one should practice single-mindedly according to the instructions.
If one applies effort in this practice without ceasing, over a long period it will naturally become proficient. Eventually, the mantra, its syllables, and the deity will merge into a single entity.
After the vital winds have been purified and stilled, one contemplates this luminous orb (*maṇḍala*). When one wishes to defecate, it becomes large;

when one wishes to urinate, it becomes small. Whatever one desires to contemplate appears, and whatever one desires to perform is accomplished—just as a skilled artisan who has mastered a hundred refinements.
The transformation of the syllables (*bīja*) without obstruction and performing ritual acts according to one's will is called the "initial seed-syllable mind.
The practitioner first performs the visualization of the deity as the sound of the syllable; when these are combined, they form the seed-syllable.

This is like a person at the initial stage of *kalala*, where life-force, consciousness, and warmth must combine to form the seed. It is also like having obtained grain and planting it in a fertile field through skillful means.
Just as nurturing [a seed] must necessarily yield fruit, so too it is with the practitioner:
having first obtained the seed-mind, one next performs the preliminary service for one month; this is the skillful means of planting.
The Sūtra states: "The practitioner, through each and every phrase of the preliminary expedient means (*pūrvayoga*), thoroughly penetrates the great renown of all Buddhas.
This refers to the preliminary expedient means for first receiving and upholding [the mantra], which is precisely the method for initial recitation (*japa*).
One should practice it fully according to the sequence of offerings for Vairocana. As for what is meant by "thoroughly penetrating each and every phrase," it is as follows:
In that method of offering, each and every yoga path is made clearly manifest before one, just as when first adorning the maṇḍala;
from the limit of the wind-circle up to the vajra-ground, all various adornments are accomplished without exception, exactly as described in the text.
Next, when using the seed-syllable to manifest as the deity, one immediately beholds bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The assembly of bodhisattvas are all seated upon lotus pedestals, arrayed within the circular light.
Because the practitioner is practicing for the accomplishment of the maṇḍala, they should arrange them according to the layout of the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-vyūha* (Great Compassion Womb Matrix).

One by one, they should contemplate their physical forms and the seals (*mudrā*) they hold; they should see the mantra-syllables and also hear their sounds. Upon reaching the time of offering, immediately—

When one contemplates this single flower as various clouds of flowers pervading the worlds of the ten directions, performing the works of Buddhas and making offerings to all worthy sages, the practitioner sees them all within the perfect luminosity. One should know that it is the same for all other articles of offering.
Just as when contemplating clouds of emanated Buddhas, one immediately sees every single [deity] within the maṇḍala of one's own body.

The Honored Ones each emit immeasurable rays of light; within these lights are immeasurable Buddhas seated upon lotus pedestals, who travel to the ten directions and, assuming bodies that all sentient beings delight to behold, guide and benefit them according to their inclinations and desires.

Furthermore, within the perfect clarity [of the light], one clearly perceives everything in its entirety. Next, one should recite the mantra according to the Dharma. Having finished the recitation, one should act as follows:
In the fifth section on the sequence of Dharma-offerings, when emerging from the maṇḍala, the practitioner further disciplines the mind through various other virtuous practices;
in each instance, one must not fail in the prescribed rules, as fully described therein.
It should be understood that the Buddhas of the ten directions cause those who uphold the mantras to have already disciplined their "oxen" and brought their "fields" to full maturity.

In order to plow the fields of the present life, sow the seeds of *siddhi*, and be capable of bringing down the great rain of compassion to extensively plant the roots of merit through offerings, this one-month preliminary practice for upholding the Dharma is taught. Furthermore, the method for recitation with a profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*) is now explained:
the practitioner should, as before, visualize the syllables of the mantra, or visualize the mudrā, or visualize the life-force of the *iṣṭadevatā*.
When the winds have subsided and one dwells in tranquil composure, one should simply illuminate it with wisdom and contemplate its meaning.
When dwelling in the gate of the letter *A*, one should contemplate the meaning of original non-arising through such phrases as the "fourfold non-arising.

When dwelling in the Vajra Seal (*vajramudrā*), one should separately contemplate the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. When dwelling in the Lotus Seal (*padmamudrā*), one should separately contemplate the lotus.
The meaning of the Flower Samādhi is to be understood by analogy with all other cases; I shall now clarify it using the metaphor of the spring pond from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
For instance, those who study the Mahāyāna all know that within this mind-consciousness there is the treasure of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
However, because they lack skillful means, each, with a mind of grasping, competes to hold shards and pebbles, claiming them to be genuine lapis lazuli.

Just as one who joyfully takes a jewel home is ridiculed by the wise, so too, when one now dwells single-mindedly through the skillful means of mantra, the three obstructions are eliminated and the nature of the jewel manifests clearly due to the power of the pure bodhicitta.
However, this is merely the contemplation of the mind and not yet its realization. At that time, one must not disturb it so that it becomes turbulent, nor...

Fearing that it might cause agitation, one should not grasp it; rather, with a single mind and through skillful means, one should enter the water calmly, as taught by the Ācārya Nāgārjuna regarding the Middle Way and Right Contemplation, and according to the ten phrases on dependent origination in this "Chapter on Abiding Mind" mantra.
One should slowly move the wisdom-hand (*prajñā-hasta*) to peel and tear [the layers] one by one until reaching the treasure-limit (*ratna-paryanta*), ensuring that each is clearly revealed.
When the jewel is in the palm, one is a person who has seen the clarity of the mind and realized the Way.

At that time, if the practitioner enters the gateway of the letter A, they immediately obtain the treasure of primordial non-arising; when entering the gateway of the letter Ha, they immediately obtain the treasure of being free from causes and conditions;
when offering incense, they immediately obtain the treasure of unobstructed precepts; and when offering flowers, they immediately give birth to great compassion.
When offering precious incense, one immediately attains universal pervasion throughout the dharma-realm; when offering precious lamps, one immediately attains the transformation of ignorance.

Thus entering immeasurable gateways—all of which should be explained in detail—one is said to have "penetrated every single phrase" because one perceives the profound meaning within each and every component. If a practitioner cultivates these mundane accomplishments...

Although one cannot yet enter the Dharma-nature instantaneously during the stage of preliminary preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*), one should nevertheless take non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as the means and practice according to one's capacity.

If one lacks even a portion of the *prajñāpāramitā*, then being among those with the three obstacles, how could one—like a member of the retinue walking on the summit—attain the fruit of the first *siddhi*?
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If one wishes to offer a single meal..."
One who wishes to support the Buddhas and their Saṃghas in each of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, should study the Prajñāpāramitā;

one who wishes to offer a single robe, flower, incense, necklace, powdered incense, unguent, burning incense, lamp, candle, banner, pennant, or parasol to those Buddhas and their Saṃghas should study the Prajñāpāramitā—this is precisely that meaning. Furthermore, regarding practice:
When the first month is about to end, within this practice of mental offering, there shall be a sign of accomplishment:

even if the weather is severely drought-stricken or various calamities arise, if the practitioner uses a single flower or anointed incense to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions and dedicates this merit,
praying for rain to fall, then according to their wish, the sweet moisture will descend everywhere.
If one wishes for remaining calamities and afflictions to be eliminated, they shall likewise be extinguished immediately according to one's intent.
One should know that the power and function of the seeds of the pure mind gradually manifest, just as roots and sprouts grow incrementally;
therefore, one should employ skillful means to nurture them, and thus perform the ritual of making offerings for two months.
The Sūtra states: "Next, one should offer whatever incense, flowers, and so forth are available, dedicating them toward one's own enlightenment for the sake of attaining perfect awakening.

Regarding the instruction that 'one should be fearless during the two months of mantra practice,' this means that once one has mastered each and every component of the ritual of offering, one should prepare the incense at the appropriate time every day."
With a universal mind, one makes offerings of flowers, incense, lamps, food, drink, and so forth to the Triple Gem,
and gives rise to great compassionate vows that extend widely to all sentient beings. Through the convergence of the power of one's own merit,
the sustaining power of the Tathāgata, and the power of the *dharmadhātu*, this ocean-like cloud of merit becomes equal to space, inexhaustible, and follows the practitioner.
Whatever is undertaken through the power and momentum of the mind is accomplished;
one immediately dedicates these merits as they truly are toward the Great Bodhicitta, so that the siddhis may be fulfilled. Because merit is perfected, all obstacles are eliminated.

Therefore, when performing the rite of accomplishment, there is nothing capable of obscuring it, just as branches, flowers, and leaves flourish once they have fully developed; from this point on, there is no interval.
Because it will certainly bear fruit, it is said: "In this manner, during the two months, one should remain fearless regarding the mantra.

Next, as for performing the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*), this is precisely for the purpose of protecting and augmenting these flowers of merit so that they do not wither or perish, but reach full maturity.

Furthermore, according to the profound and esoteric interpretation, the moon serves as a metaphor for the bodhicitta. When the practitioner enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), this mind becomes perfectly complete and pure;

therefore, it is called the "first moon. From that point onward, by means of this moon-like mind, one gives rise to the myriad practices of great compassion, makes offerings to the Triple Gem, and extensively plants roots of goodness until entering the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). This entire process is designated as "one."

The monthly offerings from the stage of Immovable (Acalā) onwards involve further using the moon as a metaphor for the mind to give rise to immeasurable activities of skillful means and wisdom, correctly dedicating them toward the *siddhi* of the Tathāgata until reaching the stage of Vajra. This is called the "two-month offering.
Once these two months are complete, one performs the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*) within the Bodhi Maṇḍala; if explained in detail:
Regarding each individual stage (*bhūmi*), there are again three types of mind—cause, root, and fruit—as explained in the first chapter.
Although what is clarified in this chapter is mundane accomplishment, profound skillful means (*upāya*) is hidden within it.
When seeking supramundane accomplishment, one must still deliberate upon these methods to establish the secret portion; therefore, this is the *Vidyādharapiṭaka*.
The Dharma is like the lineage of Indra, capable of fulfilling all manner of mundane and supramundane aspirations.
Furthermore, as previously described, the sequential rules for recitation constitute a great mundane accomplishment;
if a practitioner fully relies upon this method and attains accomplishment, they will immediately achieve the purification of the six sense faculties or realize the *āvartana-dhāraṇī*.

Possessing the *dhāraṇīs* and total retention such that they never forget, they travel through various Buddha-fields in this very body, dwelling for immeasurable lifespans, making offerings to and attending upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and extensively benefiting sentient beings;
or, by waving their hands through space, they produce various kinds of precious jewels to give to those who are destitute.
Yet, because they still possess a birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and have not yet attained the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), they are called "worldly."
Regarding the accomplishment within this interval, the ritual for accomplishment shall be explained in detail in a subsequent chapter.
Nevertheless, this method is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*); it can also comply with the inferior aspirations of worldly beings.

If practitioners wish to perform rites of worldly accomplishment—whether superior, middling, or inferior—they should consult and apply various scriptures such as the *Susiddhi*, while still relying upon [the present method].
In this chapter on the practice of mental recitation (*japa*), one need only visualize the external form clearly;
then, according to the ritual manual, one may perform all the various accomplishments (*sādhana*) without necessarily transforming it into one's own body. Thus, the verse in the *Pūjāvidhi* says:
"The wise person, as previously instructed, visualizes the original deity before them, [appearing] entirely within the bright, full moon of their heart."
One should contemplate the mantra-syllables and accordingly receive and uphold them in their proper sequence, until the mind becomes pure and free from defilement;

when the number [of recitations] reaches the appropriate time and the signs appear, one follows the scriptural teachings to fulfill the aspiration for the meaningful benefits of signs, whereby the *siddhi* of mantras is accomplished at will.
This is called the world-transcending four-limbed dhyāna-gate of possessing signs, which is further distinguished [from the mundane].
This is a distinction. If one is a master of profound practice, they should naturally possess full knowledge of the accomplishments (*siddhi*) and signs of realization within *yoga*.

Now, for those of shallow practice, I shall briefly clarify the method of supplication. Once the practitioner has completed two months [of preliminary training], they should perform it on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of either the waxing or waning moon, or on the days of solar or lunar eclipses, or simply during the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*).
Within this [rite], one should bathe for purification, don fresh and clean garments, and recite the *śāntika* mantra while offering prayers until evening.

Then, having prepared extensive offerings and performed *homā*, take a thread spun by a young girl and tie seven knots upon it, reciting the mantra once for each knot. When this is complete, recite the mantra once more.
Recite [the mantra] seven times and tie it upon your left arm; while contemplating the deity, lie down on your right side.
In your dreams, you shall see the Lord of your own family, or the Lord of Mantras, or the Vidyārāja, or the assembly of the Three Jewels and Bodhisattvas;
or you shall see yourself reciting and upholding the mantra while performing various activities, or wearing white robes, or being honored by others.
Sometimes they see themselves ascending mountain peaks; sometimes they see themselves riding elephants; sometimes they cross great rivers; sometimes they climb fruit trees;
or they ride lions, oxen, deer, horses, and the like; or they ride flying geese, peacocks, and all manner of winged birds;
or they see beautiful women adorned with necklaces and holding flower vases; or in their dreams, they receive elephants, horses, chariots, and various precious objects.
If one dreams of obtaining flowers, fruits, ghee, milk, curd, rice, or blossoms; or obtains a rosary;
or sees oneself bathing, becoming pure, and adorned with fragrant incense—know that these are all signs of *siddhi*, as described in the *Susiddhi*.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Boy Subāhu* states: "If the practitioner’s accomplishment draws near, they should apply themselves most intensely to the practice of recitation."
A mind of love and joy arises, such that one does not cling to objects of defilement, nor does one suffer from hunger, thirst, heat, or affliction.

One’s mind remains unshaken by external appearances of things contrary to the Dharma; mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects dare not approach, and *piśāca* spirits and other ghosts dare not even tread upon one’s shadow.
All the teachings and instructions one utters are received with faith and put into practice.
Furthermore, he is intelligent and skilled at composing literary works; his mastery of various scriptures, mathematics, and arts is naturally subtle and wondrous.

His mind delights in the wholesome Dharma, and he practices with diligence and vigor. His body is free from illness and defilement. If people see him or hear his name, they conceive a heart of reverence.
They may perceive hidden treasures in the midst of empty space, hear the voices of devas, or behold their forms and the *kṣetra* (fields).
If the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and their like behold such superior signs, one may then perform the rites of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Furthermore, when the practitioner wishes to perform an accomplishment, they should, according to the methods of Susiddhi, perform rites for manifesting radiance and increasing majesty;
they should bathe the deity, prepare all necessary requisites and components, and personally perform the Great Empowerment that removes all obstacles.
Having made offerings to the maṇḍala according to the ritual, one should then commence the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

As prescribed in the first chapter regarding the skillful means for selecting and purifying the ground, one should construct a square maṇḍala with four gates measuring eight cubits, seven cubits, or five cubits.
One should open only the western gate; four cubits outside the western side, one should construct the initiation (*abhiṣeka*) maṇḍala.
In the central maṇḍala, open only the eastern gate; the attendant bodhisattvas and others are described in the same manner as previously stated.
Outside the four corners of the great maṇḍala, further place tridents (*triśūla*).

Upon the eight-petaled lotus of the central womb (*garbha*) and upon each of the other three tiers, place the secret mudrās of the various deities. Furthermore, at the position of the Buddha in the central womb...
First, place the seal of the principal deity (*mūlavidyā*) and set out one flask; the remaining four flasks for the consecrations are placed at the four corners.
Outside the gate, set out another flask to subjugate the three times. All other ritual procedures for the offerings are as explained in the second chapter.
Once the offerings have been made, one should perform the three types of *homa* in order to dispatch [the deities].
To expel *vināyakas*, one should employ the *sādhana-mantra* to perform *abhicāruka* rites for one's own benefit;
to accomplish *puṣṭika* rites, one should employ the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) of the respective family;
and to pacify all calamities, one should employ the mother-mantra (*mātṛkā*) of the respective family.
To perform the *śāntika* rite, one should employ the *Gaganacakṣus* mantra or the *Upaśama* mantra from the second chapter, according to the *homa* ritual.
One should offer substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and others, reciting each with the threefold mantra one hundred times, or increasing that number. Then, [proceed as follows].
One should perform seven offerings for each of the lords of mantras (*mantranātha*), and one should likewise add [offerings] for their principal deities.
Alternatively, using the *śāntika* mantra, one may offer a total of one hundred times; however, for those who cannot manage this, they should perform seven or three offerings.
After that, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) should be performed. Regarding the central *garbha* jewel-vase, as before, one should daily use [the appropriate substances].

Once the empowerment of the mobile deities is complete for those [deities] upon the flower pedestal, one should again perform the empowerment with the mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha-citta*) for those in the four corners, and empower the four Bodhisattvas.
For those in front of the Principal Deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should hold them with their respective mantras and cause the assistants to confer the empowerment upon them in succession.
Alternatively, one may request an Ācārya to perform the empowerment. If following the *Susiddhi[-tantra]*...
Regarding the ritual of the earth (*bhūmi-vidhi*): first, one employs the Krodhavajra flask; fourth, one employs the flask held with its respective mantra;

as for the remaining two flasks, they may be used as one pleases, as explained in detail therein. When it is time to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the practitioner stands upon the lotus pedestal and visualizes the syllable *RA*, which completely incinerates his own body until it becomes a heap of ashes. Once the sprinkling of water has been completed, he returns [to his original state].

Having generated [the maṇḍala] by means of the syllable *vaṃ* and having visualized oneself as the Maṇḍala of Great Compassion through secret yoga, one should adorn oneself with ox-gall, unguents, incense, mustard seeds, thread bracelets, garments, and so forth.
Furthermore, one should pay homage to the deities, circumambulate them, and make offerings; then, in order to pacify obstacles, one should perform homa once again.
Afterward, one dispatches [the deities] by means of these causes and conditions so that the honored ones may rejoice and cause the *siddhi* to be swiftly accomplished.

The Sūtra says: "On a mountain peak, or in a cow-pen, or on sandbars of various rivers, at a crossroads, in a single room, in a shrine, or in the chamber of Mahādeva"—this is a brief explanation of the locations for performing accomplishments (*sādhanā*). The Susiddhi-tantra says: "If it is a supreme accomplishment..."
One may perform the lower accomplishment (aparasādhana) by the side of a pond, or wherever one happens to be, or at a place corresponding to a mantra;
one should perform it there. Accomplishment will be somewhat slower if performed in a place other than these.

However, within a *caitya* containing relics (*śarīra*), all mantras of the internal rites (*adhyātmika*) will attain accomplishment; yet, among the eight great stūpas, such as the place of the Buddha’s birth, this is the most excellent.
If one performs the ritual at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) as described above, no demonic activities (mārakarma) will be able to obstruct or hinder them.

For fierce accomplishments, one should perform them in a cemetery, or in an empty house, or in a temple inhabited by a single deity, or beneath a solitary tree in a remote place, or by the side of a river.
If one wishes to accomplish the rites of yakṣas, it should be done in a forest.
If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the Nāga King, one should perform it by a spring.

If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the Messenger (Dūta), one should perform it at a place where people gather. If one wishes to accomplish the rite of entering a cave, one should perform it within a cavern.
Regarding the profound and secret explanation herein: when performing a supreme accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*), one must not merely select a name.
Just as a mountain that rises above the realm of clamor and baseness abounds in clear springs and flowering fruits, one should likewise abide upon such a mountain of bodhicitta.
Because it rises above the conceptual proliferations of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and gives rise to the merit of *dhāraṇī*,
and because its internal and external factors are in harmony, one is able, through the power of inconceivable *dharmas*, to transform them into the fruit of worldly *siddhi*.
If one cannot find such a high mountain, then next one should select a level plain; therein, a cow-pen is superior because it is free from the clamor of the village and is pure.

The cow represents the mind of the practitioner of meditation—pliant, penetrating, and capable of producing the root-body of the True Dharma that is able to continue yielding the five kinds of refined essences. The pen represents the life-sustenance of non-conceptual precepts.
The winds are stilled within the field of merit and nurtured; this "high mountain of the six sense organs being purified" is next in rank.

The term *hadata* (river sandbank) carries the meaning of being an island for oneself. In the Āgamas, the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) is taken as one's own island, where the island is not other than oneself, and the refuge is not other than oneself.
Now, in this school, one manifests as the Honored One (*bhaṭṭāraka*) at the fundamental site.
The body is also the cultivation of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*).

This means that although a practitioner has not yet attained complete pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), by being able to perform this contemplation, they can wash away the defilements of karma and sever the path through which *vināyakas* come and go;
therefore, it is placed next [to the previous stage]. "A crossroads" signifies that all desired destinations are fully accessible; this refers to speech.

Although such a person may not yet be able to manifest themselves as the form of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity), if they can integrate the voice and syllables of the deity into a single aspect and dwell correctly within the contemplation of the three secrets (*triguhyasamādhi*), remaining unobstructed by the disputes and attachments of the four extremes, then whatever they turn toward will naturally be effective;
thus, they can accomplish the function of being a messenger for the Tathāgata. Next, it says:

Regarding the "single chamber" (*ekāgāra*): although one may not yet be able to fully integrate the three secrets (*triguhyasamāja*), if one can firmly abide in a single view, well-guarding the mind so that it is not disturbed by the winds and rains of the eight worldly dharmas or the mosquitoes and gadflies of evil thoughts, one may also achieve minor accomplishments according to one's capacity.
Furthermore, regarding the "divine chamber" (*devāgāra*) or "Great God’s chamber": "divine" refers to the *iṣṭadevatā* (the chosen deity), and "Great God" (*mahādeva*) refers to... [text continues].

This chamber of all Buddhas is named Great Compassion. Although practitioners may not yet be able to remain unmoved or unswayed within a single vision, they can cultivate the visualization of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) until it appears clearly before them.

Whatever they do, they take great compassion as the foundation, relying on skillful means such as counting [mantras], timing, and signs of manifestation, while being protected by the spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
If one guards the body and ensures that the signs of conditioned activity do not fail the ritual rules, one may still achieve minor accomplishments such as subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
However, from this point onward, even if one exerts oneself with diligent hardship until the end, it is feared there will be no success.

The Sūtra states: "That maṇḍala site is entirely like a vajra palace; in this place, the practitioner who performs the rite of protection and seeks accomplishment should employ the auxiliary methods when performing the central ritual. This shall be explained further in the section on the lower grade.
It also says: "Whether it be at the middle watch of the night or at the time of sunrise, the wise one should know [the procedure] as follows..."

When these signs appear—such as the manifestation of the syllable *HŪṂ*, the sound of a drum, an earthquake, or hearing pleasing words in the void—one should know that such signs indicate that the object of *siddhi* will be attained according to one's wishes. Generally, when a *siddhi* is accomplished, there are three types of signs:
if it is accomplished during the first watch of the night, it is inferior; if at midnight, it is middling; and if it occurs when the dawn light begins to stir, it is superior.
Regarding that which is accomplished from the time the sun is about to rise, it is considered supreme and wondrous. The *Bāladāraka-sūtra* states: "In this context, there are three signs, namely:
the increase of breath (*vāyu*), smoke (*dhūma*), and light (*prabhā*). By appearing in succession, one attains the three types of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

If the breath emerges, one shall obtain benefits such as being loved and respected by the people of the world; if smoke emerges, one attains the *siddhi* of transforming one's form; and if light emerges, [the supreme accomplishment] is achieved."
If the vidyādhara’s pure and subtle body manifests as a mental accomplishment, or if a painted image moves, or if one sees the movement of ornaments,
necklaces, and flower garlands adorning the body, or if various celestial flowers descend from the sky,
or if there is a gentle breeze and fine rain, or if one perceives an earthquake, or hears an incorporeal voice in the air saying: "That which you..."
I shall now explain the prayers for fulfillment: one may see the lamp-flame increase in size, its color becoming glossy and radiant like golden light;
or the light may grow even more intense as the oil is exhausted; or the hairs on one’s body may stand on end and the heart feel great joy;
or one may hear the sound of celestial music and the tinkling of divine necklaces in the sky; or one may see the form of the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā) in the sky, surrounded by a retinue.
One should circumambulate and immediately offer arghya water containing the five precious gems, flowers, and incense;

one should praise, make offerings, and pay homage while kneeling, contemplating one's own spiritual power and seeking various aspirations. Once the aspirations have been attained, one should prostrate with joy and again present arghya.
One should face that honored deity and recite the received mantra, and then perform the ritual dismissal according to the dharma, as explained in detail therein.

Regarding the expedient means, if one explains them in depth: the "first watch of the night" refers to the period from the aforementioned *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) until the time they are fully accomplished;

because the mind still dwells upon signs (*nimitta*), it is termed the "first watch. The "middle watch" is the time when the six sense faculties gradually become purified and one no longer gives rise to craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*);
this is, for example, like having already transcended the "Summit Dharma" (*mūrdhāna*) in the Hīnayāna. At that time, demerit and merit are exactly equal. From this point onward...
Subsequently, as one turns toward the proximate true illumination, the meaning of this is called the "middle night.

When the portion of the night has passed and it is metaphorically like the rising of the sun, at that time when the mind perceives the path of illumination, the dharma accomplished therein is named "supreme accomplishment" (*uttamasiddhi*).

Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of "inferior accomplishment" (*adhamasiddhi*), as discussed in the usual course of exposition, if one explains them according to the purification of the six sense faculties, it is as follows:
In the state of yoga, one sees immeasurable Vajradharas of wisdom bestowing empowerment and proclaiming this sound "HŪṂ" with the Great Lion’s Roar;
or, through the sound of the Great Dharma Drum of the Tathāgatas, their aspirations are fulfilled;
or, within meditative concentration, one sees the adorned worlds of the ten directions all quaking in six ways, and this [sound] being proclaimed in the midst of space.
The sound of the Brahma-voice that comforts and consoles is, in reality, coming from nowhere and going nowhere;
as explained in the *Prajñā-sattva-pūlaṃ* chapter, one should know that these are the signs of great worldly accomplishment for all such practitioners.

Furthermore, when the practitioner personally perceives the luminous path of the mind and realizes the gateway of the syllable *HŪṂ*, they hear the secret voice of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana’s prophetic record.
This sound vibrates within their adamantine ground of mind, causing the sprouts of the ten thousand virtues to grow and giving rise to the myriad practices of great compassion.
When such incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) great vows are universally activated, all the Buddhas of the ten directions [respond].
It should be known that when they are present together and console one another with Brahma-sounds, this is the sign of the first supramundane accomplishment for these practitioners.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to summarize the meaning of the great accomplishment herein, spoke further in verse:
The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, have proclaimed that fruit: by abiding in this mantra practice, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
It accords with all types [of practitioners]; one should always mindfully uphold the mantras spoken by the ancient Buddhas and Great Sages; therefore, one should keep them in mind.

In this context, "all types" refers to opening the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) to reveal the true aspect (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*), because each and every mantra-gate fully possesses the threefold meaning of pure bodhi.

One should know that the various skillful means of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time ultimately converge and return to this very point; therefore, within all types, [this is the case].
One should fully illuminate and perceive the true meaning of the mantra. Next, one must firmly maintain faith so that it does not fall away from the mind.
Chapter Six: The Manifestation of Siddhi.
Regarding the "Manifestation of Siddhi," as clarified in the preceding chapter, although one may fulfill the minor aspirations of sentient beings...

I vow that by means of the practice of offering and the skillful methods for taming the mind—the very foundation of cultivation—one shall accomplish the great attainments (*mahāsiddhi*) of both the mundane and supramundane realms.

For one who seeks these great attainments, if they do not perceive the true meaning of the mantra within all its various forms, they will fail to reach the stage of *siddhi* and their cultivation will not be perfected.
Therefore, the following chapter on the Manifestation of *Siddhi* is explained to clarify this point exactly as it is.

All these siddhis flow forth from the spiritual power of the dharmadhātu. That is to say, when the practitioner contemplates this fruit of accomplishment, does it arise from the power of the roots of virtue produced by the offering of a disciplined mind? Does it arise from the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment?
Or does it arise from the power of the dharmadhātu? If it were due to the power of one's own roots of virtue, it would simply arise from one's own nature.
If it arises through the power of the Buddha’s empowerment, it is born from another nature; if it exists through the combination [of conditions], it is born from a common nature;

nor does it exist without causes and conditions. If one claims that *siddhi* arises through the power of the *dharmadhātu*, then since the *dharmadhātu* is equal, it would possess no characteristic of arising.
If *siddhi* were to arise by departing from the equal *dharmadhātu*, then one would fall into error.

If one observes that within conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) the arising of phenomena is unestablished, yet claims that there is no *siddhi* whatsoever, this constitutes a denial of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.
One should know that such *siddhi* is, at the very moment of its dependent origination, fundamentally unborn (*anutpanna*).
It is thus by the nature of things (*dharmatā*), neither produced by the practitioner nor created by the Buddha; for a creator cannot be apprehended.
Because it is free from all causes and conditions, it is the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the mind; it is the true mark of *siddhi*.
Since one crosses over all demonic obstacles by means of this true mark, when performing the rite of accomplishment (*sādhanā*), there is nothing able to obstruct it.
Because everything desired within this wish-fulfilling jewel manifests before one accordingly, it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of *Siddhi*."
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his eyes of universal empowerment, again surveyed the great assembly;

having known them to be firm, profound, pure, and capable of upholding the Great Dharma, and in order to fulfill all their aspirations, he further expounded the Dharma-verse of the Perfect Wisdom of the Innumerable Gateways of the Three Times.
This was because the World-Honored One had already extensively revealed the maṇḍala of the three mysteries.

Rāga further explains that after concluding the methods for entering the immeasurable gates and advancing toward the goal, in order to cause all within this [practice] to universally achieve the fruit of *siddhi*, he further expounds upon the "Gate of All Dharmadhātu and the Seal of Decisive Wisdom. This seal of decisiveness is the true reality (*tattva*) of mantras;
it means that by means of unimpeded, pure wisdom, one realizes the dharmas of the three periods of time in a single thought-moment.
All these arise from conditions and possess no intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they do not emerge apart from the pure bodhicitta.
Therefore, they are equal to space—profound, vast, and inexhaustible—and free from all conceptual discrimination.
This is true for every aspect of their accomplishment, from the gate of the Dharmadhātu of Vairocana down to the gate of the Dharmadhātu of the lowest worldly devas; in each case, it is exactly thus.
This is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the place where all phenomena converge; therefore, it is called the "Perfect Dharma-phrase.
The opening verse states that "space is stainless and lacks intrinsic nature," which precisely describes the true nature of the mind.
This true nature of the mind is the definitive seal of wisdom (*jñānamudrā*) among all phenomena, for it is boundless, stainless, and non-conceptual.

Therefore, although it is partially likened to space, in reality it is equal to the mind of space; because the mind likewise does not abide in its own nature, it cannot be fully illustrated by that analogy.

Thus, while it is equal to space in being signless (*animitta*), it nevertheless possesses various inconceivable skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to accord with the faculties and conditions of beings, thereby guiding and benefiting them. Yet these skillful means are merely...
Arising from the conditions of responsive capacity and causes, phenomena are thus by their very nature empty and quiescent, eternally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature, they are primordially unborn; being primordially unborn, they enter the gateway of the letter *A*.

Entering the gateway of the letter *A* is the original ground-body (*dharmakāya*) of Vairocana. This is like contemplating the true reality (*dharmatā*) of one’s own mind. All [phenomena] are likewise so.
The Dharma is likewise so; therefore, all phenomena are profoundly deep and difficult to perceive, such that only a Buddha and a Buddha can realize them.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, know that all dharmas are eternally without self-nature;

the lineage of the Buddhas arises from conditions; for this reason, they preach the One Vehicle. To discuss the profound intent of that sūtra in general, it lies precisely in this single verse. If a practitioner...
Seeing that all phenomena arising from conditions are none other than the Dharmadhātu-body of Vairocana, at that moment the ten directions merge into a single Buddha-land;

this is called the ultimately pure bodhicitta. By means of this ultimately pure bodhicitta, one universally manifests simultaneously in accordance with the inexhaustible Dharmadhātu and the capacities of the realms of sentient beings, through the causes and conditions of skillful response.

Practicing the bodhisattva path with a physical body, they make offerings to immeasurable spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in every thought-moment and enter into immeasurable gates of the perfections (pāramitā).

Thus, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they constantly advance with excellence to adorn and purify all buddha-fields and accomplish all the deeds of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings without ever resting; this is called...

When one is endowed with these Samantabhadra practices and paths, one can fulfill the various aspirations and wishes according to whatever sentient beings think of in their minds, even bestowing the vow for unsurpassed bodhi; this is called the "Sphatika-maṇi" (True Crystal Jewel) of all Bodhisattvas.
One should know that although the gateways of progress are immeasurable, when discussing their ultimate principle, they all converge here.
Because all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have no other method than this single causal condition,
this gāthā is called the "Dharma-Verse for Fulfilling the Immeasurable Gates of the Three Periods of Time."
Furthermore, there may be those who give rise to doubt, wondering how the mind of the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) can perform such various conditioned activities.

To address this, the verse further provides an analogy: "Just as all the realms of existence (*gati*) in the world, along with their environments and dwellings, all abide in dependence upon space and are established by means of space, yet space itself has no basis upon which it depends."
The practice of non-attachment and non-arising is likewise so for this pure Dharma-body.
Although it is eternally quiescent and does not manifest the characteristics of dharmas, it pervades all worlds without exception and performs all deeds;
because it arises through the causal conditions of the power of roots of goodness born of compassion, rather than from delusion or karma, it is called "pure birth. It is like the Tathāgata who—
The *Sicijingjie jing* (Sūtra on the Sphere of Contemplation) states that the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra addressed the Bodhisattva Guṇagañja, saying:

"World-Honored One, from the moment he first received the prediction of enlightenment from Dīpaṃkara Buddha, [the Tathāgata] immediately entered the Tathāgata’s inconceivable sphere samādhi (*tathāgatācintyaviṣaya-samādhi*).
Constantly and effortlessly, he spontaneously manifests immeasurable buddha-activities—namely, within a single hair-tip of empty space."
Within this place, there are Buddha-worlds as numerous as the atoms of all Buddha-fields; therein, he may manifest birth in the Tuṣita heaven,
or pass away from there to descend and enter a womb, or manifest being born and taking seven steps, declaring,
"I am now the limit of birth and death," or manifest leaving the royal palace, practicing austerities, or descending [from Tuṣita].
The Māra attains perfect enlightenment and turns the sublime wheel of Dharma; he may manifest remaining in the world for immeasurable eons, or again demonstrate entry into nirvāṇa;

he may make all eons a single kṣaṇa, or a single kṣaṇa all eons, such that eons and kṣaṇas neither increase nor decrease, until all sentient beings have attained liberation, not even for a single kṣaṇa.
At that time, throughout all these worlds, he constantly performs such various Buddha-activities without ever resting; yet it is effortless, like space,
wherein within immeasurable lands at the tip of a single hair-pore, he manifests in every thought-moment the various majestic demeanors and dharmic rules of all Buddhas,
even extending throughout the entire void at the measure of a hair-tip, remaining thus eternally.

Performing the work of a Buddha to benefit sentient beings until the end of the future, never resting for even a moment, yet the Buddha-fields neither decrease by so much as a speck of dust nor increase;
why is this? Because all phenomena are like illusions and mirages, as extensively explained therein;
thus it is said that they arise in a state of complete, untainted purity.
Next, it says: "Because one cultivates the 'Universal Victorious Birth-Adornment' (*Samantavijaya-janma-vyūha*). Here, "victorious" (*vijaya*) has the meaning of being honored or preeminent;
as worldly people refer to those of long-standing virtue who serve as models for teachers as "senior masters" (*pūrva-janman*), this refers to the "previously awakened" (*pūrva-buddha*).

That which arises from the *garbhadhātu* (Womb Treasury) is called *bhoga* in Sanskrit, meaning that which is fully adorned with various kinds of wealth and treasures; this is the ancient "universal" (*samanta*).
All victors have caused the lineage of the Buddha-seeds in the world to be transmitted without interruption down to the present day precisely because they practiced these mantra-words (vidyā-mantra).
It is impossible for there to be any practitioner of the Tathāgata’s path apart from such dharma-words;
therefore, it is said that there are no other words [capable of this]. Because these are able to give birth to the practices of all Tathāgatas, they follow accordingly.
The place where the *Dharmapada* appears is precisely where a Buddha appears in the world to universally provide illumination, just like the Great Sun;

therefore, it is said that he "acts as the illuminator of the world. Because those who enter this Dharma-gate of Radiance, such as the World-Honored One, constantly and pervasively traverse the Dharmadhātu and practice the path of Samantabhadra without end, it is said that he "proclaims the method of extremely pure cultivation."
It is profound, vast, inexhaustible, and free from conceptual discrimination. Furthermore, these *ariṣa-gāthās* are phrases empowered by the Tathāgata’s spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*);
it is most excellent to praise with the Brahma-voice when performing various offerings. They are now preserved in their entirety.

Tathā-satataṃ pratyayena janmani gambhīra-dur-darśana (three phrases). (First recitation. Sadā tu viśeṣa-gamini na (one phrase). Phala.
Mokṣaṇa (supreme), nandati (bestows), vicitrān (whatever is thought of)—these two lines; yathā (as), sarvagatim (all states of existence), ālayam (the abode)—this third line;
gaganopamām (like space), apratiṣṭhitām (without fixed support), anāśrayām (without dependence), carati (he moves)—this concludes the fourth line. (Recite twice.)

*Tathāgata-viśuddha-dharma-tathatā-triloka-śeṣa-viśuddha-sambhava-caryā-tattvārtha-kṣara.* (The Tathāgata, the purity of the Dharma, suchness, the three realms, without remainder, pure in its arising, the practice, the reality, the syllable.)
The Tail (the Ornament of Supreme Birth) (three phrases): *bāvadati* (existence), *sarva-arnaka* (all the Buddhas), *gocara* (range/activity). (End of four phrases) (Recite three times).
*nānyathā-bhāvamasti durlabham* (it is not otherwise; it exists and is difficult to obtain). (One phrase) *sogha*.
Lokākaraṇatathatā (two lines) Kathyate suviśuddhadharmatācaraṇam (three lines) Tarakalpadvārttam (four lines) (Loka = world; ākara = source; tathatā = suchness. These two lines mean:
"The source of the world is suchness. (Kathyate = is taught; suviśuddha = utterly pure; dharmatā = the nature of phenomena; caraṇam = practice. These three lines mean:

"It is taught that the practice of the utterly pure nature of phenomena. (Tara = without; kalpa = conceptual construction; dvārttam = free from. These four lines conclude the verse. (Recite four times.)
Vipuladharma-gambhīra-māveya (the Sanskrit manuscript has this one line as an auxiliary sound outside the four verses;
it is now incorporated into the four verses for the sake of literary convenience).
At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana spoke this Seal of the Universal Gate of Decisive Wisdom.
The various seeds also seal the roots and sprouts of the myriad practices as well as the fruit of *siddhi*. Having finished [this], he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Each of you, from whichever gate, should manifest the spiritual power of the *dharmadhātu* according to what you yourselves have mastered;
let the phrases of the outflow of *siddhi* emerge. If sentient beings, through whichever *dharmaparyāya*, behold this Dharma, they shall rejoice."

Because one leaps up and attains abiding in peace and bliss, the "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi*) herein also carries the meaning of "dynamic manifestation" (*vikurvita*) and the meaning of "expansion," that is, from one obtaining many, even unto the immeasurable. "Flowing forth" (*niḥsaraṇa*) also contains multiple meanings;
it may be termed "attainment" or "gate," yet "flowing forth" is the primary sense. At that time, Vajradhara and the others...

They all prostrated themselves before the World-Honored One and spoke these words: "O Lord of Dharma, in accordance with Your instructions and having received the command of the Great Master, we shall with single-minded reverence and obedience dare not transgress them. Thereafter, following their inquiry, they again requested of the Buddha, saying:

"We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, will reveal the *siddhi-niṣyanda-pada* (the verses on the flow-out of accomplishment). Why is this? Because of [the power] of the Venerable One..."
It is not appropriate for the Bhagavān to personally proclaim before others the Dharma he has realized. Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray only that you may bring benefit, peace, and happiness to future sentient beings. Within this, there are generally three intentions:

first, to cultivate for oneself the conduct of shame, remorse, humility, and withdrawal, thereby demonstrating to all practitioners the ritual methods for honoring teachers and revering the Way; second...
Each of the noble ones has thoroughly investigated and attained mastery through their respective gateways into the single dharma-realm, thereby perfecting the dharma-words.

Within a single gateway, each possesses all gateways; yet, reflecting that their own mental capacity cannot reach it, they did not dare to speak of the dharmas they had realized before the World-Honored One.
First, they requested the World-Honored One to expound upon the accomplishment of the universal gateway.
Once the Dharma has been established, each of the bodhisattvas shall expound it from their own respective gateways; thus the lineages will be visible and the dharma-gates will be orderly.
These three thousand verses serve as the root, preserved in an abbreviated form; therefore, the written text does not exhaust all that is said.
When a practitioner achieves accomplishment through yoga, they shall naturally hear and see it in its full detail. The Buddha praised Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! Regarding the Dharma-Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, he praises a single quality, namely, having a sense of shame (*hrī*).

The Buddha observes that although these great beings possess immeasurable and boundless wisdom and skillful means, they know for themselves that they are like the moon on the fourteenth day—small and not yet full—and therefore do not dare to stand before the Tathāgata."

Because that which has been stated is precisely the characteristic of a virtuous person, he exclaims, "Excellent! In the Sanskrit original, the term for *hrī* (shame) is distinct from *apatrāpya* (moral dread);
however, when it is said here that one possesses *hrī*, it implies that both *hrī* and *apatrāpya* are fully present.
One should know that these two pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) are the cause of all virtues; therefore, the World-Honored One expands upon this meaning by stating, "Because of having shame..."
Two matters arise swiftly: first, one does not perform what should not be done; second, one is praised by the people of the world as a person possessed of a sense of shame.
Now, O sons of the Buddha, because you possess a mind of modesty and shame, you observe for yourselves the lineage of the Tathāgatas and do not transgress the samaya;
therefore, you are constantly praised by the holy assemblies of the ten directions.
This is a praise. Furthermore, because of the presence of shame (*hrī*), two things are swiftly produced: one attains dwelling together with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
