in short, all unfulfilled merits are brought to fulfillment, and one constantly assembles in one place with the great assembly of the Great Compassion Maṇḍala. Furthermore, because of the presence of shame, two further qualities arise.
This means that by abiding in *śīla*, one is born among humans or devas; *śīla* has the meaning of "coolness.

It is like one oppressed by the stifling heat of suffering who enters a pool of eight qualities, or like one afflicted by a toxic disease who is anointed with sandalwood from the seashore and sprinkled with nectar (*amṛta*).
At that time, both internally and externally one becomes cool, and body and mind are at peace; therefore it is called *śīla*. The practitioner is likewise so.
Because of the presence of shame, one attains entry into the foremost pure state of Great Parinirvāṇa;
yet, through skillful means, one is further reborn among humans and devas, let alone in the auspicious realms of the world.

Herein, the meaning of shame should be extensively praised by means of three, four, five, six, and so forth, up to immeasurable dharma-gates. One may grasp the general principle from this; it need not be cited in full detail. 3.
After the World-Honored One of the Corner had thus offered praise, he further exhorted them to listen attentively and then expounded the verses on the manifestation of *siddhi*.
Just as when a Buddha in his physical body emits light, there is a source from which it issues— namely, from the *ūrṇā-kośa* between the brows, up to the crown of the head,
and down to the soles of the feet and the region of the waist— from each and every one of these marks, Vairocana universally flows forth.
Vairocana is likewise; from each and every body of the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala, the signs of the dharmas of the mantra naturally cause the merits of *siddhi* to flow forth universally.
Because the practitioner of yoga attains correspondence when fully endowed with skillful means, it is called the "phrase of correspondence."

From this point forward, the section on the branches of *siddhi* is explained in detail. First, it clarifies the person who performs the accomplishment (*sādhana*), for such a person is the primary cause of *siddhi*.
If a practitioner has not yet perfected the seeds of the path and their vessel as a recipient of the Dharma is incomplete, then the fruit of the Three Mysteries cannot possibly manifest.
Within this branch, there are further many sections; the first is the vision of the maṇḍala.

Regarding "Ra," as previously stated, once the ritual for fulfilling the requirements has been completed—identical to that for one receiving the full ordination (upasampadā)—one is thereafter permitted to practice and study the various mantra rites (*mantracaryā*).

As for "being authorized by the second honored one," this means that after the practitioner has received the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), on another day they should perform extensive offerings to the *ācārya* and inquire about and receive the essential points of the mantra methods; this should be done with...
The sequential transmission of the auspicious precious vase is explained in detail within the chapter on "Receiving the Mantra Method" in the Susiddhikara Sūtra;

however, the primary intent of this sūtra further emphasizes the meaning of profound and secret yoga. If one does not receive it through the successive lineage of masters but instead practices it impulsively based merely on a literal interpretation or conjecture—just as, for example, in the Vinaya, one who leaves the household life as a renunciant without a teacher is not [a true monk]—[then such practice is invalid].
However, if one lacks merit, it conversely becomes an obstacle to the Path; even if one practices with diligence and reaches the limit of hardship, *siddhi* will not be attained.

Third, regarding the accomplishment of true speech (*satyavāda*): this means that the *mantra* one upholds is not merely [correct], but one has personally received the seal of authentication (*mudrā-pratyaya*) from the *iṣṭadevatā*.

Furthermore, when the syllables and phrases are complete and one performs methods such as increasing majesty (*vīrya-vardhana*), accomplishment through power is easily obtained, and blessings (*adhiṣṭhāna*) are bestowed.
There is a state of doubt as explained in the *Susiddhikara-sūtra*, the *Mantra-vidhi-paripūrṇa*, and the *Vīryavardhana-paṭala*.
Fourth is the generation of the bodhicitta; fifth is profound faith; sixth is compassion; seventh is the absence of stinginess—all of which are explained as in the second chapter.
This corresponds to the fourth line of the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) within the Secret Vehicle (*Guhyayāna*), which corresponds to not being separated from the bodhicitta.
The fifth phrase corresponds to the precept of upholding the mind; the sixth phrase corresponds to the precept of not abandoning the true Dharma;

the seventh phrase corresponds to the precept of not performing acts that are unbeneficial toward sentient beings; and [the eighth] corresponds to the precept of not being stingy or miserly regarding the true Dharma.
If one violates any of these individual prohibitions, no virtuous merits will ever arise; thus, these four mental states must be made to be in complete accord with those [precepts].
Because one does not transgress [the precepts], one will certainly be able to accomplish the fruit of *siddhi*. Eighth, abiding in subduing (*dānta*;

in Sanskrit, *nanda*, meaning "already tamed and softened"): this means that by means of the ten kinds of skillful methods and the points of training (*śikṣāpada*), one disciplines and controls the six sense faculties.
Consequently, all three types of action (*trikarma*) become spontaneously tamed and softened; like a trained ox or a fine horse, they are fit to be employed according to one's will.

"Riding" means reaching a destination. Ninth, "being able to skillfully distinguish phenomena arising from conditions" means being able to deeply cultivate the observation of the ten phrases of dependent origination, thereby understanding that all activities within the gateway of mantra practice are like illusions and transformations, even unto a *gandharva* city, because they are ultimately unobtainable due to their non-arising and lack of intrinsic nature. This is [the meaning].

The meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) does not obstruct the fact that such-and-such illusory appearances arise when various causes and conditions converge; thus, it is the meaning of the provisional (*prajñapti*).
Because thorough illumination of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) does not transcend the mind, it is the meaning of the middle (*madhyama*).

When a practitioner perceives in this way, various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are extinguished, and internal and external demonic activities can do nothing; only then can one accomplish the Great Achievement (*mahāsiddhi*).

Furthermore, tenth is the upholding of the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*). This is the specific code of discipline (*vinaya*) for the gateway of mantra practice (*mantranaya*), as extensively explained in the *Susiddhi-sādhana*, in the chapter on the Vidyādhara Precepts, and in the *Vairocana-pūjā-vidhi*.
If one can respectfully and obediently uphold these without doubt or hesitation, never transgressing the *samaya* teachings, then no obstacles whatsoever shall arise.
Chapter Eleven: Rapid Attainment on the Grounds. Those who dwell well in the training of the multitudes are the matters to be studied in the gateway of mantras.

Just as there were numerous branches of ritual service (*pūjā*) within the "Chapter on Entering the Maṇḍala" and numerous branches within the methods of offering, so too here, at the time of performing the *sādhana*, there are numerous branches, extending even to the skillful arts required for the maṇḍala.
In all fields of arts and sciences, one should diligently inquire and receive instruction, practicing exactly as taught;

when facing tasks, one should be free from doubt and not look to the faces of others for guidance, just as a bhikṣu who has already relinquished formal dependence (*niśraya*) within the Dharma is called a person established in the stage of abiding.
Twelfth, "possessing skillful means" means being fully capable in the performance of mantra activities and excelling in adaptive flexibility (*vaipulya*). Like a parable...
Just as the compass, square, and plumb line are common tools for all craftsmen, yet only those whose mental application is subtle and refined attain their true mastery;
so too, although one may have committed grave offenses, they are easily eliminated if one possesses skillful means (*upāya*).
Likewise, even if one has planted only slight roots of merit, they are rendered inexhaustible if one possesses skillful means—just as an echo enters a horn, or as a whirling fire consumes its fuel.
If one does not comprehend such provisional application (*upāya*), then one's efforts will be in vain and many obstacles will persist.

Thirteenth, the meaning of "valiant" (*vīra*) is as explained in the second chapter on the qualities of the *ācārya*: when performing a great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*), various difficulties will arise;
it is only after ensuring that the mind does not retreat or sink, and that one is free from fear, that success may be achieved.
Fourteenth, knowing the timely and the untimely means being able to employ *siddhānta* (established methods) and skillful means (*upāya*) regarding various undertakings;
neither acting too early nor too late, one successfully seizes opportunities so that movement yields results.

Whether it be sitting in meditation, reciting scriptures, managing affairs, transforming others, or even practicing the four dignified postures (*īryāpatha*), eating, drinking, or sleeping—each has its proper time.

Regarding the characteristic of being untimely: for a practitioner of mantra, such acts as lying down like a corpse during the day or remaining awake throughout the entire night do not accord with the meaning of "time.

Fifteenth, one who delights in practicing generosity: because they take pleasure in cultivating meritorious deeds and constantly keep the benefit of others in mind, they are able to extensively plant roots of goodness within the two fields of gratitude/virtue and compassion. Thus.
If one dedicates [merit] toward *siddhi*, the fruits of one's prayers will be easily realized;

however, if one lacks the meaning of universal salvation (*parārtha*) and is merely entangled by latent obstacles (*vāsanā*), the Jewel that fulfills all wishes will remain ever more distant. Regarding the sixteenth mind, "Fearlessness":

this meaning differs slightly from the previous "Courageous Strength" (*śūra*). It refers to being able to sustain oneself through the Dharma even when amidst a multitude of those who possess majesty and awe-inspiring power.
He maintains his dignified deportment without deviation; he possesses no heart of timidity or cowardice when faced with various difficult questions.

Even if there is something he has not yet fully realized, he skillfully consults and resolves his doubts, never causing disturbance or confusion. For this reason, the non-Buddhist scriptures call him "a person of steadfast integrity.
Because he is endowed with these virtues, even when the assembly of noble ones is present before him, he upholds the affairs of the Dharma with a mind free from delusion or error. Chapter [Number].

Seventeenth, the diligent cultivation of the methods of mantra practice means that regarding the activities undertaken within the Secret Vehicle, one never abandons them midway out of laziness or negligence, nor does one wait for future conditions;

for this would cause those who are about to attain [realization] to fail to do so, and those who have already attained it to lose it, giving rise to many obstacles to the path such that they become habitual and ingrained in one's nature.
Therefore, this single condition is, for example, like the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Honey can perfect the five perfections; therefore, it is said in the Vinaya that by means of single-minded diligence, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
How much more so for other wholesome dharmas, which should lead to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—this shall be explained in detail.
(18) One who penetrates the true meaning of mantras refers to the fact that each individual name-phrase, as previously described, is established.

Establishing the middle way, one clarifies the characteristics of the wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*), penetrates their profound meaning, and is able to freely rotate between the two interpretations—the superficial and the secret—of the various causal factors and constituent parts to skillfully respond to the diverse capacities of sentient beings.
This is like a wise minister who, from the single term *sindhu-pāla*, derives four distinct uses that delight the king’s mind; as a reward, his stipend is doubled. Thus, by means of the Dharma...
The nineteenth [chapter] concerns the womb of the realms (*dhātu-garbha*) which brings about all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

Those who constantly delight in sitting in meditation should practice the various skillful means for training the mind through yoga, as described in the preceding chapter; this is called the primary cause for the wondrous fruit of the seeds of *siddhi*.

One must ensure that the profound mind is focused on a single object, with every thought-moment uninterrupted, only then being able to realize contact with the truth and personally witness success. If...

If one cannot do so, yet merely wishes to follow the pursuit of the "single eye" by planting trees in empty space, even after a thousand million billion kalpas, there would still be no possibility of attainment;
how much less could this body achieve great accomplishment? Twentieth, regarding those who delight in performing accomplishments:
this is the great craving of a bodhisattva, for by the conditions of this craving, they become stained and attached to various realms of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Inconceivable form is like that of worldly people who, because they cannot abandon their attachment to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), perform various karmas and thereby receive a physical body;
thus, when receiving empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) in the Yoga school, the Ācārya establishes a solemn vow, saying:
"From this day forward, you must carefully refrain from severing desire; for by not severing desire, one does not sever the world."
This is the lineage of the Buddhas. It is like a skilled person who explains the king’s cuisine and delights in studying the methods of the immortals;

one who fully understands the proper application of cooking and roasting while also transmitting the secrets of flight and refinement—if such a person does not employ skillful means and has no intention to ingest [the elixir], who could force them to do so?
If one possesses these twenty virtues, they are called a person who possesses the constituent parts for accomplishment.
The Blessed One, wishing to console those who have achieved accomplishment and to cause them to have deep faith and delight in the inconceivable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
again addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying: "Lord of Secrets, it is as if, for example, among those in the desire realm who are intoxicated by the sovereign,
satisfying, and fulfilling vidyā-mantras— even up to the sons of the gods in all the abodes of desire— there is one known as the Heavenly King Vaśavartin."

By the power of one's own supernatural penetrations, merit, and wisdom, this vidyā-mantra is accomplished, enabling it to respond simultaneously and universally to sentient beings of the six heavens and four realms,
each according to their respective kind, causing all their heart’s wishes to be fulfilled and satisfied; furthermore, for all the daughters of the gods in the desire realm,
it manifests various objects of the five sensory dusts— both animate and inanimate— all of which are exquisitely beautiful.
Subtle and wondrous, it captivates the human mind, causing others to develop deep attachment and become intoxicated by it.
It can manifest before them fragrances, flowers, music, dance, food, drink, clothing, and so forth, all of which may be enjoyed;

it can even manifest transformed female forms with whom they may further enjoy themselves, as these beings are of a similar nature to living creatures. Therefore, it is called "enjoyment" and "universal enjoyment," for it is not merely something for others.
If even he— who possesses the supernatural transformations of greed and delusion— can likewise enjoy this for himself,
how much more so could the Great Sage’s mantras not universally manifest form-bodies and perform the deeds of a Tathāgata? Furthermore,
just as the Heavenly King Maheśvara possesses another vidyā-mantra called "Superior Mind-Born" (Śreyo-manojā), which can simultaneously and universally manifest the three [realms].
He brings about the benefit of all sentient beings throughout a great trichiliocosm,

even manifesting various kinds of pure and wondrous requisites to please the noble ones of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, so that they may enjoy them, experience them universally, and he himself also partakes of them.
Since his supernatural power remains so steadfast as the sovereign of a great trichiliocosm, how much more so when it pervades a single [world-system]?
Although they are masters of the Dharma-realm in every respect, they are unable to universally manifest form-bodies and perform the deeds of a Tathāgata. Setting this matter aside for a moment:
even those in the world who practice illusionary arts can, through the power of their mantras, empower medicinal herbs to manifest various groves, people, and things;
likewise, even the Asura kings, though included within the four evil destinies, possess such powers.

By the power of his own mantra, he transforms himself into the body of Śakra, Lord of Devas, and sits upon the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā), causing the assembly of the thirty-three gods to give rise to doubt;
how much more so could the Tathāgata, who has exhausted the limit of all phenomena as illusion, not exercise sovereign spiritual transformations through his Dharmatā-body?
Furthermore, setting aside this matter, consider such beings as the seven mother-demons (mātṛkā).
Furthermore, by the power of even a small degree of mastery, one can compose vidyā-mantras capable of causing epidemics and calamities among sentient beings, as well as pacifying them;

and it is seen in the world that those who hold the vidyā-mantras of the garuḍa-birds and so forth can collect and eliminate various poisons, transform cold and heat, and subdue blazing fires to make them cool. How much more so for the Tathāgata regarding all minds!
Since you are the foremost among those who possess sovereign mastery, why do you not utter words of truth to extinguish these various calamities?
The reason the World-Honored One has extensively expounded various parables is that for those whom he seeks to bring to accomplishment, until they have attained *siddhi*,
they may give rise to various webs of doubt, or they may themselves use the power of their own minds to speculate upon such matters.

Is it definitively existent, or is it definitively non-existent? Or perhaps, because they have not yet realized the inconceivable dependent origination, they grasp at the *tathatā* (suchness) and the *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality), giving rise to such views.
Now, the pure *dharmakāya* is unconditioned and signless; yet here it manifests in various forms—is this not, then, illusory?
Therefore, in order to cause [beings] to universally sever the net of doubt, the World-Honored One further...
Furthermore, he again synthesizes the various phrases to clarify the Middle Way, saying: "Good son, you should have faith in such 'flowing-out' phrases.
The majestic power (*prabhāva*) of this mantra does not emerge from within the mantra, nor does it enter into sentient beings;
it cannot be found in the place where the practitioner recites it. If the practitioner contemplates these four 'non-arising' phrases with truth..."

When one observes that various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*)—such as existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence—are extinguished, one then perceives the phrase of primordial non-arising (*mūlānutpāda*).
When perceiving the phrase of primordial non-arising, one knows that the *dharmatā* of all phenomena remains thus, whether a Buddha appears or not.
Therefore, it is said: "O son of good family, by the power of the empowerment of the mantra..."
Therefore, it is by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that this arises, without ever being transgressed;

the Buddha further explains the causal conditions himself, stating that because it does not transcend three periods of time—namely, in all worlds of the past, future, and present—it is by the nature of things that when sentient beings possess the capacity (*indriya*), the Dharma-body possesses the capacity to respond;
and when the response and the capacity are in accord, various activities of the Tathāgata arise, like a great ocean.
The tide has always been thus for a long time and never exceeds its limit. Furthermore, they explain it to one another: "For what reason is it so?

It is because phenomena arise through the principle of inconceivable conditions (*acintya-pratyaya*). For example, when the bright moon is in the sky and the water in a vessel is clear and pure, and there are no obstructions such as smoke or clouds to block it, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that its reflection arises; it cannot be resisted when the conditions come together. And so it is with every single condition.
If there is mutual deficiency, one cannot pursue or attain [the goal]; to further engage in conceptualization and discrimination is merely idle proliferation.
Therefore, when a practitioner performs an accomplishment (*sādhana*), they should simply examine their own body and mind, striving to ensure that all causal conditions are complete.

As for whether these conditions exist or not, or whether success or failure occurs—why should such matters be a cause for doubt? Furthermore, to earnestly exhort him: "Therefore, O son of good family, you should master..."
The Mantra Way is the path of constant, uninterrupted realization of the inconceivable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

When a practitioner accords with and penetrates this inconceivable nature of phenomena, they come to know that the limit of all phenomena as being like an illusion is no different from the limit of cessation (*śānti*), and that the limit of cessation of all phenomena is no different from the limit of being like an illusion.
Having thus perceived these two limits as non-dual, one realizes the boundlessness of the Tathāgata.

Regarding "response and resonance" (*ganying*): if one understands the Tathāgata’s response and resonance, one can manifest the universal form-body (*sarvarūpakāya*) through the dance of the vajra, ensuring that the seed of the Buddha in the world is never severed;
therefore, it is called the "uninterrupted path of true words" (*anupacchinna-mantra-mārga*).

The Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One again dwelt in the unimpeded power of the three times, relying on the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, and relying on the Samādhi of the Adorned Pure Treasury. From this point onward, it clarifies the constituent parts of the mantras held [by the Buddhas].
As mentioned above, each of these Bodhisattvas dwells in samādhi and speaks their own heart-mantra; now, Vairocana...
Vairocana likewise entered samādhi because he wished to proclaim the mantra of his own mind.
Just as the various physical, verbal, and mental karmas of worldly sentient beings all depend upon the mind, so it is with Vairocana;
all his unimpeded power of wisdom throughout the three periods of time, all his miraculous transformations, and his inconceivable power of empowerment depend upon the Adornment of Purity.

O Pure Treasury, although all sentient beings inherently possess the lotus-womb matrix (*padmagarbha*), because their power of unimpeded wisdom is not yet perfected, they have not attained ultimate purity;
and because their power of sustaining grace is not yet perfected, they have not attained ultimate adornment.
Furthermore, although all sentient beings inherently possess the power of unimpeded wisdom regarding the three periods of time, spiritual transformations, and sustaining grace...
Although he possesses inconceivable power, because his lotus-womb treasury has not yet attained adornment and purity, neither his illumination nor his function manifest before him;
only the Tathāgata, having fully accomplished these, is able to abide in this samādhi.
Furthermore, it shall now be explained that samādhi should be understood as being conjoined with wisdom.

Because it is adorned by the purity of the lotus-womb treasury (*padmagarbha*), wisdom is itself the Tathāgata’s eternal wisdom; it possesses no characteristics of entering, abiding, or emerging, nor is there anything to be manifested.
Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata dwells in the "Samādhi of the Adorned Pure Treasury," yet in reality, the Tathāgata’s concentration and wisdom are without [duality].
There are two aspects [to this], which follow the conventional approach of the teaching in order to facilitate understanding through differentiation;
thus it is said that "the Buddha abides in samādhi. In the Sanskrit language, *samāpatti* is the correct term for samādhi.

At the time of entering the realization of samādhi, he speaks the Mantra of the Buddha-mind from within that meditative concentration; therefore, he brings forth immeasurable speech from the inexhaustible realm.
If one explains the meaning according to the Abhidharma, this refers to the karma of the constant vocal expression of all Buddhas;
furthermore, it is that which is collectively certified by the Buddhas of the ten directions, and this certification is precisely the meaning of "expression" (*vijñapti*). Next, it says:
"By the power of the dharma-realm, the peerless power, and the power of faith and understanding in perfect enlightenment, a single sound flows forth from four places. Furthermore—
To further explain, such sounds do not arise without cause and condition; they necessarily emerge only after three powers are fully assembled.

First is the power of the inconceivable *dharmadhātu*. Second is the power of the peerless *samaya*: by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), when sentient beings who are to be saved appear, [the Buddha] bestows empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) so that the great ocean-tide of his vows arises, never failing its appointed limit. This is the peerless *samaya*.

Because it is a power, it is called "unequaled power. If it resides in a practitioner, it is called the "power of the Buddhas' empowerment," which is the power of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*) of the Perfectly Awakened One.
This refers to the roots of virtue accumulated when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path in his previous lives.

If it resides in a practitioner, it is called the "power of one's own merit," such as that of a person who recites mantras through the correct dedication (*pariṇāmana*) resulting from the conjunction of three factors.
Because all that is wished for is accomplished, the Tathāgata likewise produces vocal sounds through the conjunction of the three powers;
since these arise from various conditions, one should know that this sound is fundamentally unarisen. Regarding "one sound in four places":
for example, the single letter *A* becomes fourfold when a stroke is added below, a dot is placed above, or a dot is set to the side.
Furthermore, the sound "A" is one, yet it forms four names depending on whether it is pronounced as a short vowel,
a long vowel, a nasalized sound, or as the sound "Ha. Moreover, the Buddha-mind is one, yet it forms [four designations] depending on whether it is taken as the fundamental non-arising principle,
the fundamental non-arising practice, the fundamental non-arising bodhi, or the fundamental non-arising nirvāṇa.
Although the four meanings and four aspects differ from one another, their essence has never been distinct.

To manifest this principle, the Tathāgata, from within the perfectly luminous mind, manifests the gateways of the four characters. Within this single essence, these four gates flow forth from four locations with a single sound;
it is like the four rivers flowing from Lake Anavatapta, circulating endlessly until they fill [the world].
Because it is like a great ocean, it is said to pervade the entire *dharmadhātu* and be equal to space, reaching everywhere.
This sign of sound and syllable represents the Buddha-mind; this is the true meaning of that mantra.
The first phrase is "Homage to all Tathāgatas. The second phrase is *viśva*; in ancient translations, this is called *piśu*, which signifies "various" or "multiform."
Furthermore, "kauśalya" (巧) signifies skillfulness; "mukha" (目佉) signifies a gate, referring here to the various gates of skillful means (*upāya*).

Next, "sarvathā" (薩嚩他) signifies the gate that universally encompasses all phenomena. This means that all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time each expound upon all dharmas through immeasurable and boundless gates of skillful means, using various causes, conditions, parables, and verbal expressions. Now...
To synthesize and discuss this, tracing its fundamental purport, it does not go beyond the gateway of four characters: Ā, Ā (protracted), Āṃ (aspirated), and Aḥ.
Because of the gateway of the letter Ā, all sentient beings inherently possess the nature of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
for their sake, the Tathāgata employs various causes and conditions to cleanse away the cataracts of their eyes, so that they may attain clarity and illumination. Thus is the Dharma.
The first phrase of the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and cause it to become pure" is precisely the pure bodhicitta.

Having attained this pure bodhicitta, one should extensively reveal the various inconceivable realms within the treasury of the Dharma-realm, so that all may universally behold all spiritual friends and universally study all gates of the perfections; thus, [it is taught] in the second chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The phrase "manifesting the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" signifies the meaning of the long vowel *ā* as the ten thousand practices of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Having already perfected the ten thousand practices of great compassion, one next attains great bodhi through the wisdom of the blossoming flowers of the king of *śāla* trees;
thus, the third phrase of the *Lotus Sūtra*, "awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," signifies the meaning of the letter *aṃ*. Once Buddhahood has been attained...
By means of the skillful expedient of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), he universally manifests traces to guide and benefit sentient beings.

When sentient beings realize that [the Buddha] is eternally abiding, all the traces of the Tathāgata have completely ceased; because there are no longer any traces, it is called "entering parinirvāṇa.

Thus, the fourth phrase of the *Lotus Sūtra* states, "Entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," which is precisely the gateway of the letter *A*. This wheel of letters corresponds to the Tathāgata.

In the wisdom of skillful means for coming [to enlightenment], there is further a fifth gateway of the long-syllabled *a* (pronounced as a drawn-out sound), which is not mentioned here because it has no distinct essence.
If one wishes to point to the text to distinguish its characteristics, it is precisely the various gateways of the Tathāgatas’ skillful deliverance within the phrase "I take refuge" (*namo*).
These five syllables encompass all Buddha-dharma without exception; therefore, they are called [the *akṣara-mukha*].

It is also the mind of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Furthermore, for the time being, this is explained with distinctions of depth and shallowness based on a single path of sequential practice;
however, in reality, each of the five syllables is the wisdom of all Tathāgatas and each individually encompasses all Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, as stated in the subsequent text regarding the cultivation of contemplation, by focusing on any single mind, one immediately perceives all Tathāgatas.
Because the mind revolves without obstruction, it is called the "mind of perfect enlightenment" (*samyaksambuddha-citta*).
To manifest this meaning, O Bhagavān, when he uttered this mantra, every single sound and syllable pervaded the entire *dharmadhātu*.
From each of these four syllables, all the gates of letters (*akṣaramukha*) emerged; thus, from each and every gate of letters, there further arose all [other syllables] in succession.
One should know that it is likewise with the gate of syllables (*akṣara-mukha*), for sounds arise from syllables;

because syllables serve as the gates, it is said that "at that very moment, all sounds throughout the dharma-realm issue forth mutually from the sound that is the emblem of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Although these vocal sounds issue forth mutually in various successive distinctions, when one examines their essential substance, they do not transcend [that single source].
Therefore, when the bodhisattvas heard this signal sound, they immediately understood the Tathāgata’s mind according to its meaning;
they realized that all dharma-gates arise in succession from it, and they also knew that all dharma-gates ultimately do not depart from the Tathāgata’s mind.
Thus, having attained what they had never experienced before, their pure eyes blossomed, and they uttered these subtle and wondrous words:
The verse says: "How marvelous! The mantra practice can possess vast wisdom. This vast Brahma-sound is named Vipula;

because the sound of the mantra pervades the entire Dharma-realm, equal to space, reaching everywhere, one should know that the Buddha-mind is likewise so—thus it is called 'vast wisdom. If this wisdom is transmitted and spread further and further..."
Just as when the sounds of various banners are uttered together, they constitute the very phrase of attaining perfect enlightenment, it is said:
"If one pervades this, one becomes a Buddha, the Honored One among Two-legged Beings. The next verse, seeing such benefits, universally exhorts others to practice:
"When the pure mind is freed from the bonds of self, one shall attain such sovereign power."
The Sūtra states: "At that time, the Bhagavān again spoke these Dharma-verses for those who have accomplished the mind of perfect enlightenment...
and so forth. This clarifies the preliminary branches of recitation and offering. The first verse clarifies the location for recitation.
Within the ritual of offering, it is explained in detail that the contemplation of bodhicitta is precisely what follows in the next chapter, where it is described as being "stainless."
With the eyes gazing at the location of one’s own mind, visualize an eight-petaled lotus with the letter *A* as its gateway, causing the clear mirror to appear before you, radiant and pure;
thereafter, following the instructions of the sūtras, practice various yogas. One should know that this mind pervades and flows forth everywhere.
When first practicing contemplation, various appearances will arise, yet one should simply cultivate constancy and abide therein, without forming [conceptualizations].
By applying effort continuously over a long period with diverse objects of focus, one naturally attains clarity; thus, the various nets of doubt are gradually eliminated.
Therefore, it is said that "one eventually comes to abide in the state of not giving rise to doubt.
Within this, the cultivation of yoga is briefly explained as having two stages: first, the stage of non-equipoise (*asamāhita-bhūmi*), and second, the stage of equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
Regarding the "levels" (*bhūmi*), their definitions and correspondences should be analyzed in detail according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

What is clarified in this present sutra differs only in its use of secret visualization; that which is called "not the stage of meditative equipoise" (*asamāhitā bhūmiḥ*) refers to when a practitioner first sees the letter *A* within the lotus of the mind, and from that letter, the mind spontaneously abides in stability.
The light from the gates shines in the four directions; because the mirror of this mind is pure and luminous, all objects contemplated by the practitioner appear within it.
Next, one should rely upon the secret body of the samaya as depicted in the drawing, carefully assuming the majestic deportment and physical form of the deity and observing it with focused attention.
At first, one should close the eyes and abide in the object of focus until clarity is attained.

Afterward, upon opening the eyes, everything appears clearly and distinctly. If one wishes to receive and uphold the mantra of the mind of Perfectly Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhicitta*), one should select any one of the four syllables previously mentioned and place it upon the luminous circle at the heart of the deity while receiving and upholding it.
Therefore, it is said: "Selecting one from among those, place that one mind within the mind. In the Sanskrit original, these two refer to the two minds.
All these syllables are the *hrīḥ* seed-syllable and not the *jita* seed-syllable.

When a practitioner first begins the visualization, if the mind has not yet become pliant and disciplined, they should employ the skillful means described in the preceding chapter to visualize this heart-syllable as a stream of pure milk and as a wheel of sound.
Furthermore, one transforms the syllable of sound into the form of the deity, all as previously explained. This is how it is done.
Through the empowerment of the three secrets, the heavy obscurations of the three karmas accumulated since beginningless time are purified and eliminated;

even the life-winds (*prāṇa*) subside as they become increasingly tranquil and profound. At that time, the mind does not engage with external objects, becoming serene, peaceful, and limpid—like a motionless mirror or a waveless great ocean.
One personally realizes the state of ultimate purity, free from all defilements and impurities; although the yogic realm is vividly manifest, it remains [in its natural state].
As previously stated, it is like a high hall where a mirror hangs, making no distinctions; with this mirror-like mind, one contemplates the heart of this perfectly luminous *bhaṭṭāraka*.
Upon that heart, there is again a perfectly luminous seed-syllable (*bīja*), which is even more bright and pure, yet also exceedingly minute.
Therefore, it is said that it does not differentiate, being as subtle as a reflection appearing before a mirror. The reason for this is to symbolize the seed of the mind.

Therefore, just as one contemplates all phenomena through the gateway of the letter A, seeing that they arise successively from a multitude of conditions, one investigates their fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and finds it to be ultimately without support and without marks.

Because this fundamental limit is eternal, one thus knows that the myriad phenomena of the world ultimately do not transcend the gateway of the letter A; now, observing the perfectly luminous seed-syllable is likewise so.
Because one perceives that at the moment of its initial arising it is extremely subtle, one knows that it arises solely from the mind and ultimately has neither abiding nor foundation.

Since one knows it has no abiding and no foundation, even though it is later cultivated and expanded until it pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one knows it is not different from its initial arising.
Therefore, those who study this contemplation must proceed gradually from the minute toward the luminous.
Great! Furthermore, the reason for proceeding from the small to the great and subsuming the great into the small is to cause the practitioner’s mind to attain mastery.

Through the power of that mind, which can contract and expand without obstruction, one can gradually encompass infinite dharma-realms within a single minute atom (*paramāṇu*), and place infinite dharma-realms within a single minute atom. If this is explained as a profound secret, it is this:
In the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, the subtle wisdom of all Buddhas transcends all mental measures (*cittamātra*) and cannot be demonstrated to others;

yet, through the empowerment of their sovereign mind, there is nothing they do not perceive. Therefore, the term "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) refers to this subtlety of function, not to something that is merely small or minute.
Furthermore, because the practitioner constantly practices in accordance with it, the inconceivable *dharmadhātu* [is realized].
The insignia appear even more vividly before one; one is able to contemplate that one’s own body is itself the body of the deity, and that the body of the deity is itself one’s own body.

Thus, they are non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual. When one contemplates the mind-Buddha of the deity as being one’s own self, one then sees oneself within the perfectly luminous heart of the deity; and upon one’s own heart, there is likewise [the deity].
The subtle, luminous, and perfect seed-syllable can cause gradual expansion and allow for mastery over contraction and expansion.
When one visualizes the Buddha within one's own mind as the *iṣṭadevatā*, one sees the Tathāgata within the luminous sphere of the practitioner’s heart;

upon the heart of that Buddha, there is likewise a subtle, luminous, and perfect seed-syllable capable of causing gradual expansion and allowing for mastery over contraction and expansion—all of which are thus accomplished.
Because there are no obstructions and they do not mutually hinder one another, it is said that even the forms of the Buddhas whom one has personally revered appear.
Up to this point, it is called the accomplishment of the reflected image (*pratibimba-siddhi*), which still belongs to the stage of non-concentrated absorption (*asamāhita-bhūmi*).

Next, from the second stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) downward, one enters the stage of concentrated absorption (*samāhita-bhūmi*), whereby one is able to see the true Buddha within the mind of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-citta*).
Regarding the signs of profound faith and understanding through the empowerment of the body by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-prabhā*, one perceives that the Buddha is eternally present on Vulture Peak.
As the *Samantabhadra-vyūha* states: "The form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions do not perish; it is because my own turbid and evil eyes are obstructed that I do not see them.
Now, the central principle of this sutra takes the practitioner’s pure mind as the cause and the Tathāgata’s pure mind as the condition. From these...

Because the mind arises through causes and conditions, it is called "seeing the Buddha of one's own mind. When seeing in this manner, one does not depart from the phrase "originally unborn," and is thus termed the "body of true empowerment.

This is different from those with distracted minds who see the Buddha outside the mind, and it is also different from beginners in contemplation who merely achieve the accomplishment of a mental image.

The verse says: "Regarding the mirror maṇḍala" means that after first visualizing oneself as the samaya body of the deity, one further contemplates the heart-center as being round, luminous, pure, and subtle, like a circular mirror.
Within this mirror is a great eight-petaled lotus king, fresh white and magnificent, complete with filaments and anthers; as before, upon the center of the flower is—
When these seed-syllables transform, the meaning of these seed-forms and sounds reveals the true empowerment-body of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata,
as if dwelling in a profound cavern in samādhi, with a topknot crown upon his head and his entire body radiating immeasurable light,
adorned with inexhaustible marks and signs of excellence. At that time, the practitioner, having received the light of the Dharma, [perceives this].
The illuminated mind turns toward clarity and naturally awakens to the understanding of the ten phrases of dependent origination. One realizes that such wondrous form is not different from emptiness;
although its intrinsic nature is eternally empty, it is not different from form. Since this is the case for the characteristics of form, the same principle applies to the meaning of mind.
Because both form and mind enter the gateway of the letter *A*, one knows that the nature of mind is fundamentally quiescent, just like space.

Emptiness, which is free from all attachment, contention, and conceptual proliferation, and transcends all demonic activities—this is called the initial seed-mind of the accomplishment of the signless (*animitta*).

It is also termed the Samādhi of the Secret Contemplation Gate (*guhyadhyāna-mukha-samādhi-bhūmi*). According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this corresponds to the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties;
according to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is the moment when the reflection of the moon appears in the pond. From this point onward...
Later, gradually employing skillful means, one enters the water calmly and slowly. When observing this body of forms and images, one increasingly understands the body of the Dharma-gate.

One should know that the "phrase of perfect enlightenment" refers to the meaning of the manifestation of the perfectly equal awakening as clarified in the first chapter of this sutra regarding the characteristics of the bodhicitta;
because it is like holding a bright jewel in the palm of the hand, it is called "manifestation," not merely seeing it from a distance.
The mirror maṇḍala signifies the meaning of the pure bodhicitta which cannot be moved by any phenomena;

the great lotus king throne signifies the meaning of the wondrous Dharma-garbha (Tathāgatagarbha), which is unstained and eternally abiding; dwelling in profound depth signifies the meaning of entering deeply into the boundless;
and the crown of the topknot of dhāraṇī signifies the meaning of the perfection of myriad virtues. If one approaches this from a shallow and concise perspective:

The *Mingyi* (Exposition of Meaning) simply states "holding the topknot crown. This character "hold" (*chi*) possesses the resonance of *dhāraṇī*, meaning that [the virtues] reach the summit of the myriad qualities above and ultimately converge [therein].
It is like gathering and binding various topknots and wearing them upon the head;

thus, the translator, wishing to include both the exoteric and esoteric interpretations, translated it fully as "total retention" (*zongchi*). Next, it says "surrounded by immeasurable light," which is...
Because this refers to the meaning of accomplishing immeasurable wisdom within the verses of the first chapter, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"That which is called 'luminosity' is named wisdom," as explained at length in the section on the Bodhisattva’s deeds regarding the light of lapis lazuli. Next, it says:

"To be free from deluded grasping and discrimination" refers to the meaning of transcending the one hundred and sixty mental states within the verses of the first chapter. "Primordially quiescent like space" refers to the first chapter.

Regarding the meaning of "originally quiescent and signless" within the verse, by cross-referencing it section by section with the preceding passage on the "Seal of the Bodhicitta," one knows that this second profound and secret explanation takes the pure bodhicitta itself as the seed of *siddhi*.
If one considers the second "Perfectly Awakened" phrase of this chapter in relation to the second [category of] Buddhas explained in the preceding chapter:

The "Victorious Phrase" (*jaya-pada*) is already one layer of profound mystery; furthermore, when explained in terms of the partial realization through vitarka and vicāra, it constitutes yet another layer of profound mystery.
Entering each and every stage (*bhūmi*), there are the initial seed-minds and the meaning of the three-month recitation, which are even more profoundly secret.
According to the depth or shallowness of the practitioner’s mental capacity (*citta-mātra*), these can all bring about various accomplishments (*siddhi*); therefore, they are not in vain.
The meaning of *siddhi* is boundless. Next, regarding "gathering the mind": from one to ten is also one;

even when reaching one hundred, one thousand, or ten thousand and so forth, they are all likewise one. Because this one pervades many moments, through these many moments one is able to see for oneself.
In Sanskrit, it is called *samādhi*, which carries the meaning of "equipoise" (*samāpatti*). It is also [the state of] such meditative concentration.
The meaning of "gathering the mind into a single object" is precisely the meaning of "one-pointed mind. Regarding the second moon:
the offering of scented unguents and so forth to benefit sentient beings in various ways is similar to the worldly practices mentioned previously;
however, the intent behind its re-explanation here is distinct from that of the former. Herein, one has already attained meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).

When the mind is pure and supple, one is able to accomplish whatever task is undertaken. By offering even a single incense, one can, according to reality, pervade the entire Dharma-realm and universally reach all realms of sentient beings, performing various kinds of benefit; every undertaking is accomplished accordingly.
This is explained in detail in the section on dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Just as it is with incense and flowers, so too is it with whatever other things are employed.

In this way, there is nothing that does not accomplish the great work of Buddha-activity. Furthermore, regarding "other months," within this context there are two months of practice, by which one immediately reaches the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).

(Question again: As for "renouncing gain and honor," to explain it according to the text, it means renouncing the eight worldly dharmas and matters of compliance or opposition, because they act as obstacles to the Path.
If one interprets it with esoteric intent, this refers to the Great Element (*mahābhūta*) of this Bodhisattva.
The fruits of these roots of goodness are inexhaustible, and one currently attains the jewels of merit from immeasurable Dharma-gates;
one should not give rise to attachment or grasping toward them. If one gives rise to craving for dharmas, one will not swiftly enter the state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma);
therefore, one must relinquish such gain and honor. At that time, the practitioner further reflects correctly upon the bodhicitta and utters a compassionate vow, saying:
Because it arises in accordance with principle, it is called "reflection in accordance with principle" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).

The meaning of "reflection" here refers to such reflection in accordance with principle by which one attains mastery; that is to say, the practitioner abiding in yoga achieves accomplishment. This means:
"I shall masterfully bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings and attain all things without obstruction"—this is the generation of a resolute compassionate vow (*karuṇā-praṇidhāna*).
"How is it that sentient beings, though equally possessing such enlightened nature (*buddhadhātu*), do not realize it for themselves and thus undergo great suffering?
I shall immediately give rise to a heart of great courage and resolve, employing countless skillful means (*upāya*) to bring them to fulfillment;
I must certainly cause them all to reach the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), eliminating all defilements and obstructions so that none remain. Or, one may further make this vow:
I vow that those who desire to accomplish the *siddhi* praised by the Tathāgata— namely,
the ultimate perfection of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision, and his skillful means of wondrous liberation— if they do not attain this,
how could they appear in the world for the sake of the one great cause? I shall swiftly accomplish these subtle and wondrous expedient means praised by all Buddhas.

Furthermore, "desire" (*chanda*) is synonymous with "aspiration. At times, when all the aspirations of sentient beings are fulfilled and free from hindrances, one should generate an object of focus (*ālambana*) in accordance with reason;
such yoga is then without obstruction. One should perform the recitation by means of such an object of focus, namely, by thinking:
"By my merit, may the suffering of all [beings] be extracted," and so forth, filling [the mind] with great compassion.
It can fulfill all that sentient beings hope for—uprooting their great suffering and bestowing present happiness—and it can also bring these to fruition.
Why is this? Because the practitioner’s own mind is free from defilements and obstructions, they possess great power.

Furthermore, by removing obstacles for sentient beings according to their respective capacities, and through the causal condition of that mutual freedom from obstruction, one is able to accomplish these matters accordingly.

This is precisely the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra. What is this sign? It means that one gives rise to such great compassionate vows to cause the sufferings of mutual devouring within the realm of animals to be forever eliminated;
to cause those in the realm of hungry ghosts who lack food and drink to always be fully satisfied;
and to cause the immeasurable, extreme sufferings within the realm of hell-beings to be extinguished. By means of my...
Regarding "by virtue of merit": because of the immeasurable, supreme blessings produced by me, in the third month—following the previous months—I renounce gain and honor.

This means that regarding both internal and external things, I have no attachment; this is called "renouncing gain and honor. Furthermore, concerning external matters, I do not seek nor accept offerings.
Having renounced these gains and honors, I bestow them upon sentient beings; through the power of the mantra practice (*vidyā-mantra*), all shall attain accomplishment.
Furthermore, regarding those who repeatedly give rise to compassion through these and other methods of contemplation, such compassionate vows are of infinite varieties and cannot be fully described.

Recitation performed in the first and second months is likewise; one should make vows, though during the first two months one does so merely with a mind of faith and understanding, as the practice has not yet reached perfection. In the third month, all that is vowed is accomplished; therefore, one performs the dedication of merit.

When a practitioner who practices for the sake of both self and others attains realization, they act in accordance with each circumstance, repeatedly washing their mind with the water of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Gradually, this bodhicitta comes to possess great power;
its increasing efficacy up until the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*) is entirely due to this process. This is the first month of bodhicitta, followed by the second month.

Contemplating the form of the Buddha is called the "Phrase of Perfect Enlightenment" (Third Abode). The mantra is free from all characteristics and is called the "Three Months," or also the "Three Lakṣas.
Furthermore, there are the three phrases of vast empowerment; one should contemplate that they are the Tathāgata’s empowerment and spiritual power, accomplished through these three phrases.
Now, desiring to perform the deeds of the Tathāgata, one should bring this to mind through thought and recollection.
There are three phrases: first, by the power of my own merit; second, because it pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
third, by the spiritual power of the Tathāgata. When these three phrases are combined, the power of vast empowerment arises.
Having formed this thought, one should recite these phrases. These are the heart of all mantras. One should take the merit of these three phrases according to [one's needs].

Take flowers and other offerings and apply them by means of mental visualization; as for flowers, apply them with the Flower Mantra, and as for incense, apply them with the Incense Mantra, and so on until all instances of extracting suffering and bestowing bliss, or making offerings to the Buddha and others, are accomplished.
If one does not use the primary mantras to apply these, it is also successful to use the subsequent Consort Mantras. By the power of my merit, this shall be so here.
The realm of sentient beings is pervaded by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, equal to the Dharma-realm and all its benefits.
With the thought and desire to benefit all sentient beings, they shall all obtain the objects of their mindfulness in accordance with reality;
because they abide in reality, whatever they contemplate will be accomplished. Furthermore, by my power of merit, even the suffering of suffering shall be removed, and so forth.

Therefore, by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, by the power of the equality of the dharma-realm, and through the conjunction of these three conditions, one is able to accomplish inconceivable karma.
One who acts in this manner should be known as acting in accordance with principle; thus it is said that they "shall attain that which accords with principle."
Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi-vikurvaṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra, Scroll Eight;
Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi-vikurvaṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra, Scroll Nine.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Yi-hang.
The Remainder of Chapter Six, "The Appearance of Siddhis.
At that time, the Tathāgata further spoke the mantra of the consort Ākāśagarbha-vajravārāhī, known as "Equal to Space" (Ākāśasama-bala).
It is called "Equal to Space" because it is indestructible like space and cannot be overcome by anything.
Furthermore, as for "treasury" (garbha): it is like a person who possesses a great treasury of precious jewels; whatever they desire, they may take at will and never suffer from poverty.
The Tathāgata’s vast treasury of space is also like this: all matters that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings emerge from within it.
One takes from it the immeasurable treasures of the Dharma with sovereign ease, and because they are inexhaustible, it is called the "Treasury of Space" (Gaganagañja).

"Transformation and illumination" (*parāvṛtti-prabhāsvara*) means that "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) has the sense of being able to produce; it is able to produce this *tathāgatagarbha* and is able to produce all Buddha-activities.

It is as previously stated regarding the compassionate vows one has made: for example, when making an offering with a single flower, one directs the mind so that it pervades all Buddhas, as well as ordinary beings and sages, and having offered it to them all, one dedicates the merit toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). May all those who receive my gift, by means of this... [dedication].
By this power, may I attain the aforementioned vows. Having made such vows, if one applies this mantra, there shall be nothing that is not accomplished.
First, prostrate to all Tathāgatas and so forth. *Kuṇḍalinī* (also meaning various gates).
*Sarvatha* (all). *Khaṃ* (the level tone; emptiness; this refers to the preceding statement that all is empty; this is the seed-syllable). *Utpatti* (arising). *Svaḥ*.
*Rāhe gagaṇe svāhā*. This signifies the power of the "Space-Treasury" (*ākāśagarbha*) and its equality with space;
it means that this substance arises within the emptiness of all phenomena and pervades the entirety of space.
One who recites and maintains this mantra should offer a single flower, which will thereby become pervasive.

Having offered [this] upward to all the noble ones within the Dharmadhātu and bestowed it downward upon all sentient beings, one should generate the great vows as described above and empower them with this mantra;
then all will be accomplished. It is like taking precious objects from a treasury for oneself—the results follow one's heart's desire.
Reciting this three times, whatever one contemplates will likewise be achieved. (In all offerings of flowers and so forth, with...)

By dedicating through the three kinds of power and augmenting them with this vidyā, everything is accomplished according to one’s wishes; that is to say, by offering a single flower to all Buddhas and so forth, mastery is attained. Next, regarding the accomplishment performed on the full moon:

first, having made offerings and performed service until the signs of accomplishment are obtained, one then performs the recitation rite on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon—this is the "full moon.
According to the superior, middling, or inferior matters, one performs the method of accomplishment as follows: [Superior]...
Whether on a mountain peak, in a cow pen, in a cold forest, or by a riverbank—these locations are suitable for the superior, middling, and inferior [levels of practice].
Alternatively, one may perform it wherever the mind finds delight. When constructing a maṇḍala on such places as a mountain peak, the first layer surrounding it is painted with vajras.
This altar consists of three layers, all of which are demarcated by vajras. Its directions are as follows:
Regarding the deities such as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who appear later, they will be discussed in their respective places; they are not differentiated here.
The arrangement of these deities here is generally the same as the previous positions, with the only difference being that they are connected by vajra-marks.
The vajras drawn around the perimeter serve as the boundary. All of this is to be made pure and free from faults. To be "without fault" means it must be perfectly circular.
It is perfectly upright and wondrous;
its vajra-marks encircle it in this manner, all of which are yellow, which is the color of the vajra. In three respects, it is identical to the vajra:
it is identical to the color of the vajra, identical to the substance of the vajra, and identical to the name of the vajra. Its purity is likewise identical to that of the vajra.

"Vajra" (the adamantine) refers to purity and excellence, being identical to the vajra. Because these three matters are identical to the vajra, they cannot be destroyed, cannot be surpassed, and cannot be subdued.
Once this Vajradhātu has been constructed, all obstructing spirits will be utterly bewildered, and none will dare to cause harm.
Having become free from obstructions, the medicinal elixir [of accomplishment] is thereby achieved.
Regarding the statement that "things are easily accomplished," the phrase "four-cornered" has two meanings:
it refers to the altar being made as a perfect square, and it also refers to the vajra seal being made as a square, which likewise corresponds exactly to the four directions.
Regarding the term "vajra-knot," as described above, when vajras are placed all around with each prong connected to the next, this is the meaning of the vajra-knot.

Regarding the single gate and its conditions (*pratyaya*)—where "conditions" refers to opening a path to an empty space as described above to serve as the external condition—the "correspondence" (*yoga*) means that this gate corresponds to the specific ritual action.
For the superior accomplishment (*siddhi*), the gate faces east; for the middling accomplishment, it faces north or west;
for the inferior accomplishment, the gate is made to face south. The boundary (*sīmā*) consists of interconnected vajras, which also carries the meaning of "vajra. There are two gatekeepers.
To accomplish the ritual of attainment (*sādhana*), one must guard it most diligently; guarding the gate is therefore essential.
This refers to those previously mentioned who possess unbearable majesty and stand facing the gate. They all form the mudrā by extending their fingers upward (the mudrā is described below).
Both [deities] are red and white in color, manifesting extremely wrathful forms. A trident (*śūla*) together with flames is placed at the corner; this is the Solitary One (*Ekajaṭī*).
As for the Vajra of the Thighs, place it wherever there are corners (with flames).
Place the Vajra of Equal Joy at the four cardinal directions in opposition;
place the Crossed Karma-Vajra in the very center of the maṇḍala so that its four sides are perfectly aligned with the four directions, and construct [the design] above it.
The great lotus with eight petals and its filaments (is formed upon the vajra); since this is identical to the vajra-seat, it is called "identical to the vajra.
Binding the vajra-mudrā is precisely binding the five-pronged mudrā of Vajrapāṇi; therefore, it is called the "vajra-wisdom," which is the vajra-mudrā.
One should prostrate to all the Buddhas and repeatedly perform the protection of the medicinal substances at that place.

Regarding the purification of substances: when one prostrates to the Buddha, one should repeatedly make a personal vow as extensively described above, directing the mind toward universal compassion and vowing not for oneself alone, but for the sake of all sentient beings.

One should pray that through the power of this empowerment, these medicinal substances may quickly reach accomplishment; because they are thus accomplished, they will be able to benefit all sentient beings. As for their protection...

Medicines possess many dharmas that have existed extensively from the beginning; whenever one takes medicine, one must understand their ritual application. Whether purchasing them in the market or gathering them oneself, there are established methods and procedures.
Even for performing protection (*rakṣā*) and purification (*pariśodhana*), there are sequential ritual applications as well as rites for manifesting radiance (*prabhāsana*), and so forth.
These are not fully detailed here, and one should inquire further [or consult texts such as the *Susiddhi* which may be used in common]. Once the purification has been performed, then...
When reciting, there are likewise signs of initial, intermediate, and superior accomplishment. If one attains unimpeded accomplishment, there are three signs of superior accomplishment:

warmth arises during the first watch of the night, smoke rises during the middle watch, and flames emerge at the fifth watch (dawn). There are two signs of intermediate accomplishment: excluding the emergence of flames, [the other two].
There is one sign of inferior accomplishment: namely, the arising of warmth alone. "Transformation" means obtaining much from little; from...
Once smoke has attained its flames and so forth, and having thus been accomplished, one may either consume it or carry it;

thereby one is able to travel with mastery through the Buddha-fields, moving from one to another, dwelling for immeasurable kalpas, possessing sovereign majestic light, and attaining mastery over birth and death.
Because one possesses mastery over birth and death, one is truly a son of the Buddha. (Worldly conduct is precisely the practice of traversing the world. Substance.
Once it is accomplished, protect yourself with the Vajra-mudrā, protect the deity, and protect the object before taking it; divide it into five portions:

(1) for the Master, (2) for the previously accomplished Siddha, (3) for the companions, (4) for oneself, and (5) for the Buddhas. Regarding the Buddha-objects, they are used according to where they arise within the Three Jewels.
As for the objects of the previously accomplished Siddha, if a Siddha should come to take them, one should [act accordingly].
If [the teacher] does not come, one should take the items and divide them into two parts: one part is given to a companion and one part is taken by oneself.

If the teacher is in another location, one should hold the teacher’s property for him until he returns and give it back to him; if the teacher is not there, one should perform meritorious deeds on his behalf based on what arose from that [property].
Items such as knives and the like cannot be divided, yet one should also mark them in one's mind as the portion [of the teacher]. From beginning to end, these are all to be used [in this manner].

Having perfected the self-protection and protection of others through the Vajra [mantra], one is able to universally manifest the form-body (*rūpakāya*) throughout all worlds and perform great Buddha-activities.

Regarding the medicinal offerings, there is also a specific method: namely, making offerings to the Buddhas—as the Sūtra says, "one who turns the offering attains accomplishment"—and then carrying it to the ten directions to offer it to the Buddhas of the ten directions as many times as desired. Furthermore, there are specific proportions and methods for the *ācārya* and his assistants.
(One should ask further: If one attains such accomplishment, it is called "accomplishment with conceptualization" (*savikalpa-siddhi*).
Because it involves substances, medicinal herbs, and so forth—which are phenomena characterized by objective signs—it is termed "accomplishment with conceptualization.

Through this accomplishment with conceptualization, one attains non-conceptual accomplishment (*nirvikalpa-siddhi*); this refers to conceptualization acting as the cause. Based upon this conceptualization...
Regarding the attainment of the fruit of non-conceptuality through differentiation:

although the fruit of the unconditioned, signless, inconceivable, and untainted is not produced by causes, it is nevertheless established by taking conceptual differentiation as its cause. Thus, this untainted, unconditioned fruit is brought to fruition.
The Sūtra says: "O Secret Lord, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently present in all worlds,
having thoroughly realized the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) and the fact that the intrinsic nature of all such conceptualizations is emptiness,
through the power of the perfection of skillful means— unconditioned yet with the conditioned as its retinue— they manifest the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) for the sake of sentient beings."
"Universal" means that although this is the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it can be accomplished through conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) skillful means;
this is inconceivable. The Buddhas of the three periods—present, future, and past—all preach this Dharma-gate by virtue of their mastery of the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
By citing the Buddhas of the three periods, it is intended to clarify that they all enter into this very same text. Although...
Although one employs these conditioned means as a skillful expedient, one thereby realizes that the very nature of these conceptual phenomena is eternally empty.

Such phenomena arising through causes and conditions are free from birth and cessation, permanence and annihilation, identity and difference, or coming and going; they are merely like illusions and transformations, not distinct from the Middle Way.
If one abandons this and seeks the essence of non-conceptuality elsewhere, it cannot be found. This is because of the unconditioned.
Because their nature is not different from existence, and in order to fully realize this profound law of dependent origination,
they are able to take this very conditioned state (*saṃskṛta*) and make it the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time,
by the power of skillful means (*upāya*), although they have realized the *dharmadhātu*, are able to manifest from this fruit of the unconditioned, effortless essence through existence.
He manifests as various retinues through the power of empowerment based on the qualities of his own realization, just like the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana.

(Regarding the manifestation of the conditioned within the unconditioned: its original nature is non-active; yet, by means of activity, it is able to accomplish the unconditioned. As for "mutual correspondence":

before the recitation was performed, the nature was originally impure; through recitation, it attained purity. Now, for the sake of liberating sentient beings, he again manifests an impure body. This impure body further serves as a condition for others to become pure; this is called "mutual correspondence. It is the manifestation of the conditioned arising from the unconditioned. Manifestation.

Each of the Vajra Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds, draws in and gathers sentient beings through the gateway of mantras, causing them all to attain the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
By these skillful means, they pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*, universally responding to all sentient beings so that they may obtain benefit and profit.
Seeing the peace and bliss of the Dharma, they dwell therein with a joyful mind; thus they attain long life and the five [supernormal powers].
Desiring to play and laugh with joy, one receives this offering from the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

By uttering these words that cause all people of the world to disbelieve and revile, one attains the aforementioned matters. This benefit is seen through the sequence of the path of the mantra practice of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas;
it is spoken with a joyful heart by those who, through the skillful means of all Tathāgatas, bestow empowerment from the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).
By the power of not abandoning sentient beings, one manifests according to their needs: either causing them to see the Dharma and abide in peaceful and happy conduct;
or inspiring a heart of joy (which is the joy of the Dharma at the first stage); or attaining a long life of countless kalpas to constantly behold the appearance of Buddhas in the world;

or obtaining pure and exquisite fivefold desires for one's own enjoyment; and furthermore, being able to make offerings to all Tathāgatas—these matters cannot be accomplished through expedient means alone.
Such persons are unable to believe it; they form this thought: "The essence of mantra is identical to the dharmadhātu—unconditioned and uncreated.
How could such a thing be accomplished? If such a thing were produced, it would possess marks and involve conceptual discrimination;
how could that be consistent with reason? For this reason, they give rise to disparagement. However, in this matter, the Buddha has a secret intention, for there is no other expedient means.
One cannot understand that herein, by means of mastery over the mind, it is taught that this constitutes longevity;
such a lifespan is precisely the life-force of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-lifespan. As for the "five desires," they refer to the four immeasurables and the bodhicitta.
All noble ones take these as their present dharma to enjoy and to offer to the Tathāgata; this is the true Dharma-offering.

The Buddha is the body itself. If a practitioner, relying on the Buddha’s skillful means and the profound dependent origination, achieves accomplishment in worldly dharmas, they then contemplate the emptiness of intrinsic nature within this very state; this is the accomplishment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Such inconceivable dharmas cannot be believed by ordinary beings themselves, yet all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas clearly perceive these benefits.
One must not slander this path of the sequential stages of mantra practice as being non-existent. Why?

Because other bodhisattvas, seeking the unsurpassed path, perform difficult and painful ascetic practices as if their heads were on fire; even after passing through immeasurable eons, they may still fail to attain such accomplishment.
However, one who accomplishes these mantra practices, provided they possess skillful means, [attains it] in a single lifetime.
It can be accomplished because one understands the meaning of the ten similes of profound dependent origination;
and because although one performs various accomplishments through mantras and the like, there is no grasping or attachment, as these are not different from suchness—therefore, it is subtle and swift.

Next, the substances to be accomplished are explained: having first performed one hundred thousand recitations for one month and then two months as described above, one constructs a maṇḍala and places the substance to be accomplished within it;
by performing further recitation for three hundred thousand [times], it is then perfected.
Since the deity positions and other elements of this maṇḍala are identical to those of the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha* (Great Compassion Womb), [the procedure] herein...
Do not speak of it; rather, place within it that which one desires to accomplish, and position the Mahāvairocana Tathāgata in the cardinal directions and intermediate corners.
(Question: As for the banner (*dhvaja*), its shaft is made of bamboo and wrapped with pure silk; it should hang down to a length of one *zhang* or more, resembling a pennant.

At its top, it takes the form of a tiered structure, upon which a *vajra* is placed. The sword is made of tempered steel, and its hilt is fashioned from bone. There are three grades of parasols: superior, middling, and inferior.
The "lower completion" refers to gold, silver, and peacock feathers. Footwear made of leather is first thoroughly washed with various substances until it is extremely clean and free of odor;
it is then treated with medicinal substances so that even fire cannot burn it. Once it is also extremely fragrant, it may be used according to the ritual manuals.

To obtain a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling jewel), one takes a pure and excellent gem and places it atop a banner. For eye medicine, one uses *añjana*; this *añjana* is prepared as follows: [The text continues with the preparation of the añjana.]
There are two types [of methods]: first, the extremely light method of ascending against the current (further inquiry).

Regarding *gorocanā* (cow bezoar), there are furthermore immeasurable medicinal substances—namely, *vaidūrya*, cinnabar, realgar, orpiment, and so forth—all of which can be successfully accomplished. Furthermore, immeasurable objects such as the *vajra* can also be accomplished.
The original text fully explains the ritual procedures (*vidhi*), and the *Susiddhikara-sūtra* also contains the sequential stages, as follows:

Once the sandals are completed, one may immediately wear them to travel through Buddha-fields without obstruction; once the eye-medicine is completed, one will see the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
The rest is understandable. Furthermore, there are drawings of various forms of birds and beasts;

by taking any one of these and performing the rite, they become fit for mounting and traveling to the Buddha-fields of the ten directions with mastery. Alternatively, one may apply this method to a boy or a girl.
He shall also cause that [person] to achieve accomplishment so as to serve him, and they will then travel to the lands of the ten directions.
