To the west, there was a person who, having achieved [this], led five hundred people to ascend into the sky and depart, with no one knowing where they went. When this dharma is accomplished, one becomes a *vidyādhara* (knowledge-holder) or *ṛṣi* (seer).
Whatever objects one desires, they shall be produced; when he recites [the mantra], he shall also attain the meditative states (*viṣaya*) and be able to perform them.
In this way, with respect to any given object, one may direct the mind to perceive it as non-existent, and by so doing, the rite will still be accomplished.
As the Sūtra says: "That which all people of the world cannot believe, that person attains; such a one is called an 'accomplished practitioner' (siddha-puruṣa).
They are able to attain all those rare and marvelous things that cannot be believed. Therefore, it is said: "O son or daughter of good family, through skillful means..."
Whatever objects one desires, they are attained solely through mastery over one’s own mind; it is by such mastery over one’s own mind that they are accomplished.
This "mastery over one’s own mind" means that whatever one wishes for is accomplished simply by the turning of the mind alone.

"Solely" (*kevalam*) means that one employs only one's own mind without depending on other conditions; "solely" also carries the sense of "immediately," meaning that as soon as the thought arises in the mind, it is so.
It is accomplished.
O Lord of Mysteries, this causal desire for the goal based on the Lord of Mysteries is not something known by those foolish worldlings.
If a person, within these mantra practices, should think: "I am now performing such a cause and shall thereby obtain such a result..."
Regarding this result, one should know that this is not the correct teaching; it is merely the false conceptualization of the foolish.

Why is this? There are certain non-Buddhists who claim that all phenomena arise from a self (if it were so, then because of the Lord’s pleasure he would grant [it], and because of his displeasure he would not grant [it], and so forth—people such as these cannot understand this path). Thus, all things arise from causes; if they arise from causes, then what is this cause?
If there were intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then having intrinsic nature would entail falling into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). How could an eternal dharma give rise [to anything]?

If the cause perishes while the effect arises, it would be a dharma of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*); how could such a thing give rise [to an effect]? One should consider that as for the "cause," the cause is empty.

Since the cause is empty, how can there be an effect? This should be understood through the wisdom that extensively refutes this cause, as found in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Upon examination, even the origin of this cause cannot be found, for it is without support. That which is without support is fundamentally unarisen;
since a cause that is fundamentally unarisen cannot produce an effect, one knows that the effect is fundamentally unarisen.
Because the cause is not truly existent, and a cause that is not real can never produce a real effect, one should know that the effect is fundamentally unarisen.
Furthermore, one should know that because the nature of the cause is empty and quiescent, the characteristics of the effect are likewise so.
If, within such a law of dependent origination, one speaks of there being a cause and an effect, this is the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);

it falls into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism, or identity or difference, and does not enter the Middle Way. Therefore, one realizes that such mantras are eternally free from the characteristics of causes and karma.

This is precisely the *dharmadhātu*, the inconceivable realm. Furthermore, because there is that which is produced by causes, and since the cause involves activity, one should know that the effect likewise involves what is produced.
Since there is that which is produced, how can it constitute reality? One should know that the effect is detached from the karma of the cause;
for these characteristics of cause and effect exist only through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and thus, when correctly observed, they are fundamentally non-existent.
Because that which abides has no place of abiding, the essence of the fruit does not arise; it is identical to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, if a practitioner thinks, "By reciting mantras and practicing the mantra-path, I shall attain the fruit," they merely deceive themselves.
Although these mantras arise from conditions, they are in reality without action; from the very beginning, the *dharmadhātu* is unborn and non-existent.
How can the essence of phenomena that are neither pure nor defiled be established?
One should know that practitioners of *mantra* simply purify their own minds through skillful means; if the three karmas are purified, one will naturally attain clarity and self-awakening therein.
It is, for example, like a person who, while dreaming, practices the various six perfections and thereby becomes pure.

When the Buddha-land awakens, there is no sign of the fruition of results; it is simply that within the single thought of the mind of ignorance, there are the causes and effects of the myriad practices.

It is also like a treasure trove within a dark room: if one employs skillful means to light a great bright lamp, although it arises and ceases through causes and conditions and cannot be found when pushed back to its source—being fundamentally identical to emptiness—it nevertheless illuminates all phenomena as they are.
Rising through the power of fortune and clarifying the nature of causes and conditions, one perceives that this treasure-store does not arise apart from skillful means.

For those who cultivate the practice of mantra and conduct, the primary purpose is to eliminate delusion and karma; they should realize that the Dharma-realm is without arising or ceasing, and that purity and defilement are free from all conceptual discrimination.
They must know that the essence of this mantra is itself the essence of the Dharma-realm. If one understands this...
Knowing that the essence of the mantra is identical to the Dharma-realm and equal to great emptiness, one will naturally be able to attain the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).
Because of this signless samādhi, the *siddhi* will manifest before one; thus, one should give rise to such faith and understanding.

Next, Vajrapāṇi again asked the Buddha: "I pray that you will further explain the syllables of Perfect Enlightenment and the syllables for the accomplishment of siddhi—namely, as previously described, how a single syllable can give rise to four syllables, and so on until they pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
This is the 'Heart-Syllable' of the Buddha; I now ask about the method of accomplishment within this. "O son of good family, those who perceive this dharma..."
When virtuous women dwell in a state of joy, peace, and well-being, this is precisely what it means to practice and train within this teaching;
to achieve such perfection is called "seeing the Dharma. To achieve perfection means to realize the Truth (dṛṣṭadharma) in this very life.
Those who see the Dharma, upon hearing the Buddha teach this method of achievement, will surely [attain] profound [realization].
He inquires because he has attained the joy of the Dharma, abides in the practice of peace and happiness, and dwells in the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). As the Sūtra says:
"The intention regarding the non-harming of the *dharmadhātu* means that within this *dharmadhātu* there is nothing that can be obstructed.

Even when experiencing various worldly pleasures, these worldly pleasures are themselves the *dharmadhātu*; one never, by reason of them, harms or diminishes the *dharmadhātu*. It is not that the *dharmadhātu* is harmed.

Why is it non-harming? World-Honored One, because the Dharma-realm is the inconceivable realm, as taught by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Therefore, World-Honored One, the Dharma-realm cannot be destroyed;
when a Bodhisattva practicing the mantra path attains this, these four syllables achieve ultimate perfection and do not obstruct the Dharma-realm. These four...
Every word and phrase is the Buddha-mind; how could the Buddha-mind obstruct the Dharma-realm?

For those who dwell in this accomplishment and the Dharma-realm, there is no duality or distinction, and thus no mutual obstruction. This *siddhi* and that Dharma-realm do not obstruct one another at all.
Why is this? Because the Dharma-realm is inconceivable. Therefore, immeasurable Buddhas attain the Way and achieve accomplishment therein.
The dharma-realm does not increase when immeasurable sentient beings are liberated, nor does it decrease;

even if sentient beings advance toward excellence, there is no addition, and even if afflictions are destroyed, there is no loss. This inconceivable realm is by nature identical to a vajra and cannot be destroyed.
If there were obstruction, there would be "this" and "that"; where there is "this" and "that," there can be destruction. Now...
Because it is immediately without obstruction, it cannot be destroyed; this indestructibility also carries the meaning of being indivisible.
That is to say, various gates and various mundane and supramundane phenomena are of one single *dharmadhātu*, which cannot be analyzed to establish them as separate entities.
If one can thus penetrate this, it is the attainment of the vision of the accomplishment of the Dharma. At that time, the Buddha...
"Praising Vajrapāṇi: 'Excellent, excellent! You are indeed excellent! This is a repeated praise because he was able to inquire about such a great matter and its causal conditions.
'Out of compassion for those of the future who practice the path of mantra and conduct, you have raised such a question.
Now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.'"
"I shall explain this to you; listen attentively and reflect well upon it, for I shall explain such matters to you.
Next, [the text] says "Thus, O World-Honored One," meaning that Vajrapāṇi wishes to hear with joy. The Buddha said:
"O Lord of Secrets, that which is accomplished through the syllable *A* is the very state of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*)."

The "method for accomplishment" (*sādhana*) is performed therein. Regarding the "monastic residence," this refers to a temple, a mountain hermitage, a cave, or an interior room—any place according to one's preference.
The secret interpretation has already been set forth above. As the Sūtra says:
"One should cause the letter *A* to pervade all limbs; the practitioner who maintains three hundred thousand recitations shall mentally deploy this *A*."
The syllable *A* proceeds from the crown of the head and the eyes, ears, and so forth, pervading all internal and external parts of the body;

furthermore, by reciting this syllable *A* three hundred thousand times (*tri-lakṣa*), one achieves accomplishment. Moreover, the secret teaching states that the seed-syllable of the *iṣṭadevatā* (the tutelary deity) and the *maṇḍala* (perfect luminosity) are called the "three.
One visualizes the syllable within the *maṇḍala*, and the *maṇḍala* upon the heart of the *iṣṭadevatā*; when these three are realized as one, [accomplishment is attained].
Each of these constitutes a distinct condition (*pratyaya*) regarding these three objects; therefore, they are called "three lakṣas. *Lakṣa* here carries the meaning of "seeing.
Having recited these three lakṣas, one reaches the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, which is called the "full moon.

According to the text, once the recitation of the three lakṣas is completed, one should take the fifteenth day of the waxing moon to construct the maṇḍala for the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*). When performing this ritual:
Having made offerings to the Triple Gem with all that one possesses, when performing the *sādhana*, one should also recite these syllables (the secret explanation may be understood as before).
When performing this rite, whether it be Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, or any other Vajra—this term "respondent" (*prativādaka*) is not fixed to a specific deity;
whichever deity appears will come to grant accomplishment. However, upon seeing [the deity], there are also signs of superior, middling, or inferior [attainment]. If it is personal...

If one sees [the deity] as clearly as if facing them face-to-face, it is the highest accomplishment; if one merely hears their voice and they manifest before one to provide instruction, benefit, and joy, it is the middling accomplishment;

if one sees them in a dream and so forth, it is the lowest. Furthermore, when seeing them, by noting the distinctions between clarity and dimness, one knows whether there are obstructions or not (this secret teaching can be understood through the meaning alone).
Thus, when the *iṣṭadevatā* and others manifest before one and bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), at that very moment—
One should perform prostrations and offer argha; this consists of water with incense and flowers, further augmented by the five jewels, grains, and so forth, as previously described.
At that time, the practitioner immediately attains the samādhi of the non-forgetfulness of bodhicitta.
Because one has attained this samādhi, both mind and body achieve pliancy (pliancy means the removal of defilements and hindrances). Furthermore, by means of this very pliancy—

By practicing visualization and recitation, one attains purity of body and mind as described in the "Chapter on the Six Sense Organs," whereby all phenomena are perceived and the Buddha-mind can be known.
Because the body and mind have thus become pure, one immediately attains the "body born of thought" (*manomaya-kāya*), which arises in accordance with one's thoughts.
"Arising in accordance with thought" means that through the practice of recitation, the body and mind arise in a state of purity. This is the practice.
If one wishes to purify the faculty of hearing, one should visualize the letter *A* spread upon that faculty and recite it;

thus, one will attain purity of the faculty of hearing, enabling one to hear and retain teachings without forgetting, and to hear the Dharma preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions as well as the voices of devas and others, just as described in the Lotus Sūtra.
If one wishes to dwell for a long duration of life, one should visualize the letter *A*.
Regarding the inhalation and exhalation (meaning that by using these syllables for the breath, one makes the inhalation and exhalation distinct and uninterrupted):

if one contemplates with such mental attention during the three periods of each day, one will immediately attain eternal life. As for the secret teaching, the syllables, the phrases, and the *iṣṭadevatā* constitute the three periods.
If one wishes to subdue all poisons, one should visualize the syllable *A*—whether on oneself or another—within the body, as if it were [a flame].
Regarding the visualization for self-protection: one visualizes this syllable *A* at the site of the poison and gradually extends it throughout the body, thereby driving the poison downward.
As the poison gradually descends, the syllable follows it; once it has been completely expelled, the poison is eliminated. There are two kinds of poison: first, the poison of medicinal substances;
second, the poison of sentient beings, such as that of dragons, snakes, and the like. If explained esoterically, "poison" refers to...
If the three poisons are rampant and one wishes to eliminate them, one should expel them until they are exhausted by performing the ritual procedure as previously described.
If one wishes to cause others to feel affection and to take refuge, one should visualize the syllable *A* as one’s own body and the syllable *Ha* as the other’s body;
then, while holding a conch shell, one should further imagine holding a lotus flower with it.
If one gazes at each other while reciting this syllable *A* in the mind, even if the other is wrathful and arrogant, they will immediately submit with a loving heart.
As for the secret teaching: if one wishes to subjugate them, one should imagine one’s own mind as the syllable *A*, and imagine the other’s mind as the syllable *Ha*.
When the mind has a lotus and the hand holds a conch (*śaṅkha*), they will become compliant, and thus one will be able to subjugate them.
"Subduing" refers to the fact that even those things most difficult to subdue can be subdued; this refers to the higher afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, the Buddha told Vajrapāṇi:
"The various Tathāgatas have names derived from the mind, such as 'Acting through Karma,' 'Sporting in Play,' and 'Dancing.
These arise from the karmic activity of the Buddha-mind and perform various playful acts, manifesting the signs of various playful discourses; this is precisely the universal manifestation of forms."
"Body" refers to manifesting forms corresponding to the six realms of existence and so forth. "Dance" refers to various miraculous transformations and illusory manifestations;
these are displayed according to specific circumstances in such great numbers that they cannot be fully described.

"Sustained by the four elements" means that although this body appears as the internal and external environments and their inhabitants through the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, it arises solely from the Buddha’s mind.
The mind has a substance that is identical to emptiness and cannot be grasped; because the mind-king abides peacefully, it is equal to empty space.
Just as empty space is eternally unmoving yet contains all things, "seeing" refers to worldly fruits, while "not seeing" refers to fruits such as Bodhi;
since there are immeasurable categories such as these, they are called "vast. Furthermore, "seeing" refers to various kinds of dance and play.

That which is signless and non-perceptual is called the fruit of nirvāṇa; yet, one also perceives the various Dharma-gates practiced by the three vehicles, causing their aspirations to be fulfilled according to their wishes—this is precisely the ability to manifest all manner of visible and invisible phenomena.

Even when they pray for and seek the Dharma-gates of meditative concentration and wisdom, as well as the various jewels, [the Buddha] likewise manifests them according to their kind and bestows them upon them.
It is like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels, which bestows everything according to whatever the minds of sentient beings desire;
*samāhita* means "equipoise" (referring to the arising of supernormal powers and so forth through equipoise, not merely meditative attainment).
At that time, the Buddha Vairocana, having surveyed the entire great assembly, addressed the Lord of Mysteries, Vajrapāṇi (as explained above):
"Vajrapāṇi, the performance of the dance accomplishes all things; it is the vast manifestation of the results of creation and destruction, the bestower of all to all.

This 'dance' is a term for playful manifestation (*vikalpa*). It universally manifests the form-body (*rūpakāya*) to accord with various types, skillfully bringing them to completion and responding in manifold ways."
It is not real, but is merely like an illusion; therefore, it is called the dance of the Tathāgata.
Just as a dancer can delight the minds of the multitude, even though their various interpretations differ, he causes all hearts to rejoice; the Buddha is likewise.
However, this is not produced by the matter of the four elements; it arises according to the Buddha’s own intention, arising from the mind and following the mind.

Although the mind ceases and, while not being a permanent dharma, is able to arise and perish according to conditions—this arising and perishing occurring in accordance with conditions is called the "fruit of arising and perishing," which refers to formation and destruction. This also pervades all dharmas within the realms, being vast and boundless;
thus it is called "vast. Because what has been produced returns to cessation, it is called "formation and destruction. This formation and destruction is...

This is the meaning of transformation. Thus, this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is precisely the Tathāgata’s wondrous response, arising from the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) through the resonance of karmic conditions.
Although it arises, it does not arise; although it ceases, it does not cease. It is identical to an illusion and not different from the Dharma-realm, because that which is produced is unreal;
therefore, it is called a "dance. All Buddhas of the three periods of time perform this dance. [End of] *Qin* (Direct Encounter).
"Everything is bestowed by my own kin" means that I previously received this Dharma from a former Buddha and now bestow it upon you in person;
hence, it is said that "everything is bestowed by my own kin. "Kin" refers to those who are able to personally and directly bestow the fruits of all one's aspirations—this is the correct meaning.
First, regarding the "actual self-phase," it is as observed above: the seed-syllable mantra and the fundamental [mantra].
The Venerable One, having visualized the deity and having seen the deity, immediately transforms his own body into that of the deity;
this mutual interpenetration without mutual obstruction is the seeing of the vajra-realm, the bodhicitta.
Therefore, it is called "first establishing the mark of reality. To abide in such a sequence means that the mind dwells well within what was previously visualized.
Yexian has already personally realized the true nature (*dharmatā*). The *Ākṣara-sūtra* states:
"In this way, one first correctly contemplates," which means contemplating and recollecting the dharmas as explained in the preceding text.

One should personally form the syllable *Ā*, add the nasal dot (*bindu*), and within a square golden vajra-railing that is vast and exceedingly pleasing to the mind, contemplate and recite the names of all Buddhas.
Regarding "light pervading all places" and so forth, these are the teachings on the true nature of all Buddhas:
one contemplates the syllable *A* so that it becomes a deep yellow color; its form is upright, majestic, and beautiful, bringing joy to the mind, and it resides within one's own heart.
The Sūtra states that "adding points and expanding" means adding points above the characters; "expanding" refers to increasing them.

Furthermore, one draws four-cornered vajra-marked railings around these characters. These railings are fashioned by interlacing three-pronged vajras with one another, within which the characters are placed.
Upon seeing this letter *A*, one immediately transforms this character into Vairocana.
The form of the Vairocana Honzon is one's own body manifested as the image of the Honzon;
this image is produced according to the fundamental mudrā. This Buddha’s entire body is radiant;

this is the Buddha of the true aspect perceived within the bodhicitta, like seeing the image of pure gold within clear lapis lazuli, and is not the same as that which appears within other mental factors.
One should know that such a vision is precisely the vision of the Buddha who is the true nature of the mind;
one who accomplishes this without doubt or hesitation will be able to universally bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
The Sūtra says: "To possess that which is vast and marvelous" is like a phantom person possessing various extraordinary feats;

it is like the deeds of the great Bodhisattvas who, according to their will, benefit sentient beings. Like illusory water or the moon reflected in water, they respond to the myriad categories of beings and all things are accomplished.
This is the phrase regarding the Tathāgata’s illusion-like samādhi. If one can act in this manner...

The evil karma accumulated by the practitioner since beginningless time, the fruits of oppression from the three realms of existence, and even the heavy karma of the immediate [retributions], shall be extinguished in this very life; how much more so other karmas? To state the essential point:
all the fruits of suffering within the three realms of existence shall be extinguished. Why is this? Because the reciter has attained abiding in *samādhi*.
Therefore, if one contemplates the mind in this way according to its true nature—[the Sūtra says:

"If one contemplates that mind, it is the unsurpassed bodhicitta," meaning the practitioner contemplates the unsurpassed bodhicitta within their own mind]—this is precisely the unsurpassed great bodhicitta. If one abides in this contemplation, one is able to purify the karma of body, speech, and mind;
because one is able to purify such karma, one becomes detached from the fruits of both pure and impure karma. This is what is meant.
There is such karma that neither the pure nor the impure births can defile it.
As the Sūtra says: "Regarding 'karma of the future,' this refers to the karma for producing this pure mind in the next life; these fruits cannot be defiled. Why?
Because they are always in accord with the principle (*tattva*). It is like a lotus flower, which, though born from within the mud,"
And being thus unstained by those [defilements], such a practitioner is identical to all Buddhas.
Why? Because they are able to give birth to all Tathāgatas; this person is the most honored among the virtuous. (The meaning is:

if merely contemplating and abiding in the bodhicitta yields such a fruit, how much more so for one who has personally realized it and attained Buddhahood? At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata again dwelt in the state of subduing...

The Vajra-play Samādhi for Subduing the Four Māras: Abiding in this samādhi, one subdues the four māras, eliminates the afflictions, karma, and suffering of the six realms of existence, bestows the bliss of liberation, and fulfills the omniscience of all beings. This is the exposition of the vajra syllables.

One who abides in this samādhi is able to subdue the four māras, remove the afflictions, karma, and suffering of the six realms, grant the joy of liberation, and also fulfill the needs of all ordinary beings.
This is the aspiration of all the Noble Ones. The Buddha, abiding in this samādhi, spoke the mantra of the vajra-phrase:
*ĀVĪRA HŪṂ KHAM*. These five syllables are the mantra-phrase for subduing the four māras.
The syllable *Ā* is the practice, namely the practice of primordial non-arising (*anādikāla-anutpāda*). The addition of two dots [the vowel *i*] signifies purification.
The meaning [of the syllable *haṃ*] is that by this principle one can subdue the four māras and eliminate all suffering. The "taste" (*rasa*) signifies bondage;
when the long stroke of the *samādhi* is added above it, it becomes the "unbound samādhi," which is the inconceivable liberation.
*Ra* signifies the purification of the six sense faculties; because the six faculties are purified, there is no dust [of defilement]. The meaning of *hūṃ* has already been explained above.
The meaning of *kha* is also explained above; furthermore, *hūṃ* has three meanings, which are the three liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the Tathāgata.
By practicing and removing obstacles, one attains the three liberations, and from these three liberations, one abides in the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
"Kha" refers to this Great Emptiness. When the Buddha spoke this mantra, Vajrapāṇi, Samantabhadra, and others attained what they had never experienced before.
With eyes blossoming (as described above), he prostrates himself before all those who possess all-knowledge (*sarvajña*). Thus it is said:
"All-knowledge" refers to the Tathāgatas, who are the knowers of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-sarvajña*). "All wealth" (*sarvadhanam*)—in the Sanskrit sense, this means being without lack;
that is, the meaning of a treasury. It is said that these five syllables constitute the treasury of the Great Sage, capable of fulfilling all vows.
All wealth, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and World-Saviors— these Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and World-Saviors,
as well as Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas who have destroyed [the afflictions] (the term *sura* here is explained in the Sanskrit commentary as meaning "one who destroys the afflictions")—
who traverse the stages of practice and possess various supernormal powers; "wealth" refers here to the Dharma-jewel of the Tathāgata.
Because it provides for all sentient beings without ever becoming exhausted, this inexhaustible great treasury of wisdom-jewels is called "the one possessed of wealth.
Because the wealth of the Dharma can bestow everything upon all, this gateway of mantras is taught;
from the Buddhas above down to the śrāvakas below, there are none who do not rely on these phrases to perform various miraculous deeds.
Because it transforms and benefits all, it is said that "according to the stages of their practice, they manifest various supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*).
"Stages of practice" refers to wherever they travel; as the verse says: "Searching through lands, mountains, and forests, there is none equal.
They attain supreme wisdom—the Buddha-wisdom. This "supreme wisdom" means that they have attained not only supernormal powers, but also [wisdom] by virtue of this.
All noble sages attain wisdom through these phrases, even reaching the point of collectively achieving the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Although the wisdom of the two vehicles is also called "unsurpassed" in comparison to the mundane world, this term is repeated here to clarify the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha.

Having offered praise, he again requested the Buddha to explain the extensive method for the sequence of these five syllables, as well as the various practices such as the visualization of the mind and its placement.
Regarding "categories" (*jāti*), it is requested that all points not explicitly stated herein be explained within this context.

Regarding the arrangement of syllables and the visualization of syllables—whether superior, middling, or inferior—the various distinctions of color and function, and all diverse skillful means, are all requested of the Buddha to be extensively proclaimed.

Within these various gateways, the accomplishment, advancement, and compliant practice of this dharma is termed "instruction" (*śāsana*). As for those who personally proclaim this instruction, they request the Buddha himself [to do so].
This is an exposition. If a practitioner of the supreme mantra practices of the Mahāyāna were to hear this Dharma extensively expounded by the Buddha, they would come to see the Dharma;
those who have already seen it likewise all rejoice. "Seeing the Dharma" means to realize and attain it.
"One should abide [in it]" means that having seen it for oneself, one further imparts it to all sentient beings. By seeing this matter, both self and others together obtain the unsurpassed.

For the sake of the benefit of the Dharma, he requested the Buddha to explain this fundamental sūtra at length; it contains three thousand five hundred verses that expound the meaning of these five syllables.
"Samādhi" (the vowel *e* is drawn out) is correctly translated as "abiding of the mind on a single object.
The Buddha desired to cause the entire assembly to abide their minds on a single object while listening to the vajra-words; wishing to do this, [he spoke].
Regarding the method for accomplishing the Vajra-mantra, one should first have a vajra-throne constructed, just as when the Buddha was about to attain enlightenment at the Vajra-maṇḍala.
Once this throne is established, there is no other seat capable of surpassing it in excellence.
At that time, the Great Vajra becomes the boundary of the earth (meaning from the surface of the earth down to its limit); this boundary of the earth empowers the lower body.
In order to explain the supreme empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the letter A (the meaning being that this letter is the most excellent), and wishing to expound this Dharma, one first empowers oneself.
Regarding the lower body, from the navel downward, one should visualize it all as pure vajra. This has two aspects:
internal and external. "Internal" refers to what was described above; "external" refers to visualizing the place where one's own body is seated.
It is situated within the square Vajra-maṇḍala; as for that maṇḍala, its square layout and railings have already been described above.
It is called "Great Indra" because it is the most adamantine among all vajras; it can shatter vajras, yet no vajra can shatter it.
Furthermore, it is an intense yellow, like the color of refined gold (jāmbūnada-suvarṇa). One should visualize the syllable *A* upon this seat.
It is named the Vajracakra; within this seat, one contemplates that all things are the seat of yoga.
This is the place where those who practice according to reason sit. "Contemplating all" means that all matters are contemplated and enacted within this [seat].
Because the matters are numerous, it is called "all. This concludes the first explanation of the syllable *A*.
Having completed the arrangement of the seats, he next spoke the long-syllabled letter *A*. This letter is the primary life-force (*jīva-mūla*);
because it can sustain all other letters, it is called "life. If the letter *A* were absent, no other letters would arise;
thus, it is the phrase for summoning and gathering. If one contemplates this letter, it can summon and gather all internal and external phenomena, summoning them extensively.
Sound is itself conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*). If one touches the syllable *A*, it draws forth the activities of all Buddhas;
thus, it is called "summoning" (*ākarṣaṇa*), which means to gather [them] so that they belong to oneself for sovereign enjoyment.
This gateway of the syllable *A* can summon the merits of all Tathāgatas to return to one's own person and can also fulfill all aspirations. Next, it is explained:
If one contemplates the syllable *Aṃ*, this syllable is able to encompass all poisons, diseases, and other obstacles;
it can encompass and eliminate all internal and external obstacles. Internal obstacles refer to various factors that hinder the Path; as soon as they manifest, it can encompass and remove them.
External obstacles refer to all external things that act as hindrances; these too it can entirely encompass. Furthermore...
It removes all poisons and various diseases; whatever ailments there may be, it can eliminate them all.

Furthermore, it is able to restore those who have lost their minds, causing them to regain their original state of mind. Moreover, by means of this syllable, one can concentrate the mind on a single object and swiftly attain correspondence with *samādhi*.
Because meditating upon this syllable yields such merits as these, it is said to be "capable of gathering and bestowing."
To "bestow all fruits" means to grant them, which is to fulfill their aspirations and confer the fruit of *siddhi*.
If a practitioner, for one month, binds the Vajra-Wisdom Mudrā and recites the syllable *Aṃ* three times daily throughout that month,
the entire citadel of ignorance will be shattered, [and the darkness] of the ignorance of all sentient beings [will be dispelled].
That which is encircled on all four sides is as firm and solid as a fortified city, indestructible; yet by means of this gateway of letters (*akṣaramukha*), it can be destroyed.
That which is immovable and firm refers to that which cannot be destroyed by gods, humans, *asuras*, and others.
Whenever one wishes to perform any rite of augmentation (*puṣṭi*), one should sit upon this seat; thus, this is also called "Augmentation."
"Perfection" (*paripūrṇa*) means being able to fulfill all aspirations. If explained esoterically, "one month" refers to "one vision.
If one attains this vision, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), where all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and so forth increase spontaneously, continuing through the various stages.
When wishing to perform a rite of increase (*puṣṭi*), the reciter [should focus] upon this vajra.
Visualize the Buddha within the maṇḍala abiding in the samādhi-body, of true golden color, with a surrounding blaze of light and majestic radiance (*vibhūti*).
The meaning of "majestic radiance" is that it simultaneously clarifies the significance of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity). Such is the Sanskrit sound.
With a surrounding halo of flames, he has his hair as a crown; this is the Great Indra. This solidity of the great vajra is—
The meaning of the Buddha’s wisdom can shatter all that cannot be removed;
one should imagine this Buddha within the square vajra-maṇḍala, performing all accomplishments as desired.
The Sūtra states: "That which is called 'constant peace' refers to all such matters that should be performed within this wheel.
To accomplish the Vajra-dharma, one should fashion a five-pronged [vajra] of pure gold and place it within the maṇḍala;

furthermore, one seeks the superior, middling, and inferior accomplishments according to the ritual, as described above—namely, by reciting this syllable *A* in each case. If one wishes to accomplish Buddhahood...
Regarding the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*): one should fashion the Buddha’s crown out of pure gold and apply the ritual empowerment (*adhitiṣṭhati*).
If this is accomplished, it becomes identical to the body of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana. Alternatively, it may not be necessary to use separate materials;

rather, by visualizing with mastery that it is the Buddha’s body and applying empowerment, if it is accomplished, it becomes identical to the Buddha’s body. If one performs the *vajra-siddhi* and holds it, it becomes identical to the Vajra.
As for the Bodhisattva Hastavāla: if one wishes to accomplish the lotus, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus out of gold and perform the recitation within it;
if it is accomplished, one becomes identical to Avalokiteśvara. Regarding the sword, there is also a method for its accomplishment;

if it is accomplished, by wielding it, one becomes identical to Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta. Regarding the goose, there is a method for its accomplishment; if it is accomplished, by mounting it, one immediately [attains the same].

This body becomes the body of Brahmā. Among the external riches, one may achieve either yellow and white—namely gold and silver—or the earth (where "earth" refers to hidden treasures), or wish-fulfilling jewels and the like;
whatever accords with the rite of increase (*puṣṭi*) is all performed by means of this method. It possesses methods of the superior, middling, and inferior grades. This is the Mahendra [Ritual].
"Contemplation" refers to the visualization within the golden wheel.

Furthermore, regarding the methods for gathering and maintaining [the winds], although the previous explanations concerning the gathering of the winds and the formation of the seven points have been mentioned, they were not yet exhaustive;
these are now fully elucidated herein. All things that act as obstacles to the path are to be gathered by means of this method.
To cause them to be immovable and to unify all within a single object means to cause everyone to settle their minds and listen.
To perform this rite, first visualize Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, with eight peaks—that is, with peaks surrounding it on all four sides.
Upon these eight peaks, visualize a lotus flower, and upon the flower, three-pronged vajras with their prongs pointing upward. As the scripture says: "Place [them]."
The summit of that [vajra] is the head of the vajra. One should visualize above it the letter *A*, with its radiant flames encircling it on all sides.
Having visualized it thus, all obstacles are gathered and eliminated. Thus gathering them, one causes them to abide in a single object of focus without being able to move;
this is not the meaning of the Immovable Lord (*Acala*), but rather the sense of being firmly established, practicing the path at will with mastery and without hindrance.
Furthermore, regarding the methods for accomplishing medicinal preparations, when one wishes to accomplish such as these, there are complete sequential ritual applications;
here, however, I have merely briefly clarified the general principles. To perform the addition of the medicine to the drug, recite [the mantra] one hundred times.

Generally, whenever "one hundred" is mentioned, it refers to adding eight more times to make one hundred and eight recitations. Having finished the recitation, one may drink it oneself or give it to others; it is able to eliminate [ailments].
It can eliminate all illnesses, even those resulting from past karma; furthermore, all matters of increase and prosperity correspond with the yellow color of Vajra.
Next, the syllable-gateway *va* is explained;
it is the same as the aforementioned syllable *vi*. First, its binding (*bandha*) is clarified, which is further combined with samādhi.
As for this visualization: one should conceive of this syllable as being purely white, as brilliant and pure as a snow mountain, cow’s milk, and the like.
First, one visualizes a white lotus flower above the navel, extremely white and radiant;
one then visualizes the syllable VAṂ, pure white, situated upon that white flower. Once it has been accomplished, one then turns this syllable back.
Because he is made the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity), this is the foremost among all rites for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*).

That Buddha, as the *iṣṭadevatā*, also assumes a tranquil form; the meaning of supreme tranquility abides in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), pure white and peerless, like the moonlight of an autumn night.
That maṇḍala should be constructed as nine concentric circles, just like nine successive lunar disks.
Visualize it as having the appearance of fine, drifting white clouds and mist, and abide within it. By accomplishing this rite, all the heat of afflictions and the like are entirely pacified;
indeed, all practices corresponding to the pacification of calamities (*śāntika*) are performed herein.
Regarding "cow’s milk" and "like a string of pearls": visualize that from within these syllables, a stream of cow’s milk flows forth in continuous, unbroken drops, just as described above.

It is like white pearls pouring down and filling one's heart; whether for oneself or others, when one visualizes this pouring, there is no internal or external feverish affliction that is not removed. Or, visualize it as the moon or as pure crystal;
let the light of the moon flow everywhere, and all those who suffer from the ailment of feverish affliction will have it entirely eliminated by this infusion.
All *śāntika* rites are performed here in association with the color white.
Among these, the preceding syllable *A* is the Vajra Maṇḍala; this syllable *Va* is named the Water-Wind Maṇḍala.

[The square (gold/the earth/yellow), the circle (compassion/the water/white), the triangle (wisdom/the fire/red), and the crescent (supernatural power/the wind/black): though empty and formless, it manifests in various ways.]

Furthermore, from within the maṇḍala of the moon-disc cloud-cluster, there emerges a flow like milk that can eliminate all feverish afflictions—namely, the internal and external obstacles which are these very "fever-obstructions.
This is entirely capable of removing them; "to be freed" means to escape from this suffering and distress.
Thus, by binding the object of focus to a single point, one accomplishes [the attainment of] ghee, milk, along with pearl garlands, lotus fibers, and crystal.
Whether it be water, curd, or other such substances in great abundance, whatever one desires to perform according to one’s will,
if it is associated with the *śāntika* (pacifying) rite, it shall all be accomplished. Whether seeking long life and dwelling for immeasurable time,
or manifesting various bodies with marks that are upright, exquisite, and extraordinary— some say that "supreme" means the most supreme among those worthy of love and respect— it shall be so.

Whether one seeks to be loved and respected by others, or seeks the power of hearing and retention (*śrutadhāraṇī*), or seeks intelligence, or seeks wisdom, or seeks the cessation of all diseases—all such things shall be accomplished.
Furthermore, if a dot (*bindu*) is placed above this syllable *ba* (縛), and the syllable *pra* (𑖯) is added, it can likewise eliminate illnesses and other matters;
all internal and external poisons will be swiftly extinguished. This is the auspicious rite for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*).
The maṇḍala also encompasses and eliminates immeasurable matters; thus it is called "etcetera.
Next, the *ra* syllable maṇḍala for the removal of obstacles is explained: among all methods for removing obstacles, this is the foremost, the most authentic dharma.
This *ra* syllable is the reddest of the red, the fiercest of fires, and the burningest of burns. By means of it—
It can incinerate and extinguish various afflictions, karmas, and sufferings, even those as grave as the five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*).
If one cultivates this gateway of letters (*akṣaramukha*), it can also purify them until nothing remains. Once the transgressions have been eliminated, all manner of virtuous merits will arise.
This gateway of letters functions in conjunction with Acala Vidyārāja; yet, Acala Vidyārāja himself is capable [of this].

To perform all matters in three grades, the method is as follows: first, abide as described above in one-pointed concentration and visualize an extremely red triangular maṇḍala that is most pleasing to the mind.
This term "pleasing to the mind" means making it vivid and exquisitely orderly.
Furthermore, "pleasing to the mind" implies performing this within one's own heart; this is the secret instruction. Surround it with flames.
Visualize the syllable *raṃ* in the center of a garland that has the appearance of the blazing flames of a fierce fire.
Once this syllable has been formed, it transforms into Acala Vidyārāja, appearing in a serene form—neither wrathful nor smiling, his countenance tranquil. Furthermore, it is said:
first visualize Acala Vidyārāja, and upon his heart, visualize a triangle within which the syllable *raṃ* is formed.

It is transformed into Acala Vidyārāja; because it removes obstacles, transgressions are extinguished, and because it is tranquil, it pacifies calamities—this is the meaning of the extinction of transgressions and the arising of merit. This "accomplishment of the object" refers to this triangular mandala.
*Graha* means the retinue that seizes the sun; all eight luminaries are called "seizers. Regarding the sun...
The rites for the various deities such as the *Ābhāsvara* gods and the Fire God (*Agni*) are largely the same, performed in the southeast corner.

This refers to practices such as requiring fire for ritual use, or cooling the fire, all of which are performed within this context. However, it is said that the secret meaning is the production of the fire of one’s own wisdom (*svajñānāgni*).
The sun is likewise the sun of wisdom (*prajñāditya*). As for "gathering" (*saṃgraha*), it means gathering those who follow unwholesome dharmas and those who are difficult to discipline.
This means to make [them] pliant and subdued (the meaning is that the twenty-eight lunar mansions and twelve houses, etc., occupy the same positions as the moon and water).
Herein, "subduing wicked people" refers to being able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*) and attain mastery.

Furthermore, regarding "arousing enemies," it means being able to cause both oneself and others to achieve success (that is, by arousing those enemies, etc.). "Drying up the various limbs" means being able to cause their bodies to wither away.
It is that which is capable; it takes the three poisons as its fundamental essence and causes them to be exhausted without remainder.
To speak in terms of external signs, "drying up" refers to the exhaustion of dragon pools and the like.
All activities of the agent—all matters corresponding to subjugation—are performed within this context. Nevertheless, all are in correspondence with compassion, in order to...

"Because they have been subdued, well-tamed, and made into causes and conditions for the Buddha-way, [the syllable] Ha is the foremost reality," and so forth—this is the wind maṇḍala. The nature of wind is able to augment all things;

that which is produced by wind refers to all matters concerning the performance of the functions of wind, all of which are produced within this altar, and it is also that which gives rise to these various phenomena.
Furthermore, just as all phenomena may undergo depletion or transformation, so too is the function of these characters;
that is to say, regarding the process by which seeds arise from karma and so forth to grow and flourish, one attains mastery over them.
If a bindu (anusvāra) is placed above [the character], it can destroy all such matters of karma and its causes. As for the method: first, visualize the Principal Deity upon one's own forehead.
Form the two eyebrows into the shape of a half-moon and place a syllable within it. First visualize it facing outward, then turn it back toward oneself.
This half-moon has the appearance of great majestic power and light, with black flames radiating out everywhere;
it bears the insignia of being stirred by the wind. "Evil" refers to the image assuming an extremely wrathful form and color. Thus it is said.
However, the Honored One of the Wind-wheel is not Trailokyavijaya; his image is also made of a deep blue color (that is, a blackish hue).
If one performs this accomplishment, one can bring about various benefits for all sentient beings.

Next, regarding the accomplishments—namely, the objects listed below—they are performed within the wind; that is, by manifesting this very body, they are all attained, meaning one ascends into the void.

The "empty" refers to the supernormal powers of transformation (*ṛddhi-vidhi*) as well as the divine eye and divine ear; "disappearing" means concealing one's own body, while "opening" refers to opening the palaces of the asuras and so forth.
What follows below regarding "recollection" (*smṛti*) simply means performing it by means of the mind. These five characters are all accomplished through mental activity as the mandala.
Furthermore, one may construct the mandala through ritual methods (*kriyā-dharma*), yet one should contemplate that the mind corresponds with it. For example, by...

One should construct a mandala according to the ritual characteristics and practice the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) while seated within it; one may also place lotus roots and the like within the mandala and perform the visualization.

One should imagine that white milk flows and fills the interior. In the past, when the Buddha sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he descended from this gateway of syllables (*akṣaramukha*) to subdue the immeasurable hosts of Māra’s armies.
If a practitioner can train and practice in accordance with the Dharma, [they shall likewise achieve success].
Before long, he will likewise manifest in person like the Tathāgata and be able to subdue those armies; he of great renown is precisely that subduer of Māra.
Next, by means of the gateway of the syllable *ha*, one transforms it into the syllable *kha*; the syllable *ha* signifies "cause," for there is a cause.
Thus, there is the appearance of receiving the fruits of karma according to one's actions; however, within this primary truth (*paramārtha*), the gateway of the syllable *ha* is fundamentally unborn.
Because it is unborn, a cause cannot be apprehended. If even this cause is itself originally unborn, how much more so could there be karma and its fruit therein?
When viewed in this way, the three things—cause, karma, and fruit—are all quiescent.
If one can contemplate in this way—that which is unobtainable—one is identical to the Tathāgata sitting beneath the Bodhi tree and subduing Māra.
Because these causes and conditions are likewise unobtainable, this is its characteristic: it is like space, empty and yet further empty.
Therefore, when the Great Virtuous World-Honored One speaks of "form," he is speaking of the "form of space. Thus, it is added above.

The point (bindu) enters the gateway of the syllable *kṣa*. This gateway of the syllable *kṣa* explains that the name "Venerable" (*bhadanta*) means "the Venerable among the venerable," which is Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
If one wishes to accomplish all ritual vessels, they shall all be accomplished;
their names are manifold and immeasurable, beyond full description. Their maṇḍala is neither square nor circular, but shaped like a half-moon.
One should know that while space is signless (*animitta*), this maṇḍala manifests in various colors and can accommodate the appearance of various colored forms.
Regarding the performance together with the sword-seal (*khaḍgamudrā*): this means performing the accomplishment while simultaneously protecting it with the sword-seal.
The sword should be made of high-carbon steel (*vimala-loha*), the cord should be made of thread or lotus fiber, and the wheel should be made either of gold or of high-carbon steel.
(The place of benefit is below, named Nalaccha. These vessels are so numerous that they cannot be recorded in full; there is a separate diagram [of them] (this is named Mugalan).
Regarding the various vessels mentioned above, whichever one is used for a particular rite, it is accomplished by means of this syllable *khaṃ*.
If the superior, middling, or inferior accomplishments are attained, they are employed according to the specific task, and even when success is achieved, they are maintained and carried with them.
Wandering through the buddha-fields, they are called vidyādhara-siddhas.
Next, to explain further the meaning of the five syllables: if one abides in this principle and acts in accordance with specific circumstances, one will be able to accomplish all activities.
Therefore, the Buddha, observing the great assembly, addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying: "This is the gateway of mantras for bodhisattvas..."

When the Bodhisattva practicing *sādhana* attains all phrases and meanings through the abandonment of both internal and external things by means of the letter A in its own original color, it means that he is in resonance with the fundamental essence and original color of the letter A.
