Visualize the dot (*bindu*) as the practitioner’s head, and the remainder as the body and its four limbs. (Question: Does the water flow from the letter *A* down into the other letters? Answer: It does. By means of this practice...
Because these individuals do not yet recognize their own minds, skillful means are employed to bring about such recognition. First, they are made to contemplate the lotus flower;

furthermore, by cleansing their minds with the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), when this letter *A* is seen clearly and penetratingly, all the sense faculties and all defilements gradually become purified.
Because the six sense faculties are thus pure and free from stain, the nature of the mind is stainless, like the light of the moon reflected in clear water.
One should know that this is precisely what is called "seeing the seer. This seeing is the accomplishment; the accomplisher is identical in essence to the *dharmadhātu*.
One should know that this *dharmadhātu* is primordially quiescent and serves as the support for all sentient beings and the world-systems.
It is just as sentient beings depend upon the world-system, and so on down to the earth-disk depending upon water, water depending upon wind, and wind depending upon space.
It serves as the support for all things while itself being without support; the Dharma-realm is likewise. Because sentient beings are defiled by ignorance, they cannot understand it themselves;
now, because their six sense-faculties are purified, they see it clearly. When it was not yet seen, there were further expedient means, which are also found in another chapter.
Furthermore, when the practitioner contemplates these two characters "non" (非) and "direct" (直), they must further contemplate within themselves.
By causing all syllables to pervade and clearly distinguish each limb, at that very moment all matters become manifest, and one becomes a Vidyādhara.
Because one is able to employ these various gates of syllables with mastery, one becomes a Vidyādhara-siddha.
Furthermore, regarding what is called "seeing" herein, it is not a seeing characterized by attainment; because it is stainless, one is able to see, and this seeing is itself the Dharmadhātu.
The essence is like a mirror; because it is pure, the myriad phenomena appear of themselves. Yet it does not form such discriminations as "I am the seer" or "those various things are the seen.
Nor does it discriminate the characteristics of coming and going; it simply perceives through the conjunction of conditions.
All sentient beings are likewise identical to this essence of the *dharmadhātu*. When one perceives in this manner, that is *siddhi*.
This mark can universally manifest the form-body (*rūpakāya*) to display the inexhaustible treasury of adornments.
Because the practitioner’s mind is pure, they not only possess the exquisite bliss of the celestial realms but also attain the subtle and wondrous bliss of Great Nirvāṇa;

they also see the Tathāgata, for every phrase [of the teaching] is the seat of all Buddhas (meaning the dwelling place of the Buddha). When one sees it in this manner as described above, it is still not yet called [the true realization].
This is the vision of ultimate accomplishment.

Furthermore, there is a skillful means: the practitioner who contemplates the syllable-gate *ra* should place these two syllables above both eyes, their radiance like that of a lamp, glowing with red flames. When the practitioner sits, they should slightly bend the neck; by this means—
With eyes like the light of a stainless gem, one gazes inwardly at the mind; because the mind is like this syllable *raṃ*, one is able to perceive the nature of the mind.
The neck should be kept neither too bent nor too straight. This has two meanings:
first, to regulate the body so that it does not suffer illness, for if one sits with the body too bent or too straight, the four great elements will not be in harmony; second, it signifies purity.
Because the faculty of the eye quickly reaches the source of the mind, this syllable-gateway *ra* is the bright lamp of pure knowledge and vision;
by observing the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the lotus throne of the mind with this eye of wisdom, one swiftly attains accomplishment.
Furthermore, when sitting, the tongue should neither touch the upper palate nor hang down too far toward the lower lip; it should remain in the middle. Thus, with the purified eye, one observes.
One's own mind is likewise devoid of such characteristics as subject and object; it is only because the necessary conditions are complete that one attains such a vision.
Thus the Buddha told Vajrapāṇi: "The characteristics of coming and going—this practice arises from the mind, and the mind serves as the illumination that can perceive the path of the Tathāgata.
Practice is itself the Path. The Path is both practice and its fruition. It is not [otherwise]."
However, what I have thus spoken is no different from what has been taught by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.

As previously stated, regarding the skillful means of mantras and even the visualization of this locus of the mind as stainless and pure like a perfect mirror constantly manifesting before one, you should know that this is precisely the true mind proclaimed in common by the Buddhas of the past. Thus it is.
The nature of the mind is eternally abiding, without change or transformation, and indestructible; this is precisely the Great Parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, and is therefore called "Reality.
Because one purifies this mind through the gateway of the syllable *ra* and others, the light of the wisdom of Reality arises.
By means of this light of mental wisdom, one directly perceives the path traversed by the Buddhas of antiquity, namely, the Mantra of the Secret Treasury.

This is the gateway. When a practitioner encounters this True Word (mantra) path, consciousness (*vijñāna*) also emits light; "consciousness" here refers to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*).

As explained in the Hīnayāna, "mind" (*citta*), "thought" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are merely differences in terminology. In the Mahāyāna, however, there are distinct characteristics:
it is said that the six consciousness-bodies are merely the conjunction of three conditions and are unable to definitively cognize all phenomena.
That which discriminates is the mind. Because the mind is pure, the six consciousnesses are likewise radiant and luminous.
It is like the nature of a great precious jewel, which is eternally pure yet becomes stained by dust and grime.

If a person polishes it, gradually removing the coarse impurities until it becomes increasingly bright, it will then be able to rain down various jewels without obstruction, its light and color being beyond compare. So it is with the six [consciousnesses] of sentient beings.

Consciousness is likewise so; because the source of the mind is pure, the six consciousnesses are also entirely pure—this is what is called the purity of the nature of the six sovereign kings (*ṣaḍ-vaśavartin-rāja*).
When that practitioner of the mantra path perceives the nature of the mind in this way, they are seeing the Perfectly Awakened One, the Two-Legged One.
That which is eternally free from error and inversion is called "correct"; by means of this correct knowledge and vision, one realizes all phenomena.
Among those with two feet, humans and devas, he is the most honored, and is thus named the "Two-footed Honored One" (further consult the scriptural commentaries). Why is this so?
Because apart from this nature of mind, it is impossible to perceive a Tathāgata anywhere else; the practitioner perceives the Buddha within this very mind.
At that time, it is called the first siddhi, which is the attainment of the supreme eternal body.
There are many kinds of siddhis, with immeasurable distinctions, whether worldly or supramundane;
yet this particular accomplishment is the foremost supramundane siddhi, namely, the accomplishment of the supreme eternal body—this eternal body.
This is precisely the indestructible vajra-body of all Buddhas. When one perceives this mind, it is the perception of the Tathāgata’s state;
one knows that all phenomena are like the ten similes—neither arising nor ceasing, their nature eternally unborn.
By attaining this true wisdom, one perceives the reality-limit (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Although it is explained in this way, the practitioner is still not yet able to reach ultimate realization.
To clearly perceive the nature of the mind, there is another expedient means, namely, transforming the syllable *ra* into the syllable *laṃ*.
Previously, one visualized the syllable *ra* within the eyes while contemplating the mind; now, further transform this syllable *ra* into the syllable *laṃ*.
As before, slightly lower the throat so that it is neither too curved nor too straight, and adjust the tongue to its proper height and position.
One contemplates the letter *A* within the heart. This letter *Laṃ* signifies "form" (*lakṣaṇa*).
The dot above it represents the Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahāśūnyatā-samādhi*), which is the foremost dharma of signlessness (*animitta*) among signless dharmas.
Since all signs are inherently non-substantial dharmas, this sign, by its very nature, does not arise; thus, it is identical to Great Emptiness.
This is precisely the dharma of the firm and true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). To contemplate in this way, such that all phrases of emptiness correspond with principle, is the phrase of immortality.
The phrase of immortality is the eternally abiding body of all Buddhas.
By means of this expedient method of the letter *laṃ*, one is detached from all marks; this is the eternal body. The eternal body is the emptiness of all dharmas.

This is the verse of immortality. If one desires the vast wisdom, the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), or the *vidyādhara* siddhis and so forth, O Long-lived Youth, for as long as one has not yet attained the recitation [of this], one does not conform to the body of vast wisdom; that very body is the body of the Tathāgata.
This means that all the merits of the three vehicles, down to the five supernatural powers, longevity, and other such matters, are apart from this.
The syllable *Raṃ* is the gate of signlessness; therein, there is no sense of attainment. Why is this?
If a person’s mind clings to signs, they become bound by fetters and entanglements, revolving according to karma and failing to attain mastery.

If even worldly *siddhi* cannot be attained, how much less the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and so forth? If there is no possibility of attaining even the five supernormal powers, how much less the Tathāgata?

Is it the body of the wisdom of equality? Therefore, the Buddha taught that all the merits and benefits of the three vehicles, both mundane and supramundane, are accomplished from within the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).

Just as there are many kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), if a practitioner, through a mind free from signs and non-attachment, attains even the five supernormal powers of the two vehicles, and if they cultivate this further, then...

When one is able to attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of a bodhisattva, these five powers constitute the sovereign functioning of a bodhisattva who has ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Compared to the powers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), they are like the light of the sun compared to that of a firefly.

A *vidyādhara* refers to a practitioner who, having attained the fruit of the sublime accomplishment of *siddhi*, is able to travel universally to all Buddha-fields to make offerings to the Buddhas and bring sentient beings to maturity.

If one does not contemplate this dharma-gate of original emptiness and quiescence, which is free from all marks, even such a *ṛṣi* cannot be attained; this is precisely what constitutes entering the stages of a Bodhisattva.
"Long-lived" means possessing mastery over life, remaining eternally in the world to benefit sentient beings and drawing near to all Buddhas.
"Child" means having a lifespan of immeasurable years, always appearing as a youth of sixteen with a fresh and youthful complexion; he is also a vidyādhara-ṛṣi.
The meaning of the sūtra is that if one does not accord with such a dharma-gate that is free from all marks, even this ṛṣi [would not be able to...]
It is impossible to reach [the limit], let alone the inconceivable activity of the ultimate *dharmakāya*. The wisdom of mantra gives rise to true wisdom;
it is the supreme wealth of all Buddhas. Because one enters the gateway of the syllable *laṃ*, one is free from all marks and directly perceives the Tathāgata.
This is the wisdom of equality, the great wisdom, the true wisdom—such is the truth.
Regarding this, it is said that among all dharmas, wisdom is supreme; all Buddhas take this as their wealth, for "wealth" has the meaning of "enjoyment.
Such a treasure of the wealth of wisdom is immeasurable in number;

by enjoying it with mastery, they accomplish the Buddha-work and bestow it universally upon sentient beings—this is precisely the meaning of the Great Elder in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Thus, [the Bodhisattva]...

The Saviors of the World, as far as those who travel through the lands by means of the two vehicles and dwell in the Buddha-fields, all that they proclaim and manifest likewise proceeds from this Dharma-gate;
it is by means of this practice that they attain the Unsurpassed Way.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "To be free from all marks is what is called the Buddhas. [Siddhi is the wondrous fruit of the mantra; for the sake of this fruit, one cultivates the causal practices. Thus, herein...]
[The "accomplishment" refers to the accomplishment of activity. Chapter Eight:
The Ritual of the Maṇḍala of the Revolving Wheel of Syllables.
As above, Vajrapāṇi questioned the Buddha regarding the characteristics of the coming and going of mantras and their practices and fruits; the Buddha has now finished answering.
The Tathāgata further observed the great assembly with the eye cultivated through great compassion as he surveyed the realm of sentient beings;
this "great assembly" refers to the congregations of vajra-holders and others, numbering as many as the atoms in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
Having long cultivated the eye of great compassion throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Tathāgata’s observation of the world also possesses a specific intention, namely:
Furthermore, he will expound subtle skillful means so that all the worlds may receive great benefit.
Having contemplated thus, one enters the Samādhi of the Birth of Ambrosia (*amṛta*).

Just as when worldly people drink poison they meet with immediate death, yet if they should encounter celestial ambrosia and drink it, they immediately become neither old nor dead, and all their ailments and sufferings vanish.
There is nothing that is not healed; body and mind become cool and blissful, attaining a state of happiness never before experienced. Now, this samādhi is likewise so:

if one hears, contemplates, and practices it, one immediately attains the supreme mundane-transcending bliss, with a lifespan that is eternally abiding, and achieves the Tathāgata’s bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*). Arising from this concentration, he further expounds upon all three periods of time.
Regarding the Vidyārājñī of Unimpeded Power, "Unimpeded Power of the Three Times": throughout the three times, there is nothing capable of destroying her;
such is the power of this vidyā. Because she removes the darkness of all ignorance and afflictions, she is called a "Vidyā" (Illumination).

However, there is a distinction between the meaning of "vidyā" and that of "mantra": that which issues from the mind and mouth is called a mantra, whereas [that which issues] from all parts of the body is [a vidyā].
That which arises spontaneously is called "vidyā" (knowledge/illumination). Because it signifies the sense of growth, it is addressed in the feminine gender;
just as a king is honored by his position, his consort is likewise held in high esteem, and is thus called a "vidyārājñī" (Knowledge Queen).

As in the first volume of the *Vajrapāṇi*, where the Buddha was questioned from beginning to end and answered that entire inquiry, with no other speech interrupting the dialogue in the interim, here too—
The Buddha again reiterated his previous intention and replied as follows: Having already briefly explained the meaning of the syllable-gateway *laṃ*, the Buddha now,
for the sake of those who practice the path of mantra and conduct (*mantracaryā*) so that they may fulfill all conditions and swiftly attain the unsurpassed way,
rose from the *amṛtodbhava-samādhi* (the samādhi born of nectar) and spoke this vidyā-queen.
Gagana-same (equal to space), aprati-same (asked), sarva-tathāgata (all Tathāgatas), samantānugate (having reached the abode together with all Tathāgatas;
asked again), gagana-same (repeatedly equal to space), vara-locane (vara is the supreme vow; locana is the sign).
*Gagana-samaye*: "Gaga" has the meaning of "going. Repeating it as "gaga" clarifies that this very practice is precisely non-existence;
it is practicing without practice. This first indicates [the nature] and subsequently negates [dualistic grasping].
It means that this signless and unimpeded Dharma is identical to empty space—immeasurable, unobstructed, and all-pervasive. Yet, there is further meaning of distinction, for which reason...
What is meant by this? If all phenomena were simply like space, they would possess neither faults nor virtues.
However, although these [phenomena] herein are signless and unimpeded—just like empty space—they nevertheless possess all the true virtues of the Tathāgatas, with nothing left incomplete;
therefore, the meaning of the second phrase is now clarified. Although this emptiness is cited as a metaphor, it is not merely a comparison.
There are immeasurable and boundless virtues free from characteristics that cannot be illustrated even by empty space;
these merits are equal to the Tathāgata and are the destination of all Tathāgatas. (The second phrase is asked again.
Next, it says *gagana-samaya*: although they possess myriad virtues, they do not manifest anything, being identical to the Great [Space].

"Because it is empty, it is stated twice" (this refers to the meaning of the interrogative phrase). Herein, what is called "unimpeded power" (*anāvaraṇa-bala*) means that "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*) signifies being indestructible and also signifying being signless (*animitta*). Because it is unimpeded and signless, it cannot be destroyed.

Within samādhi, the Buddha manifests this consort (*vidyārājñī*); that which is spoken by the mouth is called a mantra-dhāraṇī (masculine gender), while that which is manifested by the body is called... [the name].
The Vidyārājñī [states]: "By means of this son of good family, the Vidyārājñī and the body of the Tathāgata are a non-dual realm.
By the power of this, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of great renown attain the unimpeded Dharma and are able to extinguish suffering.
It is said that this Vidyārājñī is identical to the body of the Tathāgata; if one does not awaken to this principle, there is no way to achieve Buddhahood. If one realizes the signless and the...
The principle of non-obstruction is precisely the attainment of mastery over all phenomena and the realization of Bodhi.
Thus, this signlessness is the profound realm of the Tathāgata; it can be known only by Buddha after Buddha, and for this reason it is called the "Buddha-realm.
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time enter through this gate, they pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
He manifests through the gates to bring sentient beings to fulfillment without end;
for this reason, he attains a great reputation that is heard throughout the ten directions, and is thus called "Great Renown.

He has attained the unimpeded Dharma because, being without obstruction, without marks, and without hindrance, he is able to eliminate all suffering of body and mind for all sentient beings, truly and without falsehood, leading them all to ultimate realization.
Ultimately, this leads to the bliss of unsurpassed great enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Because one does not comprehend the ultimate truth, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Due to ignorance, there arise formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and from these, various kinds of suffering are produced.
Although a bodhisattva has entered the stages (*bhūmi*), they have not yet comprehended the profound and secret realm of the Tathāgata; this is likewise subtle ignorance.
This is suffering; now, for their sake, the Buddha causes them all to ultimately reach the realm of the Buddha, and thus it is said that "all suffering is removed.
To remove the suffering of ignorance is to bestow upon them the inconceivable liberation, the immeasurable and boundless merits of the Buddhas, and the bliss of the present dharma.
As for the term "consort" (*bhāryā*), it is like a worldly woman who can give birth to sons and daughters.
Because this vidyā can produce all the merits of all Tathāgatas, ensuring that the lineage is never severed, it is termed "Queen" (mudrā) in its meaning.
When a practitioner cultivates the true words and practices, although there are various such expedient means as mentioned above, they must nevertheless uphold this vidyā-queen;
otherwise, the manifold virtues will not be complete.
At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana reflected upon all Buddhas, thinking: "I am primordially unborn by virtue of the power of grasping the vajra.
He then addressed the foremost Vajradhara, saying: "The Tathāgata has arisen from the samādhi born of nectar;
having thus arisen, he reflects that I am primordially unborn because all Buddhas are fundamentally unborn, being non-dual with all Buddhas."

Because it is the essence, one thus takes up the *A* syllable of primordial non-arising to empower oneself and Vajradhara, addressing them with the empowerment of the power of non-arising. All things enter the gateway of the *A* syllable;
this is the essence of non-duality. Having contemplated in this way, one then addresses the foremost of the vajras. [The foremost...]
This is not limited to the Lord of Secrets alone; rather, all the Vajradharas throughout the ten Buddha-fields are the foremost leaders.

Listen attentively, son of good family! This chapter on the practice of the Maṇḍala of the Revolving Syllable-Wheels (*akṣara-cakra*) extensively explains the Bodhisattva’s performance of Buddha-works through the gateway of mantras.
One who is able to abide before it—the "wheel" refers to the syllable-gateway *A*—this single syllable is [the essence].
The central [syllable] enters into all syllables, and all syllables enter into this single syllable; it revolves without obstruction among all phenomena.
It is like the wheel of worldly people: if it does not turn, that is one thing, but once it turns, there is no end to it;
its beginning and end cannot be discerned, and for this reason it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). Furthermore, when the wheel of the world revolves, [it is likewise without end].
It can sever all types of grasses and trees; whatever encounters this wheel—whether its roots, stems, branches, or leaves—there is nothing that is not shattered.
Why is this? Because its edges and blades are sharp. This *ā* syllable wheel is likewise able to destroy all ignorance and afflictions;
wherever it is directed, there is nothing that is not crushed and extinguished. This is the maṇḍala.
The meaning of "Purity" (viśuddhi) will be further explained below. Regarding the term "Extensive" (vaipulya): this refers to the sense within [the text] that its meaning pervades all places.

This specific section is merely one part of the whole; because the extensive meaning is like a wheel that has no end or exhaustion, and yet even this single part of the scripture does not depart from that wheel, it is given this name.
That all other sections are called "extensive" should be understood by analogy with this.
(That is to say, because the words are abbreviated and the meaning is partial, it is inexhaustible. That which is "originally unborn" is the *A* syllable wheel;

entering this wheel is to be of one essence with all Buddhas, non-dual. Because the Buddha wishes to enable Bodhisattvas who practice the path of mantra to achieve accomplishment, he first praises the merits of this *A* syllable wheel before explaining it, [stating that] if one attains this wheel, it can cause all Bodhisattvas...
The Buddha universally manifests before all sentient beings, appearing in a body that is pleasing for all to behold, and dwells before them to transform and deliver them;
because he performs the work of a Buddha through great causes and conditions, it is said that he "dwells before them."

At that time, the Vajradhara prostrated to the Buddha and, having descended into the corresponding position below the Vajra-svayambhu (the Self-Existent Vajra) and seated himself upon the lotus pedestal, he praised the Buddha. This Bodhisattva uses a lotus pedestal atop a vajra as his seat;
the vajra is the Wisdom-Seal (*jñāna-mudrā*) of all Buddhas, and it serves as the pedestal for this Buddha-Wisdom-Seal Great Maṇḍala.
Thus, there is that which is symbolized: just as when a vajra is thrown into the air, it revolves while descending to the ground, so too it was with this Bodhisattva.
Having heard the Buddha further explain the wheel of the letter A, he leaped for joy;
immediately, this platform rotated upon the vajra and descended from his seat. As he descended, he prostrated before the Buddha. At the moment of his descent—
Because it resembles a mallet thrown into the air, which spins as it descends, it is said to be "corresponding with that.
This also symbolizes the unimpeded wisdom of the Buddha. Because of reverence for hearing the Dharma, those on the lower stages pay their respects.
To take refuge in the bodhicitta is to take refuge in the minds of all sentient beings (as stated above: "This mind is the bodhicitta"). Homage!
Furthermore, those who have generated the bodhicitta prostrate to the one who can generate this mind (namely, the one who enters the gate of illumination through the pure bodhicitta).
They bow their heads to the one who practices the pāramitās of the ground, for the essence of practice consists of both the grounds and the pāramitās.
They pay homage to the original creator, for although all sentient beings...

Because one possesses this bodhicitta yet cannot fully realize it oneself, one takes refuge in those of antiquity who, having generated the mind and attained fruition, turned and showed the way to sentient beings;

thus, out of mindfulness of their great kindness, one bows once more. The repetition of the words "I take refuge" and "I prostrate at the crown of my head" signifies that while the general meaning is the same, there are slight differences in emphasis.
Such repetition is used because of the profound nature of one's reverence. Thus he praised.
The Buddha having already been invited again is like a worldly person who raises silkworms for profit and nurtures them well;
this is also like that, for in order to request the Buddha to further explain the profound meaning for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others, he first praised the Buddha.
"Realizing emptiness" means realizing the dharma of signlessness, non-obstruction, and equality. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I only pray that the Dharma..."
The King further expounded, saying: "I pray that the Dharma-King, the World-Honored One, will further explain this out of compassion for me and for all sentient beings.
I pray that you will have pity on me, protect and mind me, and act for the benefit of sentient beings.
As for the 'Dharma-King,' he is called a king because he possesses mastery over the Dharma; as the Dharma-King, may you have pity on me and protect and mind me."
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, so that those who practice the true conduct and mantras as taught may attain perfection, I pray that the Buddha will further explain the *A-kṣara-cakra*.
As for "perfection," it means that according to their respective capacities— whether superior, middling, or inferior— all shall receive benefit according to their individual natures and portions,
and all shall achieve the wondrous fruit.
Next, the Buddha addressed the Lord of Secrets, saying: "I shall now speak of the names and titles of the Buddhas, which were first proclaimed as the most supreme refuge for the world.

Before expounding the Secret Treasury, I shall first extol my own virtues, because this Dharma is difficult to believe; it is just as when one is about to preach the Lotus Sutra, one likewise extols oneself.
'First' (ādi) has the meaning of 'lifespan' (āyuṣ-pramāṇa). [Question: What does 'the refuge of the world' mean? It is like that of all [beings]."

Just as all grasses and trees grow by depending upon the earth, or as merchants depend upon a guide, those entering the sea depend upon a navigator, and those suffering from illness take refuge in a great physician—these have many aspects that should be explained in detail—the Buddha is likewise so now, acting as the support for all.
However, there is a further profound meaning; although it is said to be a self-praise, it is in fact...

The intention behind the teaching of the Dharma is as follows: regarding the term "I" (*ātman*) in the Sanskrit language, it contains the sound *a*, which signifies "fundamental non-arising" (*mūla-anutpāda*).
This essence of eternal non-arising is that upon which all things depend.
As for the title "Buddha," because I have realized this non-arising, all people in the world address me as such; it is not a mere conventional name.
The Dharma-realm has such names as these. Regarding the statement that "the Dharma is without equal or comparison":
among these incomparables, all that is taught by the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) consists of superior dharmas; therefore, they are said to have comparison.

Generally speaking, all those who do not understand the secret dharma of internal realization are non-Buddhists. This is because the Buddha taught that this [Dharma] cannot be compared or illustrated by any analogy.

Because it is the Dharma, the teaching of the Dharma is likewise peerless. Furthermore, within this, the syllable *ma* (or the sound *ma*) signifies non-arising (*anutpāda*), and it is also an exclamation used when teaching the Dharma.
[The text] further inquires: "This primordial stillness has nothing superior. Within this word "primordial" (*mūla*), there is the sound *a*, which reveals the meaning of non-arising;
because of the meaning of non-arising, it is primordially quiescent. This Dharma is the foremost and most subtle.
It is wondrous and unsurpassed; because it can pacify all the sense faculties, the six organs are eternally pure.
Because all evils are forever extinguished, it is called "pacification" (*śānta*). This syllable *A* is the heart-mind of all Buddhas.

When the Buddha now speaks this syllable *A* within his verse, he is speaking of the Dharma realized through self-awakening (*pratyātma-adhigama-dharma*). Although there is something [expressed] among all languages...
It is said that this object of internal realization can ultimately never be fully comprehended, because the dharma of self-realization is ineffable.
Although the Buddha himself praised it, he was in fact praising this syllable *A*.
Since this syllable has been the basis of the world from the very beginning, what is now described as the dharma of self-realization is not the domain of the two vehicles or of non-Buddhists.
Because within that Dharma there is nothing with which it can be compared, it is called "incomparable.

Just as one who has drunk water knows its coldness or heat for themselves, yet cannot describe it to one who has not drunk it—how much less so regarding the realm of the Tathāgata? (One should cite the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* here.
Nevertheless, by the power of his empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the Buddha taught this Dharma that is beyond verbal expression, so that Vajragarbha and the others might all attain it.

To know this matter is itself rare. (It is said that "originally quiescent" means one should know that this dharma of original quiescence and extinction is absent from all vehicles of the two types of practitioners and from the paths of externalists;
it is not within the scope of their mental objects.)
By virtue of this empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), Vajrapāṇi and all the Bodhisattvas were able to manifest the sublime vow of the Buddha’s seat of enlightenment (*bodhimanda*).

That is to say, after the Buddha had spoken these verses, he empowered them through his Buddha-power; at that moment, the Vajra-Bodhisattvas were immediately able to manifest the seat of enlightenment.
As for this "seat," it is merely a conventional worldly expression; it is simply the location of the seat. However...
In the Western [tradition], this seat is called *maṇḍa*. *Maṇḍa* signifies firmness, immovability, the sense of having no equal comparison, and the sense of pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This present Bodhi-seat is likewise like clarified butter manifesting from within curd; though all flavors are present in one place, they do not separate from one another.
It is through the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that it is thus manifested. (Question again: How is this so? It is because of empowerment.
This seat is adorned by the merits of the Tathāgata and accomplished through immeasurable great vows;
it is identical to the Buddha-body, appearing universally within all realms of sentient beings to perform the buddha-work. Therefore, it is called "Supreme Vow.
The Buddha is like space, free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), non-dual, and in accord with and perfected by principle.
The practitioner is precisely this seat; it is like space, free from all conceptualization and proliferation (*prapañca*).
Although bodhisattvas thus practice through various skillful means, there is neither duality nor distinction, for they do not depart from such a sublime principle;
hence it is called "conformity with principle. Just as the practitioner attains the fruit, so too is it the same as that.
The "accomplishment of non-duality and non-distinction in the seat" refers to the fruit attained by the practitioner.
At that time, the various limbs and parts of the Buddha’s body all manifest this syllable throughout all mundane and supramundane realms;
for those who diligently cultivate the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), and *siddhi* of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it pervades the entire body of the Buddha.

In every part, this *A* syllable mantra is manifested; this gateway of the *A* syllable is the very life-force of wisdom for both the mundane and supramundane, as well as for the meditative contemplations of the two vehicles.

(To gather the mind without distraction is called "concentration" (*samādhi*); next, one should perform "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). When the practitioner first gathers the mind, [the visualization of] the perfect luminosity and so forth is "contemplation.
The following meanings and contexts should be connected accordingly. Just as all syllables have their lifespan, this syllable shares the same seed, the same life, and the same vitality as all others.

Regarding those who share the same basis and manifest as saviors of the world, as mentioned above, all the wondrous activities performed in both the mundane and supramundane realms have the letter A as their very life-force.

Just as a person, if devoid of the life-faculty, must abandon all undertakings, so too it is with all these mundane and supramundane merits, such as meditative concentration and wisdom; if they are separated from the letter A, they likewise cease to exist.
The gate cannot achieve accomplishment through augmentation, for it is like a dead person who is incapable of acting.
Furthermore, the syllable *A* is the sound of opening the mouth; if there were no sound of *A*, one could not open the mouth.
If the mouth is not opened, all syllables would be non-existent. Therefore, the syllable *A* is the seed of all syllables; one should know that all phenomena [arise from it].
Practice is also like this, taking the letter A as its seed; if one is separated from the letter A, the world is not established.
Regarding the commonality of the locus of dependence: just as for sentient beings and others, if there were no great earth, there would be no place to dwell;
this letter A gate is also like this—if separated from the letter A, there is no locus of dependence. Regarding the commonality of being a savior of the world:
One should know that the syllable A is the great protector of all the world. At the end, it says "manifest" (mngon);
as mentioned above, when the Buddha manifested the vajra-throne for the great assembly, all these ultimate meanings were made manifest.
Next, the mantra-gate is explained: *Namo samantabuddhānām* (Homage to all Buddhas). [This means] "I pay homage to the universal..."
[This is] the Buddha, etc. (This is precisely the *A* syllable mantra-gate). O son of good family, this mantra is the heart of all Buddhas of the ten directions;

it is that which is empowered by the Dharmakāya in common. Any practitioner who relies upon this mantra is immediately able to perform the works of all Buddhas, even manifesting the form-body (*rūpakāya*) universally to reveal the Buddha’s wisdom to the realms of all sentient beings.
Just as wisdom is like a Buddha capable of performing these deeds, this syllable *A* can likewise perform them;
thus, the essence of this and that is identical to the bodies of all Buddhas. Regarding the turning of all phenomena through the gateway of the syllable *A*:
by turning this syllable *A*, one accomplishes various merits, and from this gateway of the syllable *A*, one practices and turns.
[He asked again: "Therefore, Lord of Mysteries, those bodhisattvas of the mantra-gate who wish to see all Buddhas—meaning they wish to see the pure *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas;
those who wish to make offerings—meaning they travel to all Buddha-fields to offer worship, serve, hear the Dharma, and practice;

those who wish to realize the arousal of the *bodhicitta*—meaning they realize enlightenment and purify the mind; and those who wish to assemble together with the bodhisattvas—meaning they dwell in one place together with bodhisattvas such as Nārāyaṇa..."

[It is] the bliss of the present life. For those who wish to benefit sentient beings—meaning, for example, that like Vairocana, one constantly performs the great Buddha-activities for all sentient beings in various ways—and for those who seek *siddhi*—in this regard, even the supreme accomplishment, namely the Buddha-body, can be swiftly attained; how much more so other accomplishments?

And for those who seek the wisdom of omniscience—since this gateway of the letter A accomplishes every purpose and benefit without exception—to state it briefly: even the wisdom of omniscience shall certainly be attained. One should diligently [apply oneself to] this heart of all Buddhas.
The Buddha said that for those who practice this, regarding the matters listed above which you wish to seek, there is no other method;
you need only diligently cultivate this gateway of the letter A.

The Remainder of Chapter Eight: The Practice of the Maṇḍala of the Wheel of Syllables.

At that time, Vairocana Buddha further definitively expounded this inconceivable Dharma of the Samādhi and Supernatural Powers of the True Word (Mantra) for the Arrangement of the Positions of All Honored Ones within the King of Maṇḍalas Born from the Matrix of Great Compassion.
As for the explanation, it has already been extensively set forth previously regarding the arrangement of the maṇḍala positions; why is it explained again now?

There are many reasons: it is to further develop a certain class of sentient beings, to cause those who have already heard it previously to attain even greater clarity, and because although the various stages and grounds were previously mentioned, they were not yet universally exhaustive; it is now explained again so that there shall be nothing left out.

Furthermore, because there was a deficiency [in the previous explanation], and since only their names had been mentioned previously while their forms remained largely unmanifested, they are now explained again to make them complete.
Why were they not explained all at once, but rather divided and explained here? There is a specific intention for this:
even those who deeply delight in the Dharma should not have it explained to them all at once; [this method] is intended to cause them to give rise to a sense of preciousness and reverence.

The mind is gradually guided and opened. Furthermore, if one were to take merely a painted image of the Honored One as the reality itself, then even those such as painters could achieve the qualities of an Ācārya;
yet, it is not by means of a painted image alone that one accomplishes the practice of mantra, for it must correspond in every detail with the signs of samādhi and supernormal powers.
It is only now that it may be called "inconceivable practice. Because the Buddha now wishes to reveal and clarify this, he speaks of the Dharma through *samādhi* and so forth;
that is to say, he expounds it in conjunction with *samādhi* and supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

Regarding that Ācārya’s entry into the gateway of omniscience, his abiding in the letter *A*, his taking of the thread, and his prostrating to all Buddhas, these have been explained in sequence above according to the mind.
In the center, one forms the syllable *A* and the eyes form the syllable *Ra*, as has already been fully explained in the preceding chapter.
Now, wishing to construct the maṇḍala, one must first abide in this samādhi to bring oneself into accord with the principle; with wisdom thus in accord, one applies the compass and the chalk lines.
When joining the cords, they must be handled appropriately and not too loosely; if they are not properly adjusted, it will cause distress for both the master and the disciple.
If the disciple is frequently ill and harassed by obstacles, or if the practice is interrupted during its performance, it will also cause the master to suffer loss and exhaustion.
Next, one must understand the proper directions; for this reason, one must first carefully determine the cardinal points.
If the disciple errs at the time of practice—such as mistaking east for west—it provides an opportunity for obstructing spirits to take advantage. Next, perform one prostration.

To prostrate to all Buddhas is precisely to pay homage to the essence of the *A* syllable mantra. Regarding the layout of the altar at this stage, following the *Sūtra* and the *Suspaṣṭārthā-ṭīkā*, it is appropriate to inquire of the Master:

the Master first performs the prostration on the southeast (Śun) side of the altar, facing north; the disciple then stands on the northeast (Gen) side, facing south, as they draw the cord between them.
Next, the Master turns the cord toward the northwest (Khen) and faces east, while the disciple turns his body accordingly.
Facing west, the disciple turns clockwise to the Kun corner (southwest) and faces north; the Master turns his body to face south.
Next, the Master again turns clockwise back to the Xun position (southeast) and faces west; the disciple turns his body to face east. Thus, the four cardinal directions are established.
The disciple then proceeds further to the Qian corner (northeast) to face the Master at the Xun position; thus, the Qian-Xun corners are finalized. It is said: "The corners are now settled."
[Question: Generally, when determining the four cardinal directions, one must be as careful and precise as before, without shifting them.
However, for the four intermediate corners and the central cross-line boundary, it is sufficient to simply rotate clockwise according to convenience, provided that no obstruction occurs;
this will suffice. Having performed this, Ācārya again, within the yoga, transforms the letter *A* in the heart.

One forms the syllable *vaṃ* as previously arranged; the skillful means for the syllable *raṃ* and so forth are no different from before, except that one changes the syllable *a* within the heart, whereby one becomes the body of Vajrasattva.
One must also visualize one's own body as being identical to that body and maintain the Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā.
Although one changes *a* to *vaṃ*, they are nonetheless not separate. Why is this?
Because it is non-arising, it is primordially without bondage; this is the "Single Essence with Different Gateways.

As previously described, when the cord has not yet reached the ground, one strikes it and performs this visualization. Then, together with the disciple, one enters again into the central womb (*garbha*).
Following the previous sequence, one establishes the location within the meditative concentration of the central womb.
As stated above, the mutual correspondence of non-duality with the form of the Tathāgata and the form of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is a reciprocal explanation.
To praise this non-dual form is to say it is the very form of the Tathāgata; that which is the form of the Tathāgata is precisely the form of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
As previously described, one should first take a cord and, with the master and disciple facing each other, pull it taut to determine the four cardinal directions and the four corners.
The crossroads are merely held by the cord-seal and have not yet been lowered (the markers had already been established at the four corners, and only then does one proceed).
When stabilizing [the site] in this manner, one must visualize the letter *A* as described above, pervading the entire body (all as previously explained).
Now, when the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana enters the Great Compassion Womb Matrix (*mahākaruṇā-garbha-kośa*) Samādhi—how could this Great Compassion Womb Matrix Samādhi be [anything other than...]?

Is there a difference from the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala described in the preceding chapter? It is precisely because the various directions of the previous altar were not yet complete in their colors and forms, nor were they fully equipped, that this is explained further.
Next, having finished determining the directions, the Master visualizes the syllable *vaṃ* as previously described, pervading all parts of his body.
He visualizes himself in the form of Vajradhara and enters the central womb (*garbha*). As before, he draws a line to determine the directions, extending it downward;

that is, he stretches the cord for the lower direction. (Question: Does one first determine the directions and then stretch the cord below, or does one simply stretch the cord below immediately? Suppose the square of the central womb measures six feet; taking half of that, it becomes three [feet].

One *shaku* is the measurement for the width of the first enclosure (*prathama-maṇḍala*) within the womb-section (*garbha-kosa*). This three-foot span is divided into four tiers (which constitute three boundary lines):

the first is for the walking path (*caṅkrama*), the second is for placing offerings, the third tier is the seating area for the various deities, and the fourth is the outer perimeter (*bāhya-pradakṣiṇā*).
These three tiers are all equal [in width], while the outer perimeter is narrower. One should calculate these three feet so that they are perfectly proportioned within.
To ensure they obtain their proper places, when making offerings, the master should direct his mind that all [deities] should assemble here;
however, for those who have no designated diagrams, positions, or seats, one should make offerings to them within these external conditions.

Next, divide the second courtyard by three feet, taking half of that as one foot and five inches; the dimensions of the third courtyard are likewise to be distributed evenly with four paths as described above.
Next, further divide one chi and five cun into two halves; the seven chi and five fen shall serve as the measurement for the outer enclosure.

Within these seven and a half cun, four lines shall be evenly placed so that they are appropriately positioned. At the entrance to the womb-mandala (garbha) of the first enclosure, it connects directly with the path;
a small portion should be taken there to establish the location of the gate, while the remainder is used for the passage.

Regarding the arrangement of the gates (the position of this gate): if there is ample space for the outermost gate, one may construct it as large as desired; there is no impediment even if it encroaches significantly upon the ground.
This is because the previous *maṇḍala* stated, "In the second enclosure, place Śākyamuni," while the third [text] states, "Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
These are mutually interchangeable; since the central womb (*garbha*) has already been fixed by prior determination, one proceeds directly to fix the third enclosure.
Therefore, it is said that the second [level] is not the second of the three tiers. Now, within this very text there is explicit evidence:

Mañjuśrī is in the second tier and Śākyamuni is in the third tier. One should first visualize the syllable *A* for the outer enclosure, and next visualize the syllable *Vaṃ* to form the central womb (*garbha*).
Having performed these steps in sequence, one visualizes Mañjuśrī in the second enclosure, or alternatively, one visualizes *Maṃ*.

The syllables (as before, pervading the parts of the body and so forth): next, one should visualize Śākyamuni in the third enclosure, or visualize the syllable *vaḥ* (the syllable *vaḥ* pronounced with a double sound).
Next, regarding the Vajrasattva who empowers me by grasping the vajra:

his mudrā, or the syllable *vaḥ*, or that which is placed within the central maṇḍala of the internal sense-bases—this refers to when the Master, having first completed the determination of the lines, desires [to proceed].
At the time of entering the central womb, one immediately empowers oneself as Vajrapāṇi;
however, since the Master uses the term "self" (*ātman*) to refer to his own person, he is identical to the Buddha Vairocana and should not have any personal activity of his own.
Therefore, he transforms himself into the body of the Bodhisattva Vajradhara, [realizing] that the letter *A*, which is primordially unborn, is inseparable from the letter *Ya*.

Thus, it is so that they may be employed in transformation. Likewise, in this second maṇḍala, by the power of my empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is fundamentally quiescent, there is the form of non-dual union, the form of the Buddha, and the form of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Next, one further extols the virtue of the syllable *va*;
because the meaning of the syllable *a* enters into it, it is also fundamentally quiescent. This is precisely the meaning of primordial non-arising (*an-utpāda*); it is non-dual.
Regarding "correspondence" (*saṃprayukta*): *va* is the letter *a*; they are non-dual and without division, corresponding eternally by virtue of their primordial quiescence.
Thus, even the form of the Tathāgata is empty and lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Next, regarding the two parts concerning the celestial positions, the abandonment of the outer maṇḍala, the three parts concerning the distant boundary-path, and the discarding of the eastward-extending lines and so forth: this means that for each enclosure (*kūṭāgāra*), [the same applies].
There are three levels of abandonment: first, one abandons the first level and installs the deity’s position in the third court;

next, one abandons the second court and [installs it] below the colors in the third court. (The meaning is not yet fully understood; I ask again regarding the passage in the Sūtra from the completion of the lines for the meditative positions up to the determination of the colors—the interpretation remains unclear and unrecorded, so I inquire further.)
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, Vairocana, I empower that seal. 'Extensive Dharma-realm' refers to the visualization of the colors;
as for 'the lower,' it means when applying the lower colors, the Ācārya should visualize himself as the Tathāgata Vairocana, or [as stated:
'At that time, one should visualize oneself as the Great Sun Tathāgata'], as being this very seal, which is the seal of the vast Dharma-realm. Thus it is said.
Having formed this thought, one first visualizes white light. At that time, the Ācārya visualizes his own body as being the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu);

the essence of the Dharma-realm is luminous, pure, and untainted. While contemplating in this manner, it is not only one’s own body, but all sentient beings as well who are likewise purified and made identical to the Tathāgata, free from all faults. One’s own person [is thus transformed].
"Equal to the Tathāgata" refers to the color white; white is the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, free from all faults.
Now, as for the statement that "all sentient beings are identical to the wondrous *dharmadhātu*," by what dharma is this attained? It is not that there is no expedient means (*upāya*) for this.
It is said that by entering the syllable-gateway of *ra*, at the moment one enters this syllable, one is able to cause both oneself and one's disciples [to attain it].
Because all sentient beings ultimately equal the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm body, which is forever free from all faults, it is next stated that one should visualize the syllable *ra*.
This syllable is white in color like a conch shell (*śaṅkha*)—some say this refers to a precious vessel—and its hue is supremely pure.

[The First Master says: Within this there is the syllable *a* and the syllable *va*; therefore, one visualizes the syllable *ra* as white. The word "visualize" means that its radiant light is tranquil, and the light emitted is like milk; by purifying with this, it becomes a stainless color, free from all faults.]
Furthermore, there is the *jun-ṇi* flower (a flower of the western region, also exceptionally pure white), which resembles the appearance of the bright moon;
the flames of its syllable are also white, tranquil and serene, yet radiating brilliant light.

When visualizing in this manner, one should recite the syllable *ra* one hundred or one thousand times before applying the color (*āliṭa*). Generally, for any ritual involving the consecration of colors, one first [visualizes] within the color itself.
Once the syllable *raṃ* has been visualized as having been formed, it immediately transforms into the Buddha. There are two types of *ariṭa*:
first, place the hands in the gesture of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*) at the chest, forming fists with the index fingers (*vāyu-aṅguli*) extended straight upward;
extend the right arm straight as if striking an object and raise it. Then, with the left foot pointing forward, the right foot should be about three feet away, and one should stretch the body fully.
This is so; white, vermilion, yellow, and blue are all used for this purpose. One should visualize the form of the Buddha while forming this mudrā.
Generally, there are two types of dignified postures (īryāpatha) when forming mudrās; if performing them while standing, one must maintain the proper dignified posture.
All four Buddhas assume a tranquil form and employ this mudrā. Second, regarding the lower red color that should be noted, it says "A."
Ācārya, you must examine this with careful discernment. Next, when the red color descends, one should visualize the syllable *ma* or the syllable *ra*.
The syllable *a* illuminates like the color of the rising sun—either red or yellow; this is a mixture of red and yellow.
This radiance is brilliant and dazzling; this syllable is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Buddha Ratnaketu.
This is the Buddha who is invincible, supreme, and peerless; one should also visualize oneself as being identical to this Buddha.
Regarding the other expedient means, they correspond to what was previously stated: the red syllable *ra* with a bindu added is incorrect;

it should be the syllable *a*, yet in meaning it is appropriate to use the syllable *ra* with a bindu. Next, when [the color] is yellow, one should visualize the syllable *ka* as the reality (*tattva*).
The golden color and its radiance are likewise golden; this is the Muni Buddha (*muni* being a general title for a Buddha).
*Ka* signifies the sense of action (*karma*); because it is non-action, it is eternally free from all faults. Abiding in this samādhi, it destroys all poisons, and its light pervades everywhere.
One who wishes to enter meditative concentration should rely on the instructions (meaning one should contemplate with focused intent and an undistracted mind). Next is the blue color.
At that time, one should contemplate the syllable *ma* (it is said that one contemplates this syllable *ma* above [the blue color]). This signifies the transcendence of birth and death;

it is Śākyamuni. Seated upon the Great Bodhi-throne, this Buddha uses this syllable to remove the terrors of sentient beings and to subdue the hosts of Māra armies. Above this syllable, there is an outer halo like a rainbow.
The color of the blue lotus and its light are likewise. Other expedient means are as previously described; in the West, the rainbow is called the Palace of Śakra.

Next, one should visualize the black syllable *ha* below it, which, because the fire at the time of the kalpa-ending catastrophe is so intensely blazing, emits a deep purple-black light; the light of this syllable is also like this. This is the [syllable] A.
The Tathāgata Ṣaḍakṣarī, out of great compassion, acts as a protector for all beings and subdues all obstacles;
thus he manifests the wrathful form of Bhṛkuṭī and performs the mudrā directed toward those who create hindrances (this *bhṛkuṭī* frown is as previously described).
This Honored One’s name is *Pratīcā*, which is a Sanskrit term. For this mudrā, raise the left hand, extend the left leg, and bend the right.
The feet [are likewise]; this is the general mudrā for subjugation. One should assume the form of a Vajra-anger deity; it is not necessary to assume the form of a Buddha.
These two deities are the general body-mudrās for all applications. Other expedient means are as previously described.
At that time, Vairocana Buddha arose from samādhi and dwelt in the Samādhi of Infinite Excellence. While remaining in this concentration, he—
before whom all Tathāgatas arise and proclaim the teachings that are omnipresent and possess the power of being indestructible—
dwelt in the Amṛtodbhava Samādhi and, having finished expounding the aforementioned Dharma-gate, [remained] thus.

In order to fulfill the various skillful means of the Bodhisattvas who practice the true path of mantra and conduct, he arises from meditative concentration and further enters the immeasurable and supreme samādhi.
"Immeasurable and supreme" (ananta-vijaya) carries the meaning of the power that cannot be harmed.
By abiding in this immeasurable and supreme samādhi, he causes this vidyā-queen to arise. This vidyā-queen is named Sarva.

The arising of the Tathāgata’s realm is itself the realm of the Buddha. Because of this vidyā-mantra, all bodhisattvas who practice the true mantras become identical to the realm of the Tathāgata and likewise give rise to such an inconceivable realm.
Because they have entered the realm of the Buddha, the merit they produce is also equal to that of the Tathāgata, pervading all things without exception.

The power of harmlessness is precisely the meaning of non-obstruction. It does not merely pervade the realm of the Tathāgatas, but also pervades the realms of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even down to those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment;
for anyone who can practice this vidyārājñī conduct shall likewise enter the realm of the Tathāgatas.
*Namo sarvatathāgatebhyaḥ*: "Homage to all Tathāgatas" means to take refuge in all the Tathāgatas and so forth.
Because they are born from all the Tathāgatas, they are not one; because they are not one, they are called "all" (*sarva*).
*Sarvamukhebhyaḥ* (with the two-syllable contraction): by all the Buddhas...
He is the foremost and the object of aspiration. (Questioning him further: *Asami* (unequaled; because he arises from the realm of all Tathāgatas, he is unequaled).
Furthermore, in this secret interpretation, the syllable *A* is the Buddha’s own body.

The three delusions are equal to these [Tathāgatas], and being equal to the Buddhas is precisely to be equal to the essence of the syllable *A*. *Parama* (translated as "the foremost"; because it is unequaled, it is the foremost). Furthermore...
[This is] unsurpassed. Regarding the esoteric interpretation: this syllable *bha* is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Because the preceding syllable *a* is identical to the essence of all Tathāgatas, it is equal to the ultimate truth and to the Tathāgata.

*Ācārya* [means] immovable. By virtue of the syllable *a*, it is identical to the ultimate truth. Since the ultimate truth is beyond the path of speech and the cessation of mental activity, it cannot be destroyed and cannot be overturned.
Gagane (empty, because it is also unmoving; equal to the nature of space, pure, vast, and beyond conceptualization or measure) samarasāne (to seek and recollect;

that is, to seek and recollect the meaning of the letter A—meaning to contemplate this meaning at all times and in all moments, without interruption) sarvatrānugate (pervasive; by constant contemplation...).
By contemplating this meaning, one is able to reach all places—not only reaching all Buddhas, but also reaching all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even the stages of [arousing] the mind and so forth.
*Svāhā* (the *svā* is drawn out and the *hā* is drawn out; *svā* is the base, and *hā* is the suffix). This serves to awaken the Buddhas and cause them to remember their original vows.
All those who practice these mantra-observances (*vidyā-caryā*) for which the Tathāgata formerly established such definitive great vows shall receive their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
"By establishing this, may my aspirations be swiftly fulfilled; for I now practice in this manner. This serves to awaken all Buddhas and cause them to constantly remember their original vows.
Next, regarding the method for preparing the colors: prostrate to the Buddha Prajñāpāramitā and recite this vidyā-queen eight times.
One who recites this is said to be preparing pigments to paint an image of the Tathāgata’s true form;

first, one should read and recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with reverent offerings, which constitutes the meaning of performing prostrations. Whenever one prepares the pigments, one must act in this manner.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the characters within those colors (referring to characters such as "La" and so forth), and recite these characters either one hundred times or...

Recite the mantra one thousand times, and furthermore, recite the Vidyārājñī eight times. Once the Master has adjusted the colors [having risen from his seat, circumambulated, and entered within, while the disciple visualizes the power of great compassion;
the Master himself then forms the vajra and letter mudrās], he arises from meditative absorption, circumambulates the maṇḍala, and generates a mind of great compassion.
Having empowered that disciple through this power of great compassion, the Ācārya becomes a Karmavajra.
Regarding those Bodhisattvas such as Vajrapāṇi, who are empowered by the *sattva* and the syllable *vaṃ* and grant boons,
this Ācārya— by means of the Tathāgata’s empowerment and the syllable *a*— is himself Vairocana Tathāgata;
since it is improper for the Tathāgata to perform the activity of self-creation, he further empowers himself with the syllable *vaṃ* and manifests the body of Vajrasattva.

Regarding the painting of the various images: [The syllable *bha* together with the Wish-Fulfilling Auspicious Vajra is Mañjuśrī; the seed-syllable is the letter *ma*, which is the bindu of emptiness; and *śva* is used as the letter *pha*.
At the time of creation, one should visualize it as identical to one's own body, as described above. Furthermore, one should recite this syllable *va* one hundred or one thousand times, etc.
Within the Great Maṇḍala born from the Matrix of Great Compassion (*Mahākaruṇāgarbhodbhava-maṇḍala*), the preceptor should calmly install the maṇḍala.
Having thus performed self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), one rises with composure and enters the central womb;
there, one slowly applies the various colors to fashion the image of Vairocana. This image, in its original form, sits upon a white lotus pedestal;
it wears a crown of hair and is not adorned with [external] pigments. A very fine silk serves as the lower garment, and an even finer gauze (*dukūla*) is used [for the upper].
Those garments that are lighter and finer than the lower robes are used as upper robes so that the color of the flesh may reflect through and appear within.
The body is the color of Jambūnada gold; this refers to a deep golden hue of extreme brilliance and luster.
From the bodies of these Buddha images, flames arise and merge to form a continuous garland of interlocking rings that envelops the entire body. This is why, within the maṇḍala...
One must fashion this image of the Buddha because, desiring that those disciples quickly give rise to supreme aspirations and,
through the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), fulfill the body of omniscience (*sarvajñatākāya*), one must first establish it.
Furthermore, there are superior, middling, and inferior methods for constructing the mandala.

If the disciple possesses abundant wealth and resources and is capable of extensive preparation, the master should construct a mandala of painted colors and images, in order to demonstrate the forms and hand-seals (mudrās) of the deity.

If one has the capacity to provide these yet constructs a mandala of written characters instead, one commits the offense of concealing the secret dharma. This is provided that the master observes the disciple’s [capacity].
If one possesses such extreme reverence that one is even willing to sacrifice body and life to serve the teacher, how much more so should one have no sense of stinginess?
However, for those who lack the necessary resources, it is permitted to construct a maṇḍala of written characters;

by simply inscribing the characters in the place where the Buddha is to be situated, these characters themselves constitute the very essence of the Tathāgata. Once the letter A has been placed in the center, [the rite is complete].
Outside the *garbha* (womb), write a syllable directly to the east; furthermore, place a syllable in the northeast, the direction of Īśāna.
This *ga* is the Eye of Space (*ākāśanetra*) and is the mother of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Next, in the direction of Agni (southeast), place either the *cintāmaṇi-ratna-mudrā* of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or the syllable *ka*.

Next, in the north, one should place the syllable *Vaṃ* for Avalokiteśvara and Maitreya—the Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa who are in their final birth before Buddhahood—surrounded by their retinues. Alternatively, one may place the syllable *Sa*.

Next, in the south, one places Vajrapāṇi and others, either in their physical forms or merely as mudrās (mudrās referring to the three-pronged vajra), or else one places the syllable *Va*. Furthermore, within this [central area], one should place the syllable.
If the orientation differs from that of the previous altar, inquire about it again and establish those respective positions.
Regarding the abandonment of all the *vajra* mudrās or their seed-syllables (*bīja*), the method of abandonment is as explained previously and is no different.
For the syllable and seal, one forms the syllable *HŪṂ*. Next, in the direction of the *Rākṣasa* (the southwest), one does not draw anything beneath Vairocana.
The Moving Honored One (Cala-nātha) sits upon a stone, holding a sword and a noose (*pāśa*), with a wreath of flames encircling his entire body;

he vows to subdue all those who create obstacles. Alternatively, one may simply form the mudrās above (the mudrās being those of the noose and the sword), or form the syllable *Haṃ* (with a long vowel).
Next, in the direction of Wind (the northwest), one visualizes the Victorious One of the Three Times (*Trailokyavijaya*) atop the heads of all those who create obstacles, emitting blazing light.
One should assume an appearance of great wrath like that of Yama, black in color;
even amidst things already terrifying and fearsome, one should manifest an extremely terrifying form.
In his hand, he brandishes a *vajra* (this is the three-pronged *vajra-mudrā*, which represents meditative concentration), or one may simply form the syllable *HAḤ*.
Next, one should draw the four great *bandha-rakṣā* (protective bindings) in the four directions. In the east, one performs the *Abhaya-bandha-rakṣā* (this is its name).

His body is golden in color, he wears white robes, his face has a slight expression of wrath, and he holds a staff (*daṇḍa*) in his hand. If only the seal (*mudrā*) is to be placed, one simply draws the seal of the staff;
or if only the syllable is to be placed, it is the syllable *vaḥ*. In the north, one performs the Great Protection that Destroys All Fears; he is white in color and holds a sword in his right hand.
If one forms the mudrā of the White-Robed One (Pāṇḍaravāsini) together with Jvālāmukhī, it is simply drawn in the shape of a sword;
if expressed as a syllable, it is the letter *pa* with two dots added beside it. She is so named because she is a great protector of the West who is difficult to subdue and whom none can overcome.
Her body is the color of the *anupa* flower (like the deep purple of the *shuqi* hollyhock flower here in this land), and her robes are likewise red, though slightly lighter.
Regarding his physical form, he has a smiling face and stands within a halo, appearing as if presiding over a great assembly;
this refers to the assembly in the western direction. As for the mudrā, one should simply draw a sword or the letter *ja*.
Regarding the Southern Vajra Aparājita Mahārakṣa: because it is like a vajra and there is nothing that surpasses it, it is thus named. Furthermore, regarding the Vajra...
This is an alternative name for Śakra, the Lord of Devas; however, because the power of this Great Protector (*Mahārakṣa*) exceeds even his, it is so named.
His body is black in color and wrathful in form, with knitted brows and garments that are also black, though slightly lighter than the hue of his body and face.
On his head, he merely wears a topknot, and his own body emits a halo of flames. He holds a staff (*daṇḍa*); if one were to depict him using only mudrās, one would simply [depict the hand gesture].
The staff is represented by the syllable *kṣam* (as a bimātra vowel), which serves as its seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Regarding the four great protectors mentioned above, their respective retinues are to be placed alongside them; these retinues consist of their attendants, all of whom sit upon white lotus flowers.
The practitioner of the mantra should arrange and place them in this manner.

Next, outside, one proceeds to the third enclosure and draws the Muni King of the Śākya clan, wearing a kāṣāya robe and endowed with the thirty-two marks, who bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings (because he benefits all through the teachings, causing them all to attain fearlessness).
His mudrā should be placed as a bowl, a kāṣāya, and so forth (“so forth” referring to items such as a mendicant’s staff). If it is to be represented by a syllable, it is the letter *va*. This.

The most supreme is the secret, unsurpassed meaning. Next, regarding the outer maṇḍala, for those who have set out with the bodhicitta empowered by the intrinsic nature of the dharmadhātu, they perform the meditation on the intrinsic nature of the dharmadhātu.
The dharmadhātu is the body of the Tathāgata; one meditates that one's own body is identical to the dharmadhātu-body of all Buddhas, and through this empowerment, one abides therein.

Regarding "bodhicitta" (this "setting forth" has the meaning of direction, the meaning of arrival, and the meaning of practice; this section is further questioned): "Those three parts, having abandoned the three, pay homage to the Buddha Vairocana.
Recalling him as before, "adjusting the colors" means that after setting aside Śākyamuni, one places [the others].
Next, in the second courtyard, one should pay homage to Vairocana and paint him according to the previously explained method for adjusting colors (further inquiry).
In the east, he should be depicted in the form of the Vajrakumāra of the Varada-mudrā (which is another name for Mañjuśrī), holding a blue lotus in his left hand with a vajra placed upon it;
his body is adorned with all kinds of necklaces and garlands, and a fine, exquisite silk serves as his lower garment.
The lower garment is made of extremely fine gauze as an upper robe, which is even finer than the lower garment so that the color of the body shines through.
The body is the color of *uragasāra* gold, and there are five topknots upon the head. As for the mudrā, one simply draws a blue lotus with a vajra placed upon the flower.
If one writes it in characters, it refers to the "full" syllable (maṇḍalākṣara), or one may add the words of refuge (*namas*). This is it.
Regarding the mantra: To the right of Mañjuśrī (which is the north), place the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha. All his limbs are complete;
his left hand holds a jewel net (*ratnajāla*), and his right hand holds a hook (*aṅkuśa*). If only the mudrā is placed there, one may either draw the mudrā or draw the hook.
As for the seed-syllable (*bīja*), it is the syllable *raṃ* (which suffices to place this alone). In the south, paint Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
The Bodhisattva has golden hair and a crown (it is said that there are no necklaces). His left hand holds a Cintāmaṇi jewel atop a lotus flower.
If one performs only the mudrā, place a maṇi jewel upon the lotus flower; or if one places only a syllable, it refers to the syllable *Aḥ*.
In the north, one should depict Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, whose color is like that of a *pātra* (alms bowl).
In the western direction there is the *gandhā* flower; its color is like that of millet here [in this world]. Its floral calyx is also like a grain ear and it is very fragrant.
This Bodhisattva holds a lotus flower in his hand, and his body is adorned with various necklaces (*keyūra*).
If one merely forms the mudrā, one simply places a lotus flower there. If one places a syllable, it is the letter *i*. [This is] in the western direction.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja and others likewise adorn their bodies with various necklaces;

their bodies are white in color, and they wear white garments (the color of these white garments reflects upon the body so that it appears a fleshy red, slightly different from the natural body color).

Their bodies possess blazing light, and they hold great swords—those who employ this mudrā simply draw a great sword; however, if one merely places a syllable, it is the letter *Ī* (prolonged). Now, within this maṇḍala...
As there are still many remaining stages, the statement that "it has been completed" is also an instance of alternating between the upper and lower [levels].
At the time of completion, the *ācārya* first sits outside the door, abiding in the *dharmadhātu*—[the Sanskrit text says: "Next, the reciter abides in the *dharmadhātu*;

I am the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, abiding in the *bodhicitta*"]—while simultaneously maintaining the *bodhicitta*. This *bodhicitta* is itself the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. He then faces the east.

Form the Vajra-mudrā (since the entrance to the maṇḍala opens to the west, the master faces east). Once the maṇḍala is completed, sit facing east within the maṇḍala and contemplate that you are identical to the Buddha;
the Buddha is the very essence of the Dharmadhātu. Having become identical with all Buddhas, one then performs the activities for the benefit of sentient beings.
Regarding the Action-Vajra (*karmavajra*), this refers to performing various activities as a vajra; it is the three-pronged *viśvavajra*.

(Generally speaking, whenever one speaks of "performing the Vajra," it refers to the mudrās of the syllable-body; this applies equally to performing the Buddha-activities. Fearing prolixity, I shall not state each instance individually.)
Next, regarding those who perform the offerings with earnest devotion, one should further admonish the practitioner: "One must be cautious and diligent in performing them;

do not forget the sequence. [The Sanskrit text says: "One should bind the Vajra-mudrā, then perform the Vajra-activities, and offer worship with earnest devotion to the Samaya of all manifest Buddhas, the Saviors of the World.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the manifest mudrās, samayas, and so forth," the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used because there are many *samaya*-mudrās. This refers to the offerings and the performance of activities.
One recites the *samaya* mantra three times for all [deities], as this is frequently used in ritual activities; hence the word "etc.
By performing this rite, one’s mind, according to its specific application, can pervade all directions and awaken all Tathāgatas.
Because of the Buddhas’ original vows, they are all awakened and bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). First, one should contemplate them pervading all directions.

Regarding what is called the maṇḍala: if a practitioner of deep realization directs their mind universally toward all the deities according to their respective positions within the maṇḍala, this is the samaya that reveals the actual locations of all the maṇḍala deities.
To request the ritual application for the deities, one accomplishes all matters through the two types of messengers;
by means of the mantra, one immediately attains [success]. If one possesses swift wisdom, [this is achieved] in a single moment.
One may also separately invite [the deity] using the fundamental mantra and mudrā. Next, call the disciple from outside;

having him maintain ritual purity, first summon him from outside the gate, have him approach the gate, and have him stand facing the mandala. Furthermore, one should first instruct him on how to purify himself according to the Dharma.
This completes the invitation of the Honored One (honzon). Subsequently, all rites from the binding of the boundary (kaji) to the dismissal (hansha) are performed within the offering.

In the ritual of nourishment (*poṣadha*), it may be applied accordingly. Once the protection has been established, one bestows the Three Refuges; these Three Refuges are what is called the "Seal of the Dharma" (*dharmamudrā*).
First, the seal protects the body; next, the Wheel Seal (*cakramudrā*) protects the various parts of the body;
