next, there is another seal which shall be explained below. The first seal is impressed upon the crown of the head; the next seal is impressed upon the limbs. (Regarding the next seal, further inquiry is required. Regarding the next seal, it says above: "Gold."
Sentient beings are indeed thus; by means of these three seals, one abides in the bodhicitta.

When forming the Dharmadhātu-dharmacakra-mudrā, "one should single-mindedly form one's own body" means that when the practitioner directs the mind to create this dharmadhātu, they visualize their own body as being identical to the dharmadhātu.
At the time of binding the seal, it is identical to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that mudrā. [End of upper section]
Having bound that Dharma-realm Self-nature Seal (dharmadhātu-svabhāva-mudrā), one next binds the Dharma-wheel Seal (dharma-cakra-mudrā) and asks further questions.
One should first visualize the letter *A* within the disciple’s topknot, and then seal it with the Dharma-realm Arising Seal (dharmadhātu-utpatti-mudrā), pressing down with the seal.

Next, one should recite the mantra three or seven times. Thereafter, one should cover the disciple’s face with a cloth, while the master should give rise to a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Out of compassion for them, in order to cause them to forever cross over birth and death and open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, his disciples at that time should also personally resolve upon the supreme, unsurpassed vow. This is because the Amoghapāśa [mantra] brings the perfection of Bodhi;
that is to say, it is so that those disciples may swiftly perfect unsurpassed Bodhi, according to their respective capacities of superior, middling, or inferior strength.

Having made offerings to the Buddhas, the principal deities, and others with all that one possesses, or by presenting precious flowers and the like, the master then instructs the disciple in his ear so as to cause him to form a protective bond; this refers to causing him to abide in the bodhicitta, though there are other explanations for this.
Once he has generated the bodhicitta and abides with single-minded devotion and reverence, the master himself—
Form the mudrā and place it upon the disciple’s crown. Ask him again, "Which mudrā is this? Then, have him cast a flower;
you should note the deity upon whom that flower falls. Furthermore, within the body of a single deity, there are distinctions of superior, middling, inferior, left, and right.
According to the place where the flower falls, bestow upon him the corresponding mudrā and mantra. Disciple.
"Son, because you have thus performed the samaya according to the Dharma-instructions, everything is granted.
(He asked further. At that time, the Virtuous Vajradhara again requested: "I pray that the Buddha himself will speak this Buddha-consecration rite;
I entreat the Buddha to speak it himself. Then the Buddha, abiding within the nature of the Dharmadhātu, addressed Vajrapāṇi: "Listen attentively with a single mind."
I teach this Dharma so that practitioners may attain mastery within it—what is called the attainment of the supreme teaching.
(This "mastery" also carries the sense of "swift attainment" and "sustaining," which differs from the meaning of "mastery" as the possession of great wealth mentioned above.
When I speak of the teaching of all dharmas as the "supreme mastery and sustaining," it refers to the mind possessing aspiration and seeking.
One is able to fully grasp all things and fulfill wishes with mastery, such that whatever one intends to do in a single land is necessarily accomplished.
An ācārya who performs that mudrā through the empowerment of the original form and intention of the Tathāgata shall act according to the superior, middling, or inferior rites;
whether forming the shape of a Tathāgata, or those of the Lotus or Vajra families, one should perform it according to the maṇḍala presided over by each.
Regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) manifested in form: "The empowerment of the Tathāgata’s original form" means that the *ācārya* empowers his own body with the nature of the Tathāgata;

this nature of the Tathāgata is precisely the original form. Alternatively, "using those mudrās" means empowering oneself by means of the mudrās while visualizing the syllable *A* pervading all limbs;
this syllable *A* is the very essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Because it is adorned by this very nature, one is then called a disciple only when they are identical to the Buddha-body.
If the *ācārya* has attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or has already achieved realization of the Dharma, whatever he performs will be spontaneously accomplished.
If he is unable to do so, he should perform the rites using seals (*mudrā*) and visualization (*bhāvanā*). Next, he leads the disciple toward the Great Flower King Maṇḍala.
*Rā* (referring to the location outside the maṇḍala where the empowerment altar is first prepared): the great vase empowered by the Great Bodhisattvas is made of the four jewels;
it is the vase empowered by the four Great Bodhisattvas of the central womb (*garbha*), adorned with the jewels of the Bodhisattvas.

Next, one should form the mudrā that generates all limbs and empower [the disciple] by pouring [the water] upon the crown of the disciple's head. This is to be performed at the time of every empowerment.
Once this mudrā has been bound, one takes the flask for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). If one does not use this mudrā, the ritual procedure will be incomplete;
it will prevent the disciple from abiding in the bodhicitta, leading to regression, and would be no different from sprinkling scented water into empty space.
Furthermore, prior to the consecration, one should visualize the syllable [HŪṂ] at the crown of the disciple’s head, at the junction of the ten directions.
Within his heart, one should intensely visualize the syllable *A*, and further visualize the syllable *Ra* upon the chest;

alternatively, it is sufficient to visualize the syllable *A* pervading all places. Regarding "one with golden light and hair-crown sitting upon a white lotus," this means one should visualize the white lotus in the heart of that disciple opening and becoming fully blossomed, with Vairocana Tathāgata seated thereon.
Having placed it upon [the head], one then performs the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). As the Sūtra says: "The benevolent one is none other than Vairocana Tathāgata.
If one is consecrated by means of this rite, it is equivalent to receiving the consecration from all the Buddhas of the ten directions;
by means of the water of Dharma, one receives the station of the Dharma King. Otherwise, it would be merely a vain exertion of one's own body to perform the sprinkling, accomplishing nothing at all.
[This concludes] the third fascicle. Chapter Nine:
The Secret Seals (*Guhyamudrā*). Fascicle Four.
At that time, the Buddha Vairocana surveyed the entire great assembly; the Buddha had already briefly explained the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

As the ritual procedures were concluded and the Buddha was about to speak further, he again surveyed the great assembly, which was as vast as the atoms of ten buddha-fields, perceiving that it was not without cause or condition.
This was because he was about to proclaim the seal of the Tathāgata’s body-mystery (*kāyaguhyamudrā*). He then addressed Vajrapāṇi:
"There is a seal called the 'Adornment of the Tathāgata,' which is the banner of the path to the Dharma-realm. The word "same" (*tulya*) means: [To be continued with the subsequent passage.]
Because all Buddhas take this as their adornment, they attain the body of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm;
if there are sentient beings who practice this dharma, through the empowerment of the seal (*mudrā*), they likewise become identical to the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm body.
Furthermore, this seal is the emblem of the Dharma-realm; by means of this seal, the essence of the Dharma-realm is indicated. Thus:

It is named the Banner of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-dhvaja*). Because all Buddhas adorn their bodies by means of this, they establish this insignia of supreme, great Bodhi within all great assemblies;

it causes those among the eight classes of beings who are evil and heterodox to depart from afar, while those of a virtuous root-nature draw near, receive the teachings, and practice them. Listen attentively and apply your minds with great care; I shall [speak].
"I shall now proclaim it. "World-Honored One, now is the very time; World-Honored One, now is the very time"—these two phrases spoken by the Buddha must surely have a specific meaning.
When he first spoke of the *kāla* (time), his intention was this: "Now these four assemblies are devoid of branches and leaves;
they are purely solid and substantial, capable of receiving the Great Dharma. That the Tathāgata should preach according to their capacity is precisely the right occasion."
"It is the time; it is the present moment; it is the very time for preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One dwelt in the Samādhi of the Harmless Body-Power.
Because the Buddha wished to fulfill this vow, he entered samādhi once again. This is the power of the Tathāgata’s unimpeded body and mastery; therefore, none can harm him.
Abiding in this samādhi, one utters the mantra of the three vidyās; this vidyā is named "Harmless and Unequaled Power.
By virtue of this samaya, practitioners are permitted to hear and enter the True Dharma.
If one does not act accordingly, it is improper to enter the maṇḍala, nor is it proper to hear the secret teachings. If one cultivates this vidyā, one will be able to attain [the results].
Because the purity of body and the purity of speech fulfill all aspirations and converge with the three bodies (*trikāya*), they are called the "three knowledges" (*tisro vidyāḥ*).

[The "three powers" refers to the power of the three times, or perhaps the power of the three equalities; the "unequaled power" is precisely these three powers. These knowledges shall now be explained in sequence.
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām (Homage to all Buddhas). Asame trisame samaye svāhā (Unequaled, threefold equality, O Samaya, hail!).
Regarding "A-sa-mi": herein, taking the letter *A* as the primary element is identical to the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas, which is signless and free from characteristics;
one should know that this dharma-body is without equal. Regarding the "three equals":

this refers to the three bodies of the Buddhas—the dharma, enjoyment, and transformation bodies—which, when unified as a single body, teach and transform sentient beings; their essence is likewise identical to the letter *A*.
Because this gateway is without characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and without the characteristic of separation, it is called "equal" (*sama*). *Samaya* means that which is not to be transgressed;
it is what all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have equally taught. The Buddha, abiding in samādhi, spoke this vidyā of harmlessness and equal power.
By means of this vidyā, one is able to enter the *samaya*. This *samaya* is precisely the vow (*pratijñā*).
The vow is like the command; it is the fundamental essential pledge of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

This Dharma-gate is difficult to believe, difficult to enter, and difficult to hear, because the Dharma is not fully possessed [by others]. For this reason, the Buddhas of the three periods of time together proclaim this mantra.
By means of the empowerment of this samaya-mantra, one is able to enter, hear, and practice this Dharma.
It is as the Venerable One has taught and must not be transgressed; if one does not hear it, one shall neither enter nor be permitted to hear it.

*Svāhā*. This is in the sense of "arousing. When this mantra was spoken to arouse all the Buddhas, the Buddhas were immediately aroused and arose to bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon the practitioner. Such is the power of this vidyā.
Therefore, one is able to fulfill the various stages and cause the practitioner to attain the three dharmas in the present; that is to say, there are three dharmas for accomplishment, namely:
the body of the *iṣṭadevatā*, the mantra, and the mudrā. When these three dharmas are complete, one attains accomplishment.

Next, regarding the description of the characteristics of the mudrās: "not transgressing the three paths of the dharma-realm" means that this realm is the realm for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), not the *stūpa*.
Because one proceeds through the center of the path of the realm, it is called "not transgressing.
Now, herein first the names and characteristics of the twelve kinds of *añjali* are explained; in all ritual methods of mudrā, these twelve kinds are the ultimate expressions of reverence.
One should clearly remember this first method: join the palms together with the center of the hands firmly pressed against each other, leaving the tips of the ten fingers slightly apart.
This is called the *niṣaṇṇa* (seated) *añjali* (this is the *dṛḍha-hṛdaya-añjali*, or "firm-hearted" *añjali*).
Second, align the ten fingernails so they are even and level, joining the fingertips while keeping the center of the palms slightly apart.
The third is the renowned *tripuṭa añjali* (this is called the "hollow-palmed" *añjali*);

next, join the tips of the ten fingers together so that they are level, while keeping the palms hollow and slightly arched; this is called the *kuḍmala añjali* (translated as "like an unopened lotus").
The fourth is to touch the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers together, while slightly spreading the remaining fingers.

The fifth is called *punnāga-añjali* (this is the first [type of] lotus): again, with both palms turned upward and placed side by side, facing upwards and aligned perfectly, it is called *utkṣipta-añjali* (this means "manifested").
The sixth is again to place both palms side by side and facing upward as before, while bringing the fingers together.
Slightly bend them together in the manner of a person cupping water (but do not bend them too much);

this is called the *ādarā añjali* (translated as "holding water"). For the seventh time, again have the tips of the ten fingers interlace, with each right finger placed over a left finger, like the *vajra-añjali* (translated as "homage-añjali" [Sanskrit: *praṇāmāñjali*]). The...
Eighth: Again, place the right hand over the left with the palms turned upward and interlace the tips of the ten fingers;

likewise, place the fingers of the right hand over the fingers of the left hand. This is called the *mukula-muṣṭi* (or *viparyasta*) añjali (this is translated as the "inverted-interlaced" añjali). Ninth:
Again, place the right hand palm-upward upon the left hand and the left hand palm-downward over the right hand, slightly resembling—
The form of the hand-gesture for those practicing seated meditation is called *vibhūti-saṃpuṭa* (in Chinese, "reversing the palms so they touch each other").
This is the tenth [gesture]. For the eleventh, one simply turns both palms upward, joins the tips of the middle fingers of both hands, and holds them facing up;
this is called *tiryak-saṃpuṭa* (in Chinese, "the cross-bar finger gesture"). This is the eleventh.
Furthermore, covering both palms with both hands and joining the middle fingers together is called *añjali* (in this context, "palms turned downward joined").

This is the twelfth [mudrā]. Again, covering both hands with both hands and placing the two thumbs side by side with the tips of the ten fingers pointing outward is also given the same name. Furthermore, it is called *añjalim* (also translated as "palms turned downward joined").

Now, for this Samaya-mudrā, first join the three *puṭa* palms (this refers to first extending the two hands apart, then gradually bringing them close until they touch, and finally joining the palms with a slight space remaining within).
Align the two *kaniṣṭhikā* (little fingers) side by side and extend them straight upward; do not let them be too low, nor too slanted, but ensure the two *kaniṣṭhikās* point directly upward.
In this sūtra, both hands are established as the Secret Names of Prajñā and Upāya, representing the ten fingers.

All are designated by the secret names of the five wheels (*pañca-maṇḍala*): the middle finger is earth, the ring finger is water, the middle finger of the right hand is fire, the index finger is wind, and the thumb is space.

The left hand represents *samādhi* (concentration) and the right hand represents *prajñā* (wisdom). Alternatively, the little finger of the left hand may represent the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), with the others counted upward in sequence; the index finger then represents *samādhi*. The little finger of the right hand represents the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), with the others counted upward in sequence;

the index finger then represents the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*). [According to the Yoga system, concentration and wisdom are not different from these two hands; the ten fingers take the ten perfections as their designations, beginning from the little finger of the hand of concentration for giving, and beginning from the little finger of the right hand for wisdom, proceeding upward in order: giving, morality, patience, effort, meditation,] wisdom, skillful means, vows, power, and knowledge.

"Wisdom, Direction, Vow, Power, and Knowledge"—these are the names of the ten fingers. Furthermore, these names were established by those who have transcended this [worldly] intention; they cannot be understood unless they are personally transmitted by an Ācārya, and for this reason, they are called "secret. Regarding this Samaya-mudrā:
when first practicing and performing various virtuous deeds, if one does not perform it beforehand, one is unfit to perform any of the rites.
Not only must one form this mudrā, but one must also recite the preceding Samaya-mantra while performing the ritual.
Having bound this samaya-mudrā and placed it upon the crown of the head, recite the aforementioned samaya-mantra once;
then place the mudrā on the right shoulder, next on the left shoulder, next at the heart, and finally at the throat.
At each placement, recite the mantra once. By reciting it five times while sealing these five locations, one achieves great protection. This shall now be explained briefly.
Regarding the mantra and mudrā: what are the merits of this mantra? By means of this mantra, one can eliminate past obstacles and purify oneself.
Once the body is purified, external obstacles are likewise purified; because external obstacles are purified, no hindrances can enter.
This constitutes a great protection. Through this inconceivable empowerment, merit [is generated].
As one's karmic obstacles naturally increase through spontaneous engagement, they are likewise spontaneously extinguished; the Buddhas awaken them and fulfill their aspirations.
Furthermore, the mantra for the arising of the Dharmadhātu is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ dharmadhātu*. (Dharmadhātu means "the realm of phenomena.")
*Sarva-bhāva-ātmaka-dharmadhātu*. "Dharmadhātu" refers to the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*).
The subsequent phrase, "I am," means that "I" is the dharmadhātu.
Furthermore, although this practitioner has not yet been able to realize the true nature of reality (*tattva*) in its essence, they nevertheless perform...
Reciting the mantra while forming this seal is itself identical with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). To form this seal: bend the two index fingers (the *śūnyatā* fingers) inward toward the palms;

with the left and right hands, clench the three fingers of earth, water, and fire into fists, and extend the two wind fingers straight upward (each hand forms a separate fist, with the extended wind fingers aligned side-by-side). First, extend the two wind fingers and place them at the chest, then direct them forward.
Turning inward, one forms [the mudrā] at the crown of the head by pressing with the tips of the wind-fingers (the index fingers).

One causes the two thumbs to move from both sides of the crown toward the left and right cheeks and neck respectively, drawing them slightly downward toward the heart, at which point the hands are released.
This means that first the fingers are held upright, then the tips are slightly directed downward while the backs of the fingers face inward toward the head, neck, and cheeks, gradually [moving down].
The fingertips should be close together. When reciting mantras and forming mudrās, it is like two oxen plowing together;
they must advance side by side and not one before the other. Next, to form the Wheel-Turning Mudrā (*dharmacakra-mudrā*):

first, perform the *pratyālīḍha-pāṇi-saṃpuṭa* (the reversed back-to-back palms joined), hooking the two ring fingers (*bhūmi-aṅguli*) with their tips facing inward (placing the right over the left). The remaining three fingers—water, fire, and wind—should likewise be hooked in reverse order.
Having finished the hooking, finally draw the two empty fingers (the index fingers) down to the palms so that they face inward and support one another.

This is the Seal of Turning the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana-mudrā*). By forming this seal, it causes both body and mind to be purified, enabling one to manifestly see the Buddhas of the ten directions turning the wheel of Dharma. The mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānāṃ vajratma huṃ. This mantra has already been explained above (verify further).

Next, regarding the formation of the sword mudrā (*khaḍgamudrā*): the sword is a metaphor for sharp wisdom, taking the sense of "able to sever and cut off. This refers to the removal of the mountain peaks of evil views.
Just as the peaks of a great mountain are exceedingly disordered and numerous, so too are the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Now, by forming this sword mudrā, through the power of this seal, one is able to sever and eliminate the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) along with its innate counterparts (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*). As for the method of forming this ritual seal (*mudrā*), first...

One should take refuge and join the palms (as described above). Then, bend the two ring fingers so that their tips touch, and place the two little fingers side by side, pressing and clasping them together to form the shape of a great sword. The mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām (as above). Mahākāyavīrarāja-vimala-dharma-sandarśaka-sahaja-satkāya-dṛṣṭi-nāśana.
Ṛṣicchedanaka-tathāgata-adhimukti-nirjāta-vīra-agra-dharma-niḥ... (The final syllable is likely *ṣṭhā*, as it follows the standard structure of this mantra.)

JATA (birth) HŪṂ. The Great Powerful One, the Stainless Dharma-manifestation, the Body Born of Coemergence, sees and severs [obstructions]. The Tathāgata’s faith and understanding give rise to the dharma of non-attachment.
Recite this mantra in the Sanskrit sound as it appears in the root sūtra; the commentary on its meaning is hereby concluded, as previously explained.
Furthermore, this mantra takes the initial syllable *ma* as its heart, which signifies the meaning of "self" (*ātman*).
Moreover, it is the syllable of the five void points (*pañca-bindu*), which signifies the meaning of "pervading all places. The intention here is precisely to destroy this view of self.
One should know that this sword is the great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, capable of severing all views; therefore, one uses the sword to cut through the afflictions.

The faculty of affliction (*daurmanasyendriya*) is precisely the manifestation of the stainless Dharma (*vimala-dharma*). That which is co-arisen with the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is what constitutes "stain" (*mala*);
now that this stain has been severed, one ceases from error. Yet, even though one has ceased [from error], there is still a superior Dharma that has not yet ceased:

namely, having removed this stain, one shall give rise to faith and understanding (*śraddhādhimukti*) toward the Tathāgata (this meaning is as explained at the beginning). What is this Dharma called "faith and understanding toward the Tathāgata"? It is as follows:
These are the roots of goodness, such as non-attachment. For this reason, the syllable *jaḥ* (pronounced *ja*) arises next;

here, the letter *ha* serves as the cause, and because it functions as the cause for removal (*hāna*), it has a long *ā* vowel mark (*ā*) beside it, which signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen (*anutpanna*).
Below is the letter *u*, representing samādhi, and above it is a dot (*bindu*), representing great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). One should recite this.
This enables the practitioner to fulfill the three kinds of bodies; because these characters contain three meanings, they are the manifestation of the *dharmakāya*.
The Tripiṭaka Master says that in the West, the methods for forming seals (*mudrā*) are especially secret.

When performing them, one must be extremely reverent, staying within a sacred chamber or a place that is empty, pure, and clean. One should bathe and adorn the body; if one cannot do so all at once...
First, one who bathes must thoroughly wash and rinse themselves, and only after anointing their hands with fragrant ointment may they perform the rite.

Furthermore, while performing it, one must maintain proper dignified demeanor, such as sitting in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*); otherwise, one incurs offense, which causes the Dharma not to be swiftly accomplished.
Next, perform the *śrī-śaṅkha-mudrā*. First, form the *añjali* in mid-air (as described above).
Bend the two index fingers (*agra-aṅguli*) and press them down with the two middle fingers (*tarjanī*), forming the shape of a conch shell (*śaṅkha*).

Having formed the mudrā, bring it close to the mouth and blow upon it according to the method of blowing a conch. This is the *śrī-śaṅkha-mudrā*, which fulfills all wishes; by performing this, [all desires are attained].
Therefore, one immediately fulfills all virtuous aspirations, proclaims the Great Dharma, and enables it to be heard and known throughout the ten directions;
this is the Seal of Quiescent Nirvāṇa. The refuge formula for its mantra is the same as before.
*Sarvatathāgata-hṛdaya* (the heart-mantra of all Tathāgatas). This is the core of the mantra.
"All phenomena are originally unarisen" (*sarvadharma-anutpanna*). Furthermore, the bindu above it signifies the Great Emptiness that pervades all places.
This is the essential nature of the Great Tranquil Nirvāṇa, like the stillness of all phenomena.
It pervades all places.
Next is the method for the Vajra-Indestructible Sitting Seal, also known as the Lotus Sitting Seal:

first, place the two thumbs and the two ring fingers side by side, while the remaining fingers are extended and slightly spread like a lotus flower just beginning to open; this is the aforementioned *bhadra-paryaṅka* (auspicious sitting).
The *Pāṇy-uttara-tantra* states that it should be shaped like a bell. Next, one modifies this by interlocking the earth and space fingers;
the middle six fingers remain extended as before, while the fire and wind fingers each join their respective counterparts, and the water finger remains solitary—this is precisely it.
This is the seal of the Lotus Seat, also called the Vajra Seat; one sits upon it as follows.
Because this seat is able to give birth to all Buddhas, and because all Buddhas arise from this very seat, it is named the Auspicious Seat (*śrī-āsana*);
it is therefore called the Indestructible Vajra Seat. The mantra for taking refuge is as before.
"A" (pronounced with a departing tone and a drawn-out vowel) is the heart of the mantra. This long "A" character represents *caryā* (practice), while the two side dots represent *samādhi*.
Furthermore, there is another dot to ensure that this dharma remains firm and solid. Now, regarding the method for forming the fist, there are four types.
When forming all mudrās, one should universally apply the following: first, as usual, form the fist and extend the thumb; this is the first.
Next, place the index finger within the palm while maintaining the fist; this is called the "Vajra Tathāgata Fist" and is the second.
Next, join the hands together to form a fist, causing the ten fingers to appear on the outside; this is called the "Pointing Finger."
This is the third outer fist (with the right index finger placed over the left). Next, interlace the ten fingers so that the tips of all ten fingers are inside the palms;
this is called the inner binding fist, the fourth (also with the right index finger placed over the left).
Next, perform the Vajra-mudrā: place both hands side by side and bend the index fingers (salilāṅguli) toward the palms;

join the backs of the middle fingers (vāyavyāṅguli) with the ring fingers (tejāṅguli) without touching their tips. This is the Vajra-mudrā. (The two thumbs [ākāśāṅguli] are also placed side by side and held upright, joined like the form of a five-pronged vajra.
By means of this Vajra-mudrā, one can destroy the palaces of ignorance, which nothing else can destroy. Its...
The mantra for taking refuge is as before.

The essence of the mantra consists solely of the universal taking of refuge in the Vajradhara, with the syllable HŪṂ (the meaning of which is to be explained in accordance with what was stated above).
Next, for the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mudrā: first form fists with the fingers pointing inward, then extend the two middle fingers so that they are parallel.

Next, place the two ring fingers (*vāyu-aṅguli*) upon the middle phalanges of the backs of the middle fingers, and bend the two thumbs (*ākāśa-aṅguli*) together, holding them slightly curved at the tips over the water;
this is it. (The phrase "fists with the fingers pointing inward" means the tips of the fingers are directed toward the inside. This great seal is named the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-binding.
When forming this mudrā, one is immediately identical to the Benevolent One; "Benevolent One" refers to all Tathāgatas.

This means that by performing this mudrā, one becomes identical to the bodies of all Buddhas. HŪṂ (protracted) HŪṂ (protracted). This is the mantra, and it also possesses the meaning of the three gates of liberation.

The former is the cause and the latter is the fruit. The cause is the practice of the Tathāgata, and the fruit is the attainment of Buddhahood. (Perform the combined gesture above the crown of the head.)
[Further inquiry].
Next, the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Ūrṇā (Hair-treasure) is as follows: form a fist with the hand of wisdom (*jñānahasta*) and extend the thumb straight upward, placing it between the eyebrows;
this is it. By forming this seal, one becomes identical to the Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ūrṇā. Its mantra is the *namas* (homage).
As previously [stated—further questioning the cause of practice and its arising], by means of this non-arising practice, one purifies all causes.
(*Ja* signifies that arising is unattainable).

Next, perform the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Almsbowl: with the left hand, hold the two corners of the robe (the method for this is to take the corner near the fingertips of the robe and the corner draped over the shoulder, wrap them around the elbow and insert them into the hand so that the two corners resemble a pair of ears).
Then, with both hands joined together, place the right hand over the left like the hands in the posture of sitting in meditation;
draw them upward until they are level with the navel and slightly bend them so that they form the shape of supporting an almsbowl with cupped hands—this is it. Perform it thus.
This mudrā is identical to the ritual of the Tathāgata holding the insignia of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
it is also capable of rendering all sentient beings who are not vessels fit to be vessels of the Dharma. As for its mantra, the homage is as before.
"Bhava" has the meaning of the "three existences" (trai-dhātuka). Because they are fundamentally unarisen, they are free from the three existences; the three existences are originally ungraspable.
"Attainment" means that by transcending these three realms of existence (*tribhava*), one attains the true existence of the Tathāgata, namely, the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.
Next, perform the mudrā of Bestowing Fearlessness: with the left hand as before holding the two corners of the robe, extend them to the level of the navel;
the right hand points upward and extends outward like the gesture of beckoning beings (this is the same as the Śākyamuni mudrā explained previously in the Yoga [section]).
If one forms this mudrā, it can eliminate the various fears, anxieties, and afflictions of all sentient beings, causing them to cease immediately;
it also removes their various great terrors of the future. Its mantra is as follows:
Homage as before. *Sarvatha* (all), *śāna śāna* (conquer), *bhayanaśana* (the removal of fear).
"Universal" (*prabhūta*) has the meaning of "pervasive," which is to say, pervading all places. Among all skillful means (*upāya*), it is the most supreme;

it excels them all. Because it first abandons the afflictions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and subsequently abandons the afflictions of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is stated twice—meaning it is supreme even among the supreme. For this reason, the Tathāgata is able to pervade all things.
This mudrā dwells in the universal removal of all fear and affliction.
Next, for the Tathāgata’s Mudrā of Fulfilling Wishes: the left hand is held as before, grasping the corner of the robe and extending it as previously described;
the right hand is turned outward, extended and hanging down, with the five fingers arranged like the mudrā of Ratnasambhava Buddha in Yoga practice. Form this [mudrā].
At the time of sealing, by the power of the Tathāgata, all Buddhas fulfill his wishes and he attains complete accomplishment.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before:
*Vajradhara-vajra-tmakā*. (Vajradhara means "Holder of the Vajra"; *vajra* means "diamond" or "thunderbolt"; *tmakā* means "I" or "self").
The meaning is: "I pray that all Buddhas grant me a vajra body; this is also to bestow upon me the body of great wisdom.
This is precisely the fulfillment of one's vow.
Next, for the mudrā of terrifying all obstructors, form a fist with the right hand (grasping the thumb) and extend the wind-finger (the index finger) straight.

One should place this seal vertically between the eyebrows (this means that the tips of the fingers should be placed at the midpoint of the eyebrows; "samādhi" refers to assuming the form of Bhṛkuṭī, with a face like that of a wrathful deity while the mind remains fixed on a single object without moving).

This Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of all Buddhas can manifest the power of the Tathāgata’s fierce and mighty majesty to terrify all obstructing spirits and cause them to be subdued; it can also bestow [benefits] upon all sentient beings.
When one who practices according to their vows binds this mudrā, those who create obstacles will not fail to scatter in the four directions;
even the hosts of Māra’s celestial armies, though possessed of great power, will naturally retreat and disperse.
At the Tathāgata’s site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), this mudrā is able to subdue all Māras. The mantra for taking refuge is as before.
Mahābalavatī daśabalavatī dhāpave mahāmaitrī vyūṭa-ghoṣite. This mantra is the great power of all Buddhas. What kind of power is this great power? It is the Tathāgata.
The Ten Powers are the greatest among all powers; how does the Tathāgata attain these Ten Powers?
It is because they are attained through great compassion that it is said these Ten Powers arise from great compassion.

Next, for the Buddha-Eye Mudrā: with the hand of wisdom, bend the index finger (the *ākāśa* finger) over the ring and little fingers (the *vāyu* and *pṛthivī* fingers), pressing its nail with the tip of the index finger;
then extend the middle and ring fingers (the *tejas* and *āpas* fingers). Form this with the right hand. Having done so, support the eyes with these two [extended] fingers:
first apply it to the right eye, then to the left. By means of this secret expedient, one is able to purify the faculty of the eye and achieve perfection.
Through the Buddha-eye, one is able to perceive the profound and secret realm of the Tathāgata.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before: *Gagana* (space), *vara* (wish), *raksana* (the aspect of the wish), *karuna* (compassion), *maya* (essence), *tathagata* (Tathāgata), *cakṣuḥ*.
Although empty space is signless and unobstructed, it cannot accomplish great deeds;
yet this emptiness of the Tathāgata, though having no basis, accomplishes all supreme matters and surpasses that empty space such that it cannot be equaled.
The essence of great compassion is the eye of the Tathāgata; this eye arises from great compassion and is able to give rise to [all things].
[This is] also the Seal of Great Compassion (asked again).
Next, for the Tathāgata Pāśa Seal: first form a fist with the ten fingers pointing inward;

then extend the two *vāyu* fingers (the index fingers), joining their tips so they touch in the shape of a circular ring. As for the two *ākāśa* fingers (the thumbs), press the right thumb against the left.
This is done by placing both palms together within. This mudrā can bind all those who do evil, and it can also destroy them, causing their various evils to cease.
The mantra for this is as before, beginning with the homage.
*Khe* (In this context, the sound *ha* is the cause; it also carries the meaning of samādhi. This *khe* is a call, meaning "call upon this cause for attaining Buddhahood.

Since this cause is fundamentally unborn, it is free from the characteristics of cause and effect, purifying this cause again and again. *Mahāpāśa* (This means "Great Lasso"; this cause, which is free from characteristics, is called the Great Lasso.

*Prasara* (Pervasive. *Dharyā* (Like space. [It is said that] this Great Lasso is as vast and pervasive as space, reaching everywhere. *Sattvadhātu* (It is said that this lasso is universally vast and acts...)

What is its purpose? It is said that within the realm of sentient beings, one upholds them by removing their delusion (*moha*). *Phaimuha* means delusion; it is the removal and destruction of delusion. *Tathāgata* means the Tathāgata.

*Dhimukti-nirjāta* (a compound of *dhimukti* and *nirjāta*) means born of resolute belief (*adhimukti*); it is also the arising of the original vows of all Buddhas. When the Buddhas practiced the bodhisattva path, they established great solemn oaths to deliver all sentient beings without exception.

If, by means of these essential causes, they were to attain the fruit [of Buddhahood] yet dwell in the bliss of liberation without remembering their original undertaking, they would violate their original vow. This too is called delusion. Herein, this [practice] removes such delusion and brings one to the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.
[This refers to] constantly performing Buddha-works.
Furthermore, from what does this cord arise? It is said to arise from the faith and understanding (*adhimukti*) of the Tathāgata.

The meaning of this faith and understanding has already been explained at the beginning of the sutra scroll; by the power of this faith and understanding, the Tathāgata manifests various kinds [of forms] through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*).
Whether manifesting in a form of great wrathful activity or as a vidyādhara ṛṣi possessing great power and majesty, one subdues and gathers immeasurable sentient beings,
causing them all to attain the sublime fruit of the Tathāgata; this is the meaning of the "Great Lasso" that extensively and universally pervades the realm of sentient beings.
Next, perform the Tathāgata Hook Seal (*tathāgata-aṅkuśa-mudrā*): first, with the left hand, press the tips of the four fingers excluding the thumb together so that they form a ring-like shape.

Then, insert the three fingers of the right hand into the ring; place the right thumb over the outside of the left thumb and bend it into the palm, pressing down on the three fingers of the right hand so that they also form a ring-like shape. Finally, extend the right hand.
To bend the third phalanx of the *vāyu* (wind) finger slightly so that it forms a hook shape is precisely this. This explanation differs from the sūtra;
I now suspect it is an error by the commentator (*śūstrakāra*). According to the sūtra, regarding this "Tathāgata Hook Seal" (*tathāgata-aṅkuśa-mudrā*):

with the two hands of *samādhi* and *prajñā*, interlace the fingers inwardly to form fists, then extend the *prajñā* *vāyu* finger (*anāmikā*) straight upward and bend it slightly to form a hook shape. This is the *brahma* [seal].
The Sūtra speaks in this manner, which differs from the Commentary; this point should be further questioned to reach a definitive conclusion.

By forming this hook-seal (*aṅkuśa-mudrā*), one can summon all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions to assemble at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and can also fulfill the stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*);
how much more so would those among the eight classes of beings who have not yet given rise to a wholesome mind not come?
Ākarṣaya sarvatrāṇapratihate tathāgatakośa bodhicaryāparipūraya.
In this context, "practice" refers to that practice by which one can summon the great ocean of merit of all Buddhas.
Just as a worldly hook has a specific location and limit and cannot summon or attract across all places, the hook of the Tathāgata is not like that;
it reaches everywhere, adding its influence to all without exception, even unto the ability to summon Great Bodhi.
To state the essential point: it completely fulfills all the merits of the Tathāgatas and universally summons all sentient beings, causing them likewise to attain this path.
Therefore, the next line says: "Pervading all harms" (where "harm" refers to the hooking and summoning of the remainder).
It pervasively harms all those who are unsubdued, causing them all to incline toward the practice of Bodhi and to attain fulfillment in the sublime fruit.
Next, for the Tathāgata Heart Seal: perform the aforementioned Hook Seal (*aṅkuśamudrā*), but further extend the wisdom-fire wheel (*tarjanī*) and bend it like a hook;

the concentration-hand (*samādhi-hasta*) bends both the wind and fire wheels (*anāmikā* and *madhyamā*) together into the palm. This is it. The method is all according to the previous [seals], with the only addition being that the fire finger (*tarjanī*) is extended.
These two fingers extended are those with their third joints bent. The mantra’s homage is as before:
*jñānodbhava* (the arising of wisdom). This refers to the wisdom of all Buddhas;
this wisdom is not obtained from another, but arises from the Buddha-mind itself.

Next, the Tathāgata Navel Seal is also based on the previous [seal], with the addition of extending the water-finger (the ring finger) [the diagram differs; consult further]. Generally, when three fingers are extended, the third joint is also bent;
this refers to the wisdom hand (*prajñā-hasta*). Now, this seal also differs from the sūtra. The commentator states:

"Extend the three wheels" [referring to the three fingers]; the sūtra only mentions extending the wisdom and water fingers, while the rest are crossed inwardly. The Sanskrit sūtra also agrees with this explanation.
It is appropriate to examine this again. The mantra for taking refuge is as follows: *Amṛtodbhava*. "Amṛta" (Nectar) is an epithet for wisdom;
it can eliminate the feverish afflictions of body and mind, and by partaking of it, one does not age.

Death may be used as a metaphor for the wisdom of the Tathāgata; now, by means of this wisdom, he removes the feverish afflictions of all sentient beings and enables them to attain a body of eternal life. This flavor of ambrosia also arises from the mind of the Buddha.

Next, the waist mudrā of the Tathāgata is performed according to the previous Tathāgata-hook mudrā; the difference is that the wind fingers (middle fingers) are tucked inside while the wisdom-water fingers (ring fingers) are extended.

These water fingers should be stretched straight and need not be bent at the third joint. (Regarding this right hand: the mudrās in the sūtra, the commentary, and the diagrams all differ from one another.

The sūtra states that the water-wheel [ring fingers] are stretched straight and the others are also held upright. The commentary states that the others are all crossed inward, with only the middle wisdom and water fingers upright. The diagram shows the two water fingers joined and held upright, while the others are all bound inward. Now, these three versions are inconsistent; it is appropriate...)
Question: One who transmits the Dharma of the Great Vehicle alone knows the fixed direction of the pointing finger at the water.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before: *Tadyathā* (the Tathāgata), *prabhāsuvāva* (arising).
One should know that this Wisdom Seal (*jñāna-mudrā*) arises from the Tathāgata. Generally, all seals and mantras are named after themselves.
The meaning of each [mudrā] is briefly provided here;
all others should be understood by analogy. Next, for the Tathāgatagarbha-mudrā: first, form the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) hollow-palms gesture.

The fingers of water (*vāri*) and wind (*vāyu*) are both bent into the palms (with the fingertips facing one another). The two fire (*tejas*) fingers are extended straight upward, with their tips joined together. II.

Place the two *śūnyatā* (space) fingers side by side and press them against each other; the two *vāyu* (wind) fingers [should be] on the two hands; the two *pṛthivī* (earth) fingers should also be extended so that the tips of the fingers do not touch, but rather slightly bent, making them all curved—this is it.
Regarding this seal (*mudrā*), there are also differences in the sūtras and commentaries. One sūtra says: "Bend the two *vāyu* fingers and insert them within;
the two *ākāśa* (space) fingers press down upon them; the two *tejas* (fire) fingers are extended and joined; the two *pṛthivī* and the two *ap* (water) [fingers are likewise]."
To slightly bend it is this; the diagram is the same as the sūtra.

*Ra* signifies "stainless," and the upper dot is the Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahāśūnyatā-samādhi*). The first syllable removes the obstacles of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*);
the second syllable abides in the emptiness of the Tathāgata’s nectar (*amṛta*). To the side of the next two syllables, two [dots] are added.

The word "Dian" (點) signifies the meaning of purification: the first character removes the defilements of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and the second character removes the defilements of those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Next, for the Binding of the Great Boundary Seal (*mahā-sīmā-bandhana-mudrā*), follow the method of the Tathāgata Hook Seal (*tathāgata-aṅkuśa-mudrā*) as previously described;

however, simply raise both hands so that the fingers of the water-position (*ap-kara*) are held straight and upright. (This was further questioned, but it was not clear. If one performs the seal according to the explanation in this commentary, the seals will not accord with the diagrams in the sutra.

According to the *Benjie chabie jing* (The Scripture on the Fundamental Distinctions), one first bends the two wind-wheels (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) and presses them with the two space-wheels (*ākāśa-maṇḍala*). The two fire-wheels (*tejas-maṇḍala*) are extended straight and joined together.

The two earth-wheels (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*) and the two water-wheels (*ap-maṇḍala*) are all made to stand apart. According to the diagram, the wind and fire wheels follow the scripture, while the two space wheels are raised side-by-side without pressing down.
The tips of the fingers of the wind wheels, the two earth wheels, and the two water wheels are all held upright. Regarding these three explanations, it is unknown which is correct.

Regarding the meaning of the "Great Boundary" (*mahā-sīmā*) herein: it refers to the period from the initial generation of the mind of great enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) until the attainment of Buddhahood;
during this interval, not allowing for interruption, not sinking into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and not regressing from enlightenment—this is the meaning of the Great Boundary.
The mantra’s homage is as before:
*Lī* (the samādhi of detachment from marks), *Ru* (the syllable *ra* forms the mark of the two vehicles), *Pu* (the ultimate truth;
the ultimate truth is unattainable), *Li* (detachment from defilement), *Vi* (detachment from bondage), *Ku* (the sound of manifestation), *Lī* (detachment from marks).
These seven are all samādhis; the Tathāgata uses these various samādhis as adornments, and there is nothing superior to them—this is the Great Boundary of all Buddhas.
Next, perform the Great Protection Seal according to the previous method:
using the Tathāgatagarbha Seal, extend the two water-fingers (ring fingers) so that their tips touch one another.
As for the "Mountain Peak" mudrā: its two fire fingers (middle fingers) also touch each other at their tips and are slightly bent, resembling the shape of linked rings;

furthermore, the two space fingers (pinky fingers) are opened with a distance of two inches or less between them—this is it. (*Note: This mudrā varies across the sūtra, the commentary, and the diagrams. The sūtra states: "Bend the two wind fingers (index fingers) so their nails face each other;

place the two space fingers side by side and bend them down; join the tips of the two fire fingers to form a circle; extend the two earth (ring) fingers and the two water (pinky) fingers. The diagram largely agrees with the sūtra, differing only in that it depicts the two space wheels separated and held upright.*)
The mantra is as follows:
*Sarvatathāgatebhyo namaḥ* (Homage to all Tathāgatas); *sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhitāya namaḥ* (To the one empowered by all Buddhas;
this is also a praise of the Buddha and an act of homage); *viśvamukhebhyaḥ* (To those with various doors; this also carries the meaning of "skillful" [referring to the Buddhas]).
This is the skillful manifestation of various gates of merit. *Sarva-ta* (the pervasive; meaning all times, all places, and all directions). *Haṃ khaṃ*:

*Haṃ* signifies cause, and *khaṃ* signifies emptiness; the dot (*bindu*) is also emptiness. By means of this pure emptiness, all causes are purified. Furthermore, that which is empty—this emptiness itself is also empty. *Rakṣa* (to protect):

not only protecting the followers of the two vehicles, but also protecting all Buddhas. Because of this, the Buddhas do not abandon sentient beings, constantly performing Buddha-works without rest, and do not abide in quiescent extinction. *Mahā-male* (Great Power).
This is the tenfold power of knowledge (*daśa-jñāna-bala*) of the Tathāgata. *Sarvatathāgata* (the Tathāgatas); *bhiṣanīya* (to be feared); *nirjāte* (born;

this means that these powers are born from the merits of the Tathāgata). *Hūṃ hūṃ*: [The first *hūṃ*] removes obstacles through terror; [the second *hūṃ*] is repeated for the sake of fulfilling the three qualities of a Buddha, meaning "extreme terror. *Trātaya trātaya* (protect, protect):
[this means] to subdue, to subdue both internal and external obstacles, and furthermore, to accomplish the Buddha-body (*dharmakāya*). Repeated for the same purpose.
Regarding the term *apratihata* (meaning "unhindered" or "without obstruction"): this name signifies the Great Protection of Intolerance (*akṣānti-mahārakṣā*).
Because its majestic radiance is so fierce and intense, it is like a newborn infant who cannot endure the light of the blazing sun; likewise, nothing at all can endure it or dare to eclipse it.
Therefore, it is called the "Great Protection of Inability to Endure," by which those who practice the mantra (vidyā-mantra) are protected.
Next, for the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-mudrā: join the two middle fingers (the *dvyaṅguṣṭha*) side by side and bend them into the palm;

extend the two index fingers (*tarjanī*) straight upward (each not touching the other, both held upright); join the tips of the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*) with a slight gap between their joints, forming the shape of a sword’s edge; as for the remaining fingers...

This is the same as the previous one (Note: This mudrā differs from the sūtra; the hands for fire, wind, and space are largely the same, while the two wheels of earth and water differ from the sūtra text.
In the sūtra, the two water fingers are held upright with their tips separated, while the two earth fingers are joined and upright. The diagram matches the sūtra). The mantra is: Homage as before.
Jvala (Jva is birth; va is binding; ra is appearance [light]; it has the bindu ā, which signifies non-arising; thus it is signless and unarisen [called light]).

Mālinī (Mā is "I"; li has a long vowel sound; nī is appearance; ī has the meaning of perception, that is, contemplation; it is free from both existence and non-existence). Tathāgataraśmiḥ (This is the light of the Tathāgata;
the light of the Tathāgata arises from within signlessness, non-contemplation, and so forth).
Next, for the Tathāgata-nail seal (*tathāgatāṅgulimudrā*), join the palms in the *tripuṭa* gesture;
place the two wind-fingers (*vāyu-aṅguli*) alongside the backs of the middle fingers and align them parallel. Its mantra is as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ pracaṇḍavajra-jvala-viśuddha-prabhā hūṃ. (The above mantra has been verified against the new edition. These three meanings are as explained above;
regarding other questions concerning the Upādhyāya, it is essential that one who is like a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood must receive this.
Seated upon the Vajra-throne for the sake of unsurpassed Bodhi, one subdues all Māra armies and attains perfect enlightenment;
for this reason, practitioners of the mantra path must don this armor to perform the Buddha-work.

Regarding this Tathāgata Armor Mantra and the Tathāgata Tongue Seal, they were previously omitted from various Chinese translations of the sūtras and their commentaries, until later the Upādhyāya Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra [restored them].
This was verified through consultation with the Sanskrit manuscript and the diagrams.

Next, for the Tathāgata-jihvā-mudrā (Tongue Seal): form the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) *añjali*; bend the two water-wheels (*tarjanī*) and the two wind-wheels (*anāmikā*) into the palms so that their nails face away from each other;
open the palms and place each of the two space-wheels (*aṅguṣṭha*) against the side of its respective wind-wheel. This is the Tathāgata-jihvā-mudrā.

The previous seal for the tongue is formed by pressing the tips of the index fingers into the palms while the remaining fingers remain as before; this is the seal for the tongue (omitted in the collated manuscript).
The mantra of the Tathāgata’s tongue is: "I take refuge," as before.
*Tathāgata-śāsana-dharmasthitir* (The Abiding of the Dharma of the Teachings of the Tathāgata). "Tathāgata" means "thus come" (*tathā-āgata*).
Just as the tongue of a Tathāgata always utters speech that is suchness (*tathā-vāda*), it never utters deceptive speech.
Because the language of others is based on such reality, it is eternally abiding.
Next, regarding the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Gate of Speech (the "gate of speech" refers to the mouth), follow the previous seal:

first form the *tri-puṭa* joined palms, then bring the tips of the water-fingers (*tarjanī*) and wind-fingers (*anāmikā*) together within the palms, and press them down with the two space-fingers (*aṅguṣṭha*) placed side by side. Its...
The second [mudrā] consists of the two fire fingers (tarjanīs), which are held straight with their tips side by side like a mountain peak;

this is it. (Note: This differs from the diagram and commentary. The diagram states that one may also form the *tripuṭa* hand by slightly opening the palms, bending the two wind fingers (*anāmikās*) so their tips touch, and placing each of the two space fingers (*aṅguṣṭhas*) beneath the respective wind fingers. The mantra for taking refuge is as before.
*Mahā-vāk-tara* (this refers to speech); *viśva-vid-jñāna* (various skillful wisdoms); *mahā-dhaya* (greatly vast).
This means that this speech arises from the Tathāgata’s skillful wisdom of immeasurable gates; this wisdom is vast and immeasurable.

Next, for the Tathāgata’s Tooth Seal: perform the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) añjali, bend the two *vāyu-aṅgulī* (ring fingers) into the palms so that the backs of their joints are aligned. The mantra of taking refuge is as before.
*Tathāgata-daṃṣṭrā* (the fangs of the Tathāgata), *rasa-rasāgra* (the supreme flavor among flavors,
which is the flavor of the Dharma of the Tathāgata), *agra-sampad* (attainment of the supreme), *sarva-tathāgata-viṣaya* (the domain of all Tathāgatas).
*Trambhava* (meaning "arisen," signifying that this supreme flavor arises from the realm of the Tathāgata).
Next, perform the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Fourfold Eloquence (*catur-pratisaṃvid-vāk*): join the palms in the *tri-puṭa* gesture;

hook the two *vāyu* fingers (the index fingers) and place them upon the backs of the two *tejas* fingers (the middle fingers), ensuring their tips do not touch. It is by means of this seal that the Tathāgata dwells amidst the assembly.
Fearlessly expounding the True Dharma for others, even within a single syllable containing infinite meanings—such eloquence is inexhaustible.
The mantra for taking refuge is as before.
Acintya (inconceivable), ānupūrva (successive), akṣara-vibhāga (the analysis of syllables— this too is marvelous), vāk-samanta (universal speech—
when the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, it reaches before all sentient beings; wherever it reaches, each person thinks,
"The Buddha uses my own voice to preach the Dharma to me"), prabhāsvara (luminous purity), sarva-ruta (all sounds).

Furthermore, because the speech and sounds uttered are free from all faults of verbal karma, such as coarseness and harshness, and are subtle, pure, and pleasant for others to hear, they are called "pure speech and sounds.

Next, regarding the seal of the Tathāgata’s ten powers: bend the fingers of the earth (ring finger) and space (middle finger) so that they rest within the palms, join the tips of the thumbs together so they touch, and form the *tripuṭa* with the remaining fingers; this is the seal. The mantra for taking refuge is as before.

Dara Hūṃ (Hūṃ represents the three virtues; Ma represents emptiness; Bindu represents samādhi; Ja has the meaning of "to produce. It also means "to summon"—furthermore, it is asked [meaning "to summon"]. This mudrā can uphold the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata.

These three syllables are combined at the end of the phrase, as in the Sanskrit original. Dha (entering) Śavalan-ga (the light of the limbs of the ten powers; regarding the word *laṅ* above, this refers to the ten powers.
Specifically, the long vowel *ā* attached to this *laṅ* is connected with *ga*, signifying the limbs).
"Dhāraṇī" means that by the power of this seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*), one is able to uphold the constituent parts of the Tathāgata’s ten powers (*daśabala*).
Next, for the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Applications of Mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), perform the *tri-puṭa* joined palms (these palms are joined like uncut lotuses in mid-air). Furthermore...
(Examine the preceding text to ensure there is no error. This refers to joining the two *śūnyatās*, the two winds, and the two earth-wheels (*bhūmi-cakra*) together.
As for the method of joining: the four fingernails should be made to touch one another, and the tips of the six fingers should be made to touch.
The commentary text mentions only "four fingers" and does not specify "two earth-wheels. The *namas* (homage) of the mantra is as before.
*Tathāgata-sitātapatra-sattvārtha-karodgata-gaganasama-asama*. (The Tathāgata’s White Parasol for the Benefit of Beings, Arisen Equal to Space, Peerless.)
It is said that this mindfulness is equal to space and immeasurable; yet, because space cannot serve as a comparison, it is further described as "unequaled.
The reason for this is that space, being of a non-existent nature, cannot bring great benefit to all sentient beings;
however, this mindfulness of the Tathāgata can bring great benefit to all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*.
Because it pertains to the Buddha’s work, it cannot be illustrated by analogy.
Next, for the Seal of Awakening to the Equality of All Dharmas, perform the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) *añjali*:
join the two water-fingers and the two space-fingers together so that they touch one another; this is it. For the *tripuṭa* *añjali*, bend the two earth-fingers and the two water-fingers inward.
With the palms, join the two *aṅguṣṭha* (thumbs) and place the two *tarjanī* (index fingers) upon the fire; this differs from the commentary.
Regarding the transmitter of the Dharma: the *namas* (homage) is as before.
*Sarvadharma-samantabhadra-pāraprāpta* (all dharmas are equal; having reached the further shore of all dharmas being equal).

*Tathāgata* (the Thus-Come One; "tathā" meaning "thus" or "rightly," and *āgata* meaning "come" or "attained")—it is called "Thus-Come" because he has come in accordance with reality, having attained such awakening as that [of the Buddhas].
Next is the Samantabhadra Seal of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel. As for why he is named Samantabhadra, it is because of all that this Bodhisattva possesses...
The three karmas are universally virtuous and excellent, for they are revered and praised by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. To form its mudrā, one makes three *puṭas*:
with the two wind fingers (the index fingers), one turns them over and places them behind the two fire fingers (the middle fingers), aligning the joints so that they are rounded.
The rest is as usual (*[The commentary states there are discrepancies and errors; further verification is required]*) . The mantra’s invocation is as before.

Samantānugata (pervading all equally), Vairocana (stainless and free from dust), Dharmadhātujāta (born from the Dharma—meaning this stainlessness arises from the Dharma), Mahāmahā (this term is repeated for emphasis, just as one says "the God of gods";

because the Bodhisattvas and others make offerings to the Buddha, and the Buddha in turn makes offerings to Samantabhadra—since the body of Samantabhadra is equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, this is the "Great among the Great," the offering within offerings; therefore, it is stated twice).
Next, for the mudrā of Maitreya Bodhisattva: form the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) palms and bend the two ring fingers so that their tips reach below the root of the middle fingers;
join the two little fingers together and press them down. The rest is as usual.
This mudrā is like the shape of a stūpa because it holds the Dharma-body stūpa of all Tathāgatas, just as Avalokiteśvara holds the Buddha’s body.
Thus it is. The *mantra* for taking refuge is as before:

*Aśitaṃ* (formerly called *Ajita*; this is his name, and its meaning is "Unconquerable," for among all afflictions of craving and views, even those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), there is none that can conquer him).
*Jaya* (victory; attaining victory within the unconquerable). *Sarvasattva-āśaya-nudya* (the dispelling of the dispositions of all sentient beings).
"Many" (meaning "to know" [arise]; "arise" is the meaning of "know," referring to knowing the nature of all sentient beings).
Each character (the Ācārya says this is the seed-syllable of Maitreya).
Next is the Ākāśagarbha mudrā: join the palms with the hollows facing outward, then bend the two space-fingers (the thumbs) together and insert them into the palms; this is it.

Alternatively, join the palms with the hollows facing outward, place the two wind-fingers (the index fingers) over the two fire-fingers (the middle fingers), and tuck the two space-fingers into the palms;
this is another version. These differ from the commentary, so they should be further examined. The mantra for taking refuge is as before.

Ākāśa (space), samanta (equal, meaning equal to space), nugata (attained; previously explained as "knowing," here explained as "reaching/attaining," which also accords with the former sense), citra-māvara (where *māvara* is a term for clothing, and *citra* means various;
thus, it means wearing various garments). This refers to wearing various garments while being like space—colorless yet able to manifest various forms.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; like space, he is able to fulfill various aspirations and benefit sentient beings.
Next is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin: join the palms three times (tri-puṭa);

bend the earth and water fingers into the palms, while the others remain as usual (the earth and water fingers being joined). Join the palms three times (tri-puṭa); bend the earth, water, and space wheels [fingers] inward.
Placing [the hands] within the palms so that wind and fire are joined vertically is correct; the commentaries differ on this (the *Jiǎ* commentary states they are to be pressed against one another).
The mantra for taking refuge is as before:
*Asattva-hita* (*A* has the meaning of "able to remove," and *hita* has the meaning of "benefit," meaning to benefit sentient beings); *pāya* (a conjunct syllable); *uḍ* (this character *uḍ*...).

[Enter with the long vowel of the preceding syllable. *Ghaṭa* (meaning "to remove" and also "to develop," causing one's virtuous nature to manifest). *Taraṃ taraṃ raṃ raṃ*. Regarding what is called "removal" above—what is it that is removed?

It refers to the removal of the four stains: first, the stain of craving and views; second, the stain of the śrāvakas; third, the stain of the pratyekabuddhas; and fourth, the stain of bodhisattvas. Because one removes the stain of sentient beings, one enters the stage of the śrāvaka;
because one removes the stain of the śrāvaka, one enters the stage of the pratyekabuddha; and so on, until because one removes the stain of the bodhisattva, one enters the state of complete purity.
Next is the Seal of Avalokiteśvara: first form the "opening-lotus" *añjali* by joining the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*) and the two index fingers (*tarjanī*), pressing them together;

the remaining six fingers are extended upward and spread apart, with the fire and wind fingers (middle and ring fingers) both held upright with their tips pointing outward, while the two water fingers (pinky fingers) alone are held erect. This is it. The mantra: [Mantra follows]

*Sarvatathāgata-avalokita-karuṇā-maya-rara-ra-hūṃ-ja*. [Sarva-tathāgata]: All Tathāgatas. [Avalokita]: "Avalokita" means to observe; it refers to the observation of the Tathāgatas. [Karuṇā]: Compassion. [Maya]: Essence.
This means that great compassion constitutes the essence; body and mind, internally and externally, are entirely embodied in great compassion. [Rara-ra]: The three defilements. [Hūṃ-ja]:
This syllable *hūṃ* signifies the practice of liberation, great compassion, and emptiness as the triad. *Ja* has the meaning of "birth," referring to phenomena produced from conditions.

Regarding the "contemplation of the Tathāgata" herein: although this bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, they manifest as equal to a Buddha because they perceive the nature of the aggregates (skandhas);
thus, it receives the name "contemplation. It takes emptiness and compassion as its essence.

This compassion and emptiness arise from being free from the three poisons and are produced through the roots of goodness such as non-attachment, thereby forming the three gates of liberation. Therefore, there are the three syllables *ra*.
Next, for the mudrā of Mahāsthāmaprāpta: form the *tripuṭa* (three-fold) añjali, bend the ten fingers so that they touch one another, making them perfectly round like an unopened lotus.
This unopened lotus is the Tathāgata’s precious casket, just as it is before it has blossomed.
This is because they are joined together. The mantra:

*Jhan* (the syllable *jhan* signifies "birth," while *sa* signifies "equal wisdom"). [It is further asked: "How does one depart from worldly birth and transcend the birth of a bodhisattva? [The answer is that] one abides in the midst of equal wisdom.
Next, for the mudrā of Bodhisattva Tārā: first, form fists by crossing the index fingers inward; then join the palms and extend both [index fingers] upward.
Join the two index fingers like the point of a needle; extend the two middle fingers side by side and press them down—this is it.
The mantra is:
*Tare* (O Savior), *Tāriṇi* (She who ferries [one] across, like one who places a person on the further shore of a great river), *Karuṇe* (Compassionate One).

Uṇnava (the character *uṇ* here is the residual sound of *ṇa*; this phrase means "arising"): because this Bodhisattva arises from compassion, he also leads sentient beings across to the realm of compassion.
Next is the Vajracarcikā mudrā: as with the previous mudrā, form fists facing inward and join the palms;

extend both index fingers (*vāyu-aṅguli*) together and upright, but let them be slightly offset so that the right finger overlaps the left—this is it. Its general form and posture are largely the same [as the preceding].
The *tāla* and *daṃśa* mudrās differ only in the positioning of the fingers.
The mantra is as follows: *Sarvabhaya-trāsaṇi* (O you who terrify all fears; among all fears, you further terrify them with terror, causing them to retreat and scatter.
Thus, those who are unsubdued are further subdued by fierce power, so that they may not commit further wrongs. *Hūṃ* (the three meanings are as above). *Phaṭ*.
(This also carries the meaning of "dispersing and destroying," causing those various fears to retreat and scatter.
Among all mantra recitations, this *Vijayā*, the Mother of Recitation (*Japamātṛ*),
is supreme in its efficacy, like a mother.

Next, for the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Śvetaketu: bend both ring fingers (water-fingers) into the palms; the two index fingers (space-fingers) are also placed side by side and bent so that they touch each other;
the remaining fingers form the *tripuṭa* joined palms. The mantra is as follows:
*Tathāgataviṣayaja* (born from the realm of the Tathāgata), *sambhava* (arising—meaning arising from the realm of the Tathāgata), *padmamālini* (garland;
an ornament for adorning the body; this refers to that which gives rise to the merits of all Buddhas as adornment, thereby adorning the Dharmakāya). Next, perform the Hayagrīva mudrā:
form three *puṭas*, bend the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*), join the nails, and tuck them beneath the root of the space-fingers (*tarjanī*).
The two empty fingers are held side-by-side, slightly raised so that their tips do not touch by about the width of a single grain of barley.
The mantra is:
*khādaya* (to devour—to devour all obstacles), *bhañja* (to shatter), *sphoṭaya* (to strike this obstacle and cause it to scatter in four directions).

The mantra:

Form the right hand in the same manner and insert it into the scabbard.)
This is the seal of Acala (Ajita). The sheath-hand is turned upward and the blade-hand is turned downward. (The mantra is as previously stated;

the mantras for all deities following this chapter shall likewise conform to those in the preceding chapter. The seal of Trailokyavijaya is identical to that of the five-pronged vajra. (Inquire further.)
Next, perform the Buddha-Eye Mudrā (*Buddhalocanā-mudrā*): form three *puṭas* by bending the earth and water fingers double and inserting them into the palms;
join the two fire fingers upright like a needle; rotate the two wind fingers to press upon the third joints of the two fire fingers, forming the shape of an eye;

and hold the two space fingers side-by-side upright, slightly bent, positioned directly below the middle fingers, pressing against the sides of the wisdom-water fingers so that their tips resemble upright eyes.
The form is that of the three eyes. As for the earth and water fingers, they are joined inwardly according to the method previously described;

this is called the *Buddhamātṛ-mudrā* (Seal of the Buddha-Mother), and here it is also called the *Uṣṇīṣa-mudrā* (Seal of the Buddha’s Crown) or the *Buddhabodhisattvamātṛ-mudrā* (Seal of the Mother of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas).
Next, for the mudrā of the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa: extend the left hand with the tips of the five fingers separated by about one inch to form the parasol;
make a fist with the right hand and extend the index finger (vāyu-aṅguli) upward to serve as the handle, resting the handle against the center of the palm of the left hand.
(In all instances where "making a fist" is mentioned, the thumb is placed on the outside; others should be understood accordingly. The mantra is as explained in the preceding chapter.
Next, perform the Seal of the Victorious Uṣṇīṣa; it is the same as the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Sword described previously. That is to say:
form three *puṭas* by joining the fire-fingers (the middle fingers) upright, and interlace the wind-finger (the ring finger) with the space-finger (the thumb). This is it.
Next is the mudrā of the Most Victorious Uṣṇīṣa; it is the same as the previously described mudrā of Turning the Wheel of Dharma.
Next is the mudrā of the Karma-Removing Uṣṇīṣa; it is formed by both hands making the hook-mudrā as before, which means:

forming the gesture of palms joined with fingers interlaced toward the body, bending the ring finger (*vāyu*) of the right hand so that it resembles a hook, and likewise twisting the two thumbs (*ākāśa*) to the right.

The "Left Hand of Aversion" (now, with one hand alone, form a fist with the right hand and extend the index finger, slightly bending its upper joint) is the same as the mudrā for the invocation in the Mañjuśrī Assembly mentioned in the preceding text.
Next, the fire-cluster *uṣṇīṣa* mudrā is the same as the previous *uṣṇīṣa* mudrā.
Next, the *vipula-janman* *uṣṇīṣa* mudrā is like the five-pronged *vajra* mudrā described previously.
Next, for the *janma-utpāda* *uṣṇīṣa*, perform the lotus mudrā (which is the same as the previous Avalokiteśvara mudrā). For the *apramāṇa-svara* *uṣṇīṣa*, perform the conch (*śaṅkha*) mudrā.
The mudrā is as previously described (namely, the three *puṭas*: double-bend the two thumbs and press them together with the two index fingers).
Next is the Ūrṇā-mudrā: form a fist with the right hand and place the thumb against the space between the eyebrows;
this is called the Cintāmaṇi, which is the Ūrṇā-mudrā.

The Buddha-eye mudrā is formed as previously described for the Buddha-mother mudrā; the slight difference therein is that one opens the *vāyu* fingers (the index fingers) and separates them from the backs of the *tejas* fingers (the middle fingers) by the distance of a single grain of barley, so that they resemble the form of a five-pronged vajra. This is it.

Next is the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Aparājita: place the right hand at the heart in the manner of holding a lotus flower (the wind and space fingers [index and middle fingers] are pressed together at their tips, the fire finger [ring finger] is bent down into the palm, and the earth and water fingers [pinky and thumb] are held upright). This is identical to the previously described mudrā of the Arising of Great Compassion, with this slight difference:
extend all five fingers of the left hand upward and outward, supporting it (the fingertips are spread apart); hold the hand slightly above the head. This is it.
(The manner of standing is as previously described for Pāṭalī).
Next, for the mudrā of the Vidyārājñī Aparājitā: form fists by interlacing the fingers inwardly;
then, extend the two index fingers parallel to each other, separating them as far as possible from the fists and bending their joints so that they resemble hooks—this is called the "mouth" gesture.
This is the mudrā of the Vidyārājñī Aparājitā.
Next, extend the right hand and rest it against the right cheek, tilting the head slightly so that it touches the hand;
this is the mudrā of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika devas (this is the *cintā-mudrā*, also known as the *Īśvara-mudrā*).

Next, as before, extend the right palm; slightly incline the head of the middle finger toward the inside so that it forms a staggered alignment with the water and wind wheels (the ring and little fingers), creating a slight row-like shape.
This is the seal of the Devaputra Samantakusuma (Hand placed at the side of the chest).
Next, as before, extend the right palm and bend the ring finger so that its tip touches the palm; this is the mudrā of the Devaputra Jyotiṣprabha (Light-Garland).
Next, as before, extend the palms and join the tips of the ring fingers and thumbs in the shape of holding a flower; this is the mudrā of the Devaputra Manobhirāma (Satisfied-Mind).
The *putra-mudrā* (the finger-seal of the son): [the remaining three fingers are held together side by side]. The above are both the seals of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika devas.

Next, with each hand, join the tips of the *ākāśa* (thumb) and *jala* (ring finger) fingers; with the ends thus joined, cover both ears. This is the seal of the Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin (or Samantaghoṣa) devaputra.

[With the *tejas* (middle finger) and *vāyu* (index finger) tips covering the ears—this is performed on the ground before the deity, signifying that one's voice shall be made known to all; this is also a seal of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika devas.]
Together with the seals of the Śuddhāvāsa deities, these constitute the five heavens [also known as the "seals made by the Hand of Solitary Wisdom," according to the collation].
Next, for the seal of the Earth Deity (Pṛthivīdevatā): first join the palms; bend the tips of all ten fingers together and press them against one another to form a circle.
Hollow out the interior of the palms so that their shape resembles a small flask (*kumbha*); this is it.
Next, as before, form the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), but bend the ring finger so it rests against the palm;
this is the seal for summoning the Fire God (*Agnideva*).
Form the hand of granting fearlessness, and with the ring finger, pinch the second joint of the little finger; this is the seal of all the *ṛṣis*. (From here...)
The second [mudrā] below is that of the Universal Sage (Viśvadeva).
First, press the second joint of the little finger with the thumb; then, stand the remaining three fingers upright and parallel. Following the sequence:
first extend the index finger, next the middle finger, then the ring finger, and finally the little finger, keeping it slightly separated from the earth; then, release all five fingers completely.
This refers to the five great sages (*pañcamahā-ṛṣi*) according to the sequence of the sūtra.
Next, for the seal of Yama: form three *puṭas* (folds) by bending the two wind fingers and two earth fingers into the palm so that their tips meet;
with the two space fingers, pinch the back joints of the two wind fingers (at the second and third phalanges); slightly bend the tips of the space fingers so that they face the fire finger.
This refers to that [the *daṇḍa-mudrā*].
Next, extend the fingers of the right hand, covering the palm so that it takes the shape of a bell, and let it hang downward; this is the *Yama-rājñī-mudrā*.
