Next, with the hand of concentration, bend the earth and water fingers into the palm; extend the fire and wind fingers so they are parallel;
slightly bend the head of the space finger so that its tip touches the base of the wind finger. This forms a fist as is customary. This is the Seal of the Night Sky (the Seal of Queen Yama).
Next, as with the previous mudrā, simply bend the index finger and press its second joint with the tip of the thumb;
this is the *Rudra* mudrā (the mudrā of the Queen of the Lord of Freedom). [The mudrā of the Queen of the Lord of Freedom is also inquired about.]

Next, with the left hand, form the seal of Brahmāṇī, which resembles the shape of holding a lotus flower (that is, extend the palm and join the thumbs and ring fingers to press the middle fingers, which are bent inward against the palm;
in the diagram, they are also shown extended straight). Question: Since Brahmā is without desire and lacks a female body, why is she called a "consort" (*rājñī*)?
Answer: This is the consort of the Brahmā King. "Consort" (*vidyārājñī*) has the meaning of *samādhi*; because this is a seal (*mudrā*), it is figuratively called a "consort."
Next, extend the palm of the left hand and bend the earth (thumb) and water (index finger) fingers into the palm;
rotate the wind (ring finger) and press it against the back of the fire (middle finger);

slightly hook the space (pinky) finger and place it beneath the wind finger—this is the *Kāmarūpa-ḍhakkī* mudrā (*ḍhakkī* refers to a musical instrument, as shown in the diagram). This is the son of Maheśvara named Kṛttikā; this is *Kāmarūpa*.
This is the name of his consort.
Next, extend the three fingers of earth, water, and fire of the left hand outward so they are each spread apart; then, with the wind finger (ring finger), touch the space finger (thumb).
This is the mudrā of Nārāyaṇī’s consort (hold the Flower Mudrā over the chest and turn this mudrā outward to support it).

Next, form a fist with the left hand and extend the index finger straight upward; this is the mudrā for the Seven Mothers of King Yama and their attendants (this mudrā is used universally for all seven mothers).
Next, extend the left hand and bend it into the shape of supporting a skull, holding it facing upward against the chest;
this is the seal of Cāmuṇḍā.

With the left hand, place the thumb upon the earth and water fingers (the little finger and ring finger) and extend the fire and wind fingers (the middle finger and index finger) together and upright; this is Nairṛti.
This is also the Sword Mudrā.

Next, extend the left hand alone and relax it as before; it is like the previously described Wheel-Turning Dharma Mudrā, with the difference that only a single hand is used without the fingers being interlaced or entwined. This is the Nārāyaṇa Mudrā.
With the hands in the mudrā of concentration, extend the four fingers upright and bend only the thumb (the *aṅguṣṭha*) across the palm.
Next, extend and spread the ten fingers and cover them with the two thumbs, interlacing them; this is the seal (*mudrā*) of all nāgas.
Next, place the right hand over the left as before; this is the mudrā of the Nanda Nāga King. Rotating the left hand to be over the right is the mudrā of the Lesser Nanda Nāga.
As with the previous nine-headed dragon mudrā, place the two palms flat together, extend the four fingers of each straight out, and divide them into two wings with a space between them.
The fingers are interlaced like a beak; this is the seal of the King of the Garuḍas, also known as the King of the Kinnaras. It also causes [the opponent] to tremble with fear.
The hand is held palm upward (generally, most seals used for those dwelling on the earth are performed with a single hand).
Next, extend the left hand with the fingers held upright so that the fingertips do not touch, spreading them wide like the shape of a trident.
Then, join the palms at the space between the thumbs, pressing the small fingernails together. This is the *triśūla-mudrā* (trident seal) of Śaṅkara (the Lord of the Skeleton).
Forming the previous mudrā while joining the three fingers together is the Umā mudrā; according to another version, it is called the Narmadā mudrā.
This is the consort of Śaṅkara. (The two mudrās are similar; whereas in the former the index finger is slightly bent, here it is held straight and upright, fanned apart.)
Form the half-lotus mudrā with the left hand exactly as in the method for forming the Avalokiteśvara mudrā, but perform it with only one hand;
this is the Brahmā mudrā. An alternative version states that it is formed by pressing the space-element finger against the earth-element finger.

On the following day, when the celestial chariot and seals manifest, one joins the palms and bends the tips of the two wind fingers (the ring fingers) so that they press against the third phalanges on the backs of the two fire fingers (the middle fingers), while the tips of the two water fingers (the little fingers) are brought into alignment with them; these two water fingers likewise rest upon the backs of the middle fingers.

According to an alternative version, one places the wisdom hand and the dhyāna hand palm-to-palm and uses the thumbs (space fingers) to each press against the second phalanges of the two water fingers.
The phrasing regarding the wind and the various [elements] is identical to the back of the fire; thus, examine it carefully as being different from the commentary.
As for the moon seal, it is no different from the seal of Brahmā, with the sole distinction that one should visualize a white moon disc.

Next, join the palms and bend the *vāyu* (ring) and *pṛthivī* (little finger) fingers into the hollow of the hands; then bring the *tejas* (middle) and *ap* (index) fingers together to form a circle, bending them like a bow.
This is the *Raudra-syāpi-duya-mudrā*.
Next, the mudrā of Vāyu is as described before: that is, extending the left hand with the palm facing sideways and bending the earth (thumb) and water (ring finger) fingers.
This is the Vāyu-dhvaja-mudrā. Regarding this mudrā, the sūtra, the diagrams, and the commentaries differ from one another. The sūtra simply states it is "as before, the dhvaja-mudrā.
Furthermore, there is no such dhvaja-mudrā mentioned previously; rather, the diagram depicts it using the wisdom hand (right hand), while still bending the fire (middle finger).
The *vāyu* (wind) mudrā is placed on the palm; the remaining three fingers are all extended upward. For now, I have recorded them all together, though it is not known which is correct.
First, turn the left hand upward against the navel in the manner of holding a lute (*vīṇā*).

With the right hand, join the *vāyu* and *ākāśa* (thumb and ring finger) together, while the remaining three fingers are extended loosely toward the body. Move them as if plucking strings; this is the seal of the goddess Ghoṣavatī (and it also subdues the gandharvas).
[These] are the Devīs and also belong to the class of Gandharvas.
Next, as before, the noose mudrā is the mudrā of all the Nāgas (that is, forming the inner-interlaced fist and extending the wind-finger [index finger], hooking it and bending it to touch the thumb).
Performing it with the left hand alone constitutes the seal of the Nāga King Vāsuki (this seal is not present in the aforementioned scripture).
Next, form the seal of the Asura with the left hand as shown in the diagram for the seal of the Music God (*Gandharva*):

bend the wind-finger (*vāyu-aṅguli*) of the right hand over the back of the fire-finger (*tejas-aṅguli*), extend all other fingers, and place the palm facing downward upon the left hand. This is the seal of the Asura.
In another version, the wind-mudrā (vāyu-mudrā) is bent and placed upon the surface of the space-mudrā (ākāśa-mudrā), while the remaining fingers are all extended.

Its mantra is: *Gara-lā-yan* (*Ga* is because movement is unattainable; *ra* is because it is stainless; *la* is because it is free from characteristics; *yan* is because there is nothing to be obtained; the dot above signifies the Great Space).
The gandharva forms the inner-palm fist with the tips of the water-fingers (tarjanīs) joined together; this is the samaya of this family.
If one performs the *karmamudrā* alone, it is as follows: place the thumb upon the three fingernails and extend the ring finger straight;
this is the *gandharvamudrā*. The mantra is: [Mantra]
*Phuṣṭa* (entry), *dhau* (purity), *sarva* (sound), *ravahe* (emit). [The meaning is: "emit the sound of purity";
these are all worldly samayas.
Next, form a fist with the left hand, bending the ring finger (*vāyu*) like a hook so that it does not touch the tip of the index finger (*ākāśa*) even slightly.
This is the seal of all yakṣas (it may also be performed by joining the hands). An alternative version states: "The wisdom and dhyāna [hands] are interlaced within like hooks;
the two earths and two waters are joined and held upright; this is the seal of all yakṣas. This is according to the sūtra. The mantra is as follows:

*Bhaiṣajya* (the term *bhaiṣajya* means "remedy"; the meaning of the word-element is "to consume"). *Īśvara* (meaning "sovereign"; he is so named because he has attained mastery over all afflictions).
Next, with the left hand, press the tips of the nails of the ring fingers against the ground, extend the water and fire fingers, and press the thumb with the wind finger.
This is the mudrā of all yakṣiṇīs on the finger joints (it may also be performed by joining them). Regarding the mudrā of the yakṣiṇī according to the sūtra:

it is formed by joining the remaining three fingers while the thumb and ring finger are held apart like the appearance of empty space, with the others extended upward. According to the diagram: form a fist by crossing the wisdom-finger (middle finger) and the mind-finger (ring finger) within;
extend the other fingers upward, with the tips of the two fire-wheels (index fingers) separated by half an inch. This is the mudrā of all yakṣiṇīs. True.
The words are as follows:
*yakṣa-vin-dhara* (the term *yakṣa* means "to eat"; *vi* has the sense of "binding," meaning that one devours these fetters of affliction; *dhara* means "to hold" or "to clarify").
Next, with the left hand, pinch the three fingernails with the ring finger (*anāmikā*), then extend the middle finger upright; this is for all *piśācas*.

This is the mudrā (it may also be performed simply by forming a fist and extending the middle fingers; according to the sūtra, it consists of crossing the two hands inward and raising the fire-fingers [index fingers]; the illustration matches the sūtra). The mantra is as follows:
Viśacagati (Gati means "going"; since the ultimate goal is unattainable). Next, following the previous method, slightly bend the middle finger;
this is the mudrā of the Viśacī woman. (The Tang and Sanskrit versions both provide the same illustration:
interlace the inner hands of concentration and wisdom, extend the two index fingers, and slightly bend them so that their tips do not touch. The mantra is as follows:

*Viji viji*. (*Vi* is the ultimate negation; it means to transcend birth and death. Because one knows the ultimate truth, one transcends birth and death. The repetition of the term signifies the absolute transcendence of birth and death.
Next, join the two hands in *añjali*; the two index fingers (the *ākāśa-aṅgulī*) should also be aligned and extended fully, keeping them separated from the other fingers.

Gṛhila is what kind of *mudrā*? (This is a distinct class of being, neither human nor ghost, capable of terrifying people; that which is possessed by such a non-human [being] is this; it is not this [other thing];
it is a planet (*graha*), and if it is near a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), one should take the nine planets as the fixed rule).
*Kelike* (meaning "action," "defilement," or "cause"), *śavariya* (meaning "sovereignty"), *prapto* (meaning "attained"), *rudra* (meaning "light";
it is called light because of the various luminaries), *maya* (meaning "nature"; it means to attain sovereignty within the nature of light; one calls that name and attains sovereignty therein).
Next, first perform the *tripuṭa* [mudrā]: interlace the two fire fingers and the two space fingers, pressing the right over the left.

This is the seal of all the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*). The mantra is: *nakṣatra-nir-datiye*. *Nakṣatra* refers to the lunar mansions. *Nir* means sound; *datiye* means food, thus it means "the food of all sounds.

*Na* has the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and *kṣaya* has the meaning of exhaustion; thus, it means "all are completely exhausted. *Tra* is as before, having the meaning of defilement (*mala*) and so forth.
To speak according to its etymology, it means "to consume" the various defilements and stains; thus, this pure sound is universally disseminated as the so-called "stainless sound.
All such mantras mentioned above employ melodious tones to proclaim their true virtues, awakening them and causing them to rejoice.
Next, form three *puṭas* by double-bending the two water-fingers (*anāmikā*) and inserting them into the palms; the rest is as in all previous mudrās.
This is the *rākṣasa-mudrā*. Regarding the mudrās of the terrestrial deities mentioned above, whether the *sūtra* states they are formed with both hands or with one hand, either is acceptable.
If, due to circumstances such as recitation or other duties, one lacks the leisure for both hands, [one may use one hand].
As for the manual execution, it is accomplished by using only the left hand (as stated above in the sūtra regarding "two hands" while drawing with the left hand, this is what is meant).
The mantra is as follows:
*Rākṣasa* (where *ra* means "stainless," with a dot beside it indicating the sound *a*, which signifies "action"; *kṣa* means "traversing space"); *dīpate* (meaning "king," referring to his virtue;
having caused others to hear this, they rejoice and fulfill the wishes of sentient beings).
Next, extend the left hand to cover and conceal the mouth, and touch the tongue to the palm; this is the *ḍākinī-mudrā*.
The upper part of the letter *ha* is free from causes and stainless; the *samādhi* dot (*bindu*) above it indicates wrath.

*Ha* signifies the meaning of cause, and the dot likewise signifies wrath. Those that take these as their heads—beginning with the various mudrās mentioned above and ending with Ḍākinī—are, when expanded to include all categories and retinues, of infinite varieties, as stated in the tenth chapter of the Mahātantra-sūtra.
That which is explained in this chapter from among the ten thousand verses is merely a brief citation of its primary points;
it is like raising the main ropes of a net, whereby all the meshes of the net are raised.
Lord of Mysteries, such as these, the signs of bodhisattvas born from the Buddha’s faith and understanding have already been realized by the Tathāgata as equality.
Because the Dharma-realm, through the power of its original vows and great compassion, manifests this gateway of the secret body by means of the empowerment of its spiritual powers,
so that all sentient beings may attain faith and understanding and together enter the stage of omniscience—
it should be known that such mudrās as these arise from the faith and understanding of the Buddha; it should be known that such mudrās as these are thus.
These are the insignia of these bodhisattvas; because they manifest the virtues of the Tathāgata’s internal realization through these skillful means, they are called "insignia" (*cihna*).

Just as a seal is applied to many things, even down to the movements and postures of the body, so too, if an ācārya clearly understands yoga and deeply penetrates the secret intent, he is able to purify the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Because they have attained mastery over the secret dharma through the purity of mind, whatever they do is for the benefit and subduing of sentient beings;
in all their actions, there is nothing that does not accord with the majestic deportment of the Buddha.
Therefore, every movement and action of the entire body is none other than a mudrā. This is not limited to physical karma alone, but extends even to all [other activities].

All speech is likewise the mantra. For this reason, Lord of Mysteries, a bodhisattva practicing through the gateway of mantras who has already resolved upon bodhicitta should abide in the maṇḍala of the Buddha-ground;
if one acts otherwise, it constitutes slandering the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, and is a transgression beyond the three [vehicles].
Regarding the statement that "the violation of the *samaya* leads inevitably to falling into the evil destinies":

this means that in the present degenerate age, those Bodhisattvas of mantra practice who have already resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) should first abide in the stage of a Buddha before constructing a maṇḍala.
If one acts otherwise and constructs it arbitrarily, that constitutes slandering the Buddha. Therefore, the aforementioned Ācārya should understand this.
Knowing that each of these methods, such as the mudrās and mantras, does not deviate from their respective rules,
one should also long cultivate the practice of yoga to purify the karma of body, speech, and mind. By understanding the practice of the dharma-gate of the equality of the three karmas,
and through the empowerment of this yoga, the mantras, and the bodily mudrās, one becomes identical to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

One’s own body is identical to the state of the Buddha; through this samādhi, phenomena and principle do not conflict, and one establishes the circular maṇḍala, as well as its locations, forms, and so forth, such that each accords with principle without error.
One should know that by skillfully understanding the sequence, one will certainly obtain great benefit without fail. If it is otherwise, one transgresses the samaya.

The "sin of violating the samaya" refers to one's own vow. It is the vow established by all Tathāgatas with the desire to universally open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for all sentient beings, causing them all to become like myself;
thus, this dharma is established through skillful means. Therefore, it is like the edict of a great worldly king, which must not be transgressed; were it to be transgressed—
One will inevitably incur severe retribution. Therefore, one should act while remaining in accord with the bodhicitta and abiding on the stage of a Buddha;
for if one does not follow the teachings, it is merely a waste of effort and a vain squandering of time that results in nothing accomplished, only inviting sin and guilt without any benefit.
Thus, the practitioner should carefully seek out the sūtras and the Dharma, and seek out an enlightened teacher. Do not...
The detailed explanation for those who have erred themselves is now complete.
*The Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
*The Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*, Scroll Eleven.
The *Commentary on the Single Practice* (Ekavyūha-ṭīkā) by Śramaṇa Yi-hang.
Chapter Ten: The Wheel of Syllables.
The Buddha again addressed Vajrapāṇi: "As for what was previously asked by Vajrapāṇi, the Buddha has already answered it in successive order."
Since there were points in the preceding text that were not fully exhaustive, I shall now explain them further; therefore, I command you to listen attentively.

There is a dharma-gate called "Pervading All Places. That which is the station of the syllable-name of that Bodhisattva—the dwelling place wherein all activities and tasks are accomplished—is precisely this Dharma-gate of the Syllable Wheel (*akṣara-cakra*), which is the Dharma-gate that pervades all places.
If a bodhisattva abides in this Dharma-gate of the Syllable Wheel, then from the initial generation of the sublime mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood,
all various activities for one's own benefit and the benefit of others occurring during that interval shall,
by virtue of entering this Dharma-gate, be entirely accomplished without any hindrance. Furthermore, regarding what has been explained above:
The meaning of the *ācārya* abiding in the stage of Buddhahood has not yet been fully understood; it refers to this very gateway of syllables (*akṣara*).

The initial syllable "A" is itself the bodhicitta. If one contemplates this syllable and attains correspondence with it, one is identical to the essence of the Dharmakāya of Vairocana. This is because contemplating the wheel of this syllable "A" is as follows:
Just as the radiance of a peacock’s tail-wheel surrounds a practitioner who dwells within it, so too does one dwell in the state of Buddhahood.
(Question again: This wheel of syllables should be made threefold; the syllable *A* is placed in the center, while the other syllables as its retinue are placed on the outside.
Furthermore, this syllable *A* has five types, and at the beginning of each wheel of syllables...
First, there are the threefold heart-mantras of taking refuge in the Triple Gem, namely the syllables *A*, *Sa*, and *Va*.
These manifest the meaning of the three families (*kula*): the syllable *A* is the Tathāgata family, the syllable *Sa* is the Lotus family, and the syllable *Va* is the Vajra family.
Each of these three families revolves according to the five-syllable wheel, corresponding to their respective meanings as previously described.
Regarding the term *maṇḍala*, what is now called a "wheel" (*cakra*) is precisely the meaning of *maṇḍala*. In the former ritual of the altar (*maṇḍala*), the center is Mahāvairocana Tathāgata;
this is identical to the letter *A* within this [present] context. To the north, the lotus and its various retinues are placed together in one location;
this is the letter *Sa* within this context. To the south, Vajrapāṇi and his various retinues are placed.
The "affiliated" (shǔ) refers precisely to the syllable *va* within this context. Now, from the syllable *a*, four further syllables arise;
these are the petals of the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha). Because many syllables are generated from a single syllable, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*).
Once the practitioner has brought forth the primary syllable *a*, which is the essence of the bodhicitta, there follows...
The five sounds *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and *ṅa* (excluding the fifth vowel from each) all take four characters;
next, one further takes *ya*, *ra*, and so on, up to *kṣa* (a conjunct), all of which are masculine sounds and enter the wheel of the letter *A*.

Since the practitioner has already generated the bodhicitta and should proceed to cultivate the conduct of the Tathāgata, the wheel of the letter *Ā* (departing tone) is explained next as that conduct. Its...
The three families refer to the three syllables [A, Va, Ra].
Next, from the syllable Ka up to Kṣa, all are likewise provided with a dot at the upper corner to serve as the wheel of the long Ā (ā-kāra).
Since one who has already perfected the conduct of the Tathāgata achieves awakening (*bodhi*), the wheel of the syllables A and Ma is explained next. These are the three families.
Furthermore, this letter *A* with a dot above it signifies the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*). Because this bodhicitta is free from all characteristics, it is called the Buddhas;
this is the accomplishment of bodhi. This letter *Ka*, and so on up to *Kṣa*, each with a dot added above, constitutes the wheel of the syllable *Aṃ*.
Having already accomplished bodhi, where should one go? It is called Great Nirvāṇa (*mahānirvāṇa*).
Following the *bha* [wheel], the wheel of the syllable *aḥ* is clarified; this is the wheel of the three families (*trikula*).
From *ka* up to *kṣa*, all have two dots added as sub-scripts, which constitute the wheel of *nirvāṇa*.

The single character *aḥ* (with the *praśleṣa*) is the wheel of skillful means (*upāya-cakra*), and for this reason it is not present here; this is the wheel of Śākyamuni Buddha (the Karma family, which pervades all wheels).
Therefore, there is no separate mandala; this is what is meant by "yoga. Generally, the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*) is divided into three parts: first, the syllable *A* constitutes one part;
next, from the syllable *Ka* up to the twentieth syllable constitutes the second part; and next, from the syllable *Cha* up to the syllable *Ha* constitutes the third part.
The syllable *Kṣa* is excluded because it is redundant (that is, it contains both the sounds *ka* and *sa*, and is thus repeated). By means of these...
The characters above are all syllables of wisdom (*jñāna*). Next, there are the eight syllables *i* (high tone), *ī* (low tone), *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*;
when these eight syllables are added, they accomplish *samādhi*. These are all sounds of *samādhi*.
Their meaning can be understood as they also revolve according to the five wheels (*pañcacakra*). Next, there is *ga* (pronounced like *yu-ke*).

[Reverse: If [it can be reversed], *Ṭha* (upper tone, read as *mù kě fǎn*) and *Na*. This character pervades all places, meaning it pervades both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, these five characters also rotate according to the five wheels (*pañcacakras*), which means that by adding side strokes, adding a circular dot above, or adding two dots beside, these five [forms] all become the five characters. That is to say:
Regarding the "wheel of syllables" (*akṣaracakra*): from this wheel of rotation, all syllables arise. "Wheel" has the sense of "generation.
For example, from the single syllable *A*, four syllables are generated: *A* is the bodhicitta; *Ā* (long) is practice; *Aṃ* (nasalized) is the accomplishment of bodhi;
and *Aḥ* (aspirated) is great quiescent nirvāṇa. *Aḥ* (protracted) is skillful means, just as in the case of *A*.
Regarding the syllables (*akṣara*), one should know that the letter *ka* also consists of five letters;
likewise, one should know that up to the letter *kha*, there are twenty letters in total. Following these, there are twelve letters, namely:
The two characters are identical to the horizontal strokes above the letters, which signify *samādhi*.
The five characters *aṅga*, *na*, *na*, *maṅ*, and *ya* are likewise identical to the dots (*bindu*) atop the letters; they signify "also.

The eight characters *ka*, *ca*, *ra*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa* are identical to the side-dots (*anusvāra*) of the letters, which carry the meaning of "excluding. One should know that this wheel of syllables pervades all mantras.
Within this, if one sees the syllable A, one should know it explains the meaning of bodhicitta;
if one sees the long Ā, one should know it reveals the conduct of the Tathāgata; if one sees the syllable Am, one should know it reveals tripiṭaka-bodhi;
if one sees the syllable Aḥ, one should know it reveals mahāparinirvāṇa; if one sees the long Āḥ, one should know it reveals the power of skillful means.
Likewise, if one sees the twenty syllables beginning with *ka*, they should be explained according to their respective categories and meanings;

it should be known that all these syllables are wisdom (*prajñā*). If one sees the eight syllables beginning with *ra*, it should be known that they are identical to the side-dot (*bindu*), which is also a corresponding application according to its category (meaning that the syllable *ra* is "stainless" and so forth). If one sees [the vowels] beginning with *i*, it should be known that this reveals meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
If one sees the five characters beginning with "Yaṃ" (仰), one should know that they manifest the bindu of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).

That Great Emptiness, which is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), is the very meaning of attaining Buddhahood. If a practitioner realizes this in such a manner, they are able to enter the meaning of all *dhāraṇīs* and revolve therein without obstruction; therefore, it is called the "Wheel of Characters" (*akṣaracakra*).
Thus, the *Guhyapati Akṣarapathadvārasaddharmamantrayānavihārakrama-buddhādhiṣṭhita-samyaksambuddhamārga-satpuruṣacaryā-nartana-sūtra* states:
"In this way" refers to the aforementioned wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*).
As explained above, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and so forth, are precisely the gateways to the Buddha-way (*buddhamārga*). They are capable of—
This is the path to attaining perfect enlightenment. If one understands the meaning of these syllables, one will be able to abide in the path of mantra;

therein, one will fully comprehend and clearly master the sequential methods of entry, the characteristics of realization, and the distinctions between the stages, as well as the points of obstruction and penetration, without any doubt or stagnation.
Furthermore, even worldly children constantly [learn] these Siddhaṃ letters.
How can one cultivate [the path] so as to suddenly accomplish such a feat?

It is because these syllables are all issued forth from the Tathāgata’s internally realized essence by means of the Tathāgata’s power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that they possess this inconceivable activity and function.
If a person clearly understands the underlying intent herein, that skillful means is itself the penetration of *sambodhi*.
If one can penetrate the Way, it means they understand the faculties, dispositions, and desires of all sentient beings;
they should know by what dharma one enters the Way and through which gate one attains awakening.
Being able to comprehend such infinite and boundless matters, they bestow the sublime Dharma upon sentient beings according to their needs, causing them all to reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, as for those who dance, they are like worldly dancers who, in the midst of a great assembly, manifest various physical actions— bending, extending, bowing, and looking up—
and produce various subtle, exquisite, and skillful sounds and melodies. According to what sentient beings desire and enjoy, they cause that great assembly to experience joy,
or to feel sorrowful reflection, or to feel terror, all through what is produced by their single body and voice.
Through skillful means, the benefits conferred upon sentient beings vary, for he well understands how to proceed and how to desist in accordance with their minds;

the Bodhisattva is likewise: manifesting various modes of deportment, there are none that do not constitute the *mudrā*, and from these he produces various sublime dharmas, all of which are mantras that respond perfectly and universally, bringing great benefit to all. Therefore, this is called the "Bodhisattva Dance."
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have all made this teaching—having taught it, now teaching it, and shall teach it. Such is the gateway of syllables, the mantra-purified path;
the path of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods is identical, and all manifest their form-bodies in this same way.
They reveal the Buddha-way through various gateways, just as a dancer follows the rhythm of the music to accord with human sentiment. Therein is neither "other" nor "self. I...
With the Buddha-eye, one universally observes that in all Buddha-fields throughout the three periods of time, this very gate is taught;

all Buddhas are no different from me, and all Buddhas are likewise no different from those other Tathāgatas. Because there is no divergent teaching, it is said that there is neither "other" nor "self.
This is precisely what should be cultivated according to the teachings of all Buddhas; were it otherwise, [it would not be so].
"Skillful means are not complete. For this reason, the Tathāgata concludes that meaning and addresses Vajrapāṇi;
in addressing Vajrapāṇi, one should know that he is addressing the entire great assembly.
That is to say, if a bodhisattva of mantra practice wishes to attain the Dharma of the ancient Buddhas, they should train in this manner throughout.

By diligently hearing, contemplating, and practicing this Dharma-gate of all places, one may, within a single lifetime, attain the various dances, plays, and songs of all Tathāgatas to delight sentient beings. Regarding the addition of the beginning, middle, and end:
this refers to the five syllables beginning with *A* as the "beginning," and the twenty syllables beginning with *Ka* as the "middle."
The eight syllables beginning with *ra* all possess the side-dot (*bindu*). The twelve syllables beginning with *i* all have the upward-stroke (*ūrdhva-mātrā*).

The five syllables beginning with *aṃ* all have the upper-dot (*visarga*). These various syllables are called "subsequent distinctions" because they serve to assist in completing the meaning of the words.
Generally, all [consonants] such as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* belong to the gateway of the syllable *a*; the syllable *a* is the Buddha.
Regarding the visualization of the mind within this context, the addition of the initial, middle, and final marks is as follows:
if the syllable *A* stands alone, it is the bodhicitta; if a stroke is added to the corner, it is the practice of *A*, which is the bodhicitta together with its practice;

if a dot is added above, it is *Am*, which is the bodhicitta together with the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) that transcends all characteristics, thereby accomplishing bodhi. If [the syllable] is *A*...
When two dots are added to the side of a character, it signifies the bodhicitta and the attainment of nirvāṇa through the removal of all obscurations;
others should be understood by analogy in this manner. These may be added cumulatively, whether they carry one meaning, two meanings, or three meanings.

Furthermore, there are cases where, although there are no dots above the letter *A*, there is a subsequent character that is a reduplicated form, possessing both the "upward-facing" (*ānkuśa*) and "downward-facing" (*bhūmi*) aspects.
The sounds *ṇa*, *na*, *maṃ*, and so forth, when joined with the preceding [vowels], constitute the syllable *aṃ*.
This is because these [consonants] such as *ya* (the upward-pointing stroke) are applied as bindus to the preceding [vowels], whereby the syllable *a* becomes the sound *aṃ*.
Alternatively, if the syllable *a* lacks the bindu, there follows a doubling of the character; for instance, the four characters *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *gha* are doubled and applied.
The character for *ya* (仰) is used as the dot (*bindu*), and the character for *cha* (遮) with the character for *jia* (闍) and *she* (社) uses the character for *niang* (壤) as its dot;
others follow this pattern. The sounds such as *ra* are assigned to the preceding [vowels] to form the syllable *aḥ*.
This is because all sounds such as *ra* possess two lateral dots (*anusvāra*), which, when joined with the preceding vowel *a*, produce the sound *aḥ*. (Further inquiry). As for...
The essence of the Dharma is ineffable and free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);

nevertheless, because all Tathāgatas, through the power of their sovereign empowerment and spiritual transformations (*adhiṣṭhāna*), have formed this wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), they are able to perform the deeds of a Tathāgata for the benefit of all beings.
This explains the chapters on Ka, Ca, Ṭa, Ta, and Pa; the Samādhi chapter; the realization of the Bodhicitta; the practices bestowed by the Buddhas; and Nirvāṇa.
The addition of the syllables and so forth constitutes the mantra teaching, complete with its beginning, middle, and end (this is the scriptural text; the explanation of the text is now finished).
One who knows this and recites it according to their will should resolve to apply each individual phrase with focused intent.

By perceiving and bestowing the phrases that are supreme and most excellent, one who knows thus knows what is called the "wisdom of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*), which is a designation for the difference [in realization].
Furthermore, if a practitioner understands the meaning of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*) in this way, they will be able to achieve all that they desire.
To state the essential point: what is called "everything being accomplished according to one's will" refers to the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
If one accomplishes this, they are identical to the Dharma King with respect to all phenomena.
Having attained mastery, one also fulfills original vows to open the pure knowledge and vision for all sentient beings, enabling them to attain the wisdom of a Buddha.
Who attains this benefit? It is said to be those who, according to principle, fully possess the conditions and skillfully maintain the recitation;
therefore, it next says "the practitioner of recitation. Furthermore, who attains this resolute intention? It is said to be the person of wisdom who is skillful...
Because one awakens to and understands the meaning of the wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*), one should follow each individual letter-gate, such as *A* and the rest;
through whatever practice is undertaken, the fruit of awakening will certainly be accomplished, so do not give rise to doubt. Among these, what dharma is awakened to?
It is as follows: the syllable *A* is the bodhicitta; adding the bindu (*anusvāra*) to it is the bodhisattva conduct; and adding it to the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*) is the result.
This is precisely the attainment of Buddhahood. If the bodhicitta is purified and all veils and hindrances are removed, that is itself the Great Parinirvāṇa;
there is no other meaning. To thus penetrate and fully understand each of these points is to receive the unsurpassed and most excellent phrase.
The unsurpassed phrase is the attainment of Bodhi. This is unsurpassed Bodhi.
This mind is the spontaneous wisdom of all Buddhas; truly, there is no one who can bestow it.
However, when a practitioner is fully endowed with skillful means and thoroughly understands the meaning of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), they naturally attain it.
This itself constitutes the bestowal of unsurpassed bodhi.

In this way, one should know that this wheel of syllables revolves; for the practitioner who maintains the recitation, it is always manifest in the world, just as the World-Honored One Vairocana turns the wheel.
Just as when a worldly wheel is revolving, its beginning and end cannot be known, and it has no limit and is inexhaustible, so too should one know each individual wheel of syllables.
Furthermore, from the letter A, all other letters are thus born through rotation;
this wheel of letters pervades the names of all mantras, revolving as a dhāraṇī without limit or end, its source encompassing all places—this is the hundred-thousand-million-fold rotating dhāraṇī.
If a practitioner can understand it in this way, [they shall attain liberation].
If one understands the meaning of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), one is able to use this constant luminosity to illuminate the world;
this constant luminosity is the very body of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, who turns the wheel of Dharma as Vairocana.
Herein, this constant luminosity is the sun of great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*). This sun is the essence of the letter *A* of the bodhicitta. It is without [end].

Because it is born of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), is without change, and is not produced by causes, this wisdom of the eternally abiding true reality (*dharmatā*) is called "Ever-Luminous" (*nityaprabhāsa*).
If a practitioner exerts effort and cultivates for a long time without slackening or retreating, they will certainly attain it.
However, as for the methods and applications of the mandala procedures described above, from the scattering of flowers and the conferral of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*)...
Furthermore, some are given a bright mirror, as if using a golden scalpel to clear away cataracts from their eyes;

such methods are all for the sake of those who have newly resolved to attain Bodhicitta. Through the application of skillful means and empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), these sequential ritual practices serve to make their resolve firm and act as a gradual stage for entering the Buddha-dharma.
Now, the secret essence herein lies in the wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*). Why is this so?
If a practitioner acts as an ācārya for others and intends to construct a maṇḍala, they must first abide in the station of the World-Honored One;
that is, by means of these syllable-gates (*akṣaramukha*), one integrates and accumulates them to form a body, which is identical to that of a Buddha.
This means that when a yoga-ācārya achieves success through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), whatever is performed according to their intention is spontaneously accomplished.
Because one clearly perceives this wheel of syllables pervading all parts of the body, it is identical to the Buddha; thus, one occupies the same station as the Buddha.
Furthermore, when arranging the syllables, they should be divided into four sections, which constitute the four-layered maṇḍala.
The head constitutes the first section, which is the position of the *akṣara* "A," the bodhicitta. From "Ka," "Kha," "Ga," "Gha," "Ṅa," "Ca," and so forth, up to "Śa" and "Sa."
Hā! All that belongs to the first tone is the Bodhicitta. One should contemplate the letter *ka* from the location of the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between the eyebrows of the practitioner;
from *kha* onwards, one should rotate to the right following the path of the sun, arranging them in succession so that they form a continuous, circular connection.
Next, from the throat downwards constitutes the second division, which belongs to [the second tone].
The long *ā* syllable gate should also be aligned vertically with the center of the ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft of hair), extending downward;
it is arranged clockwise for one full circuit and joined together—this is the practice of bodhi. Next, from the heart downward is the third section, which belongs to the syllable *aṃ*;
likewise, starting from above the heart, the *aṃ* syllable is arranged, followed by a clockwise rotation for one full circuit and joined together. Next, from...
The area below the navel belongs to the syllable-gateway *Aḥ*. This is the Great Nirvāṇa, and from within it, the syllable *Aḥ* is placed, which then revolves clockwise once to pervade everywhere.
The head constitutes the upper portion; the throat and heart constitute the middle portion;

and the navel constitutes the posterior portion (I privately maintain that the arousal of the bodhicitta is the initial practice, the fruit is the middle, and great quiescence is the latter). This fifth syllable *Aḥ* (protracted) pervades all.

In this regard, whatever one wishes to do is accomplished; this occurs outside the body, like the light of a Buddha’s body which functions according to one's will, and does not reside within the body in the positions where syllables are arranged. The syllable *ka* is likewise identical to *a*.
Once the master has thus perfected the body, he should arrange the maṇḍala in the same manner and should also visualize the disciple.
Causing these three matters to be performed in this manner so that they are all accomplished is called the Secret Maṇḍala.
If one does not thoroughly understand the intended meaning herein, then even if one performs the rites according to the preceding methods, it is not called performing them well;
it is a mere waste of effort and nothing will be achieved. Furthermore, this method of arranging the syllables is the Secret Maṇḍala itself; unless one is long... [omitted].
Only those who have practiced the conduct of true illumination and are capable of transmitting it may receive its meaning through oral transmission; it cannot be conveyed by means of written texts.
Therefore, the Master transmits it orally, saying that what is not explained in the scriptures is simply like the revolving wheel of Vairocana.

Furthermore, the practitioner must know the colors of the various syllables: namely, the initial syllable *A* and the twenty-five syllables beginning with *Ka*, up to *Ya-ra* and ending with *Ha*, all of which belong to *A* and manifest as its yellow color, which is the color of the Vajra.
The second *Ā* (long *ā*) transforms into a yellowish-white color, which is the color of tranquility. This is the syllable *A*.

The essence of the *samādhi* of yellow is white because it is a combination of two colors; thus, it is yellow-white. Regarding the third addition of a dot, it is also made yellow-white, representing the syllable *aṃ*.
The syllable *a* is yellow because its great space is white; thus, it is yellow-white. Regarding the fourth, the syllable *aḥ*:
the wheel of the syllable *aḥ* is made yellow-black, because the syllable *a* is yellow and the two dots are the color of nirvāṇa, which is black; thus, it is yellow-black.
Furthermore, these two dots signify the meaning of subjugation; just as *nirvāṇa* destroys, annihilates, and crushes all obstructing phenomena, this [syllable] is likewise.
Therefore, the two dots are made black. Regarding the fifth "evil" (*ā*) syllable: the body of the syllable *A* is yellow;
the dot at the upper corner is white, while the side dot is black. One should know that it thus possesses various aspects.
It is of variegated colors. In constructing the maṇḍala, it likewise consists of three layers.
The first layer, extending from the syllable *ka* to *ha*, encircling the interior, is called the Vajra-wreath (*vajravalaya*).
This vajra-wreath sustains all phenomena, just as the vajra-wheel in the world sustains the universe. It is the practitioner’s initial bodhicitta.
The "wheel" refers to the inner wheel (*garbha-cakra*), which is established first in order to stabilize the bodhicitta. Next is the second wheel;
this refers to both the *Dīrgha-āgama* and the *Andhakāra* wheels, which share the same middle section.
If one uses syllables as wheels, it is unnecessary to place a syllable-wheel; if one uses syllables as wheels, it is unnecessary to employ a syllable-wheel.
(I personally maintain that these are the practice, the cause, the realization, and the fruit. Next, for the third wheel, employ the syllable *Aḥ* wheel;
it is also arranged from the center as described above, forming a continuous circle. The twelve syllables beginning with *I* are scattered on the outside like blazing flames.
This is the meaning of the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma. Having thus arranged them, the practitioner who recites [the mantra]...
One immediately becomes a vidyādhara body, equal and no different from the empowerment of the spiritual power of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata;
this wheel is also called the Wheel of Causes and Conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-cakra*). Both the master and the disciple, as well as the maṇḍala wheel, all constitute such a secret wheel.
Furthermore, since these various syllables are themselves the wheel of mantra, there are thus four kinds in total.
Furthermore, regarding the "wheel" (*cakra*), the Sanskrit term is *akṣara-cakra*.
*Akṣara* means "immovable. This immovability refers to the letter *A*, which is the bodhicitta.
Just as Vairocana dwells within the essential nature of bodhicitta and manifests in various ways through the universal gate to benefit all beings, so too does this wheel.

Although it manifests in immeasurable and boundless ways, and though its traces thus descend infinitely and inexhaustibly, it is in reality eternally abiding and immovable, and possesses no characteristic of arising or ceasing. It is like a chariot wheel:
although it revolves without end, the axle-pin within never wavers. Because it is immovable, it can govern all movement without limit. This is the letter A.
It is likewise so: because it is unarisen, it is without movement or regression, yet it gives rise to all wheels of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) revolving without end;

therefore, it is called the "Immovable Wheel. If a practitioner can thoroughly comprehend this Immovable Wheel and deploy the various vidyās, then by the natural nature of these syllabic forms, whatever the body expresses is none other than a secret seal (*mudrā*), and whatever the mouth articulates is none other than a mantra.
Whatever is spoken is all mantra; whoever sees, hears, touches, or knows it will certainly be destined for unsurpassed bodhi.

The benefits and merits thus accomplished are true and not false. If one can act in this way, one is identical to Vairocana, performing buddha-deeds and constantly illuminating the world. When a practitioner recites, they should contemplate the syllables.

The wheel, or rather the *pada-cakra* (wheel of phrases); as for what is called the *pada-cakra*, one visualizes that upon the heart of the deity there is a luminous orb, within which the syllables of the mantra are arranged in a circular wheel, revolving and connecting with one another until they appear clearly before one.

When reciting, one visualizes these syllables as being like white milk, flowing down in succession and entering the practitioner’s mouth, or pouring onto the crown of the head, in an uninterrupted stream.
It pervades his entire body and extends even to its limbs; the syllable within that luminous orb is always clearly manifest, like a constant flow of water that never exhausts.
When one becomes utterly weary from such recitation, one should simply abide in a tranquil mind—this refers to contemplating the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The method for this contemplation has already been fully explained above. If one succeeds in seeing the seed-syllable...
Immediately, the deity manifests from within the seed-syllable. Once this is accomplished, one is able to pervade the entire wheel of syllables and transform into the body of a Vidyādhara;
only then is one fit to perform all ritual activities. For instance, the syllable *A* signifies immovability and is the essence of the vajra.
Whenever one wishes to make an activity firm and unshakable, or [to establish] oneself or others...

The immovability of the mind of others and so forth are all applied by adding the syllable *A*; likewise, all other syllables are to be applied according to their respective functions and characteristics.
Chapter Eleven: The Secret Maṇḍala.
At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana again entered the samādhi called "The Tathāgata’s Eye-Pervasion of the Entire Dharma-Dhātu,
the Swift Manifestation of the Treasury of the Dharma-Dhātu, and the Equal Adornment-Treasury," in order to manifest the inexhaustible adornments of the dharma-dhātu.
By means of this gateway of mantra practice, he fulfilled his original vow to deliver the entire realm of sentient beings without exception.
Regarding "because it is complete": the preceding section on the *Akṣara-cakra* (Wheel of Syllables) has been concluded.

Because it is secret, everything that has been taught therein is the majestic power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata. If one were apart from the majestic power of the Tathāgata, it could not be expressed;

therefore, this chapter is titled the "Chapter on the Wheel of Syllables Empowered by Majestic Power. (All other chapters are to be explained in this same manner. Thus, these syllables have been explained.
Having completed the "Chapter on the Wheel," in order to further accomplish this wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), he again enters samādhi;

what is described here in the sūtra is the name of the samādhi from which he emerges. "The entire dharma-realm" refers to the signless dharma-realm (*animitta-dharmadhātu*), which is viewed by means of the Buddha-eye and so forth.
Furthermore, according to the secret interpretation, the aforementioned wheel of syllables is itself all the Buddhas.
When one observes this dharma-realm with the Buddha-eye, one should know that this Buddha-eye is itself the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*);
apart from such empowerment, it cannot be described. As for the "Dharma-realm treasury" (*dharmadhātugarbha*), this "treasury" (garbha) in its Sanskrit original is *kośa*, which means a sheath.
Just as a sword in the world resides within a sheath, so too does this treasury.
Therefore, it is translated according to its meaning. Thus, what is here called the "Dharmadhātu-garbha" (Dharma-realm treasury) refers to the source from which the Tathāgatas emerge;
that is to say, all Tathāgatas abide within it. "Vikrīḍita" (exertion/playfulness) has the sense of flowing forth and the sense of overflowing.
It is like a lion king who, while dwelling unmoving within a deep cave, occasionally emerges from his lair and stretches himself with vigor.
Movement is its very essence, yet it is fundamentally unmoving; it is now moving because it has departed from its usual place. The Buddha is likewise so:

while dwelling securely within the profound and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, he could not have been shown had it not been for the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s spiritual majesty, for he is subtle, wondrous, quiescent, and beyond reach. Now, however, he manifests an inexhaustible variety of body, speech, and mind.
The pervasive manifestation of forms and sounds throughout the Dharma-realm is the *vikrīḍita* (heroic stride) of all Buddhas.

To manifest the Tathāgata’s Treasury of Equal Adornment (*samatā-vyūha-garbha*) is precisely this Treasury of the Womb (*garbha-kośa*). Entering into this Dharma, the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are entirely equal and uniform;
because the Way of every Buddha is identical, it is called "Equal" (*sama*). This is the Adornment.
This refers to adorning one's body; that is, using the infinite gateways to the Buddha-way to adorn the Dharma-body in order to deliver sentient beings.
Because one uses the equal Dharma-realm to adorn the Dharma-body, it is called "adornment" (*vyūha*).
It is just as in the world, where a place with great banners and insignia belonging to a host of armies is called "adorned"; this samādhi is likewise so named.
It is named as such because this samādhi can manifest the secret matters of the Tathāgata.

In this context, "treasury" (garbha) is the Sanskrit term *gaha*, which signifies an inexhaustible flow of adornments and displays that cannot be exhausted, like a great treasury of jewels. This treasury of the equal dharmadhātu is precisely the Tathāgata.
The meaning of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is that the adornments of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) are inexhaustible, just as the revolving wheel of syllables is inexhaustible;
therefore, it is called "Inexhaustible Adornment. For what reason does the Tathāgata abide in this samādhi?
It is certainly not without cause or condition; rather, it is precisely for the purpose of revealing the profound and secret essentials of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the subsequent sutra [states]:

It is said that because he has fulfilled his original vow by delivering the entire realm of sentient beings without exception through the gateway of mantras, the Buddha—having established the great vow while practicing the bodhisattva path to cause all sentient beings to enter together into the treasury of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm—now manifests with vigorous power out of the fulfillment of that wish and great compassion to deliver sentient beings. As it is said: [The Buddha] manifests with vigor to deliver sentient beings.
The treasury of the adornments of the Dharma-realm is inexhaustible, and the realm of sentient beings is likewise inexhaustible.

Now, by means of the gateway of true word practice (*mantra*), one desires to universally and impartially benefit all beings, causing them all to open and purify their vision and knowledge until nothing remains;
this is the fulfillment of one's original vow, which is why it is said that "the original vow is fulfilled."
Furthermore, because the preceding dharmas were not yet fully perfected, practitioners of the mantra path could not swiftly achieve the Unsurpassed Way;
now, in order to definitively resolve these matters and cause them all to be clearly manifested, he enters this samādhi.

Next, regarding "abiding in samādhi," it means that the Buddha dwells in meditative concentration and manifests rare and wondrous deeds to universally benefit all sentient beings while within this samādhi.

What kind of rare phenomenon manifests? It is that for all realms of sentient beings without exception, through the gateway of sound and so forth, according to their mental karma, there arise the accomplishment and reception of various fruits of retribution—manifesting as form, appearance, and voice—and the path to the fruit of the Dharma is taught in various ways according to their minds, bringing joy to every single sentient being.
From every pore and so forth, the Dharma-realm increases, and from the body emerges this Brahma-sound.
Sound is also a roar, just as when a great dragon appears and thunders with a voice that all hear and which reaches everywhere;
the roar of the Tathāgata is likewise pervasive throughout the realm of sentient beings without exception.
This realm is immeasurable, and his voice is heard universally, unlike the worldly dragon which has limitations within the realms of sentient beings.
Because one obtains retribution according to karma of superior, middling, or inferior grades, it is called "the maturation of birth through karma.
It is like when people receive food; as long as they have not yet eaten it, it cannot yet be called "received.

Only after they have accepted and consumed it is it called "receiving that food offering. The experience of ripening retribution is likewise: if one receives it by conforming to prior causes, [it is then truly received].
The fruits [of their actions] differ in their forms, colors, and other qualities in ten thousand ways; their speech, intentions, inclinations, and understandings are likewise each distinct.
The Buddha, with a single, sublime, and impartial voice, universally accords with their minds;

according to their aspirations and following their respective languages, he reveals and awakens them, stimulating their thought and awareness through skillful means and guidance, so that all attain joy. This is the third [supernormal power].
Within this state of obscurity, no auspicious signs have ever appeared. Here, regarding the various [phonemes] that are explained, it is as in the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*):
for instance, when three sounds combine to express a single meaning, if that meaning is not yet complete, another syllable is added to fulfill it;
if four sounds together express a single meaning, one uses only three sounds, and once the meaning is fully established, one syllable is removed. It is thus.

One should increase or decrease [the syllables] as appropriate; here, too, it is the same. Simply by means of the single gateway of the letter *A*, all meanings are fully encompassed, and because there is nothing regarding phenomena that is not complete, this is called "speaking," which is not the same as the speaking of ordinary dharmas. There is a difference in the Sanskrit pronunciation;
furthermore, regarding the question of the emergence of the body of the increased Dharmadhātu: the ultimate quiescence of the equal Dharmadhātu is non-existent.
There are characteristics of entering and exiting; by means of the Tathāgata’s empowerment through supernatural power (*ṛddhi-adhiṣṭhāna*), he manifests inexhaustible physical bodies.
This refers to the manifestation from each and every pore of the Buddha of the aforementioned roaring sounds as well as various forms;

thus it is called the "increased body of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-vardhamāna-kāya*). In reality, these arise from conditions and are without birth or intrinsic nature. Such true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is identical [to the ultimate].
In the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, how could there be any increase, birth, or cessation? Although the nature of dependently arisen phenomena is eternally suchness,
by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, a roaring sound manifests from each and every pore—
whether in gentle words or harsh speech, whether profound or shallow— accordant with the mental capacities of beings, never exceeding its constant limit like the tide of the great ocean.

His body is likewise: sometimes large, sometimes small; sometimes in a wrathful form, or manifesting through the practice of the six perfections, or subduing others through majestic power—manifesting in myriad distinct ways according to the beings to be saved, without any error.
Having previously shown the wheel of syllables, he now manifests forms and sounds from within the wheel of the Dharma-realm.
Having emerged, throughout worlds equal to space, a single sound manifests the Dharma-realm as the birth of the Tathāgata. A verse says:
"Just as space has no boundaries, so too is this sound; it is equal to space. "Manifests" (pary-ava-sthā) means to indicate or represent;
that is, it is the vocal activity of the Tathāgata’s manifestation, which expresses itself such that all sentient beings may understand.
It is the realization of the equal Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because this wondrous sound represents the Dharma-realm, it is called "the manifestation of the Dharma-realm.
This single sound is the gateway of the letter *A*; its revolving cycle is inexhaustible, equal to empty space and filling the Dharma-realm.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time are born from such wondrous verses; therefore, they are called "born of the Tathāgata. Now, the Buddha...

It is named as such because, from this gateway of a single sound, he speaks sublime verses so that all worlds without exception may hear and know them equally, each attaining understanding according to their own kind.
As explained above, the wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) is intended to manifest the merits of the Tathāgata;
therefore, the Buddha emits sublime sounds from every single pore, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, and therein speaks these syllables.
The profound meaning of the wheel refers to the verses that can give birth to all Buddhas.
If there are sentient beings who understand the meaning of such a wheel of syllables, they will immediately attain Bodhi; therefore, it is said that "all Buddhas are born from this.
However, the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas is free from arising and ceasing. If one perceives the Tathāgata as having birth, this is merely attachment to signs.
Those who cling to signs cannot even escape from birth and death, much less achieve great Bodhi. What is here called "birth" is, in fact, birth that is free from all signs.

Although the pure Dharmakāya is free from all signs, the Buddha, through the power of his *adhiṣṭhāna*, employs this wheel of syllables to reveal the secret, internally realized virtues of the Tathāgata. By means of...
Because it is sustained by the Buddha’s sovereign supernormal power (*ṛddhi-vaśitā-adhiṣṭhāna*), one is able to give rise to the signless through the expedient means of signs.
Just as when one has not yet awakened to reality, one uses this wheel of syllables as an expedient means to gradually attain thorough understanding;
by observing the gateway of the syllable *A*, and because of entering the gateway of *A*, one is able to ultimately realize the sovereign Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Furthermore, the verse says: "That which can produce the dharma-characteristics of all phenomena according to their respective forms" refers to entering the gateway of the letter *A*;
this is precisely the equal Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Because of this signless Dharma-body, one is able to respond to conditions and manifest universally.
The physical body manifests the wisdom of the Tathāgata by assuming various forms according to the species [of beings] and appearing in whatever form is pleasing to behold.
As the verse says: "The Buddhas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the world-saving Bodhisattvas who advance with valor, are all likewise like the Buddha."
Because this body is without arising and without marks, all Buddhas are born from it;

it is not merely that the Buddhas are born from this, but rather that all the various stages of practice for Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas—even up to the stage of "one-life-to-Buddhahood"—are all produced from the principle of this letter A. It is not merely that one [Buddha] is born.

All the fruits of the sages and worthies, as well as the various distinctions and successive developments of the entire world of sentient beings and the receptacle world, all likewise arise from the meaning of this syllable *A*. Within this, there are briefly three types of arising;
the superior type of arising refers to the arising of the fruit of the Tathāgata’s true, pure, and eternally abiding *dharmakāya*.
Regarding the essence, it successively gives rise to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and those of the Two Vehicles; wherever they may abide, it eliminates their respective hindrances.
As for the inferior grade of arising, both sentient beings and the receptacle world are likewise established from this very Dharma-gate.
Regarding phenomena such as arising and abiding, those which are produced are eternal; however, what is explained here differs from the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Although all phenomena arise from causes, those causes are without marks; although they arise from conditions, those conditions are without marks;
although they originate from conditions, phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; and although they arise and cease from conditions, there is neither arising nor abiding.
Because its characteristic is such, it is eternal; this is not the same as the views of the non-Buddhists, which is why birth, cessation, annihilation, and permanence are discussed.
A verse says: "Possessing wisdom and skillful means, while simultaneously being free from lack of wisdom and doubt, one thoroughly understands the meaning of the wheel of the letter 'A.
That all phenomena are ultimately empty, non-existent, quiescent, and signless in essence, and that they are unarisen from the very beginning—this is wisdom."
Furthermore, mantra, body-mudrā, yoga, and so forth, can cause the practitioner to achieve great benefit and enter the wisdom of the Buddha;

these are the skillful means (*upāya*). If one relies on skillful means but lacks wisdom, or possesses wisdom alone but lacks skillful means, one will ultimately be unable to accomplish the inconceivable and sovereign function. It is essential that both skillful means and wisdom be fully possessed.
Only then can one enter the secret treasury of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*).

Those who are devoid of wisdom and doubt—know that such persons, being separated from these two dharmas, are people lacking wisdom; because they lack wisdom, they will give rise to doubt in every situation and will be unable to advance.
Furthermore, if a practitioner possesses both wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), they will naturally be free from the lack of wisdom.
This gives rise to wrong doubt.
The verse says: "Regarding this path taught by all Buddhas, it is not only I who speak thus; all Perfectly Enlightened Ones speak thus without any difference.
This is because the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are identical in this regard.
The Way is frail yet without differentiation; it is a single mark and a single flavor, with no divergent paths.

At that time, the bodies of the Tathāgatas born from the Dharma-realm—the clouds of manifestations of their own bodies throughout all dharma-realms—pervade the pores of Vairocana’s sovereign mind. Among these, the successive births of Buddhas are the "Dharma-realm-born" herein.
The body is itself the Dharma-body of Vairocana; because it arises from the reality of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is called "born of the Dharma-realm.
Regarding "the manifestation of one's own body throughout all dharma-realms": "manifestation" means that which enables all beings to know and see.
This refers to the fact that within all dharma-realms, clouds of self-manifestations and transformations completely pervade everywhere. This means:
The physical manifestation of the Tathāgata’s body appears universally as a form-body (*rūpakāya*), just like that great cloud which pervades the *dharmadhātu*.

"Cloud" here carries the sense of "pervasive filling. This means that the cloud of this transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) fills the *dharmadhātu* and extends throughout the worlds of the ten directions, being immeasurable and limitless.

Regarding the phrase "mastery of mind" (*citta-vaśitā*) herein, it is translated according to its meaning. The *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) states: "Mind-cāi" (*citta-cāi*) refers to "just as" (*cāi*).
In the brief moment of concentrating the mind, one is able to manifest such vastness and pervasiveness without the exertion of effort;
this demonstrates mastery over the mind. Regarding the successive empowerments of the Buddhas arising from within all the pores:
it is like the Tathāgata, upon merely entering samādhi, immediately and instantaneously manifesting such wondrous and rare events—this is the empowerment of the Tathāgata.
"Supernatural power" (*ṛddhi*) refers to mutual interpenetration. From the pores of one Buddha’s body, various Buddhas flow forth;
from the bodies of those Buddhas, the bodies of Tathāgatas and *iṣṭadevatās* (honored deities) flow forth in succession, interpenetrating one another.
Each individual body manifests the aforementioned supernatural powers, transforming again and again without end. These meanings should be further [elucidated].
To explain in detail, "successive empowerment" (*krama-adhiṣṭhāna*) refers to being empowered by the sovereign spiritual power (*vibhutva-ṛddhi*) of the Buddha;
this is precisely the empowerment of the wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) of the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-svabhāva*) as described above.

From each and every pore of the Buddha’s own body, various clouds of bodies (*kāha-megha*) emerge, categorized according to their superior, middling, and inferior divisions: namely, the head is the inner womb (*garbha*), and the heart is... [the center].
The area above this constitutes the first court; from the navel upward is the second court; and from the navel downward is the third court.

These correspond respectively to the four positions of the aforementioned circular altar, manifesting the bodies of the Honored Ones according to their respective left, right, front, back, upper, middle, and lower divisions.
Each emerges from within the world-system according to its original position, performing the Buddha-activities from each [position].
Because his body manifests successively to perform the various deeds of a Buddha, it is called "successive manifestation" (*krama*). At that time, Vajrapāṇi also understood the Buddha’s intention:
"Now the World-Honored One manifests this unprecedented event; it cannot be without cause or condition.
He will surely further expound the profound and secret Dharma—namely, whatever remains unclarified or omitted from what has been taught above, he will certainly explain it. Truly so.
Because his mind remained fixed in longing and aspiration, the Buddha further addressed him, saying: "O Lord of Mysteries, listen well! It is excellent;

contemplate it with great care as I explain for you the sections for the positions of the holy deities of the maṇḍala, along with their seed-syllables and their symbolic marks. At that time, the Buddha—

When the Vajradhara and other deities have manifested the aforementioned states and performed their various buddha-activities, they return from their original positions and enter the body of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
Because the sequence of their entry is no different from that of their emergence, that sūtra states:
"They re-enter the palace of the Dharma-realm. As for the seed-syllables of the deities' positions, it is as follows:
The deities above are all the virtues realized internally by the Tathāgata, each manifesting individually the profound nature of the *dharmadhātu* revealed by the Tathāgata.
Now, if there is an ācārya who wishes to construct a maṇḍala, he must first abide in yoga;
just as [the deities] emerged from the body of the Buddha, one should visualize each position in its respective form and color, and then—
Upon his heart, one visualizes a luminous orb; within that luminous orb, one contemplates those seed-syllables.
Only when they are thus established one by one does the ritual procedure become complete.

If it were otherwise, one would ultimately be unable to empower or establish those dharmas, and the disciple likewise would not receive the title of *ācārya*. As previously stated, once the seeds of affliction have been severed...
Next, the seed of the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) that arises is the equal seed of all sentient beings.
This equal seed of the nature of the dharma-realm is that which grows from the stage of the Tathāgata’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
Just as the various grasses and trees in the world, each differing according to its own specific nature and portion, all depend upon the great earth; so too does this seed.
The roots, stems, branches, and leaves that grow and develop are diverse in their various forms; they increase in size and differ in their essential natures.
Yet all of these are of the nature of the great earth, arising from the earth. Although there are various distinctions, they ultimately all return to the earth.
It is only through the conjunction of causes and conditions that growth and development occur; yet in reality, they possess no self-nature, being neither born nor arisen.
Furthermore, once sentient beings have been established with such seeds, they are identical to the stage of the Tathāgata.
Because these seeds arise from the nature of the *dharmadhātu* and are capable of producing the *dharmadhātu*, they are called "seeds produced from the *dharmadhātu*.
That which is produced from the *dharmadhātu* is precisely the self-nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) of the Tathāgata. As for their "characteristics," they are like worldly seeds.

Each is distinct and differentiated. If one observes the seeds of even a small blade of grass with wisdom, although they have not yet grown, one already knows their inherent nature, their magnitude, and the ultimate extent of their potential.
If one sees the conduct of sentient beings, their causal-stage seeds are likewise all thus; yet these present seeds are, in fact, the seeds of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
One should know that this nature is certainly able to give birth to the Tathāgata’s body of equalizing wisdom; therefore, it is called a "mark" (*cihna*).
Furthermore, each and every position within this maṇḍala possesses its own seed-syllable to mark the gateway to the differentiated *dharmadhātu*.
One should know that by entering each [position] into the letter *A*, one perceives the mark of internal realization. Thus it is understood.

Because they are the virtues realized within by the Tathāgata, they are called "signs" (*liṅga*). Those who emerge from the four successive stages (*avasthā*) are the very insignia (*cihna*) of the Buddha;

that is, they may emerge from the stage of a Buddha, or from the stage of a Bodhisattva, or from the stage of the Two Vehicles, or from the stage of the eight classes of gods and nāgas. One should know that the distinctions between these respective levels are as follows:
Each [category] has its own distinct order. At that time, after the Buddha had addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi said to the Buddha:
"I wish to hear it, desiring to cause it to be circulated and disseminated for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings, and also for the benefit of the great assembly."
Therefore, we request the Buddha to expound upon it. Although the methods of the maṇḍala have been explained above, the secret treasury of colors and seed-syllables has not yet been taught;
therefore, listen with a single mind as we pray that the Buddha will expound them.
Next, the Buddha told Ānanda: "In general, when an ācārya wishes to establish disciples within the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-vyūha*, he should first abide in yoga and contemplate his own body as follows:
from the navel downward, he should visualize a vajra-wheel, yellow in color and firm; next, from the navel upward to the heart, he should visualize a water-wheel, white in color."
From the heart upward to the throat, one should visualize a fire wheel, red in color. Next, from the throat upward to the crown of the head, one should visualize a wind wheel, black in color.
Furthermore, the earth wheel is square, the water wheel is circular, the fire wheel is triangular, and the wind wheel is the shape of a half-moon.
Above all, one should visualize a single dot representing space, possessing various colors, situated at the crown of the head.
It is placed upon a cross-stitch; this is the wheel-form, which perfectly accords with the constituent parts of the body.

As for these five positions: they are the previously mentioned five syllables—place the syllable *A* within the square, the syllable *Liṃ* within the circle, the syllable *Raṃ* within the triangle, the syllable *Haṃ* within the half-moon, and the bindu within the point.

The missing characters should be verified in the preceding fascicle. Once the Master has thus observed his own body in its successive stages and performed the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of his own form by visualizing and placing the seed-syllables (*bīja-akṣara*), he next contemplates the ground of the maṇḍala. He visualizes it as being overturned and inverted:
at the very top he creates the vajra-wheel (*vajramaṇḍala*); beneath the vajra-wheel he creates the water-wheel (*toyamaṇḍala*); and beneath the water-wheel he creates the fire-wheel (*tejomaṇḍala*).
Below the fire-wheel (tejas-cakra) is the wind-wheel (vāyu-cakra), and below the wind-wheel is the space-wheel (ākāśa-cakra). Why is this so?
Because all worlds are supported by these five wheels. When a world is formed, it first arises from space as the wind-wheel;
from the wind arises the fire-wheel, from the fire arises the water-wheel, and from the water arises the earth-wheel. This is the arrangement of the maṇḍala.
This establishes the sequence of dissolution: when [the world] disintegrates, the earth element perishes first, until only empty space remains;
this is the sequence of the Master’s own empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). (Question: Now, the practitioner’s cultivation of the path is also similar to this:
first arises the mind of faith, next the bodhicitta, and finally even the great emptiness. (Question: Since the Ācārya has thus bestowed empowerment...

Having held [the visualization], one should immediately install the various deities according to their respective positions and contemplate each one through yoga, according to their directions, colors, and forms.
Upon the heart of each deity, one places a luminous orb (*maṇḍala*); within that luminous orb is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
One should cause each of these to be clearly manifest and unobstructed. One who is able to act in this manner is the Maṇḍala of the Matrix of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-garbha-maṇḍala*).
