The stage of *lā* enables all Tathāgatas to collectively bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and all the Honored Ones to assemble together to empower the practitioner, establishing the disciple so that they ultimately do not regress from Bodhicitta;
otherwise, one would merely waste effort without benefit. Furthermore, this seat of yoga is the square wheel of golden vajra.
The square is the seat of Vajra for pacifying; the circle is for increasing; the triangle is for subjugating; the half-moon is for summoning;
and the bindu is for accomplishing all activities. This wheel of space is performed by means of mental visualization alone, as it does not rely on physical forms.
Even when the world is destroyed, it first perishes from the wind-wheel, and from that, the earth arises.

Fire follows fire, and after that comes wind (further inquiry). One should understand that when constructing the five wheels (*pañcamaṇḍala*) in this manner, there are space-wheels (*ākāśamaṇḍala*) both above and below.
This is because wind, fire, water, and earth arise from the space-wheel, and because one ascends gradually from the earth-wheel up to the space [wheel];
therefore, there is space above and below. When constructing the maṇḍala, the master should personally contemplate his own body and...
Furthermore, the Ground observes that the disciples to be delivered should likewise be established according to the Teacher’s Dharma;
if it is not so, it is not called "in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi entered the ground of the body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata Vairocana, ascending to the level of the Dharmadhātu.
Regarding "Equal Contemplation" (*samadarśin*): because this Bodhisattva is able to know the secrets of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind, he is named "Lord of Secrets" (*Guhyakādhipati*).
As for the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret of mind, only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully comprehend it; as it is with the mind, one should know that the same applies to the body and speech.
Now, since this Bodhisattva is also able to know them, one should know that his stage is identical to that of Great Enlightenment.
In order to deliver sentient beings, he manifests as a bodhisattva to inspire them. Herein, "body-secrecy" (kāyaguhyaka) refers to the various mudrās;
for each deity within the four major maṇḍalas, there is a specific body-mudrā.
By contemplating this body-mudrā, one comes to know the secret virtues manifested by that deity, according to the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior types.
There are further immeasurable varieties. *Vāgguhya* (the secret of speech) refers to the mantras belonging to each of the honored ones;

upon hearing these mantras, one immediately comes to know the virtues realized within by those honored ones. *Cittaguhyā* (the secret of mind) refers to the visualization of the yoga of the *iṣṭadevatā* (chosen deity);
this also differs according to each of the four directions, and by corresponding with this, one enters into the Tathāgata.

This is the treasury of the secrets of mind. Within this, if one were to discuss the secrets of body, speech, and mind extensively— from the stages of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas down to those of the two vehicles,
the various heavens, and the eight classes of beings, with their immeasurable distinctions, even as numerous as the atoms within ten worlds,
each being different— if one were to speak of them briefly, the positions indicated in this sutra all represent the Tathāgata.
If one can understand the virtues of the secrets of body, speech, and mind as they truly are, one is identical to the Lord of Secrets.
Now, the Bodhisattva Lord of Secrets, dwelling in the contemplation of the equality of the dharmadhātu,
in order to cause all future sentient beings everywhere to tear apart the great net of doubt, spoke this Great Mantra King before the Buddha, according to the text.
It may be understood thus. The mantra says:

there is no logical way for it to be achieved. The practitioner is also like this: if they have not personally awakened to the teacherless wisdom (*asat-saṃvāda-jñāna*), yet desire [to lead others], [it is likewise impossible].
"There is no possibility that another could hear the Dharma and attain realization [without this].
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, having praised the Tathāgata with these verses, then further spoke an udāna verse to question the Buddha;
"udāna" signifies a summary or a comprehensive synthesis, as the meaning of a single verse is thereby condensed.
Because the inexhaustible dharma-realm is a dharma free from marks and possesses immeasurable dharmic meanings, it is said to be "encompassed.
Having finished reciting these verses of praise, he considered those sentient beings of future ages who practice the true words and deeds;

fearing that they might fail to swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi due to deficiencies regarding this Maṇḍala Born of the Great Compassion Treasury, he sequentially questioned the Buddha concerning its secret essentials.
Regarding the phrase "expedient means also sever all doubts": if one cannot universally sever the various nets of doubt of sentient beings, one is not called an Omniscient One (*sarvajña*).
It is only by being free from the net of doubt within all phenomena oneself that one can then sever those of others.
Since the Buddha has now personally severed all nets of doubt, I now respectfully inquire: I pray that you will sever my doubts for me.
Furthermore, one who is free from feverish affliction is said to have eternally severed the roots of the three poisons.
Now, for the sake of all sentient beings, I inquire of the Teacher; because he is able to guide them through all dharmas and lead them to the wisdom of a Buddha, he is called the Great Teacher.
Next, the questions are posed in verse in their proper sequence; this is now set forth before the verses are concluded. What is it that must first be done regarding the maṇḍala?

(That is to say, since there are many types of matters concerning the maṇḍala, what is it that should be performed first? That is to say, what action should be undertaken first? How many kinds of ācāryas are there? (This too is explained.
Furthermore, how many kinds of disciples are there? (The Great Muni also explains this. How does one know the characteristics of the ground? (That is to say, regarding good and bad grounds...)

[This concerns] the requirements for middling and lower levels of accomplishment, and so forth. What is the method for discerning the site? Having discerned it, how does one perform the purification (*pariśodhana*)? [According to the text, there are three questions here. Once purified, how does one abide?

[Although the purification has been completed, fearing that one might again be troubled by obstructors, the question is asked: "How does one attain stable abiding? According to the text, there are three questions [here]. [Furthermore, another question:

"For what purpose does one perform the purification for the disciples? May the Buddha explain this. [The previous question concerned the types of disciples; now that disciples have been obtained, the question is: "What should be done first for them?"]
What are the characteristics of that which has been purified? (This refers to the intermediate master’s three questions regarding the site, the disciple, and the three matters.

Regarding binding, protection, sprinkling, and holding, there are many meanings; what protection is used for the site, and how is the protection performed? (This also asks about the master performing protection for himself, protecting the site, and protecting the disciple—three questions.
How is the site empowered (*adhiṣṭhāna*)? Binding, protection, sprinkling, and holding have many meanings. (This also asks about the three matters. What is the first?

Regarding the ritual action (which refers to the tasks to be performed at the site of the maṇḍala after the purification of the ground is complete): there are two kinds of tasks to be performed herein—the external task, which refers to the various matters concerning the construction of the maṇḍala;

and the internal task, which refers to the various yoga methods such as the master visualizing his own body as Vairocana Tathāgata and so forth. [By what mantras and other methods? One first performs protection and first purifies; this asks about the sequence of the preceding matters. These two matters constitute the ritual action. How many kinds of cords are there, and how is the ground measured?
[This refers to using the cord to measure and using the cord to establish the boundaries. Furthermore, how many types of offerings are there?

What are the flowers, incense, and so forth? (In this context, there are further items such as ointments, lamps, jeweled nets, jeweled pavilions, trees, and various other objects of offering; all should be treated according to this same principle. Thus, the term "and so forth" [indicates] plurality. Question:

What is the method for offering incense and flowers? To whom should the flowers be offered? (This means that since there are various types of flowers, the deities to whom they should be offered also differ.
What flowers are used for offering to the Buddha? What are used for Bodhisattvas, devas, and others? The same applies to the incense and other offerings. (Follow the pattern of the flowers.)
And it is said: When offering flowers, how is it done? By what dharma are they offered? It means there must be the empowerment of mantras and so forth. By what dharma are they used for the offering?

The same applies to incense and other offerings (to be explained according to the rules for flowers). How does one offer food and the like? (Within food, there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior. How is homa performed? (Question:

What is the sequence between offering to the Buddhas and performing homa? The arrangement of the ritual rules constitutes the sequence; this is the general name. How does one present the seats for the various deities? (The Buddha and Bodhisattvas...)

Regarding the seats of the eight classes of *sattvas* and others: upon what do they sit together, and how are offerings presented? May the Dharma-teachings, the rules of conduct, the methods, the sequences, and the ritual procedures all be made manifest. Regarding their colors, shapes, and so forth: "Color" refers to the various deities' blue, yellow, red, white, and other hues;

"shape" refers to matters such as sitting or standing, large or small; and "form" refers to appearances such as those of joy, laughter, wrath, or tranquil abiding. [These are the three questions; I pray you explain them in sequence, not in a manner that contradicts the established rules. Regarding the seals (*mudrā*) of the deities and their respective seats:
this refers to the seats for one's own regular recitation, such as mats of *kuśa* grass and the like. I pray that the Teacher will explain these. Furthermore, from where do the seals arise?

What further purpose does this seal (mudrā) serve? (Just as worldly seals are used for kings and others to ensure that people trust them and do not doubt their authenticity, what then is the case for the Seal of the Tathāgata?

What is the name of this seal? For what reason is it called a "seal"? How many kinds of consecration (abhiṣeka) are there? (This is because one wishes to know and understand. How many kinds of samaya are there?
For how long must the practitioner of recitation maintain the recitation? By diligently practicing the true mantra-conduct (mantracaryā), what is attained?

[Question: How does one accomplish the path of a Bodhisattva? (This is the request for the All-Knowing One to speak. At what time should one realize the Truths? (This refers to the meaning of attaining correct knowledge and vision through the Gate of Mantras;
it is a question regarding the [proper] time. How many kinds of *siddhi* are there? (This is the desire for an explanation. When do the various *siddhis* arise?

Furthermore, how is it explained that at the time of *siddhi*, one ascends into the void? What is the secret of the body? And how is it that one attains the state of a celestial being (*deva*) without abandoning this present body?

Once the body of a sage has been accomplished, how do the various transformations arise? (That is to say, all things are accomplished according to one's thought; from where do they arise? From one’s own mind, or from another?

Who produces these various transformations, and from what do they further arise? How are the sun, moon, fire, directions, planets, times, and so forth, as well as the various inauspicious clouds, removed?

(The sun and moon transform into the calamity of fire; or there are strange constellations in the directions, namely the twenty-eight lunar mansions and the various stars; and separately, regarding birth, death, and the suffering of rebirth...)

Regarding "arising," how is it that all [defilements] are completely extinguished? (This refers to the meaning of non-existence as extinction. Regarding "how does one practice," how does one constantly assemble in one place with all Buddhas? How many kinds of *homā* are there?
(In this context, the question concerns how many kinds of fire are required for the time of *homā*; this is what one wishes to know. Within the fires, how many further increases of majesty are there?

(This refers to the method of increase (*puṣṭi*). "Increase of majesty" is used in all instances, such as for flowers and so forth. "The nature of the various venerable deities of different classes" (this means the forms and natures of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the eight classes of beings; one must recognize their essential nature).
[May the Teacher of Peaceful Joy and Wrath explain this vow! How many are the world-transcending realms and the measures of the supramundane fruits?

What are their numbers? [The "supramundane" refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the "mundane" refers to the eight classes of beings and so forth. There are six questions regarding the duration of attainment, the fruits, and the numbers. Question: What are the mundane and supramundane samādhis?
They refer to the distinguished meditative concentrations, which together with the preceding ones make eight; these are for the accomplishment of activities.

In what place [is there non-attainment] (when one asks where the attainment of the fruit of feeling resides, and asks the same regarding that which is not yet attained)? Furthermore, at what time can one be free from the production of the fruit of karma?
In what state does one attain liberation?
At that time, Vajragarbha, riding upon the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, spoke in verse to question the Buddha;
for there were still deficiencies in his practice of the mantra path, and the essential methods and skillful means had not yet been fully perfected.
Then the World-Honored One, the All-Knowing Vairocana, who is free from all afflictions, hearing those questions concerning the secret essentials, uttered this praise:
Excellent, excellent, O Great-Minded One of Diligent Valor! (This refers to the Great Mind, Great Vow, and Great Practice that are great at all times.

Regarding the "Decisive Arrangement of the Honored Ones' Positions in the Secret Maṇḍala" (which means the definitive establishment and arrangement of the seats of the various Sages), "Secret" refers to the profound treasury of the Tathāgata’s mysteries.
This essential point has been long kept in silence; it is spoken only at the proper time, like the Udumbara flower, and is not revealed unless the person is worthy.
This is not like the common, manifest teachings of ordinary instruction. The maṇḍala possesses manifold virtuous meanings;
it is the secret virtue of the Tathāgata, self-adorned like a blooming lotus. The term "decisive" (*kai-ketsu*) carries the meaning of discernment (*viniścaya*).
Thus, within this secret treasury of the lotus, various states and positions are distinguished.

All matters that ought to be done are here definitively resolved (*niścaya*; "decisive" means to explain with certainty). The root-source of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)—arising from the fundamental source of Great Compassion—is the unsurpassed secret of all Buddhas of the Mahāyāna;
that is to say, this maṇḍala is the very root-source of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
This is because this bodhicitta takes Great Compassion as its root, and is like a *garbha* (womb-matrix).

This refers to the "Root," meaning that a practitioner of the Mahāyāna Mantra Vehicle, by virtue of being fully endowed with skillful means, traverses the great direct path without any obstacles and reaches the ultimate reality.
It is like riding a well-trained horse along the great direct path to reach the great city; this is the most supreme and secret essential dharma of all Buddhas.
If it were explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even throughout all future kalpas; now, I shall explain it briefly by means of skillful expedients.

Because even within a single word all meanings and flavors are contained, it is called a "brief explanation" (the secret matters of all Buddhas that you are able to ask about, I shall now explain briefly).
At that time, the Buddha, having already first praised the Dharma and granted permission for a brief exposition, proceeded to answer the questions in their respective order.

The Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi: "Listen attentively! Regarding the Great Power Maṇḍala of the Twelve Branches, the Birth of the Vidyārāja of Great Power (the initial practice of the maṇḍala is answered first): that which should be performed first is precisely the twelve branches as explained above."
The arising of phrases proceeds from twelve supporting phrases; this Great Powerful Vidyārāja arises from these twelve phrases as the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Therefore, one should first manifest this Vidyārāja, for by means of this Vidyārāja, all mantras of the mundane and supramundane realms are entirely subsumed within it.
(When first constructing the maṇḍala, one should first abide in the samādhi-king of that Vidyārāja; this is none other than Mahāvairocana.)
This means that one should place the first of the twelve syllables within the heart to sustain the body. When one wishes to construct a maṇḍala, it is essential to first recite [the mantra];
that is, when about to create the maṇḍala, one must first recite it and then abide in yoga.
Yoga is the practice of this Vidyārāja in accordance with principle. Having abided in yoga, one should correctly observe what is now being performed as appropriate.

By what means is this known? It refers to the various applications of the five syllables as described above according to the five families—whether square, circular, triangular, crescent-shaped, or otherwise—and their appropriate use within the upper, middle, or lower mandalas;
furthermore, one must know the specific faculties and dispositions of the disciples. Only after knowing all such details may the rite be performed. Within these matters, regarding the mantras:
The King has not yet fully understood the various distinctions among these matters; therefore, he asks again. Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who possess prior knowledge:
first, the masters who have seen the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya), who, regarding such kings of mantras, perceive all faculties and conditions with unobstructed penetration;
second, those who have not yet seen the Truth, who must rely upon the instructions.
Furthermore, it is also secondary to examine the essential meaning transmitted by one's teacher;
once this has been examined and understood, one should perform whatever actions are appropriate. Therefore, one must first employ this King of Mantras.
Having sustained the body through the fundamental samādhi and first mastered the path of yoga, one may then perform all activities according to one's will. However...
Explaining this through the esoteric [teachings], these twelve mantra-kings are themselves the Vajrasamādhi.

Because the Bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and enters the Vajradhātu, he receives the simultaneous empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of all Buddhas of the ten directions and is sustained by their collective support, thereby attaining entry into the rank of a Buddha.
To enter the rank of a Buddha is precisely to achieve the Great Compassion Treasury-born Great [Vairocana].

This is the ultimate meaning of the maṇḍala. Because Vajrapāṇi entered this King of Mantras, he too has received the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas of the ten directions within this sūtra. Now, let us further resolve the treasury of great compassion;
for if it were otherwise, how could one receive the empowerment of all Buddhas and attain the station of a Dharma-King Tathāgata? Thus, [it was] composed.
Regarding the Maṇḍala ritual, it must first be performed by an Ācārya; therefore, this is answered next. One should know that there are two kinds of teachers.
As for the rank of an ordinary teacher, they must possess a thorough understanding of mantras, mudrās, and the characteristics of the *iṣṭadevatā* (sacred deity).

They must master each of these individually without doubt and clearly comprehend the distinctions between the superior, middling, and inferior methods. Furthermore, those [teachers] are of two types. (The "two divisions" refers to...)

This is for two reasons: first, to understand the profound mysteries; second, to master the concise and manifest teachings. What is called "profound" refers to the ability to comprehend that which is deep and vast.

This means attaining the practice of samādhi within the path of mantra-activity (*mantracaryā*), skillfully knowing the underlying principles (*naya*), extensively understanding the Mahāyāna, and being worthy of receiving the entrustment.
Here, "worthy of receiving the entrustment" refers to one who skillfully knows the appropriate timing, understands the capacities and natures of beings, and is capable [of such realization].
One who receives [this teaching] becomes an unasked friend, ensuring that one does not lose the causal conditions for the Great Matter;
as for those who are not yet capable, one should protect their inclinations and further instruct, benefit, and gladden them within other profound teachings.

For this reason, they are said to be "capable of being entrusted. It should be known that these are the Buddha’s eldest sons, because they have seen the Truth (the vision of the Dharma refers to seeing the retribution of the present life). Thus it is said.

Because one does not grasp at the characteristics of phenomena and is free from the realm of mental construction and discrimination, it is called "detachment" (meaning detachment from seeking the Buddha-way through worldly sharp wisdom and the like).

One should know that this master is one upon whom the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest before him, each extending his right hand to stroke his crown, conferring the empowerment of the Dharma and entrusting him with the Dharma-treasury. As for the second master, he has only attained the mundane...

The benefit of accomplishment (which is the advantage in the present life) consists in constructing a mandala for that purpose—specifically, by adding mindfulness and recollection within the extensive phrases.

Furthermore, one who possesses the understanding of various skillful means such as constructing the maṇḍala without error, having received initiation from a master and attained the rank of ācārya, is also said to be "authorized by the Buddha. Because of this, he personally faces the [deities] within the maṇḍala.
Because he is honored and receives the position of the Master of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), it is called "authorization" (*pratibodhana*).

From the section on empowerment onwards, this is a reiteration concerning the Master of Profound Practice. It should be understood that herein, those who receive empowerment from the Buddha are the masters of profound secrets, while those who receive transmission from a worldly master are the *ācāryas* of the manifest and concise [teachings]. All that was asked by Vajragarbha pertains to these.
The Buddha also answered in successive verses regarding what is required for the maṇḍala; these verses have not yet had their lines finalized and shall be embellished with prose later.
Having answered the master, he next described the characteristics of the disciple. The reason for this is that although there may be a master alone without [a disciple],...
Because disciples lack the conditions for transmitting the Dharma, the lineage of the Buddhas cannot continue;
therefore, next, the characteristics of disciples are distinguished into four types. First, disciples who maintain recitation; second, those who are untimely;
third, those who are both timely and untimely; fourth, those who are neither timely nor untimely—these are the four. As for what is meant by "timely":

If disciples seek an ācārya and request a master of the mantra-practice (vidyādhara), and if that master is one who has realized the Truths (dṛṣṭasatya), he shall naturally perceive the conditions of the disciple’s realm and know their capacity for a particular task.

He shall then grant them the practice and command them to perform recitation for a fixed period, whereby they will attain accomplishment; furthermore, he shall provide the skillful means for further accomplishment. Even if the teacher is a worldly one, although...
Without observing the immediate circumstances before him, the master simply acts according to the instructions, causing the disciple to recite mantras while praying for signs of mutual resonance.
The master likewise recites himself; if there is a correspondence, the disciple will attain the state, and the master shall know when it is permitted to receive the Dharma.
Once the correspondence is achieved, he transmits the ritual practice to him, also instructing him to recite as described above.

This also possesses its proper method (fāngguǐ). [Question: Regarding "non-timely" (*akāla*), it is as previously taught in the dharma: one should practice the mantra rites at the appropriate time so that accomplishment may be attained.
However, if the signs of success do not arise despite following the timing, one must perform additional preparatory practices (*prayoga*);
therefore, it is called "non-timely. Regarding "both timely and non-timely": although one has received the teacher’s oral instructions as described above, one has not yet attained [the realization].

When one practices according to the Dharma but has not yet reached accomplishment—being neither in this [present] time nor in a non-time—it is called a "concurrent phrase" (*sahita-pada*) because it is like the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*).
As for "neither concurrent nor non-concurrent," it refers to those who have merely resolved their minds and taken refuge, yet have not yet established the successive stages;
although the teacher has already accepted them, they await the proper time and conditions, and as these are not yet fully present, they have not attained [the goal].
Because that mantra-dharma is essential, it is called "neither [existent] nor [non-existent].

Furthermore, regarding those who possess all the marks, there are two kinds of marks: first, external marks, which refer to the limbs and so forth being complete without deficiency, as shall be explained in detail below;
second, internal marks, which refer to possessing the bodhicitta and being capable of [the practice].

Those who possess the equipment of the Dharma, such as a sense of shame and remorse, and who are able to practice each and every instruction of their teacher according to the Dharma—daring not to disobey the Buddha’s commands—these are the internal characteristics. (One should know that "the Buddha's commands" refers precisely to the teacher's instructions, because the teacher acts in accordance with the Buddha's teachings.
These four types of persons are all at the stage of training and have not yet reached fulfillment. Since there are now disciples for the first time...
The teaching on the characteristics of the stages and the mind-ground shall now be explained in succession. Regarding this so-called "mind-ground," one should construct a maṇḍala;
since one must first select the site for constructing the maṇḍala, the selection of the site is clarified next. That which is called "the ground" is none other than the bodhicitta;
purifying this mind first is precisely purifying the ground first. Having performed the purification, first—

Regarding the explanation: one should perform the eight petals and so forth as previously described. As for the previously mentioned skillful means of purifying the bodhicitta, it refers to visualizing an eight-petaled lotus;
upon the center of the flower, one visualizes the letter *A*, continuing up to placing the letter *Am* at the crown of the head.
One should also place the letter *Ra* on the eyes and visualize the heart. Furthermore, the throat should be kept neither too low nor too straight.
All such instances as these are skillful means for purifying the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*).

Once the ground of the mind has been purified, one next places the syllable *laṃ* upon the two eyes and contemplates it; this is the selection of the ground of the mind and the further removal of all impurities.
These skillful means have already been explained in detail previously; one should simply practice them as described before.
If one attains fearlessness by departing from the ground of faults, it is because one can purify the bodhicitta and the mind is free from signs;
thus, one is able to depart from all faults—namely, the delusions of afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), views, and craving.
Therefore, having departed from such faults, one departs from the perils of affliction, the terrors of the evil realms, and various forms of insecurity, thereby attaining [fearlessness].
Because it is of a nature of security, it is called "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*). Regarding the phrase "one shall attain all purity":
because one is free from all faults and the mind is without fear, one is able to bring the bodhicitta to ultimate purity.
If one has reached such a state, one should remain firmly established therein; that is, having attained freedom from all faults, one is no longer subject to the category of defilement.
Even if one is defiled by other things, one should maintain it without wavering and not allow it to be lost; one will certainly be able to reach unsurpassed bodhi.
To see this pure bodhicitta thus, without exception and to its ultimate extent, is itself the accomplishment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
To dwell firmly in the pure ground is to obtain the vision of tri-bodhi; "knowing" means knowing in this way. Thus it is said.
This knowledge is itself the vision of the Buddha; otherwise, it cannot purify the ground.

If one dwells in conceptual discrimination, the ground is not purified—meaning that if the ācārya does not purify the ground of the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala in this manner, it cannot be called the purification of the ground, because he is unable to free himself from deluded conceptualization.
Because one is constantly unable to escape from fear and affliction amidst various faults due to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), how can such a place be called a perfectly pure maṇḍala ground?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If a practitioner who maintains the recitation dwells within conceptual discrimination, it is not a pure ground.

[The practitioner dwelling in discrimination—if they were to perform purification, it would not be pure, O Lord of Secrets, because they are devoid of bodhicitta; thus both types of masters must abide in...]

Regarding the *bodhicitta*, although the Master may have purified the ground, it is not yet perfected; one must still abide in *bodhicitta* for a short time, for without this, [the rite] will not be accomplished. As explained previously in the section on constructing the mandala:
starting from a distance of one cubit (*hasta*), one should excavate away the "evil earth" and select out sand, gravel, hair, shards, stones, and the like.
Furthermore, since it is impossible to individually and exhaustively examine every minute impurity, even if the area within one cubit is purified, beyond that—
Even if one cubit were filled with various kinds of filth, it could not be sorted out;

how then could this maṇḍala attain ultimate purity? Therefore, you should know that if one can purify this bodhicitta, casting off the dung of all conceptual proliferation and discursive thought, and thus purify the ground of self-awakening, then this is what is called [purity].

To cultivate those stages well: if a person takes the teachings according to the literal text and merely follows the sequential application of the methods as previously stated, acting according to the specific matters at hand, one should know that such a person remains on the level of an ordinary fool and is unable to comprehend the secret function [of the teachings].
One should know that to form such an understanding is not what has been taught by the Omniscient One. This is why.
If one cannot purify this ground of mind, because of the existence of discriminative conceptualization, one has not yet abandoned the cause of suffering;
therefore, this is not what is taught by those who have attained perfect enlightenment. Since the internal and external are purified through the purification of the mind, the ground is purified.
Therefore, one should abandon discrimination and thoroughly cleanse all grounds, objects, and activities related to the ground. This concludes the general answer.
Having completed the purification of the bodhicitta, one should nurture it within the womb of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*).

Regarding the various maṇḍalas taught therein, I shall explain them in their proper sequence (this "sequence" refers to following the ritual procedures). Those who do not rely on what must first be performed out of ignorance fail to understand;

they merely inquire about the results—superior, middling, or inferior—without knowing how to abide in the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*). If one seeks liberation without abiding in the mind, [it cannot be attained].
It is impossible for a Buddha, the unsurpassed one in the world, not to possess this; nor is he called "Omniscient" otherwise.
Furthermore, as long as one cannot abandon these causes of suffering rooted in conceptual discrimination, it is for the sake of purifying the bodhicitta that one performs such deeds.
To exhort disciples to generate the mind in this way is to abide in the bodhicitta, lest they fall back or sink away.
Therefore, it is necessary to perform the rite of protection (*rakṣā*). The sutra continues by stating that one should guard [the disciple] with Acala; this refers to the Vidyārāja Acala.
One should take the heart-mantra of Acala to protect the disciple—this is the "Gate of the Letter Ha" (*ha-dvāra*), which is the syllable *haḥ*.
The syllable is the meaning of "cause. This refers to the pure bodhicitta which first abides;
both the master and the disciple abide in this bodhicitta, and subsequently they are protected by these two honors. It is the cause of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
The long vowel *ā* on the side signifies "practice," while the circle above signifies "realization"; it has the meaning of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). By means of this wondrous cause...
One should give rise to right practice, act with equanimity toward all things as being like space, and use these three dharmas to protect the mind so that it can never be moved or taken away.
If one does not employ this immovable protection, even using the Vidyārājas of the Three Times will suffice;
for the world says that the three poisons are like those [Vidyārājas], and by subduing the three poisons, one attains great sovereignty within the world—therefore they are called the "Three Times."
This is indeed superior, yet there is also a skillful means for further inquiry: if a disciple is able to accomplish this matter, they are not possessed by delusion (*moha*).
Delusion is attachment; where there is attachment, one cannot abide in detachment. To be free from delusion is precisely to be immovable.
Whatever is grasped or attained is all delusion. This means not being moved by false attachments; it is certain.
It is perfected as unsurpassed bodhi— pure, stainless, equal to space, unshakable, vast and boundless,
yet capable of containing all forms and images; one should know that the mind of omniscience is likewise so.
Next, regarding the empowerment of the ground: this refers to the gate of the syllable *A*. One should empower it with the syllable *A*;
this is the teaching of all Buddhas. All Tathāgatas in the past attained perfect enlightenment through this gate.
To protect the mind by means of this, or to apply *AṂ* to the crown of the head and *RAṂ* to the eyes and so forth, constitutes the firm bodhicitta.
Therefore, one achieves the karma of mastery; if it were otherwise, one would not attain mastery over the mind. Thus it is said: "Not other, not other.
This means that for all Tathāgatas to achieve Buddhahood, there is no path other than this; it is solely this single gate.
The first stage, the Stage of Empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-bhūmi*), relies upon the Buddha's teaching; "Buddha" refers to the letter *A*. The second is mastery over the mind.
This refers to the *bindu* (the point). Because this *bindu* is the very essence of samādhi, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), one attains mastery over all things.
Furthermore, one should not deviate from this teaching. Initially, relying on the Buddha, one generates the mind [of enlightenment], which is the letter A;

subsequently, upon attaining Buddhahood, one becomes equal to the Buddha, which is the letter Āṃ. Since the bodhicitta arises in reliance upon the Buddha, all conceptual discrimination is thereby eliminated.
That which has not yet attained Buddhahood is the seed of the unconditioned (*anālambana*).

Having already completed the question-and-answer regarding the empowerment of the ground (*adhiṣṭhāna-bhūmi*), one must next employ a cord (*sūtra*) to determine the positions within the maṇḍala. Regarding the cord:
its Sanskrit name is *sūtra*, which carries the meaning of "continuity" or "binding. It is called a cord because it binds together all virtues, preventing them from dispersing.
The sutra states that there are four kinds: white, yellow, red, and black; furthermore, there is one more kind, namely the color of space (*ākāśa-varṇa*).
To "mind" this means one should maintain mindfulness of it. Space can contain all forms and images, and thus it possesses all colors.
If one relies solely on manifest color (*varṇa*), it is a light blue color, like the color of the leaves of trees and grasses. White is...
Yellow represents faith, red represents diligence, and black represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the color of concentration is identical to the color of *nirvāṇa*.
Wisdom is the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*); because the Great Emptiness possesses all characteristics while being without characteristics, it constitutes all forms.
Whenever the lines are joined, if one follows the ritual for each step individually, one should separately construct a maṇḍala and install it there.
One should prepare various offerings, such as precious vases, incense, flowers, unguents, lamps, and diverse foods and drinks (further inquire regarding the specific methods).

Thereafter, one should have a young girl join [the threads]. First, she should receive the eight precepts, don fresh and clean garments, bathe with scented water to ensure internal and external purity, and sit within the mandala to perform the joining. As for the method of joining the threads, one should first prepare fine [threads] in advance.
The silk threads must be made perfectly even in thickness; their size and tension must all be adjusted appropriately.
Furthermore, they must not be interrupted in the middle, but joined together. When combining them, cover the mouth with a piece of silk.

As each colored thread comes and goes, fold and layer them so as to form nine strands, and then combine these into a single thread (the threads have only one end, which is folded and layered in the middle; no joining is permitted between sections). This constitutes one thread.

The single color consists of five colors combined into one cord. If the cord is made by combining [the colors] such that the tension, looseness, thickness, or fineness are uneven, or if it is not crafted with full attention, it will give rise to obstructive dharmas, harming both the master and the disciple, or even causing them to fall into madness and confusion;
therefore, one must be careful. I privately maintain that the young girl is *samādhi*, for through *samādhi* she is perfectly balanced.

Through equalizing and harmonizing, the five powers (*pañcabala*) and five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are accomplished; by means of these faculties and powers, one is then able to sustain all practices. (Question:

Regarding "equilibrium in empty space" [ākāśa-samādhi], in other versions it is "equilibrium such as empty space"; "equal" [sama] refers to universality. "Sustaining" [dhāraṇa] means that one should act in this manner.
"Acting" [karaṇa] means knowing the magnitude. First, one determines emptiness. "Equal position" [samatva] means equilibrium.)
Second, regarding the placement of the thread upon the site of the maṇḍala, there are two types.

If it is a master of profound practice who wishes to construct the altar, once the ground for bodhicitta has been purified, he should—within the context of yoga and for the sake of guiding his disciples—correctly contemplate the empowered positions of the Womb (Garbha) Great Maṇḍala; that is to say, he must first ascertain its dimensions.

"Fixing" means that all positions are clearly manifest as if facing them directly before one's eyes. "Universal" refers to the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) within the space [of the mandala] and so forth.
"To act" means that one should act in such a manner; "equal" means uniformity. Second, one places a cord upon the ground of the maṇḍala;
however, for the sake of measuring for others and conforming to worldly convention, these directions are applied to the altar.
Once the ground has been prepared, one should then establish the directions using five-colored threads and other materials.
Even for a *ācārya* of shallow practice, it is necessary first to use these threads to establish the directions;
thereafter, one must arrange everything with focused attention so that all the directions appear as if before one’s eyes. Alternatively, one may record them separately on paper and with a brush.
When it comes time for actual application, one must not be hesitant or mistaken during the performance of the rite. Regarding the phrase "in the air" and so forth mentioned here:
this refers to what was explained above—first, together with the disciples, one draws a line to establish the orientation without letting it touch the ground.
First, one draws lines in the air facing each other, aligning them with the heart; then, following the proper sequence, one ensures they form a complete perimeter.

If there is no disciple fully endowed with the required qualities who is capable of constructing the maṇḍala together with the master, one may also perform the rite by placing ritual pegs at the disciple’s location.
Once the boundaries have been thus fixed, one should then direct the mind to arrange the sequence of positions; only after that may the cords be stretched and the lines drawn.
If the yoga-ācārya performs this within the same space, he shall behold all the Buddhas as they appear in their respective directions.
The Bodhisattvas, celestial deities, and others are clearly established in their respective positions in accordance with worldly conventions;
they are delineated by marking out lines and determining their locations according to their forms and colors to manifest them. One should know that this constitutes the supreme arrangement.
"All the sons of the Buddhas, all the wise ones" (this refers to the sons of the Buddhas praising the Bodhisattvas for their possession of wisdom).

"The lotus that delights the mind, the supreme auspiciousness praised by the world"—this means it is praised by the world as being auspicious. This next passage answers the representation of the seating arrangement;
just as people in the world regard the lotus as auspicious and pure, capable of pleasing the hearts of all, so too [is this Bodhisattva].

Within the Secret Treasury (*Guhyakośa*), the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-maṇḍala-saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is also the most profound and secret auspicious gateway of all empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and its embodiment sits upon this lotus pedestal.
Yet, even among the lotuses of the mundane world, there are immeasurable gradations;
that is to say, they differ in size, whether they are open or closed, and in their colors and forms—each being distinct. Such is the nature of the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*).
The lotus pedestals also possess distinctions such as provisional and real, opening and closing; therefore, it is said that the wise should know this.
If it pertains to the stage of a Buddha, one should visualize an eight-petaled *puṇḍarīka* (white lotus), causing its petals to open fully and spread in all directions.
If it pertains to a Bodhisattva, one likewise visualizes this flower as a seat, but causes the flower to be only half-open, not allowing it to be fully blossomed.
[Their flowers may be white, yellow, or made of precious lotuses; all are acceptable, but those that are red in color are worldly flowers and remain below.

If Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas are to sit, they shall sit upon the petals of these flowers, or upon the petals of the *kumuda* flower. [The shallow-minded tradition claims that what is transmitted as such is merely a partial wisdom.
This is the blue lotus (*utpala*); this is simply a blue-colored lotus, yet there is another distinct blue lotus.
The "seeds" are not of this category; they are lotus leaves, specifically the green lotus leaves that grow from the lotus.

As for the gods of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) up to the Brahmā heavens of the First Dhyāna (who are designated as "Brahmā" by worldly convention), they all sit upon red lotuses, which are pure red in color (referred to in the world as "sitting kings").
As for the gods of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those dwelling on earth, each sits according to their respective station.

These are used as representations; for instance, in the case of an image of Śakra, one depicts the King of Mountains, Sumeru, with the mountain deities seated upon the mountain, the water deities seated upon the water, the tree deities seated upon the trees, and the city deities seated within the city.

There are many such cases that can be understood through one's own reflection. (From here on, the various devas are distinguished by their respective abodes, such as the heavens of the desire realm, where they may sit upon grass or dry leaves, etc. "Recollection" [smṛti] means mindfulness and the act of holding it in mind without forgetting. — Tripiṭaka Master.

It is said that there are many kinds of lotuses in the Western [Pure Land]: First is the *padma* (in Chinese, *bōtóumó*). [Furthermore, it has two varieties: first, the red variety, which is the lotus in question here;

second, the white variety, which is the white lotus found here [in this world], and not the *puṇḍarīka*. Second is the *utpala* (in Chinese, *yǒubōluó*). [It also has two colors, red and white, and there is also a variety that is neither red nor white, shaped like the *nīlotpala* flower.

Third is the *kumuda* (in Chinese, *jùmùtóu*). [It has two types, red and blue. It is also said that the *kumuda* is the blue-colored lotus. Fourth is the *nīlotpala* (in Chinese, *nílǔbōluó*). [This is offered...]

That which grows from cow dung seeds and is exceedingly fragrant, held by Mañjuśrī, with eyes like blue lotuses—this is also it. Furthermore, there is the *sukandika* flower, which is similar but smaller. The *pāṇḍarīka* flower has about a hundred petals;

the petals overlap one another in a perfectly round and lovely arrangement. The outermost petals are extremely white, gradually turning pale yellow toward the inside, until those at the very center are nearly the same color as the filaments. This flower is also exceedingly fragrant.

Formerly, when King Vairōcana was harming the Śākya women, Mahākāśyapa took this flower at Lake Anavatapta, wrapped it around eight kinds of meritorious water (*aṣṭāṅga-guṇodaka*), and sprinkled it upon the bodies of the women, whereby their minds and bodies attained peace and happiness, and they passed away.

The cause for rebirth in heaven was that a woman threw flowers into the pond, whereupon they grew into plants that exist there even to this day. The flowers are very large, measuring over one chi in diameter, and are especially lovely. This is what is extended from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
it is precisely this eight-petaled *maṇḍala*.

Next, the meaning of making offerings is explained. Although the responses herein may not follow the sequence of the questions, they all accord with the meaning of what was asked and do not deviate from the principle.
One should know that there are briefly four kinds of offerings:

first, the offering of incense, flowers (as well as unguents, lamps, and so forth, up to food and drink—this is worldly offering, consisting merely of presenting material objects); second, joining the palms (which refers to prostration; this is the mudrā); third...
The four stages of the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) refer to the stage of mental application where one visualizes incense and flowers filling the entire Dharma-realm;
having done so, one then employs the mudrā of palms joined. Thus, both the palms-joined gesture and the three matters of compassion are all mental applications.

Although the sutra does not explicitly mention incense, flowers, and so forth, they must necessarily be present according to the meaning. "The Flower-Hand Arises" (this is a restatement of the palms-joined mudrā; these flowers arise from the hand). [One] offers them.
Regarding the visualization of the Bodhicitta-seal that binds all Buddhas and generates all limbs, it is said that the *Kusuma-hasta* (Flower-in-Hand) arises;
this means that once the seal has been formed, one should immediately direct the mind toward making offerings.

As for this "seal that generates all limbs," although the mantra was previously present, it is stated here that the seal had not yet been mentioned; one should verify this accordingly. Having thus empowered [the object] with the seal, one should...
Contemplating the mind of enlightenment, one visualizes these flowers emerging from the hands as an offering.
Each and every Buddha gives rise to this mental application, as do their respective offspring.

With earnest devotion, they offer these faultless, exquisite, fragrant, and luminous flowers to the King of Trees (the Bodhi tree), manifesting them throughout the Dharma-realm. (Note: Visualize the trees pervading the entire Dharma-realm.)
Regarding "making offerings of flowers": through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of mantras, most excellent, wondrous, and vast clouds arise within the Dharma-realm;

from these, flowers rain down before all Buddhas and so forth. This means that one makes offerings by employing the respective mantras and mudrās according to their original forms for all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and even the two vehicles and the eight classes of beings, thereby consecrating the objects of offering.
When the practitioner makes offerings of incense and flowers, they should empower them with mantras and mudrās; for instance, when offering flowers, one uses the Flower Mantra and so forth.
If the mind does not abide in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), how can this be achieved? It is said that it is through mastery over *samādhi*.

Thereafter, one directs the mind [with the thought]: "May these flowers and incense be fragrant and beautiful, free from all faults and evils, and may I be born in a supreme and wondrous realm, abundant [in merit]."
Just as a great cloud arises from within the dharma-realm, so too do flowers rain down from it (arising from the dharma-realm).

Constantly producing various kinds of light that pervades before all Buddhas, these flowers and other offerings likewise pervade the entire dharma-realm as a single great tree, no different from the celestial *kalpavṛkṣa* tree.
They rain down clouds of various flowers, fragrant banners, canopies, and the like, as well as food and drink.
One should perform various offerings before all Tathāgatas—immeasurable, boundless, and inexhaustible—making them pervade each and every one.

To cultivate the mind in this way and empower it with mantras means that for each individual honored one, one performs offerings while empowering them respectively with their own specific mantra and mudrā. Next, those inferior to this are the eight [offerings].
The various sections and so forth also each employ mantras and mudrās according to their respective original categories. Furthermore, these deities are inferior to these celestial gods;

next, the celestial gods will be explained. Alternatively, there may be mantras within the sūtras that correspond to their original yoga—that is, they correspond to their respective tutelary deities (iṣṭadevatā).
For example, for wrathful deities, one uses red [colors] and so forth, as with flowers.
The application of scented unguents and so forth should also be performed with appropriate visualization.
Regarding these deities, some sūtras contain mantras and mudrās while others lack them; in such cases, there is a separate general auspicious mudrā:
one should join the tips of the two fingers representing space (the thumb) and water (the ring finger), while extending the other three fingers. One should empower all objects using this mudrā.
Furthermore, all the implements for offering within the mandala may be augmented with these [mantras], and they will all be successfully accomplished.
If one has forgotten the specific mudrā of the principal deity at the time of practice, it is also permissible to augment it with a general mudrā.

As for the mantras for incense, flowers, and so forth, they are the same as the mantras for incense, flowers, lamps, and so on mentioned in the previous chapter, each applied according to its respective category.
As for its application, it is as described in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*: if one wishes to universally make offerings to all Buddhas with a single flower, one should cultivate this *prajñāpāramitā*.

This means that by simply directing the mind toward a single flower or incense, through the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one is able to universally make offerings to all worthies and sages throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*.

This means that these roots of goodness shall be inexhaustible. If one does not perform the Universal Auspicious Seal (*sāmānya-maṅgala-mudrā*), there is alternatively the Vajra Fist Seal or the Lotus Seal (and the Avalokiteśvara Seal;
however, these are performed with the right hand only). For the earth-dwelling deities (*bhūmi-cara-devas*), one joins the left hand;

yet, fearing that the left hand may be occupied holding something, it is also permissible to perform the addition of the object with the right hand. When making offerings, one should first apply the seal and then hold [the object] up.

One should direct the mind toward making an offering before placing them at the location of the various deities. If it is scented unguent (*vilepana*), one may apply it to the bodies of those deities;
otherwise, it should be placed as appropriate in a place of adornment, or simply set before them. When holding flowers and the like, there are likewise distinctions of height:
for a Buddha, [the offering] should be held high, level with the body or the crown of the head; for a Bodhisattva, [it should be held] at the level of the head.
Regarding the positions: those of the Two Vehicles are below the heart; those of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas hold [the mudrā] at the heart;

the Worldly Deities are at the navel; this is the fixed rule. The Śuddhāvāsakāyika and other deities are below the navel. Having performed the mudrā-binding, they are led upward into the sky to make offerings to the Buddha.
Then, descending by degrees, they reach the Earth-dwelling deities and so forth, causing them to descend further. As above, there are the four classes of honored ones.
From the body of the Buddha, flowers are now offered; their height and depth are also according to the previous standard, aligning them with their respective positions in the maṇḍala.
However, there are two types of masters: if one is accomplished in Yoga, they need only employ the mastery of the samādhi-mind;

because they have already attained penetration into the gateway of mantras, whatever they perform according to their mind is immediately accomplished, without necessarily depending on ritual procedures.

It can also be accomplished; however, if one is a teacher of the second [class] in the world, it must necessarily rely upon substantial phenomena (*vastu-dharma*), employing mantras and mudrās for consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) before success can be achieved.

Next, regarding the meaning of *homā* (fire ritual), one should know that there are two kinds: first, the internal (*ādhyātmika*), and second, the external (*bāhya*). These are what are called the internal and external.
"Realm after realm" is a specific commentary. *Homa* has the meaning of "burning. Through internal *homa*, one is able to burn away and eliminate all karma.
Since all sentient beings are born from karma, they revolve through the wheel of rebirth without end due to that birth.
Because karma is eliminated, birth is also eliminated; this is precisely what constitutes liberation. If one is able to burn away karma, it is called "internal."
From what does homa attain liberation? It is said that it attains liberation from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering.
Having departed from the world, it gives rise to the seed, namely the pure white bodhicitta.
Just as worldly fire, once it has burned an object, results only in ashes, this is not so; for it burns away all afflictions.
The afflictions are like the fire at the end of an eon, which leaves nothing behind; yet from within this very state, a sprout arises, namely the sprout of bodhi.
That which can burn is wisdom itself. As previously described, one contemplates the syllable RAṂ surrounded by a wreath of fire;
now, imagine that this fire completely envelops the body, and that the body, moreover, holds a sword and a noose.

Because of this letter-gateway *ra*, one attains the exhaustion of all karma and the complete purification of all obstacles; once the karmic obstacles are purified, one gives rise to the seeds of pure whiteness.
Therefore, one should next contemplate the bodhicitta; it should be understood that the seeds arise in dependence upon the bodhicitta.
When contemplating in this manner, one should visualize the letter *va* pervading all parts of the body and the pores.
From within [the vessel], white nectar flows forth, pervading the ten directions and sprinkling upon the bodies of all sentient beings.
By means of this causal condition, it is able to cause the seeds to grow gradually; therefore, it is called "inner homa" (antar-homa).

Next, the explanation of "outer homa" (bāhya-homa) consists of three types: first, the *bhagavat* (honored one); second, the mantra; and third, the mudrā. (The coarse *bhagavat* is for the purpose of making offerings.)

Place it according to the specific school one follows; alternatively, it may be placed within the position of the maṇḍala. Furthermore, inquire regarding the location for placing the fire in the coarse hearth (*sthūla-kunda*). This is the mantra; within the fire is the coarse seal (*sthūla-mudrā*), which is the seat of the *ācārya*.
One’s own body is itself the seal. When performing the outer homa (*bāhya-homa*), these three positions correspond exactly.
These three also signify the purification of the three karmas. The three positions are: the body, the hearth, and the deity. Each of these three has its own triad, namely: the deity... [text ends].
Mantras and mudrās purify the three karmas and accomplish the three activities—namely, *śāntika* (pacification) and so forth. [Commentary:

"Purifying the three karmas" means that the *homa* deity is the mental karma (*manas-karma*), the mantra is the verbal karma (*vāk-karma*), and the mudrā of the master’s body is the physical karma (*kāya-karma*).

Through these causes and conditions, one is able to purify the three karmas and accomplish the three activities, namely: pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), and subjugation (*abhicāruka*). These are the paths of the three karmas.

This path is the convergence of meaning; when words and principles accord, they are said to converge. The practice you all perform is the Bodhisattva path, which is the three paths returning to a single consistency.

Furthermore, regarding the visualization of the three syllables, each character differs: for the *śāntika* (pacification) visualization, one should place a dot above the syllable *raṃ* and visualize it as white;
for the *puṣṭika* (augmentation) visualization, the syllable is *raḥ*, which is yellow; for the *abhicāruka* (subjugation), [the syllable is *kṣaḥ*].
Visualize the syllable as either black or red; just as the syllable is, so too are the colors of the Honored One and oneself.
When these three factors correspond, success is achieved. Within this, there are further distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior:

pacification (śānti) is superior, enrichment (puṣṭi) is middling, and subjugation (abhicāra) is inferior. One who practices in this manner performs what is called external homa; this should be understood.
Both outer and inner homa are called "supreme"; if one does not accord with this [principle], practicing them in vain is of no benefit.
Because one performs outer homa, it is possible to lead [the practice] into inner homa. However, the principle of the inner and outer is fundamentally without distinction;
this differentiation is made for those seeking worldly accomplishments so that they may perform outer homa. If...
Those who differ from this—meaning those who do not rely on the prescribed methods and procedures—should be known as having no understanding whatsoever;

their efforts are in vain and will yield no fruit. Because they act perversely according to their own ignorant minds, divorced from the wisdom of mantra, they will ultimately never attain the fruits of *siddhi*, whether mundane or supramundane; therefore, it is said that they "do not obtain" them.
This is the result.
Next, in response to the question regarding color and form, there are generally three families. Vairocana belongs to the Buddha Family;
he is the body of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm and is consistently white in color. Next, Avalokiteśvara is [the embodiment of] Amitābha.
The Buddha’s body is yellow; next, Vajragarbha is Śākyamuni, whose body is reddish-yellow (that is, variegated).

Regarding the various mantras spoken by the Buddha and those spoken by the Buddhas: the preceding mention of "the Buddha" refers to the Buddha division, while the subsequent mention of "those spoken by the Buddhas" refers to the mantras spoken by Vairocana.
Within the Tathāgata family, all mantra sections—from those born from the Buddha down to those permitted by the Buddhas—belong to the Buddha family.
As for the phrase "all Buddhas" mentioned below, it refers specifically to that which was spoken by the Buddhas and does not extend to [the teachings of] Bodhisattvas and those below them.
These two types both possess two colors, namely white and yellow; this merely states that they are appropriate.
It should be understood that "white and yellow blended" means neither too yellow nor too white; "variegated color" means possessing all five colors.

One should know the sequence: the section on the respective activities of the mantras of Vajrapāṇi, the various classes of Avalokiteśvara, and the others, refers to their application according to the specific purpose of each activity. The Buddha Family is exclusively for the pacification of calamities (*śāntika*).
Regarding their colors: for one's own ritual activities, Avalokiteśvara is purely white; however, within his family (kula), he transforms according to the specific activity.
The Lotus Family is exclusively for the purpose of augmentation (puṣṭi) and uses the color gold.

The Vajra Family is exclusively for the purpose of subjugation (vaśya) and uses various colors—that is, it possesses all five colors—or else follows the specific requirements of each respective family.
There are three types of ritual applications within the Buddha Family itself: namely, pacifying (*śāntika*), increasing (*paustika*), and subjugating (*abhicāruka*).
If performing pacification, one should follow the original rite and employ white; if the Buddha Family performs increasing, one follows this same rite but employs yellow;
and if the Buddha Family performs subjugation, one follows this same rite but transforms it into variegated colors.
This is as follows: just as with the Buddha Family, it should be understood that the Lotus Family and the Vajra Family categories are to be interpreted in the same way.
Regarding "the division according to their respective functions," this means that their activities are divided according to their respective colors and types.
As for "the various mantras of Avalokiteśvara," the various sounds mentioned here cite the Lotus Family as an illustration by analogy for the Buddha and Vajra Families.

Next, the shapes of the maṇḍalas are explained. Although the rite for pacifying (śānti) was mentioned first, here we follow the sequence of the sounds and the practical application, placing the rite for increasing prosperity (puṣṭi) first.
For all rites of increasing prosperity, the maṇḍala is square (□) with yellow in the center. The altar for pacifying is circular (○) with white in the center.
The altar for subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa) is triangular (△) with black in the center. The altar for summoning (ākarṣaṇa) is a half-moon.

Regarding the "summoning by various colors," this refers to summoning by taking up various objects and so forth. The Sūtra states that "the four directions are all [square]" to provide an illustration for all cases.
For example, if the central mandala is square, then everything down to the outer enclosure is square;
if the center is circular, then everything down through the successive tiers to the outer enclosure is circular. If the center of the mandala is square, then all parts are universally square.
The circle is likewise in this sequential manner; the triangle and so forth are also the same. The construction of the homa hearth is also thus:
if the altar is square, the fire-hearth is also square. All other cases should be understood by analogy.

Next, the "categories of form" (*rūpa-jāti*) are explained; this refers to physical appearance (*ākṛti*). It should be understood that "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) is the correct meaning, though it may also be termed "form-image" (*rūpa-bimba*).
The verse states: "The form-image should first be known. "First" means "I shall now explain.
Now, the categories of form for these deities vary in many ways; speaking generally, there are briefly two types: male and female. The male represents wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, it is called the "Foremost Woman" (*Mukhamātṛkā*); this samādhi is the second [of its kind]. Alternatively, regarding those that manifest form and color in all places:

as in this sutra, or in other sutras where the honored form manifests according to all places, manifesting form and color in accordance with objects—because these manifestations are not fixed, they are called "inconceivable. Although each is distinct, they are categorized by their common type.
If one says that white is for *śāntika* (pacification) and yellow is for *pauṣṭika* (augmentation), the rest is easily understood;
by observing the differences between those men and women, as well as their complexions and appearances, one will know the appropriate application. Regarding the arising of inconceivable wisdom:
although one should act as the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) in white, when performing a *pauṣṭika* rite, one must perform it according to the practitioner’s mental visualization.
The yellow color possesses the function of augmentation and shifts according to the mind;
yet all that is produced is real and not false, for it is made so by means of inconceivable wisdom.
Now, it is said that within a single form of the *dharmadhātu*, there are all forms, and because the observing wisdom is also subsumed within the object, such mastery is attained.
Its function is to eliminate ignorance; thus, various kinds of wisdom arise. Although immeasurable wisdoms are known, in reality they are but a single wisdom.
As stated previously, wisdom is "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvajñā); it is by means of this single wisdom that all wisdoms are manifested.
The previous question concerned the dimensions—large or small—of the forms of the Honored Ones; this is now answered.

Since the Buddhas manifest through the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) solely to respond to the capacities of sentient beings, and since those capacities differ in ten thousand ways, one should know that the manifestations they extend likewise have no fixed size.
When discussing the form of each individual Honored One, there is none whose measure does not equal the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), being without boundary or limit, and devoid of beginning or end.
Because wisdom has degrees of depth and breadth, and because its measure is either great or small, the bodies perceived by each practitioner differ accordingly.

Therefore, one should know that the size of the visualized deity (iṣṭadevatā) follows the capacity of the practitioner’s mind and has no fixed limit. (This clarifies the three secrets of the Guhyakapada Sūtra.
That which is called "realized wisdom" (pramāṇa-jñāna) is precisely the Buddha; it is the realization of the inexhaustible realm through inexhaustible wisdom.
As the box is large, the lid is also large.
Previously, in the inquiry concerning the venerable form and dimensions, the question also included the seat and the mudrā; now they are answered as well.

Since the body has no fixed measure, one should know that the seat and the mudrā are likewise so. (This extends to the point where) if the mind can be vast, the seat is also commensurate with that measure, and the mudrā is likewise so. Their sequence is according to their magnitude.

[This] is also small [to make it] commensurate with the seat of the Honored One. Next, as for answering from what this mudrā arises—[furthermore, the sequence is from the Buddha down to the devas]—the Buddha said:
"Just as the place from which a Buddha is born, so too does the mudrā arise from that very source. Why is this?
Because all Tathāgatas arise from the seed of the Buddha-nature, the bodhicitta; one should know that all mudrās likewise arise from this."
The Bodhicitta arises; the seal (mudrā) arises from the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and seals the disciple, just as a king uses a seal to stamp [his edicts] so that all may believe and accept them.
Now, by sealing with this seal arising from the entire Dharma-realm, it is the Dharma-seal (dharma-mudrā);
it is the seal of the marks of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa). Next, to answer the question of what use this seal serves: it is by means of this seal arising from the Dharma-realm.
The seal upon the disciple signifies the meaning of that which cannot be transgressed; for it is not transgressed by oneself or by others.
That is to say, from the initial bodhicitta until the ultimate wisdom of a Buddha, there is no falling back and no turning away during this interval.
For this reason, the world designates such a person as a *bodhisattva*. By means of this seal, one abides in the bodhicitta.
Because it is non-retrogressive, it is called "non-transgression. One should know that this seal is precisely the seal that closes the gate of birth-and-death and opens the path to the Dharma-realm.
To speak briefly, the measure of this seal is equal to the Dharma-realm;
by sealing with this seal of the Dharma-realm, one causes that person to bear the insignia of the Dharma-realm and to become identical with the universal gate of the Dharma-realm.
Because it is embodied, it is called a "seal" (mudrā) for disciples; the Dharmadhātu-mudrā is its abbreviated form, meaning that one seals [all things] with this single Dharma-seal.
If expanded, they would be beyond counting; this is the distinguishing mark of a Great Being.

Regarding the previous question concerning the types of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), we shall now answer it. "O Son of the Buddha, listen well"—according to the authentic language of the Sanskrit original, this should be stated fully.
One must listen with earnest attention. Why is it that in the preceding questions it was not said "listen well," yet it is only here that it is mentioned?

It is because if one does not listen well to other teachings, the resulting forgetfulness entails a relatively minor fault; however, if one does not listen well to the consecration... [the fault would be great].
If the consecration (abhiṣeka) is not performed, it is improper to hear the mantras, mudrās, and so forth; none of these may be practiced.

Since this fault is exceedingly grave, one must strictly admonish against it. It is, for example, like the case in the world where those of the Kṣatriya caste, desiring to continue their lineage so that the royal bloodline is not severed, perform the consecration for their eldest son and draw water from the four great rivers.
The water was contained in vases made of the four precious substances and adorned in various ways; furthermore, the Prince’s person was decorated, and all necessary articles were fully prepared.
A great elephant was also adorned, and holding the vase upon its back, it was made to carry the Prince to the center of the altar.

All those under his command assembled, and from atop the elephant's trunk, they poured the water so that it flowed down over the Prince’s crown. Having performed this consecration, they raised a great cry.
He proclaimed three times: "You all should know that the Prince has already received his consecration; from this day forward, you must all carry out every command.

Now, the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, is likewise; in order that the lineage of the Buddhas may not be severed, he has poured the water of the nectar-like Dharma upon the crown of the Buddha-son’s head, so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall never be interrupted. Thus, in accordance with [the tradition]...
Because this is a worldly dharma, there is this method of empowerment through the seal (*mudrā*);

from this point forward, all the assembly of noble ones shall hold them in reverent esteem, and they shall know that such a person will ultimately never regress from unsurpassed *bodhi*, being certain to succeed to the rank of Dharma King.
Whatever activities they undertake—be they mantra, physical seals (*mudrā*), or the practices of *yoga*—none shall dare to transgress them.
However, there are three types of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). The first is performed solely through the method of mudrās, free from all ritual activities;

this refers to entry into the secret maṇḍala. It is for those disciples who possess sincere and earnest hearts, who deeply delight in the practice of mantras, and who aspire to the Mahāyāna, yet lack the necessary resources.
If one were to require them to seek out every single requisite item, it would instead lead to [frustration].
When there is such a person who creates obstacles on the Path, the teacher should give rise to deep compassion and observe that person’s mental conduct to guide and attract them.
However, one may do this for only this single individual and must not do so for many people. Why?
For fear that those who possess the resources and capacity to provide support might develop a sense of indolence and fail to devote their whole hearts to planting the roots of all virtues.
While performing [the rite], one should prepare a modest offering according to one's means to worship the Triple Gem;
this is the foremost and most excellent method, for it unifies the body, speech, and mind of the *iṣṭadevatā* into one, as all three are pure. One should seal [the practice] with this mudrā;

this is the most excellent. The Master’s secret transmission includes such mantras and hand-mudrās (first, the mere hand-mudrā; second, the complete ritual procedure; third, the samādhi-consecration).
Second, regarding empowerment through the performance of ritual activities (*karmaprasara*): this refers to both the master and the disciple first performing ritual activities.
This means, for instance, that one first causes the disciple to perform sincere prostrations and repentance for seven days;
likewise, the master also performs recitations for seven days to seek a response from the deity and to prepare various offerings, such as incense.
All items required for the altar, such as various kinds of flowers, must be prepared one by one. This consecration is not different from the previous one;
however, because there is available wealth and power, one is made to exhaust all one's strength to perform inexhaustible offerings within the ocean-like assemblies of the Buddhas.
For this reason, the fruit of the merit bestowed is inexhaustible; therefore, it is necessary [to proceed].
Third, regarding the exhortation to perform the empowerment through the mind alone:
such an empowerment does not require selecting a specific time or direction (meaning that it is permissible to set up the seat facing east, south, or any other direction).

Because this disciple has already cultivated the practice of mantra and is thus capable within the Secret Treasury, it causes the master’s heart to rejoice; furthermore, this is the most supreme method.
Furthermore, both master and disciple attain the yoga of mind-to-mind consecration (*cittābhiṣeka*), which is like the bestowing of a prophecy through the touching of the crown of the head.
Moreover, by serving their master with all their heart in various virtuous deeds without transgression, they cause the venerable one to rejoice;
for this reason, the *yogācārya* performs the mental visualization consecration (*manasikārābhiṣeka*). As for the method of this consecration, it is as follows in the *Yoga-ācārya[-tantra]*:
First, enter the pure chamber and abide in samādhi as previously described;
arrange the four sections of the body to form the four-layered maṇḍala positions exactly as they appear in the manifestation of Vairocana, without any difference.
