Having done so, through secret empowerment, cause the disciple to wait outside the gate for the command.
Spontaneously receiving the majestic empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Vajrapāṇi, one is led to enter;
spontaneously, one also understands how to form the mudrās and so forth, each according to the ritual rules.

Having entered the chamber, because of the empowerment bestowed by Vajrapāṇi, the positions of all the deities of the maṇḍala appear vividly before one’s eyes, as do the forms and mudrās of each individual deity.

The practitioner also fully understands the equality of all syllables. At that time, by the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), a sublime flower spontaneously appears in the practitioner’s hand, with which they make offerings to the assembly.

Wherever the deity to whom they are naturally linked resides, that deity immediately arises and comforts them with a sublime voice, granting them protection and guidance. Thereupon, the deity takes one...

Having drawn the water of the nectar-samādhi from the presence of all the honored deities of the great assembly, he then bestows the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) upon that disciple in their very presence.
At that time, the ācārya merely sits in one place, enters samādhi, and remains silent and unmoving, yet is able to accomplish such a supreme feat.
This is called "bringing joy to the Honored One" (*devatā-saṃtoṣaṇa*), which refers to the service (*sevā*) of the *iṣṭadevatā* (the chosen deity).
One should perform the empowerment through the manifestation of the practitioner with joy, by means of the prescribed number of recitations and the completion of the ritual procedures.
Through service and mantra recitation, one causes the Honored One to be pleased and to manifest and preach the Dharma; one should act according to what has been taught.
This follows the previous example: just as a disciple can serve a master and cause him to be pleased, so too does the master bestow empowerment and instruction.
Next, to answer the question as to how many types of samaya there are: the World-Honored One now replies that, briefly, there are five kinds. Regarding *samaya*:

it is like a person who, in the midst of a great assembly of kings and ministers held in high esteem, speaks for themselves and makes a solemn vow, saying, "I shall never again commit such a thing. Such is [the nature of samaya].
Regarding the practice of these matters: when one makes a sincere declaration in the presence of a person worthy of trust, should one violate it, one incurs a grave offense.
Therefore, *samaya* means that which must not be transgressed; in brief, it carries the meaning of "precept.
Among the five types mentioned herein, the first is merely being able to see the mandala from a distance.
This refers, for example, to when one is constructing a maṇḍala and perceives it as being fully complete.
Suddenly, there are people who, with virtuous minds, rejoice in the work and desire to pay homage and make offerings. At that time, the ācārya permits them to be led in;

however, they are made to worship from outside the altar, scattering flowers, incense, and so forth from afar into the site of practice (maṇḍala) as an offering, thereby attaining the vision [of the maṇḍala].
Because of such an assembly of the Dharma, immeasurable karmic offenses are all extinguished; however, one has not yet been authorized to receive the mantras and mudrās—this is the first [stage].

The second is seeing the seating positions within the maṇḍala: it means leading the person into the center of the altar to perform prostrations and offerings, scattering flowers upon their designated seat, and the master addressing them: "Your flower has fallen upon the position of such-and-such a Honored One."
The Master explains the name of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) and [the disciple] enters the inner precinct of the maṇḍala, seeing all its positions;
this person is said to have attained the second *samaya*. If one requests mantras and mudrās, they may also be bestowed according to what is appropriate.
The third stage is the vision of the maṇḍala and the positions of the mudrās, wherein one performs all the rites; this refers to the *ācārya*.
From beginning to end, [the master] constructs a maṇḍala for this person, and further instructs them individually on all the deities, mudrās, and so forth;
he also transmits the mantras and hand-seals, teaching every ritual procedure—this is the third [stage].
As for the fourth, [the disciple] is already able to follow the ritual procedures to cultivate the gateway of mantra according to all its prescribed rules.
Having thoroughly understood each [aspect] and possessing full knowledge of the expedient means and various arts required for the ritual mandala, he is capable of holding the rank of a master;
pleasing the master’s mind, the master then creates for him the *kriyā-tantra* mandala and declares: "From this day forward, you shall be no different from me.
You must construct mandalas and initiate disciples so that the Dharma may endure for a long time and the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed."
This is the fourth. The fifth is the secret samaya; as it is taught, the mudrās, the maṇḍala, and the arrangement of positions are all visible.
If one does not enter this secret maṇḍala, secret wisdom will not arise.
Therefore, one should receive empowerment according to the ritual within the secret maṇḍala; this is called the fifth, which the wise should know. If it were otherwise...
This is not called the *samaya*. It refers to that which was previously described as entering during the third consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
If one differs from these five matters, it is not called "skillfully performing the *samaya*. Furthermore, within the secret maṇḍala itself, there are five types:
the first is when, having received the mantras, mudrās, and dharmas from the master, one practices according to the instructions and [unites] with the *yoga*.
In the *Ga* [section], one may see the great assembly of deities within meditative concentration, yet has not yet been granted entry [into the mandala] (this is like the first person).

Next, the second person has been granted entry into the secret maṇḍala and is able to perform circumambulation and offerings, yet has not yet received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) manifested by the holy deities.
Thirdly, having been granted entry into the midst of the great assembly of sages, from the beginning until—
Each and every secret practice of the final [stage] is received through the skillful means and instructions of the Noble One, like the third person.
As for the fourth, having already well practiced the essential path of secrets, they currently receive the secret transmission and samaya from the various Honored Ones;
they are thus employed by the Tathāgata to perform the deeds of the Tathāgata. The fifth has already completed the preceding [stages].
Furthermore, one may see oneself within a great assembly acting as the *ācārya* teacher; this is one who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*).

As soon as such a person enters samādhi, they see all the assemblies of Buddhas, even those as numerous as the atoms within ten worlds, and are able to gather them all together, occupying a position equal to that of the Honored Ones therein. If one observes this in the mind...
Susthitamati (addressing Vajrapāṇi): One who awakens their mind and does not find [reality] in three locations is called a Bodhisattva; this name is obtained by way of its meaning.
Because one has self-awakening, one does not cling to these three locations—namely, the phenomena observed within oneself, the time of accomplishment, and [the result].
If one clings to these three, it is not called awakening the mind. Because there is no attainment regarding these three, one is called a Bodhisattva.
Previously, the meaning of "bodhisattva" was explained according to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); now, it is named here according to its essential meaning.
Regarding Vajrapāṇi’s previous question as to when one obtains the name "bodhisattva," the answer is given here:

if one contemplates the mind and awakens to the well-established state of the three places, yet is unable to maintain the recitation, this is called "contemplation. This refers to beginning from the time one receives [the teachings] from the teacher.
The yoga method briefly consists of three matters: the mind visualizes the deity, the mouth possesses the mantra, and the body possesses the dharma-seal (mudrā).

You should contemplate in this manner. Once you have received the teaching, practice as you have heard it until it is clearly and thoroughly realized, like seeing one's own face reflected in a mirror;
this is "contemplation" (dhyāna). As for "awakening," it is the awakening to and realization of the realm of one’s own mind.
This is the reality of the Dharma. "One who dwells well" refers to Vajrapāṇi, whom the Buddha addressed by name after delivering this teaching.
Alternatively, it may refer to a practitioner who, having realized their own mind, attains a state of dwelling without dwelling;
thus, they are called one who "dwells well. Having attained such a state in accord with the Dharma, one is able to behold the Honored One.
When the practitioner’s sphere of activity is vast, sublime, pure, and inconceivable,
they then employ "non-apprehension" as a skillful means and observe with wisdom whether such phenomena arise from within, come from without, or arise from a combination of both internal and external.
For the practitioner, their own body and mind are what is termed "internal," while the realm of the *iṣṭadevatā* (the chosen deity) is the "external."
That which is the object of perception is called "external. The conjunction of these two is called "intermediate.

Observing in this way, one understands that these various inconceivable phenomena do not emerge from within, do not come from without, nor do they exist in the intermediate state as a combination of both internal and external.
One should know that they are fundamentally pure and ultimately unapprehendable.

That which is produced—namely, the external objects, the internal body, and the mind as the middle [factor] through contemplation—all three of these things being entirely eliminated is the primordial purity, the single characteristic of equality.

Why is this so? Because when the practitioner correctly contemplates the conjunction of the internal mind, the external objects, and the mental conditions, the conjunction of these three things brings forth the presence of the inconceivable object of contemplation.
Because the three factors arise from the convergence of conditions, one should know that they are non-arising, devoid of intrinsic nature, and ungraspable.

Furthermore, when the practitioner possesses the secret seal of the body, the mantra of the speech, and the visualization of the deity’s realm within the mind—since these three factors are ultimately non-arising—they constitute the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-pariśuddhi*) and the equality of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa-samatā*). Thus it is said.
The practitioner, having abandoned the three attachments and purified the three spheres, becomes free from the four marks; from this point onward, one attains the name of Bodhisattva.
(The four marks refer to the self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span, as distinguished in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.)
Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra,
Fascicle Eleven Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra,
Fascicle Twelve Recorded by the Śramaṇa Yi-hang (Ichigyō)
The Remainder of Chapter Eleven, the Secret Maṇḍala:
Now, when the practitioner performs this contemplation of non-arising and lack of intrinsic nature, the mind finds nothing to grasp and does not cling to internal or external signs;
this is because all phenomena are ultimately empty and entirely unobtainable. Thus, from the moment the thought of enlightenment was first produced...
How is it that the various meritorious deeds practiced and the myriad conducts cultivated for the benefit of sentient beings do not fall into the error of nihilism within this ultimate emptiness?
It is because the practitioner possesses the power of skillful means (*upāya*) that they do not incur such faults.
Why is this so? Because when the practitioner first contemplates, regarding the various marks of existence...
The object is precisely the dharma that arises from conditions; because it arises from conditions, it is not self-generated, not other-generated, not co-generated, and not without cause.

Therefore, it is eternally unarisen. If there is no arising, this dharma of causes and conditions is identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in its profound stillness and purity, fully endowed with all inconceivable natures and the arising of meritorious qualities that respond to conditions.
The capacity [of the Buddha] is like a reflection in a mirror or the moon in water: it exists and yet does not exist; it does not exist and yet exists.
Although it arises from conditions, it does not fall into the two extremes. Therefore, although it is ultimately empty, it can accomplish various merits to universally benefit all sentient beings.
Because great compassion transforms beings, one does not fall into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Thus, the Sūtra says: "By the power of skillful means..."
One should know that for the sake of sentient beings, the wisdom of the practice of objectless contemplation (*anālambana-bhāvanā*) acts as the seed of Bodhi.
O Virtuous One, this very person is one who has accomplished Bodhi. This objectless contemplation is precisely the inconceivable contemplation of the Middle Way.
Since the Buddha has already abandoned all attachments, he plants this "seed of seeds" in order to deliver sentient beings; thus, when he has attained Buddhahood, he obtains it.

The practice of non-conditioned awakening (anālambana-bodhi) arises within the fundamentally quiescent Dharma as a skillful means (*upāya*) to benefit others; it employs skillful means to benefit sentient beings. By what skillful means?
If one were to abide solely in fundamental quiescence, it would contradict one’s original vow. Therefore, through skillful means, one plants the seed of Bodhi for the sake of sentient beings.
Because this cause specifically benefits others, it is termed "delivering people" (*puruṣa-tāraṇa*); thus, one turns the non-conditioned toward [the goal].
This is the meaning of "having conditions. A "benevolent one" (ren-zhe) is a name for a Buddha; "transcending sentient beings" means surpassing ordinary people.
A benevolent one is one who has attained mastery over the root of tranquility.

The previous question asked, "What is meant by 'seeing the truth'? Now, the answer is given: the fundamental quiescence of dharmas is that they lack intrinsic nature; those various [states] are established...
Abiding in the inherently quiescent Dharma with a mind equal to Mount Meru is called "one who has seen the truth" (*dṛṣṭasatya*); such are the practitioners of those paths.
Because they know that all phenomena are inherently quiescent and devoid of intrinsic nature, they are as immovable as Sumeru; this is what is meant by "seeing the truth.
As stated above, one first receives the mantras and the skillful means of contemplative practice from a teacher, thereby attaining correspondence with samādhi.

Having clearly and directly perceived this, one then correctly contemplates, in accordance with reality, that these three things are all unarisen, without intrinsic nature, and utterly unapprehendable.
By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to realize through direct awakening that all phenomena have, from the very beginning, been characterized by constant quiescence.
In this context, "those phenomena" refers precisely to the objects of observation and illumination mentioned previously; it is within this [that they are realized].
Having realized that which is inherently quiescent and abiding in the principle of self-realization, one attains stable dwelling within the true wisdom of such a dharmic essence;
thus, doubt and regret are forever exhausted, remaining as immovable as Sumeru, the King of Mountains.
"Sumeru" carries the meaning of being unshakable. Abiding thus, from this point onward, it is so named.
This is for the sake of seeing the Truths (*satyadarśana*). That which is real is like emptiness; reality is precisely like emptiness, just as emptiness is.
Being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is called "real," and that which is real is precisely like emptiness. "Real" means it is not false speech. Next, it says:
"That which is seen is like the Buddha" (seeing the Truths is identical to becoming a Buddha); the Buddhas of the past also saw in this way, and I likewise see in this way.
Therefore, it is said "and" (*ca*). Next, it says: "By means of this reality and emptiness, one does not speak falsely;

together with what is seen, as [a Buddha], seeing thus is the meaning of 'seeing the truths' (*satyadarśana*). Now, as for "seeing while abiding," this refers to abiding securely within the wisdom of reality;
therefore, it is called "reality. Because one awakens to the emptiness of intrinsic nature and the purity of the fundamental nature, one should know that all... [the various dharmas].
All phenomena are empty and void; this means dwelling apart from false conceptualization and abiding in the principle of truth—both of these constitute reality.
One who perceives this principle is one who sees the path perceived by the Buddhas of antiquity; their understanding is identical to the intent of all Buddhas.
The Tathāgatas of the past likewise proceeded along this very path to achieve perfect enlightenment. Having thus attained such spontaneous wisdom, [one realizes it].
Furthermore, one should transmit this to sentient beings, for what I have now attained is no different from this; therefore, it is called "the real.
"The real" carries the meaning of being without falsehood or deception. Regarding the previous question concerning those who have attained the bodhicitta, their siddhis are unsurpassed;
beyond these, there are five further kinds of siddhi.
"What is called *siddhi*, and how many kinds are there? Now, first answering regarding the fruit:
that which is called the accomplishment of *siddhi* refers to abiding in the bodhicitta. This bodhicitta is precisely the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment;
this is what is called *siddhi*. Because it is the most exalted among all *siddhis*, a sutra says: "Of those *siddhis*, there is nothing further."

Next, in response to the question regarding the stages of entry into practice, this refers to the stage of faith (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*). Next, in response to the question of how many kinds of *siddhi* there are, it is said that prior to this unsurpassed *siddhi*, there are briefly five kinds of *siddhi*: first, faith; second, entry into the stages; third, the five [supernormal powers]... [and so forth]. The worldly five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) belong to those such as the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas. [and so forth].
The four [levels] are the two vehicles (*yāna*), and the five are the attainment of Buddhahood; these constitute the five kinds of *siddhi*. First, regarding the practitioner who abides in faith:

this refers to one who is able, according to their capacity, to purify the various faculties, who possesses deep faith in the Tathāgata’s secret treasury without any doubt, and who believes that the Buddha possesses such-and-such skillful means (*upāya*) and that if one practices accordingly, one will certainly attain *bodhi*. This is the stage of practice through faith prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*).
Next, "entering the stages" refers to entering the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). This corresponds to one who has realized the Truth (*dṛṣṭasatya*) within the Śrāvaka teachings.

Third, regarding the "five supernormal powers" (*pañcābhijñā*): it means thoroughly understanding that the objects of the five worldly supernormal powers are like illusions, dreams, the moon reflected in water, or images in a mirror, and thus they are not to be grasped or clung to. At that time, one attains the name of the "Stage of the Sages of the Five Supernormal Powers."

Thirdly, regarding your question concerning the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*): it means that when the mind observes the spheres of the two vehicles and attains non-attachment, one does not fall into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
At that time, one transcends the spheres of the two vehicles; this is when one reaches the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*).

From the ninth stage onward, one cultivates the path of awakening (*bodhimārga*), progressively advancing until the state of a Tathāgata is accomplished. Thus, according to various sūtras and śāstras...
The Master’s general outline is largely as stated above; however, regarding the meaning within the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*), there is further distinction:

it is said that on the first Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) there are ten mental states (*citta*). From the first mind through the fourth, one attains mastery over the sphere of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*);
from the fifth through the eighth, one attains mastery over the sphere of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; and from the ninth mind onward, [one proceeds] exclusively toward...

Practicing the path to enlightenment until reaching the tenth mind is called "attaining Buddhahood. "Buddha" means "awakened," referring to the awakening to the nature of one's own mind as pure, inherently quiescent, and characterized by primordial cessation.

Within these ten stages of mind, the first through the eighth are called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the ninth through the tenth are called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). "Seeing" refers to the direct perception of the principle of the Truths (*satya*).
Progressing in cultivation based on this is defined as exclusively contemplating the Tathāgata’s inconceivable realm and secret merits.
Such a secret state is not an object of perception, as it transcends the measure of the mind; therefore, it is specifically termed the "path of contemplation.

"Awakening" (jue) carries the meaning of contemplative knowledge (*vipaśyanā*); having already transcended the realm of the two vehicles, one thoroughly understands the minds of the two vehicles and those of bodhisattvas.

There is a distinction. If one enters the second bhūmi, one likewise reaches the fourth mind to transcend the five supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), the eighth mind to transcend the two vehicles (*yāna*), and the tenth mind to attain Buddhahood.

Following this principle, although the names of the ten minds of faith and the entry into the stages do not differ from those of the first bhūmi, these ten minds here are further illuminated and purified of defilements. This continues up to the tenth bhūmi as well.
The ten minds constitute one hundred minds in total; that each successive stage is increasingly superior can be understood by analogy.

This may be understood through the metaphor of refined gold in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Upon the fulfillment of these ten minds of the first bhūmi, one is able to manifest bodies in a hundred buddha-fields and so forth, as explained in detail therein.
However, the attainment of Buddhahood through these one hundred minds is specifically taught in the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
This sutra, which is profoundly deep and subtle, has not yet reached the Eastern lands. By practicing without ceasing, one causes the mind to become pure in every moment.
Next, the answer regarding the practice of activities without cessation until the mind is continuously purified refers to the non-interruption of one's functional effort (*prayoga*).
Such maturation—meaning that which is not yet matured is brought to maturity—will result in the attainment of *siddhi*. It may also be said that "he shall attain *siddhi*"; this is the next response.
Regarding when *siddhi* arises, the Sūtra states: "From lifetime to lifetime and birth to birth, until karma can no longer obstruct the ripening of the fruit—at that time, *siddhi* is accomplished.
When it must arise through karma so as to be attained within one's own person, for the practitioner of recitation, *siddhi* emerges from the mind.
(This is the text of the Sūtra. This "from lifetime to lifetime and birth to birth" is an expression of profound meaning (*arthavāda*). In Sanskrit, it is called *saṃsāra*.
*Tāna* refers to consciousness, which is to say, that within the internal mind.

Just as sentient beings in the world perform various kinds of karma and, by virtue of this karma, undergo its retribution—whether in a single lifetime or across hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions of lifetimes—and this karma is never lost, such that when it ripens, one receives the retribution;
now, the answer to this is that the arising of *siddhi* is also like this, according to the practitioner’s superior [capacity].
In the middle and later periods, by practicing according to the essential principles of the mantra-dharma, one attains *siddhi*.
Because this *siddhi* resides within the body, it remains constantly within the practitioner’s body throughout every successive lifetime, just like the ripening of karma.
Although it arises from a multitude of conditions, it is eternally empty and quiescent—neither existent nor non-existent—and yet it neither perishes nor vanishes. From this point onward...

*Siddhi* is that which is accomplished; it receives its fruit in every lifetime without failure. Because one receives that fruit by means of the karma of *siddhi*, it is called "the family of *siddhi*.
Once born into the family of *siddhi*, until the attainment of Buddhahood, one never loses or destroys it;
therefore, it is said that "karma cannot remove it. As the Sūtra says: "That which is matured—maturity is itself the fruit"—it causes [the fruit] to be realized.
"Ripened" means the sense of the fruit of enjoyment. "At one time" refers to a single moment;
that is to say, once the practitioner has first relied upon the dhāraṇī for recitation and attained the meditative state (*viṣaya*), he is permitted to perform the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Thus, within this single night, he attains *siddhi*. Because it is accomplished in a single moment, its influence persists in the body over a long duration.

In the interim, it remains undestroyed; just as poison placed within milk can kill a person even when it has reached the stage of clarified butter (*mārdvika*), so too, when one creates karma for rebirth in the heavens and receives its fruit according to that karma, once the celestial reward is attained, it is obtained immediately upon thought without the need for further effort, being accomplished simply by the power of recollection.
This *siddhi* is likewise: in all births, one constantly attains whatever one desires through the mere power of thought.

Therefore, it is said that [the siddhi] arises according to one's will. At that time, when the practitioner arises from the pure karma produced by their cultivated practice, the practitioner subsequently attains siddhi.
The pure karma arising from the will and the mind that gives rise to it are equal and without distinction;
when the karma and the mind are equal, at that very moment siddhi is accomplished.
Next, the response to "How does one ascend to the realm of space? is as follows:

It means that the practitioner, by the power of *siddhi*, traverses the realm of space with sovereign non-obstruction, just like a magical illusion (*māyā*). Regarding "attaining fearlessness within the phenomena of illusion":

"fearlessness" refers to being able to fully comprehend the methods, procedures, and rules of illusory phenomena without doubt or difficulty; thus, whatever is desired is accomplished, just as in that [illusion].

Just as a magician creates various realms and manifests them according to people's desires, yet that magician remains truly unmoved and undergoes no change, but merely deludes the minds of the multitude through the causal conditions of mantras and medicinal herbs;
so too is this *siddhi*: without abandoning this body, one walks upon the realm of empty space and travels among all [realms].
The various buddha-fields appear with sovereign mastery, yet they have never wavered;
it is only because they are produced by the illusion of mantra that such a state is attained. This "mantra of the illusionist" is named Śakrā-jāla (Indra’s Net);
just as that net displays appearances in all matters, manifesting various forms while in reality there is not a single substantial entity among them, it is therefore called Śakra.
This "net" is a metaphor for the worldly mantras of those illusory people, used to illustrate the illusory nature of supramundane mantras.

(Alternatively, it is said that "net" carries the meaning of "uninterrupted. Just as a net causes people to become deluded and unable to escape on their own, this mantra-net likewise causes the minds of people to be deluded, leading them to perceive things falsely; hence the name.)
Next, regarding the answer concerning the secret of the body as being like a city of the *gandharva*:
those inhabitants therein are neither body nor consciousness. Next, regarding the answer to "What is the secret of the body?":

it is said that this person of *siddhi*, without abandoning this body and without abandoning this consciousness, is able to keep their body secret, just as various things are seen within a city of the *gandharva*.
The characteristics of the palace, its inhabitants, and its various objects, though appearing to exist, are in reality non-existent;
yet they are not non-existent in the sense that they may sometimes be seen and sometimes be absent. This practitioner’s concealment of their body is likewise:
like a city of the gandharvas, it arises from a multitude of conditions and is neither real nor unreal, appearing and disappearing according to circumstances.
Due to the various causes and conditions of mantra practice and contemplation, this body likewise arises and ceases in accordance with those conditions.

Furthermore, it is like a dream; as stated in the scriptures, for example, it is as if a person in a dream ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and experiences the various sublime pleasures of the gods, yet while wandering through the celestial palaces in that dream, they do not abandon their current body.
Nor does one actually travel to that place; though a kalpa may pass, upon awakening from the dream, it is but a brief moment.
That person does not abandon this body nor go to that celestial realm, yet through the mind in the state of sleep, such inconceivable phenomena occur.
This cannot be fathomed by the ordinary cognitive faculty; now, those who have accomplished *siddhi* travel to various [realms].
The world is also like this; it exists only through the causal conditions of yogic dreams, whereby various phenomena arise as if they were real and not non-existent.
Yet one knows that all these are like the ten similes and does not give rise to grasping or attachment.
Because the body is purified, *siddhi* occurs like a rainbow; mantras are like wish-fulfilling jewels, and *siddhi* is like a rainbow. Mantras are like rainbows.
The merit and activity of the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) is *siddhi*.

Just as a rainbow appears in the sky from whence it is unknown, yet its various colors can be seen, so too does the mantra arise in manifold ways according to body, speech, and mind, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.

It produces all requisites in accordance with one's thoughts; though they arise, they are without conceptual differentiation, arising precisely through non-differentiation. Furthermore, it is like a multicolored rainbow.
The five colors in the sky are brilliantly radiant and clearly visible; observing this phenomenon now, does it arise from space or from the vapors of the earth?
If it arises from space, space itself is originally devoid of phenomena—how then could such colors exist there?
If it arises from the earth, that too is impossible, yet here is this matter which delights the human heart; one should contemplate and understand its nature.
Phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor from another, nor from both together, nor without cause; they merely arise through the convergence of various conditions.

Now, the body of *siddhi* is likewise so: by the power of the merit of reciting mantras, there come to be such inconceivable and manifold supernatural transformations, just like that rainbow. Furthermore, to resolve further doubts, it is as if someone were to say:
How can this dharma of the ritual characteristics of mantras accomplish the true dharma of the vision of reality that is signless?
Indeed, this mark of reality does not depart from causes and conditions; by contemplating the true nature of these dependently arisen phenomena, one enters the inconceivable realm.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel atop a banner-pole, which can fulfill the aspirations of all people.
According to one's desires, it fulfills their requests and accords with their minds even until now. Now, consider this:
does it arise from the jewel, or does it arise from the person’s mind? If it were produced from the jewel, why would it not emerge at all times?
It must wait for the person’s heart to have a longing wish before it emerges. If it were produced from the person’s mind, then why would that mind not seek [the result] for itself?
One should know that when waiting for a pearl, it does not emerge from the pearl itself, nor does it emerge from the human mind;

it is neither independent nor causeless, but exists only through a combination of conditions. Likewise, the accomplishment of *siddhi* and its inconceivable miraculous transformations are also like this:
they are achieved solely through the conditions of the mantra, the visualization of the deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), and the bodily mudrās. Because of the mantra, the vocal karma is purified.
Because the mudrā of the intentional karma of contemplating the Honored One purifies bodily karma, and because the three karmas are equal in their activity, inconceivable karma arises spontaneously;
yet it is also not to be differentiated, being without thought and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

If that were so, since it would be like a wish-fulfilling gem, one might think it is a phenomenon possessing characteristics (*sanimitta-dharma*). To eliminate such a view, the analogy of the great void is further explained.
Just as space is signless and non-conceptual, yet all the various activities of sentient beings—
coming and going, advancing and stopping— are accomplished by means of space;
and just as all myriad things and all forms and appearances are manifested by means of space, yet the nature of space is eternally non-conceptual and without arising.
The mantra of the marks is likewise: its original nature is eternally pure, identical to empty space;
it cannot be defiled by any conditioned phenomena, yet it can accomplish various activities and manifest inconceivable transformations through the universal gate.

What are the characteristics of existence? One should know that among the various phenomena of the world characterized by existence, grasping these forms and appearances is called "characteristic" (*nimitta*).
Based on such conceptual discrimination, one establishes names; this is called "name" (*nāman*). These phenomena of name and characteristic are all identical to the ten similes;
they exist only because of causes and conditions, and because they arise from inversion, it is said that they are non-existent.
In truth, non-arising and the absence of intrinsic nature are identical to the dharmadhātu and the suchness-nature (*tathatā*).

If one can contemplate in this way, it is as if one has assembled in one place with all the Tathāgatas. Although such a person may not yet be able to exhaustively realize the Buddha-wisdom, their understanding is identical to that of the Buddhas;
because their understanding accords with the Dharma and is the same as that of the Buddhas, they are indeed [the Buddhas].

It is to be in a single assembly together with all Buddhas. Just as space is devoid of all conditioned activities—[this clarifies that the ten directions are empty]—so too the practitioner of mantras is unstained by any activity of conceptual discrimination.
Observing thus in every way and understanding that it is merely ideation, when the practitioner of mantras contemplates in this manner, all Buddhas rejoice along with him.
Regarding the two kinds of *homa*: although the characteristics of *homa* were briefly explained previously, they are now further distinguished as outer and inner *homa*.

As taught by the Two-legged Honored One (*dvipadottama*), there are two kinds of *homa*: outer *homa* refers to performing rites to eliminate obstacles such as afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
inner *homa* refers to the cessation [of conceptualization] as taught by the Buddhas, the Two-legged Honored Ones.
All objective spheres are produced by the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Now, the external *homā* and internal *homā* serve as the skillful means, which are themselves the cause. To this, an objector says:

"If one performs this offering of *homā* now and seeks that fruit, it involves having expectations; how can this be said to accord with principle? The respondent answers: "I have no expectations whatsoever now."

Question: If this is so, why does one not follow the constant law of *dāna* (generosity) by giving universally to all who are poor and suffering, but instead perform this burning and consuming in vain? What is the purpose of this? Answer: Indeed, when ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) give something and there is a recipient, they immediately harbor a mind of aspiration—either seeking a reward in return or hoping for the fruit of the gift. Because of this, [the act is not pure]. However, in this case, there is no recipient; since there is no recipient, there is no hope for a reward. Furthermore, because there is no recipient, there is no fear of retribution. Since there is neither hope nor fear, it is called "pure giving. Therefore, although the firewood is burned and consumed, it is not in vain. This is called the "Dharma-giving of the Bodhisattva. These causes and conditions cannot counteract the mind of longing; because they cannot counteract it, they cannot sever the source of craving and attachment.
For this reason, they cannot serve as the causal condition for internal homa.
Now, burning this offering is precisely intended to sever those faults and act as their antidote, serving as the cause for non-attached wisdom and functioning as the internal [homa].

It is through the skillful means of *homa* that one acts in this manner. By offering these ritual substances to the Honored One (*bhattāraka*), one knows that the mind of aspiration is no different from the objects themselves.
Just as fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted, there is nothing to be grasped and no location;
thus, internal *homa* serves as the causal condition. (In performing the rites of increase—whether superior, middling, or inferior—there is increase...)

[Regarding "diminution"]: Just as when offering flowers, one first removes all impurities and then further enhances their majestic radiance before making the offering—just as it is with flowers, so it is with *homa*.
A master of profound practice performs the internal *homa*, whereas a practitioner of shallow capacity performs external rites, which ultimately serve as the cause for the internal rite.

Furthermore, the distinct characteristics and essential natures of the various deities must be personally realized; that is, by observing the forms and examining the colors of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, followers of the Two Vehicles, and celestial beings, whether superior, middling, or inferior, they may be known.
Furthermore, there are various distinctions among the practices of mantra cultivation; I shall now analyze them.

If worldly persons practice the cultivation of mantras by relying upon the honored deity of their own respective lineage—such as Maheśvara and others—there are immeasurable varieties, each different from the other, which cannot be recorded in full.
The sūtra merely cites one corner [of this diversity] as a general illustration.

The sovereign [deity] is the foremost; yet, when those practitioners perform ritual offerings (*pūjā*), each hopes to attain the fruit of the *iṣṭadevatā* (personal tutelary deity) of their own family (*kula*).
According to the differences in their respective natures and stages, they each harbor distinct aspirations and seek to achieve those fruits;
thus, their minds are limited, and the fruits likewise differ accordingly. This is what the Tathāgata has taught regarding the practice of *homa*.
This is the nature of the Dharma. The mantras and so forth of the world explain the worldly dharmas.
The mantras taught by those known in the world as gods, lords, and possessors of merit, as well as their powerful mudrās—
All manifest their results in this very life; therefore, they are said to be valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*).
Those that possess some slight difference are called phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; because they lack any enduring stability, it is said that they do not exist in future lives.
As for those called "valid cognitions," the Buddha taught that they are phenomena with limited duration; thus he spoke. This is because worldly people seek only [results in this life].

Because one desires to realize the fruit of those very deities and spirits of the mundane world, the Buddha likewise established the worldly *homa* method as an antidote; thus, there exists the *mantra-practice homa* method.
However, if a person among those worldly beings has reached the ultimate perfection within their own fundamental ritual system, they may simply act as a representative for that fundamental deity.
The categories [of practitioners] may not exceed their respective levels; the same applies to their mantras and mudrās.
However, according to the depth of merit planted and the power one can sustain for that particular deity, one speaks of the mantras, mudrās, and the principal deity (iṣṭadevatā).

According to that power, one may only achieve the fruit of that specific deity, and furthermore, one can only achieve results in the present life, ultimately attaining only mundane accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*).

One cannot achieve supramundane fruits; however, if one cultivates the mantras and mudrās of the Tathāgata, it is not so, for through these causes and conditions of *siddhi*, one never regresses and ultimately achieves wondrous enlightenment.
Furthermore, from life to life and birth to birth, there is never an exhaustion or loss of this—this is the distinction. It is like a puddle in a cow’s hoofprint, even if it were to remain...
Water dries up of its own accord when it reaches the limit of its own power; however, if one places this water within the great ocean, there is no principle by which it could be exhausted.
Why is this? Because it has merged with the nature of all waters into a single flavor, it cannot be depleted.
It is the same for those who practice the mantra-vidyā of the Tathāgata: they continue in this manner until they attain Buddhahood.
From this point forward, through life after life, one shall receive the fruit of this siddhi, which can never be exhausted; by virtue of this power, one shall ultimately attain bodhi.
Why is this? Because one has already become of one flavor with the great ocean of all Tathāgatas.
The various mantras of those who have transcended the world are primordially unarisen (meaning non-constructive);
they sever the arising of all karma, are free from the faults of body, speech, and mind, and constitute the mantras of the Buddhas,
Pratyekabuddhas (the treatise says "rhinoceros horn," or alternatively "unicorn horn"), as well as the assembly of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
I shall now explain its measure: it transcends the three times and arises from conditions.
Whether visible or invisible, the fruit arises from body, speech, and mind; this is what is proclaimed by the world.
The fruit may endure for an eon; thus has the Perfectly Awakened One taught.
Mantras transcend the number of kalpas;
these mantras of the supramundane are fundamentally and originally uncreated and unarisen.
Yet, the mantras spoken by the worldly lords such as Maheśvara are all conditioned phenomena. From those lords, the supramundane mantras are produced. Thus...
It is not so; this is neither created by the Tathāgata himself nor was it created by the Buddhas of antiquity.

Therefore, one should know that these mantras, mudrās, and so forth have been such by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) from the beginningless limit (*anādikāla*); they do not arise through deliberate creation.
Question: If you say there is no creation and no arising, yet we now see practitioners currently seeking the fruit of *siddhi*, [how can this be?]
If one diligently applies skillful means and thereby achieves that fruit, and since there is both the arising and the fruit, there must be something produced;

how then could it not arise? The answer is: this reasoning is incorrect. For the nature of the mantra and the mudrā, as well as the essence of the one who maintains and recites them, are identical to empty space;
the fruit that arises is likewise so. This is because [the fruit] proceeds from the mantra, the mudrā, and the *bhagavān* (deity).
Through the causal conditions of the equality of these three matters, one is able to purify the obstacles of the stages of body, speech, and mind.
Once the three obstacles are purified, from this arises the inconceivable fruit. Therefore, the magnitude of this inconceivable fruit cannot be apprehended;
like those mantras and mudrās, its measure is equal to space. One should know that this fruit is likewise identical to space. Thus it is said.
The mantras belonging to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are likewise equal in measure to that;
they all transcend the three times—the three times being past, future, and present.

Because they are free from the three times, one never loses or destroys the fruit of this siddhi, ultimately attaining unsurpassed bodhi. This is the arising of the fruit through dependent origination.
This means that because various conditions—such as mantras, mudrās, and the honored deity—are fully assembled, accomplishment is attained;
therefore, this measure is the true mark (lakṣaṇa) of the Middle Way of equality. This fruit is of two kinds:
first, the visible dharma, which refers to attaining accomplishment in the present life; second, the invisible dharma, which refers to the fruit of the future.
Because retribution is eternally inexhaustible, one receives its fruits life after life, progressing ever further until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Yet this is neither manifest karma, nor matter, nor mental phenomena; it neither exists nor perishes, and thus it is never destroyed.

Nevertheless, it arises through the pure causal conditions of the actions of body, speech, and mind, and yet it is unborn and devoid of intrinsic nature. (There are many other types of answers above; consult the original text and its corresponding questions.)
Next, to answer the question regarding the number of fruits and the duration of their lifespan: the power of all mantras belonging to those honored in the world is at most no more than one *kalpa*.

Those spoken by the Buddha, however, exceed the number of *kalpas*—meaning they surpass one *kalpa*, and again surpass another *kalpa*, in such an immeasurable manner until the attainment of Buddhahood. Therefore, the *siddhi* and lifespan obtained by worldly people [are limited].
Regarding the measure and its fruit, there is a numerical limit that does not exceed one kalpa; now, however, his lifespan is not lost and is inexhaustible, surpassing the measure of all kalpas.
If explained in terms of actual events, it means that according to one's power and capacity, one may pass through several kalpas or even immeasurable kalpas without the lifespan being exhausted;
this is also what is meant by "surpassing" those worldly devas. Hence, it is said: "transcending."

The term "kalpa" is a general expression that encompasses indefinite time; speaking in terms of actual reality, it refers to the immeasurable life span of Amitāyus, which transcends the number of kalpas, and his retribution, which is likewise limitless.
The Great Sages who are the Buddhas, and the assembly of Buddha-sons in samādhi, are pure and free from all conceptualization;
those with conceptualization belong to the world.

Next, regarding the answer concerning samādhi: briefly, there are many kinds. If one speaks of the Buddhas and the Buddha-sons as well as the followers of the Two Vehicles, they are termed "free from conceptualization."
If this samādhi is a mundane yoga, it is called "samādhi with signs. Here, *sam* has the meaning of "equality," and *ādhī* has the meaning of "wisdom.
By means of wisdom, one contemplates that the three things [the subject, object, and act of cognition] are all empty as previously described.
Because the essence of these three things is empty, they are equal and free from all signs; when these three things are equalized and unified into one, this is called *samādhi*.
However, the samādhis of both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are all free from marks and pure. By means of this samādhi, they correctly contemplate that these three matters are equal;
because they are further without discrimination and detached from all marks, their original nature is purely white and free from all defilements, and is therefore called "pure.
If there were marks, it would refer to all worldly samādhis, which involve practicing according to their respective fruits.
Cultivating causes with the hope of attaining fruits involves having expectations that extend at most to the four dhyānas and eight samādhis; because one cannot go beyond these, it is not pure.

Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain purity, they have not yet attained all-encompassing purity, for they have not yet fully understood both the afflictive and cognitive obstacles (kleśa-āvaraṇa and jñeya-āvaraṇa); thus, their purity is not yet absolute. Furthermore, there are worldly samādhis...

There are two kinds: first, the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), and second, the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). Those with the view of annihilationism are entirely without conceptual differentiation, while those with the view of eternalism possess a slight degree of conceptual differentiation.
Regarding the attainment of results from karma: there is the accomplishment [of the cause] and the ripening [of the result]; if one attains *siddhi*, [the result is realized].
Mastery over karma is attained; one may obtain what must be experienced, yet also obtain its non-experience.
Because the mind has no intrinsic nature, the nature of the mind is free from cause and effect.
Liberation from karma—birth, life, and so forth—is like space; when the fruition of karma is accomplished and ripened, the attainment of *siddhi* results in the reversal of that very karma.
Because the mind lacks intrinsic nature, cause and effect are not separate from the karma that gives rise to birth; thus, one can be liberated from birth like space.
This refers to the worldly *sanimitta-samādhi* (meditative concentration with signs), which is called "maturation" because it is cultivated while still having karma and its expected retribution;
attaining this maturation is termed *siddhi*. If one uses this worldly concentration to dedicate toward the mind’s lack of self-nature...
Since its essence is devoid of characteristics and equal to empty space, and because empty space is boundless, its merit is likewise vast.
As for this mind that lacks intrinsic nature: "mind" is called *citta*; *citta* is like a collection adorned with various colors, thus it is named *citta*.
Because it is produced by a multitude of conditions, it has no intrinsic nature. This is...
This is the cause. Since the primary cause lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one should know that the fruit produced from it likewise lacks intrinsic nature.

Why is this so? If the cause were to have arising, the fruit could have arising; however, since the cause itself must depend on conditions to be established, it is without arising and without intrinsic nature.
One should therefore know that the arising of the fruit is unattainable. Because both cause and fruit are thus, [emptiness] is attained.
This is liberation from all karma. Some may say that if this were so, it would mean there is neither cause nor effect, falling into the view of nihilism;
however, this is not the case. It is simply that one is free from the nature of birth through karma.

Since one is free from the nature of birth through karma, there is the arising of the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena), which is equal to space. Because space is boundless, one should know that the accomplishment of the goal is likewise so.
Because the deeds of virtue that benefit sentient beings are likewise boundless and inexhaustible, they are not subject to cessation.
The above constitutes a brief explanation in verse answering the questions of Vajrapāṇi; it is further explained here in prose.

As for the phrase "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*), it is used because there are matters not yet fully exhausted from what was previously stated, and this [section] continues to clarify them; hence, it says "Furthermore."
"Listen attentively" means that because this dharma contains profound and secret essential points, he strictly exhorts them to listen with care.
Herein, five matters are briefly explained: namely, the seal (*mudrā*), color, honored rank, abiding, and samādhi. "Seal" refers to hand-seals and pledge-seals, which are here rendered as "forms.
"Color" refers to the distinctions in the divisions and segments of the honored deity’s form (the term "placed" refers to shapes such as square, circular, or half-moon).

[The category of the "horns," etc. "Venerable position" refers to the fact that within the maṇḍala, each residing direction has its own specific location (the arrangement of the positions of the sages).

"Residing" means that the image of the principal deity (*honzon*) is not merely painted; rather, through the invocation of mantras and mudrās, it arrives at its original seat, manifests majestic power, and remains there.
[This is the manifestation of awe-inspiring efficacy. "Samādhi" refers to [the practice] according to the superior, middling, or inferior [capacities].
This refers to the ritual procedures for the various states of tranquility, wrath, joy, and so forth.
It means that one requests the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) to duly assume their seals (*mudrā*) and physical forms, and to manifest their majestic power and presence while abiding in *samādhi*.

"The place where one abides" is called the "destination" (*gati*), which refers to the destination of *samādhi*. One must fully understand these five conditions of the expedient means; thus, they are called the "five."
Regarding "destinations" (*gati*), the term signifies "distinctive differentiation. Because they are differentiated by these five conditions, they are called "five.
By possessing these five, one is able to fully comprehend all maṇḍalas, both mundane and supramundane.
Furthermore, these five matters are the practices of the Buddhas of antiquity who attained supreme perfect enlightenment within the dharma-realm and the void of space.

The Buddhas have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; their practice within the dharmadhātu and empty space is such because they accomplish the conduct of a Tathāgata through identity with the essence of the dharmadhātu.

Thus, for the sake of delivering sentient beings in the realm of no-remainder (*anavaśeṣa-dhātu*) by virtue of their original vows, and for the benefit and happiness of those bodhisattvas who practice the gateway of mantras, the Buddhas have expounded this; therefore, you should receive it with earnest and attentive devotion.
Thus it was. "So be it, World-Honored One," replied Vajrapāṇi, the World-Honored One;

and having heard this, the great assembly of ten world-systems headed by Vajrapāṇi, as well as the great assembly of ten world-systems headed by Samantabhadra, all responded with one voice upon receiving the Buddha’s instruction.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "Indeed, World-Honored One, I wish and desire to hear it. For this reason, the Buddha further expounded the secret Maṇḍala-dharma. The Buddha said:
"There is the Maṇḍala of Perfect Enlightenment, known by names such as 'The Most Secret,' 'The Innermost Secret,' and 'The Source Born from the Unsurpassed Treasury of Great Compassion.
If there are other mundane or supramundane maṇḍalas that are identical to these, they are the Tathāgata’s supreme and correct [maṇḍala]."
Awakening (*bodhi*) is the ultimate teaching; yet, since this Great Compassion Treasury (*mahākaruṇā-kośa*) was already fully explained previously, why is it explained again?
What is the distinction? Although that which was previously explained is indeed secret, there is a secret within the secret, a secret within the secret of secrets.
If one does not obtain this Dharma, even if one attains mastery in the previous teachings, one will still not achieve success.
This is the most essential and secret [teaching]. If one understands this, it may be employed for all mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas;

there is nowhere it cannot enter. Regarding its ritual procedure: first, construct a square maṇḍala, the boundaries of which are formed by connecting the *karmavajra-jñāna-mudrā* (the wisdom-seal of the action-vajra) all around.
It is held that its path consists solely of the Gate of Peace (*śānta*).
Within it, one also forms the *vajra-mudrā* of the cross, performing it just as before, with the only difference being the use of a cross.

Upon this cross-shaped *vajra-mudrā*, one draws a lotus flower facing upward and half-opened, such that the cross serves as the stem of the flower. Upon the flower, one places an eight-petaled [lotus].
The flowers correspond to the positions of the five Buddhas and four Bodhisattvas mentioned previously;
one should mentally place nine points, which represent the central pedestal and a point within each of the eight petals.

These points are the realization of the Great Void and signify the meaning of attaining perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Upon these eight petals and the center, one should construct square and circular maṇḍalas.

When painting the image of the Principal Deity (Bhagavat), the Buddha's mandala is square and that of the Bodhisattvas is circular. This is intended solely for the practitioner to create for themselves and must not be shown to others.
When performing the ritual, one should sit freely at the gate of the mandala and personally perform the empowerment and other rites;
only then may one carry out all dharmas. This matter is especially secret; it should be kept in mind alone and must not be manifested outwardly.
Regarding the calligraphy, one should further visualize the twelve-syllable King of Mantras as described above upon the altar, ensuring each character is clearly distinct and placed upon the mandala.

(If asked: "Are they arranged in a continuous chain? What is their sequence? Furthermore, it is said that "placing a seed within the flower" means drawing lotus seeds, whether numbering ten or more or fewer; there is no fixed requirement.)
The Sūtra states that "flowing forth" means that once one understands this secret dharma, all mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas flow forth from within it;
this may be understood according to its corresponding meaning. Briefly, there are four types of secret methods for accomplishment:

namely, activity (which refers to the various rites to be performed at the maṇḍala from beginning to end), form (referring to the manifested divisions of the deity’s form), and siddhi (that which is the fruit accomplished).
Regarding the "Placement of Positions" (which refers to the positioning of the principal deity): understanding these four dharmas provides mastery over all methods that flow forth from them.
Furthermore, it was asked: "Do all the maṇḍalas that flow forth from this follow what is taught in their respective original scriptures? [The answer is: Yes.
"Buddha-son" (Buddhaputra) refers to him who is addressed, namely Vajrapāṇi. Furthermore, as for the four bodhisattvas, their positions are as follows:
Samantabhadra is in the Southeast (Xun), Mañjuśrī in the Southwest (Kun), Maitreya in the Northeast (Qian), and Avalokiteśvara in the Northwest (Gen).

In the assembly listed in the preceding "Origination of Conditions" (Nidāna), sometimes Gaganagañja (Chagai-zhang) replaces Avalokiteśvara, and sometimes Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin (Chu-yiqie-ewoqu) replaces Mañjuśrī; the meanings of these various substitutions differ according to the ritual practice.
One may also employ a single practice; herein, the employment of Avalokiteśvara is taken as the primary one. The above concludes the Maṇḍala of Vairocana.
Next, first to be explained are the Maṇḍalas of the Buddhas, which refers to the initial teaching on the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the Buddha Family.
In general, when constructing an altar for any other Buddha, if one is constructing an altar for Amitābha, one simply moves Amitābha into the center;
as for the Buddha Mahāvairocana, he is moved to take the position of Amitābha. If it concerns the various [deities] of the Two Vehicles...
The deities and others shall not be made to sit upon the eight-petaled lotus;
they should instead depart from it and sit upon their respective seats within the square mandala.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas on the eight petals each move slightly closer to their respective positions on the outer perimeter.
As for the Buddha Mahāvairocana, he should occupy the same location as Ratnaketu; there is no other place for him to the left or right. Nevertheless, he must remain within the Garbhadhātu-maṇḍala.
If Yama is placed within [the inner court], his original position in the outer court is merely indicated by the earth-seal (pṛthivī-mudrā) and offered there.
Regarding the method for nurturing [the deity]: this is also applied equally to the *śāntika* (pacifying) and *vaśīkaraṇa* (subjugating) rites.
As for the method of using thread, place a stake in the center and wrap the thread around it; there are two types: placing it in the air and placing it below.

Furthermore, it is said that while the master holds the thread in the center, the disciple circles around it, forming a shape like the letter "Pa" (半月). Having constructed this Maṇḍala of the Buddha Family, one should make it circular.
The maṇḍala is circular like the moon and white like the color of a conch shell. Within this circle, first draw a white lotus flower;
upon the flower, paint a triangle. Inside this triangle, create a red area, within which one should paint an image of a Buddha (ask further which Buddha).
Surround the triangle with a vajra-enclosure as shown in the diagram. Place dots around the triangle; these dots serve as markers. (Ask further.)

The outer wheel is fashioned like a light that repels enemies; it is circular, and its outer perimeter is adorned with dots (it is now uncertain whether each of these dots represents the position of a principal deity, so one should inquire further, or perhaps characters should be placed there).
"Light flows forth everywhere" means one should visualize the light flowing from within the Buddha’s body, gradually spreading outward beyond the triangle.
(The "Mantra Lord" refers to the Principal Deity; light flows forth from every part of his body. This is within the aforementioned Great Mandala.
There is also a triangular seal (*tri-kona-mudrā*), which differs from the application of this [previous one].

The former is merely a seal; here, one places either a Buddha or a seal, completing the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) therein. (Regarding those drawn as both mundane and supramundane: these may likewise be called "existent.

It is said that there are immeasurable mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas; listen well as they are about to be explained. This should be understood as being placed above, for it is the initial altar born of compassion. Next is the Lotus Family (*padma-kula*). (This phrase belongs to the aforementioned.)
This is merely the secret maṇḍala. If performing śāntika and other rites, the square, circular, red, white, and celestial [maṇḍalas] and so forth each follow their respective originals.
Although one constructs a circular maṇḍala, the seats of the principal deities and others may be either square or circular, each according to its ancient tradition.
When constructing a square maṇḍala, draw a conch shell within it, and upon the conch shell, a lotus flower.
Upon a lotus is a vajra; upon the vajra is another lotus. Upon the flower, one should place the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, or alternatively, install a mudrā or a syllable.
Upon all the mudrās, one should install seed-syllables (bīja-akṣara), namely on the conch, the vajra, and the flowers.
In the next courtyard, one should install Mahāsthāmaprāpta and others, making light pervade everywhere; do not give rise to doubt.
The doubts and hesitations are also skillfully established by means of their fundamental seeds and serve as the seed-syllables.
In the empty space, one should place seven white auspicious ones (*śrīvatsa*), each having two messengers (*dūta*). This scripture merely mentions them briefly;

they are fully recorded in the separate ritual methods of the Avalokiteśvara section, which should be consulted in detail elsewhere. (Further inquiry: [Regarding] the Consort (*vidyā*) and the Mistress of Wealth (*vasudhārā*).
These are those who can bestow [blessings] with mastery upon those who seek them, as well as Mahāsthāmaprāpta and others, who act according to the Dharma.
They are lords who have attained mastery and hold their characteristic seals;

they should be depicted with exquisite detail, such as Hayagrīva within a triangular mandala, drawn according to the ritual rules while abiding in the triangle. As for the other deities, each likewise has [their own].
The distinctions of color, shape, and so forth—including square, circular, semi-circular, triangular, and other forms—are all as described in the extensive version.

What was previously stated regarding the necessity of comprehending the five matters refers precisely to this: color, shape, the seal (*mudrā*), the principal deity (*bimba*), and the position. (As it says:

"When painting that deity, what colors and images should be used, and each has its respective seal. The former, the Great Compassion Treasury Birth (*Mahākāruṇagarbhodbhava*), was the general assembly maṇḍala; now, within this [context], it follows the three [specific types].
Each family has its own distinct [mandala] as follows: within this Lotus Family mandala, the central womb (garbha) is the Auspicious Mandala, with Avalokiteśvara as its presiding lord.
Outside the womb, a space is left vacant; beyond this vacant space is the second seating area, where all the deities of the Avalokiteśvara family are installed.
All other matters are exactly as in the method for constructing a great mandala. In that vacant space, one should also install the Buddhas of the Ten Directions.
The third seating position is likewise occupied by the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭakāyika*), which may be understood according to the preceding description.
Within the triangle, there is a radiance like that of the rising sun—meaning it is reddish-yellow like the sun when first appearing.
Those situated at the side of the Vidyārāja are at the side of Mahāsthāmaprāpta. If one constructs the Hayagrīva Maṇḍala, they should be placed within the triangle.
The three outer maṇḍalas should likewise all be made triangular. When doing this, why?
Kṛṣṇa is moved to the center, and Avalokiteśvara is shifted to take the place of Mahāsthāmaprāpta; the remaining retinue surrounds him.
All other [arrangements] are interchanged, which can be understood through one's own discernment. Next, construct the second maṇḍala.
"Rā" refers to the Lotus Family (*padmakula*), where the lotus is the first and the vajra is the second family;
"I shall now proclaim" means it is well-spoken. It is not said before or after, but is taught according to sequence.
The mandala is made square on all sides, surrounded by vajras, with the boundary-marks formed by three-pronged [vajras].
Within the enclosure of the enclosure, in the center, place a yellow lotus; upon the flower is a flask, white as the color of the moon.

It may be encircled by a vajra or encircled by other substances (meaning that according to the mudrā of that particular deity, one proceeds to make it the center and likewise encircles it with that same mudrā).
Above that flask is a great wind, which is crescent-shaped and has the appearance of black clouds (like rain).
At that time, clouds gather and hang low in blackness; beneath them, the forms appear like banners, their shapes moving and surging as if driven by a great wind.
That crescent moon is like a fierce flame of fire, forming a triangle. Its three corners are also encircled by vajras.
Within the triangle, it is red like the color of the rising sun; in its center is placed a lotus, which is intensely red like the great flames at the end of a kalpa.
Regarding the color (meaning a deep, rich red, or perhaps reddish-black), paint a vajra upon a lotus (meaning either the form of the principal deity, the five-pronged mudrā, or a syllable).
From that vajra, various tongues of flame stream forth. If the form is painted, place the seed-syllable upon the heart; this refers to the syllable HŪṂ.
If the mudrā is painted, place the syllable upon the mudrā. One should visualize the syllable HŪṂ and recite it while performing the empowerment.
"This is your maṇḍala," because the Buddha spoke this directly to Vajrapāṇi, he declared, "This is your maṇḍala.
All Buddhas of antiquity have spoken thus, and I now speak likewise. Regarding the various vidyārājas each sitting according to their respective categories and forms:
this refers to the assembly of the Vajramātṛs, the Vajrasūcī, the Vajrapāśa, and so forth.

The numerous vajra retinues each follow the distinctions of their respective principal deities' forms and colors—either by being depicted in form, or by forming mudrās, or by placing seed-syllables (*bīja-akṣara*).
Each follows its own ritual sequence in accordance with the teachings, for the sake of accomplishing the sublime *siddhi*.
According to this, Vajrapāṇi constitutes the central womb (*garbha*), while the various classes [of deities] constitute the second enclosure (*maṇḍala*). All of these have been explained.

The central matrix is transformed into the immeasurable mandala. Regarding what was previously mentioned as being placed on the right and what was subsequently mentioned as being placed on the left, the distinction between right and left is determined according to the direction of the opened gate. Furthermore, I have previously explained the various names of the many Vajras;
"sovereign" (*īśvara*) refers to attaining mastery over the Vajra. Moreover, this explains that I hold the Vajra myself.

These are: Gaganāmala-vajra, Vajracakra, Vajradaṃṣṭra, and Surata.

Vajra (meaning "wondrous abiding," which refers to dwelling together in peace); Vajra of Renowned Great Portion (meaning the portion of the great, which is the essential nature of sentient beings with the great mind);

Śāntavajra (the meaning of "tranquil" is like the meaning of *nirvāṇa*); Mahāvajra (the name); Nīlavajra; Padmavajra; Viśālākṣavajra; and Dhṛtisuvarṇavajra.
Dharmavajra-vajra (named simply after the single vajra), Vajra-abiding-in-non-conceptuality, Vajra-boundless-walking-in-vajra-space—these and others are listed by name;

each is placed in its own location within the great maṇḍala. Maṇḍalas such as these, whether square or circular, follow the preceding [rules] regarding their colors and shapes, and are established accordingly.
They are arranged according to their names in sequence, revolving again and again. White and yellow.
Regarding the colors—red, black, and so forth—they follow the sequence of the text: first white, then yellow, then red, then black;

They are to be fashioned according to their respective original types of shape and color. These vajras are as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields and are listed at the beginning.
It should be understood that among these assemblies, there may be mutual appearances and absences—meaning that what exists here may not exist there.

Furthermore, regarding the mudrās held by these Vajras: they may be three-pronged, single-pronged (which refers to a needle; following the previous sequence, one first forms the three-pronged and then proceeds in rotation), or double-headed.
These two heads constitute the five-pronged [vajra]. This mudrā is used to form four sickles all around, as follows:
Among the four vajras, there is one that resembles a five-pronged [vajra] but does not open; it may be a garland, or it may hold a vajra-garland.
Each of these vajras has its own name as the mantra; specifically, the most excellent syllable within that name serves as the seed-syllable (bīja).
One should place the *hūṃ*, along with the specific or general syllables, upon the heart.
Regarding the hand gestures (*mudrā*), the five-pronged golden vajra seal is used universally.
In the Maṇḍala of Acala, both wind and fire are present; "wind" refers to the crescent moon and "fire" refers to the triangle.
This means that within a crescent-shaped altar, a triangle is drawn, and within that triangle, Acala is depicted. As for his being in the *Nairṛti* direction, it is because he is Vairocana.
In the southwest, one should perform the rite; upon his heart, one should place the seed-syllable, and the three corners should be encircled by a sword.

Alternatively, regarding the "Victorious One of the Three Times," "different" refers to his location in the direction of wind (the northwest), which makes him distinct; otherwise, he is identical to Acala. In the three locations, [one should use] gold.

The Vajraprākāra (Vajra-enclosure) is also within the half-moon; by means of the primary Vajraprākāra—meaning the mudrā held [in the hand] is positioned within the half-moon—at the three locations, which refers to either the form, the mudrā, or the syllable.

However, if this Maṇḍala of Acala is constructed separately, Acala is in the center, Vairocana is in the middle court, and the other Vajra-retinue deities surround the perimeter in the eastern direction.

The four sides are of vajra-color, encircled by a vajra boundary; this is the most supreme.

Upon the vajra, place a lotus; the lotus is yellow. Upon the flower, place an alms-bowl (*pātra*).

Furthermore, for the Most Victorious Honored One who transcends all honored ones, the lotus is the seal (*mudrā*). For the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa of Immeasurable Sound, one should visualize it according to its color-class—meaning, as previously explained, visualizing the color-class such as white, yellow, red, and so forth.

these seals are used for the purposes of the Dharma-equality, consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and the accomplishment of ritual substances, while for rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), they are applied accordingly.
