The consort Aparājitā holds the lotus mudrā—meaning one pinches the lotus with the empty-space and wind fingers while extending the other fingers—and she holds it before her heart. As for the various deities...

Regarding those who possess mudrās, they should be placed according to the textual descriptions; if no description is provided, one should take the principal mudrā of their respective family and place it, following the same principle as for seed-syllables (*bīja*).

For the Unconquerable King (*Ajita-rāja*), one forms the mouth-mudrā (*mukha-mudrā*) upon a black lotus, which means drawing an angry face with both fangs protruding upward. These positions for the various Buddhas are [established] with Śākyamuni as the standard.

In the central [hall], the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa and others are arranged in the second court; if one selects any single principal deity from among them to serve as the presiding lord of the maṇḍala, then Śākyamuni is moved to the exterior, and all other cases may be understood by this same principle.
Next, the *Suddhāvāsadeva-mudrā-sūtra* states: "The practitioner of the Pure Realm takes meditative concentration as its flavor and purity as its practice.

The mudrās are now listed in sequence: The *Cintā-hasta* (Thinking Hand)—meaning slightly touching the ground with the water finger (ring finger), pointing toward the palm, the other three fingers extended like the prongs of a trident, tilting the head, and bending the hand inward so that the index finger points toward the cheek.
The *Kalyāṇa-hasta* (Good Hand)—meaning the sense of being excellent; this refers to the hand bestowing fearlessness, which is performed with the left hand, though the right may also be used.

The Laughing Hand (meaning: turn the hand of reflection toward the front of the heart, keeping the three fingers pointing upward); the Flower Hand (using the wind and space fingers to pinch a flower while extending the three [other] fingers;

these three fingers may be spread with the palm facing upward, or extended vertically—either is acceptable); the Space-Facing Hand (meaning: tilt the right hand with fingers splayed and held in mid-air).
These deities may perform acts such as laughing, reflecting, or granting boons, all of which are permissible (the rules for their depiction mean they should be painted according to these methods).
Next, for the Earth Goddess mudrā: form a circular white jewel-vessel (*ratnaghaṭa*) in which various jewels, grains, flowers, fruits, and so forth are inserted;
adorn it and encircle it with a vajra. Next, for the Fire God (*Agni*) invocation mudrā:

extend the right hand sideways, slightly bend the third joint of the index finger (*tarjanī*), and bend the upper joint of the middle finger (*madhyamā*) toward the palm, as if first straightening it and then bending it.
This is the invocation; if one first bows and then extends [the ritual], it is the dismissal.
He is surrounded by the great ṛṣis—namely, the ṛṣis Kāśyapa, Gautama, and so forth—all of whom should be painted in succession within the fire-courtyard.
The fire-courtyard is the triangular mandala; its color is red, and thus it is called the "Red Courtyard. Its...
The mudrā is as described by the five classes of ṛṣis who possess the supernatural powers; it is the *veda-mudrā*. This is a secret notation for those who practice the *brahmacarya*.
When one who recites the Vedas sees this hand gesture, they will know which treatise or which school it belongs to.

As for the Ṛṣi Gautama: while traveling through the void, he had two drops of semen that fell and defiled the earth. From the earth grew sugarcane, which was scorched by the sun, giving birth to two sons who became the kings of the Śakras.
Makhanā (this refers to one who sat in meditation while ants built a mound over his entire body; fearing they might be harmed, he entered meditative absorption once more).
Khecarṣi (a mountain name; he was named after the location). Vasiṣṭha ṛṣi (this is the one formerly called the Rishi Vasu). Aṅgiras (this means "body sweat";
this ṛṣi was not born from a womb but was born from sweat, hence he received this name). Yama, King of the South, shall act.
In the wind mandala, draw the seal of Buta (Butara). [If the seals are such that one corner of the mandala faces the practitioner and one corner faces outward, or otherwise as convenient.
To the right of the King, draw the Queen of Wrath; her seal is a bell, which she holds in her hand if depicted in bodily form.
To the left, draw the Queen of Darkness; her seal is a banner.
This is the banner (in Sanskrit, *ketu*, which also means "flag"). Maheśvara’s wrathful form performs the *śūla-mudrā*;
this is the *śūla*. The consort of Maheśvara’s son performs the *śakti-mudrā*;
this is the *śakti*. This is the vidyā of Mahābrahmā-deva-rāja.
The Consort forms the Lotus Mudrā, which signifies an unopened lotus.
Nārāyaṇa forms the Wheel Mudrā. The Seven Mothers likewise all use the Mustard Seed (Mūlaka) Mudrā (this is it).
Kubera forms the Skull Mudrā (at the crown of the head). [In the Vīra...]

"O Śramaṇa, this is the skull, which is bone. [He] holds it with the "smiling hand" gesture (meaning: bend the water and earth fingers into the palm while extending the remaining three fingers in the shape of a smiling hand, holding the cranial bone like one holds an alms bowl).
The retinue of the Seven Mothers consists of crows, vultures, foxes, and *vāśī* birds (resembling small owls or crows, yellowish-brown in color with yellow beaks;
they belong to the class of hawks and possess a secret method of concealing their bodies). These all surround the Seven Mothers within the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
(All the classes of King Yama reside within the wind-wheel. If one holds a flower, one may also obtain these birds and so forth, and likewise hold the mantras of the Seven Mothers;
for each of these there are their own respective methods of recitation, but they are included here because they enter this maṇḍala assembly.
(As an adornment: In the direction of Nairṛti, one forms the seal of the great sword, [dedicated to] Nārāyaṇa.
The Deva is also called the Wheel Seal (as above). Kumāra is called the Śakti Seal [the son of Maheśvara].
The Nanda Dragon Brothers perform the Cloud Seal (within the clouds there are lightning and water forms;
they are both situated at the edge of the mandala gate). King Śaṅkara performs the Trident Seal.
Śaṅkara’s consort forms the *pātrī* (bowl) mudrā;
Candradeva forms the white flask together with the lotus mudrā;
Sūryadeva forms the chariot mudrā within a golden wheel (which is the square altar); and Jayā-Vijayā form the bow.
The seal [is also] placed in the center of the wheel in the [western] direction; there must be an arrow beside the bow. The Wind Deity forms the wind-banner seal;
Sarasvatī forms the lute seal; Varuṇa, the Nāga, forms the noose seal (as before).
One should construct a circular maṇḍala and surround it with the fundamental seed-syllables (meaning that the syllables should be at the heart, with the seal).
[Encircle it. I shall now inform the Vajradhara. To the right: these are brief indications of the seal-explanations (*mudrā-vidhi*).
If one were to elaborate upon them, they are fully contained within the ritual manuals (*dharmaparyāya*), namely the specific practice methods for each respective mantra.
This concludes the section on the Śākya family.
The following clarifies the Maṇḍala of the Bodhisattvas (this is the second tier of the Great Maṇḍala, consisting of the positions of the various Bodhisattvas).
The Maṇḍala of Mañjuśrī is square and surrounded by vajras as previously described; within this, a triangular fire is also fashioned.
The "emergence" refers to the triangle. Within the triangle, one draws a blue lotus;
the "mantra syllables" taken therein are the seed-syllables (*bīja*).

Reciting them, one visualizes them pervading the interior and places them within it (it is not only placed within, but is also placed along the four sides). This refers to the boundary lines along the interior of the triangle.
One should surround the perimeter of the path with small blue lotuses; this is the seal (mudrā) of the Great Blue Lotus.

The reason for forming this seal is to identify the meaning, purpose, and so forth of this honored one’s dharma-gate. Therefore, one should observe each according to its shape and color to recognize the secret intention.
One takes the seed-syllable according to the ritual method, and that seed-syllable [is the placement of this syllable as the seed]. It...
In the center, one forms these mudrās in their respective order; these are the mudrās of the "Vigorous Heroes" (*vīra*), which are the *pūrṇa* [mudrās].

That is to say, one performs them according to the ritual sequence, such as the lotus seed-syllable (*bīja*) and so forth. One should recognize their secret significance by observing their shapes and colors.
The youth *Jālinīprabha* forms the hook-mudrā (*aṅkuśa-mudrā*); the youth *Ratnamukuṭa* holds a jewel as his mudrā; and the youth *Vimalaprabha* holds an unopened flower.

The practitioner who recites [the mantra] should know that messenger according to what is appropriate. Regarding the performance of that mudrā through correspondence with the Dharma:
a young girl or a wise maiden is identical to Mañjuśrī; she may also be called "Endowed with Virtue" (Guṇavatī) or Kaitasini.
(The *mahā-khaḍga* is the seal. *Kṣudra-gaṇeśvara* (the *śūla* is the seal). The multi-colored messenger (*citrapaṭa-dūta*) uses a staff as his seal. Dharaṇīmati uses a banner (*dhvaja*) as his seal.

The summoning messenger uses a hook (*aṅkuśa*) as his seal. (The above are all female messengers. All the messengers who carry out the teachings universally form the small-knife seal (*kṣudra-khaḍga-mudrā*).

(As in the sūtra and the diagrams, this knife is shaped like a saw-toothed blade. [Note: "small knife" is not a literal translation. ) All that has been described above is performed within a square maṇḍala.
One forms the mudrā encircled by blue lotuses; the above constitutes the retinue of the Mañjuśrī division in the eastern direction.

If Mañjuśrī is the central seed-syllable (garbha), the other bodhisattvas form the second layer, and the eight classes [of deities] form the third layer; others are to be understood by extension from this.
In the south, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin uses the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) as his seal;
he also forms a four-sided vajra wheel, within which a triangular mandala (known as the fire-wheel) is made.
Inside the triangle, one draws a wish-fulfilling jewel surrounded by his retinue. All the bodhisattvas below this one are likewise situated here.
One should know that the retinue should surround [the central figure]; now the characteristics of those mudrās, the retinue, shall be explained in detail.
Within that [mandala], one should perform the drawing of the mudrās according to their sequence;

this is the correct method. In that text, there is this word indicating [the deity] as follows: the Bodhisattva Duryodhana (i.e., *Kārttikeya*). His mudrā is the Vajra-mudrā, which is said as follows:
(Ōshuku): The Vase-born Vajra is depicted making the vase gesture, with one prong of a vajra inserted into the vase so that half of it remains within.
The Bodhisattva Abhayadatta performs the *abhaya-mudrā* (the gesture of fearlessness; as described in the *Yogatantra*, this is the seal of Śākyamuni).

The Bodhisattva Durgatipariśodhana is painted with his hand raised (*utkṣipta-hasta*)—that is, the hand is extended with the palm facing upward, lifted from below toward the top. The Bodhisattva Citta-viśuddhi performs the *karuṇā-mudrā* placed at the heart—that is, the thumb and ring finger are joined in the water-and-space gesture.

When the mind is focused on others, extend all [fingers] outward (the thumb and index finger are brought toward the heart). The Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā performs the Flower-Holding Mudrā (join the thumb and ring finger like holding a flower;

extend the remaining fingers outward and hold them upright). The Bodhisattva Karuṇāmaya (bend the middle finger toward the front of the heart; extend all other fingers outward)—this is the name of this Bodhisattva as spoken by the Wise One.

The Bodhisattva Tāpana-nivāraṇa performs the Wish-Fulfilling Hand Mudrā (extend the fingers with the palm facing upward, with nectar-water flowing downward; "fingers" refers to all the fingers). Not [so].

The Bodhisattva Cintamanicakra (思議具慧者) performs the gesture of contemplation (with hands identical to those of the Bodhisattva Cintāmaṇicakra, as previously described for the seal of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika gods).
Possessing inconceivable wisdom, both [hands] form square altars upon which lotus flowers are placed (meaning that these hands and so forth are to be depicted).
These are all the retinues of Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; the remaining meanings are as explained in the section on Mañjuśrī.
The Seal of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva of the North (the Great Indra-wheel): Within a vajra-wheel, one creates a ground adorned with jewels (which means first placing a seat therein).
Upon this ground, one draws a lotus flower of various colors; atop the flower, one erects a banner (*dhvaja*), and at the top of the banner, one places a jewel.
One does not draw the actual form [of the deity], but merely draws the banner. If one performs this seal, it is of the highest excellence; this is its form.
This is the mark; this teaching is called the "Supreme Form," which is a term of praise. If one forms this seal (*mudrā*), it is the most victorious, supreme, and exquisite among all seals.
One should diligently draw the seal therein. This Bodhisattva has immeasurable retinues;
now, for the sake of brevity, I shall briefly describe their leaders as follows. [The seal of] the Bodhisattva Ratnakara is three-pronged gold.
The *Gang* (Vajra) is placed upon the jewel. (It is simply the mudrā made upon the jeweled ground; if one draws the form, it is likewise seated upon a lotus, according to the method of Kṣitigarbha.
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi forms a single-pronged vajra and places this vajra upon the jewel. The Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara forms a double-headed vajra and places it upon the jewel.
(Within the single prong, there is the form of five prongs, as in the previous mudrā. This is the Jewel-Seal-Hand (*Ratnamudrāhasta*).
The Bodhisattva Seal forms a five-pronged vajra placed upon a jewel (which is the vajra of the five Buddhas);
the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati forms a ten-pronged vajra (which is the karma-vajra), also placed upon a jewel;
all those on the right are likewise installed within that maṇḍala.
In each of the square wheels, one should create a jeweled ground; upon this ground are placed jewels, and atop the jewels are seals.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha of the western direction is the presiding lord of the western division within the Mañjuśrī assembly.

He forms a circular maṇḍala that is made exceedingly bright, pure, and white, sitting upon a white lotus. In his hand he holds a sword; if one does not depict the form of the Bodhisattva, [one should instead draw the seal].
One merely draws a sword; that sword is extremely sharp, like frost (this means it is likewise firm and keen). It is further made solid by surrounding it with seed-syllables.
The wise person seeds it with their own seed-syllable, which is the installation of the fundamental seed-syllable.
This is also surrounded by the fundamental [syllable], which is in turn encircled by a wheel. This fundamental element is the syllable itself.
Next, the mudrās of the retinue are listed. Regarding the forms of the Bodhisattvas' mudrās, they are as taught; that is, all are to be performed according to the instructions and the Dharma.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Ākāśamala is the wheel (which is the four-pronged vajra-wheel); it is placed within the wind mandala, and the wheel itself also encircles it.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Ākāśamati is the conch shell (which is the half-moon mandala); it is placed within the wind mandala. Pure...
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati draws the white lotus mudrā upon the wind-maṇḍala;
the Bodhisattva Gati-prajñā places a conch within the wind-circle, and within the conch is inserted a blue lotus;
the Bodhisattva Vihāra-prajñā draws a blue lotus upon the wind-circle, and upon the flower is placed a vajra. Thus, in this Great Maṇḍala of the Mahākaruṇā-garbha, Mañjuśrī...

In each assembly, there are four bodhisattvas; one bodhisattva serves as the presiding lord and is placed in the central altar, while the others are arranged according to their respective directions in the second court.
In the third court, the eight classes of supernatural beings (*aṣṭakulika*) are placed.

If this refers to the second court within the Great Compassion [Maṇḍala], even if Avalokiteśvara is taken as the head of that division, the Vajra family, the Buddha-Usnīṣas, and so forth [are likewise included].
These are all arranged according to their respective directions to form the second court. In the third court, the eight classes of spirits (*aṣṭau devanikāyāḥ*) are placed;
it is not necessary to place the Bodhisattvas of the Mañjuśrī assembly. As for the Śākyamuni assembly, it is as described above (ask further about this).
This teaching is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (This matter should be further questioned and examined. △
Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Entering the Secret Maṇḍala.
Regarding the "Chapter on Entering the Secret Maṇḍala," it refers to the secret treasury of the body, speech, and mind of all Buddhas;
because only the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets is able to know it, the Buddha spoke to him once again. Now, as for this Vajradhara...
This is the emanation-body of Vairocana, manifested for the purpose of elucidating this profound and secret Dharma.
There is no one capable of posing questions regarding this Dharma; it can only be understood through the mutual inquiry between Buddhas.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Accumulations" in the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, after the Buddha had entered samādhi, syllables emerged from within his body.
The forms and seals manifest as the bodies of the various Honored Ones of the Original Vows, each emerging from their respective directions to perform Buddha-works.
This is what is called the "Great Cause and Condition" for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Having performed these acts, they again enter the body of the Tathāgata.
At that time, a voice inquired about the Dharma from within the void, asking the Buddha for his one hundred and eight names: "What is meant by 'Buddha'? What is meant by 'Samyaksaṃbuddha'?"
From the knowledge of equality up to the questions addressed to the sixteen great bodhisattvas, as well as the mantras and mudrās, were explained in detail as previously described.
At that time, the Buddha himself uttered this praise: "Excellent, excellent! You are able to ask about such matters," and he answered according to each question.
Then the great assembly attained what they had never experienced before and thought to themselves: "Now we ask the Buddha concerning the Buddha’s own body."
Just as illusory phenomena, though without action or birth, can accomplish the work of a Buddha, so too is this Vajradhara:
he arises from the Buddha’s seal of vajra-wisdom, and again, by holding the Tathāgata’s seal of vajra-wisdom, he is able to pose questions to which the Buddha provides answers.
Fearing that others might not believe it, had he asked and spoken for himself, it would not have been so.
Because he is worthy of the highest respect, he inquires about the Buddha-body by means of the Buddha-body.

Furthermore, the reason he is named Vajrapāṇi is that he is able to uphold the secret body, secret speech, and secret mind of the Tathāgata; therefore, he is called the Holder of the Vajra-Wisdom Seal.
At that time, the World-Honored One further proclaimed the method for entering the secret maṇḍala.
Having already answered Vajrapāṇi regarding the secret maṇṍala, but not yet having clarified the method for entering it, he next proclaimed this:
"The practitioner who recites mantras, the wise one, and the mantra-holder should study the secret maṇḍala everywhere (that is, in all places)."
One must understand this: the "Wisdom Secret Mandala" (wherein "wisdom" means thorough penetration) is so named because it is free from all doubt and obstruction;

thus it is called the "Wisdom [Mandala]. The Wisdom [Mandala] completely incinerates all sins. A disciple who maintains and recites the Dharma in this manner is one who has attained accomplishment—that is, an *ācārya*.
One should study it universally; however, only a Buddha and a Buddha can know and study it universally.
Only one who possesses all these virtues regarding all dharmas may be considered a teacher. Now, in this final age, such a person is difficult to find;

how then could there be a Dharma-transmitting master? Nevertheless, although an ācārya has not yet attained the level of a Buddha and must therefore know everything exhaustively, he must clearly understand, point by point, the essential tenets, the sequence, and the ritual applications of this sūtra, as well as remain in accord with what this sūtra teaches.
That is to say, one should thoroughly understand those dharmas required for the maṇḍala, and should practice the yoga of conduct;

having clearly discerned the various faculties of sentient beings— whether sharp or dull, obstructed or unobstructed— as well as the categories of the *vidyā-mantra*, body, and seals (*mudrā*) of the *iṣṭadevatā*,
one may then transmit the Dharma and perform the rite of initiation into the secret maṇḍala for disciples.
Because these essential teachings of the Buddhas are now extremely profound and difficult to understand, they are collectively guarded and not proclaimed recklessly;
this core principle has been kept silent for a long time and not expounded hastily.

If teachers in the final age cannot discern demonic activities or the sequential stages of entering the Path, yet teach people erroneously, they will cause a mismatch with the students' capacities and lead others astray; therefore, [this must be done].
The so-called "wise one" is precisely this person of universal learning (*sarva-śikṣita*).

Because they are able to know what should and should not be given, what should and should not be entered, and various other such matters, they are called "wise. If one is not proficient in skillful means (*upāya*), despite having much to say, one cannot cause others to establish unsurpassed roots of goodness (*anuttara-kuśala-mūla*) or to swiftly enter into all suchness (*tathatā*).
To come to this stage and further invite extremely great obstructing dharmas that harm oneself and others—how can such a person be called a wise one?
Disciple, "the Dharma is thus" means entering the maṇḍala according to the Dharma and performing the ritual procedures.
As for the burning away of the disciple’s transgressions: it is like one who, from beginningless time, has possessed immeasurable and boundless, profound and deep obstructions.
If these are not removed, the vessel of the body is impure; because obstructions still remain, it is inappropriate to preach to them the path fully perfected by all Tathāgatas.
This is just as it is inappropriate to confer the precepts upon those with the thirteen impediments and so forth, as in the case of the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, regarding the burning away of that life-force so that it does not arise again and reducing it to ashes:
how could one now use the fire of the mundane world to incinerate that body and cause the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) to cease, thereby turning it to ash?
Rather, there is here a sublime skillful means—the great wisdom-fire—which incinerates that body of karma and afflictions so that it may not arise again for all sentient beings.
All [beings] obtain growth through the continuous accumulation of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), such that the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) never ceases; therefore, it is called "life.
Now, one burns these so that they are exhausted without remainder. Karma and afflictions serve as the fuel, and skillful means-wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) serves as the fire.
By means of these causes and conditions, [the fuel] is exhausted without remainder. Once this fuel is spent, the remedial method itself is also discarded.
This means that "burning" is the literal meaning of the syllable; one should take the syllable *A* as the body of the disciple and cause it to pervade his entire being with the syllable *A*.
Next, one adds the syllable *Ra* above it; the syllable *Ra* is the fire of great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*), and by means of this wisdom—
The syllable *ra* incinerates that mine of the true gold of bodhicitta so that no impurities remain;
thus, it burns the syllable *a*. Now, having been incinerated, is it like the extinction and ashes of the two vehicles, from which there is no further arising?
It is not so. Once the fuel of all impurities has been exhausted, there is a wondrous arising, which is called "purity."
The bodhicitta truly arises; this arising is itself the pure nature, the seed of the Tathāgata.
By what skillful means does the Master cause these ashes to sprout again with wondrous shoots? That which was burned away is like ash, yet it arises once more.
Regarding the "syllable that burns the syllable," it refers to visualizing the syllable *ĀḤ* as being identical to the disciple within the square mandala.
Visualize the syllable *raṃ* in the center and burn it; because it is burned, it becomes one with the body. The body is identical to the syllable *a*, which is then burned by the syllable *raṃ*.
All afflictions and sins are eliminated, and even the physical form is removed until the essence is identical to the golden wheel—this refers to the *va*-gate.
One should visualize a brilliant orb upon the heart and place [the syllable] within that brilliant orb.
From this syllable *vaṃ*, the water wheel arises; it is like white milk that is poured forth.
By this expedient means, the seed of the Buddha—the pure bodhicitta—is further produced.

This pure body is born free from internal or external defilements, like gold refined a hundred times and further polished until it may be fashioned into vessels according to their use. One should know that fire then moves.
At that time, it is together with the wind; the "wind-wheel" (vāyu-cakra) is the meaning of the syllable *ha*.
Furthermore, when a dot (*bindu*) is placed above the syllable *va*, this dot is the "gate of the letter *kṣa*" which is the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*).

The subtle and wondrous water of the Dharma pours from emptiness to purify the vessel of the mind; one should know that this thus possesses the meanings of the five syllables: earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
However, all of these are the secret meanings of the Tathāgata and are not merely as they appear in the text; one should contemplate them well.
Once the practitioner has attained such a pervasive purity and stainlessness, their life-span is restored and they become entirely stainless.
Furthermore, so that this mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) may be made firm, there is yet another expedient means for the sake of this mind-made body.
By placing twelve syllables, they correspond again to the twelve links of dependent origination—namely, the phrases of the twelve links.
This refers to the previously mentioned twelve-syllable King of Mantras, which should be used to pervade the entire body.

First, there are four syllables to be placed in the upper portion, meaning from the crown of the head down to the forehead. One syllable is at the crown of the head, the syllable *Ākāśa*; two syllables are in [the forehead].
The syllable *E* is located on the nape of the neck; it is auspicious to begin from the eyes according to the original nature.
Next, there are four syllables in the middle portion, namely: two on the shoulders and one each on the heart and the throat. Next, there are four syllables in the lower portion, namely:
one above the navel, one on the waist, one on the thigh, and one below the foot; however, both the thighs and the feet possess [syllables].
Second, by placing [the seed syllable] at only one foot, both feet are encompassed;
one should know that these twelve bases (*āyatana*) likewise encompass all other individual parts of the body, just as the word "two ears" encompasses the two eyes and so forth.
Regarding the aforementioned syllables, one should take the first syllable from the King of Mantras and arrange them in sequence downward.
However, there are three ways to perform this expedient means: first, the master lays it out himself; second, he uses it to construct a maṇḍala (further inquiry:
how does one begin laying out the syllables?); third, he applies it to the body of the disciple—this is the secret empowerment of yoga.
Having performed it in this manner, one is immediately able to become a vessel for the Dharma; therefore, it is said that "one makes them into a vessel. Thus it is.
Having performed [this], one accomplishes the *samaya*. That which is called *samaya* has the meaning of "equality.
This means that we are equal to the Buddha and the Buddha is equal to us; there is no duality and no division, for all are ultimately equal.
The *ācārya* is equal to the Buddha, and the Buddha is equal to the disciple. This disciple is not merely equal...
Regarding all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as all Bodhisattvas, all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
and the multitudes of celestial seers and spirits of the world— if one is equal toward all such beings,
this is precisely the body of Vairocana Buddha; therefore, it is said that he is "equal to all worlds."
"Same and compliant" also means that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* does not contradict the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); one should understand it in this way.
It is equivalent to being the same as all Buddhas; this is the interpretation of the samaya.

Just as those who have entered the secret maṇḍala and attained mastery over all the teachings of the various maṇḍalas understand them in this way, so too do I understand this samaya-secret maṇḍala. By entering the various maṇḍalas within all the teachings, one attains mastery;
even without entering them, one attains mastery and can encompass them, just like us who maintain the recitation.
(This means that the self and that practitioner are not different, but are unified as one; this is called the *samaya*). For the reciter, being non-different from the *samaya* is termed "explaining";

"explaining" has the sense of understanding and the sense of knowing. If one understands this, entering the secret maṇḍala through skillful means is equivalent to universally entering all maṇḍalas. This disciple thereby universally enters all [maṇḍalas] together.
Because of the maṇḍala, one immediately attains mastery and practices all dharma-gates without any hindrance.
Since the Buddha explains the name "samaya" as the ultimate equality of all dharmas, it is called the "Exposition of the Name Samaya."

Just as at the beginning of the sutra there are the various teachings such as entering the Maṇḍala of the Womb of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇagarbha*), these teachings are taken as the essential methods;
they are not explained earlier but are explained here. If one does not understand this, the maṇḍalas constructed above will ultimately fail to be accomplished.
This is why the sequence is interchanged, with the preceding and succeeding parts not following one another in a linear progression.
Is it that the Buddha has anything he begrudges? It is simply because those who wish to enter the True Dharma must learn by relying upon a teacher.

Just as the Buddha, in the *Śrāvaka-sūtras*, rebuked those who dwell like thieves, saying: "Having obtained a full complement of preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and instructors (*ācārya*), and having received the precepts according to the Dharma, one should joyfully practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Why do you dwell like a thief? Thus, in this final age...

The student is likewise: if they do not strive to draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to inquire about and receive the essential points of the Dharma, but instead take themselves as their own teacher and hope to achieve the sovereign activities of a Tathāgata;
or if they merely open the texts and wish to act upon them immediately, hoping to achieve success—there is no principle by which such success can be attained.
Not only do they harm themselves, but because they seek fame and profit, they falsely assume the role of a teacher to others.
Since one has already violated the Dharma oneself, how can one hope to establish unsurpassed roots of goodness in others? There is no such reason for this, as it is ineffective;
moreover, it invites the conditions for slandering and destroying the Dharma, thereby constituting the karma of an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
How could a person who has committed an immediate retribution ever achieve the sublime fruits of benefiting both self and others? Therefore, a practitioner must strive to seek clarity.

The Master consulted him on each point until the subtle meaning was fully understood and made clear. Having first established himself, he became capable of establishing others in unsurpassed roots of goodness.

Just as in the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, by accomplishing the five dharmas one personally realizes the fivefold body of the Dharma (pañcadharmakāya) and can also bring about the fivefold body of the Dharma for others;
having attained freedom from reliance, he reached the rank of a Teacher. At that time, he...
One may transmit the Dharma to benefit others; however, if it is otherwise, one must take care not to recklessly wield a sharp tool and wound one's own hand.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "To preach the Dharma with a mistaken mechanism for the sake of humans and devas is to become their enemy.

It is just like this when one does not first study the treasury of Vidyādhara-yoga thoroughly, yet desires to transmit the Dharma to others according to their individual conditions—this is likewise the case upon entering the maṇḍala.

At that time, there were samaya verses, numbering perhaps fourteen or fifteen, which constitute the essential words of the vows for bestowing the bodhisattva full precepts upon disciples and providing them with instruction and admonition; these have simply not been transmitted to this land.
Next is the thirteenth chapter, "Abiding in the Secret Maṇḍala.
The preceding chapter explained the expedient means for entering the secret maṇḍala, namely the three kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
This refers to empowering the body of the master with mantras, as well as the maṇḍala to be entered, and further empowering the disciple so that they abide in firmness and stability.
Because one subsequently attains stable abiding within the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*), the chapter on "Abiding in Realization" is explained next.
At that time, the World-Honored One Mahāvairocana entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of realization for the sake of future sentient beings;
regarding the meaning of "abiding in the state of realization from within samādhi," this has already been explained above, and now it shall be further explained.

That which is called Vairocana is the sun. Just as the sun in the world can dispel all darkness, cause all things to grow, and accomplish the activities of all sentient beings, so too is the Dharmakāya Tathāgata;
therefore, he is used as a metaphor. However, the worldly sun has spatial limitations; if it shines upon the exterior, it does not [shine within].
The sun that illuminates the internal sciences illuminates only one side and not the other; it can illuminate only by day, and its light does not reach the night.
The sun that is the Tathāgata is not like this: it illuminates both internally and externally without partiality, making no distinction between day and night.
Perfectly bright and eternally abiding, when all sentient beings encounter the rising of this sun, they are able to give birth [to awakening].
He increases the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas and performs the work of a Tathāgata;
because he cannot be compared even to the sun of the world, which represents only a small fraction of his merit, he is given the name "Mahā" (Great).

The reason the Buddha enters this samādhi is that, while abiding in the dharma of ultimate signlessness and quiescent extinction, he dwells in samādhi out of great compassion to cause [all beings] to...

All the great assemblies and immeasurable sentient beings who behold this subtle dharma of the Great Assembly of the Adornment of the Maṇḍala of the Matrix of Great Compassion see form within the signless;
yet although there is form, it arises from causes and conditions, which is the meaning of non-arising. This is identical to the dharma of intrinsic purity, yet each and every sentient being...

In accordance with their original conditions, they see various forms, hear various sounds, and obtain various dharmas; each, according to the vessel of their own mind, practices in accordance with the Dharma.

Because there are such great causes and conditions, and furthermore, in order to fulfill the questions asked by Vajrapāṇi so that they may be made clear and exhaustive, he enters samādhi. "Samāpatti" (equipoise) is another name for samādhi. [End of] the above.
Regarding the statement "at that time," and then again "at that time" when the Tathāgata entered into samādhi:
this is distinguished from the preceding causal conditions because there is subsequently this further matter; thus it is said "at that time. (Question: What is meant by) "attainment" (*samāpatti*)?
It means that all Tathāgatas of the past have all ridden upon this path to reach the attainment of perfect enlightenment; as it was for those of the past, so it shall be for those of the future.

All Tathāgatas of the present are likewise thus; all attain perfect enlightenment by following this path and employing these skillful means, which is why it is called "attaining equality" (*samatāgama*). Just as the Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained perfect enlightenment, so shall I do;
just as I now ride this path to reach the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), so too do all Buddhas. Buddha after Buddha is entirely equal to the original source.
Because they are ultimately and entirely equal, they are called "attainments" (*samāpatti*).

Furthermore, just as the arrangement of the directions and positions of the great maṇḍala previously shown was manifested by the Buddha while entering a samādhi, so too, when an ācārya abides in meditative concentration to initiate disciples, he should likewise lay out these directional positions; they shall not differ from that [original manifestation] in the slightest.
All these are the universal gateways of practice for the spiritual friends who enter the Dharma-realm.
If a teacher performs this contemplation to empower a disciple, it will likewise enable them to see such a great assembly.

Because what is contemplated within the inner mind and what is manifested externally are equal and without distinction, it is called the Samādhi of Equanimity (Samāpatti). When the Buddha enters this samādhi...

Because [the assembly] was in a state of obscurity, Vajrapāṇi and the other great Bodhisattvas were unable to satisfy the doubts they held regarding the matters manifested by the Buddha within samādhi;
for that manifestation was intended to demonstrate the methods and applications of the various directions. Therefore, the Buddha entered this samādhi.
When that Buddha entered samādhi, his buddha-field and so forth—[“and so forth” meaning it was equal to others]—became level and even, specifically the ground.

"Level" refers to samādhi; it means that one attains the vision of the adornments of the Pure Land, where the ground is even and upright, free from tiles, stones, mountains, sand, gravel, and the like. This, however, is the meaning of the pure bodhicitta:
by the power of faith, one levels the ground of the mind and removes all the sand contained within the ālayavijñāna.
With the exception of the ground that is the essential nature of the ultimately equal and pure bodhicitta, such as gravel, stumps, and stumps of trees—
if one can level and purify this ground, one may then accomplish the majestic array of the Great Compassion Womb Matrix (Mahākaruṇā-garbha) Buddha Assembly.
"Interspersed with the five treasures" refers to the five treasures, such as gold and silver, and their respective colors;
it means that the ground is interspersed with these five-colored jewels. The five colors are, in order, white, yellow, red, green, and black. "Interspersed" (kancata) means demarcated by boundaries.
White is faith (*śraddhā*), yellow is diligence (*vīrya*), red is mindfulness (*smṛti*), green is concentration (*samādhi*), and black is wisdom (*prajñā*). [End of] upper section.
The commentary states: first white, then red, then yellow; taking this explanation as definitive, the previous one was incorrect.

From here on, each and every adornment has a specific doctrinal interpretation, though they have not yet been explained individually here; they will be matched to their respective *dharmamukhas* in other places.
It is not merely that the ground is interspersed with the five jewels; there are further "adornment gates" (*vyūha-mukha*) which serve as headings for further sections.

The "signpost" (*sūcaka*) is the gateway to the Great Compassion Womb Matrix (*Mahākaruṇā-garbha-kośa*); it serves to make known the directional characteristics of the gateway through which one enters.
This signpost is that which has been illustrated above; however, there are both those made as paintings and those erected as structures.
The painted version is as depicted in the diagram, while the erected signpost is also constructed according to these same characteristics. This gateway possesses pillars.

The crossbeam atop the pillar marks it as a gate; the gates of the four directions are the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), while this marks the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
*Niryūha* is a gate, a *toraṇa*, and also a banner or a marker.
As for the variegated colors, they are not merely the colors of the five directions, but include various other mixed colors; these mixed...
The colored banners are broad and long in appearance, positioned atop the gate markers.

As for the great jeweled canopy (*mahāratnacchattra*), it is above, covering [the space] like the square of a ritual altar (*maṇḍala*). This canopy is called "great" because its dimensions cover all Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*).
Furthermore, white whisks (*śveta-cāmara*) and jeweled bells (*ratna-ghaṇṭā*) are suspended from these markers as adornments; the former were the colored banners, while these are—
Jewel bells and banners, as well as precious canopies and streamers, are suspended and interspersed among them;
furthermore, various kinds of multicolored silks and famous garments hang down and are distributed all around, bound in sections by bundles of fine cloth—this refers to the "multicolored silks.
I personally believe this signifies the meaning of wearing robes of variegated colors. It is from the foremost dharma of signlessness that these are produced.
In this way, the manifestation of the various physical forms born from the treasury of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-kośa*) explains immeasurable dharmas through diverse skillful means;

this is the meaning of "variegated colors" (*citra-varṇa*). Variegated banners have always been placed upon the gate-signs (*dvāra-lakṣaṇa*); "erecting" refers to setting up the banners at these signs.
In the eight directions and intermediate corners, great *maṇi* victory banners (*dhvaja*) are erected; these banners are made of *maṇi*. As for "banners," it refers to—

Upon the pillars, there first appear columns for tiered terraces; in the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate corners, jeweled *maṇi* banners of wondrous wish-fulfilling gems are erected.
Beyond this, there are further pure and exquisite bathing pools of the eight meritorious waters, serene and limpid.
Within these pools, immeasurable water-birds frolic at will, producing various subtle [sounds].
The sounds are pleasing to all and produce various seasonal flowers—meaning that flowers of the six seasons each appear according to their respective times.
Not only are there named flowers, but there are also various precious jewels arranged in rows, distributed throughout the eight directions (where "fen" means "directions").
Five-jeweled necklaces are strung together as cords; around these eight pillars, precious cords are wound in every direction.
They are interconnected in this manner. Regarding the term "necklace" (*hāra*) used here, its Sanskrit pronunciation differs from that of the "ornaments" (*ābharaṇa*) mentioned previously;
it refers to necklaces hanging down like upward-facing crescent moons, with strings of jewels surrounding them and joined together.

The ground is fine and smooth like cotton, and like cotton garments, it is pleasant to experience and provides supreme tactile pleasure—just as there are garments made of pure cotton in the Western Regions.
Such things as the cotton cloths of this ground are exceedingly soft and smooth; when pressed down, they sink, and when lifted, the entire body returns to its former level as before.
Their touch is most subtle and gives rise to the sensation of supreme bliss. Furthermore, immeasurable musical instruments fill the air;
suspended in mid-air, they resonate spontaneously without being struck, their sounds profound and wondrous, causing those who hear them to delight and experience joy and happiness.

Upon this ground arrayed with adornments, there further arise immeasurable mind-made seats and palaces, produced by the merit of the various bodhisattvas and born from the Tathāgata’s faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).

These seats are arranged in three tiers, following the same sequence as the arrangement of the Maṇḍala Born from the Great Compassion Treasury mentioned above; each is according to the purity of the respective bodhisattva.
From the sublime merits and the sensory delights of the five objects, various distinctions arise;
to state the essentials, there are as many as the number of atoms in ten worlds, each distinct and arranged in their respective positions.
All of these are within the pillars of the eight precious banners, and they all arise from the Tathāgata’s power of faith and understanding, through the power of the Tathāgata’s original vows.
By virtue of this power, he manifests through the universal gate within the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and samādhis.
That which marks the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) arises from the Dharma-realm and is thus its very insignia;

herein lies the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*), for in the Sanskrit original, the term for "insignia" (*cihna*) implies "nature. The essential nature of the Dharma-realm is primordially and eternally pure.
In the first [mandala], which is adorned by the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is a great Lotus King.
This flower is identical to the Dharma-realm, pervading all places, and its intrinsic nature is pure.
One should know that the Tathāgata who dwells therein—since the flower’s magnitude is equal to the Dharma-realm—his Buddha-body is likewise so. This is the Central Womb (*garbha*).
It is the eight-petaled flower. A great lotus flower arises, and the Tathāgata dwells therein within that dharmadhātu.

It is the foremost of those who possess the joy of sentient beings through their resolute belief and understanding (*adhimukti*); it is the foremost dharmadhātu-body which, according to the resolute beliefs and understandings of all sentient beings, causes them to attain joy.
This "foremost" is of an extremely subtle nature, most difficult to perceive; therefore, it is "extremely subtle."

Furthermore, this "first" in meaning should be translated as "nature. Regarding "according to inclination," it means that by the power of the Buddha’s original vows, in order to deliver all sentient beings, he manifests through the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) in various forms according to what each being delights to see;

thus, he guides and benefits them according to their capacities, causing them to attain joy. Those various limbs of the Tathāgata arise from the unimpeded power of faith and understanding in the ten powers.
Regarding the birth of a body adorned with immeasurable colors and forms: the limbs of the Tathāgata possess unimpeded power, which is called "indestructible power.

Because the powers of all worldly beings, celestial seers (*ṛṣi*), those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas are still subject to obstruction, there may be superior powers capable of destroying them due to that very obstruction. However, the power of the Buddha is unimpeded.
Because it can destroy all things like a vajra, it is called the power of non-obstruction. From where does this power of non-obstruction arise?
One should know that it arises from the Tathāgata’s ten powers of knowledge (*daśa-jñānabala*).
From the upper, middle, and lower parts of the Buddha’s body, it flows forth in various forms; even from every single pore, it flows forth in various kinds.
There are various forms and colors, each distinct—whether square, circular, triangular, or crescent-shaped; or blue, yellow, red, white, or black;

including forms such as those of peaceful, joyful, or wrathful deities. These are immeasurable in number and consist of the various principal deities, all of whom should be seated upon thrones manifested by the mind.

Now, from what do these ten powers arise? They arise from the Tathāgata’s cultivation of the six perfections, the ten perfections, and even hundreds of thousands of millions of unspeakably unspeakable *asaṃkhyeya* perfections throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
It is through the merit of these various practices that the *dharmakāya* is nourished and brought to maturity, and thus they manifest. This is due to their merit.
Through the nourishment and growth of virtue, his body appears; having appeared, within the great assemblies of all dharma-realms—
that is, throughout the ten directions— he does not merely manifest his form, but further produces various wondrous sounds to proclaim and disseminate the inconceivable,
eternally quiescent, and secret Dharma of mantra practice, so that all may universally hear and know it.
Furthermore, the bodhisattvas born therein each spoke various sublime verses to praise the Buddha;
that which expresses such speech through sound is called "verse" (*gāthā*). It is just like the assembly that emerged from below.
While Mahāvairocana Tathāgata still remains in samādhi, this is the manifestation within the lotus pedestal produced by that samādhi: the World-Honored One Vairocana—
Within the constituent parts [of the body], this body is manifested.
When the Buddha emerges in various forms from this lotus of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, various sounds also issue forth from the Buddha’s body to expound the wondrous Dharma.
As the Sūtra says: "That which is expressed by sound is that which is expressed by speech. This is a brief verse summarizing the exposition of sound.
There are two verses; the first verse says:
"How marvelous! The skillful means of all Buddhas are inconceivable. Regarding the nature of non-storage, they contain it within wisdom by means of wisdom."
This verse praises the Buddha’s intention; because he has manifested inconceivable matters as shown above, it extols the Buddha’s merit as being most extraordinary.
Since praising a single Vairocana is equivalent to praising all Tathāgatas, it says "all Buddhas.
One should know that the extraordinary marks manifested by the Tathāgata are themselves the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, within skillful means, this inconceivable karma arises. Why is it inconceivable?
It is because while abiding in the nature of non-storage (*anālaya*), one is able to manifest that which has storage.

"Storage" (*ālaya*)—in Sanskrit, *ālaya*—is translated here as "storehouse," or carries the meaning of a "palace," "residence," or "dwelling. Just as with dwellings in the world, all sentient beings each [possess their own].
Abiding therein according to one's own portion, once such a cave-dwelling exists, there is the containment of both good and evil from which one cannot emerge on one's own.
Because the Tathāgata has already departed from such a cave-dwelling of the ālayavijñāna, it is said that he possesses no nature of concealment (*asaṃvṛti*).

Although the Buddha is devoid of all concealments, through the skillful means of wisdom, he manifests a "concealment" of birth; that is to say, within the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*), [he manifests birth].

Yet, within the non-delusory realm of phenomena, they manifest various signs and produce various sounds to preach, using this very treasury to lead all beings to the state of being without a treasury.
The subsequent verse says: "If one realizes there is nothing to be attained, then all phenomena lack a fixed abiding mark.
By attaining that which is unattainable, one becomes a Buddha, a Guide. This means that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is unattainable and inconceivable.
One should not conceive of the meaning of emptiness as something to be attained; if one attains this, that is the Buddha.

If there is anything to be attained, it is then characterized by delusion and concealment, and is not the Tathāgata’s teacherless wisdom. That which can be cognized is merely the sphere of mental activity and is not the ultimate, supreme truth.
This is why the Buddha’s inconceivability is praised: it lies precisely in this state of non-attainment.
That which can be known and attained is what is called the aforementioned realm: signless yet possessing signs, causing all sentient beings to attain through non-attainment.
Who attains this Dharma? It is the Buddhas, the Guides. Furthermore, the verse says: "How marvelous!
In the Sanskrit sound "how marvelous" (*āścarya*), there is the syllable *ā* at the very beginning; this is the verse.
The exposition of the Dharma has now been completed. This is precisely the meaning of "primordial non-arising" (*an-utpāda*): it is that which gives birth to all phenomena.
This refers to the various forms and sounds manifested by the body of the Tathāgata, all of which arise from the letter *A*.
Having manifested these various forms, they then return into the Buddha-body; that body, in turn, returns into the inconceivable Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. Each [returns] in this manner.
Because it enters according to the place from which it emerges, the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, one enters that inconceivable Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
This inconceivability—Sanskrit *acintya*—also contains the sound *a*; its meaning clarifies that it emerges from *a* and also enters into *a*.
These two ends, pointing upward and downward, indicate that the two *a*-syllables clarify oneness.
The arising and ceasing of all phenomena are identical to the essence of the Dharma-realm.
That Buddha spoke to the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries, saying: "That Buddha is Vairocana.
You should further inquire of that Buddha whether he is the one manifested within this samādhi, or whether he is the original Tathāgata."
This must indeed be the Tathāgata. From this point onward, after the Buddha has arisen from the samādhi of equality (*samatā-samādhi*), he addresses Vajrapāṇi.

The reason the Buddha dwells in samādhi and manifests various rare signs as previously described—ranging from the ground being level like the palm of a hand to the arrangement of the deities and the eight-petaled lotus in their respective positions—is that he desires...
By showing the realm of the internal yoga of Vajradhara and others, he uses the external to illustrate the internal and thereby express the meaning.
Therefore, now arising from meditative concentration, he again explains the method for entering the secret treasury of the internal mind-maṇḍala and reveals it to Vajrapāṇi:
"O Son of Good Family, listen attentively! This is the internal [mind]; the maṇḍala within the heart is that secret."
The ground of the principal body is the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*; it is empowered by the empowerment of mantra and mudrā.
Its intrinsic nature is pure because it has purity as its causal condition.
As previously described, having first empowered oneself as Vairocana, one then performs activities by means of the empowerment of Karma-Vajrasattva, as stated in the Great Root Text (*Mahāmūla*).

There are twenty signs that urge one to listen attentively: the Buddha, for the sake of Vajradhara, those who have removed all dust and defilements, and the various Bodhisattvas practicing mantra-vidyā, has taught these essential dharmas; yet without possessing them, one cannot swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Now, furthermore, I shall explain so as to fulfill the previous meanings and bring these essential dharmas to completion; if one does not know or understand this—
Since the preceding teachings were not yet fully exhaustive, for these reasons I exhort you to listen attentively.
These twenty kinds of causes and conditions shall now be explained in detail. What was previously presented was due to the power of this samādhi;
that which was presented as external objects is now to be contemplated internally. Within the practitioner's own mind, the great ocean of the Buddha-assembly is complete.
When these directions are unified as a single buddha-field, it is understood only by oneself and not seen by others; therefore, it is called the Secret Maṇḍala.
It is just as when constructing an external maṇḍala, one must first prepare the ground by removing sand, gravel, stumps, and the like (the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span);
next, one must level and stabilize it so that it is entirely firm, even, and upright, and only then may one [proceed] within it.

The establishment [of the ground] here is likewise so. For one who wishes to establish the great maṇḍala within the inner mind, one must first level the ground by removing stumps, stumps, and other such defects;
this which is called "the ground of the body" (kāyabhūmi) implicitly includes earth, water, fire, and wind.
How is it purified? It means that one should first establish the seat of yoga. The seat of yoga is the syllable of the mantra to be held;
one should empower it. Taking the very first syllable of that mantra to be held, one empowers that initial syllable, which is the heart of the mantra (*hṛdaya*).
That syllable should be stripped of its nasal dot (*bindu*) and so forth, and only the [consonant] itself should be taken.
The fundamental essence is such that the essence itself is the letter A; this letter A is the Vajra-ground. Why is this so?
It is because when Śākyamuni first attained perfect enlightenment, he entered the Vajra-samādhi to achieve that enlightenment, and beyond the Vajra-ground, there was nothing capable of surpassing it.
Now, this is likewise: for the purpose of establishing the inner mind, [the Vajra-ground is established].
Because this is the Great Maṇḍala Assembly of Vairocana, if one does not first establish the adamantine ground of the mind (*vajracitta*), it cannot be firmly established.

The letter *A* is the adamantine wheel; because one desires to ascend the adamantine throne, one first contemplates the letter *A* as the beginning, and then, by means of the adamantine, one maintains the adamantine. One should contemplate this letter as being square.

The form of this character is likewise square; observe that this character is perfectly square and manifests the color of vajra, pervading the practitioner’s inner body just as the earth element pervades the body without exception.
Next, regarding the practice of the Water Samādhi: this refers to visualizing the syllable *ba*, which resides within a sphere of perfect luminosity.
Its color is pure white and it likewise pervades the entire body; furthermore, the shape of this syllable is also circular.

Having previously visualized the syllable *a* so that it pervaded the whole body, it now again pervades the body just as the element of water thoroughly saturates the body without obstructing the element of earth. Next...
Visualize the syllable *ra* as a red triangle; this syllable itself takes the form of a triangle.
The syllable *ra* also pervades all places, just as the fire element (*tejas*) pervades the body. Next, visualize the syllable *ha* in the shape of a sideways crescent moon, black in color;
that syllable is situated in the center, its color being even deeper black, and it also pervades the body, just like the body itself.

Regarding the great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind within the body: when these external objects are illuminated from the internal, they are the syllable *Avaloka*, which is added to the body.
This *A* is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, for since all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, they are identical to the *dharmadhātu*.
Because of this *A*, one should know that the remaining elements—water, fire, and wind—are likewise so.
The nature of the purity of the *dharmadhātu* arises from causes and conditions yet is fundamentally unarisen;
one should know that these individual syllables of the mantra, through their empowerment, are by nature pure.
"Condition" (*pratyaya*) means that [something] is produced on account of this (it likely carries the sense of "therefore").
Karmavajra-sattva-āśrita-sarvaraja-sattvāyuṣmat-pūrṇamanu-janita-manas-rṣi-janaka-ādi-sthāṇu-doṣin. There are two kinds of vajra: first, jñānavajra;
second, karmavajra. This [latter] is called *vajrakarma* in Sanskrit, which refers to that which is performed.
Regarding this activity, because it is empowered by this vajra-activity, that ground is purified and cleansed.
"Free from all dust" means that "dust" refers to faults, afflictions, and so forth. To level the ground, one must first remove pebbles, gravel, stumps, and the like—namely, all defiled views.
Next, its characteristics will be briefly explained: [it concerns] sentient beings, life-span, and persons.
Those born of Samadṛṣṭi and Pūrṇaka constitute one class of non-Buddhist views;
they hold that Pūrṇaka is the self and that everything arises in dependence upon him. Those born of the seer Manu hold that everything arises from him;
this too is a view of one class of non-Buddhists. These are all natures characterized by defilement, obstruction, and inequality; now, [this] is also like gold.
By performing the rite of firm wisdom (*vajra-karma*), one eliminates those uneven past [obstructions];

once that stump and thicket are purified, one constructs the secret great maṇḍala upon this ground of the mind. It has four corners and four gates, with the western gate always open for entry and exit.
Alongside the entrance, a perimeter is established as previously shown, including the outer features, the markings of the central gate, and the surrounding [enclosures].
Surrounding the eight directions are great precious pillars, upon which hang precious necklaces, white whisks, and various other ornaments;
now, the internal yoga is likewise no different from that.
However, each of these is a dharma-gate of the inner mind; one should further inquire into their names and meanings.
Within this, there is a great lotus-king born from the mind with eight petals, a stalk, and filaments, adorned all over with exquisite colors.
In its center, the Tathāgata—the most honored among all people—ascends the stages of body, speech, and mind, and the stages of the mind, attaining the sublime ground of the mind-ground.
Regarding the "Bestower of the Fruit of Supreme Delight," it refers to the great lotus king-throne within the inner ground of the Great Level Adornment.
As for the great flower-king manifested above, its essence is pure and subtle, its magnitude equal to the *dharmadhātu*;
because what is now visualized within this inner ground is like that, it is called the "Great Flower King. This flower possesses a stalk.
There is a calyx with various colors interspersed, all exquisitely painted; this is said to be produced through internal visualization.
Just as a painter applies various pigments to create diverse forms, although these arise from the conjunction of many conditions and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their features appear vividly.
Above this is the Honored One among all humans, namely Vairocana. This is the stage of practice (*caryā*).
This intrinsic nature, the teacherless wisdom of the Great Vairocana Buddha, does not come from without.

Those who transcend body, speech, and mind ascend to the ground of the mind; by transcending the ground of body, speech, and mind, they reach the ground of the mind and obtain the delightful, sublime fruit.
By transcending the defiled ground of the mind, they reach the ground of the fruit of the pure mind. It is as with all things.
Because worldly people have not yet attained the threefold equality of body, speech, and mind, they are unable to enter this Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground.
The Tathāgata has completely abandoned all faults of the three karmas and attained the threefold equality;
he has reached the Mind-ground of all Buddhas, which is to say, he has attained the pure Bodhicitta—the delightful Mind-ground of Vairocana Tathāgata—and thus, among all things, [he is supreme].
Furthermore, Venerable One, all sentient beings equally possess this nature—the secret treasury of the Tathāgata—which is complete and without deficiency;

yet they cannot have confidence in it themselves, nor do they understand it for themselves. The Tathāgata, having clearly realized and personally witnessed it, universally opens and awakens them to it, and causes them likewise to attain this Dharma.
For this reason, he is called the Honored One among all sentient beings, O Pleasing One.
"Result" refers to the ultimate fruit; one should know that those who attain this "ground of mind" are none other than Vairocana Tathāgata.
"Bestowal" means that while there may be someone who transmits it to another, one must personally observe and practice to attain this fruit.
It is like a person giving away a fruit: one realizes it for oneself and does not obtain it from another.
As described above, Vairocana is seated upon the flower pedestal; following him on the eight petals are: in the east, Ratnasaṃkusumita Buddha, also named Ratnaketu Buddha;
in the south, Saṃkusumitarājendra Buddha—*Indra* here also carries the meaning of "king," and since repeating the word "king" would be redundant, the Sanskrit term is retained;
in the north, Duṇḍubhisvara Buddha (the name *Akṣobhya* was previously used, but has now been changed to this).
In the west is Amitābha; at its four corners are Samantabhadra in the southeast, Avalokiteśvara in the northeast, Mañjuśrī in the southwest, and Maitreya in the northwest.
Within the filaments of its flowers are placed the various Mother-Deities (Buddhamātṛs), such as the Prajñāpāramitās and the Samādhis;
these Mother-Deities are, for instance, Gaganalocanā and others. Beneath these flower filaments are placed the various Vidyādharas.
The wrathful deities and others are all situated beneath the petals; their flower-stalks are held by Vajrapāṇi Guhyapati, who serves as their stalk.
The "infinite great ocean assembly" refers to the vajras. There are also various offering implements, such as flowers and incense;
these have been briefly explained here, though further arrangements will appear in the subsequent text. As for those flower-stalks:
Looking downward, one visualizes the great ocean waters; for the sake of accomplishing the samaya, one must prepare flowers and other offerings.

Desiring to cause all [beings] to enter the mandala, one mentally contemplates the flowers and causes them to enter. Beyond the seashore, the terrestrial devas each visualize their respective positions and arrange themselves according to their directions.

The verse beginning with "The lamp-flower of the mind" (*manas-toraṇa-puṣpa*) follows. Regarding "painting with diligence": it means that the practitioner who performs the recitation applies [the visualization] to their body and mind as if painting it.
Because there is a Buddha in the center of this mental maṇḍala, it is called the "Great Self" (*mahātman*);
"Great Self" is an epithet for the Buddha. "Creating by oneself" means creating through internal contemplation.

This is to understand it clearly and distinctly. However, regarding this secret maṇḍala, if the master perceives that the disciple is truly a vessel for the Dharma and sincerely seeks [initiation], yet lacks the power to provide the various conditions required for a grand production as described above, the master may perform this rite of transmission for them.
In other cases, one must require the full array of conditions; it cannot be the same as this. However, if the disciple...
Once the disciple has attained the state of a yoga master and one wishes to lead him into the secret assembly of the Buddha, one proceeds in this manner as well.

Regarding the purification by means of the syllable *ra*: (First, having already performed the purifications with the syllables *a* and *ra*, one now purifies the disciple according to the method described above.

That is to say, using the aforementioned skillful means, one contemplates the fire of the syllable *ra* and burns away those obstructing dharmas and accumulated karmic residues until they are entirely purified; only then does one again use the sweet...
By sprinkling the water of the Dharma, one causes the sprout of the Way to grow from within the ashes of death; therefore, next, the syllable *Aṃ* is bestowed.
The Master, abiding in the seat of yoga, should visualize this syllable *A* with a dot (*bindu*) placed upon it and set it at the crown of the disciple’s head, within the fontanelle.
One should know that the dot above it is the nectar-water of the Dharma.
Regarding "using [the water] to consecrate the crown of the head" and "recalling the Tathāgata":

this means that because the master intends to lead the disciple into the secret treasury, he recalls the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, desiring that they may together realize and together protect and uphold it.
Once the master himself has settled into the seat of yoga, he uses his own body and mind to form an assembly of the ocean of Buddhas; thus, he alone is clearly manifest.

This is understood by others who do not see it. Next, the master gives a flower to the disciple and instructs them to cast it upon the body of the master as an offering to the Buddha within the heart, while contemplating their fundamental affinity (*mūla-pratyaya*). Following that fundamental affinity, one contemplates whether they are a vessel for the Dharma.
If the disciple is embraced by the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the master perceives this within the flower without error; however, this applies only to disciples who have not yet attained *yoga*.
It is seen to be upon his body; where the flowers are cast down, the general layout of the mind constitutes the eight-petaled position.

From the navel to the heart is the Vajra Terrace (*vajrapīṭha*); the navel is the great ocean. That which is below the navel is the position of the deities who dwell on the earth. What does this signify?
It means that from the ocean of the great compassion of all Buddhas, Vajra Wisdom is born; from Vajra [Wisdom]...
Wisdom gives birth to all Buddha-assemblies; among all maṇḍalas, this is the most supreme and peerless.

(The phrase "seeing for oneself and then explaining to others" means the place where the teacher perceives within his own mind. As stated in the preceding text, the practitioner visualizes the internal body—specifically the flesh and heart—as divided into eight parts, forming an eight-petaled lotus in full bloom, and places the letter RA upon the eyes and so forth. If the practitioner...
It is not as effective as practicing until one achieves accomplishment, for there is no way for an ordinary person to perform this Secret Mantra rite;
rather, one must first achieve accomplishment oneself, be capable of abiding in the station of a yoga master (*yogācārya*), and receive the authorization of an *ācārya* before one can undertake it.
Although what is being done here is a skillful means for guiding others, the practitioner must maintain [the practice] for themselves.

When reciting and contemplating, one should likewise practice according to the Dharma; by using this method of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) to sprinkle oneself, all obstacles are removed and one swiftly enters the assembly of Buddhas.
While the preceding chapter was titled "Entering the Secret," the present one again speaks of "entering";
this "entering" is an entering of realization (*praveśa*), just as when a person has already entered a house or dwelling, each [room] becomes clearly manifest.
Having clearly distinguished the entry and exit [of breath], one knows all that exists within the house, unlike a person who has merely entered the door for the first time.
Next is the fourteenth chapter, "The Secret Eight Mudrās."
At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana surveyed the great assembly and addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:

"O Lord of Secrets, there are eight secret mudrās that are profound and most secret. As the Tathāgata previously taught in the preceding chapter—having completed the explanation of the method for entering and abiding in the secret maṇḍala—the great assembly again had this thought: 'Such is this secret...'"

"What further expedient means, endowed with perfect characteristics, can cause practitioners of the *mantra* path to swiftly attain accomplishment regarding this most profound and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing the thoughts of the assembly— wondering whether there was something even more secret within this secret,
or whether this [teaching] was the limit— since they could not fathom it and none dared to ask, the Buddha [spoke].
Without waiting for a question, he speaks of his own accord; that which is called "having divine efficacy" is as follows:

when a practitioner arranges the seats of the maṇḍala of those deities, whether internally or externally, because they are empowered by these eight mudrās and mantras, it is highly effective to install them within the positions of the deities.
"Miraculous efficacy is identical" means that it is equal to the majestic spiritual power (*vīrya*) of the Honored One (the Principal Deity).
Those various deities naturally descend to the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), fulfill the practitioner's vows and objectives for correct practice, and then depart.
This is the law of inconceivable response and resonance; even the reflection of water and fire, or the sun and moon in a mirror, cannot be conceived, let alone that of the Tathāgata.
This is the resonance between the inconceivable *dharmadhātu* and its response; it is the seal practiced by the *ācārya*, which must not be practiced haphazardly.
Even those who have already entered the *maṇḍala* are not permitted to perform it before [the deity] recklessly, let alone others.
It is not merely that there are the mantras of the *iṣṭadevatā*; there are also insignia (*cihna*) representing the *iṣṭadevatā*.
The "mantra-gati" (mantra-path) serves as the sign (*cihna*). "Gati" refers to [destinies] such as the six *gatis*; this is the mantra-gati.
"Perimeter" (*jū*) means the sense of being complete or fully endowed. It is not merely the mantra, but includes the maṇḍala as well. Regarding "correspondence with the Honored One" (*honzon-sōō*):
just as the Honored One possesses such virtues, I too possess them; therefore, it is "endowed. This is the same for all matters mentioned above.
That "Venerable One" refers to the form and posture—whether sitting or standing—and one should know that one's own body abides in the form of the *iṣṭadevatā* (the chosen deity).
Having known this, by abiding as the *iṣṭadevatā*, one attains *siddhi*.
If a practitioner, in accordance with these eight mudrās, mantras, and maṇḍalas, aligns them with their respective positions and can understand this, they will draw near to *siddhi* before long.

As for attaining the state of abiding as the Honored One (Bhagavān) himself: although the preceding sections have been correlated with the Secret Maṇḍala, if one wishes to invoke the Honored One, it is only by performing this rite that success is achieved; if one does not perform this, the practice remains incomplete.

Throughout this scripture, the preceding and succeeding sections complement one another to form a single matter, their texts interwoven; therefore, practitioners must carefully cross-reference them before proceeding.
When a practitioner performs recitation, they must also perform this [mudrā]; by thus inviting the deity and making their desired aspirations, one will swiftly achieve self-establishment.
As for the first mudrā: form the *tri-puṭa* (three-fold) hollow-palms gesture;
extend straight and open the two earth-fingers (*tarjanīs*) and the two wind-fingers (*anāmikās*), while the others remain as before. This is it.
The Seal of the Arising of the Majestic Power of Vairocana Tathāgata arises from within this;
herein is born the Great Majestic Power of the Tathāgata, which is the illumination of the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Its maṇḍala is triangular in shape, and as its four sides are further surrounded by four triangles, it is called "encircled. Within it, one should visualize Vairocana.
The World-Honored One Vairocana is situated therein. As for this triangular maṇḍala, one should visualize it upon the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus;
that is, one constructs this triangular maṇḍala upon the aforementioned yoga-seat.
Its apex points downward and its color is red. Although previously it was said that the apex of the triangle points upward, here it points downward.
The meaning and function are distinct. One should visualize the Buddha within this [mandala] and perform the *Vibhīṣaṇa-mudrā*. Its mantra is: OṂ LAḤ.
Second, as before, form the mudrā and bend both ring fingers (*anāmikā*) to press the tips of both thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*), causing them to meet.
The shape of the letter *ṇa* (ṇa) is this seal of the indestructible vajra. "Vajra" refers to the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
because this wisdom does not arise from conditions and cannot be destroyed, it is called the "indestructible vajra.
The form of its maṇḍala is circular like the letter *su* (*sa*, the fifth vowel), and it is surrounded by vajras (which should be vajras possessing light).
Jvala). Its vajra is likewise located at the four sides of the maṇḍala as described above.
That which is called the syllable VA is this very maṇḍala, perfectly circular and white; it is also situated upon the flower pedestal.
Within it is the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, from whom all [the following] emanate. However, regarding these eight mudrās, the reciter may select any one of them according to the specific rite.
This is to be used according to the specific rite during the recitation.
