This is not like the Śrāvakas, who loathe all afflictions and seek the noble Dharma separately. It is the same with the unwholesome: by transforming this wholesome nature, one makes it unwholesome, just as with a knot.
Water becoming ice has no distinct nature. Regarding "mother" and so forth, "mother" carries the sense of that which gives birth;
it means that because of wrong views, one can give rise to all unwholesome dharmas, just as a mother does.
For this reason, a bodhisattva does not give rise to wrong views even in jest or while looking on; to state the essential point, they do not produce even a single thought that violates this.
If even a mind of wrong view regarding the precepts is so grave, how much more so when it is frequent?
In the Śrāvaka sūtras, jesting speech and the like are not considered violations of the training rules; however, this is not the case here.

Even within jesting and the like, to engage in acts such as wrong views is impermissible, let alone intentional karma. Nevertheless, because a Bodhisattva possesses wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), [it is otherwise].
One is able to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without being moved by any views, thereby entering into correct characteristics from within erroneous characteristics.
Why is this? Because sentient beings have practiced these methods extensively since beginningless time, making it difficult for them to be established in what is truly correct.

This is like the skillful physician who first conforms to the patient’s activities and subsequently seizes their authority, as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and elsewhere. Furthermore, it is like...
In the Jātaka section of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, it is said that in the distant past there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a king named Brahmadatta;
however, this occurred many eons ago. The name of the city today is precisely that same original site.
One should know that within that world-system, places repeatedly return to their former sites and regain their original names. Yet, in recent times...
The King of Vārāṇasī was also named Brahmadatta; his name was the same as that of former kings. At that time, a son was born to a brahmin who was a minister of that king.

When the son was born, clouds of blue, yellow, red, and white appeared in the four directions of the sky, each according to its quarter, spreading with brilliant colors across the entire Jambudvīpa and bringing down a fine rain. All the brahmins...
According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, when a son is born, one must invariably invite a celestial sage of holy wisdom to first examine his physical marks and establish a name for him.
At that time, the minister sought out a seer and had him examine the child. The seer asked, "When this child was born, what auspicious signs were there?
We shall establish the name based upon these. The father recounted the previous events to him. The seer said, "I am Wei..."
The Vedic scriptures state that if a person is born with such marks, they will certainly master the four Vedas;
as they cause the flow of the Dharma’s grace to spread throughout the four quarters, they are named "Auspicious Cloud" (*Kṣemambara*).

Furthermore, because the ministerial caste practices the four Vedas and this is the tradition of the *maṇava*, he is designated by his original title as a *maṇava*. As this youth gradually grew older...
Having established the transmission of his practice, he thoroughly understood all the essential tenets of the Four Clarifications (Caturvidha-prakāśa). He then formed this thought:
"It is not merely through intellectual understanding that one attains meaningful benefit; rather, one must contemplate and select what to practice.
He then investigated the essential tenets throughout this text, considering by what method one might achieve liberation. Why was this? Because this youth had cultivated merit in his past lives.
Because his fundamental nature was long nurtured by wisdom, although he had been born into a school that held divergent views, he was able to spontaneously give rise to this mind of awakening.
Nevertheless, as he investigated each of the scriptural traditions one by one, he found they only led to rebirth in the Brahma Heaven and lacked the path for transcending the world.
He then said to his father: "Among those I have studied thus far, there is no path for transcending the world. What further dharma is there that might serve as an addition?"
The father said, "From my ancestors down to myself, we have inherited only this dharma, which is the most sublime. Furthermore, it was spoken by the Brahma King;
it should simply be followed. How could one seek a dharma superior to this? The son thought again to himself, "I have not yet completed what I am learning now;
how can I be indolent? I must certainly seek further wisdom. He heard that among the Snowy Mountains there was a great rishi.

Regarding those who, outside of the four Vedas, possess a definitive understanding of the profound meaning, they are called Kātyāyana (this name signifies "one who follows [the mind] through question and answer").
It is because of this teaching that this seer is named the Seer Kātyāyana. I shall now go to question him.
His father said, "This seer dwells in a place so precipitous and remote that it is not accessible to human tracks; how can you possibly reach him? Then the son departed.

Without ceasing his mental resolve, he immediately went there. At that time, the various devas, perceiving that this youth would surely be able to benefit the multitude, collectively bestowed their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon him, whereby he reached the abode of the seer.
When the seer beheld his countenance, which possessed an extraordinary appearance surpassing that of ordinary men, he first greeted him with kind inquiry;
once the youth had taken his seat, the seer was attended by five thousand other seers.
The leader, who was constantly expounding the profound Dharma, asked the youth, "By what means have you come here?
The youth related his previous circumstances in detail and said to the Great Seer, "I studied these four scriptures among men;

fearing that my interpretations may be biased or inconsistent with their original intent, I request that you first explain them yourself, so that I may receive your seal of approval. At that time, he extensively set forth his understanding, and the Great Seer praised him, saying:
"This youth’s wisdom and awakening surpass those of men; what I understand cannot reach his level.
Yet, regarding the supramundane path spoken of by this youth, I have personally heard from the Brahma King that there shall appear in the world a great seer named Sarvajña (All-Knowing One).
Only such a person can expound this Dharma; it is beyond the scope of our own aspirations."

Furthermore, when he was fully instructed in the principles of analytical discernment according to his own understanding, the youth— having heard the name of the Omniscient One through the roots of merit from previous lives—
attained what he had never experienced before. Deeply grateful for his teacher’s kindness and desiring to repay it,
he reflected that according to the brahminical tradition of repaying a teacher, one must provide a garment of deer skin with a yellow sacred thread and five hundred...

With the thought that he wished to repay [his teacher] with wealth, and hearing that there was a king in the south who was about to be established and desired to manifest his majestic virtue by receiving the consecration (*abhiṣeka*),
he intended to seek it there. However, those brahmins told the king that he must prepare a thousand sheep, horses, and men for each person,
slaughtering them to manifest his majesty as part of the consecration ceremony, hoping thereby to achieve a reputation that would spread far and wide, O youth.
Later, when the time came, King [Prasenajit] heard of his reputation and was greatly delighted, thinking, "I have established myself and now encounter this worthy man of great auspiciousness.
He immediately invited him as a guest of honor and commanded him to help determine the ritual procedures. The youth summoned the various Brahmins and questioned each one exhaustively:
"What scriptural authority is there for this sacrificial rite involving the killing of living beings? He scrutinized them with extreme rigor until they were brought to their knees.
Using logical reasoning, he addressed the king, saying: "This rite of consecration is not the true path.
Your Majesty should, within a single day, prepare all manner of offerings at the four city gates and bestow them upon whoever comes seeking them;

the merit will be immeasurable and your fame will spread far and wide. The king, having previously possessed roots of goodness, understood this immediately upon hearing it and respectfully followed his advice.
The Teacher instructed him to prepare the rites with great care; the youth took only five hundred gold coins and a deerskin cord and departed.
On the way, he reached the city of Ratnasaṃbhava (this city was near the borders of Gandhāra). The king’s name was Jaya (he was so named because his armies were always victorious in battle).
As the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was first appearing in the world, the king had adorned the city and its precincts to welcome him, having purified the streets and arranged various offerings.

The flowers and incense were exceptionally different from their usual state; having seen this, the youth asked people, "For what reason is it thus? Is it because I have arrived, or is there some other cause?
(At that time, the youth’s fame was spread far and wide, and he was received with great hospitality and respect wherever he went; therefore, he suspected [the change] himself.
The people of the city replied, "A Buddha has appeared in the world, named Dīpaṃkara-rāja, and they wish to welcome him. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, the youth was suddenly enlightened.
Mahāprīti thought: "This name that has now emerged must surely be something beyond the traditional scriptures, spoken by a Great Sage.
Because of this, I wish to seek out offerings with the wealth I have acquired to present them to the Buddha.

At that time, because his resolve was so great, the celestial Māra feared that he would lead immeasurable multitudes of beings beyond his realm; thus, he obscured all people so that no goods could be purchased.

At that time, there was a woman who, due to the karmic merit of her past deeds and a long-standing causal connection with the youth, could not be obstructed by Māra when he sought to buy flowers from him.
The youth replied, "I wish to offer these to the Buddha; even for a single flower, I would not sell it for a hundred pieces of gold.
The woman said, "You have already agreed to sell them," and so she purchased one flower for a hundred pieces of gold.
When he reached five stalks for the price of five hundred gold coins, the woman immediately made this demand:
"I will not give them to you unless you can be my husband in every lifetime. The youth thought deeply to himself, "A woman obstructs the path of a Bodhisattva;
I would rather not buy these flowers and leave them here. The woman said, "I desire that in every lifetime we may assist each other in realizing the True Way."

Ultimately, they did not obstruct one another, as described in detail in the sūtras and vinayas. When he carried flowers to the Buddha’s presence and scattered them as an offering, they formed a canopy in mid-air as he followed the Buddha into the city.
The youth attained what he had never experienced before, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, whereby he deeply realized the benefits of the Dharma.
Furthermore, on a muddy section of the road, he wished to spread his deerskin garment so that the Buddha might step upon it; at that moment, Māra...
The king threw [the bowl] away five times and said to him: "Young man, you who practice the truth are the most supreme in all the world;
why do you abandon the true path to study the heterodox ways of the śramaṇas? He did not take this to heart at all.
Seeing a narrow path ahead that was muddy, he thought, "The Buddha will surely pass through here," and so he waited for his arrival.
At that time, [the Buddha] covered himself with his robe and hair so that the Buddha might step over him. Next, a disciple wished to follow the Buddha across, but the Buddha said, "Stop, stop!

This one possesses a great mind; if you all were to step over him, it would destroy your great merit. Thereupon, the Buddha pressed down upon the disciple's crown and bestowed a prophecy upon him, saying:
"At that very moment, you shall see the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all being pressed down by him."
Upon receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), he immediately ascends to the ninth stage of a Bodhisattva.

At that time, through the causal conditions of this Great Being, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all abandon false views and enter the Right Path. This demonstrates the Bodhisattva’s wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*);
for having first demonstrated entry into the wrong path and exhausted the tenets of its school, he is then able to turn their minds back [toward the truth] and lead them [to liberation].
Because those [virtues] are immeasurable and of the same kind, they are called the "perfection of the skillful means of wisdom. One should further consult the sūtras for the complete details.

At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, may the World-Honored One explain those ten paths of wholesome action and the precepts regarding 'extreme severance' and 'root severance.
This refers to the following: severing like grass, where although it is cut, it grows back again; whereas severing a *tāla* tree..."
"Not arising again" is called "ultimate severance"; this explains the power of the precepts.

How is it that a Bodhisattva, possessing sovereign power over a royal throne, dwelling in a palace, surrounded by parents and kinsmen, and experiencing celestial delights, does not give rise to transgressions?
Having spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Lord of Mysteries! You should..."
Listen attentively and apply your minds well; I shall expound the secret skillfulness regarding the definitive Vinaya of the Bodhisattvas.
Secret Lord, you should know that there are two kinds of Bodhisattvas. What are these two? They are the householder and the renunciant.
Secret Lord, the householder Bodhisattva accepts the five precepts, possesses sovereignty over a royal throne, and employs various skillful means on the path.
According to the time and place, they exercise sovereign mastery (to act with mastery according to time and place, such as manifesting the treatment of wrong views for those with great delusions).
Seeking omniscience, they are endowed with skillful means; they manifest in various artistic fields, such as dancers, temple priests, and so forth.
Through those respective skillful means, they gather sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), causing them to aspire to supreme enlightenment.
To observe the precepts against taking life, taking what is not given, false speech, sexual misconduct, and wrong views—these are called the five precept categories for laypeople.
A bodhisattva should accept and uphold these virtuous precepts as they have been taught, train well in them, and possess full faith, following the training grounds of the Buddhas of the past;
that is, learning by following the example of the Buddhas of antiquity. This is because they abide in existence.

Because those who possess wisdom and skillful means are able to attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, auspicious, and unconditioned aggregate of precepts (śīlaskandha), and because students reflect upon and train in them, they are attained.
Thus, the exposition of the ten characteristics of the precepts is complete.
Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying: "I pray that you will explain the precepts of the ten paths of wholesome action regarding the severance of the roots.

How is it that a bodhisattva, while possessing sovereign power over a royal throne and surrounded by palaces, men, women, kinsmen, parents, and the enjoyment of celestial delights, does not commit transgressions?
The intent of this question is: what further factors can harm the roots of these precepts so that wholesome dharmas do not arise?"
"Extreme" means that one possesses all harmful [conditions] for wholesome qualities. The meaning of the question is: how can one remain within worldly phenomena without being defiled by them?
However, for the sake of sentient beings, a bodhisattva must always remain in the world;

it is necessary to possess the skillful means of ethical discipline (*śīla*) so as not to harm their wholesome qualities. After the Buddha had praised this, he commanded them to listen attentively and then spoke: "Bodhisattvas..."
Regarding the certainty of mastery and the certainty of skillfulness: it is said that all evils bring about one's own ruin, while all virtues arise from them;
this is what constitutes intrinsic goodness (*svabhāva-kuśala*). There are two types of Bodhisattvas: the householder and the renunciant.

As for those who live as householders, they receive the five precepts as previously described. Even while possessing sovereign power over a royal throne, they do not hinder the practice of the Bodhisattva path by means of these five [precepts].

"Affairs" refers to the various skillful means (*upāya*). "Time" refers to the mastery in gathering [beings] at the proper moment for the pursuit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is called the perfection of skillful means.

"Place" refers to manifesting in various artistic venues, such as dance halls, temples, and so forth, in accordance with those skillful means to gather sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);
this is the meaning of the scriptural passage. "Time" means observing the proper and improper times, not waiting [indulgently] and never missing the opportunity, just like the tide of the ocean.

Furthermore, "according to the region" means responding to whatever dharma is appropriate for a particular place in order to enter the Path; this accords with the *loka-vyavahāra-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint).

Because they are fully endowed with the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*), they exercise various forms of sovereign action to gather in sentient beings and establish them on the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
This is not like those who observe the five precepts without skillful means, who merely restrict themselves and aspire solely to protect their own selves.
Because they embrace all beings by observing their benefit, they enter various paths;

even entering celestial shrines themselves, they demonstrate to their fellow students what those students have learned, gradually leading them with right view. Since such skillful means are boundless, the benefit is likewise limitless.
They then lead others into the Buddha-way by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). These four methods of attraction are like the Jewel Cloud Bodhisattva.

This is explained in detail in the *Saṃyuktāgama* and other scriptures. If a lay bodhisattva upholds the five precepts—namely, refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and wrong views—and maintains them through skillful means (*upāya*), then regarding all other matters, they remain unimpeded, solely intent on leading others into the Buddha-way.
By taking these five precepts as the foundation, one is able to achieve omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Because it is the stage of the Tathāgata, it is said that one "attains the nature of untainted precepts and achieves [enlightenment]. By abiding in this, one possesses both wisdom and skillful means; this constitutes the training (*śikṣāpada*).
This fundamental nature is fully endowed with all myriad virtues, and these precepts are precisely the unconditioned precepts (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*).

To explain this again, it is no different from what was stated previously; this is merely a restatement because what was not yet clear before has now been made manifest. As for the aforementioned "Bodhisattva":
There are two types, namely the lay and the ordained. These five precepts are those observed by the lay bodhisattva;

because they remain in the world amidst various affairs, by observing these five precepts and because these five precepts are endowed with wisdom and skillful means, the afflictions and evil karma cannot harm them. By this cause and condition, [the goal] is accomplished.
The Buddha himself said in a sutra: "Thus, one who possesses good precepts, practices them well, and is endowed with faith—this is an exhortation to uphold [the precepts].
The intent of this exhortation to uphold them is that the Buddha cites the Buddhas of the past as witnesses;

because the Buddhas of the past upheld these five precepts, they remained within the world, engaging in the various activities of sentient beings to gather them in, yet without hindering their own practice, thereby attaining success.
The Buddha’s precepts, which are the untainted self-nature endowed with the perfection of ten thousand virtues, also arise from this. As for the possession of skillful means and wisdom:
these skillful means consist of the body seal (mudrā), the oral mantra, and the mental visualization of the deity in samādhi;
taking these as the means, there is furthermore sublime wisdom, which is to contemplate these three matters as arising from conditions and thereby entering into the true reality (dharmatā).
Therefore, one attains Buddhahood by suddenly perfecting the myriad practices.
Just as in the Śrāvaka sūtras, the reason a layperson observes the five precepts is to protect body and speech so as to enter the vision of the truths (satyadarśana); here, too, it is the same.
By using these phrases of the five precepts as a skillful means to protect oneself, one attains the practice of the mantra and perceives the truths.
Not only do lay bodhisattvas [observe these], but all those who have gone forth also practice these five points together.
Furthermore, there are four root prohibitions which those who cultivate the practice of mantra (vidyā-mantra) must not violate even at the cost of their lives.
What are the four? First, slandering the various dharmas; second, abandoning the bodhicitta; third, being stingy with the Dharma; and fourth, causing affliction [to others].
Why is it that harming sentient beings is so? Because these four are intrinsically defiled and do not constitute the upholding of the bodhisattva precepts.
The following verse states that this nature is defiled because it does not constitute the upholding of the bodhisattva precepts; this refers to the preceding scriptural passage.
For a practitioner of the mantra path (*mantracaryā*), these four grave prohibitions are equivalent to the four root offenses of a śrāvaka. If one commits these...

This means that the root of wholesome karma is severed, such that no meritorious qualities whatsoever can arise—just as in the Śrāvaka sūtras there are analogies such as the cutting down of a *tāla* tree.
However, within the Mahāyāna, there is no sense of permanent severance; rather, one receives a new self, which is precisely what "arising" means.
If one commits this offense, one is no longer a Bodhisattva, just as a Śrāvaka who commits a grave offense is no longer a Bhikṣu.
The reason for this is that these four matters, within the Dharma of the Bodhisattva, are capable of defiling one's nature and obstructing all merits so that they cannot arise;
therefore, even at the cost of losing one's life, one must not violate them.
Next, the Buddha further provides scriptural evidence, stating that all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have attained [enlightenment] only by being endowed with wisdom.
To practice these precepts and thereby attain the training for unsurpassed bodhi and achieve great *siddhi* is the fruit of sublime conduct, namely the realization of bodhi.

"Without outflows" refers to the nature-precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*). The phrase "the skillful means of departing from the spheres of knowledge" also refers to the scriptural passage concerning the entry of the śrāvaka great heroes; the intended meaning is that the Buddha [taught this] for the sake of the śrāvakas.
It is heard that they also speak of the complete precepts, the four grave offenses, and so forth;

however, because this was a provisional teaching intended to guide those of a certain class with inferior faculties, it is not the ultimate truth. Therefore, these precepts lack both skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
If one can enter the study of the Mahāyāna and cultivate the sublime precepts, only then will one be able to fully possess the Bodhisattva precepts. Great!
The term "valiant one" refers to Vajrapāṇi, who was addressed as follows:

The Buddha’s purpose in bringing inferior sentient beings—who lack the aspiration for the Mahāyāna—into the house of the elder, rather than leaving them long in the impoverished village to exhaust themselves in vain without gaining anything, was to lead them in through this Dharma;
it was not the Buddha’s original intent for his appearance in the world.
Therefore, this precept is not the Buddha’s wisdom—the untainted, inconceivable precept;
rather, once one enters the Buddha’s untainted wisdom, it is realized through self-attestation alone. (The above concludes the "Chapter on Receiving the Training in Expedient Means.")
Next is the nineteenth chapter, "The Explanation of the Generation of the Hundred-Syllable Mantra.
At that time, Vairocana Buddha surveyed the great assembly and spoke this teaching of Amogha, which brings accomplishment according to one's desires;
it is the sovereign of all mantras, the king of mantras, the guide of mantras, and possesses great majesty.

The Virtuous One, abiding in the perfection of the three *samayas*, (at this stage of abiding, as if seated, lying, or standing upon a chariot), addressed the Great Powerful Vajrapāṇi with exquisite words: "O diligent hero, listen with one-pointed mind!
All mantras and the Teacher of Mantras shall immediately abide in the Samādhi Born of Wisdom; according to their respective desires, all mantras [shall manifest] of themselves."
The Mantra Master of Great Majesty, having spoken thus to complete the three samayas, said:
"Although the various expedient means of mantras have been explained above, they are not yet exhaustive; therefore, I shall speak further.
I observe this great assembly once more to illuminate their mental capacities, for within this multitude, all are universally upright and sincere, and capable [of receiving the teaching]."

Furthermore, he observed them again in order to preach to those who were vessels for the Dharma; moreover, he did so by empowering them with inconceivable supernatural power (*acintya-rddhi*) so that they might attain the power of the Dharma and become capable of hearing this sublime teaching.
The mantras have already been explained extensively above; this is the heart of the single-syllable mantra, which is the most supreme among all mantras.
First, one should know that this is the mantra of the *Amogha* (Non-empty) teaching.
It is called "non-empty" because for all sentient beings, whatever they see, hear, touch, or cognize, there is nothing that passes them by in vain; they are all destined for unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, it is able to fulfill their virtuous vows, even unto the great vow for the bodhi of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is able to fulfill all needs, just as a great jewel king atop a high banner satisfies everyone;
therefore, it is called "Unfailing" (Amogha). All who are masters of mantras are like the Tathāgata, who is the sovereign of all dharmas and possesses mastery over them;
this mantra is likewise so, for it has attained mastery over all mantras. By means of this—
The causal conditions are also called the King of Mantras and the Guide of Mantras.
Just as many people entering the ocean rely upon a guide until they reach their destination and obtain a great hoard of jewels to bring back for their own use, so too is this King of Mantras;
he is the guide of all mantras. This guide is the Savior of the World.
It is said that this mantra is identical to the Buddha. Furthermore, the power of the Tathāgata’s great majesty, sovereignty, and secret supernatural faculties all arise from this.
If a practitioner can practice according to the Dharma, they likewise become identical to this mantra and attain such [realization].
Regarding the "three samayas of sitting," this refers to the three samayas of body, speech, and mind.
The mantra of the mouth, the dharma-mudrā of the body, and the principal deity (honzon) of the mind—further inquire into the meaning of their seats;
it is now said that these are the Vajra-seats. The "perfection of the three dharmas" refers to the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. The teaching is that which has been explained above;
here, beneath the teaching, these three dharmas are fulfilled to ultimate completion without remainder. The Buddha uttered a wondrous sound and addressed Vajrapāṇi.
Vajrapāṇi, I shall now speak this Dharma; you, a hero of great power and diligence, listen with a single-minded attention.
Why was it not explained earlier when the Chapter on Mantras was taught, but only now? [This is] for the sake of those who, being deluded, search through the text of the sūtra.
If the Buddha possesses great compassion, why did he not explain it immediately instead of confusing sentient beings? The answer is as follows:

It is not that I am stingy; rather, I say this because there are various teachers in the world who, relying on their own sharp faculties and the power of analytical wisdom, explain the common characteristics of all phenomena and master the literal words.
Yet, due to their prideful minds, they do not rely upon a teacher but instead arbitrarily search through the scriptures, wishing to practice them on their own.
However, these teachings are subtle and profound; if one does not rely on a clear guide, one will ultimately be unable to achieve success. Furthermore—
Fearing that those who act recklessly might harm themselves or others, he concealed the text so that they could not reach an understanding through their own intellectual power alone;
thus, they would abandon their arrogance and rely upon a teacher. For this reason, and so that the conditions for the destruction of the Dharma would not arise, it was necessary to act in this way.
When the Buddha was about to speak this mantra, the Guide immediately entered the samādhi called Skillful Wisdom-Arising.
This samādhi is so named because it can give rise to the Tathāgata’s skillful wisdom of the universal gate.
Regarding the mantra of "Hundred Lights Shining Everywhere," it means that from this single syllable, the light of a hundred dharmas flows forth everywhere.
However, if one were to translate this character as "pervading" (bian), it would not be entirely accurate to its meaning; if translated as "emitting light" (fang guang), it is likewise [incomplete].
The meaning is also not yet exhaustive; it is generally intended to signify "pervasive emergence. It is from this that the light of a hundred majestic powers emerges.
This mantra was spoken after first taking refuge in all Buddhas.
The Sūtra says: "Vajrapāṇi, this mantra is the Savior of the World; the Buddha of Great Majestic Virtue is himself the Muni, the Sovereign of All Dharmas.
The Buddha told Vajrapāṇi: "This entire mantra is the Savior of the World;
its accomplishment of great majestic virtue is the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Muni, the Sovereign of All Dharmas (meaning, regarding all dharmas, he is himself...)"

[He] destroys the darkness of all ignorance like the orb of the sun appearing everywhere; he is my own essential body, a Great Muni who, through empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), manifests as a divine transformation (*vikurvaṇa*).

[The original text says "manifesting transformations," meaning he creates transformations. He benefits sentient beings according to their desires (benefiting and enriching them according to whatever they wish).
[The above is not required. He brings benefit to all sentient beings, even to the point of causing everything to follow their thoughts and wishes.
"Arising" means that whatever the mind thinks or wishes for, it causes that very thing to arise; it is able to perform all such supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

This is the unsurpassed phrase. Therefore, among all categories (meaning, regarding all desires, meaning, among all objects of desire), and regarding all matters, there is nothing like seeking this phrase of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Consequently, one should [attain] a body that is pure in every respect.
"Free from all hindrances, one should constantly and diligently cultivate the phrase 'seeking the purity of the body of perfect enlightenment.
Being free from hindrances means that the practitioner purifies their own body, causing it to be free from all obstacles as they engage in practice.
'In every way' means cultivating within all types of skillful means and forms. It is like the sun's orb appearing, equally seen by all, which shatters the darkness of all ignorance."
"From this time forth, I shall empower the Great Sage to manifest transformations for the benefit of sentient beings;
until all such beings have conceived the thought [of awakening], I shall constantly perform these supreme transformations.
For this reason, one should diligently cultivate all various skillful means according to principle and act to purify the self. This is the aforementioned scriptural passage.
This mantra is the Muni who possesses mastery over all dharmas; it is another name for Vairocana.
The light of wisdom and skillful means of this mantra can shatter all the darkness of ignorance, just as when the great sun rises, all obscurity vanishes of its own accord.
It causes all sentient beings to suddenly eliminate all their ignorance.
"Furthermore, you should know that this syllable is empowered by me; it is identical to me and no different from me.

'I' refers to the Buddha speaking of himself. By means of this gateway of mantras, I universally manifest form-bodies according to the various types [of beings], pervading all classes of sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, appearing as whatever kind of body they joyfully behold, able to manifest them everywhere at once."
His body manifests in accordance with the desires of his mind, not merely by manifesting his physical form alone;

for his mental vows and thoughts are immeasurable and diverse, such that even within a single moment, he is able to satisfy all immeasurable inclinations and desires—hence it is said, "the arousal of wisdom.
Furthermore, because he gives rise to the capacity for others to enter the Way, it is called "the arousal of wisdom."
This is the supreme phrase for abiding in the state of abiding; therefore, one should diligently practice and study these various skillful means.
If one practices them, one immediately attains the pure self. Herein, "the pure self" is Vairocana.
Now, in the very center of this wheel of syllables (akṣaracakra), one places this King of Mantras; next, on the outer wheel, there are twelve syllables.
This refers to the twelve samādhi-sounds from *i* to *au*. Next, the outer wheel is arranged with one hundred syllables:
first, twenty-five beginning with the letter *a*; then another twenty-five; then another twenty-five;
and finally another twenty-five. Among these, the five syllables *oṃ*, *āḥ*, *hūṃ*, *na*, and *ma* constitute the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).

Because these points pervade all places, they are arranged in the same manner. (Furthermore, another interpretation at a different time states: "These five characters [are placed] outside, while the twelve characters are arranged in a circle. Question:

If one arranges them in five layers, it is also permissible for these twenty-five characters to constitute the first wheel, the next [twelve] the second wheel, the next [five] the third wheel, and the remaining [three] the fourth wheel.
(Question: *Note: The original text contains parenthetical remarks and questions inserted by the commentator or editor regarding alternative arrangements of the seed syllables.*

The intention [of this] is not yet exhausted; the sequence of its characters rotates to the right day by day. [The preceding section on the "Chapter of One Hundred Characters" is concluded. Next, this chapter explains the fruits of this King of Mantras.]
Next, the twentieth chapter, the Chapter on the Correspondence with the Fruit of the Hundred Syllables:
"O Lord of Secrets, if one attains entry into the stage of the empowerment of the Great Compassion of Perfect Enlightenment, one will see for oneself that one abides in the three samaya-words.
O Lord of Secrets, if one enters this manifestation of the form of the dhāraṇī of the empowerment of the Great Wisdom of the Bhagavat—"
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, performed buddha-activities by appearing before all sentient beings and proclaiming the three samaya-syllables.
Then, Vairocana addressed the Secret Lord Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, enters the stage of the empowerment of great wisdom and attains the three samayas, he brings body, speech, and mind into equality."

Regarding the passage: "For the sake of unifying them, while abiding in the view of self, the Lord of Mysteries manifests this Buddha-activity as the form of the *dhāraṇī* for the empowerment of great wisdom (*mahājñānābhiṣeka*) upon entering Buddhahood"—this refers to the aforementioned scriptural text. The stage of the empowerment of great wisdom is precisely the eleventh stage of the Tathāgata.
It is by abiding in the eleventh stage and entering the empowerment of great wisdom that one is able to perform [these deeds].
For the sake of the Tathāgata’s work, this ground of great wisdom is transformed into the body of *dhāraṇī* to perform Buddha-activities;
by means of this, one is able to perform Buddha-activities for the benefit of all sentient beings.

As for the form of *dhāraṇī*, it refers to the synthesis of the preceding wheels of mantras into a single body, thereby constituting the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*) body. This is because one abides in this totality.
Because he maintains his body, he manifests a form pleasing to behold before all sentient beings and preaches the Dharma according to their capacities without error,
so that they may equally enter the Buddha-wisdom.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in accordance with the three samaya-phrases of the buddha-activities for all sentient beings, proclaimed the secret lord’s abiding in the wheel of syllables of my speech;
this miraculous transformation extensively and infinitely pervades the world-systems, being the gate of universal purity.
Such is the nature by which all sentient beings are made joyful, and it is likewise the gate of the dharma-realm manifesting according to the various types [of beings].
Now, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, who is distinct from the realm of empty space, pervades all worlds and diligently performs the Buddha-work; O Secret Lord,
it is not because he is a sentient being that you can know the Buddha— this is because the marks of his wheel of speech flow forth,

and by means of the garland of ornaments of his wondrous awakened voice, he produces the images of Buddhas, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy according to their dispositions and desires.
Having thus spoken as above in the current passage, the Buddha next addressed Vajrapāṇi:
"You should contemplate the wheel of my speech," which refers to the sphere of the syllable-wheel (*akṣara-cakra*) of the Buddha-dhāraṇī-body.
Through the empowerment of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*), the Buddha caused the great assembly to behold the sphere of the wheel of his speech, extending far and wide beyond mere limits.
The gate of purity in immeasurable worlds manifests according to the original nature of all sentient beings;
the gate of the Dharma-realm that accords with their various types causes them to give rise to joy.

Just as the present Śākyamuni World-Honored One pervades the inexhaustible realm of empty space, diligently performing Buddha-work in all lands within great assemblies, it is not only Vajrapāṇi who attains this vision.
The entire great assembly may likewise behold this inconceivable and wondrously sublime realm. Why is this so?
Because this body of great wisdom eternally abides in quiescent extinction, transcending all causes and conditions; it is not an object within the sphere of the conceptual mind.
Apart from the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha’s spiritual power, it is not within the domain of any bodhisattva. Since the Buddha has...
Having manifested this, he addressed them, saying: "You should now observe the realm of my wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*), which is immeasurable in its breadth and length.
'Length' means that it exceeds what humans can reach; 'height' refers here to its loftiness.

Its breadth extends horizontally throughout the realms of all sentient beings, and its height reaches vertically to the very limits of the Buddha-realm; therefore, it is called 'broad and long. Such a body, broad and long as it is, pervades everywhere."
How could all these things be obtained? They are manifested from this single syllable, the King of Mantras.
Through the body of a single mantra, all bodies are revealed; through the phonemes of a single mantra, wondrous sounds emerge and pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
and through the mind of the deity of a single mantra, the realm of all wisdom is universally displayed.
Śākyamuni is precisely this body of Amoghadarśin, which enters universally into the world to perform the buddha-work;

therefore, that which is shown here is the body of Muni. When the Buddha causes the buddha-work to be performed, it is this Śākyamuni who emerges from the syllable-wheel of Vairocana. Yet, being neither two nor distinct, they both pervade all places.
Since these syllables are identical to the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) in their fundamental non-arising, one should know that the body of the hundred syllables is likewise so.
The distinction is this: the body of the Tathāgata’s three samayas pervades the world and extends throughout the ten directions of empty space;
there is no place within empty space that it does not pervade. One should know that empty space itself is immeasurable.
The body is likewise thus, performing the work of a Buddha throughout its vast and boundless extent. O Lord of Secrets,
no sentient beings can know that from this wheel-mark of the World-Honored One’s speech, there flow forth the various Buddhas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones,
such as the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Citta*, the *Sughoṣa*, and the *Buddhaghoṣavyūhahāra*, all emerging from the *Garbhadhātu*.
The adornment of the images (forms) of the Buddhas refers to adorning their forms with speech; these Buddha-forms arise from the *citta-garbha* (the womb of the mind).
Vast and boundless, they perform the Buddha-activities. That which is not known by sentient beings is this very wheel of syllables (*akṣara-cakra*) of the Buddha;
it is not the domain of bodhisattvas, and unless one possesses supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*), one cannot perceive it.
How much less could sentient beings know the places from which they were born, or the realms to which they go and where they dwell?
Among all vocal sounds, the Buddha is supreme; he is adorned with the sixty kinds of qualities and so forth, yet in essence, he is adorned by the signless (*animitta*).
From his mind, he manifests births, assuming bodies according to the various types of beings, because he abides in this Samādhi of Sublime Sound.
He manifests universally before them, causing them to attain joy and faith-and-understanding according to their own natures.
Hereafter, regarding the "Womb-Treasury Adorned with Subtle Sounds": it is called the "Womb-Treasury" because it arises from a single syllable.

Taking this single syllable as the womb, that which arises from it serves as its reflected image, just as when a mirror is perfectly clear and pure, it faces all forms; yet the forms themselves do not [enter the mirror].
The mirror does not come, nor does it go; yet, through the harmony of causes and conditions, the image appears vividly.
It is neither born nor extinguished, neither one nor different, neither coming nor going, neither permanent nor discontinuous. It is identical to that substance and is inconceivable.
The images of the Tathāgata are likewise: without thought and unconditioned, yet they respond to all things, manifesting in accordance with their minds.
Attaining joy, they manifest the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings; indeed, with the single speech-sound of one Buddha, one can produce all Buddha-works.
If even those whose six sense organs are purified can fill the trichiliocosm with a single sublime sound, how much more so the Tathāgata’s six sense organs, which are ultimately perfect and pure?

At that time, the World-Honored One, within the gateways of the ocean of immeasurable worlds—which is also the meaning of "mouth"—earnestly exhorted the realization of Bodhi through the formation of Bodhi within the Dharma-realm;

he brought forth the birth of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows. Therein, within the ocean of the lineage of this world adorned with a matrix and with its ground strewn with exquisite flowers, he took birth and purified [all beings] through various gates of essential nature and purity.
"Abiding in the manifestation of the Buddha within the bodhimanda of the buddha-field" refers to the aforementioned scriptural passage.
"The gateways of the immeasurable oceans of worlds for the empowerment of this great wisdom" signifies the points of entry from which one enters.
The "gateways of the immeasurable oceans of worlds" refers to the gates through which all streams flow and enter. By knowing these immeasurable [realms]...
Because it is the gateway to the oceans of worlds, one diligently cultivates bodhi; yet this bodhi is not merely a single bodhi, but extends throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Because sentient beings are immeasurable, the dharma-realm is immeasurable; thus, one now causes all to universally attain bodhi.
Having already passed through differences and entered the dharma-realm, this is the practice of great bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, within the Dharma-realm of the gateways to the ocean of immeasurable worlds, earnestly exhorted, inspired,

and brought to fulfillment the Bodhisattva practices and vows of Samantabhadra (Samantabhadra being the merit of the Tathāgata). By giving rise to these Bodhisattva practices and vows of Samantabhadra and through this empowerment,
he manifested signs as described below, within this matrix where exquisite flowers are spread upon the ground.

Regarding the term "this world," it refers to this Sahā world. Within the ocean of spiritual lineages (*gotrasamudra*)—where "lineage" refers to the place of rebirth and "ocean" signifies being uninterrupted, vast, and manifold—one takes birth.

Through various gates of purification of these lineages, one purifies Buddha-fields, manifests the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and performs Buddha-activities (which means that through empowerment, one performs Buddha-activities such that they are nowhere not pervasive).
Furthermore, awakening (bodhi) is no different from what was described above; entering equally into the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is precisely the practice of great awakening.
To set forth such a practice is the practice of Samantabhadra; to give rise to such a vow is the vow of Samantabhadra.
It is for this purpose that the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind [on awakening]. As for the "flowered ground," it is like being purified and leveled.
The ground is swept and sprinkled for purification, and various flowers—pleasant to the eye, nose, mouth, and body—are scattered about;
it is surrounded by a dignified and majestic arrangement, and one sits upon it. Now, this heart-ground of the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha) is also like this.
The "womb" (*garbha*) is the place of initial arising; that is, the place where the Tathāgata arises, because it is born from the Tathāgata-nature, and from the Tathāgata-nature it is born.
This means that it arises from this very syllable. Such an arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is precisely the first stage (*bhūmi*).
"Ocean" refers to the ocean of the Tathāgata’s lineage (*gotra*); from this true nature (*dharmatā*), all the merits of the Tathāgata arise.
"Womb" means that taking this as the fundamental basis, by abiding in the conduct of Samantabhadra, the Tathāgata emerges from the ocean of the Tathāgata-nature.
Within this embryonic treasury (*garbha*), all parts of the six sense faculties of all Tathāgatas gradually become fully perfected.
This Universal Gate Body (*samantamukhakāya*) accords with the various differences in the mental activities, dispositions, and desires of sentient beings;
it purifies their minds through pure and wondrous gates. That which cannot be fully grasped or comprehended—this very purification of the mind—is itself the adornment of all Buddha-lands.
Furthermore, when a practitioner thus abides in the first bodhisattva stage, they are immediately able to universally manifest throughout all worlds by means of the gateway of the letter A,
manifesting the body of a Tathāgata seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and purifying the wheel of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

They are also able to fully comprehend all phrases— namely, the realization of Buddhahood— and are further able to fulfill their vows according to their desires and inclinations, such that these never go in vain.

Therefore, the subsequent sutra states: "Furthermore, one who aspires to the state of *samyaksambodhi* (perfectly complete enlightenment) knows that the mind is immeasurable, and thus knows that the body is immeasurable;

seeking it, they delight in the immeasurability of the mind and know the immeasurability of the body; realizing the immeasurability of the body, they know the immeasurability of wisdom and realize the immeasurability of wisdom.
Furthermore, those who joyfully seek this again cultivate the bodhisattva path; this is precisely the Buddha."
This is the matter: because sentient beings perceive that path, they are immediately inspired to train in the Way.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "joyfully and diligently seeking perfect universal knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*): to know that the mind is immeasurable is to know that the body is immeasurable;
to know that the body is immeasurable is to accomplish immeasurable wisdom; and to know that wisdom is immeasurable is to realize the immeasurability of sentient beings.

Knowing that sentient beings are immeasurable and realizing that space is immeasurable, one attains this; O Lord of Mysteries, through the immeasurability of the mind, one attains the four immeasurables and thereby realizes perfect enlightenment.
Knowing that sentient beings are immeasurable, one immediately knows that the realm of space is immeasurable.
O Lord of Mysteries, by means of the immeasurability of the mind, one attains the four kinds of immeasurables (namely, [compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity]).

[The phrase] "Mind, the remainder, body, wisdom, sentient beings, and space" refers to the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment, the possession of the ten powers (*daśabala*), the subduing of the four Māras, and the lion’s roar, and so forth.

Having accomplished the ten powers, subdued the four Māras, and attained fearlessness through the lion’s roar—this is the supreme locus of training for all heroic ones of wisdom, consisting of one hundred gates taught within the hearts of all Buddhas. This concludes the aforementioned scriptural passage.
The mental discourse [states]: because one enters this gate of the empowerment of great wisdom and abides in the lineage of the bodhisattvas, one immediately knows that the mind is immeasurable;
because one knows the mind is immeasurable, one immediately knows that all bodies are immeasurable;

because one knows bodies are immeasurable, one immediately knows that wisdom is immeasurable; and because one knows wisdom is immeasurable, one immediately knows that space is immeasurable. For this reason:
What is this? All phenomena are thoroughly understood through the mind; thus, because the phenomena are infinite, one knows that the body is also infinite.
The body manifested through conditions is the wisdom of the gate of responding to capacities and delivering beings;
arising in accordance with those [capacities], it is likewise infinite, each and every instance being equal to space. This is because the body, wisdom, sentient beings, and space are all infinite.
These are called the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*). Because these immeasurables arise from the mind, they are termed the "four immeasurable minds" (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*).

If one attains these four immeasurable minds, one achieves perfect enlightenment, possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*), subdues the four māras, and is able to roar the fearless lion’s roar; all such matters result from abiding in these four immeasurable minds.
Because one attains accomplishment by abiding in the supreme dharmapadas of all phenomena, this is the fruit of the *nāma-siddhi*.
These hundred gates are not spoken by me alone; all Buddhas likewise speak them in this way.
This refers to the "valiant hero" of the aforementioned ten powers and other virtues; that is, the Lord of Secrets (*Guhyakādhipati*). Thus, he is the most supreme of diligent heroes.

The phrase "The Awakened One" refers to the mind taught by all Buddhas within the hundredfold gates of training (the intent being that one becomes a Buddha by training in this mind of the hundredfold gates).
The above constitutes the "Fruit: Enjoyment of the Hundred Syllables," which means that one enjoys [the practice] according to whichever gate is appropriate for each individual.
Next, the twenty-first chapter, "The Accomplishment of the Hundred-Syllable Position of the Mantra.
At that time, the Lord of Secrets Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying: "How marvelous, World-Honored One!

[The following] verses describe the mantra of the Savior of the World (referring to the Sovereign King of the Hundred Gates), which is capable of generating all mantras. This is the mantra of the Savior of the World."
Regarding the statement, "How are the various mantras born of knowledge? By whom, where, and from what great sage were these mantras produced?
How were they spoken?"—all this was spoken by the Great Hero, the Grantor of Boons.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Lord of Secrets, having attained what he had never before experienced, addressed him, saying: "It is marvelous, World-Honored One, that you have spoken this."
The Mantra Savior is none other than the Buddha. Just as the Buddha is the great refuge and place of protection for all sentient beings, so too is this mantra;
among all mantras, it is equal to the Savior and serves as the place of protection for those various mantras. Just as the Buddha is the destination for all, so is this...
The mantra is likewise; it is the place of refuge for all mantras.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, this Great Holy One was able, by means of a single syllable, to manifest immeasurable mantra-bodies, with distinctions of body, speech, and mind, displaying various forms according to the dispositions of sentient beings, preaching various dharmas, and manifesting various supernatural transformations. Because of these [manifestations], he asked: "What is this mantra?"
Furthermore, who realizes birth? In what place does birth occur? These are the three matters asked about (further questioning regarding what has not yet been understood).
The Great Muni praised them, saying: "How is it known? First, by whom is it known? Second, in what place—meaning from where is it obtained? Third, who produces the various mantras?
The previous question was "by whom can this be known," while the subsequent question is "who is the one that produces [them]? O Great Hero!

This is the Buddha; he is the one among those who speak all vows who speaks the supreme vow. "Supreme among those who speak vows" means that he possesses omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and is the one who grants vows.
This is a praise of the Buddha’s virtue: because he is able to grant all vows and fulfill them, he is named the "Vow-Granting One" (*varada*).
Thus, having requested the Buddha to speak, [the text says]: "The Great Dharma-Master, the Sovereign Muni, is fulfilled."

When he had spoken thus, the World-Honored One, the Great Dharma-Sovereign, the Muni, Vairocana Buddha of the All-Pervading Dharmadhātu, the Omniscient One, addressed him, saying: "Excellent, Mahāsattva!
O Virtuous Vajrapāṇi, I shall explain everything for you—that is, I shall explain it all to you—the most rare secret, the essential mystery of all Buddhas, which the non-Buddhists do not [know]."
One who is able to know the Maṇḍala of Compassion Born from Empowerment for all Mahāyāna [which is the empowerment of the maṇḍala arising from this],

who is gentle, endowed with virtuous conduct, and always compassionate in benefiting others— such a person, though observing Bodhi through their karmic connection, will never be able to see it (it is unattainable to see). When the Buddha,
wishing to proclaim this heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) that pervades the entire world, employed his spiritual power...
By the empowerment of his power, [the Buddha’s voice] pervaded the entire Dharma realm, and with these words he addressed Vajrapāṇi:

"O Sarvajña Vairocana, well done, well done! O Great Being Vajrapāṇi, O Noble One, you have spoken my all-secrets, the foremost among rarities, the most secret of all Buddhas, this scripture that transcends all heterodox paths."
The Buddha praised Vajrapāṇi, saying, "Excellent, excellent, O Great Virtuous One, Wielder of the Vajra! You are endowed with ten thousand virtues.
This Dharma is the secret among all secrets of all Tathāgatas; it stands at the very pinnacle of all secret treasuries."
That which is collectively guarded over by them and not recklessly given to others is the foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-attain Dharma.
Now, the secrets of these various Dharmas cannot be known by any non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, there are two kinds of non-Buddhists:
first, the various worldly non-Buddhists; second, those who are "non-Buddhists" within the Buddha-dharma. This is because, although they have entered...
Within the Buddha-dharma, those who have not yet been able to know the Tathāgata’s secrets are still acting with minds of false views;
because their principles lie outside [the truth], they are also called "outsiders" (*bāhya*). This Dharma is something that the two kinds of non-Buddhists cannot know;

within this Buddha-dharma, these "non-Buddhists" are actually those of the Two Vehicles. Since the Buddha does not falsely bestow it upon others, he has long remained silent regarding this essential point, waiting for the proper opportunity before imparting it.

Who, then, is fit to hear this Dharma? Therefore, it is said next: "If there is a person who has attained entry into the Great Vehicle and received the empowerment of the arising of great compassion, only such a person is fit to hear it; otherwise, they shall not."
Next, one must further distinguish them; although they may be led into the initiation (*abhiṣeka*), they must be examined.
If a person’s nature is gentle, upright, and honest, and is endowed with all virtuous conduct, only such a person may be led into the rite of initiation.
Furthermore, those who possess constant compassion are fit to be led into the maṇḍala. "Constant compassion" refers, for example, to someone like this: [text continues].
Compassion may exist at one time and not at another; it may exist in one place and not in another;
or it may exist toward those who are dear while being absent toward those who are enemies. Now, however, it is not so: compassion is always present at all times and in all places.
Furthermore, it is vast, universal, and impartial. Only such a person may be led into the consecration (*abhiṣeka*); once the consecration has been obtained, only then may they hear [the teachings].
This is not like the sutras that are commonly circulated. Within these verses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one should also explain the criteria for selecting those who may be cited.
Furthermore, even those who possess conditions for contemplation are not permitted to hear this Dharma. The Buddha-dharma is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and free from all conditions (*pratyaya*).
If there were marks or conditions, it would not be free from the views of annihilationism or eternalism; therefore, it is not so.
Having now heard this Dharma, what is meant by "being without conditions"? Does it mean that all dharmas are utterly non-existent? It is not so.
Although the Buddha-dharma is free from the marks of conditions, through skillful means it is fully endowed with all virtuous merits, inconceivable spiritual powers, and various realms;
thus, it is both form and formlessness, and while being formless, it is complete.
"All marks are precisely non-conditions; being non-conditions, they yet possess all conditions. This does not mean that they are merely empty or simply nothing at all.
"Possessing the great meaning" refers to possessing the great practices and great vows of a Bodhisattva, having given rise to the Great Mind.
It is only for such a person that this may be taught.
Regarding the previous question as to from what [this mantra] arises, the answer now is that it arises from the mind of the Buddha. The "Guide" (nāyaka) is none other than the Buddha.
If one follows the Guide, wherever he dwells, this mantra likewise arises following him; that is to say, it arises from all his limbs.
One who is able to know this is the Great Self (mahātman) within the inner mind; this refers to praising this very mind. Following its...
From the state of one’s own mind up to all sentient beings, it is likewise so:
the Teacher dwells in a most exquisite and perfectly round moon disc upon an eight-petaled lotus born of the mind;
stainless like a mirror, he constantly abides there as the Mantra-Savior, golden-hued and possessing radiant flames that destroy poison, dwelling in samādhi, difficult to behold like the sun.
"To contemplate all sentient beings in the same way" means that this flower pedestal arises from the mind and intention;
it is precisely the contemplation of one's own mind as an eight-petaled lotus. This flower does not arise from any other place, but arises directly from the intention;
thus, the intention and the flower are non-dual and indistinguishable. This flower pedestal is perfectly luminous like the moon, pure and stainless, identical to a perfect mirror.
Since there is nothing else in the world that can serve as a metaphor, only the circular mirror can be used as an illustration to enable one to grasp the meaning and forget the words;
yet in reality, it exceeds that by hundreds of thousands of millions of times and cannot truly be compared to it.
Now, within this circle dwells the World-Savior who possesses great merit, who is golden-colored and endowed with blazing light.
Abiding in the stillness of samādhi, one should contemplate this single-syllable king of mantras.
From this king of mantras, one then contemplates the deity, whether it be the Great Vairocana or another, as explained in the aforementioned yoga methods.

Since the oral instructions were not fully clarified, one should inquire further; however, the details can be found by consulting the full text cited above. "Harm" refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*).

All afflictions have been eliminated, and its majestic radiance is like the combined brilliance of hundreds of thousands of millions of suns—so fierce and intense that even a seven-day-old infant cannot look up at the scorching sun, yet can behold its light; this Buddha-light is likewise.
While all sentient beings may gaze upon the solar disc, they cannot see its essential nature; such is the case with this Buddha-light.
It is also like this. As the Sūtra says: "Constantly, throughout the inside and outside, one universally bestows empowerment;
with such an eye of wisdom, one understands it within the mirror of the mind. It is also possible to take the clarity of the mind as the mirror of the mind.

Because the practitioner of mantras observes this circular mirror with the eye of wisdom, they shall see their own form and color (i.e., they see their own physical body), and the signs of tranquil, perfect awakening will arise.

The body gives rise to the reflected-body; that which is produced by the body serves as the superior condition for the body. The upper part is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and with-outflow (*sāsrava*), while the lower part is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The mind arises from the mind-produced mind, and from that mind, pure mind is produced.

It constantly produces various kinds of self-performed karma (the karma of the defiled *ālayavijñāna* is able to produce pure karma). Impure karma is eliminated, and pure karma manifests; once it has manifested—
The light produced shines universally like lightning.

Next, within that light, a circular radiance appears like a flash of lightning; however, this does not take the meaning of "lightning" itself, but rather takes the sense of a perfect, manifold-colored light.
This perfectly complete light of various colors illuminates all; the mantra-practitioner is thus able to accomplish everything.

The Buddha-activities pervade both the internal and external; one should know them through the mirror-like mind. Here, "mirror" refers to the circular brilliance, and the central Chinese platform should be understood as this mirror.
One should know that this mirror is the mind, and one should know that this mirror is one's own heart.
By what skillful means is it observed and known? It is by the aforementioned skillful means: placing the syllable *raṃ* upon the two eyes with this wisdom.
Because one observes the true mark with the eye of the perfect mirror-like mind, it becomes clearly manifest before one. Who is able to observe it?
It is the practitioner of mantra. This practitioner uses the eye of the syllable *raṃ* and the light of sublime wisdom to observe the mirror of the flower pedestal.
First, performing the external visualization, [the object] appears vividly and distinctly within this perfect luminosity, as if—
From their arrival until their sounds and forms are all seen to be boundless—having thus clearly understood this—one draws them in to become one’s own internal body.
That is to say, one regards the body of Vairocana previously visualized, in its state of tranquil meditative absorption and its boundless majestic radiance, as one's own body;
thus causing one's own body to become identical with that Honored One within the circle of perfect luminosity.
Abiding in stillness, one is identical to that Buddha. Because one is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), yet manifests marks, this is called the "true mark.
The reason for this is that this lotus arises from the mind; first, one places the syllable *ra* upon the eyes and contemplates the mirror of the heart-lotus pedestal.
This is external seeing, and by means of this external seeing, internal seeing is accomplished.

This is because one immediately realizes one's own mind; thus the Sūtra says: "The wisdom-eye observes in this manner. For the practitioner who recites with the wisdom-eye, it is like looking into a mirror to see one's own form and color:
the Buddha’s marks and body appear in profound stillness. From the conditions that give rise to the body, the mind arises;

it is eternally pure, and the various karmas of oneself follow in succession. Its light is like the brilliance of lightning. This refers to the one who upholds the mantra performing all the works of the Buddhas.
If one perceives [the object] as pure, I also say that all activities are performed through the mental intention; this refers to the aforementioned scriptural passage.
What is called "arising" means that the arising of body, speech, and mind occurs first by contemplating the golden color and other attributes of the perfectly luminous Buddha-image.

One should know that this arises from the mind, which draws the outward [perception] inward, such that the body becomes identical to the Buddha’s body-seal (*mudrā*), speech becomes identical to the Buddha’s mantra-voice, and the mind [becomes identical to the Buddha’s wisdom].
The same as the Buddha-mind arises, all arise from the mind; because by giving rise to this very arising one can purify all karma, it is said to be "ever-pure.
The various karmas one has created for oneself refers to being free from all karma. If one is free from all karma, one is then called a Buddha.
If one awakens to and knows it in this way, one is able to universally illumine with a circular light. As for "universally illumining":
This is precisely the performance of Buddha-activities. Adorned by the pervasive illumination of body, speech, and mind, constantly performing all Buddha-activities, one is identical to Vairocana.
Who is able to perform these Buddha-activities? It is the one who upholds the mantra.
All of this is the Buddha’s answer concerning the source from which the mantra of Vajrapāṇi arises; it means that this mantra proceeds from—
If a practitioner’s body, speech, and mind arise in such a manner, knowing this is itself the performance of Buddha-work through internal and external purity.

As the Sūtra says: "One's own karma is itself Buddha-work. This refers to the universal manifestation of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), or the demonstration of practicing the Bodhisattva path in various places, the eight phases of attaining Buddhahood, and the infinite and boundless deeds of previous births (*jātaka*). To summarize the essential point: [it is the realization that one's own actions are the work of the Buddha.]
All that has been said is the Tathāgata’s own karma. If one can know it thus, this is the attainment of Buddhahood.

For the holder of mantras who dwells in the stages prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) through the sequential skillful means of contemplation, this mantra practice involves the dependent origination of the body;
there is nothing more excellent to arise, and nothing more excellent or different from the Buddha. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Those who see [this] attain purity."
Hearing this teaching is likewise so; those who see, hear, touch, or know it all attain complete purification. Herein, the character *na* (能) contains many meanings:
it signifies that which is capable of accomplishing all things according to one’s thoughts. Next, "light" refers to the radiance of lightning;
"that" refers to the practitioner of mantras performing all the deeds of the Buddhas. If purified, I too declare that they perform all things.
The same applies to mental formations (*manasikāra*).
O Lord of Mysteries, this is the bodhisattva practice of the mantra gateway wherein such a body gives rise to dependent origination;
it is that which is "without Buddha" yet "supreme. This is the scriptural passage. Since the Master’s explanation was not clear, you may inquire further (for now...).
Contemplate their meaning and assign them in sequence. Regarding the "image" and "dependent origination": this refers to contemplating the eight-petaled lotus of the mind;

the perfect luminosity upon the flower is like a pure mirror. Initially, it is not immediately clear, but through the skillful means of the wisdom-eye of the syllable *raṃ*, it gradually becomes clear by itself.
Furthermore, within that circular mirror, one sees one's own body as being identical to all Buddhas and so forth.

Such arising of phenomena is precisely that which arises from causes and conditions. If it arises from conditions, then by contemplating this gate of non-arising, one enters the essential nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Taking the eye of wisdom as the cause and the pure mirror as the object-condition, immeasurable Buddha-activities—such as those of one’s own karma—arise from conditions;
yet in reality, they are not self-born, not born from another, not co-arisen, and not non-existent.
This is because it accords with what is taught in works such as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. This Dharma is supreme and unsurpassed;

it is said to be free from all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), without opposition, and without objective conditions (*ālambana*). Now, does performing this contemplation and so forth not contradict that?
Just as all letters arise from the letter "A," and at the very moment they arise, they are already free from the meaning of "original non-arising" (*anutpāda*), so too is this case.
Thus, by the power of skillful means, the Buddha performs this practice of yoga within the signless and quiescent Dharma;
he teaches various signs within that which is signless, for these very signs are themselves signless.
That which is called a "sign" is a phenomenon produced from conditions; yet in reality, it is not self-produced, nor is it produced by another, being free [from such origins].
Regarding the eight negations, they are precisely the primary signlessness (*animitta*); it is not that one speaks of a separate signlessness that exists apart from signs.
To speak in such a way would be identical to the "emptiness of annihilation" (*uccheda-śūnyatā*) held by outsiders. However, an objection may be raised:

"Now, this contemplation of the various objects such as the body, speech, and mind of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) constitutes 'signs,' and signs are worldly phenomena; how then can you now speak [of them as signless]?"
Why is it that, while the practice of attaining Buddhahood through mantras is thus clarified, the worldly samādhis and the dharmas with signs are further explained?
Therefore, the Buddha subsequently provides analogies to clarify them.
Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries, regarding those who cultivate the bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras, the "reflected image produced from the body" refers to the body itself.
The "arising of images" refers to the defiled body, while the "body" refers to the pure body; that which arises from this cannot exceed the Buddha.
Just as the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are perceived, so too is their intrinsic nature empty, existing only as names.
To grasp [reality] as being identical to empty space and free from all attachment, yet to arise from causes and karma like a reflection—this is precisely the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

This characteristic is itself a worldly phenomenon (*laukika-dharma*). Now, since the Buddha has taught the practice of attaining Buddhahood through mantras, why does he further clarify the dharmas of worldly samādhis that possess characteristics? Therefore, the Buddha next provides an analogy to elucidate this.
Just as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and so forth—these four great elements (mahābhūta)—appropriate their own nature which is empty, being merely names;
that which is grasped is identical to space and free from attachment;

and that which arises from causes and karma is equal to a reflection—this is the meaning of the scriptural passage concerning "characteristics" (*nimitta*) and "images" (*pratibimba*). Here, "cause" is like a mirror and "karma" is like the body.
It is like a reflection appearing when facing a mirror. Just as a practitioner first contemplates external conditions as the clear mirror of the mind, they then draw them into their own body;
if self and other are equal and non-dual, this is the accomplishment of yoga.

Taking one's own body as the cause and those objects as the conditions, through the union of cause and conditions, the reflection arises. If one understands these causes and conditions, one achieves equality.
Who is it that attains perfect awakening? It is the practitioner of mantra. This meaning is as follows:
just as in the world, the five sense faculties and so forth arise from the causes and conditions of the four great elements and karma;

although they possess characteristics and objects, their intrinsic nature is empty and is thus identical to the foremost markless dharma. Now, this yoga is likewise: although it possesses marks, it arises from...
The reality of dependent origination is the very essence of the *A* syllable, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). How can it be difficult to say that this possesses characteristics?
If one realizes this meaning, one attains perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Thus, the Sūtra says:
"Just as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and the four great elements, encompass and sustain themselves, gathering together to attain perfect enlightenment, so too do they [mutually]..."
The dependent origination is uninterrupted; within this continuity, if that which arises through conditions is produced, it is the production of an image.
Therefore, the various root deities are myself, and I am the root deity; they mutually give rise to one another.

Because they arise from one another, from the body there arises the bodily deity, and from the bodily deity there arises the celestial form of the image. This refers to the "pure birth" and "birth-body" mentioned in the preceding scripture.
The cause of my arising is due to seeing the image of one's own body appear when looking into a round mirror;
because one had not previously seen the perfect clarity, the Tathāgata’s purification and attainment of perfect enlightenment occur through mutual dependent origination.

Just as images arise within a mirror and those images mutually produce one another without the causal conditions being severed, so too does a pure body arise from a defiled body of one's own, with those two mutually producing each other.
There is no interruption; even within what appears to be interrupted, there is continuity, which is precisely what is meant by "uninterrupted.
If something arises from conditions, it is like the arising of a reflection; this clarifies that it is not separate from causes and conditions.
Therefore, the deities are myself, and I am the deity; they mutually inspire one another. Because they arise through mutual generation, body gives rise to body (meaning: the pure body is produced).

In this way, the physical body produced from the venerable form-image is called the "defiled body," whereas the production of the pure body is the pure body itself—the form of the Buddha and the Honored One (Bhagavān).
