O Lord of Secrets, those bodhisattvas who have realized the three samayas and practice the path of awakening through the gateway of mantras achieve accomplishment according to the rules of mantra; they are unattached to any false conceptualizations, and no one can create obstacles for them.
In contrast, there are others who are called "the indolent," who do not desire [practice] and engage in useless talk.
One who lacks faith yet has extensively accumulated wealth should refrain from two things: namely, drinking various liquors and sleeping on a bed.
Lord of Mysteries, observe that this is the sūtra passage concerning those bodhisattvas of the mantra-gate who practice the dharma of mantras;
they maintain their recitation, do not cling to any false attachments, abide in the unconditioned, and obstruct the hindrances.
The Buddha told Vajrapāṇi: "Observe that all that has been explained above arises from abiding in the three samayas.
By abiding in these three samayas and reciting according to the Dharma with an uninterrupted mind—meaning by not clinging to any false attachments—obstacles arise because of such false attachments.
If one abides in this equality of the three, one does not cling to anything at all."
If all false attachments are immediately these three equalities, which are themselves bodhi, by what means could any obstacles arise?
This is the great principle for being free from all obstacles. Furthermore, there are other causes for the arising of obstacles, namely:

lack of aspiration (which refers to the sudden absence of desire due to the presence of obstacles within this very mantra practice; or, because of the arising of a mind of lack of desire, obstacles enter). Lack of desire is precisely the absence of seeking.
[...is equal to... laziness (because of a lack of diligent progress, it is like extinguishing a fire before it has grown hot by repeatedly pausing; thus it obstructs entry).

Furthermore, engaging in useless talk regarding the practice of mantra, failing to recite, and failing to apply oneself to cultivation—thus wasting time in vain—is likewise an opportunity for obstacles to gain access.
Moreover, lack of faith (because of this lack of faith, obstacles gain access). Furthermore, amassing vast amounts of wealth and seeking worldly distractions.
By failing to guard against diligent effort, one suffers when the opportune time passes;

through various causes and conditions such as these, obstacles are created that allow [adversaries] to gain an advantage. All of the above are conditions for the arising of obstacles. Furthermore, there are two types:
first, not abstaining from drinking alcohol, for alcohol is a condition for the arising of obstacles. Because of drinking alcohol, all manner of unwholesome states arise.
It is because one has been born [into this state], and furthermore, for this second reason, one must not lie upon a bed.
This is because various desires and thoughts of negligence arise while resting comfortably on a bed; therefore, one may not do so. One should instead spread a mat of grass.

Those who practice recitation in the West mostly use auspicious *kuśa* grass as a mat, which brings many benefits. First, it is because at the time the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, [he sat upon such a mat].
Because it is the seat upon which all the world considers itself auspicious, the practitioner who relies upon it will not encounter obstacles.
Furthermore, if various venomous insects or the like spread this [grass] out, none shall reach that place. Moreover, its nature is exceedingly fragrant and pure.
Because this grass is extremely sharp to the touch and easily breaks, its shape is like that of a double-edged sword. Thus says the practitioner.

When resting during intervals from recitation, one should lie upon this grass mat; for if one is heedless and indulges in self-indulgence, one will be harmed by it, and thus one must not give way to arrogance.
Furthermore, the reason the Buddha himself made use of this grass was to eliminate worldly pride;
when he was a prince, amidst all manner of pleasures, he sat and lay upon jeweled beds and rested his feet upon jeweled stands.
If one who has left the household life still practices such things, they are no different from when they were originally at home.

Because he is able to renounce such matters and sit upon a mat of grass, all humans and devas give rise to a heart of reverence; they likewise emulate him by eliminating arrogance and entering the True Dharma.
If even the Buddha was like this, how much more so should we? The practitioner contemplates these merits and therefore cultivates this practice.
Chapter Twenty-Six: Explaining the Tathāgata At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets addressed the Bhagavān, saying:
"What is a Tathāgata? What is the Honored One among Men? What is called a Bodhisattva?"
Why is the Buddha called the Guide, the Great Muni? I have a doubt regarding this;
I pray that you sever my uncertainty. O Bodhisattva of great renown, casting aside the mind of doubt, one should practice the Mahāyāna.
This practice of the King is unsurpassed.
At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana surveyed the entire great assembly and addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Vajrapāṇi! That you are able to ask me about such a meaning is well done.
Listen attentively and apply your mind with great care; I shall now expound the verses on the Mahāyāna path. He spoke these verses:
Bodhi has the characteristic of space; it is free from all conceptual discrimination. One who joyfully seeks that bodhi is called a Bodhisattva.

Having accomplished the ten stages and so forth, they possess sovereign mastery and skillfully penetrate the emptiness of all phenomena as being like illusions. They know that all these are identical [meaning: they know that all these are the same].
Because he knows the destinies of all worlds, he is called a Buddha. The Dharma has the characteristic of space:
non-dual and of a single nature. Perfectly awakened, endowed with the ten powers—this is called *sambodhi*.
It is wisdom alone that destroys those [afflictions]; its intrinsic nature is ineffable.
Because it is the wisdom of self-realization, it is called the Tathāgata.
Hereafter, according to the Sanskrit text of the sutra: "The Mahāyāna path has the characteristic of space; awakening is free from all conceptual construction.
If a bodhisattva seeks that awakening with longing, this is the answer as to the name of the bodhisattva. Space has no characteristics.
Awakening is likewise like space: it is without marks and without conceptual differentiation.
Furthermore, while space is without marks, it is the basis upon which all virtues depend and the foundation by which all phenomena are established. Awakening is also like this:
ultimately without marks and without conceptual differentiation, yet it possesses all merits. To seek to realize and attain such a true reality is called [the path].
Bodhisattva.

Next, the meaning of "Buddha" is explained: hereafter, according to the Sanskrit text of the sūtra, one attains mastery in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and thoroughly penetrates the knowledge that all phenomena are empty and like an illusion;
this entire process constitutes the practice of the same path, whereby one knows all worlds and receives the name "Buddha."
The answer is that "Buddha" (Fo) signifies one who has fulfilled the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and attained sovereign mastery and thorough penetration.
Within each and every stage, he has skillfully mastered them and attained sovereign knowledge. He understands that all phenomena are identical to emptiness and illusion;

furthermore, he knows the deep-seated inclinations and the mental orientations of sentient beings. Because he possesses these virtues, all the world designates him as a Buddha. Thus, he is called "Buddha."
The name "Awakening" (*bodhi*) arises from this. Below this, the Sanskrit text states: "The characteristics of space and the nature of phenomena are non-dual;
they are but a single characteristic. This refers to the Buddha of the Ten Powers, who is called the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*), and is also titled Śākyamuni.

Previously it was merely said that one knows phenomena are empty and like illusions; now it is said that the phenomena of space are entirely without characteristics—this is precisely what is realized herein.
Because he has attained mastery, he knows all phenomena universally through the ten powers (*daśabala*), such that there is nothing he does not know;

as it is extensively explained in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, the ten powers are most vast. This bodhi is like space, devoid of dual characteristics; within this single characteristic, the mind abides nowhere.
By means of this, one attains the ten powers of a Buddha; because one correctly abides in these ten powers, one is called a "Perfectly Awakened One" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).

The names "Buddha" and "Samyaksambuddha" differ in designation but are one in essence. Because he has skillfully disciplined his body, speech, and mind, and possesses mastery over subduing them, he is able to conquer all māras;
not only does he conquer external māras, but he also universally subdues internal obstacles.

Because he is the most honored among both the mundane and the supramundane, he is further titled "The Honored One Among Men. This meaning is omitted from the text of the sutra and is not explained therein.
Other passages explain it in this way.
Below, the Sanskrit text states: "The wisdom that destroys [ignorance] is the self-realizing gnosis (svasaṃvedana-jñāna) which is by nature beyond verbal expression;

this is called the Tathāgata. This answers the question regarding the name "Tathāgata. Because this wisdom can destroy ignorance, it is called "wisdom that destroys" (*prajñā-han*), even though it is not explicitly stated [in other texts].
That which is harmed by the fire of ignorance is ignorance itself; thus, its meaning is self-evident.

This realm of self-realization transcends the path of language. Knowing that self-realization cannot be proclaimed or transmitted to others, one abides in such wisdom and thereby attains the name "Tathāgata.
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s principle is realized spontaneously and naturally, he is called the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, just as the path traversed by all Buddhas is the place where they naturally realize [enlightenment], I likewise proceed in that same manner; therefore, I am called "Tathāgata" (Thus-Gone).

In the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra], this is answered in full with over a hundred verses for each case, but the transmitters of the Dharma have merely abridged the essential points, providing a single verse as an answer for each.
Although abbreviated, the general meaning is fully contained therein.
Next is the twenty-seventh chapter, "The Ritual of Mundane and Supramundane Homa.
In the non-Buddhist scriptures of the *Veda* treatises on pure conduct, there are methods for fire worship; likewise, within the Mahāyāna Mantra Vehicle, there are also fire rituals.
The reason for this is that they are intended to subdue and gather a certain class of beings by means of the Buddha’s *vīra-cakra*.
Although [the Buddha] subdued them by means of *dhāraṇī*, their underlying intent remains as vast as heaven and earth and cannot be compared with it.

Now, wishing to distinguish the characteristics of the heterodox and the orthodox so that practitioners may no longer harbor further doubts, the transmitter of the Dharma has extensively set forth the causal origins within this chapter.
The Buddha desired to eliminate the prideful minds of various pure practitioners in future ages.
Therefore, he himself recounted his past lives, and while acting as a Brahmā-king, he expounded the Vedic scriptures of external teachings so that the minds of those of heterodox sects were subdued;
only thereafter did he teach this correct practice of the gateway of mantras.

Furthermore, Guhyapati, at one time in the past, when I was a bodhisattva practicing the bodhisattva path, I dwelt in the Brahma heavens practicing the bodhisattva path; that is, this very Brahma heaven.
At that time, the Brahma asked, "Great Brahma, I wish to know how many kinds of fire there are. Then I spoke thus to him, making such an explanation to him.
That fire is named *asmitā-svayambhū* (the self-arisen "I-am-ness"). Next, the fire produced by the son of Brahmā is named *pāvaka-guṇa*;
this is said to be the very first fire in the world. It means that in a previous life when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I manifested as the King of Brahmā (*brahmendra*).
At that time, there were practitioners of the Brahma-conduct who came and asked me: "How many types of fire-offering rituals (*agni-hotra*) are there?"
I have fully explained the fire-seed; now that I have attained perfect awakening, I realize that what was previously taught was incorrect and what is now taught is correct.
Therefore, practitioners should follow this current, correct practice of the fire-dharma and should not employ the former false and incorrect dharmas.
The following sections distinguish the methods of heterodox schools regarding fire-worship; all are taught within the Vedas.

First, the origin of the Fire God is explained: initially, the Great Brahmā King possessed such a conception that "all things arise from me," and because he held this conceit of self (*asmimāna*), and further conceived of himself as being spontaneously eternal, he received the name of *ahaṃkāra* (the "I-maker").
Furthermore, the one with the title of "Self-Existent" (*svayambhū*) is the Great Brahmā King (*mahābrahmāṇa-rāja*). Next is the son of Brahmā, named Brahmāputra;
this Brahmāputra is none other than the Great Brahmā King’s mental offspring.

Because he was born by the mere thought of the Great Brahmā King desiring sentient beings to exist, he is considered his own son. This son of Brahmā is the foremost among the gods of that celestial fire.
The first [is that which arises spontaneously].
Next is the *bāva* syllable produced by the son of Brahmā (this is the name of the worldly fire-god).
From this point downward, those generated in succession are all fire-deities within that dharma; they are merely objects of worship and have no practical function.
...as well as Brahmāṇḍaja (the son of Brahmā, i.e., the son of the son of Agni),
Pitāmaha (his grandson), Vaiśravaṇa (his grandson), Hāvana (the name of his son), Kapivāhana (his grandson), and Vāsava (his grandson).
*Atamaṇa* (also *Ataki*), *Bhataṭa* (also *Bhaki*), and *Puskarautu* (also *Pakki*)—the above are all deities of offering. These are used when placing the embryo;

they are for use when a practitioner of purity first marries and conceives. [The fire deity is used] by adding the mantra of this fire deity's name. The names of the fire deities are found in the sūtra.
[Included here as per the instruction "this does not appear below" regarding the context of the womb].
For one who wishes to bathe her later [at the time when the husband bathes her six months after conception, still binding her hair in a topknot as a sign;
this is the mantra of the fire-god named Vahanaṅga], he uses the Maṅgala fire at the time of bathing his wife.

Regarding those performed after the birth of a child (after seven days from the birth of the child, one bathes the wife and mother; this fire-god is used for loosening the hair; his name is Pāka-purīṣa).
Regarding the time of bestowing a name (*nāmakaraṇa*): (when the son has been born and the seer is invited to perform the rite of naming, this fire is used; its name is *Pāvaka-anagni*).

Regarding the use of this fire at the time of eating: (it means that when the child is able to eat, the parents first empower the clarified butter (*sarpis*) and other foods with this fire-mantra before consuming them;
each Vedic ritual has its specific application, and this is named *Śuci-anagni*).

When making a topknot for one's son (meaning when the son has gradually grown and the hair from the womb [the topknot] is shaved, leaving only the *śikhā* topknot), this Fire God is used; his name is Śikhī Agni.

When receiving the prohibitive precepts (this refers to the time when the youth gradually grows up and maintains the precepts of his own lineage), there is a *vīraṇa* grass resembling bamboo found here; it is made into a three-stranded cord and tied around the body, crossing over the back. One holds a curved branch—what the ancients called a "three-forked branch"—and this is named *samovāva*.

[One] wears a fire-vessel (*kamaṇḍalu*) and dons a deer-skin garment; this is the dress of the precept-holder. He maintains the precepts for twelve years, constantly begging for food with a red copper bowl.

When begging for food, he speaks these words: "If there is anyone [who would give], stay for a short while and do not depart immediately. Upon returning to the hearth, he divides the food into three portions. Having bathed, he takes one portion of the food to offer to the fire deity, and takes an ash-seal three times.

Having attended upon his parents and teacher, he gives one portion of his food to them; whether they eat it or not is left to their discretion. Only then does he eat his own portion. For twelve years he diligently studies the Vedic laws (*veda-dharma*);
when the twelve years are complete, he emerges from the lineage of Brahmā (*brahma-kula*) to take a wife. This is called *samāvartana*.

When the period of the vow is complete and he gives the cow as a gift—meaning that once twelve years of observing the precepts have passed, he must repay the teacher’s kindness by offering material compensation, including a mother cow and her calf—to the teacher;

and after the teacher has accepted them, he further arranges for him to marry. Therefore, he explains the circumstances of taking a wife, saying: "In a past kalpa, when the Brahmā King descended to the world, he took the form of a bull and engaged in sexual intercourse, thereby giving rise to progeny. From this came the Brahmin caste. Now, this mother cow giving birth to a calf is precisely that inherited practice;

you should emulate it to ensure the continuation of the Brahmin lineage," and so forth at length. At that time, he uses this fire to consecrate them; they are all names of fire-deities (*sūrya-homa*).

At the time of one’s marriage (specifically, according to that marriage rite, when taking a wife, one recites the original mantra of the Fire God and Brahmā; its general meaning is as follows): "The original intention of Brahmā [is such and such]. I now continue to perform the 'Brahma-cow' practice (*brahmacaryā*).
This birth canal is identical to the mouth of Brahmā, and from it the four castes are produced; thus one performs the 'cow' practice, which is called *yogāgni*."

Regarding the time of performance (that is to say, when first undertaking these various rites such as offerings, the fire deity has a distinct name; subsequently, during the performance, there are further fire deity mantras and so forth according to the specific matter, such as the *Upānaya* fire).

Regarding those who make offerings to the celestial deities (*devatā*): when performing that ritual offering (*dharmapūjā*), one takes copper bowls with two handles and fills them with flowers, fruits, leaves, rice, and various other foods.

The ritual manual states: "Offerings are made to all celestial deities. One offers in this manner to each individual deity—such as those of the household well, the hearth, the door, and the hall—placing a handful of food at each location while reciting the mantra of that respective deity.
Once the offerings to the doors are completed, the remaining food is placed upon the roof to be given to the ancestors (*pitr*) and the hungry ghosts (*preta*). This is called *bali*.

Next, construct a dwelling (using the *brahma-agni* [Brahma-fire] to erect the dwelling and so forth; it must also be consecrated by means of the ritual, whereby it becomes pure; otherwise, it is impure. *Brahma* refers to the *brahma-agni*).
When practicing the giving of gifts (that is, giving to those of one’s own kind), this practitioner of purity does not give objects [even] to those of the three castes; he gives only to his own kind.

At the time of giving, he invokes the name of this Fire God and adds a mantra, the original meaning of which is: "This object was obtained from Brahmā; now it is returned to him [Brahmā]. You, too, are Brahmā. The subsequent phrase also says "Svāhā," which is named *śānti* (pacification).

Regarding the time for binding the sheep: it refers to when one’s observance of the precepts is complete, the Brahma-lineage has emerged, and the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) are fully established, such that one may slaughter and eat the sheep.

Their doctrine states: "Since the Brahmā-born produced the four types [of castes], one marries women of the four castes, and each gives birth to sons; thus the Brahmā-born produce the four types. However, among those born sons there are naturally distinctions of superior and inferior:

at the time of slaughtering the sheep, the son born of a *śūdra* serves [the victim]; the son born of a *kṣatriya* kills it; the son born of a *vaiśya* carves it; and the son of the *brāhmaṇa* caste eats it. At that time, one also applies mantras to this; this is the bequeathed dharma of the seer (ṛṣi) Vasu, known as the *Āpaddharma*.

Vaho [Niṅ]. Regarding the time of defilement by touch (meaning the loss of the pure dharma, such as when a śramaṇa violates the precepts): it refers to times when, due to negligence, one is unaware that people have cut off one's hair, or that the cord binding the body has snapped, or that the triple-jointed staff has broken, or that at the time of eating one has been touched by a śūdra, and so forth.

Desiring to repent and undergo self-punishment, one gathers two or three hundred kinsmen and the great assembly, and confesses before them. At that time, all those practitioners of purity speak with one voice, saying: "The sun, moon, and various devas bear witness that from this day forward, this person..."

Once they have departed, they become pure again as before. At that time, the one performing the repentance makes offerings to them; then, this fire-deity mantra is applied to the ritual, known as the *mīṣa* [up to the fire].)

Regarding the time for cooking food: [When one wishes to prepare food, one first takes raw grains and other such items, consecrates them with this fire-deity mantra to purify them, and only then cooks them.
If one errs and does not do so, the rite is lost and the food is not rendered pure. This is called the *Sahasa* Fire.]

Regarding those who worship the sun and moon: when the sun has not yet risen, the practitioner joins their palms toward the east and gazes at the sun; as soon as the sun rises, they prostrate and recite mantras. This is performed according to the ritual for the Fire God (*Agni*).

When the sun is about to set, they again send [the offering] westward according to the aforementioned method. They perform this daily in this manner. Furthermore, there are places where many people gather to perform it together. (Daily, one uses *Svāhā*;

when returning from the fire, upon the rising of the moon, one again welcomes and pays homage at home. The mantra used is different: for the sun, one uses *Svāhā*; for the moon, one uses *Nidhi*. Regarding "filling the burner": this is the method for offering food to the fire. One takes food and fills a vessel, then burns it within the furnace.
[This is named the fire Amṛta]. For pacifying calamities (i.e., using this fire to cause all matters of disaster to subside), the mantra of the fire deity is named Nārāyaṇa.

For the purpose of augmentation (using mantras for pacification and so forth), this [mantra] is as fierce as the fire at the end of an eon, its power being extremely intense; it is the mantra of the Fire God, known as Kṛtānta-vahni.
Removing Obstacles (this refers to subjugation; it employs the name of the wrathful fire deity).
Summoning (this refers to when one desires to accomplish whatever is sought, such as making others behold one with joy, etc.; it employs the *kāmanu* fire).

Burning forest trees (*vanadāha*). [This dharma does not involve burning forest trees and the like; rather, there are times when one desires to burn a dense thicket or withered brush so that it may become renewed and lush—the purpose of this dharma is for the fire.]

"Warming the abdomen" (meaning that greed [causes] the fire within the body to warm the food in the abdomen so that it is digested; its function is to ensure the food is free from disease, etc.). The meaning of the mantra is:
"If, by upholding me, [the spirit] emerges from my body, it is my child," and is named *Śatāru* Fire.
Bestow [the mantras] for use with the fire-oblations and so forth (further inquire regarding the use of the *vācaka* fire).

Next, as for the fires of the ocean named *Vaṇa-bhokṣaka*, the *kalpa-dhvaṃsa* fire, and the *yugānta* fire—these are merely mentioned by name and have no practical application. Regarding pure conduct (*śīla*), there are householders and renunciants; if one is a renunciant, [proceed from...]

The conduct of the youthful truth-seeker (*kumāra-bhūta*) involves entering the mountains to seek the Way until one attains the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*); therein is no such practice as taking a wife.
All the above are the heterodox methods of *homā* for those who serve the sacrificial fire according to Brahmanical rites.
The Buddha has set these aside in order to manifest the true Dharma; O Lord of Secrets, at that time I did not know the nature of those various fires.
Performing various *homās* is likewise not the practice of *homa*.
Furthermore, it is not the attainment of karmic fruits. For you, O noble ones, I have briefly explained these forty-four types of Vedic fire-practices as transmitted through the Brahmacarya.
What I spoke at that time (the twelve fires explained in sequence):
I further taught the twelve kinds of fire upon attaining bodhi. What are those fires? The fire of wisdom is foremost, named Mahendra.

The Buddha’s intention was this: "At that time, I was the Great Brahmā King, and when the various hosts of Brahmās came to question me, I expounded for them based on the Vedic scriptures, causing them to rely upon these to practice and thereby attain worldly matters such as the five supernormal powers.
However, at that time I had not yet realized the intrinsic nature of fire nor its functional utility; because I did not know these things, it should be understood that at that time..."
The actions performed are not called well-executed, nor can they be termed *homa*; they are neither practice nor karma, and their fruit cannot be obtained.
Only when I have attained *bodhi* will the self-nature of fire and the expedient means of its causes and effects be fully understood.
That which is called the self-nature of fire is precisely the light of the Tathāgata’s omniscience.
The reason the Buddha spoke thus was that he wished to subdue the various non-Buddhists who discriminate between the heterodox and the orthodox, so that they might know there exists true homa.
These [non-Buddhists], through their various pure practices, had developed pride based on what they themselves claimed were the secrets within the Vedic scriptures they venerated;
now, the Buddha himself explained the original source of the Vedas and, therein—
This further clarifies the authentic Vedic *homā* method of the Buddha; one should know that this is the foremost among secret treasuries.
Upon hearing it, one will give rise to a sense of wonder and immediately develop faith and understanding. Previously, before I had attained perfect enlightenment, I knew nothing at all.
What has been briefly explained above consists of forty-four types of fire rituals; in their full extent, they are immeasurable.
As clearly elucidated in those Vedic scriptures, he has now attained perfect enlightenment; furthermore, it speaks of the twelvefold dharmas of the fire of true wisdom—
namely, that which accomplishes the great task by utterly eliminating the darkness of all defilements and obstructions,
thereby achieving the great task in a manner unlike the practices of the heterodox paths and unrighteous conduct of the past.
The first [deity] is named Jñānāgni-dik (Fire of Wisdom Direction). She is yellow in color, dignified, and increases power;
she abides in the Samādhi of Fire-Flame Radiance and possesses the perfection of wisdom. Herein, "fire of wisdom" refers to the light of prajñā of the bodhicitta.
Her square shape and yellow color signify the Vajrāsana (Diamond Throne). "Dignified" refers to her internal adornment.
This fire of wisdom takes the form of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) because it possesses all the merits of the Buddhas;

thus, its "increased majesty" (*vibhūti*) refers to external matters, namely the function of the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth. This fire of wisdom is of such a nature that it is fully adorned with internal and external merits;
because it can bestow the ten powers, it is called "increased majesty. By recognizing this fire, one burns away [the afflictions] from beginningless time.

The fuel of ignorance that has come forth is now exhausted without remainder; like the conflagration at the end of an eon when fire and ashes are utterly consumed, it is completely purified and free from defilement.
Thus, the merits of all Tathāgatas are spontaneously accomplished. Furthermore, this Fire Deity is none other than Wisdom itself;
its appearance is majestic and dignified, possessing the color of vajra, and it is surrounded by a circular halo of blazing flames as it dwells herein.
Within the light, he enters the samādhi of tranquil meditative absorption; by abiding in this samādhi, the nature of wisdom is fulfilled.
This radiance of wisdom is none other than a specific name for Vairocana. It is through this very Honored One that this wisdom is manifested.
If one contemplates at the initial stage, one contemplates this Fire Deity, who is capable of accomplishing all tasks; if one understands deeply...
Its nature is as explained above. Herein, the square altar is called Mahendra in Sanskrit;
this is an epithet for Śakra, the Honored One, and is also an epithet for the Vajracakra.
Wisdom is that which is internally realized, while its external manifestation takes the form of a vajra; the shape of this square seat is similar to that.
However, it is simply this: that which is the Honored One within the four-cornered altar (this head of the vajra is four-cornered in shape).

What is called "increasing majesty" (*vīrya*) above, when discussed in terms of what is represented by its iconographic form, refers to the words for a physical appearance that is perfect and fully endowed.
Yet, according to the words of ultimate principle, it is the dharma-gate of the mind. Furthermore, fire possesses two qualities; if one [considers] only...
