This is called the Inner Fire Method (*antarāgnividhi*). If one constructs a mandala for the sake of gathering worldly beings, one should fashion a square hearth surrounded by flames.
One should also wear yellow robes and visualize this very essence within the fire of the hearth.
After abiding in the Samādhi of the Divine Dwellings as described above, whatever is undertaken will be accomplished; otherwise, it will not be accomplished.
This dharma corresponds to the pacification of calamities (*śāntika*) and is a firm and stable method. It is aligned with the initial bodhicitta, namely the Gate of the Letter A.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, wisdom is fully perfected. Second, "fire" is named the fulfillment of practice (*caryā-paripūri*); this refers to...
The name expresses the meaning, and its Sanskrit sound is itself a mantra. First one generates the bodhicitta, and next one cultivates practice;
when that practice is fulfilled, one is called a Buddha. (My personal commentary: this is the root of great compassion, followed by the seed-syllable *āḥ* of bodhicitta.
His form is like the moonlight of an autumn night, shining brilliantly in all four directions; his body is clad in white robes and endowed with all manner of virtues.
(That is to say, the body is majestic, well-proportioned, and pleasing. His right hand holds a rosary, and his left hand holds a *kamaṇḍalu*.
This image abides within a moon disc. As explained above, this is the meaning of the mind-nature being perfect, luminous, and pure;
it is by means of the fire of these sublime practices that one burns the fuel of the defiled mind’s conceptual proliferation and impurity. If one performs [this practice]...
When contemplating the time [of practice], one should likewise contemplate this as the form of the Honored One (Bhagavān). As stated in the preceding text:

"Because all are the outward manifestation of the Tathāgata’s internally realized virtues, they are represented by means of Dharma-gates. If one is an external practitioner, one should use a round incense burner and smear it with powdered white sandalwood;
offer white flowers and the like as offerings; and personally wear white robes. This is the rite for pacification (*śāntika*).

These are the phenomena of calamity; calamities are immeasurable, referring to various external disasters in the world such as floods, fires, insects, and frosts, as well as all internal afflictions of the body, which manifest in myriads of forms. One is able to purify these for both one's own body and the bodies of others.
Furthermore, since beginningless time, there has been a doubting mind, which gives rise to hesitation regarding the profound Dharma.
The inability to decisively believe this is itself an obstacle; that this fire can purify and remove such obstacles is also the meaning of *śāntika* (pacification).
This *śāntika-homa* also has two types: performing the fire ritual through yoga-corresponding recitation (*japa*) or through external *homa*.
However, if one is able to provide the offerings, one must also attend to the constant performance of virtuous deeds.
If one does not prepare [the materials], merely performing it with the mind will still result in having the substance available for the rite;
yet, if one performs it with the mind alone without doing so, it is likewise not in accordance with the Dharma. The third Fire Lord is named Vāyuśoṣa (Wind-Dryer);
he is born from wind and is thus the son of wind, his form being dry and black. This refers to one whose internal color is black while the exterior is applied with dryness, as described above.
The ashes and so forth [are placed] within the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) of this deity’s location, which is in the shape of a half-moon;

it is also depicted in the form of seated samādhi. This means that although the practitioner has first resolved upon bodhicitta and wishes to advance, because the root of beginningless delusion and affliction has not been eliminated, these repeatedly draw back and shatter the contemplative mind, adding obscuration; therefore, one must perform this.

The "Dharma-wind" signifies the meaning of non-abiding. Just as the wind in the world can destroy heavy clouds, this fire of non-abiding likewise has the power to disperse and destroy all obstructions. This Venerable One sits upon a wind-mandala;

in his hands he holds a silk cloth at a distance of three to five inches from his head, grasping it at both ends in the shape of a celestial garment (*devavastra*). Its color is blue (this represents the meaning of wind; further questions may be asked). This.
This *ābhicāruka* rite also consists of two types of methods, internal and external.
Fourth, [the deity] is red like the radiance of the sun, abiding within a triangle; with his right hand he holds a sword, sitting upright upon the blade’s edge.
This represents sharp wisdom that severs the fetters, like the light of the sun’s rays, and like the color of the world’s sun when it first rises. Just as the world’s sun—when first...
When emerging, because darkness is removed at night and light appears when the day has ended, one perceives this color.

The fire deity likewise possesses such a form and color, and its flames are also thus; its physical appearance is upright, majestic, and perfect as previously described, abiding in samādhi while manifesting a slightly wrathful form.
The fifth is Mṛḍana, which signifies the union of fires; this venerable one performs [this].
"Pale yellow" refers to yellow mixed with the color of fire. "Combined" means that two dharmas are joined together;
its image consists of two halves of the body, with the left side manifesting an expression of wrath and the right side manifesting a joyful, smiling form.

(This smile is one of dwelling in tranquility, being neither angry nor excessively delighted. Regarding the hair upon the body—referring to the beard, mustache, and head hair—it should be somewhat more abundant, yet it must not be excessive.
If too many [deities] are placed, it will not be dignified. His neck is long and possesses great majestic light;

his body color is red on one side and yellow on the other (the angry side should be red). His sitting posture is also such that the right side is a half-vajra seat (half-vajrāsana) and the left side is a triangle (half-fire seat).
He holds a sword in his left hand and a *vajra* in his right; there are two methods for the inner and outer [mandalas], following the previous examples.
This union is able to universally accomplish all rites of summoning and pacification.

Internally, it is the light of wisdom (*jñānāloka*), wherein afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished and non-arising (*anutpāda*). If performed externally, one must likewise employ both types [of substances] such as incense, flowers, and vestments.
During recitation, one should also assume this form like that of the deity (*devatā*): with one eye wrathful and one eye tranquil, calamities will be eliminated.
Because the vows are fulfilled all at once through these universal principles, such functions are possible; this differs from the teachings of limited or partial approaches.
The sixth fire deity is named Krodha (Wrath); the mantra and other elements are based on the meaning of this name as explained above.
As for his body being smoke-colored, it means it is neither extremely black nor extremely white, but is closed [in its nature].
One eye is like that of Acala; his hair is disheveled upward like a wild mane, and he makes a great roaring sound, as if opening his mouth to let out a loud roar.
His mouth has four fangs, two protruding above and two below; these also symbolize two elements:
fire and wind. The seventh is called "Warming the Abdomen," which is like being within the mundane fires of the world.
This refers to the fire within the body that digests food and sustains the physical frame; however, the meaning in this True Dharma (*saddharma*) is not so.
The fire within the abdomen is, in fact, the wisdom of internal realization (*pratyātma-vedya-jñāna*).
"Swift" means that its form becomes even more wrathful than before. "Utterly wrathful" means manifesting this syllable *Aḥ*. It possesses various colors.

This means that his form is endowed with the five colors; the meaning follows the previous [explanation]. The eighth is named *Phenapa* (Consumption), which carries the sense of "removal" or "dispelling.
It means to cause all matters such as karmic defilements to be eliminated without remainder. This Honored One can remove all obstacles within the body;
that is, he causes all those of the *Vināyaka* class to be consumed and exhausted. His color is like a mass [of light].
The manifestation of a multitude of lightning flashes, difficult to behold, is of the same category as the Vajracakra (Vajra-wheel).
The ninth is named Manomaya (Mind-born), which refers to phenomena produced from the mind that are accomplished according to one's will;
it is able to assume all manner of forms and can achieve whatever is intended. It is skillful and appropriate, being Viśvakarman.

This refers to the meaning of the universal accomplishment (*samantamukha-siddhi*) of manifesting bodies according to the various classes [of beings], and the sovereign wisdom (*vaśitā-prajñā*) by which whatever is performed is accomplished;
it possesses great power. The tenth is the fire named "Receiving Food" (*āhāra-grahaṇa*), which means "to withdraw the subtle";

this signifies the sense of receiving food when making an offering to the fire. As for "receiving food," it means that when the fire-food is offered, one receives and consumes it. (Further inquiry. Its—
The Venerable One’s performance of the *Oṃ* syllable mudrā is the ritual method of the Brahmins.
For practitioners of purity, whenever there is speech, they all incline their right hand to form the mudrā and raise it while pronouncing the sound of *Oṃ* to manifest the sign;
therefore, this is so. The text for the eleventh fire is missing. The twelfth fire is named "Complete Accomplishment" (*Sarvasiddhi*).
This means that being able to fully accomplish everything is the sense of subduing Māra at the site of the tranquil *bodhimaṇḍa*, where what was to be done has already been completed.
Furthermore, it is like a class of sentient beings who are consistently evil and cannot be restrained; even if one offers them exhortations, their wickedness only increases.
If they are left unchecked, they will proceed toward the evil realms; therefore, by means of skillful expedients (*upāya*), one subdues their bodies.
Causing them to become bewildered and confused so that they know nothing at all, by means of this causal condition, one is unable to create either good or evil;
immediately thereafter, one gradually guides them to enter the True Dharma. As stated in the *Vajraśekhara*, the meaning of Vajrapāṇi’s subjugation of Maheśvara is as explained above.
All of these are the deeds performed while abiding in the path of skillful means, O Lord of Secrets.

These substances held by the fire-colored [deities] correspond to their own colors—that is, the color of the fire deity—and the medicinal substances and so forth likewise accord with those colors; as it says in the verse:
By performing the external homa, one accomplishes siddhi according to one's wish.
Furthermore, O Lord of Secrets (referring next to the internal method), the single nature possesses three; the three locations are unified as one.
This is the yogin’s internal homa: the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion—this is the rite for pacifying calamities (śāntika).
That which is endowed with joy is the method for increase; from the womb-matrix, wrath performs manifold activities.

Furthermore, O Lord of Secrets, according to the places as they have been described (meaning their application according to type), and according to those corresponding matters, one burns [the object] in accordance with faith and understanding.
One’s own form and the medicinal substances are identical to those used in external homa;

thus, for one who attains siddhi according to their wish, it is said that these twelve kinds of forms, colors, and held objects must have their natures understood. Having previously discussed the combination of the internal and external, what is now explained is the external.
The triad of elements constitutes fire, which is no different from the deity, and the deity is no different from one’s own body; they are all identical.
Self and other are identical. Regarding the internal agent: the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) is fire, and fire is one's own body. Now, as for the explanation according to principle:
the *iṣṭadevatā* is Vairocana; this Vairocana is not different from the fire of natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), and this fire is not different from my own body.
Thus, the unification of these three within a single self-nature is called "internal."
Homa is also a union; that is to say, the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) is identical to fire, and fire is identical to oneself—these three things are equal.
Regarding the "spontaneous accomplishment" (*siddhi*) mentioned above, worldly, intermediate, and superior matters are accomplished according to one's will.
If one does not understand this, there is no way for the fire-rite to succeed. This may also be illustrated by internal phenomena. If one understands this, it is the fire of wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding the threefold union (*trisaṃnipāta*), this refers to body, speech, and mind.
When the body’s mudrā, the speech’s mantra, and the mind’s *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) are united and ultimately equalized, this is called the threefold union.
If one can contemplate the honored deity, then one’s own body gradually becomes purified; purification is [the state of...]
When one perceives the single nature within the deity, the three matters are simultaneously purified; all are equal.
Next, the internal homa method is explained: within these three equalities, when pacifying rites (*śāntika*) are performed, one employs great loving-kindness and great compassion.
When these three equalities and great loving-kindness and great compassion are in union, all the deities of the pacifying class [arise].
First, if one performs an act of augmentation (*aupacayika*), it is through the union of compassion (*karuṇā*) and great joy (*mahāmuditā*).

If one is wrathful, fire is the womb; the "act-womb" is the mind itself. This means that when there are causes and conditions requiring the performance of a wrathful act to subjugate others, wrath arises from within the heart. This wrath is not like that of the mundane world.

Wrath (*krodha*) also refers to the realization of the true nature of anger from within a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and its arousal through skillful means (*upāya*) to subdue unwholesome phenomena.
By performing such [rites] as internal *homā* (fire-offering), one is able to accomplish all tasks.
Thus, the general meaning of *homā* is to burn the fuel of afflictions (*kleśa*) with the fire of wisdom until nothing remains.
This is the meaning. Now, in this context, the fire deities employed and the internal and external correspondences have been explained in brief;

one should know that within all other dharma teachings, there are likewise fire-dharma rites. Whatever task is to be performed according to the circumstances, one should act by conforming to this method while abiding in samādhi and applying it in accordance with its specific correspondence;
thus it will be accomplished. If one does not do so, [it will not be accomplished]. But...
If one burns firewood until it is completely exhausted as an offering, it ultimately conflates with external dharmas and cannot achieve [the goal].
Furthermore, what the sutra refers to as "objects" (vastu) means the objects of perception, namely the dharmas of fire, fuel, ghee, food, and various requisites.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what is it? World-Honored One, what is the fire-hearth samādhi?
What is the sprinkling? What is the orderly spreading of the *kuśa* grass? We pray that the Buddha will explain. Vajrapāṇi further questioned the Buddha:
"I have heard this method of fire many times before, yet I am still undecided as to where it should be applied."

Regarding the disposal of fire, where should the hearth and so forth be placed, and what further methods are there? This refers to the questions asked of the Buddha concerning the scattering [of ashes], the spreading of *kuśa* grass, and the use of other materials.
The Buddha addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, saying: "Lord of Secrets, that fire-hearth should be measured according to the span of an elbow."
It is universally four finger-widths on all four sides, encircled by a vajra-rim;
below this, the Buddha answers in verse, stating that the fire-pit should be one cubit in measurement, universally four finger-widths on all four sides and encircled by a vajra-rim.

This means that at whatever location it is established, it should be dug one cubit deep, and its square dimensions should likewise be so. Upon the opening, a rim is installed, both its height and width being four finger-widths (using the joint of the thumb as the measure).

Measure it again with greater precision. Encircle it with a vajra-fence (the four sides each join as described above among the eight mudrās). "Universal" means that the depth and the dimensions are equal;
as for the shapes, such as square, triangular, crescent, or circular, they may be understood accordingly.
Use green *kuśa* grass to surround the hearth, circling it to the right. Do not place the tip over the base; rather, the base should be placed over the tip (meaning do not use the end).

"One should press the roots [of the grass] with the roots [of the next]. This means that one should sprinkle the *kuśa* grass in sequence from right to left while it is still green and moist, and then spread it by circling clockwise;
this refers to the method of laying out the grass along the perimeter. One must ensure that the root and the tip press against each other; "tip" refers to the uppermost sprout.
For example, when laying it out toward the east, the roots of the grass are in the north and the tips are in the south; one should then press the tip against the next [blade] to the south.
One must not allow the roots to suppress the sprouts. Arrange them by circling clockwise in sequence until reaching the south;
at that point, the roots must face east and the tips of the sprouts face west. Proceed in this same order for the north as well. Sprinkling water refers to *arghya* water;
there are specific methods for *arghya*, as explained in the *Siddhi* [texts]. However, regarding this sprinkling of water...
There are two methods: one is to take a small bundle of *kuśa* grass, place it within an *argha* vessel, and sprinkle [water] from it;
when sprinkling, one must sprinkle in a clockwise direction (*pradakṣiṇa*). Alternatively, one may sprinkle directly with the hand, but even then, it must be done in a clockwise direction.
Furthermore, there are two types [of timing]: when first purifying the fire, one must sprinkle in a clockwise direction; when making offerings after purification is complete, one should...
Sprinkle [the water] directly; it is not necessary to rotate it. This is as distinguished in the *Siddhi* [treatises]. Before sprinkling, one must invite the Fire Honored One (*Agnideva*);
the mantra and mudrā for this have already been explained in the Superior Section (*uttara-paṭala*), and these are what are employed here.

Having finished sprinkling, offer flowers and perform the sequential offerings of all articles. At that time, one should visualize the form of the Principal Deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) within this hearth and take [it up].
The "Superior Mantra" refers to the universal sprinkling. "Full Oblation" (*pūrṇāhuti*) means using a ladle to cast the substance into the fire.
There are two kinds of ladles: first, the large square ladle called the "Full Oblation," which should be filled to the brim before being cast into the fire;
second, the small ladle, used for successive offerings into the fire, which likewise must be filled to the brim. There is also a separate method, as described in the *Siddhi* [section].
It is said that for now, the three matters of pacifying (*śāntika*), increasing (*pauṣṭika*), and subjugating (*abhicāruka*) shall be briefly indicated;

one should know that all rites are to be performed according to this standard. The ritual instructions should be followed thus: one should offer scented unguents, flowers, and lamps to the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*).
With *mṛttikā* fire, one should make an offering of a single flower and establish it at the seat. Having established it, the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) should further sprinkle [water].
The wise perform the fulfillment offering (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra, followed by the pacifying homa (*śānti-homa*).
Alternatively, one may ask about the method for increasing prosperity (*puṣṭi*); such worldly homas are called external rites.

Furthermore, regarding internal homa, one extinguishes the arising of karma—that is, the cessation of karmic birth. One thoroughly understands one's own *manas* (the mental faculty), which is the "mind.
One remains far removed from form, sound, and so forth, as well as the karmas of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, speech, and mind.

Furthermore, in internal homa, having understood the cessation of the arising of karma, that which is the "mind" (*manas*)—desiring to know the mind—one should depart from its objects. Once one has departed from objects, one should...

Cognition is also detached from the sense organs (meaning its function is subsumed under the tongue). Body, speech, and mind all arise from the mind; they originate depending upon the sovereign mind-king (*cittarāja*).
The arising of the discrimination of the eyes and so forth, as well as objects such as forms, involves delusion based on the sovereign mind-king before wisdom has arisen.
To cease this, one employs the wind to dry and the fire to extinguish it—namely, by means of the wind and fire of wisdom.
"Scorching" means to burn away false attachments so that one may attain the pure bodhicitta;
"closing the mouth" refers to pure speech. This is called internal homa, which is taught for all Bodhisattvas. Wisdom is the fire, which arises from the wind;

wisdom is the cessation that purifies the mind, serving as the basis for contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The above clarifies worldly matters; now, this internal homa is explained as it emerges [from the transcendent].
Worldly affairs refer to the removal of karma, birth, and so forth by means of the fire of wisdom. One undergoes birth from karma, and from birth one again creates karma, revolving without end.
What is now called *homa* is precisely the purification and removal of this karma, so that the Dharma of purity may arise.
Once karma and birth have been removed, one then applies the mind; "mind" (*citta*) is simply another name for the "King of Mind" (*cittarāja*). This...
Phenomena arise from the mind; they are detached from form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects, and detached from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
All these are based on the mind as the primary factor; they abide by and arise through this sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*), giving rise to discrimination.

One should purify this sovereign mind with wisdom, for when the sovereign mind is purified, all phenomena are purified. However, before wisdom has arisen, one is moved by obstructive phenomena; in such cases, one should follow the method described above.
The text takes up the wind that dries and burns it away; this must be understood according to the profound meaning of the preceding passage.

Because wisdom has not yet arisen, there is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*); due to this discrimination, there exist the defilements and obstructions of the sense faculties, objects, and so forth.
Now, one uses the fire of drying wind to purify and remove them—this fire is none other than the *bodhicitta*. It is by means of this *bodhicitta*-fire that delusions are incinerated.
To completely purify and eliminate all things such as perceptions is what is called the meaning of internal homa.
One who knows this may be called a bodhisattva. What are termed "mundane" and "supramundane" refer to the two dharmas of phenomenon and principle.
Phenomena are the fires added through skillful means; the supramundane is the fire of the nature of wisdom. If it is a mundane fire, it is produced by the gods.
The form of Brahmā is now that of the inner Dharma-fire deity; he abides in the samādhi of the *samayamudrā*, dwelling in profound stillness.
Next is the twenty-eighth chapter, "The Samādhi of the Principal Deity.
At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain the various deities so that their majestic efficacy may be realized."

"Manifesting the forms of the Honored Ones before them, even those Bodhisattvas who practice the Bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras manifest their forms so that the practitioner may contemplate and take them as objects of focus.
By regarding the form of the Honored One as identical to one's own body, free from all doubt, one attains *siddhi*.
Having spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets: 'Excellent, excellent!'"
Thus spoke the Buddha: "Lord of Mysteries, the various deities have three kinds of forms, namely: syllables (*akṣara*), seals (*mudrā*), and physical appearances (*vigraha*).
Those syllables are of two kinds: sound and bodhicitta. Seals are also of two kinds: with signs (*nimitta*) and without signs;

this refers precisely to the meaning of form—namely, having an image or lacking an image. The forms of the deities are also of two kinds: pure and impure; that which realizes purity is [the pure form]."
"Formed forms" refers to the body or the physical form; it is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). It is not a body that possesses the mark of purity, for it possesses manifest forms and various colors.
Because these two types of honored forms constitute two types of phenomena with marks, they accomplish *siddhi* with marks;
because they are without marks, they give rise accordingly to *siddhi* without marks. This principle should also be applied to what follows. Next, the Buddha is cited as evidence.
The Buddha has always taught that if one maintains the perception of signs, one will achieve a Buddha with signs; if the mind abides in signlessness, one will achieve signlessness.
These words of the Buddha are first set forth as a heading. Therefore, in all respects, one should abide in signlessness.
Since phenomena follow the mind, and because they follow the mind, one should seek transcendence from the world. Having contemplated the form of the Honored One, one shall become free of doubt.
Regarding the attainment of *siddhi* as described above, Vajrapāṇi asked: "The 'Principal Deity' (*bimba*) refers to the *brahmasvara* (divine voice) *sādhitavya*.
If one says simply *devatā*, it directly conveys the meaning of 'the one who is honored.
The 'Principal Deity' is also called 'Self-Honored,' meaning the deity whom one personally holds as one's own. Thus, that practitioner...

Just as through the union of these three factors—the body-seal (*mudrā*), the mantra, and the visualization of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity)—the deity descends to the ritual site (*maṇḍala*) and bestows its grace;
yet, when this practitioner first begins their practice, they are still an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) and possess no personal power of merit.
How, then, could the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas respond to their words and manifest immediately? It is solely due to that [power of the Three Jewels].

Because Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others have previously established words of sincerity and great vows, if there are sentient beings who rely upon this Dharma of mine to practice it without violating its principles, I will certainly respond in secret; or even if I do not come in person, I shall provide protection from afar.
If the practitioner follows the principles of the Dharma yet I do not respond, that would constitute a violation of my original vow.
The response is necessarily made, just as water descends when a square pearl faces the moon, or fire arises when a round mirror faces the sun;
through the correspondence of causes and conditions, there is no intentional thought. This phenomenon may serve as a metaphor:

it is not that the Buddhas possess mental activity and respond to beings like ordinary people do. If the mind were not in correspondence and the conditions were lacking, [the response would not occur].
If no signs of efficacy appear because the tutelary deity has not bestowed protective mindfulness, it is not the fault of the Buddha or the Bodhisattvas.
Rather, the practitioner, on account of this matter, must correctly contemplate the pure body of the tutelary deity;
having seen it, they should regard that very body as their own. For one who is thus free from doubt, there is no *siddhi* sought that will not be accomplished.
The Sūtra also states: "Contemplation based on conditions" means that each practitioner performs such contemplation in accordance with their respective tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
"Without doubt" means that because one is in resonance (*yoga*) with that deity, there is no longer any mind of suspicion or difficulty.
Therefore, what is cultivated will necessarily be accomplished. Thus ends the preceding inquiry.

The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Lord of Secrets! Since you are able to ask me about such a matter, O Vajrapāṇi, because you have applied your mind so skillfully, I shall now explain it—listen with eager desire as far as you wish to hear.

Furthermore, because Vajrapāṇi has been able to inquire after his doubts in proper sequence, this is for the sake of encouraging all Bodhisattvas of the Mantra practice in the future, and also to provide them with consolation."

This is an exhortation and admonition. Next, the Buddha said: "Lord of Mysteries, there are three aspects to the form of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity), namely: syllables (*akṣara*), seals (*mudrā*), and forms (*vigraha*).

'Form' refers to the form of the honored one. Regarding those syllables, there are two kinds: the sound and the bodhicitta. The 'syllable' refers to the initial stage of the practitioner's cultivation."
There are two ways of contemplating the meaning of the syllables (*akṣara*): first, one contemplates the bodhicitta alone; this bodhicitta is itself the syllable.
This refers to [the sequence] *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and so forth;

it mentions only the initial [syllable], yet all syllables are included. Because they take this as their primary head, it is called "bodhicitta. Alternatively, one may contemplate the syllables themselves.
"Cakra" (wheel) refers to visualizing the mantra one holds as a wheel-form entering the body, as explained in the "Chapter on Recitation";

or it may refer to visualizing seed-syllables; or, without visualizing the syllables, it refers to recollecting the sound—visualizing this sound, such as the ringing of a bell, as proceeding in succession without interruption, and using this sound to regulate the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, as described above. All these are [the cakras].
This concludes the explanation of the syllables.
There are also two kinds of mudrā-forms: those with form and those without form. "Form" refers to colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white;
shapes such as square, round, and triangular; as well as categories such as bending and extending, sitting and standing, and the places where one dwells. "Mudrā" refers to...
The seals (*mudrā*) that are grasped are those such as the sword, the staff, the noose, and the vajra. For a beginner, one contemplates with a distinct object of focus;
this means first contemplating a painted image of the deity and so forth, and observing in accordance with these is called "having form.

Later, as one gradually becomes proficient, through the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), [the deity] manifests spontaneously in correspondence with the mind. At that time, this tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) arises solely from the mind.

It is called "formless" because it does not depend on external conditions in its manifestation. My personal view is that perhaps at first, when one attains the worldly samādhi, one perceives the principal deity (besson) with such a form, such a color, and such a dwelling place; [one sees them] sitting or standing within such a maṇḍala, holding such mudrās, and so forth.
Because these are still characterized by signs, they are called "having form. Subsequently, when one maintains the mantra, [the deity appears] vividly as before.
To see directly [the deity] as being like a reflection in a mirror—wherein there is no characteristic yet it appears as a characteristic—is called "formless.

Next, there are two kinds of forms for the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored one): namely, pure and impure. This means that the practitioner, at the initial stage, uses a sign (*nimitta*) to lead into the signless (*animitta*).
First, one contemplates the perfectly luminous body of the Buddha or Bodhisattva seal; initially, one does not perceive it by relying on a painted image.
Observing this with equanimity, as the power of the Dharma gradually exerts its influence, one attains progressive clarity;

yet there still remains some obstruction such that when the eyes are closed, one sees, but when the eyes are open, one does not see. Next, as the eyes are gradually opened, one is able to see clearly both with eyes closed and open.

Gradually, even without applying deliberate attention (*manasikāra*), one sees, and eventually even touching the body encounters resistance, just as if one were facing ordinary people with one's eyes wide open.
Next, by means of these signs, one is gradually introduced into the state of purity; because they possess signs, they are called "impure.
Because this *samādhi* is induced by such [signs], one abides in the state of purity, which is tranquil and signless, and is thus called "pure.
"Pure" refers to the fruit, while "impure" refers to the cause. "Impure" refers to form, color, and seals (*mudrā*).
This is like the case of an image; thus, that which is not pure is led to purity, and through the cause of impermanence, one arrives at the fruit of permanence.
I privately maintain that each of these three matters has two aspects, which constitute the sequence of practice: first, one contemplates the mantra while observing the order of the syllables;
next, one observes the sound becoming gradually subtler; next, one observes the form of the Honored One becoming even subtler; finally, one contemplates without relying on external conditions.
Furthermore, one should next observe in detail that within the "objectless" (anālambana), there are both the mixed-impure and the purely pure;
alternatively, these three matters may be explained horizontally, as each arises through both mundane and supramundane expedient means, and thus each possesses two aspects.
The Sūtra states: "Those two kinds" refers to the fact that each of the three aforementioned matters has two types. Within those two types, there are two kinds of accomplishments:
because there is the perception of signs, there are signs; because there is the non-perception of signs, there are signless *siddhis*, such as spontaneous birth, and so forth.
This means that if one perceives through the observation of phenomena with signs, then because the characteristics of the phenomenon possess signs, there is accomplishment through attainment.
Furthermore, by practicing the signless (*animitta*), one also attains the accomplishment of the signless *siddhi*.

It is also said that among these three matters and two types [of practice], one may achieve accomplishment through any single matter; however, all involve both mundane and supramundane accomplishments, as well as accomplishment through phenomena (*dharma*) and accomplishment through principle (*tattva*).
Therefore, within each of the first three types, there are two kinds of accomplishment regarding these two matters.
The Sūtra says: "If one dwells in signs, one seeks to accomplish signs; if one dwells in signlessness, then signlessness is accomplished.
Therefore, to accomplish various matters, one should dwell in signlessness. This is an exhortation to abandon all signs and dwell in signlessness; it is a summary exhortation.
Because the principle of dwelling in signlessness is accomplished, all inconceivable spiritual transformations occur without the application of the mind.

These signs arise spontaneously as wondrous activities; they are not like the accomplishments of the mundane world, which reside within the arising and ceasing of mental activities and are thus limited in power and non-ultimate. Therefore, one is exhorted to seek that which is superior.

I personally maintain that while matters concerning the purification of the contemplative mind are fully explained in works such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, there must nonetheless be a fundamental basis for them. Now, the practitioner...

First, one should practice the contemplation of specific dependent origination, up to the point where one perceives the various realms such as the assemblies of Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions as *siddhi*.
Only after that should one wash away and purify these through Prajñā, whereby the inconceivable great function is realized and one enters the fruit of Buddhahood instantaneously.
If one does not understand the sequence of practice, merely reading the texts will not lead one into the profound.
The wise often misunderstand the intent of the sutra by entering directly into emptiness and thereby losing the path of the Perfect and Sudden;
therefore, one must most carefully contemplate the meaning of these one or two chapters.
Next is the twenty-ninth chapter, "The Samādhi of Signlessness."
Furthermore, the World-Honored One Vairocana addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries, saying:
"Lord of Mysteries, those bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras and desire to accomplish the signless samādhi should reflect in this way:
'From what do these signs arise? Are they from one's own body, or are they from one's own mind? That body arises from karma,' and so forth."
It is said that the nature of grasses, trees, tiles, and stones is thus; it is said that the nature of the body born of karma is thus.
"Stolid" means being like wood or stone; "born of karma" means arising from the mind. This contemplation involves having signs (*sanimitta*);

"having signs" refers to the external, such as all things including the body and speech. One contemplates them in this way, remaining stolid like grass and trees, with a nature free from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
This means that karma arises from the mind; that which arises from the causal karma is internal. The external refers to what is constructed of earth and wood;
this is the external.
The Buddha told Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Mysteries: "That is the mantra-gate of the vow for the accomplishment of the Samādhi of Non-conceptualization."

When Bodhisattvas practicing the path thus contemplate from what source their own bodies and their own minds arise, they are practitioners of yoga who have already been able to visualize the deity and so forth, even attaining various wondrous states;
yet, these are still encompassed by worldly samādhi and they have not yet attained the wisdom of the three equalities. Now, furthermore—

This reveals the entry into the three equal contemplations (*samabhijñā*). If one clearly understands the true reality (*dharmatā*) of body, speech, and mind through this contemplation, one enters the initial Dharma-illumination gate (*dharmāloka-mukha*) of the pure bodhicitta and ascends to the stages of the Bodhisattvas. (This is my own interpretation; the general meaning is as follows.
First, regarding the contemplation of the true reality of the body, the Sūtra says: "The nature of that bodily karma—such as producing grass, trees, bricks, tiles, and so forth—is as follows..."
This is the scriptural passage stating that one should act free from stubbornness as if acting externally, or that karma arises like the perception of forms and images.
What was previously stated—that one should abide in the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) and so forth—refers to this present chapter:
if a practitioner of the path of mantra practice wishes to attain the accomplishment of this samādhi of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they should cultivate this contemplation.
The Sūtra says: "One's own body and one's own mind" means that from the mind, volition arises;
the mind is pure, while the mental faculty (*manas*) is discrimination. (Question: Yet, this body is like wood or stone, its nature being dull and ignorant.

This means that if these four great elements are separated from the mind, they are identical to wood or stone. As it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* within the *Kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*: "As follows..."
When a person with clear vision observes within their granary the various kinds of rice, wheat, and other grains, this body is also like that.
When the contemplation of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is opened, one sees for oneself the thirty-six components, each with its own distinct characteristic.

At that time, the [notion of] bodily form is immediately removed, just as the name "granary" is removed when the granary is opened and the rice and wheat are seen. Thus, even down to each single [component], they all arise through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
This is an exposition of the stages in depth.

Next, it further clarifies that the body is identical to an image. For example, one who creates an image uses a combination of earth, wood, and various other materials to fashion an image—whether of a Buddha, a deva, or some other form such as a parent—and because of their improper contemplation, they give rise to [attachment] accordingly.
Regarding the perception of what is beloved by the Venerable One, one should observe each part minutely: it is merely a convergence of various conditions and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
My own body is likewise so; because the various elements (*dhātu*) are a provisional combination and lack self-awareness, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises.
When observed minutely, they all lack intrinsic nature; they arise from the mind like illusory or dream-like objects, produced by conditions, and are in reality ungraspable.
Furthermore, this body, because it is caused by the mind, appears as if it possesses the six consciousnesses and is endowed with cognition; yet in reality, it is not so.

It is like when the human mind does not observe: there is a state of dwelling [in ignorance], whereby even the brilliance of the sun and moon may sometimes fail to be seen, or the roar of thunder may at times go unheard.
It is also like a bhikṣu who was once single-mindedly engaged in meditative contemplation in the past.

Furthermore, when one is traveling on a road and a great army passes by without seeing it, one should know that if one is separated from the mind, this body—though endowed with faculties such as eyes and ears—is like wood or stone, devoid of cognition. Moreover, it is like the analogy of an image:
if these images of wood, stone, and so forth were to be burned by fire, destroyed by water, wounded by a blade, or shattered by a diamond and the like.
If one were to address it with angry and harsh words, it could not be moved even slightly; nor would its mental disposition give rise to displeasure.

Even if various offerings were made—clothing it in exquisite garments, presenting it with famous delicacies, anointing it with wonderful fragrances, dazzling it with brilliant colors, and placing before it an abundance of all the finest offerings of humans and devas—it would still not experience joy. One should know that such is the nature of that image.

That intrinsic nature is inherently empty arises from the conceptual discrimination of my own mind; thus, whether there is increase or decrease, whether disparagement or veneration, all are merely inverted and unreal.

Just as one who contemplates an external image must use this contemplation to observe their own body, at that time they do not perceive the characteristics of the body and are free from conceptual discrimination.
Observing the body in this way, one perceives the true reality of the body and immediately realizes the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because this is the samādhi of perception, when observing at any time, one must first rely on the conditions of characteristics and that which possesses characteristics to enter gradually and deeply;
then, naturally, characteristics will become non-characteristics and conditions will become non-conditions.

If one does not obtain this skillful means but merely observes emptiness directly without knowing by what causes and conditions it is empty, one will become attached to this dharma of emptiness and give rise to many divergent views. Therefore, [this method is necessary].
The stages of practice must be appropriately guided. Why is this?
Because foolish ordinary beings, regarding the self-nature of emptiness, give rise to the notion of a "self" based on forms;

they produce the discrimination of a self, claiming it arises from their own bodies. Through such inverted and unreal conceptions, they give rise to various discriminations—either making offerings or rejecting offerings.
Whether one is honored or reviled, one should abandon [such thoughts] in all cases. However, when observing the body, speech is included within the observation of the body;
therefore, it is not explained separately. To briefly clarify this now is precisely the intention of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Now, from what does this speech arise?
It is said that it arises from the throat, pharynx, lips, tongue, navel, and other such conditions, through the mutual interaction of the movement of the mind and the wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*).
Because of mutual contact, this sound arises, like an echo in a valley; it has no inherent nature (*svabhāva*) at all.
Because ordinary beings do not understand this, they feel delight upon hearing what is pleasant and give rise to anger when hearing what is contrary to their feelings.

Now, by seeing the true reality (*dharmatā*) of sound in this way, one knows that this sound is neither arising nor ceasing, being identical to the true reality itself. This is the entry into the wisdom-nature of the equality of sounds. Next, one then...

Contemplate the mind through the formlessness of phenomena; one can awaken to this by first practicing coarse contemplation to realize the equality of this body and the equality of speech, thereby knowing for oneself that one has entered deeply and is easily able to observe.
Furthermore, Guhyakādhipati, one should contemplate that the nature of the mind is free from all conceptual signs and that its nature is emptiness.
Guhyakādhipati, when sought throughout the three times, the mind cannot be found; it is free from those three times.
One should contemplate its nature in this way, remaining free from signs.
Furthermore, O Secret Lord, when the practitioner has thus observed external appearances, they next realize that the internal mind is also empty.
This mind is free from all characteristics; it cannot be found when sought throughout the three periods of time.
Just as space transcends the three periods of time, so too does this mind transcend the dharmas of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Furthermore, Guhyapati, those who possess mental conceptions are so called because they are discriminated as such by foolish, ordinary worldlings;
that is to say, by apprehending signs through the mind, they are unable to understand that these are unreal, and thus falsely give rise to such notions.
Their lack of knowledge according to reality means that due to this false clinging, they cannot know things as they truly are. Such reflection refers to the reflection of ordinary worldlings.
To give rise to such a thought is what is meant by saying that ordinary persons possess this discrimination; the above belongs to the section on the mind.
O Lord of Secrets, it is said that the bodhisattvas who practice the path to enlightenment through this gateway of mantras [explain the appearance as being without appearance].
One should understand that while there are signs, one gives rise to signlessness. This means that when a bodhisattva contemplates in this way, they realize the samādhi of signlessness.
O Lord of Secrets, because they abide in the samādhi of signlessness, that person shall attain the manifestation of the true reality of the mantra’s essential nature through the removal of delusion;
it will be ever-present whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. As it is said:

Regarding the mantras that have been explained, they always abide in direct presence before one; by recognizing the essence of the mantra as being like the ten previous metaphors, this is itself the sign of *siddhi*.

However, because ordinary fools do not understand the true nature of the mind, they give rise to various notions of bondage and attachment—thinking "this is my mind," "I am ignorant," "I am wise," "it is favorable to me," or "it is adverse to me"—due to the emptiness of the mind.
Because it is false, all that pertains to body and speech is likewise entirely illusory. What is it that they do not know?
It is that they do not perceive reality; because they do not perceive reality, they are like infants who lack understanding.
When one perceives the true nature of the mind, one naturally becomes free from all such conceptual proliferations and discriminations. This is because they do not know the true nature of the mind.
Therefore, the arising of false attachments is what is called being an ordinary fool; if one understands this, one is a Buddha.

The subsequent sutra states: "Lord of Mysteries, when a practitioner of mantra (mantra-yāna) bodhisattva realizes the signless samādhi and abides in that signless samādhi, they attain the true mantras taught by the Tathāgata and face them directly, and those [mantras] abide eternally. This scriptural passage is cited here, though it is not fully detailed.

Examine the sūtras and observe closely this meaning: when a bodhisattva of mantra practice thus practices while free from signs, it is called "abiding in the state of non-conceptual absorption" (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*).
Because one abides in this samādhi of non-conceptualization, all mantras spoken by the Tathāgata manifest before one and are realized;
therefore, it is called "direct confrontation. At the time of such realization of the principle—
This is precisely what is called "abiding eternally. To abide eternally is to abide as a Buddha. This chapter is now explained in conjunction with the sixty mental states discussed previously;
the sequence of the doctrinal exposition here differs from that prior account because it would have been inconvenient to present it there.

I [the commentator] privately maintain that the general purport of the preceding scriptural text does not exceed three practices: namely, the oral recitation of mantras, the bodily performance of dharma-mudrās, and [the mental cultivation of samādhi].
One should contemplate the Buddha with the mind; yet these three matters are all dependently arisen phenomena that exist only through the convergence of conditions.

They possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), being neither born nor extinguished—this is the gate of the letter *A*, the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Ordinary beings do not know this, and thus how could they enter it?
Therefore, the Buddha first taught these three mantra-gates so that one may gradually attain samādhi and eventually behold the Original [Buddha] face-to-face.
Venerable One, because you have seen various realms of supernatural transformations, your mind has become attached to them, and thus you have not attained abiding in the threefold equality.

Now I shall explain the Dharma-gate for entering the threefold equality: if a practitioner, within the state of *yoga*-mind, can further observe in this manner and remain free from the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of body, speech, and mind, they will immediately realize and manifest the mantra.
The reality and the characteristics are identical; abiding in one's own essence is identical to the Tathāgata’s abiding (concluded in the "Chapter on the Samādhi of Signlessness").
This concludes the thirtieth chapter, the "Chapter on Mundane and Supramundane Recitation.
The purport of this entire scripture is solely to clarify the recitation for the practice of mantra and conduct by all bodhisattvas who enter [the path].
Regarding the Dharma of the Path, this present chapter specifically receives its name; one should know that it provides a comprehensive exposition of the essential principles of the entire section.
Furthermore, O Lord of Secrets, I shall now explain the secret method of recitation, which also requires the individual recitation of all mantras.

The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others have taught this individually; that is to say, one should select each one from among them—that is, each separately—and perform mental recitation (*manas-japa*) for each individual mantra.
Second, one performs recitation through the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpāna-japa*).
These two methods are the most supreme and correspond perfectly. One should always practice these two methods in this way.

This is called the first stage of recitation (*japa*); do not differ from this. If one differs from this, there will be a deficiency in the recitation because its constituent parts (*aṅga*) are incomplete.
However, when divided according to the correspondence between the internal and external, there are four [stages], which I have already explained previously.
From here on, I shall explain them further. Regarding that "worldly" [recitation], it involves an object of focus (*ālambana*), namely, among the three types:
One simply contemplates the syllable-seal (*akṣaramudrā*) and, through this contemplation, recognizes its intrinsic nature: that the seal is the syllable and the syllable is the body.
When mind and body are unimpeded and the mind is profoundly still, this is recitation. If one takes the syllable as the inhalation and exhalation, the syllable is the very essence of the mantra;
because these inhalations and exhalations sustain the body, they are called "inhalation and exhalation. However, between these two [methods], by means of the inhalation and exhalation...
Because the breath has a limited object of focus, one should know that mental recitation (*manas-japa*) is supreme.
Even with the noble syllables and mudrās, which are free from conceptual differentiation, one may also achieve the inhalation and exhalation [of the breath].

Although Vajrapāṇi had previously asked the Buddha about the method of recitation at the beginning of the sūtra, and there were brief answers given therein, they were not yet complete. Therefore, for the sake of definitive resolution, [the Buddha] speaks further.
This constitutes the practice for fully discerning the essential points of the system. Regarding its secret aspects:
although that which has been elucidated in the preceding chapters is not without secrecy, the essential points herein represent the most profound secret among all secrets.
Whether reciting each [mantra] individually, performing mental recitation, or reciting through the inhalation and exhalation of the breath—these clarify the different methods of specialized practice.
"Reciting each [syllable] one by one" means reciting the mantra with focused attention through the mouth;

as the sounds emerge from the mouth, each sound and syllable must be clearly perceived without interruption or distraction. "Mental recitation" (manasikāra) refers precisely to holding the mantra in the mind and performing mental visualization and recitation without vocalizing the sound.
"Recitation through the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation" (ānāpāna-smṛti) is as described above: it is the mastery of the winds (vāyu).

"Equal" means this; "two factors are in harmony" refers to the mental attention (*manasikāra*) and the inhalation and exhalation of breath during the three types of recitation—these are most harmonious and supreme.
"Always do not differ" means one should always act in accordance with these and not allow the mind to wander toward other objects or other thoughts.
If one does otherwise, it is a mere waste of effort and brings no benefit. Thus says the Mantra-holder.

"Omission of the *kṣipa*" (defective articulation) refers to cases where a syllable has a dot [the *anusvāra*] but is not pronounced as such, or where a syllable is omitted, or where one should pronounce a long vowel but instead calls it short;
there are many such instances, all of which are termed "recitation with omitted *kṣipa*.

To the right, these internal and external correspondences together constitute four kinds of recitation (which are the four colors). It is said that in the world, there exists a continuity of conditions...
This means that each syllable and phrase represents a step taken in walking. One should contemplate these syllables as being like individual steps; the syllable itself is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
As previously explained regarding the supramundane recitation, the body, syllables, and mudrās are unified into one, and by employing any one of them, the goal is attained.
Now, for mundane recitation, they are differentiated: one may contemplate the syllable, or contemplate the deity, or contemplate the mudrā.
This means that among the methods of recitation for both the mantra-syllables and the deity within the mundane context, the recitation of the inhalation and exhalation of breath is supreme.

In the former [mundane] case, the breath is transformed into syllables; thus, during the mundane recitation, one perceives the syllables clearly and distinctly within the inhalation and exhalation, which constitutes conceptual discrimination. In the latter [supramundane] case, such discrimination is not performed.
Within the mantra, when distinguished as two, there is the aspect of form; when they are of one essence and without distinction, that is the aspect of formlessness.
Both are objects of conditions. Next, regarding those who recite in the mundane world: they possess a continuity of syllables and phrases as their objects of conditions.
Within this, one may take a single syllable as an object or take a phrase and so forth, visualizing it upon the heart of the deity as previously described.
This constitutes the external recitation (*bāhya-japa*). Taking a single syllable refers to either a seed-syllable (*bīja-akṣara*) or the initial syllable of a mantra.
If the mantra is short, one may visualize the entire phrase as described above—like a linked chain—within the luminous sphere at the heart of the deity.
These two types, whether a syllable or a phrase, follow the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.
Recite without interruption or pause, ensuring that the words are just audible to one's own ears. As the breath goes out, let the word go out;

as the breath comes in, let the word come in, so that it follows the movement of the breath. This is what is meant by the Tiantai tradition when they say that reciting the sutras is "perfect stillness" (*yuanji*) and counting the breaths is "this very intent.
By taking this single object of focus and joining it with the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, the mind will naturally continue in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment.
Without distraction and in a state of tranquility, it is easy to enter samādhi; this is the supreme among all worldly recitations.

Furthermore, a sutra clarifies this meaning: just as one clearly sees the reflection in a mirror, so too when one contemplates the syllables, contemplates the word "seeing," contemplates the seal, or contemplates the honored one, one sees them immediately.
This is the stage of having signs (*sanimitta*). If the practitioner perceives this reality, they will not dwell [in the conceptual].
Although there are signs, one has not yet entered signlessness; if one contemplates the bodhicitta, it is entirely signless.
This mind is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is oneself. Because one’s own body attains Buddhahood and this single mark is no different from other marks, it is called signlessness.
"Following" means that whether coming or going, it follows the mind.
In the mundane recitation, the inhalation and exhalation of breath are supreme; one should know that in the supramundane mental recitation, one is far removed from all syllables.
The "single integrated form" (ekalakṣaṇa) refers to the non-destruction of the union between the syllables and the deity—that is, not dividing them into two and grasping at them as distinct.
This "integrated form" means to unify them into one, ensuring that one does not grasp at them while maintaining this state of non-destruction.
"Non-destruction of the mental aspect of form" means that the image of the form is not distinct from the mind; hence it is called "non-destruction.
"Do not differ from the Dharma" means that the teaching is thus. Abiding by this Dharma, one recites three *lakṣas* as previously explained.
The various types of recitation I have taught refer to the number of repetitions, the time, the appearance of signs, the enhancement, and so forth—the three *lakṣas*.
*La* means "repeatedly," which refers to the mundane; *loka* (or *lakṣa*) refers to the supramundane.

It refers to seeing the three characteristics—namely, the syllable (*akṣara*), the seal (*mudrā*), and the deity (*devatā*)—and taking whichever one of these corresponds to the specific visualization. Seeing the body, speech, and mind of the syllable, seal, and deity is what is meant by "seeing.
Furthermore, it enables the practitioner to purify themselves and eliminate all sins; if they are not purified, [one should practice] for another month.
The details are as previously stated. However, the recitation counts mentioned here refer back to the preceding text; one should not deviate from these ritual rules.
Furthermore, regarding the "honored deities" clarified above, this method of reciting the syllables and phrases applies to all deities.
From the Buddha’s retinue above down to the eight classes of spirits below, whenever there is recitation, it must be performed in this manner. Its...

In the recitation of the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*), as well as in the various ritual procedures for each individual deity, there are likewise these methods of practice.
Regarding the supramundane, one should know that this method of mental recitation is free from syllables;

however, it does not mean that one must first discard the preceding mantra syllables and so forth to be called "free from syllables. It is not like that; rather, it means being able to penetrate the fundamental nature of syllables.
This is precisely the perfect luminosity, eternally abiding, and fundamentally unborn; that which is unborn is the very mind itself.
The essence of the mind is perfectly luminous, pure, and replete with all virtues, yet free from conceptual discrimination. One should contemplate these words in this manner.
These words are none other than the syllables and phrases of the mantra of the aforementioned *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity). It is simply a matter of understanding this.
These characters arise from the mind; since the mind is itself perfectly luminous, profound, and tranquil, the nature of the characters produced from the mind is likewise so.
What is meant by "being detached from characters, sounds, and so forth" refers to being detached from the discriminating, conceptualizing mind and from notions of sound and the like.
However, when reciting and chanting, there may be both recitation and contemplation, which can be practiced concurrently, or one may cultivate only the contemplative observation.

"Recitation" refers to focusing on sounds, syllables, or the inhalation and exhalation of breath as described above; "illumination" refers to contemplating the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of these syllables.
However, when first practicing this contemplation, it is accompanied by signs (*nimitta*). If one contemplates a single seed-syllable, its luminous clarity (*prabhāsvara*) initially appears small;
if one contemplates a full phrase or the like, the luminous clarity appears large. Its form is like a continuous chain and so forth, visualized with the mind.
Having visualized [the object] until it appears vividly clear, one then contemplates its nature from that very basis.
