Compassion is Mahāvairocana Tathāgata; there is no separate compassion apart from Mahāvairocana Tathāgata. It should be understood thus.
Know that, according to this teaching, all the myriad virtues are likewise so; it is just like the meaning of the Dharma-body, Prajñā, and Liberation in the Tiantai school.
If there were only the Dharma-body and not the other two, it could not be called "the class of the Dharma-body," which accords with this principle.

Question: Does the sequential arrangement of each of the one hundred syllables of the wheel, both externally and internally, signify the meaning of being gradually led into the maṇḍala and reaching its center? Answer: This refers to the sequence of cause and effect.

If a practitioner first generates the bodhicitta, next proceeds toward practice, next attains perfect enlightenment, next abides in nirvāṇa, and next gives rise to skillful means, it is thus performed.
Such is the sequence. If explained from the perspective of the ground of one's own fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), then the letter *Ka* is situated most inwardly;
next is Practice (*caryā*); next is Bodhi; next is Nirvāṇa; and finally, Expedient Means (*upāya*) is situated most outwardly. These letters are identical to the essence (*svabhāva*);
they constitute the fruit of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) itself, and do not represent the causal stage of generating the bodhicitta. This proceeds from the Dharmakāya.
Arising, it should flow outward in succession to deliver sentient beings, just as from the central womb of a maṇḍala one proceeds to the positions of the eight classes of worldly deities;
furthermore, drawing them inward from the outside to the fruit of Buddhahood,
just as from the outer perimeter of a maṇḍala one returns to the beginning of the eight minds, up to the means for accomplishing Bodhi— this is called *ānyāna* (仰壤拏那).
Syllables such as "ma" also follow the meaning of entering and exiting; they may be within the hundred syllables or outside the hundred syllables.

Furthermore, it is asked again: Moreover, it is asked regarding the practitioner’s mind—contemplating the practice of visualization to form the maṇḍala, which is the meaning of the Great Compassion Treasury (Mahākaruṇā-garbha)—that is, by means of the center.
The *garbha* (womb) is the bodhicitta; its gradual progression outward, even unto the celestial realms of the world, constitutes the *upāya* (skillful means).

For those who practice as ordinary beings, there is a sequential order: first, one should perform the recitation according to the ritual, employing mantras and mudrās, and contemplate the perfect luminosity (*paripūrṇa-prabhā*), or contemplate only the syllables, or contemplate only the mudrās. Whichever of these three practices is performed, once it is accomplished—these being the three matters—[the goal is attained].
When achieving this, although one initially contemplates the perfect luminosity (*paripūrṇa-prabhāsvara*), one cannot see it immediately.

By means of hand gestures (*mudrā*), mantras (*mantra*), and the recollection of the *iṣṭadevatā*, the three karmas gradually become purified. Because the obstructions are purified, one gradually perceives the perfect luminosity.

When perceiving the perfect luminosity, within it there may appear the original seed-syllables (*bīja-akṣara*) clearly manifest, exactly according to their respective forms and colors; thus one sees them.
At that time, the turbulent thoughts of one's own mind are stilled and eliminated, and the mind remains profoundly tranquil, always unified and unmoved by external conditions.
Having thus seen that these [appearances] are still external conditions, one should next draw the attention inward from the outside and observe as follows:
"This perfect luminosity emerges from my own mind; know that the internal is likewise so. Indeed, this perfect luminosity is pure.

The essence of the mind itself is not a separate phenomenon; because one diligently observes the inner mind through skillful means, one sees that this luminous seed-syllable is solely one's own mind and no longer an external object.

Even when seeing the central luminosity of an external circle, such as the visualization of a deity through the aforementioned skillful means, at the time of internal contemplation, it is one's own body that becomes Vairocana.
Since the principal deities such as Vairocana are thus in accord with the principles of yoga, they are accomplished according to their respective capacities.
Through this correspondence with yoga, whatever is visualized according to one’s intent is immediately realized.

Visualizing this mind as an eight-petaled lotus according to the aforementioned expedient means, one takes the heart of this lotus-flower pedestal as the central womb (garbha) of the maṇḍala; its outer eight petals are likewise [to be understood].
[This] is the distribution according to the positions of the Buddhas. [Another version states: "These eight petals are the second enclosure of the Great Compassion Treasury (Mahākaruṇā-garbha).
At that time, the practitioner visualizes the eight-petaled heart as the central womb (*garbha*); he contemplates his own body as the maṇḍala: from the heart upward is the first enclosure;
from the heart downward to the navel is the second enclosure; and from the navel downward is the third, the worldly deities.
The forms, colors, and marks of the various honored ones within the sanctuary each differ from one another, appearing vividly as if within one's own body;
facing them is like personally entering a Buddha assembly. However, those who have not yet seen the Truth are still unable to perform various spiritual transformations like Vairocana;
they merely achieve this through the contemplation of the mind. Nevertheless, there is one matter that is truly real.
That which is called "not false" is precisely this "I am. "I am" means to have decisive and true conviction that I am the *dharmadhātu*, I am Vairocana, and I am the universal gate of all bodies;

this matter is not erroneous, as it was stated above in the section on the meaning of the empowerment of mantras: "I am the *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, it is said that the *dharmakāya* possesses sovereign spiritual powers.

That this transformation is sustained by empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not open to doubt; as explained at length with hundreds of similes in the *Yogatantra* and the *Vajraśekhara*, its meaning is as follows:

just as when Śakra dwells in his celestial palace, the entire ground consists of lapis lazuli, pure both inside and out, such that each member of the divine host, while residing within their own palace chambers, perceives Śakra to be constantly present there.
Their palaces stand in perfect symmetry; why is this? Because this ground and all else are composed of exquisite jewels that reflect one another and mutually inspire one another.
They do not come here nor go there, nor do they combine, yet because conditions are complete, they appear thus.
In reality, however, there is no arising and nothing exists; one must not fail to believe this. Furthermore, it is like all [other phenomena].

While the gods were excessively indulgent in the Nandana Grove, by the power of their past karma, a voice of Dharma teaching issued from within the leaves of the trees, rebuking those devas and urging them to abide in right conduct.

At that time, the gods momentarily ceased their heedlessness and turned their minds toward virtuous deeds; yet, though they searched within each tree and so forth, they could not find it, nor did it cease.
This matter is accomplished neither by itself nor by another, arising from within the celestial body;
it is like when the celestial drum sounds during battle with the asuras, comforting the heavenly hosts and inspiring thoughts of valor and strength while causing the asuras to fear and retreat.
Yet, in reality, this drum has no form and no abiding place, being produced solely through the various conditions of the merits of the devas.

All these things are inconceivable; how much more so the Dharmakāya! Furthermore, it is like the Great Brahmā King who, while remaining within his own palace, appears before all the celestial hosts whenever they desire to see him;

for all those gods know that he possesses pure conduct and that his marks and signs of physical excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are supreme, and thus their minds of affliction, craving, and desire are stilled.
They give rise to immeasurable virtuous aspirations and cultivate pure conduct according to their respective capacities;
yet the Brahma King remains unmoved and unshaken within his own palace, without even forming the thought, "I shall universally respond to them by appearing before each one.
Nevertheless, each of them thinks, "He has appeared for me alone; he is preaching the Dharma for me. Such people of the world, with even small merit and aspirations, [attain such results].
If such inconceivable functions exist, how much more so must the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* be able to accomplish such sovereign spiritual powers, empowerments, and miraculous transformations?
Yet, in common discourse on the Dharma, it is sometimes said that the *dharmakāya* is pure and quiescent like space, devoid of all activity;
thus, they never mention its being fully endowed with such powers and functions, which is merely a view arising from the perspective of ordinary beings.
All these divine transformations are the power of the samādhi of the conditioned mind; that the essence of the Dharma is not mentioned therein is because it has not yet been fully realized.
Question: In the first court of the maṇḍala, why is there only the triangular space-eye and the wish-fulfilling jewel in the eastern direction?

Regarding the question of how there are vacancies among the three matters: the answer is that as found within the mantras and mudrās—such as the *ūrṇā-kośa* (hair-treasure) of the Tathāgata, the tongue of the Tathāgata, the fangs of the Tathāgata, the teeth of the Tathāgata, the navel of the Tathāgata, and the fingernails (*nakha*) of the Tathāgata—all of these are included here in this [section] and shall be listed in their proper order.
As for the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown-protrusion) of the Buddha, it belongs to the third enclosure (*prākāra*) and is not present here.
Question: What is the meaning of "Jewel Banner" (Ratnaketu)? Answer: This is the bodhicitta.

Just as in a worldly army there is a banner that is the foremost among the ranks, the insignia of the host, and which all gaze upon so that the movements and halts of the troops follow it without exception;
likewise, all myriad practices take this bodhicitta as their standard and their master.
Therefore, he receives that name. Next, why is Ratnaketu called Flower-Blossoming Buddha? The answer is: this refers to the meaning of practice;

because the ten perfections and myriad practices nourish the bodhicitta, causing it to flourish in succession—its sprouts, stems, leaves, and flowers blooming in full splendor and becoming lovely—it receives that name.
Next, why is Flower-Blossoming called Amitābha? This is the Enjoyment Buddha (saṃbhogakāya). That is to say:
This constitutes the attainment of great fruits; the enjoyment of those fruits is immeasurable, inconceivable, and includes all that is called the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*).
Next, as for the Buddha Drum-Sound (*Duṇḍubhisvara*), he represents skillful means (*upāya*). Having already attained the great fruit, how could he merely enjoy it for himself?
Rather, he expounds it for all sentient beings through various skillful means. His wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is like a celestial drum.
The name is derived from the fact that his voice accomplishes all activities without conscious thought. Furthermore, the previous mention of Akṣobhya in the north is an error in the scripture;
this [name] follows the *Yogācāra* interpretation and does not correspond to that [tradition], for it is established that he is the Buddha Drumghoṣa (Dundubhisvara).
The Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-sūtra on the Attainment of Buddhahood through Spiritual Transformation and Empowerment, Volume Fourteen (End).
Postscript to the Re-engraving of the Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-sūtra on the Attainment of Buddhahood through Spiritual Transformation and Empowerment:
These fourteen volumes of the commentary on the meaning of the Vairocana-sūtra were brought by Great Master Jikaku and transmitted [to Japan].
Circulated among humanity for over eight hundred years, the current printed editions contain numerous discrepancies and errors that are not few;
readers suffer from these defects. The Ācārya Tongkong resolved to correct them with keen intent, extensively seeking out excellent manuscripts.
Desiring to rely upon these to collate, revise, and re-carve the text for public distribution throughout the realm, he gathered various versions for comparative study and selected the most refined.
He followed this course, transcribing and preserving the work until its completion was not yet finished. As he approached his death, Jì entrusted me with these words:
"I have reached old age and am afflicted by illness; I cannot rise again. After I pass away from my bed, you must carry on my will well:
seek out excellent copies and re-edit them with care, then have them carved for printing and distributed. Only then shall I have no further regrets. I looked up in alarm.
"I accept. Yet, I, Yu, am unworthy and unable to bear such a responsibility. Furthermore, due to a lack of funds for carving the blocks, the project has been deferred for many years.
Nevertheless, I have long harbored within my heart the charge entrusted to me by Master Kōng; thus, I now wish to obtain a superior copy to re-examine and correct it."
Having searched extensively and sought it everywhere without success, I then took Master Kong’s original manuscript and re-collated it, further commissioning someone to transcribe it anew.
Subsequently, I obtained an unusual version from an ancient collection, which was inscribed at its conclusion:
"Copied from the Changyan manuscript and collated with the Gu manuscript; this is the edition of the Tangyuan Monastery, the finest among all versions. Because of this...
Having carefully collated, corrected, and revised this new edition, I have now entrusted it to the carvers.

As it has been completed at this time, I consider myself to have fulfilled the words of Master Kōng; thus, I have briefly recorded the beginning and end of the matter as a preface appended to the end of the volume.
In the tenth month of winter in the sixth year of the Bǎolì era (the Bingzi year),
the Bhikṣu Dàwéi (Cíyǒng) Mánṭí, a junior disciple of Tiantai Zhēnāyé, composed this work in twenty fascicles;
fourteen fascicles were cross-referenced against various editions of the earlier version, yet it was impossible to avoid instances of both gain and loss.
That [work] was clumsy while this one is skillful. On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, the bhikṣu Yuánzhào recorded this at Sanjing Temple in Jingō.

On the thirteenth day of the third month in the seventh year of the Zhenguan era, at the northern courtyard of the Ran-dian (Dyeing Hall), he began reading the commentary on the "Bai zi sheng pin" (Chapter on the Hundred-Syllable Birth) and below; he completed it in twenty-seven days. Recorded by [Wang*].
This commentary on the meaning, in ten fascicles, was obtained through earnest entreaty before the Great Master Daejeon,
a Virtuous One who maintained recitation at Changseongjeom Hall under the Abbot of Consecration at Cheongnyongsa Temple; may those who read it understand its origins.
Recorded on the eighth day of the fourth month in the tenth year of the Dàzhōng era by the śramaṇa Yuánjì of Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei in the Kingdom of Japan. Generally,
regarding the characters noted in the left-hand margin and those marked with the "卜" (fu) symbol, one must understand that they are distinct and must not be used interchangeably.
Furthermore, the records written behind [the scrolls] also accord with the previous deliberations. Between the seventh and eighth months, there shall be another examination.
Upon returning to our own country, we shall examine them once more; though they may differ slightly, they will remain the same in their fundamental essence. Recorded by [Wang*].
Furthermore, there are many instances of double-layered annotations; one should know that the former relies on the Sanskrit text while the latter explains it in the language of Tang (Chinese).
If one follows the text accordingly, there will be no discrepancies.
Moreover, the fourteen fascicles from the Heian period are the original versions prior to the re-editing of the scriptural text. Now...
This is the second edition of the text, revised after the original; may readers take note of this. Recorded by [Wang*].
Regarding the origins of the *Record of the Preface to the Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, it is as I have heard:
the commentary on the meaning arrived in our country from the Great Tang, and there are five parts to it.

Regarding the originals currently extant, there are four: first, the eleven fascicles brought by the Venerable Daikō (or written as Tokū) from the Great Temple of Saihō-ji (arrived in Tang China in the seventh year of Dali;
the year of his return is unknown); second, the twenty fascicles brought by Kūkai Shōnin from Kōyū-ji (the temple name being Shingo;
arrived in Tang China in the twenty-first year of Zhenyuan and returned to the court in the first year of Daidō); and third, the ten fascicles brought by Master Jikaku from this very temple.

The four-fascicle [version] (brought to Tang in the third year of Kaicheng and returned to the court in the fourteenth year of Jōwa); my own bestowed manuscript in ten fascicles (brought to Tang in the seventh year of Dàzhōng and returned to the court in the second year of Tiān'ān).
Having collated them all, they are largely identical with minor differences; it cannot be avoided that there are variations in skill and artistry.

Furthermore, I have heard that there is a copy at Saigai-ji on Mount Hiraoka (the dharma-name of the temple is Kōfuku), which Master Genbō brought back from Tang in the past. My late master of Hieizan [possessed this].
The Great Master borrowed the Fang edition to examine it, but finding it unfit for transcription, he returned it immediately. He then transcribed the Xi Da edition himself for his own study.
Because that manuscript lacked the internal titles from the second fascicle downward, the Great Master transcribed them anew based on the external titles and added them;
furthermore, he recorded the chapter titles to indicate the beginning and end of each section explained within the respective fascicles. Consequently, this was included in the canon.
There are two versions, an earlier and a later one. As for the Kaohsiung version, because it was widely circulated in the world, it was not included in the canon;

now, I shall record the titles of several versions to provide a basis for future generations to reconcile their contents and distinguish between what is correct and what is erroneous. "Erroneous" refers to this commentary (*shu*);

"correct" refers to the exegesis of the meaning (*yi-shi*). Regarding the substance of the commentary: first, it discusses the Great Thesis using written language, providing a concise summary of the explanation.
The general outline of the commentaries by various masters was such that after the title, they further opened chapters and divided sections for explanation;
however, this is not the case here. Therefore, the title of the commentary does not accord with its conclusion, though their meaning can be discerned upon examination.

As for the commentator, he simply explains the text directly without dividing it into chapters and sections, as he considers the Esoteric Teaching to differ from the common exoteric traditions regarding public lectures.

Yan only understands the literal meaning and the underlying intent of the Buddha’s words, yet we have not mastered them; whenever there is an explanation, it is mixed with mere talk and treated as a commentary (*śāstra*).
This is simply because those who study have not encountered a true master. The titles and headings of various editions from ancient times to the present differ;

one should not, based on the expectations of various virtuous elders, judge what is right or wrong merely by whichever version happens to come into one's hands. Within a family lineage, there is no lack of those who would revise [the text].
The ink-stained hair-like strokes are sparse and broken, and the brushwork is called "explanatory" (*śe*). If one can understand this principle, how could one harbor biased attachments?
Lamenting my own loss of the original, I regret that I did not personally transcribe it early on; recently, by chance, I recovered it and recorded its headings.

Both the headings and the two lines of text at the beginning are still preserved, though some omissions remain. May readers examine them carefully and choose what is appropriate. It should be said thus.

On the twenty-sixth day of the fifth month in the year of Jiachen (884), the eighth year of the Genkei era (according to the *Sandai Jitsuroku*, it should be the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month, a Yiyou day), the monk Enchin—
who had previously entered Tang China to seek the teachings— was staying at the □□ Ward of the Sōji Office in front of Enryaku-ji Temple.
This was recorded according to the *Kaigen Shakkyō Kōhon Rekishō*.
First, the manuscript preserved at Enryaku-ji Temple, one volume in fourteen fascicles, Part One (Upper):
*Bimporashana-jōbutsu-kyō-shōki* (Excerpts and Notes on the Vairocana-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra),
*Daibirushana-kyō-giki* (Record of the Meaning of the Mahāvairocana-sūtra), Fascicle Two, Upper.

The second [section], consisting of fourteen fascicles (newly copied), is the *Great Vairocana Tathāgata-buddhahood-Abhiṣeka-vikurvaṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra-artha-ṭīkā*, Volume One, Part One (upper) (Sanzan-ke Kantei-bon).
These aforementioned fourteen fascicles were further transcribed from the Sai-dai-ji manuscript; it is said that this [latter] consists of three fascicles.
The titles at the bottom and the indications within this fascicle clarify that although these are not separate texts, they are clearly from the same original source;
let the wise understand this. Third: One fascicle of the Northern Edition (Beibon) from the Office of Kōyū-ji Temple, consisting of twenty volumes.
*Daibirushana Jōbutsu Kyōsho*, Scroll One. Recorded by the Śramaṇa Acharya Ichigyō.
The aforementioned twenty scrolls are the edition transmitted from the Western Capital by the Venerable Kūkai of Kōyū-ji Temple.
One must also change the character "shū" (疏) to "gishaku" (義釋).

Fourth, the preface to the fourteen-fascicle *Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra* (Vairocanābhisambodhi-vikurvaṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra-gishaku), from a copy held in the Zōbō-in (總持院) collection (commented by Onko).
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*,
Fascicle One, composed by the Śramaṇa Ichigyō.
The above fourteen fascicles constitute the text from the Juntoku-in, which is the copy brought back by Daisōjō (Chishō Daishi) from Chang’an.
This edition, which was transmitted by An, includes a preface that differs from the three other versions; is it not worthy of our highest esteem?
Fifth, the copy carried by Enchin: one fascicle in ten volumes (the preface is separate).
